edge_semantics.descends_from: actual transmission of building practice; carries the kit cascade
edge_semantics.references: claimed or quoted ancestry imitated without descent; does NOT carry the cascade
edge_semantics.reacts_against: defined by inversion of a predecessor
edge_semantics.hybridizes_with: reticulation; a co-parent of comparable weight
edge_semantics.regional_of: variant to its parent style; carries the cascade

slots.name: Composition parti
slots.note: The whole-building compositional law: symmetry class, bay parity, where the centre is and whether there is one. Added in 0.2.0 — the Georgian exercise found that a style whose identity IS strict bilateral symmetry had nowhere to say so, and could not forbid a picturesque parti because no slot existed to forbid it in.

slots.name: Roof pitch
slots.note: One of the highest-signal, lowest-cost style tells. A 4:12 Georgian reads wrong at any level of trim quality.

slots.name: Eave condition
slots.note: Where the wall meets the sky. Boxed-and-returned, exposed rafter tail, closed soffit, flared, clipped — arguably the single most diagnostic detail in the whole kit.

slots.name: Chimney
slots.note: Position (central, gable-end, exterior-end, paired) is a plan-logic decision, not decoration. It is the fossil of the heating strategy.

slots.name: Storey proportion
slots.note: Ratio of ground-floor to upper-floor height; the graduation that makes a facade sit down rather than float.

slots.name: Construction type
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. The ontology recorded appearance and not construction, so nothing could state whether Flemish bond was physically possible or was half-bricks glued to a backup. Nearly every honest-material question resolves here.

slots.name: Wall thickness, masonry
slots.note: Split in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #12), the fourth and last of the same trade-conflation family as window_head, corner_treatment and window_surround (window_head_masonry/window_head_wood, corner_quoin/corner_board, window_surround_masonry/window_surround_wood, all split in 0.3.0) -- it had simply never been added as its own slot at all, under any name, before now. A solid-masonry or masonry-veneer wall's thickness is load-bearing geometry or a fixed veneer-plus-cavity-plus-backup buildup: 13-18 in for a two-wythe brick bearing wall, 18-30+ in for coursed stone, a veneer wall's own figure driven by code minimum cavity and backup rather than by any proportional module. Discriminate with construction_type.

slots.name: Wall thickness, frame
slots.note: Split in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #12), paired with wall_thickness_masonry. A framed wall's overall thickness is stud depth plus sheathing plus cladding plus interior finish -- typically 6-10 in for a 2x4 or 2x6 wall with modern insulation and siding -- and is a code and energy-code question, not a proportional one. The opposite assembly reaching a comparable overall dimension by a wholly different logic, the same relationship reveal_masonry/reveal_frame already models.

slots.name: Secondary cladding
slots.note: Material change is usually a storey-line or wing decision, never arbitrary.

slots.name: Material transition rule
slots.note: Where a material may change and what must occur at the joint. Prevents the 'brick blanket on the front only' pathology of production building.

slots.name: Corner quoin
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. A quoin is an ORDER element governed by the masonry module. Applying its dimension to a framed corner is roughly 2x wrong, and did in fact produce a live bug in facade-classical.

slots.name: Corner board
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. A corner board is TRIM, measured at 6-10 in on surviving frame work, and sized by the clapboard it terminates rather than by any module.

slots.name: Reveal, masonry
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. 4-8 in of reveal in a mass wall, with no architrave. The depth IS the expression, and it is what tells the eye the wall carries load.

slots.name: Reveal, frame
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. 3/4-2 in of reveal plus a 5-6 in architrave doing the work the depth cannot. The opposite assembly reaching the same effect.

slots.name: Main cornice
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13). The entablature's own cornice component when a full classical apparatus is bound (`entablature` in Classical Apparatus) -- and it, `frieze`, `modillion_dentil`, `crown` and `chair_rail` are the same object at different scales, three of them literally the same run. This cross-reference is not a regrouping: every one of the six keeps its own id and every existing kit binding stays valid. Where no `entablature` is bound at all -- the common case, since most vernacular envelope-only Georgian work states cornice and frieze directly without a full engaged order -- `cornice` is the de facto standalone module source the other four should still agree with.

slots.name: Frieze
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13). Sits directly below `cornice` in the same entablature run; see `cornice`'s note for how this cross-reference resolves when no `entablature` is bound.

slots.name: Rainwater strategy
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. Gutters and leaders ruin more traditional eaves than any other single element, and the eave slot is about the cornice.

slots.name: Colour strategy
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. Highly diagnostic, period-specific, and the cheapest thing on a house to get right or wrong.

slots.name: Window proportion
slots.note: Height:width of the sash opening. Governs whether a facade reads as vertical (traditional) or horizontal (modern default).

slots.name: Window head, masonry
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. A gauged brick jack arch is the mason's: structural, cambered by roughly opening/96, four courses deep, laid up on a centre before the wall closes.

slots.name: Window head, wood
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. A moulded wood cap is the carpenter's: non-structural, nailed on after the wall is closed, and free to be any profile the plane can cut.

slots.name: Window surround, masonry
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. In masonry Georgian the canonical value is NONE, and that is a design decision rather than an absence: the opening reads as a hole cut in a mass, and adding a surround destroys the reading.

slots.name: Window surround, wood
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type.

slots.name: Grouping & rhythm rule
slots.note: Singles, pairs, ribbons; bay spacing; alignment of upper to lower. The grammar of the facade.

slots.name: Shutter
slots.note: Must be sized to actually close over the opening, hung on real hardware. Half-width shutters are the most common single tell of a fake traditional facade.

slots.name: Door surround
slots.note: In most traditional styles the entry is the single most elaborated element. The surround is where the style declares itself.

slots.name: Garage strategy
slots.note: No historical precedent exists. Every traditional style needs an explicit, authored answer or the car eats the facade. This slot is where a modern kit-of-parts earns its keep.

slots.name: Glazing assembly
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. Insulated glass changes muntin width, which changes the window, which is most styles' first tell. The trade-off needs somewhere to live.

slots.name: Column / post
slots.note: Entasis, diminution, and plinth height are parametric and must scale with the order, not with the lumber yard.

slots.name: Entablature
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13): the root of a six-slot cross-reference family, not a regrouping. When bound, this IS the module source `cornice`, `frieze`, `modillion_dentil` (Envelope / Classical Apparatus), `crown` and `chair_rail` (Interior) should agree with -- see `cornice`'s note. This slot itself has no `derives_from_module`; it derives from the proportion pack's order, not from another slot.

slots.name: Modillion / dentil course
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13). A coursework detail within the cornice band; see `cornice`'s note for how this cross-reference resolves when no `entablature` is bound.

slots.name: Porch depth
slots.note: Depth decides what a porch IS, and different traditions want different answers. A Craftsman or Queen Anne porch below about 7 ft fails as an outdoor room; a Georgian entry portico is 5-6 ft and is a piece of the order rather than a room, and enlarging it to satisfy a Craftsman threshold makes it wrong. Bind the threshold in the style's kit, not here. (0.2.0: this note previously asserted the Craftsman figure as universal, which the Georgian authoring exercise caught.)

slots.name: Entry sequence
slots.note: Number of thresholds crossed from street to hall. Phenomenologically the most consequential decision in the whole kit and the one most often unmade.

slots.name: Trim profile family
slots.note: A single coherent profile family per style. Mixing families is the interior equivalent of mixing typefaces.

slots.name: Crown / cornice
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13). In high-style interior work this is the same run as the exterior cornice at a smaller scale, not an independently invented moulding; see `cornice`'s note for how this cross-reference resolves when no `entablature` is bound.

slots.name: Chair rail
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13, the ruling's own named example). Its module should derive from the same run as the exterior cornice rather than being independently invented; see `cornice`'s note for how this cross-reference resolves when no `entablature` is bound.

slots.name: Room adjacency overrides
slots.note: Demoted in 0.4.0. The UNIVERSAL adjacency rules now live on the room records in rooms/, where they belong — they are properties of a dining room, not of Georgian. This slot holds only what a style ADDS or SUPPRESSES: Georgian permits chambers entered through one another, which the neutral rule forbids; the Creole cottage suppresses the corridor rule entirely. Same element-first-with-style-as-facet pattern as the fault corpus. A style that states a universal rule here is duplicating data that will drift.

slots.name: Storage strategy
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. Closets are a plan element and built-ins are joinery; they are not the same slot. Styles that predate the closet need an authored answer here.

slots.name: Mechanical & services strategy
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. Chases, stacks, ducts, equipment. Where the plumbing stacks go decides whether a centre-passage plan survives contact with an MEP layout, and the ontology was silent on it.

slots.name: Grade relationship
slots.note: How the building meets the ground. Plinth, berm, cellar-exposure, terrace.

massings.name: Single-Cell Hall

origin.note: The irreducible unit. Nearly every Anglo-American type is an elaboration of it.

massings.description: One heated room entered directly from outside. All domestic life - cooking, eating, sleeping, work - occurs in a single volume differentiated by furniture and habit rather than by walls.
massings.structural_logic: A single framing bay, roughly 16-20 feet square, set by the practical span of hand-hewn joists.
massings.expansion_logic: Grows by adding a second pen (double-pen), a lean-to at the rear (saltbox), or a second storey. Every expansion path from this cell generates a named type.
constraints: Hearth must be on an exterior wall or centred; a single-cell plan cannot carry an interior chimney without eating the room.
massings.notes: Teaching this type first makes the rest of the catalog legible as variation rather than as a list.

massings.name: Hall and Parlor
massings.description: Two unequal rooms side by side: the larger hall for work and public reception, the smaller parlor for the best furniture and sleeping. The first appearance of social gradient in the Anglo house.
massings.structural_logic: Two framing bays. Asymmetry of room size is functional, and produces the characteristic off-centre door.
massings.expansion_logic: Adding a through-passage between the two rooms produces the center-hall plan and, with it, the entire Georgian project of symmetry.
constraints: Door placement is governed by the hall/parlor size difference, not by facade symmetry. Forcing a centred door here destroys the type.

massings.name: Center Passage, Single Pile
massings.description: A through-passage divides two rooms, opening front to back. The passage is a climate device as much as a circulation one: opened at both ends it draws air through the house on a summer afternoon.
massings.structural_logic: Single room depth keeps every room cross-ventilated and daylit from two sides - the reason the type persisted in the South a century after the North had gone double-pile.
massings.expansion_logic: Rear ell for service; or fill in behind to become double-pile at the cost of the through-draft.
constraints: Both ends of the passage must have doors or the type loses its reason for existing.

massings.name: I-House
massings.description: Two storeys tall, one room deep, at least two rooms wide - a tall thin slab of a house that announced a farming family's arrival at prosperity. Named for its prevalence in Indiana, Illinois, and Iowa.
massings.structural_logic: Depth of one room means no interior bearing wall and a simple common-rafter roof; the height is pure social signalling, visible across open farmland.
massings.expansion_logic: Almost always acquires a rear ell or kitchen wing, producing a T or L. The ell is where the house actually lived.
constraints: Reads as a facade from the road and a thin wall from the side. Any attempt to thicken it into double-pile turns it into a different type.

massings.name: Saltbox
massings.description: A two-storey house with a lean-to added across the rear, the roof carried down in one unbroken plane nearly to the ground on the north side. Accretion made permanent and, eventually, built that way from the start.
massings.structural_logic: The long rear slope faces north, shedding snow and burying the coldest wall in a low, unheated service zone. Thermally intelligent before anyone used the word.
massings.expansion_logic: This IS the expansion. Once formalized, further growth goes to an ell off the kitchen end.
constraints: The rear slope must be unbroken - dormers or a break in the plane collapse the whole figure.
Orientation matters: a saltbox with its long slope to the south is a costume, not a type.

massings.name: Cape Cod Block
massings.description: A low, broad, steep-roofed box hugging the ground, its massive central chimney the structural and thermal core. Sized in named increments: half, three-quarter, and full Cape, each a stage of a family's growth.
massings.structural_logic: Low eave and steep pitch resist Atlantic wind; the central stack heats four rooms from one mass of masonry and anchors the frame.
massings.expansion_logic: Half to three-quarter to full by adding bays to one side of the door, then dormers or an ell. The increments are the type's grammar.
constraints: Eave must sit low - within a foot or so of the second-floor sill. Raising it to gain headroom produces a different, worse house.
Central chimney is not optional; a Cape with gable-end chimneys is a different type.

massings.name: Gambrel Block
massings.description: A double-pitched roof buys nearly full headroom on the upper floor while keeping the eave low and the volume visually modest. The most efficient traditional answer to the problem of a second storey.
massings.structural_logic: The break in slope allows a shorter rafter run and a usable upper floor without a full second-storey wall - a tax and material advantage as much as a spatial one.
massings.expansion_logic: Flared eaves and a full-width shed dormer are the standard growth moves; both are period-correct if handled with restraint.
constraints: Upper slope should be roughly half the pitch of the lower; equal slopes read as a barn.
The break line should align with the upper floor level, not float arbitrarily.

massings.name: Four-Over-Four (Georgian Double Pile)
massings.description: Four rooms per floor around a central stair hall - the canonical Georgian box. Symmetry is not applied to this plan; it is generated by it, which is why the type survives every change of ornament.
massings.structural_logic: Two rooms deep requires an interior bearing wall, which the stair hall supplies. Paired end chimneys serve four fireplaces per floor.
massings.expansion_logic: Flanking dependencies connected by hyphens (the five-part scheme), or a rear service ell. Growth must respect the axis or the whole logic fails.
constraints: Facade symmetry is a hard constraint, not a preference.
Window bays must align vertically; a misaligned upper window is a structural admission that the plan is not really Georgian.

massings.name: Five-Part Palladian
aka: main block with hyphens and dependencies
massings.description: A dominant central block flanked by subordinate wings, joined by low connecting hyphens. Hierarchy made visible: the family in the middle, service and specialized functions stepping down and out to either side.
massings.structural_logic: Separates the hot, smoky, and noisy from the ceremonial while keeping them connected under cover - a functional diagram before it is a compositional one.
massings.expansion_logic: Wings may lengthen or gain a second storey, but the hierarchy of heights must be preserved. The centre must always win.
constraints: Wing ridge must sit demonstrably below the main ridge - a token difference reads as a mistake.
Hyphens must be lower and shallower than both elements they join.

massings.name: Side-Hall Double Pile
massings.description: Stair and passage pushed to one side, rooms lined up in an enfilade beside them. The plan that makes narrow-lot urbanism work, and the ancestor of every efficient town house since.
massings.structural_logic: Party walls carry the load; light comes only from the two short ends, which drives room depth and the deep-parlor proportion.
massings.expansion_logic: Vertical, not horizontal. Extra storeys, then a rear ell over the yard.
constraints: Only two elevations get windows; the plan must place service and stair where light is not needed.
Room-to-window ratio sets a maximum depth of roughly 25 feet before the middle goes dark.

massings.name: Charleston Single House
massings.description: One room wide and turned end-on to the street, with multi-storey piazzas running the long south or west flank behind a false street door. A climate machine disguised as a house.
massings.structural_logic: Narrow section plus tall ceilings plus a shaded piazza produces continuous cross ventilation in a subtropical climate. Every dimension serves airflow.
massings.expansion_logic: Lengthens to the rear; kitchen house sits detached in the yard.
constraints: Piazza must face south or west to catch the prevailing breeze and shade the long wall.
The street door opens onto the piazza, not the house - removing this move destroys the type.

massings.name: Creole Cottage
massings.description: A hall-less plan of four square rooms opening directly onto a full-width front gallery, with small cabinets flanking a rear loggia. No corridors: the gallery is the corridor.
massings.structural_logic: Eliminating interior passages maximizes cross ventilation; the gallery shades the wall and keeps rain off the openings.
massings.expansion_logic: Rear cabinet-loggia range fills in; the house grows backward, never forward past the gallery line.
constraints: Four front openings, no centred door - symmetry here is even-numbered, which reads wrong to an Anglo eye and is exactly correct.
Gallery is structural to the type, not applied.

massings.name: Raised Cottage
massings.description: The living floor lifted a full storey above grade on a masonry base, wrapped in deep galleries reached by a broad exterior stair. Flood response and social elevation in the same gesture.
massings.structural_logic: Masonry base survives inundation and damp; the elevated timber floor catches breeze above the ground-level heat and insects.
massings.expansion_logic: Gallery may wrap from front to sides; the base may be enclosed for service.
constraints: Base must read as masonry and the upper floor as lighter construction; a uniform material collapses the logic.
Stair is exterior and ceremonial.

massings.name: Dogtrot
massings.description: Two log pens under one roof, separated by an open central passage. The passage is the coolest place on the property in August and the reason the plan exists.
massings.structural_logic: Log pen size is limited by log length; two pens plus a gap is cheaper and cooler than one large room. The shared roof ties them together.
massings.expansion_logic: The breezeway is often enclosed later, converting it to a center-hall plan - the single most common type-transformation in Southern vernacular.
constraints: Passage must be open at both ends and unheated.
Pens should read as separate volumes under a shared roof.

massings.name: Shotgun

origin.region: New Orleans, Gulf South, urban African-American communities
origin.note: West African and Haitian plan antecedents, not simply an Anglo economization.

massings.description: One room wide and three to five rooms deep, each room opening into the next with no hallway, the gable end and its porch turned to the street. Maximum house on a minimum lot frontage.
massings.structural_logic: Narrow lots taxed on frontage; single-pile depth keeps every room lit and ventilated from two sides with aligned doors drawing air the length of the house.
massings.expansion_logic: Rear rooms added indefinitely; a camelback adds a second storey only at the back, preserving the street reading.
constraints: Doors must align front to back or the ventilation logic fails.
Porch is not optional - it is the house's only social space.

massings.name: Gable Front
massings.description: The house rotated ninety degrees so the gable faces the street, presenting a pediment-like front. Born of Greek Revival ambition and kept alive by narrow urban lots long after the temple idea faded.
massings.structural_logic: Gable to the street fits deep narrow lots and gives a naturally pedimented facade at no extra cost.
massings.expansion_logic: Side wing produces the gable-front-and-wing, one of the most widespread American forms.
constraints: Facade proportion should approach a pediment; too tall and narrow and it becomes a tower.

massings.name: Gable Front and Wing

origin.region: Northeast, Midwest, and throughout rural America

massings.description: A gable-front block with a lower side-gabled wing, the porch tucked into the inside corner. Arguably the most-built American house form of the nineteenth century and the most adaptable to any style.
massings.structural_logic: Two simple volumes, each independently framable, joined at a right angle; the reentrant corner is a naturally sheltered entry.
massings.expansion_logic: Wing lengthens; further ells accrete behind. The type absorbs growth gracefully, which is why it lasted a century.
constraints: Wing ridge must be lower than the main ridge.
Entry belongs in the inside corner; moving it to the gable front produces two front doors and no hierarchy.

massings.name: Cross-Gable Block
massings.description: Intersecting gabled volumes producing an animated roofline and a plan that can grow in three directions. The workhorse of Gothic Revival, Italianate, and Folk Victorian alike.
massings.structural_logic: Balloon framing and machine-cut lumber made intersecting roofs cheap for the first time; the type is a direct consequence of the sawmill.
massings.expansion_logic: Any arm may extend. Danger is unlimited growth without hierarchy.
constraints: One gable must dominate; equal arms produce an indecisive house.
Valleys are the leak points - the type demands disciplined flashing detail.

massings.name: Massed Picturesque Block
massings.description: A deliberately irregular agglomeration of bays, towers, porches, and projecting gables composed for the moving eye rather than the frontal view. The plan follows the picture, and occasionally the picture follows the plan.
massings.structural_logic: Light balloon frame permits complexity that heavy timber could not afford. Complexity is the point, not a byproduct.
massings.expansion_logic: Absorbs additions almost invisibly, which is both its great virtue and its great temptation.
constraints: Requires a dominant mass and a dominant roof or it disintegrates into noise.
Every projection must be justified by a room, not by the elevation.

massings.name: Mansard Block
massings.description: A full usable storey concealed within a steep-sided roof, capped by a shallow deck. Modernity in the 1860s sense: the newest fashion from Paris, and an extra floor the tax assessor once treated as attic.
massings.structural_logic: The steep lower slope is effectively a wall carrying dormers; the flat deck above sheds to internal drains.
massings.expansion_logic: Central or corner tower with its own mansard is the standard elaboration.
constraints: Mansard must be visually continuous around the building or it reads as a hat.
Dormer rhythm should relate to the bay rhythm below.

massings.name: Towered Villa
massings.description: An asymmetrical villa organized around a square tower or campanile, usually at the inner angle. The tower is a vertical accent and a stair, and it announces that this house is composed, not merely built.
massings.structural_logic: Tower absorbs the stair and gives cross-ventilation at the top; low-pitched hips with deep bracketed eaves shade the walls.
massings.expansion_logic: Wings extend from the tower's two faces.
constraints: Tower must rise at least a half storey above the main ridge or it is a bump.
Eave bracket rhythm should be consistent across tower and body.

massings.name: Foursquare
massings.description: A near-cubic two-storey box, four large rooms per floor, hipped roof with a broad central dormer, full-width front porch. The most volumetrically efficient American house ever built, and the clearest proof that massing is not style.
massings.structural_logic: A cube has the best floor-area-to-exterior-wall ratio available to a two-storey wood frame house. Cheap to build, cheap to heat, easy to ship as a kit.
massings.expansion_logic: Rear ell or a widened dormer. The cube itself resists distortion, which is part of its dignity.
constraints: Porch must be full width; a partial porch destroys the base of the composition.
Roof overhang must be generous - a Foursquare with clipped eaves reads as a shoebox.
massings.notes: Routinely dressed as Craftsman, Colonial Revival, Prairie, or Mission with no change to the volume. The canonical demonstration case for separating the massing catalog from the style grammar.

massings.name: Pyramidal Cottage
massings.description: A single-storey square under a steep four-sided roof, four rooms around a central chimney. The economical Southern answer to a compact family house.
massings.structural_logic: Pyramidal roof needs no ridge beam and sheds efficiently in all directions; the square plan minimizes wall length.
massings.expansion_logic: Rear shed or ell.
constraints: Roof pitch must be steep enough to read as a pyramid rather than a hip.

massings.name: Bungalow (Linear)

origin.note: Term via Bengali bangla by way of British India.

massings.description: A low, ground-hugging house of one to one-and-a-half storeys, its deep porch under the main roof, its living and dining rooms flowing together around a hearth. The first mass-market American house to abandon the formal parlor.
massings.structural_logic: Low profile, deep overhangs, and exposed structural members express the frame rather than concealing it; the whole is sized to a small urban lot.
massings.expansion_logic: Shed dormer for upper rooms; rear ell for service. The airplane bungalow adds a single second-storey room.
constraints: Porch must be under the primary roof, not applied to it.
Eave overhang of 24-36 inches is definitional; less and it is not a bungalow.

massings.name: Airplane Bungalow
massings.description: A bungalow with a single small room perched centrally on the roof, windowed on all four sides - a sleeping porch or study lifted into the breeze.
massings.structural_logic: The pop-up catches cross breezes above the roof plane; a hot-climate cooling device before mechanical air conditioning.
massings.expansion_logic: Rarely grows; the type is complete as drawn.
constraints: Upper room must be centred and clearly subordinate.
Its roof should echo the main roof form.

massings.name: Prairie Cruciform
massings.description: Wings pinwheeling from a central masonry hearth, roofs low and broadly overhanging, the whole composition emphatically horizontal against a flat horizon.
massings.structural_logic: The chimney mass is the structural and compositional anchor; cantilevered eaves shade banded windows and shed the horizontal line outward.
massings.expansion_logic: Terraces and low walls extend the composition into the site rather than adding volume.
constraints: No vertical accent may compete with the horizontal.
Hearth must be central and expressed in mass.

massings.name: U-Courtyard
massings.description: Three ranges around an open court, the fourth side held by a wall or left open to a view. Rooms reached from the court rather than from interior corridors.
massings.structural_logic: Single-pile ranges are lit and ventilated from both sides; the court moderates microclimate and provides outdoor room in hot-dry conditions.
massings.expansion_logic: Close the fourth side to become a full courtyard; extend ranges outward.
constraints: Court must be proportioned to admit winter sun and exclude summer sun for its latitude.
Circulation through the court means the gallery must be continuous and covered.

massings.name: Full Courtyard
massings.description: Rooms enclose a court on all four sides, presenting a nearly blind face to the street. The house turns its back on the public world and opens entirely inward.
massings.structural_logic: Thermal mass plus shaded court plus cross-ventilated single-pile ranges - the most durable hot-climate house diagram in existence.
massings.expansion_logic: Second court added behind the first, service functions to the rear court.
constraints: Street elevation must be substantially closed; a courtyard house with a picture window on the street is a contradiction.
One controlled entry - the zaguan - carries the entire threshold sequence.

massings.name: Connected Farmstead
aka: big house little house back house barn
massings.description: House, kitchen ell, workshop, and barn joined in a continuous descending chain so that winter chores never require going outdoors. Architecture as a response to five months of snow.
massings.structural_logic: Each link is independently framed and sized to its use; the descending ridge line sheds snow and expresses hierarchy without ornament.
massings.expansion_logic: The type is defined by its capacity to grow - each new need becomes a new link.
constraints: Ridge heights must step down monotonically from house to barn.
Each link should be visibly a separate building, not a continuous extrusion.

massings.name: Telescope House
massings.description: Two to four sections of diminishing height and width strung in a line, each added as the family prospered. The house's own history is legible in its silhouette.
massings.structural_logic: Each section is a complete small house; joining them at the gable end requires no structural negotiation.
massings.expansion_logic: Add another, smaller section. That is the whole rule.
constraints: Each successive section must be lower AND narrower.
Sections should share a common front wall plane or a consistent setback rhythm.

massings.name: Temple Front with Wings
massings.description: A pedimented, colonnaded gable front flanked by lower recessed wings - the Greek temple pressed into service as a farmhouse, courthouse, and everything between.
massings.structural_logic: Wings hold service and bedchambers so the temple block can keep its pure form; the portico shades the principal south wall.
massings.expansion_logic: Wings lengthen or gain their own porticoes; the temple block never changes.
constraints: Portico columns must be full height of the block - a two-storey facade with one-storey columns is a different and lesser thing.
Wings must be set back from the temple front plane.

massings.name: Octagon

origin.note: Popularized by Orson Squire Fowler's A Home for All, 1848.

massings.description: An eight-sided house arranged around a central stair and often a central ventilating shaft, argued into existence on grounds of enclosed area per foot of wall.
massings.structural_logic: An octagon encloses about twenty percent more area than a square of equal perimeter; the central shaft provides stack ventilation.
massings.expansion_logic: Essentially none - the geometry is closed. A defining limitation and the reason the fashion died.
constraints: Triangular residual spaces at the corners must be programmed as closets and stairs or the plan wastes its own advantage.
massings.notes: Included partly as a cautionary type: a massing generated by argument rather than by use, and unable to grow.

massings.name: Row / Terrace
massings.description: Individual houses sharing party walls in a continuous street wall. The unit is the house; the architectural subject is the block.
massings.structural_logic: Party walls halve the exterior envelope and carry floor loads; the street wall does the urban work that no single facade can.
massings.expansion_logic: Rear ell into the yard; vertical addition where the cornice line permits.
constraints: Cornice line, floor levels, and material must coordinate across units or the street wall fails.
Individual expression belongs at the door and window detail, not the massing.

massings.name: Linear Ranch
massings.description: A long, low, single-storey house stretched along the street, its garage brought into the composition and its living spaces turned to the rear yard. The first American house type designed around the automobile.
massings.structural_logic: Single storey on a slab or crawl space, long span trusses, and a wide lot - the type is a direct expression of cheap suburban land and cheap cars.
massings.expansion_logic: Extends at either end; rear wing to form an L.
constraints: Garage placement determines whether the street elevation is a house or a wall of doors. This is the type's central unsolved problem.
Length demands a break in plane or material every three to four bays.

massings.name: L-Ranch
massings.description: A ranch bent into an L, with the garage or bedroom wing turned forward to define an entry court and shelter the front door.
massings.structural_logic: The bend creates a wind-sheltered entry and shortens the apparent street frontage of a long plan.
massings.expansion_logic: Either leg extends; a third leg produces a U with a real forecourt.
constraints: The inside corner must hold the entry, or the L is merely a bend.

massings.name: Split Level
massings.description: Living, sleeping, and family zones stacked at half-storey offsets around a short central stair, usually exploiting a sloped lot.
massings.structural_logic: Half-level offsets suit a cross-slope site and separate noisy from quiet zones without a full second storey.
massings.expansion_logic: Poor. The section is rigid and additions rarely reconcile with the offsets.
constraints: Requires actual grade change; on a flat lot the type is arbitrary.
Roof planes at the offset are the hardest detail and the usual point of failure.

massings.name: Double Pen
massings.description: Two equal rooms side by side under one roof, each with its own exterior door and its own end chimney. No hierarchy, no passage - two rooms that happen to share a wall.
massings.structural_logic: Two log or frame pens of equal size, built at once or in sequence; equality of rooms distinguishes it from hall-and-parlor.
massings.expansion_logic: Rear shed; enclosing the two front doors into one entry converts it toward a center-hall plan.
constraints: Two front doors are definitional. One centred door makes it a different type.

massings.name: Garrison Block
massings.description: A two-storey box whose upper floor overhangs the lower at the front, often with turned drops at the corners - a medieval English framing habit carried across the Atlantic and long misread as a defensive feature.
massings.structural_logic: The jetty derives from English timber framing practice, where it stiffened the frame and gained floor area; in America it survived as a decorative memory of that craft.
massings.expansion_logic: Rear lean-to or ell.
constraints: Overhang should be modest - 10 to 18 inches. Exaggerated overhangs are a 20th-century revival exaggeration.
Overhang occurs at the front, occasionally the gable ends, never all around.

massings.name: H-Plan Manor
massings.description: A central hall range with projecting wings at both ends, producing an H in plan - the Tudor and Jacobean great-house diagram, descended from the medieval hall with its screens passage.
massings.structural_logic: Single-pile ranges keep every room lit from both sides; the wings hold the two social poles, family and service, at opposite ends of the hall.
massings.expansion_logic: Wings deepen or gain a further range; a long gallery is added at the top floor.
constraints: The hall range must remain the compositional centre.
Entry through the screens passage - offset, not centred - is the diagnostic survival of the medieval plan.

massings.name: Gallery House
massings.description: A compact core wrapped on one or more sides by a deep roofed gallery that carries circulation, shade, and social life. The gallery is not a porch attached to a house; the house is a core inserted into a gallery.
massings.structural_logic: Deep shade keeps the wall out of the sun entirely; the gallery roof is often a continuation of the main roof at a broken, shallower pitch.
massings.expansion_logic: Gallery wraps further; core deepens.
constraints: Gallery depth of 8 feet minimum - shallower and it fails as a room.
Where the gallery roof breaks pitch, the break must be consistent all around.

garrison-revival.name: Garrison Revival

geography.hearth: eastern Massachusetts and the Boston suburbs

lineage.note: A massing variant. Kit, openings and entry are the parent style's; only the jettied second storey and the seventeenth-century reference differ.
The claimed ancestor: the fortified plank-frame houses of frontier Maine, New Hampshire and Massachusetts, and more loosely the jettied first-period houses of Essex County.
Where the drops, pendants, and casement-derived window pattern actually come from - the seventeenth-century English framing tradition as transplanted, not from any garrison.
Same offices, same builders, same market; Royal Barry Wills's practice produced Capes, saltboxes and garrisons from one drafting room.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The mid-century builder's Colonial: a rectangular two-storey box whose upper floor projects 8 to 18 inches over the lower on the front elevation, decorated with turned drops, and derived from a seventeenth-century framing condition that the twentieth century reproduced with no structure behind it.
description.long:
Garrison Revival is the clearest case in this branch of a structural detail surviving as pure imagery. The jetty - a second-floor framing overhang - was a genuine feature of English medieval and early New England timber framing, where the second-floor joists cantilever past the first-floor plate and the upper storey posts land on their ends. It appears on Essex County houses of the 1670s and 1680s, sometimes with carved or turned pendants at the corners where the corner posts drop below the framing. The 'garrison house' proper is something else again: a fortified frontier dwelling of thick planks or logs, built in Maine and New Hampshire for defence, which sometimes but not always jettied. American builders of the 1930s conflated the two, named the result Garrison Colonial, and sold it by the hundred thousand.

What made it a mid-century staple is that it solves a builder's problem elegantly. A jetty of 9 to 12 inches on the front elevation buys 20 to 30 square feet of second-floor area at almost no cost, gives the facade a shadow line and a horizontal accent that an otherwise plain box badly needs, and reads immediately as Colonial without requiring a portico, a cornice, or any masonry. From the mid-1930s and especially in the postwar suburbs, it became one of the two or three default two-storey builder plans in the Northeast, alongside the Cape and the split-level. The typical example is five bays wide, two rooms deep, with a side-gable roof at 7:12 to 9:12, a centred entrance under a small pedimented hood, 6/6 or 8/8 sash, an end chimney, and an attached garage in a wing.

The claim being made is the ordinary Colonial Revival claim - settled ancestry, New England descent, respectability - with a small extra note of hardiness. The name says garrison, and the sales copy of the period leaned on it: this is the house of people who held the frontier. That the actual buyers were commuting to an office in Hartford is not a criticism; every style in this branch is doing something similar, and the garrison does it with unusual economy.

The experience is modest and depends almost entirely on the overhang doing its job. When the jetty is deep enough - 12 inches or more - and carries real drops, the front elevation acquires a horizontal shadow at the second-floor line that organises the whole facade and makes an inexpensive house look composed. When it is 4 inches deep and the drops are plastic, the shadow disappears, the overhang reads as a mistake in the siding, and the house is simply a box. There is very little else to the variant; it is one move, and either it is made properly or it is not made at all.

defining_characteristics: Second storey projecting beyond the first on the front elevation, forming a continuous jetty across the full width
Two full storeys, rectangular plan, two rooms deep, under a side-gable roof
Turned or carved pendant drops at the outer ends of the overhang, and often at intermediate points
Symmetrical five-bay (or near-symmetrical four- or six-bay) front with a centred entrance and a modest pedimented hood or pilastered surround
Multi-light double-hung sash, 6/6, 8/8 or 8/12, aligned vertically between storeys
Clapboard or shingle wall, minimal cornice, and an end chimney
diagnostic_tells: The overhang appears on the front elevation only and stops at the corners. Genuine seventeenth-century jetties usually turn the corner and continue on the gable ends.
Drops are turned wooden or cast pendants applied to the soffit; on originals they are the carved lower ends of continuous corner posts and are therefore structurally continuous with the frame above.
Overhang depth is the whole diagnosis: 8-18 in. reads correctly, 4-6 in. reads as a siding error, over 24 in. is implausible as joist cantilever.
Everything else on the house is standard Colonial Revival, including the attached garage that dates it after 1935.

Against the actual garrison house: real garrisons are plank- or log-walled defensive buildings with very small openings, no symmetry, and no classical entry. Nothing about the revival's face is defensive.

distinguished_from.difference: The original is a fortified plank-frame or log dwelling on the seventeenth- and eighteenth-century northern New England frontier, built for defence, with small openings and no symmetry. The revival takes only the overhang - itself borrowed from a different, non-defensive framing tradition - and applies it to a symmetrical Colonial Revival box.
This is the parent style with a jettied second storey. Remove the overhang and the drops and nothing distinguishes it.

The genuine first-period jettied houses of Essex County have steep 12:12 roofs, casement or very small sash, massive central chimneys, and jetties that turn the corner. The revival has a 7:12-9:12 roof, large double-hung sash, an end chimney, and a front-only overhang.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The jetty depth against the storey height. The overhang must read as a plausible joist cantilever - roughly one third of the joist depth times its span-to-depth allowance - which in practice caps it near 18 in.; everything else follows the parent style's bay-and-catalog logic.
typical_ratios: Overhang 8-18 in., most commonly 9-12 in.
Drops 5-8 in. in diameter and 8-14 in. long, at the corners and sometimes at 1/3 points
Storey heights 8'6"-9'0" first and second - lower than high-style Colonial Revival, because this is a builder type
Roof pitch 7:12 to 9:12, side gable, with a 6-12 in. eave overhang
Footprint 26-30 ft deep by 36-48 ft wide
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five bays at 8'0"-10'0" on centre in the symmetrical case; postwar examples frequently run four or six bays with an off-centre door, which is tolerated but weakens the type. Second-storey openings align with those below.

massing_affinities.note: The variant is this massing: a two-storey side-gable box with a front jetty.
The plan below the overhang is a standard centre-passage double pile.
Narrow-lot version with the entrance to one side; the overhang still runs the full width.
Where a rear lean-to is added, producing the garrison-saltbox hybrid common in 1950s New England builder catalogs.

constraints.statement: Overhang depth 8-18 in., continuous across the full width of the elevation, with the soffit framed and finished as a soffit - not as a siding transition. Overhangs under 6 in. or over 24 in. are forbidden; neither reads as a joist cantilever.

test.note: Tests the overhang depth range. Continuity across the full elevation width, soffit framing/finish, and the wider outer bounds (under 6in / over 24in forbidden) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Pendant drops are required at both outer ends of the overhang, turned or carved in wood, 5-8 in. in diameter and 8-14 in. long, aligned with the corner posts. Applied plastic or foam drops void the variant.
Where the overhang returns onto a gable end it must continue for the full depth of that elevation and terminate in a drop; a partial return is forbidden.
Roof pitch 7:12 to 9:12 side gable. Below 6:12 the box loses the proportion that makes the overhang legible; above 10:12 the house reads as a Cape or a first-period reproduction.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch range. The explanatory bounds below 6:12 / above 10:12 restate the same variable and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Entry treatment limited to a pilastered surround or a small pedimented hood not exceeding 6'0" in width. A two-storey portico is incompatible with a jettied elevation.

exemplars.name: Webber House
exemplars.note: Harry Morton Ramsay. Second-storey shingled overhang with decorative pendants; a documented architect-designed example of the type at its origin.

exemplars.name: Royal Barry Wills Associates garrison designs
exemplars.note: Wills's practice produced garrisons alongside Capes and saltboxes; the drawings are held in the Royal Barry Wills Associates collection at Historic New England. The type's design standards descend from this office.

exemplars.name: Stanley-Whitman House
exemplars.note: Not a revival building. Included as the genuine first-period jettied house with a framed overhang and carved drops that the revival imitates - the correct comparison for judging any Garrison Revival overhang.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Royal Barry Wills, Houses for Good Living (1940)
Abbott Lowell Cummings, The Framed Houses of Massachusetts Bay, 1625-1725 (1979)
John Milnes Baker, American House Styles: A Concise Guide (1994)

proportion_packs.note: The pack this variant most directly needs, and explicitly listed in its applies_to. The node's own hard constraint c01 states the overhang 'must read as a plausible joist cantilever' at 8-18 in.; the pack does not carry a jetty-specific rule (its scope is the structural bay generally: post spacing, window-to-post clearance, wing depth against the main frame), but that general framing discipline -- what a real cantilevered second-floor joist can plausibly do -- is the standard the node's own constraint is invoking, and the pack's window-clearance rule (about 15 in. clear of a post) is the same logic the jetty depends on for its drops to land on real corner posts.

Explicitly listed in this pack's applies_to. Governs the door and window rectangle and the single-head-datum rule across the jettied storey break, which the node's own defining_characteristics require ('aligned vertically between storeys').

JUDGMENT BINDING: garrison-revival is not in gibbs-doric's own applies_to list. Bound at the everyday, plainer order only -- no Ionic frontispiece -- because the node's own hard constraint c05 caps the entry at 'a pilastered surround or a small pedimented hood not exceeding 6'0" in width' and states flatly that 'a two-storey portico is incompatible with a jettied elevation.' Doric is the order the parent style uses for its plainer, secondary doorways, and this variant is a builder type through and through, per its own description.

JUDGMENT BINDING, inherited: the node's lineage states 'kit, openings and entry are the parent style's,' and the front is symmetrical or near-symmetrical five-bay per the node's own defining_characteristics, matching this pack's bay arithmetic directly.
Explicitly listed in this pack's applies_to. The interior below the jetty is ordinary Colonial Revival trim, inherited from the parent per the node's own lineage note.

JUDGMENT BINDING: not in this pack's applies_to list, but the node's own typical_ratios state storey heights of 8'6"-9'0" for both floors, explicitly 'lower than high-style Colonial Revival, because this is a builder type,' and the whole node reads as an economical mid-century production plan -- 'one move' done cheaply or well, in the node's own words. That register is closer to this pack's daylight-and-span-constrained ordinary room than to room-harmonic's designed Palladian one, which the node's own text never invokes.

gothic-revival-british.name: Gothic Revival (British)

revival_periods.note: Domestic Gothic dissolves into Tudor Revival and Arts and Crafts; only ecclesiastical and collegiate work continues the pointed arch into the twentieth century.

geography.hearth: Twickenham for the Gothick phase; Ramsgate, Westminster and the Ecclesiological Society for the archaeological one

lineage.note: The claimed ancestry, and the reason this node exists in the taxonomy. The Revival quotes medieval Gothic from measured drawings, sketchbooks and — after 1840 — photographs. There is no transmission of practice: the masons' lodges had gone, the trade had forgotten how to cut tracery, and Pugin and Scott had to teach it back to their own contractors from published plates.

The real descent. Every Gothic Revival house was built by Georgian-descended trades using Georgian carcass construction, sash-window joinery, plastered ceilings and brick or ashlar walling, and the earliest Gothick was published as a Georgian pattern book — Batty Langley's Gothic Architecture Improved by Rules and Proportions (1742, reissued 1747), which supplied five invented 'Gothick orders' for a carpenter to work from.
The castellated picturesque villa of Nash, Wyatville and Atkinson is the direct predecessor of the Victorian Gothic house, and supplies the asymmetrical composition before the archaeology arrives.

Pugin's Contrasts (1836) and The True Principles of Pointed or Christian Architecture (1841) attack classicism as pagan, dishonest and socially corrupt. The argument is explicitly moral rather than aesthetic, which is what distinguishes this revival from every other.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The moral revival of the pointed arch: a style that quoted medieval Gothic from books while descending entirely from Georgian building practice, and which invented the modern idea that construction should be visible and honest.
description.long:
The Gothic Revival has two distinct halves and the split matters. The first, from Horace Walpole's Strawberry Hill of 1749-76 onward, is Gothick: an antiquarian mood applied as thin decoration to Georgian rooms, with fan vaults in papier-mache and battlements on sash-windowed villas. Batty Langley's Gothic Architecture Improved of 1742 shows exactly what this phase was — a pattern book that reduced Gothic to five invented orders with published proportions, so that a jobbing carpenter could produce it from a plate. Gothick is Georgian architecture in fancy dress, and it knows it.

The second half begins with Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin, who converted to Catholicism in 1835 and spent the fourteen years before his death in 1852 arguing that Gothic was not a style at all but the only truthful way to build. His two principles, published in True Principles in 1841, are among the most consequential sentences in architectural history: that there should be no features about a building which are not necessary for convenience, construction or propriety, and that all ornament should consist of enrichment of the essential construction. The whole modern movement's rhetoric of honesty comes from a Catholic convert defending the fourteenth century. In practice these principles produced houses planned from the inside out, with asymmetrical massing expressing internal function, steep roofs, tall clustered chimneys, gables, bay and oriel windows, and after 1850 the structural polychromy of Butterfield and Street — walls banded in different coloured bricks so that the pattern is the material rather than a coating on it.

The conditions were industrial, religious and political. Church-building on an enormous scale followed the Church Building Act of 1818 and the Catholic Emancipation Act of 1829; the Ecclesiological Society at Cambridge from 1839 policed the correctness of every parish church in England; the rebuilding of the Palace of Westminster after the fire of 1834 was made a Gothic competition by statute, on the grounds that Gothic was the national and constitutional style. And under all of it lay industry: plate glass, cast iron, machine-cut stone, railways to move it, and the money of manufacturers who wanted country houses with pedigrees. Ruskin supplied the theory in The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849) and The Stones of Venice (1851-53), and with it the ethical anxiety about machine work that eventually turned into Arts and Crafts.

A Victorian Gothic house is a heavier, darker, more emphatic experience than any of its medieval sources. Materials are hard and richly coloured — encaustic tile, polished granite shafts, stained glass, banded brick — and the detail is sharper than any hand-cut medieval work because it was machine-dressed. The rooms are tall and the windows are large but the glass is often coloured, so the light arrives tinted and heavy. What stays with you is the insistence: every arch is pointed, every chimney is clustered, every surface declares its construction, and the whole building argues with you continuously about how architecture ought to be done.

defining_characteristics: The pointed arch used consistently, and after 1840 used structurally rather than as applied decoration
Asymmetrical massing and plan, generated from internal function rather than from an elevation — the plan drawn first, the facade a consequence
Steep roof pitches (45-60 degrees), prominent cross gables and dormers, and tall clustered or shafted chimney stacks
Structural expression as an ethical requirement: exposed roof timbers, visible lintels and relieving arches, and ornament confined to the enrichment of real structural members
Polychromy in the material itself after 1850 — banded and patterned brickwork, contrasting stone courses, encaustic tile, marble shafting
Label or drip moulds over openings, buttresses where thrust actually occurs, and traceried, cusped or plate-traceried windows
Vertical emphasis throughout: tall proportions, steep gables, finials, spirelets and a silhouette designed to be broken
diagnostic_tells: Banded structural polychromy — courses of red and black brick or two stones alternating — which is a High Victorian invention and appears in no medieval English building
Machine-sharp mouldings and perfectly repeated carving, against the tolerant irregularity of genuine medieval stonework
A steeply gabled asymmetrical front with a projecting buttressed porch, a bay window and an entrance placed wherever the plan required it
Clustered polygonal chimney shafts on a moulded base, taken from Tudor precedent and used at three times the frequency any Tudor house had them
Plate glass or two-pane sashes behind pointed or square-headed stone openings in domestic work — the Victorian window betraying the Victorian date

distinguished_from.difference: The core distinction of this whole taxonomy. The original is a continuous building practice that had no name for itself; the revival is a theory reconstructing that practice from books. Diagnostically: revival work has regular floor levels, damp courses, flues that work, plate glass, machine-cut repetition and a plan with corridors. Medieval work has none of these.

Same decades, same clients, different quoted source. Baronial takes crow-steps, corbelling and bartizans from Scottish tower houses and avoids the pointed arch almost entirely; Gothic Revival takes tracery, buttresses and pointed openings from English churches.

The successor that kept Pugin's ethics and discarded his archaeology. Arts and Crafts abandons the pointed arch, the polychromy and the church detail, keeps truth to materials and plan-driven asymmetry, and turns to English vernacular sources instead of medieval ecclesiastical ones.

proportional_system.governing_logic: No applied system. Proportion is derived from medieval precedent by measurement and from Pugin's rule that form follows construction; composition is picturesque, balanced by mass and vertical accent rather than by axis.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 45-60 degrees, with 50-55 degrees typical in slate or plain tile
Window proportion 2:1 to 3.5:1 height to width in principal openings; grouped in twos and threes under a shared label
Gable width to apex height roughly 1:0.7 to 1:1
Chimney height above ridge 1.5 to 2.5 times the stack width, with shafts of 300-450 mm each
Storey heights 3.3-4.3 m at principal level, generally uniform rather than graduated — the loss of Georgian graduation is itself a diagnostic
Buttress projection 1/3 to 1/2 of its own width, stepped and weathered
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and functional. Openings are grouped by room and by internal need, giving clusters of two or three windows separated by blank wall; the resulting rhythm is syncopated and deliberately unresolved when read frontally.

massing_affinities.note: The High Victorian country house and vicarage: an agglomeration of gabled masses with a dominant tower or entrance gable.
The intersecting gabled block is the workhorse form of the smaller Gothic Revival house, parsonage and school.
The entrance or stair tower placed at the reentrant angle, sometimes carrying a spirelet.
Where the client wanted a great hall and the architect obliged with a screens passage — Scott and Pugin both did this repeatedly.
A symmetrical double-pile box with a centred door contradicts the plan-driven asymmetry that defines the style after 1840.

constraints.statement: Every arch is pointed and every pointed opening must be structurally plausible — a real arch with voussoirs or a real relieving arch above a lintel. Applied pointed trim over a square opening is precisely what Pugin's True Principles forbids.
Buttresses may occur only where thrust exists — at an arcade, a vault or a tall gable wall. Decorative buttresses on a two-storey wall are forbidden.
Polychromy must be in the material — different bricks or stones bonded into the wall — never painted or rendered on. This is the one rule High Victorian architects never broke.
Roof pitch not less than 45 degrees, and the entrance must not be centred on a symmetrical front. Plan generates elevation, not the reverse.

test.note: Tests the roof-pitch floor. 'The entrance must not be centred on a symmetrical front' is a categorical exclusion (not-equal) with no direction the vocabulary supports, and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Classical apparatus — orders, pediments, entablatures, quoins, symmetrical porticoes — is forbidden throughout.

exemplars.name: Strawberry Hill
exemplars.note: Built by Horace Walpole in phases between 1749 and 1776 with his 'Committee of Taste'. Gothick at its purest: chimneypieces copied from medieval tombs, papier-mache fan vaulting, and a wholly Georgian house behind it.

exemplars.name: Palace of Westminster
exemplars.note: Built 1840-70 by Charles Barry with A. W. N. Pugin responsible for all Gothic detail and fittings. A rigorously symmetrical classical plan clothed in Perpendicular detail — the contradiction that Pugin himself acknowledged bitterly.

exemplars.name: The Grange
exemplars.note: Built 1843-44 by Pugin for himself beside his own church. The first house planned entirely from the inside out on his stated principles, and the direct ancestor of every asymmetrical, plan-driven English house that followed.

exemplars.name: Tyntesfield
exemplars.note: Remodelled 1863-65 by John Norton for William Gibbs on a guano fortune. A complete High Victorian Gothic country house with its chapel, service wing, fittings and collections intact — the style in full domestic operation.

sources: Kenneth Clark, The Gothic Revival: An Essay in the History of Taste (1928)
A. W. N. Pugin, The True Principles of Pointed or Christian Architecture (1841)
Mark Girouard, The Victorian Country House (1971, rev. 1979)
Chris Brooks, The Gothic Revival (1999)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England (county volumes)

proportion_packs.note: This style is named directly in facade-picturesque's own applies_to list, and the fit is more than nominal: c04 (roof pitch not less than 45 degrees, entrance never centred on a symmetrical front) and c05 (no classical apparatus) are the same design logic the pack reconstructs from measured Victorian Gothic and Queen Anne fabric — a dominant mass, at least two unbroken horizontal datums, and a hierarchy made by massing and projection rather than by axis. The pack's own sources (Robinson, Curtis, Downing) postdate this style but describe the composition method Pugin's plan-driven asymmetry actually produced a generation earlier.

Judgment binding: gothic-revival-british is not in room-vernacular's applies_to, and its rooms — vicarage studies, High Victorian drawing rooms — sit above the anonymous vernacular median in scale. No better fit exists in the library: room-harmonic is a Palladian ratio system, and c05 forbids classical apparatus throughout, so applying a treatise proportioned from the orders would contradict the style's own founding argument against classicism. Bound instead for the pack's most transferable content, the daylight-depth relationship (a room lit from one side reads dark past about 2 to 2.5 times its window-head height), which is physics rather than period style and which Pugin's own principle — nothing admitted that is not necessary to convenience, construction or propriety — is a moral restatement of. Scoped to ordinary chambers and service rooms, not to the double-height hall or stair, which the style's own massing affinities (villa-tower, h-plan-manor) already govern.

shotgun-house.name: Shotgun House

revival_periods.note: The shotgun returns as a small-lot infill and cottage-court type in New Urbanist and post-Katrina rebuilding practice, where its 14-foot width and front-porch social logic solve exactly the problems that produced it.

geography.hearth: New Orleans, Louisiana

lineage.note: The New Orleans building trade that produced the shotgun was the Creole trade: the same carpenters, the same cypress, the same hall-less planning logic in which rooms open directly into one another and circulation happens outdoors. ACKNOWLEDGED GAP: the West African (Yoruba) and Haitian ti kay ancestry described at length in this node has no target node in the taxonomy, so the graph currently understates it. The resolved cascade is Franco-Norman only and should be read with that caveat until an African/Caribbean trunk exists.
French colonial framing practice (briquette-entre-poteaux, cypress sills, full-width galleries) supplied the construction system into which the African-Caribbean plan was built.

Later shotguns borrow raised-floor and gallery details from the region's higher-status buildings, and after 1880 borrow Italianate and Eastlake millwork brackets wholesale, without descending from either.

description.short: A house one room wide and three to five rooms deep, gable and porch to the street, its doors aligned on a single axis - a New Orleans type with documented West African and Haitian plan antecedents, not an Anglo economization of a narrow lot.
description.long:
The shotgun is a plan before it is anything else: a single file of rooms, each twelve to fourteen feet square, opening directly into the next with no hallway, the whole strung front to back on a narrow deep lot with the gable end and a porch turned to the street. Three rooms is the minimum, five is common, and the rooms are typically parlour, bedroom, bedroom, kitchen in sequence, so that reaching the last room means passing through every private space in the house. The doors align on one axis, which is the ventilation strategy - open the front and back doors on a July night and the whole house becomes a single duct - and which also produced, at some point in the later nineteenth century, the folk etymology that gives the type its name. The camelback variant adds a second storey only over the rear rooms, preserving the one-storey street reading and, not incidentally, the property tax assessment that went with it.

The origins are the substance of this node, because the popular explanation is wrong and the scholarship correcting it is solid. The folk account says the shotgun is simply the cheapest way to fit a house on a narrow lot taxed by frontage. That is true as far as it goes and explains nothing distinctive: narrow lots exist everywhere and produced side-hall townhouses in Philadelphia, back-to-backs in Manchester and railroad flats in New York, none of which look like this. John Michael Vlach's work of the mid-1970s - his 1975 dissertation and the two-part 1976 Pioneer America article 'The Shotgun House: An African Architectural Legacy' - traced the plan to the Yoruba two-room house of West Africa, roughly twelve by twenty feet with the entrance in the gable end, carried to Saint-Domingue in the slave trade, where it fused with Arawak and French Caribbean building to produce the Haitian ti kay. The transmission event is documented: between 1809 and 1810 roughly ten thousand refugees from the Haitian Revolution - white planters, free people of colour, and enslaved people in nearly equal thirds - arrived in New Orleans by way of Cuba, doubling the city's population. Jay Edwards has since identified some 140 linear cottages in New Orleans built before 1840. The name may itself be African: Vlach proposed the Fon word to-gun, 'place of assembly', reaching English through Louisiana Creole, which would make the shotgun-through-the-doors story a later folk rationalisation of a word nobody recognised. Not every claim in this chain is equally secure - the etymology is the weakest link and Edwards has argued for a more complex Creole synthesis than a single African line - but the central point survives all of the criticism: the shotgun is a Black architectural tradition that arrived in North America through the Caribbean, and calling it a poor man's cottage erases the only interesting thing about it.

The conditions that made it a mass type are industrial and post-emancipation. From the 1860s the shotgun became the standard rental and owner-built house for Black urban communities across the South and, with the Great Migration, into Louisville, Memphis, Houston, and industrial towns as far as Los Angeles; thousands were built in New Orleans in the 1880s and 1890s alone. Mill-sawn cypress and pine, machine-cut nails and catalogue millwork made it fast and cheap to build; a builder could produce a row of them on a single subdivided lot. It absorbed whatever ornament the era offered - Italianate brackets, Eastlake spindlework, Queen Anne gable shingles - all of it concentrated on the street gable and the porch, because that eight feet of frontage was the entire public face of the household. Its subsequent history is a story of policy: shotgun neighbourhoods were redlined, cleared for urban renewal and interstate construction, and after 2005 flooded and demolished in enormous numbers, so the surviving stock is a fraction of what was built.

Standing on the porch of one, the first thing you notice is that the porch is the room the house does not otherwise have. It is five to eight feet deep, full width, raised two or three feet above the banquette, and it faces a street of identical porches four feet away across a narrow yard - a social machine of extraordinary efficiency, and the reason former residents describe the type in terms of neighbours rather than rooms. Inside, the axis is the whole experience: standing at the front door you see straight through four doorways and out the back, a hundred and twenty feet of aligned openings, and the ceilings are ten to twelve feet so the volume feels far larger than the fourteen-foot width. There is no privacy in the modern sense and there was never meant to be; the plan assumes that circulation happens on the porch and in the yard, exactly as it does in the West African compound and the Caribbean village the plan came from.

defining_characteristics: One room wide, three to five rooms deep, with no hallway - rooms open directly into one another in an enfilade
Front and rear doors and all intervening doors aligned on a single longitudinal axis
Gable end turned to the street, with a full-width porch under or attached to the front gable
House width of 12-16 feet overall, set by the room, not by the lot
Ceiling heights of 10-12 feet, disproportionate to the plan width, for stack ventilation in a subtropical climate
Ornament concentrated entirely on the street gable and porch, whatever the current millwork catalogue offered
Growth by adding rooms to the rear, or by the camelback: a second storey over the rear rooms only
diagnostic_tells: Sight line straight through the house from the front door to the back door - no other American type does this
Front facade of one or two openings only, a door and a window, under a gable
Porch full width and at least 5 feet deep, raised on brick or cypress piers with an open crawl beneath
Camelback profile: a house that is one storey from the street and two from the alley
Rows of identical units at 3-6 foot spacings on subdivided lots, sharing a rhythm but not party walls

distinguished_from.difference: The Creole cottage faces the street broadside with four openings, no centred door, and a hall-less four-room plan two rooms deep. The shotgun turns ninety degrees and goes to one room wide. They share carpenters, cypress, ceiling heights and the refusal of interior corridors.

A massing, not a style, and much broader. A Greek Revival or Folk Victorian gable-front house is two or three bays wide with a side hall; the shotgun is one room wide with no hall at all. Width and the absence of a passage are the test.

Different ancestry and different climate logic. The farmhouse is Anglo-descended, two rooms deep or more, has a central or side passage, and grows by ell. The shotgun is Afro-Caribbean in plan, single-file, and grows only backward.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by the room and by airflow. Width is one room, depth is a repeated module, and ceiling height is set by stack ventilation rather than by any proportional canon; the street gable is proportioned by the porch.
typical_ratios: Overall width 12-16 feet; individual rooms 11-14 feet square
Total depth 40-70 feet across 3-5 rooms
Ceiling height 10-12 feet, giving a room whose height nearly equals its width
Porch depth 5-8 feet, full width; floor raised 18-36 inches above grade on piers
Roof pitch 6:12 to 10:12 front-gabled; camelback rear section 1.5-2 storeys
Lot frontage 25-32 feet with 4-8 feet of side yard, from the New Orleans standard 30 x 120 foot lot
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Street facade of two openings (door and window) or three on a double shotgun; the side elevation carries one window per room at even spacing, which is the plan module made visible.

massing_affinities.note: The type and the massing are the same object.
Wider gable-front cottages of two rooms' width are a related but distinct type and should not be labelled shotgun.
Shares the region and the builders but not the plan; the four-opening broadside face is the opposite move.

constraints.statement: All door openings must align on a single longitudinal axis within 3 inches, front door to rear door. Offsetting an interior door breaks the ventilation path that is the type's entire environmental strategy.
Overall width 12-16 feet, one room wide throughout, with no interior hallway. A hall added down one side converts the building to a side-hall cottage and is a different type.

test.note: Tests the overall width range (12-16ft) via facade_width_ft, the narrow gable end that addresses the street. 'No interior hallway' is also cleanly testable via corridor_present = 'no' but is left as prose here since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Ceiling height minimum 10 feet (11-12 typical), with a transom over every interior door and operable windows on both side walls of every room. The section is the cooling system.

test.note: Tests the 10ft minimum ceiling height. The interior-door-transom requirement and the two-side operable-window rule are left as prose.

constraints.statement: Full-width front porch of at least 5 feet depth (6-8 preferred), raised 18-36 inches above grade. The porch is the house's only social space and its only public face; a shotgun without one is incomplete rather than merely plain.

test.note: Tests the minimum full-width porch depth (5ft) via gallery_depth_ft. The raised-floor height above grade (18-36in, testable via floor_height_above_grade_in) is left as prose here since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Growth is to the rear only. A camelback second storey must begin at least two rooms back from the front wall so the street elevation remains single-storey; a full second storey over the front rooms destroys the type.

exemplars.name: Elvis Presley Birthplace
exemplars.note: Built by Vernon Presley; a two-room wood-frame shotgun with a hipped roof and a front porch on thin wooden posts. The irreducible minimum version of the type, and precisely dated.

exemplars.name: Shotgun House (Santa Monica Conservancy Preservation Resource Center)
exemplars.location: 2712 Second Street (original site), Ocean Park, Santa Monica, California
exemplars.note: Three rooms in line, board-and-batten, front porch, with Queen Anne shingling on the street gable - evidence of the type's migration to the Pacific Coast as worker and resort housing. Relocated 2014, opened as a preservation centre 2016.

exemplars.name: Faubourg Marigny and Bywater shotgun rows
exemplars.note: The densest surviving concentration of the type, mostly 1880s-1890s, single and double shotguns and camelbacks with Italianate and Eastlake millwork on the street gables. Cited as a district because the individually documented early examples largely did not survive.

sources: John Michael Vlach, 'The Shotgun House: An African Architectural Legacy', Pioneer America 8 (1976), parts 1 and 2
John Michael Vlach, Sources of the Shotgun House: African and Caribbean Antecedents for Afro-American Architecture (PhD dissertation, Indiana University, 1975)
Jay D. Edwards, 'Shotgun: The Most Contested House in America', Buildings & Landscapes 16 (2009)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
64 Parishes (Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities), 'Shotgun House'

proportion_packs.note: The closest available match for the shotgun's 11-14 ft enfilade rooms and 10-12 ft stack-ventilation ceilings, offered with an explicit caveat rather than as a clean fit: room-vernacular's module is reconstructed from Anglo-American measured fabric, and this node's own lineage entry flags the shotgun's real plan ancestry -- a documented West African (Yoruba) and Haitian antecedent -- as an 'ACKNOWLEDGED GAP' in this taxonomy with no target node of its own. The physical constraints room-vernacular reconstructs (joist span, daylight depth, a hearth or stove's reach) are constraints of physics rather than of any one building culture, so the numbers plausibly transfer even though the plan-generating logic does not. What does NOT transfer is the room_adjacency_overrides rule's direction: the shotgun's rooms are strung front-to-back along the depth of a one-room-wide lot rather than tiled across a frontage, the reverse of every Anglo type the pack was built from.

Bound narrowly, for one thing only: the type's hard constraint that every interior door carries an operable transom (c03) is exactly the ventilation-transom device this pack's window-head notes describe, and its transom_sidelight rule -- that a transom must take the same light module as the windows it is glazed with, 'because they came out of the same box of glass and the same joiner's shop' -- is a free internal-consistency check across the street gable's one or two openings and the interior transom run.
