Not bound for light-count dating: the type's ornamental era (Italianate and Eastlake catalog millwork, mostly 1880s-1890s) is already carried by the node's own description and constraints, and forcing a divided-light pattern onto what were commonly large 1/1 or 2/2 panes by that date would misdate the building.

classical-mediterranean.name: Classical Mediterranean

description.short: The trunk of column, entablature, and proportional order that runs from archaic Greece through Rome and the Renaissance into every classical revival since.
description.long:
This is the longest continuous design tradition in Western building, and the only one that has ever been written down as a system. Its distinguishing property is not a set of shapes but a set of relations: a module is chosen — classically the diameter of the column at its base — and every other dimension in the building is derived from it. The result is that a Doric temple and a Georgian farmhouse can share a grammar while sharing almost no dimensions.

The tradition survives three near-deaths and three resurrections. Rome absorbs and industrializes the Greek orders, adding the arch and the vault that Greek trabeated construction could not produce. The Latin West largely loses the system for a millennium, keeping fragments as spolia and half-remembered proportion. Fifteenth-century Florence recovers it by measuring ruins and reading Vitruvius, and Palladio converts the recovered system into a design method transmissible by book — the decisive act, because a book crosses oceans and a guild does not.

What makes the classical stream matter for a kit of parts is precisely that it was always already a kit of parts. The orders are a parametric system with inheritance: choose Tuscan or Corinthian and a hundred subordinate dimensions follow. Any attempt to encode traditional design as software is, whether it admits it or not, re-implementing something Vitruvius, Serlio, and Gibbs each attempted with the tools of their century.

defining_characteristics: Proportional derivation from a governing module rather than from absolute dimensions
The orders as a graduated system of character, from robust Tuscan to delicate Corinthian
Trabeated expression — the visible logic of support and load, retained even where it is no longer structural
Bilateral symmetry as the default state of a composition
Transmission by treatise and pattern book, making the system portable across geography and craft tradition

iberian-mediterranean.name: Iberian & Mediterranean

description.short: The courtyard, thick wall, and tile tradition of the Iberian peninsula, carrying an Islamic inheritance into the Americas by way of Mexico.
description.long:
The Iberian tradition is the one Western stream shaped decisively by Islamic building culture. Eight centuries of al-Andalus left a permanent inheritance: the inward-turned courtyard, water as an architectural element, geometric surface ornament in tile, the blind street wall, and a fundamentally different relationship between house and public realm than anything in the Anglo world. A Georgian house presents its best face to the street. An Andalusian house presents a wall and a door, and keeps its face for itself.

Carried to the Americas by conquest and mission, the tradition met adobe construction, indigenous labor, and a scarcity of skilled masons, producing a simplified, massive, plain-surfaced architecture that has almost nothing in common with the Baroque churches of Spain except its plan diagrams and its tile. That simplification is not a loss — it is the emergence of a genuinely new regional language, and the direct ancestor of Mission Revival, Spanish Colonial Revival, and the entire architecture of California and the Southwest.

The tradition's hot-dry climate logic — thermal mass, small openings, deep shade, courtyards, cross-ventilation at night — is now the most technically relevant traditional inheritance available to builders in the American Sun Belt.

defining_characteristics: Inward orientation: courtyard and patio as the organizing void, street elevation substantially closed
Massive wall construction — adobe, rammed earth, rubble stone, brick — with deep window reveals
Small, deeply-set openings and generous shaded transitional space
Low-pitched or flat roofs, clay tile, parapets
Surface ornament concentrated at the entry and in tile rather than distributed over the facade

monterey-revival.name: Monterey Revival

geography.hearth: Monterey and Los Angeles, California

lineage.note: A deliberate resurrection of a style that had itself lasted barely twenty years, after a gap of roughly eighty.

The revival draws its sash, shutters, panelled doors, and much of its trim from the Colonial Revival vocabulary rather than from anything Californian — reproducing at second hand the same Anglo-Hispanic hybridity the original had at first hand.
The professional channel: California offices trained in academic composition, working from the state's own newly-valued historical fabric.

description.short: The 1930s revival of California's brief Anglo-Hispanic hybrid, defined by a full-width second-storey cantilevered balcony running across a two-storey block under a low-pitched tile or shingle roof.
description.long:
The original Monterey style existed for about two decades. Thomas Larkin, a New England merchant who arrived in Mexican California in 1832, built himself a house that used adobe walls in the local manner, a hipped roof and framing in the manner of the Massachusetts he had left, and a two-storey balcony across the front that belonged fully to neither. Others copied it, California became American, redwood and milled lumber arrived, and the type was gone by the 1850s. It is a genuine hybrid produced by a genuine collision, and the collision lasted about as long as such things usually do.

What makes the revival interesting is that it is a hybrid of a hybrid, and its second-generation blending runs in exactly the same direction as the first. The 1930s Monterey house takes the balcony, the two-storey mass, and the low roof from Larkin's building, and then furnishes it with double-hung sash, operable shutters, six-panel doors, and clapboard or board-and-batten on the upper storey — all of which come from the Colonial Revival millwork catalog rather than from anything in California history. The result reproduces, by an entirely different mechanism, the same Anglo-Hispanic doubling the original had achieved by accident. That is not a criticism of it. It is the reason the style works: the revivalists correctly identified what the original was about and rebuilt it from the materials they had.

The balcony is the whole thing, and it is a better piece of architecture than it usually gets credit for. Running the full width of the elevation, cantilevered or carried on slender posts, roofed by the main roof, it shades the entire upper south wall, gives every upstairs room an outdoor extension, and holds the two-storey mass down against the ground so that a fairly large house reads as a low one. It also solves the problem that defeats most two-storey traditional houses in hot climates: what to do with an upper storey that has no porch. The answer here is unusually elegant, and it is available to any builder willing to commit to a continuous element rather than a decorative fragment.

Monterey Revival was popular enough in California suburban tracts through the 1940s and early 1950s to constitute one of the last genuinely traditional production styles before Minimal Traditional and the Ranch absorbed the market. It is worth studying as the end of a line.

defining_characteristics: Two full storeys — the type does not exist as a single-storey house
A cantilevered or post-supported balcony running the full width of the principal elevation at the second floor, roofed by the main roof
Low-pitched side-gable or hipped roof, 3:12 to 6:12, in clay tile or wood shingle
Stucco at the ground floor, frequently with a lighter material — clapboard, board-and-batten, or shingle — at the second storey
Double-hung sash with operable shutters, panelled entry door, and trim drawn from Anglo-American rather than Spanish practice
Simple rectangular or L-shaped massing with restrained ornament; iron or turned-wood balcony rail
A deliberate, legible pairing of Spanish and New England elements within one composition
diagnostic_tells: The balcony runs the entire elevation without interruption — a partial or centred balcony is a different and lesser thing
Stucco below and wood siding above, with the material change occurring exactly at the balcony floor line
Shutters and double-hung sash appearing on a tile-roofed stuccoed house
A slender, almost thin balcony rail and posts, quite unlike the heavy iron of the parent style
Roof overhang modest and even, with no decorative rafter tails

distinguished_from.difference: The original, c. 1835-1855, is built of true adobe with walls two to three feet thick, has small irregular openings, and was produced by an actual collision of Mexican and New England building practice in a place where both were present. The revival is frame construction with stucco cladding, has larger and regularly spaced openings, and reconstructs that collision deliberately from published sources eighty years later.

The parent style is asymmetrical, courtyard-oriented, ornamented at a focal entry, and predominantly single-storey or irregular in height. Monterey Revival is a frontal, near-symmetrical two-storey block whose entire architectural argument is a single horizontal balcony.

Colonial Revival shares the sash, shutters, and trim vocabulary but places them on a steep-roofed, symmetrical, wood- or brick-clad Georgian-derived box. Monterey Revival puts the same trim on a low-roofed stuccoed mass with a full-width upper balcony, which no Colonial Revival house has.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by the horizontal balcony line, which divides the elevation and sets the reading of the whole. No classical module.
typical_ratios: Balcony depth 6'-8'; below 6' it fails as usable space and reads as trim
Ground-floor storey height 9'-10'; second floor 8'-9'
Balcony line placed so the lower mass reads as the heavier of the two, roughly 55:45
Roof pitch 3:12 to 6:12
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three to five bays, evenly spaced, with the entry centred or set one bay off centre.

massing_affinities.note: The Monterey balcony is a gallery raised to the second storey and reduced to one face.
Single-storey massing eliminates the balcony and with it the type.

constraints.statement: The balcony must run the full width of the principal elevation and be not less than 6 feet deep. A centred or partial balcony, or one under 6 feet, converts the house into an ordinary two-storey stucco box with a decorative appendage.

test.note: 'Must run the full width of the principal elevation' has no matching vocabulary variable (no balcony-width variable exists to compare against facade_width_ft) and stays prose.

constraints.statement: The balcony must be sheltered by the main roof or by a continuous integral roof, never by a separate applied canopy.

Where a material change occurs between storeys it must fall exactly at the balcony floor line and continue around any return. A material change that stops at an outside corner is the characteristic production-housing failure.

Shutters, where used, must be sized to cover the full opening and hung on real hardware. Half-width shutters are more conspicuous on this style than on most, because the sash is the only Anglo element carrying the hybrid argument.

test.note: Unlike the family's usual half-width-pair rule (shutter_leaf_to_sash_ratio = 0.5, e.g. colonial-revival, dutch-colonial-revival), Monterey Revival's shutters must each cover the full opening on their own -- the statement itself calls out this reversal. 'Hung on real hardware' is qualitative and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Principal balcony elevation should face within 60 degrees of south or west, where the shading it provides is worth its cost.

test.note: A genuine disjunction ('within 60 degrees of south or west') tested at its safe shared bound: the angular distance to the nearer of the two target bearings, reusing piazza_bearing_deg for the balcony's facing direction.

exemplars.name: Larkin House
exemplars.note: The original from which the revival takes its name and its balcony; National Historic Landmark. Cited here as the referent, not as an example of the revival.

exemplars.name: Casa Amesti
exemplars.note: Adobe with a full-width second-storey balcony; interiors remodelled by Frances Elkins in the 1920s, which is itself part of how the type re-entered fashionable circulation.

exemplars.name: Cliff May's early Monterey-mode houses
exemplars.location: San Diego and Los Angeles, California
exemplars.note: May's pre-Ranch work in the early 1930s; individually documented examples are best cited through the Cliff May papers rather than by single address.

sources: McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses
Gebhard, Architecture in California
Kirker, California's Architectural Frontier
Winter, Toward a Simpler Way of Life: The Arts and Crafts Architects of California
Hess, The Ranch House

proportion_packs.note: This style's own defining_characteristics list 'double-hung sash with operable shutters, panelled entry door, and trim drawn from Anglo-American rather than Spanish practice' outright, and its lineage records hybridizes_with colonial-revival at weight 0.6 with inherits_kit true. Bound for the door and window rectangle logic on that explicit, in-file textual basis -- this is the one node in the cluster where an Anglo classical-derived opening system is not a stretch but the style's own stated borrowing. Governs the sash and door proportions only; the balcony itself, which is this style's real governing datum, is not modeled by this or any pack in the corpus.

Bound specifically for the shutter rule, which this style's own c04 tests with shutter_leaf_to_sash_ratio = 1.0 -- note that this REVERSES the family's usual half-width-pair convention (0.5, as bound on georgian-colonial-american) and the constraint's own note flags the reversal explicitly: each shutter leaf must cover the full opening on its own, 'because the sash is the only Anglo element carrying the hybrid argument.' That is this style's most specific, most sourced proportional claim, and it maps onto this pack's vocabulary exactly.

A judgment call, not a documented one. This style hybridizes_with colonial-revival (weight 0.6, inherits_kit true), and trim-classical's own applies_to list already names colonial-revival directly -- so the chain from this style to this pack runs through one inherited-kit lineage edge rather than through a source specific to Monterey Revival's own interiors. Bind at low precedence for the panelled door and shuttered double-hung sash this style borrows wholesale from Colonial Revival millwork; do not extend it to the ground floor, which is stuccoed Spanish mass and takes no wood trim family at all.

The pack's own applies_to list names monterey-colonial directly -- the actual 1830s original this style revives (lineage edge type 'revives', weight 1). Bound for the gallery-house logic: the full-width balcony is 'a gallery raised to the second storey and reduced to one face' (this style's own massing_affinities note), and the upstairs rooms it shades are governed by the same daylight-depth mechanics as any single-loaded gallery room, at the pack's lower 1.8x multiplier because the balcony's own roof lowers the effective head the way a porch does elsewhere in the pack.

georgian-revival.name: Georgian Revival

geography.hearth: Philadelphia, Boston, and Tidewater Virginia

lineage.note: The accurate, brick, high-style wing of Colonial Revival. Same offices and same catalogs, held to a stricter standard of precedent.
The direct claimed ancestor, and the one this variant actually tries to reproduce rather than merely evoke.
The English source is quoted directly here in a way that plain Colonial Revival avoids - Gibbs surrounds, Wren-Baroque doorcases, and English brick bonds.
Westover, Carter's Grove and Stratford Hall supply the five-part parti, the belt course, and the Flemish-bond brickwork that this variant depends on.
Interior register - delicate plaster, attenuated pilasters, elliptical fans - applied inside houses whose exteriors are earlier in reference.
The academic apparatus that made accuracy possible: measured drawings, the analytique, and offices with libraries.

description.short: The scholarly, usually brick, high-style wing of Colonial Revival, which after about 1915 replaced free invention with measured accuracy drawn from the Georgian houses of Virginia, Philadelphia and England.
description.long:
Georgian Revival is what Colonial Revival became when it acquired a library. Where the general style tolerates - even prefers - an oversized entrance and a foursquare body, this variant holds itself to documented precedent: five or seven bays, Flemish-bond brick with glazed headers, a moulded water table, a belt course at the second floor, segmental or flat gauged-brick arches with keystones, a modillioned cornice of correct projection, a hipped or gambrel roof with pedimented dormers, and a doorcase taken from Gibbs or from a specific Virginia house. It is the register in which the Colonial Revival is judged on scholarship rather than on charm.

The conditions for that shift were documentary and institutional. The Georgian Period portfolios began appearing in the 1890s, the White Pine Series of Architectural Monographs from 1915 supplied measured drawings of specific New England and Mid-Atlantic buildings monthly, and from 1928 the Rockefeller-funded restoration of Colonial Williamsburg by Perry, Shaw & Hepburn produced an authoritative catalog of profiles, brick bonds, hardware and paint colours that spread through the profession within a decade. Simultaneously, university architecture programmes and the growing prestige of the country-house practice - Trumbauer, Delano & Aldrich, Mellor Meigs & Howe - made Georgian the polite default for institutional work as well: dormitories, banks, schools, embassies.

What this variant claimed, on behalf of clients who could afford it, was not merely ancestry but discrimination. Anyone could buy a white house with shutters; a Georgian Revival house said that the owner and the architect knew the difference between a Philadelphia doorcase and a Charleston one. This is why it became the American establishment style and why it survives at the top of the market with almost no loss of prestige - it is the only style in this branch whose claim was always partly about knowledge.

It is a quiet, dense, rather serious thing to stand in front of. The brick is dark and the mortar joints are fine, the water table and belt course give the wall a horizontal grip that clapboard never achieves, and the openings are regular enough that the eye counts them without being asked. The entrance is elaborate but held in - a proper doorcase with a pediment, not a two-storey portico - and the cornice runs across the whole front at one height and turns the corner properly. Inside, the rooms are square, tall and panelled, the stair is generous, and the whole thing is more formal than modern life quite needs, which is a large part of why people keep building it.

defining_characteristics: Masonry primary wall, most often brick in Flemish bond, with a moulded water table and a belt course at the second-floor line
Strictly symmetrical five- or seven-bay facade with a centred entrance and rigorous vertical alignment between storeys
Openings with gauged brick flat or segmental arches, or stone lintels with keystones, and 9/9, 12/12, or 6/6 double-hung sash
A documented doorcase - pilasters or engaged columns with a full entablature and a triangular, segmental, or swan's-neck pediment - scaled to a single door leaf
Hipped, side-gable, or gambrel roof with pedimented or arched dormers and a modillioned or dentilled cornice of correct classical projection
Chimneys at the gable ends, paired and expressed as mass, not as flues
diagnostic_tells: Flemish bond with glazed or darker headers, a moulded water table, and a belt course together indicate the accurate phase; running bond with no water table indicates general Colonial Revival.
Sash carries 9 or 12 lights per unit rather than 6, with muntins near 3/4 in. - this variant is where the revival actually tries to match the original's glazing.
The doorcase is elaborate but never more than about 8 ft wide overall. If the entrance grows into a two-storey portico, the building has become neoclassical-revival.
Dormers are pedimented or arched with pilastered cheeks, not shed or gabled boxes.
Against the genuine Georgian original: revival storey heights are still a foot taller, the plan is still two rooms deeper, and there is a garage.

distinguished_from.difference: The parent style admits free interpretation, frame construction, foursquare massing, and invented detail, especially before 1915. Georgian Revival is its documented wing: masonry, five- or seven-bay symmetry, correct bonds and profiles, and detail traceable to a specific precedent.

The original is smaller, has thinner and more numerous glazing bars, lower ceilings, single-pile or shallow double-pile plans, no corridor circulation on the upper floor, and hand-shaped mouldings. The revival matches its face and not its dimensions.

Georgian Revival keeps its entrance emphasis to a doorcase and, at most, a one-storey portico. Neoclassical Revival raises a colossal two-storey portico and changes the whole compositional argument from wall to screen.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Documented Georgian practice, checked against published measured drawings. The brick course and the sash light are the working modules: openings are dimensioned in whole brick courses and glazing bars are sized to the original's.
typical_ratios: Five bays by two storeys plus dormered attic; seven bays on large examples
Storey heights 9'6"-10'6" first, 9'0"-9'6" second; still taller than eighteenth-century practice but closer than general Colonial Revival
Window openings 3'2" x 6'2" typical, proportion near 1:2, with sash of 9/9 or 12/12
Belt course 4-8 in. deep, water table 4-6 in. projection, cornice 14-20 in. total depth
Doorcase 6'0"-8'0" overall width for a 3'0" x 6'8" leaf; pediment apex not above the second-floor sill line
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even and strict. Five or seven bays at 8'6"-10'0" on centre, the centre bay widened only enough to take the doorcase. Every second-storey opening aligns with the one below within an inch.

massing_affinities.note: The reference case: centre passage, two rooms deep, five bays, hipped or side-gable roof.
The Tidewater parti - centre block, hyphens, and dependencies - on estate sites.
The urban town-house version, three bays with the entrance to one side.
The Mid-Atlantic and New England gambrel-roofed Georgian; overlaps dutch-colonial-revival.
The overhang belongs to the seventeenth-century reference, not the Georgian one.

constraints.statement: Brickwork must be laid in Flemish or English bond with joints 3/8 in. or finer, a moulded water table at grade and a belt course at the second-floor line, and openings headed with gauged brick flat arches, segmental arches, or stone lintels. Running-bond veneer with no water table is not this variant.

The doorcase must be dimensioned for a single 3'0" x 6'8" to 3'0" x 7'0" leaf, overall width not exceeding 8'0", with the pediment apex below the second-floor sill line. Double doors and two-storey porticos are forbidden in this variant.

test.note: Tests the door leaf width, stated as a fixed 3'0". Leaf height range (6'8"-7'0"), overall doorcase width (<=8'0", no matching vocabulary variable -- an entry-surround-width variable distinct from door_opening_width_ft is missing), and the pediment-apex-below-sill-line clause stay prose.

constraints.statement: Sash shall be 9/9 or 12/12 on principal elevations, muntins 5/8-7/8 in., with true divided lights or full-depth simulated bars with an interior spacer. 1/1 and 6/1 sash void the variant.

test.note: Muntin width (5/8-7/8in, matching glazing_bar_width_in but not tested here) and the true-divided-lights-or-full-depth-simulated-bars construction clause stay prose -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Cornice total depth 14-20 in. with modillions or dentils spaced to the bay module, carried fully around the building including gable returns of not less than 18 in.

test.note: Modillion/dentil spacing to the bay module and the gable-return minimum (18in, no matching vocabulary variable) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Chimneys must be built at the gable ends, minimum 3'6" x 2'0" in plan, rising not less than 2'6" above the ridge. Interior ridge chimneys and flush metal flues are forbidden.

test.note: Chimney position (gable-end, expressible via chimney_position but not tested here) and the 3'6"x2'0" plan footprint (no matching vocabulary variable) stay prose -- one test per constraint.

exemplars.name: Whitemarsh Hall
exemplars.note: Horace Trumbauer for E. T. Stotesbury, 1916-21. Neo-Georgian at Beaux-Arts scale, 147 rooms; demolished 1980 and still the largest American house deliberately destroyed.

exemplars.name: Governor's Palace (reconstruction)
exemplars.note: Perry, Shaw & Hepburn. The reference library for the whole variant: bonds, profiles, hardware, dormers and paint, all published and copied for forty years.

exemplars.name: Widener Library, Harvard University
exemplars.note: Horace Trumbauer with Julian Abele. The institutional register, and evidence that the variant's brick-and-limestone grammar scales far past the house.

exemplars.name: Griffith-Sowers House
exemplars.location: Rowan County, near Salisbury, North Carolina
exemplars.note: Five-bay centre block with connected wings, slate roof; a well-documented ordinary-scale example, NRHP 2009.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
William B. Rhoads, The Colonial Revival (1977)
The White Pine Series of Architectural Monographs (1915-1940)
Richard Guy Wilson, The Colonial Revival House (2004)

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in this pack's applies_to, and the node's own description names the source directly: 'a doorcase taken from Gibbs or from a specific Virginia house.' Unlike colonial-revival, this variant's own proportional_system states the order is checked 'against documented Georgian practice, checked against published measured drawings' -- the full computational rigor of the parent georgian-colonial-american node applies here, not the looser catalog reading bound on plain colonial-revival.
Explicitly listed. The everyday order for secondary doorways and the plainer examples of the variant.

Explicitly listed. Governs the strict five- or seven-bay composition the node's own constraints require, including the odd-bay rule and the ranking of water table, belt course and cornice that the node's own defining_characteristics name individually.

Explicitly listed. The node's own hard constraint c02 (doorcase for a single 3'0" x 6'8"-7'0" leaf, overall width not exceeding 8'0", pediment apex below the second-floor sill) restates this pack's door_surround and entry_door slots directly.

Explicitly listed. The node's own hard constraint c03 (9/9 or 12/12 on principal elevations, muntins 5/8-7/8 in.) is this pack's light-count and muntin logic verbatim -- this variant is, per its own diagnostic tells, 'where the revival actually tries to match the original's glazing.'

Explicitly listed. Storey heights 9'6"-10'6" first, 9'0"-9'6" second per the node's own typical_ratios -- still taller than the eighteenth-century original but closer to it than plain colonial-revival, exactly the graduated relationship this pack records.
Explicitly listed. The interior register the node's own description names directly -- 'panelled, tall, more formal than modern life quite needs.'

Explicitly listed, and effectively governing rather than truly optional here: the node's own hard constraint c01 requires Flemish or English bond with a moulded water table and belt course, which is this module pack's whole subject. Kept under the 'optional' role label used elsewhere in this branch for the masonry module, but its precedence is high because the bond IS the diagnostic that separates this variant from plain colonial-revival, per the node's own diagnostic tells.
Explicitly listed. The node's own description -- 'the rooms are square, tall and panelled' -- and its academic, measured-drawing-driven design process match this treatise-based room system directly.

arts-and-crafts-british.name: Arts and Crafts (British)

revival_periods.note: A continuous minority practice in British house-building, and the reference point for most serious contemporary work in regional materials.

geography.hearth: The Surrey and Sussex Weald, the Lake District, and the Cotswolds around Sapperton

lineage.note: Office descent and doctrinal descent together. Philip Webb and William Morris met in G. E. Street's Gothic office in 1856; Pugin's principles — nothing unnecessary, ornament as enrichment of real construction — pass through Ruskin into the movement's core, and the plan-driven asymmetry comes with them.

And a rejection of the same style's method. Arts and Crafts keeps the ethics and discards the archaeology: no pointed arches, no tracery, no ecclesiastical quotation, no structural polychromy. Morris's founding of the SPAB in 1877 was an attack on the Gothic Revival's habit of 'restoring' medieval buildings out of existence.

Study on site rather than quotation from books. Webb, Shaw, Lutyens and Voysey measured and sketched Wealden and Surrey farmhouses, and took from them the long roof, the low eaves, the catslide, the tile-hanging and the dominant stack.

The Sapperton group — Ernest Gimson and the Barnsley brothers from 1893 — learned Cotswold masonry and stone-slating from men still practising it, and this is one of the very few revivals to reacquire a living craft rather than reproduce an appearance.

Overlapping personnel and overlapping decades. Shaw's Old English and the Bedford Park houses are the immediate context; Arts and Crafts cools the palette, removes the ornament and lengthens the horizontals.

description.short: A house built from the materials of its own county, planned from the inside out around a hall and a hearth, and detailed so that every visible thing is doing structural work — the last coherent traditional style in Britain, and the one that stopped quoting.
description.long:
Arts and Crafts is the point at which the English revival tradition stops copying periods and starts studying construction. Its founding building is Red House at Bexleyheath, designed by Philip Webb for William Morris in 1859: red brick left unrendered, a steeply pitched red tile roof, sash and casement windows of different shapes placed where the rooms wanted them, and no style label available to describe it. What Webb had done was take the Gothic Revival's demand that the plan generate the form and apply it to a house with no ecclesiastical pretensions whatever. Everything that follows — Shaw's Old English, Webb's Standen, Voysey's white roughcast houses, Baillie Scott's halls, Lutyens's Surrey manor houses with Gertrude Jekyll's gardens, Gimson's Cotswold work — is an elaboration of that move.

The intellectual conditions are Ruskin and Morris. Ruskin's chapter on the nature of Gothic in The Stones of Venice, published in 1853 argued that the roughness of medieval work was evidence of a free workman's mind, and that machine-perfect ornament records a degraded life; Morris founded his firm in 1861 to act on it, and the Art Workers' Guild (1884) and the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society (1887, which gave the movement its name) institutionalised the argument. The economic conditions were less romantic: the railway had made national materials cheap, and using local stone, local brick and local tile was becoming a deliberate and slightly expensive choice rather than the default. This is the first style in Britain in which regional material is a decision.

The formal result is unusually consistent across very different architects. Massing goes long and low, with big unbroken roof planes and eaves brought down toward the ground; walls are of one material honestly used — roughcast over stone or brick, local stone, brick, or tile-hanging above brick; windows are casements with leaded lights, grouped into horizontal bands under stone or oak mullions, so that the wall reads as a solid punctuated by a ribbon rather than as a grid of holes; chimneys are large and structurally frank; and the plan is organised around a hall with an inglenook, with rooms of different sizes and heights disposed for sun and view rather than for symmetry. Ornament, where it exists, is craft ornament: a carved beam, a wrought hinge, a leaded pattern, a fireplace tile.

To be in one of these houses is to notice how much of the design is aimed at the body rather than the eye. The eaves come down low enough to make the entrance feel sheltered; the inglenook is a room within a room, with a bench, a window and a fire; window seats are cut into thick walls; ceilings drop in circulation spaces and rise in the hall. Light is handled carefully and often sparingly, so a long low room ends in a bright bay. The whole effect is of a building that has been thought through in section as well as plan, by someone who imagined living in it. That is the tradition's real bequest, and it is why almost every good small house built in Britain since has been, at some level, an Arts and Crafts house.

defining_characteristics: Truth to materials: one honest local material per mass, left as itself — roughcast, local stone, brick, tile-hanging, oak — with no imitation of another material anywhere
The plan generated from the inside out around a hall and hearth, with rooms sized and placed for use, sun and view rather than for external symmetry
Long, low massing with large unbroken roof planes at 45-55 degrees and eaves carried down close to the ground, often to first-floor sill level
Casement windows with leaded lights, grouped into horizontal bands under continuous stone or oak mullions and a shared lintel
Massive, structurally frank chimney stacks, frequently expressed as buttressing masses on the elevation
Ornament limited to craft enrichment of real construction — carved beam ends, wrought ironwork, leaded glass, tile and plaster — and never applied as a period quotation
House and garden designed as one composition, with terraces, walls, steps and planting continuing the plan outdoors
diagnostic_tells: Horizontal bands of small leaded casements under one long lintel — the exact inverse of the Georgian vertical punched opening, and instantly readable at distance
Eaves brought down unusually low, often with a sweeping catslide over an entrance or an outshot, so the roof dominates the elevation
Battered (sloping) buttresses and chimney bases, with roughcast render carried over them in one continuous white or cream surface — the Voysey signature
A chimney stack that is the largest single element of the composition and is placed where the fire is, not where the elevation wants it
No classical order, no pointed arch, no shaped gable, no period quotation of any kind: the absence of quotation is itself the tell

distinguished_from.difference: Queen Anne quotes 1700 in red brick and white paint with sashes, shaped gables, terracotta sunflowers and cheerful eclecticism. Arts and Crafts stops quoting: casements instead of sashes, roughcast or local stone instead of red brick, ornament removed, horizontals lengthened, palette cooled.

The American branch, arriving through Gustav Stickley's The Craftsman from 1901 and the Greene brothers, translates the movement into timber: exposed rafter tails, shingle, deep porches, Japanese-influenced joinery, open plan. British work is masonry-minded, more enclosed, and keeps distinct rooms.

Tudor Revival applies half-timbering, four-centred arches and leaded diamond panes as costume over a conventional plan. Arts and Crafts uses the same regional sources structurally and refuses the period signals; a Voysey house has no half-timbering at all.

proportional_system.governing_logic: No applied system. Proportion is derived from construction and from the body: the span of a beam, the depth of an inglenook, the height at which an eave feels sheltering, the sill height for a window seat. Composition is balanced by mass, not by axis, and is designed in section as much as in elevation.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 45-55 degrees; roof plane frequently occupying 40-55 percent of the elevation's total height
Eaves height 2.4-4.0 m, often below first-floor head height, with 450-750 mm overhang
Window band proportion horizontal overall (2:1 to 5:1 wide to high) built from individual lights of 350-450 mm by 700-1100 mm
Leaded quarries 100-150 mm across, rectangular rather than diamond in the stricter work
Wall thickness 400-600 mm, giving window seats of 350-500 mm depth
Chimney stack width 900-1800 mm, rising 1-1.5 m above the ridge
Batter on buttresses and stack bases 1:10 to 1:6
Ceiling heights deliberately varied: 2.3-2.6 m in passages and low rooms, 3.5-6.0 m in the hall
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Grouped and irregular. Windows cluster into horizontal ribbons where a room needs light and disappear entirely where it does not, so long stretches of blank wall alternate with continuous glazing. There is no repeating bay and no vertical alignment requirement.

massing_affinities.note: The composed but irregular agglomeration — Standen, Cragside's later phases, Lutyens's Surrey houses — built up from a plan rather than drawn as a picture.
The long low range with subordinate service wings stepping down, taken directly from farmstead precedent and the natural form for the style.
The hall-with-wings figure returns, sometimes opened into a butterfly plan (Prior, Lutyens) to catch sun on both flanks.
The single-storey house with rooms opening to a garden, and the point at which the British movement feeds directly into the American and colonial bungalow.
A symmetrical double-pile box contradicts the plan-driven method, though Lutyens's later classical phase deliberately returns to it.

constraints.statement: Every visible material must be doing the job it appears to do. Applied half-timbering, veneer stone, false beams and imitation finishes are forbidden outright — this is the movement's founding rule.
One primary wall material per mass, changing only at a floor level or a change of volume, and then with a proper structural transition (oversail, tile course, plinth).
Windows are casements grouped into horizontal bands under a common lintel and mullion line. Isolated vertical punched openings in a regular grid belong to the classical stream, not here.
Eaves height not more than 4.0 m on the principal elevation, with the roof reading as a dominant plane. A tall wall under a small roof inverts the style.

test.note: Tests the eaves-height ceiling. 'The roof reading as a dominant plane' is qualitative and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Primary materials should be sourced from the building's own region; the choice of local material over national material is a defining act of the style, not a preference.

exemplars.name: Red House
exemplars.note: Built 1859-60 by Philip Webb for William Morris. Unrendered red brick, steep red tile roof, windows placed by plan rather than by elevation — the movement's founding building and the first English house of its century with no style label.

exemplars.name: Standen
exemplars.note: Built 1892-94 by Philip Webb for the solicitor James Beale, with Morris and Co. interiors. Local sandstone, brick, tile-hanging and weatherboarding used in distinct masses, and a plan wrapped around the sun and the view.

exemplars.name: Broadleys
exemplars.note: Built 1898-99 by C. F. A. Voysey for Arthur Currer Briggs. Roughcast walls with battered buttresses, low sweeping eaves, and three great bow windows facing the lake — Voysey's manner at its most complete.

exemplars.name: Blackwell
exemplars.note: Built 1898-1900 by M. H. Baillie Scott for Sir Edward Holt. A double-height hall with inglenook and minstrels' gallery, and one of the most intact Arts and Crafts interiors anywhere.

sources: Peter Davey, Arts and Crafts Architecture (1980, rev. 1995)
Mark Girouard, Sweetness and Light: The 'Queen Anne' Movement 1860-1900 (1977)
Alan Crawford, C. R. Ashbee: Architect, Designer and Romantic Socialist (1985)
Margaret Richardson, Architects of the Arts and Crafts Movement (1983)
Nikolaus Pevsner, Pioneers of Modern Design (1936, rev. eds.)

proportion_packs.note: arts-and-crafts-british is named directly in facade-picturesque's applies_to. governing_logic states 'No applied system... Composition is balanced by mass, not by axis, and is designed in section as much as in elevation,' and symmetry is recorded as 'balanced-asymmetrical' — the pack's dominant-mass and continuous-datum logic is the closest formal description available of what Webb, Voysey and Lutyens were actually doing, even though the pack's own sources postdate the movement's founding building (Red House, 1859) by decades.

arts-and-crafts-british and british-arts-and-crafts are both named directly in trim-craftsman's applies_to, which is a deliberate crossover: this pack is sourced from American bungalow millwork catalogues, and no purpose-built British Arts and Crafts trim pack exists in this library. The underlying logic transfers cleanly — 'this system is not derived from the orders... the module is a board,' which matches c01 (every visible material must be doing the job it appears to do) exactly, and both traditions descend from the same Pugin-via-Ruskin refusal of applied classical trim. Caveat: British practice runs oak rather than fir, favours exposed structural members (a carved beam end, a wrought hinge) over the catalogue's flat-stock casing family, and Voysey's own joinery is often plainer still. Use the pack for its structural-honesty logic and its butted-not-mitred discipline; do not import its specific American stock-board dimensions uncritically.

Judgment binding (not in applies_to). Justified by direct lineage: this style descends_from english-cottage-vernacular (weight 0.7) and cotswold-vernacular (weight 0.6), both of which are room-vernacular's own source material, and Webb and Voysey are recorded as having 'measured and sketched Wealden and Surrey farmhouses' directly. The daylight-depth rule and the varied ceiling-height logic both suit a movement whose houses are 'designed in section as much as in elevation' — though the double-height hall, where present, exceeds the pack's ordinary-room scale and should be read against its own text instead.

richardsonian-romanesque.name: Richardsonian Romanesque

geography.hearth: Boston and Chicago

lineage.note: The round arch, the squat column, and the massive wall are quoted; Richardson's own sources were closer to Auvergne, Provence, and Salamanca than to England, and none of them transmitted building practice to him.

Real transmission. Richardson was the second American to study at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts, and the plan discipline, the parti, and the compositional hierarchy of his buildings are Beaux-Arts training applied to Romanesque forms.
Against thin, brittle, applied eclecticism and the mansarded pile, in favour of mass, weight, continuity, and material presence.
Specifically against High Victorian polychromy and linear ornament; Richardson replaced pattern with mass.

description.short: H. H. Richardson's personal manner and its national imitation: rock-faced ashlar, deep round arches springing from squat columns or from the ground, and a wall so heavy and continuous that the building reads as a single geological mass.
description.long:
This is the only American style named for a person, and the attribution is honest, because the style is one man's solution and everything after Trinity Church in Boston, won in competition in 1872 and finished in 1877, is imitation of varying quality. Henry Hobson Richardson trained at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris in the 1860s, and what he brought back was not a vocabulary but a method: establish the parti, subordinate everything to a single dominant idea, and make the building one thing. He then took a vocabulary, southern French and Spanish Romanesque, that nobody in America had a claim on, and used it to make masses instead of pictures. His imitators took the vocabulary and mostly missed the method, which is why there are ten thousand rock-faced arches in America and perhaps forty buildings that work.

The style stands at an unusual angle to the technological rupture that organises this branch. Everything else here rides cheap light framing and cheap machine ornament; Richardsonian Romanesque insists on load-bearing masonry at exactly the moment American construction was abandoning it. Its own enabling technologies are different ones: mechanised quarrying and the pneumatic and steam stone saw, which made large rock-faced blocks of granite, sandstone, and brownstone economically shippable, and the transcontinental railroad that moved them. There is also a labour story. The style depends on the presence of skilled stonecutters, many of them recent Scottish, Irish, Italian, and German immigrants, in American cities in the 1880s, and it dies in the 1890s partly because steel frame construction made the load-bearing masonry wall obsolete for tall buildings and partly because those crews and their wage rates could not be sustained.

What it rejected was the entire Victorian assumption that a building should be interesting all over. Richardson's walls are large, quiet, and mostly blank; his openings are few, deep, and grouped; his ornament is concentrated in narrow bands of carved foliage at a capital or a string course and is otherwise absent. The effect is a hierarchy of attention that no other Victorian style attempts. He is also the only architect of the period whose buildings improve as you approach: from across the street you read one mass and one arch, from the sidewalk you read the coursing and the tooling of the stone, and at the door you find the carving, which is worked at exactly the scale of a hand.

In front of one, the dominant sensation is compression and weight. The entrance arch springs from near the ground or from columns so short and thick that they read as pressed down by the wall above; the voussoirs are large enough to count; the wall recedes into a deep reveal so that entering is genuinely a passage through thickness rather than through a plane. Inside a Richardson house the surprise is warmth: heavy oak, inglenooks, low broad openings, and rooms that are dark at the perimeter and bright at the windows, which are always fewer and larger than you expect. It is the only Victorian style that feels like shelter rather than display.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing masonry construction, in rock-faced squared ashlar of granite, sandstone, or brownstone
Deep semicircular arches at the principal entrance, springing from short heavy columns or directly from a plinth or the ground
Massive continuous wall surface with a low proportion of opening, and windows deeply recessed in the wall thickness
Broad simple roof forms, low hipped or with a few large gables, subordinate to the wall mass
Towers that are round, squat, and conically capped, engaged with the mass rather than attached to it
Ornament confined to narrow bands of carved Byzantine or Romanesque foliage at capitals, string courses, and the entrance arch
Polychromy by stone selection and coursing, never by paint or applied pattern
diagnostic_tells: The arch springs from the ground or from a column no more than three diameters tall; a tall slender column under a round arch indicates a later commercial imitation
Rock-faced stone with quarry tooling left visible, laid in broken-range or random coursing, with the face projecting 2 to 4 in beyond the joint
Window openings grouped in bands of three or five under a single relieving arch or lintel, rather than distributed one per bay
The tower, if any, is round and squat with a conical cap and is engaged into the corner of the mass; a slender detached tower is a different style
Compared with Queen Anne: no texture change, no applied ornament, no porch. The wall is one material top to bottom

distinguished_from.difference: Contemporary and often on the same street, but opposite in every value: mass versus articulation, one material versus many textures, few large openings versus many small ones, load-bearing stone versus balloon frame.

Shares Richardson himself and shares the doctrine of continuous unbroken surface, which is precisely why the two are linked in the graph. The difference is material and weight: shingle is a taut light skin over a wooden volume, ashlar is the mass itself.

The quoted source. English Norman work is genuinely twelfth-century, thin-jointed, with cushion capitals and chevron ornament and a real structural logic of pier and vault; the Richardsonian arch is a nineteenth-century masonry veneer of feeling with a steel or timber floor system behind it in all but the largest examples.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by mass and by the arch. The entrance arch is the module of feeling for the whole building: its span sets the wall's apparent thickness, the coursing scale, and the depth of every reveal. Beaux-Arts parti discipline organises the plan beneath it.
typical_ratios: Wall opening area 20 to 35 percent of any elevation; the wall must win
Entrance arch span 8 to 16 ft, with voussoir depth 1/8 to 1/6 of the span
Column height 2 to 3.5 shaft diameters where columns are used at all
Ashlar course height 8 to 14 in, face projection 2 to 4 in beyond the joint plane
Window reveal depth 12 to 24 in
Tower diameter 12 to 20 ft, height to eave 1.2 to 1.8 times diameter
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Grouped and hierarchical rather than repetitive: a large arched opening, a band of three or five smaller openings, and long stretches of blank wall. The rhythm is A - BBB - A, not A-A-A-A.

massing_affinities.note: Picturesque in outline but massive in substance, which is the style's particular achievement.
Round, squat, engaged, conically capped.
The rock-faced brownstone row of Boston, Chicago, and Denver.
A mansard converts mass into crown and destroys the continuity the style depends on.

constraints.statement: Exterior walls shall be load-bearing masonry of not less than 16 in nominal thickness at the ground storey, with window reveals of 12 to 24 in. Thin stone veneer over a frame wall is prohibited; the style is entirely an argument about wall thickness.

test.note: Tests the wall-thickness minimum, the clause the statement itself calls the governing one ('the style is entirely an argument about wall thickness'). The paired window-reveal range (12-24 in, reveal_depth_in) is a second numeric fact the schema's single test object can't also carry, and stays prose alongside the thin-veneer-over-frame prohibition.

constraints.statement: Principal arches shall be semicircular. Pointed, segmental, and elliptical arches are forbidden at the entrance. Where columns support an arch, shaft height shall not exceed 3.5 base diameters.
Openings shall occupy not more than 35 percent of the area of any elevation, and shall be grouped rather than evenly distributed.

test.note: Tests the opening-area ceiling. 'Grouped rather than evenly distributed' is a spatial-distribution fact with no matching vocabulary variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: One wall material shall run from water table to eave on every elevation. Texture, colour, and coursing may vary within the material; a change of material at a storey line is prohibited.
Carved ornament shall be confined to capitals, the entrance arch, and not more than two continuous bands per elevation, and shall total not more than 8 percent of the elevation area.

exemplars.name: Trinity Church
exemplars.note: H. H. Richardson, competition won 1872, dedicated 1877. The building that established the manner and made Richardson the most imitated architect in America.

exemplars.name: John J. Glessner House
exemplars.note: H. H. Richardson, designed 1885, completed 1887. Granite street walls turned almost blank to the corner with the rooms opening to a private south courtyard; the definitive domestic statement of the style.

exemplars.name: Allegheny County Courthouse and Jail
exemplars.note: H. H. Richardson, 1884-88, completed after his death in 1886. Richardson himself considered it his best work.

sources: Jeffrey Karl Ochsner, H. H. Richardson: Complete Architectural Works (1982)
Henry-Russell Hitchcock, The Architecture of H. H. Richardson and His Times (1936; rev. 1961)
James F. O'Gorman, Three American Architects: Richardson, Sullivan and Wright, 1865-1915 (1991)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: Explicit in this pack's applies_to, but its governing role is narrower here than on the wooden Victorian styles: the node's own proportional_system says the elevation is 'governed by mass and by the arch,' with hierarchy made by grouped-vs-blank wall (A-BBB-A) rather than by the pack's dominant-mass-vs-subordinate-mass logic in the usual sense. What transfers cleanly is the datum discipline (the pack's continuous-horizontal rule, which matches this node's wall material running unbroken water-table to eave) and the one-feature-window logic. The dominance ratio and wing-strategy rules are a poor fit for a single-block masonry mass and should be read loosely if at all.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to. Governs the ashlar coursing scale (8-14 in course height per the node vs. the pack's whole-course arithmetic), the water table, and the general discipline that every horizontal is a whole number of courses off one datum — genuinely applicable to load-bearing stone as well as brick, since the pack's coursing logic is generic to coursed masonry. It does NOT cover the style's defining semicircular entrance arch: brick-course's arch rules are segmental and flat-jack-arch derivations, and this node requires full semicircular arches (c02) springing from squat columns, which is a real gap — see report.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to. Bound low and secondary because the style's few, deeply recessed, grouped windows (20-35 percent opening area) are still real double-hung sash of the 1872-1905 period and would carry the same late-cylinder/plate-glass light counts as the rest of the corpus's Victorian nodes; but the pack's window-head and casing rules are calibrated to wood-frame construction and are secondary here to brick-course's masonry-specific window_head_masonry rule for the actual opening geometry.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to. Bound over room-vernacular because the node explicitly credits 'Beaux-Arts parti discipline' organizing the plan beneath the Romanesque forms, and Richardson is documented as the second American to study at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts — a formally trained, hierarchically composed plan is closer to this pack's rank-and-suite logic (adjacent rooms differing by one term of the series, breadth held constant across a suite) than to room-vernacular's structurally-constrained folk room. No specific source ties Richardson's own room dimensions to Palladio's ratios, and this binding should be read as 'the closest available system for a formally planned room,' not as a documented fact about Richardson's practice.

flemish-vernacular.name: Flemish Vernacular

revival_periods.note: Belgian Neo-Flemish Renaissance, adopted as a national style after independence and exported to English seaside and Kentish work as the 'Flemish gable'.

geography.hearth: Flanders and Brabant

lineage.note: The eastern half of the region — Limburg, the Kempen, the Maasland — builds vakwerk that is structurally continuous with Rhenish Fachwerk. The border is modern; the carpentry is not.

Antwerp Mannerism, and specifically Vredeman de Vries's engraved sheets published there from 1560, quote Italian ornament onto a wholly Flemish wall. The prints, not the buildings, are what travelled.

description.short: The brick, stone-banded and timber-framed building culture of Flanders and Brabant, whose stepped gable, long-facade farmstead and enclosed square farm were the common architecture of the richest agricultural region in medieval Europe.
description.long:
Flanders was, from the thirteenth century, the most densely urbanised and most intensively farmed ground north of Italy, and its vernacular is the architecture of that density. The land is flat, wet, treeless in its western half and clay-rich everywhere, which means brick from an early date and brick made locally in small kilns — a hard, small, red-orange brick laid in thick lime mortar. Where good building stone was needed it had to be barged in, principally the white Ledian and Gobertange stones of Brabant, which is why the characteristic Flemish wall is not stone and not plain brick but the two alternating in horizontal bands. The bands are usually explained as decoration. They are more honestly explained as a rationing system: the expensive material goes where it does the most work — sills, jambs, arch voussoirs, string courses at the floor lines — and the pattern is what is left over.

The rural type is the langgevelhoeve, the long-facade farm: dwelling, byre, stable and barn strung in a single low range under one continuous roof, entered from the long side, the doors and windows falling wherever the internal function put them. Where a farm prospered it did not lengthen indefinitely; it broke into separate ranges and closed them around a yard, producing the vierkantshoeve, the square farm, a walled and gated agricultural courtyard with a single wagon entrance. That progression — one range, then an L, then three sides, then a closed square with a gate — is the whole growth grammar of the Flemish countryside, and it is driven by the same logic in every case: the farmyard is the working floor, and enclosing it protects stock, manure, and tools in a landscape that had been fought over more or less continuously since the fourteenth century.

In the towns the same building culture produces the stepped gable, the crow-stepped brick screen that Flanders exported over half of northern Europe — to Holland, to Scotland's east coast, to Kent and East Anglia, to the Baltic — largely through the movement of Flemish weavers, masons and merchants under religious and economic pressure. The Flemish stepped gable is heavier than the Dutch one that follows it: fewer and deeper steps, more stone in the wall, more often a real gable ending a real roof rather than a screen in front of one. What the tradition was negotiating with, from the sixteenth century on, was a Renaissance ornament it received as printed pattern rather than as building. Antwerp bought Italy in sheets and applied it to a wall it had no intention of changing.

Standing in a Flemish farm courtyard is a specific and quite un-picturesque experience: you are inside a low, hard, whitewashed or bare-brick enclosure with a beaten or cobbled floor, roofs that come down close over you on all four sides, a single arched gate that frames the only view out, and a dungheap in the middle that was, until living memory, the most valuable thing on the property. The buildings are not composed. They are the walls of a room whose ceiling is the sky.

defining_characteristics: Small hard local brick laid in lime mortar, frequently banded with imported white stone (speklagen) at sills, lintels and floor lines
Stepped (crow-stepped) gable as the standing urban and farm gable form, with the steps capped in stone or tile
Long-facade farmstead: dwelling, byre and barn in one continuous low range entered from the long side
Growth by enclosure — from single range to L to three-sided to a fully closed square farm with one gated wagon entrance
Timber-framed with brick nogging in the eastern (Limburg, Kempen, Maasland) half of the region; solid brick in the west
Steep clay-pantile or thatch roof with the eave carried low over the working side
Functional, not compositional, fenestration on rural buildings: openings occur where the internal use requires them
diagnostic_tells: Crow steps with stone or tile capping, on a gable that is genuinely the end of a roof rather than a screen in front of one
Horizontal white stone banding through red-orange brick — the 'bacon' wall
A farm reading as a closed rectangle from outside, with one arched gate and no other opening in the outer face
Pantiles (golfpannen) rather than flat tiles, and a roof that comes down to about head height over the byre side
In the east, close-spaced vakwerk posts with whitewashed loam panels standing on a brick plinth

distinguished_from.difference: The Dutch canal house is a narrow, deep, pile-founded urban object whose gable is a free-standing screen and whose facade leans forward for a hoist. Flemish work is broader, lower, more often rural, heavier in the wall, and its gable is structural.
Where the two overlap in Limburg they are the same craft. West of the Scheldt the Flemish wall is solid brick and the frame disappears entirely, which never happens in the German heartland.

English framing is oak, wide-panelled or close-studded, and almost never combines with the banded brick-and-stone wall. Flemish brick reached England as an import — the 'Dutch gables' of Kent are Flemish craft, not English development.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The structural bay of the roof, and the brick. Rural ranges are set out in bays of roughly 3.5-4.5 m fixed by the spacing of the roof trusses or the vakwerk posts; the range is a whole number of bays and grows by adding one. In the towns the brick course plus joint (about 60-65 mm) is the real module, and the gable steps are dimensioned in whole courses.
typical_ratios: Farm range depth 5.5-7 m clear, one room or one byre deep
Gable step rise to tread roughly 1:1, three to seven steps per side
Roof pitch 45-55 degrees for pantile, 50-60 for thatch
Closed farm courtyard roughly 1:1 to 1:1.5 in plan, 20-40 m across
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Additive and irregular in the countryside — bays are structural, not visual, and openings ignore them. Regular and countable in town, where each floor holds two or three openings and the gable reduces them upward.

massing_affinities.note: The langgevelhoeve is the type specimen: house, byre and barn merged in one range, growing by extension at either end.
The vierkantshoeve — a fully enclosed working farmyard with one gated entry — is where a prosperous Flemish farm ends up.
The three-sided intermediate stage, before the fourth range or a wall closes the square.
Urban Flanders builds party-walled brick rows with stepped gables to the street.
The cottier's one-room brick or vakwerk cell, the irreducible unit of the rural landscape.

constraints.statement: Timber frame and solid brick are alternatives, not layers. A vakwerk elevation must stand on a fired-brick or stone plinth at least 400 mm above grade, and must not be applied decoratively over a masonry wall.

test.note: Converted from the source's 400 mm to in. Tests the plinth-height minimum only. 'Timber frame and solid brick are alternatives, not layers' / 'must not be applied decoratively over a masonry wall' is a construction-method prohibition with no matching vocabulary variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Stone banding must fall at real structural lines — plinth, sill, lintel, floor level, springing. Bands that float free of those lines read as wallpaper and are prohibited.
Pantile roofs at 45-55 degrees; thatch not below 50. Eaves overhang at least 300 mm, carried lower on the working (byre and midden) side to shelter the doors.

test.note: Converted from the source's 300 mm to in. Tests the eave-overhang minimum, which is unconditional. Roof pitch is a material-conditioned disjunction (pantile 45-55 deg, thatch not below 50 deg) with no safe shared bound -- testing at the looser bound would pass a 70 deg pantile roof the statement forbids -- so it stays prose, as does 'carried lower on the working side'.

constraints.statement: A closed farm must have exactly one wagon gate; secondary pedestrian doors are cut through a range, never through a second arch in the outer wall.
Crow steps are set out in whole brick courses and must be capped; an uncapped step erodes within a generation and is not a permissible detail.

exemplars.name: Vleeshuis (Butchers' Hall)
exemplars.note: Herman de Waghemakere; the fullest surviving demonstration of the banded brick-and-stone Flemish wall at civic scale.

exemplars.name: Groot Begijnhof
exemplars.note: Founded 13th century; the surviving brick and sandstone houses are largely 16th-17th century. UNESCO World Heritage 1998. An intact street-scale sample of Brabantine domestic building.

exemplars.name: Begijnhof
exemplars.note: Founded 13th century; houses mainly 17th century, with stepped gables and banded walls at cottage scale.

exemplars.name: Openluchtmuseum Bokrijk
exemplars.note: Relocated and reconstructed Flemish and Limburg farmsteads dating from the 16th to the 19th century, including vakwerk and langgevel types.

sources: Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World
Weyns, Volkshuisraad in Vlaanderen
Bral & Vandevyvere, Bouwen door de eeuwen heen in Vlaanderen (inventory series)
Rudofsky, Architecture Without Architects

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to. The langgevelhoeve's byre and dwelling rooms are span- and function-limited exactly as the pack describes — this node's own text states fenestration is 'functional, not compositional... openings occur where the internal use requires them,' which is close to a direct restatement of the pack's additive-vernacular bay_rhythm language.

Judgment bind: flemish-vernacular is not listed in brick-course's applies_to, but this node's own proportional_system states outright that 'the brick course plus joint... is the real module' and that 'gable steps are dimensioned in whole courses' — precisely the coursing-governs-every-horizontal logic this pack encodes for Anglo-American brickwork. Recalibrate before use: the pack's default course (2 3/4 in, a 2 1/4 in Anglo-colonial brick with a 1/2 in bed joint) must be reset to this node's own continental figure (~60-65 mm per course) rather than used as-is; the derivation — courses set the water table, string course and step heights — carries over even though the absolute unit does not.

Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to, but applies only to the eastern (Limburg, Kempen, Maasland) vakwerk half of the region, which this node's own lineage entry describes as 'structurally continuous with Rhenish Fachwerk' — the western solid-brick half has no frame for this pack to govern. Bound secondary and narrow in scope for that reason.

craftsman-bungalow.name: Craftsman Bungalow

geography.hearth: Streetcar suburbs nationwide; the type is defined by its distribution channel rather than by a place

lineage.note: Strictly this is a variant by scale and distribution rather than by region: the Craftsman grammar reduced to what fits a 40-to-50-foot lot, a 900-to-1,400 square foot programme, and a precut lumber package. It is the form in which the style was actually built, in the hundreds of thousands, across every American climate.

The same local carpenters, the same lumberyards, and the same customers. Folk Victorian's habit of ordering a house as a stock plan plus a trim package is the commercial apparatus that the bungalow inherits and perfects.

description.short: The Craftsman grammar compressed into a one-to-one-and-a-half storey, nine-hundred-to-fourteen-hundred square foot house sold as a plan book design or a precut kit, and built across the United States in numbers that made it the first genuinely national American house type.
description.long:
The Craftsman bungalow is what happens when a style becomes a product. The word bungalow describes a type — a low, broad, mainly single-storey house with living space partly in the roof and a porch across the front — and the type is older and wider than the style; the Craftsman bungalow is the intersection, and the intersection is where nearly all the buildings are. The formula is tight: a rectangular body twenty-four to twenty-eight feet wide and thirty-two to forty-four feet deep on a narrow lot, ridge running front-to-back or side-to-side, a porch under the main roof across the whole front, one or two bedrooms off a short hall, a living room with a hearth and flanking built-ins, a dining room behind it with a built-in buffet, a compact kitchen, and a single bath. Between eight hundred and fourteen hundred square feet contains an entire middle-class domestic programme with no wasted circulation, which is a level of planning efficiency that American production housing has rarely matched since.

What produced it was a distribution revolution, and the specifics are worth holding onto. From 1908 Sears, Roebuck sold Modern Homes as precut kits — every stud numbered, the nails counted, the plan shipped by boxcar to the nearest siding — a business it ran until 1940; Aladdin, out of Bay City, Michigan, had begun the same trade in 1906 and continued it into the 1980s. Beside them ran a shelf of plan books that sold drawings rather than lumber: Stickley's own Craftsman Homes (1909), Henry L. Wilson's The Bungalow Book, the Radford and Ye Planry series, Bungalow Magazine out of Seattle and Los Angeles. Local lumberyards issued their own catalogs and assembled millwork packages to match. The financial condition underneath all of it was the pre-FHA mortgage — short-term, high down payment — which meant that a house had to be cheap in absolute dollars rather than cheap per month, and the bungalow's whole economy is organized around that constraint. The streetcar line supplied the lots.

The significance of this node for anyone building a design system is difficult to overstate, and it is not sentimental. The Craftsman bungalow is the first fully specified traditional kit of parts in history: a grammar reduced to a bill of materials, an assembly sequence, and a small set of enforceable dimensional rules, shipped to unskilled builders, and executed at national scale with a quality of proportion that holds up a century later. It worked because the rules were absolute lengths rather than derived ratios — a thirty-inch overhang, a seven-foot porch, a thirty-inch pier base, a divided upper sash — which a carpenter could follow without understanding the theory. It is the strongest available evidence that traditional design logic can survive productization. The Levittown chapter of this branch is the counterexample; both are true, and the difference between them is precisely which rules were kept.

On the street, a block of them reads as a coherent whole made of small differences: the same body, the same porch depth, the same eave, but the ridge turned ninety degrees on alternate lots, the pier bases in brick here and river stone there, the gable shingled or stuccoed or half-timbered. The porch does real work — it is deep enough for two chairs and a swing and it faces the sidewalk at conversational distance. Inside, the rooms are small and the ceilings are eight and a half feet and the built-ins mean there is very little wall left to furnish, which reads today as either an unbearable constraint or a relief, depending on the occupant.

defining_characteristics: One to one and a half storeys, 800 to 1,400 sq ft, on a lot of 40 to 50 ft frontage
Low-pitched gable roof with 24 to 36 in overhangs on eave and rake, exposed rafter tails and knee braces
Full-width or near-full-width front porch framed under the primary roof, on battered piers with masonry bases
A compact plan with no formal hall: front door opens into the living room, which contains the hearth and flanking built-ins
Dormer, usually shed, providing habitable roof space in the one-and-a-half storey version
Divided upper sash over single-light lower sash throughout
Sourced from a published plan or a precut package rather than from an architect's commission
diagnostic_tells: Front door opens directly into the living room with no vestibule — the plan's fingerprint
Porch piers of clinker brick or fieldstone carrying tapered wood posts, with a solid porch balustrade of the same masonry
Shed dormer set well back from the eave line, with its own small overhang
Three- or four-over-one sash, and a wide flat casing 4 to 5 in deep around every opening
The whole street shares one massing with the ridge alternately parallel and perpendicular to the road

distinguished_from.difference: The sibling variant. The Californian type is lower-pitched, deeper-eaved, more often stuccoed, and includes outdoor rooms — sleeping porch, pergola, court — that the national type has no climate for. A bungalow with a 3:12 roof and an unheated sleeping porch in Ohio is a Californian design built in the wrong place.
The parent style covers architect-designed work at any scale, including the Greene and Greene houses. This node is specifically the mass-market type: small, published, and precut.

Both are small builder houses, and Minimal Traditional is what happened to this one after 1935: the same footprint with the eave cut to six inches, the porch deleted, the built-ins deleted, and the trim reduced to a clamshell profile.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Inherited from Craftsman — porch beam datum, aligned head datum, exposed framing rhythm — but bounded by two additional economic constraints that determine almost everything: the lot width, which caps the body at 24 to 28 ft, and the precut package, which standardizes every member length. The plan-book house is proportioned by catalog page, not by module, and it holds together because the catalog was internally consistent.
typical_ratios: Body width 24 to 28 ft; depth 32 to 44 ft; depth-to-width roughly 1.4:1 to 1.6:1
Roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12
Eave and rake overhang 24 to 36 in
Porch depth 7 to 9 ft; porch width 70 to 100 percent of the facade
Ceiling 8 ft 6 in; window and door heads at 6 ft 8 in on a single datum
Porch pier base 24 to 30 in wide, tapering to 10 to 14 in at the beam
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Two or three openings per elevation face, grouped in pairs or triples with wide plain wall between; the porch occupies the whole of the front and is itself the principal bay.

massing_affinities.note: The definitional skeleton; front-gabled and side-gabled subtypes are both this massing with the ridge rotated.
Occurs on corner lots and where a rear ell was added; usually a later accretion rather than an original design.
The two-storey answer on the same lot; the plan-book trade sold both from the same catalog.

constraints.statement: Front porch depth not less than 7 ft clear and width not less than 60 percent of the facade, framed under the primary roof.

test.note: Tests the porch depth. Porch width as a percentage of the facade has no vocabulary variable for porch width itself, and 'framed under the primary roof' is categorical -- both stay prose.

constraints.statement: Eave and rake overhang 24 to 36 in; roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12. Below 18 in of overhang the node degrades to minimal-traditional.

test.note: Tests the pitch range. The eave/rake overhang range (24-36 in, expressible via eave_projection_in) and the 18 in degrade-to-minimal-traditional threshold are a second independent numeric clause and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Conditioned floor area 800 to 1,600 sq ft on one to one and a half storeys. A full second storey disqualifies the node and moves it to the foursquare massing under the parent style.

test.note: Tests the storey-count bound. Conditioned floor area (800-1,600 sq ft) has no vocabulary variable -- there is no floor-area measure in build/constraint_vocabulary.py -- and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Dormers must be set back not less than 24 in from the eave line and must not exceed 60 percent of the roof plane's width.
The hearth and its flanking built-ins must occupy a full wall of the principal living room; if the plan has no hearth wall the node is a bungalow in massing only.

exemplars.name: Bungalow Heaven Landmark District
exemplars.note: More than 800 modest bungalows built c. 1900-1930 and designated a landmark district in 1989 — the type at neighbourhood scale, largely from published plans.

exemplars.name: Sears Modern Homes
exemplars.location: United States, shipped nationally from Chicago
exemplars.note: The precut kit programme, 1908-1940, which sold roughly 70,000 houses; surviving examples are documented in most Midwestern and Eastern states. Listed here as a product line rather than a single building because that is what the node actually is.

exemplars.name: Craftsman Farms (the Log House)
exemplars.note: Stickley's own house, whose published plans and derivatives seeded the plan-book trade this variant runs on.

sources: Clay Lancaster, The American Bungalow, 1880-1930 (1985)
Gustav Stickley, Craftsman Homes (1909)
Katherine Cole Stevenson and H. Ward Jandl, Houses by Mail: A Guide to Houses from Sears, Roebuck and Company (1986)
Alan Gowans, The Comfortable House: North American Suburban Architecture 1890-1930 (1986)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)

proportion_packs.note: Same composer as the parent style, bounded harder here by the lot: this node's own governing_logic states that the body is 'capped at 24 to 28 ft' by the standard 40-50 ft lot, which is a real-world instance of this pack's dominant-mass module (18-22 ft for 'a bungalow or a cottage where the dominant mass is a single gable') at the small end of its documented range.

The type IS this pack's own primary evidence base -- Sears Modern Homes, Aladdin, the Radford and Ye Planry plan books are cited by both the node and the pack as the same distribution mechanism -- so this is as close to a one-to-one binding as this corpus gets outside the Georgian order packs. Governs the picture-rail datum, the door-head-datum-not-ceiling rule that explains why a house this small tolerates both an 8 ft and a 9 ft 6 in ceiling, and the three-board casing family this node's own diagnostic tells describe directly (a wide flat 4-5 in casing, no mitre).

Bound for the plan's own tight small-house arithmetic: this node's diagnostic tell that the front door opens directly into the living room with no vestibule is exactly the additive, furniture-and-circulation-first room logic room-vernacular reconstructs, and its ceiling-height rule (post-1900 bungalow band, 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft) matches this node's own 8 ft 6 in figure precisely. Not given the top role: the plan is a catalog product bounded by the lot and the precut package before it is bounded by any physical room constraint, which this node's own proportional_system says outright.

neoclassical-revival.name: Neoclassical Revival

geography.hearth: Chicago, by way of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition
