lineage.note: The colossal portico had been dormant in domestic work for forty years. Neoclassical Revival puts it back, at a larger scale and on a plan that owes it nothing.
The imperial register - domes, coffering, Corinthian and Composite - reaching the office through Ecole plates rather than through Rome.
Order profiles, especially Ionic and Doric, taken from Stuart and Revett by way of nineteenth-century handbooks.
The actual descent. Same offices, same draughting conventions, same exposition; Neoclassical Revival is Beaux-Arts with the sculpture budget removed.
Ecole des Beaux-Arts composition - axis, parti, the hierarchy of masses - as taught to Americans in Paris and re-taught at MIT, Columbia and Penn.
In domestic work the two are continuous: the same catalog trim, the same symmetrical plan, differing chiefly in whether the portico is one storey or two.
The White City was a deliberate repudiation of Richardson's weight and of Victorian polychromy in favour of white, thin, axial classicism.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The academic classicism launched by the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, in which a colossal columnar portico - two storeys tall, correctly ordered, and almost always structurally unnecessary - becomes the standard American emblem of institutional and personal permanence.
description.long:
Neoclassical Revival is the residential fallout of a single event. The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago assembled the country's leading offices under Daniel Burnham's coordination and produced the Court of Honor: white, uniform-corniced, colossally colonnaded, and visited by roughly a quarter of the United States population. Within two years the vocabulary was everywhere - banks, courthouses, libraries, railway stations, and, for anyone who could pay for it, houses. The domestic form is straightforward and remarkably stable for fifty years: a symmetrical rectangular block, a low hipped or side-gable roof, a full-height portico of columns rising two storeys to a pediment or a flat entablature, and a correctly detailed order carrying a cornice that runs the whole building.

The conditions were professional before they were popular. By 1893 American architecture had acquired schools, licensing campaigns, and a generation trained at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts who had learned to compose in plan by axis and hierarchy and to render precedent with authority. Classicism was what that training produced, and the Exposition proved it could be produced at speed and at scale. Behind the profession stood a national argument: a country that had just industrialized past Britain wanted a civic architecture that looked like Rome rather than like a mill town, and the City Beautiful movement carried that argument into every state capital. Behind that stood the buyers - bankers, planters, senators, and the professional class of small cities - for whom a two-storey portico was the cheapest available demonstration that a fortune made in the last twenty years had been made in the last two hundred.

What the style claims is permanence, and it claims it with a peculiar honesty about its own thinness. The colossal portico is very rarely doing structural work; it is a screen in front of a conventional balloon-framed or brick-bearing house. In the South especially, where the type became so common that the public renamed it 'Southern Colonial', it was frequently applied to older houses, so that a Greek Revival or even a Federal box acquires a 1910 portico and a new identity. This is not deceit exactly. The portico is understood by everyone involved as a public face rather than a structure, in the same way a suit is understood not to be a body.

The experience is one of scale ambiguity. From the street the house looks larger than it is, because the giant order sets a module the eye then applies to the whole building. Under the portico the effect reverses: the columns are close together, the ceiling of the portico is often only a painted board soffit, and the front door - normal-sized, with a fanlight - sits at the far end of a shadow far too grand for it. Inside, the ceilings are high and the rooms are conventional. The best examples resolve this by giving the portico real depth, 10 to 14 feet, so it becomes a room; the worst press four columns flat against the wall and leave 4 feet of porch, and the whole composition reads as a stage flat, which is exactly what it is.

defining_characteristics: A full-height entrance portico with columns rising two or more storeys to a pediment or entablature, dominating the primary facade
A correctly executed classical order - Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, or Composite - with entasis, capital, base, and entablature in academic proportion
Symmetrical rectangular main block with a low-pitched hipped or side-gable roof and a continuous cornice, often with a balustrade or parapet
Centred entrance with fanlight and sidelights or a decorated door surround, subordinate to the portico above it
Regularly spaced double-hung sash aligned vertically between storeys, frequently with a Palladian or lunette window on the axis
Smooth or lightly rusticated wall surface treated as a plane behind the order rather than as a texture
diagnostic_tells: Columns run two full storeys. One-storey columns on an otherwise similar house make it Colonial Revival, not Neoclassical.
The order is correct - the shaft tapers, the capital is turned or cast to a published profile - where Colonial Revival will accept an untapered box column.
Roof pitch is low, 4:12 to 6:12, and often invisible behind a balustrade; Greek Revival originals carry a shallow pediment as the roof itself rather than hiding one.
The cornice runs continuously around the whole building at one height, including the rear, which no Greek Revival or Colonial house bothers to do.
Portico depth under 6 ft with columns pressed near the wall indicates a late or budget example; 10-14 ft indicates an architect.

distinguished_from.difference: The original, 1825-1860, is a temple in its own right: the gable faces front and is the roof, the order is heavy and often Doric, and the entablature is deep. The revival hangs a lighter, usually Ionic or Corinthian, portico on a hipped block whose roof continues behind it.

Beaux-Arts is richer and wetter - paired columns, rusticated bases, swags, cartouches, sculptural groups, exuberant stone carving. Neoclassical Revival is the same grammar stripped to plain wall and single columns, which is why it could be built in wood in a county seat.

Colonial Revival claims descent from American colonial building and keeps its columns to one storey; Neoclassical Revival claims descent from antiquity and goes to two. In practice the same office built both, often in the same year.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The classical order, module equal to the column diameter at the base, taken from Vignola or from an American handbook derivative. Unlike Colonial Revival, the order genuinely governs: column height, entablature depth, and intercolumniation are all derived from the chosen diameter.
typical_ratios: Ionic shaft height 9 diameters, Corinthian 10, Doric 8, measured including capital and base
Entablature depth 1/4 to 1/5 of column height; architrave, frieze, cornice in roughly 3:3:4
Portico columns 18-24 ft tall on a two-storey house, diameter 20-28 in. at the base
Intercolumniation 2.25 to 3 diameters clear (eustyle to diastyle); wider than 3 reads as slack
Portico depth 10-14 ft on architect-designed work; below 6 ft the portico ceases to be a space
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Four or six columns across the portico with the entrance on the centre line between the middle pair; the wall behind carries five or seven bays at a constant rhythm that ignores the columns, producing the characteristic mismatch between screen and wall.

massing_affinities.note: The full academic case - portico on the centre block, lower wings either side.
The common domestic case: a two-room-deep centre-passage block with a portico applied.
Grand examples on estate sites, hyphens and dependencies included.
Budget version - a hipped cube with a two-storey portico, common in small Southern cities 1905-1925.
The portico wants a symmetrical facade; a side-hall plan fights it.

constraints.statement: Columns must be built to a published order. Shaft entasis is required: minimum taper of 1/6 the base diameter over the shaft height, with the taper beginning no lower than 1/3 the shaft height. Untapered cylindrical or box columns are forbidden at colossal scale.

Entablature depth must be between 1/5 and 1/4 of column height and must be carried on the return elevations for at least one bay. An entablature under 1/6 of column height reads as a fascia board and voids the order.

test.note: 1/5 to 1/4 of column height. The return-elevation-carry and under-1/6-reads-as-fascia clauses stay prose.

constraints.statement: Portico depth must be a minimum of 8'0" clear from wall face to column centreline, and preferably 10'0"-14'0". A colossal order in front of less than 6'0" of porch is a stage flat and is forbidden.

test.note: A colossal-order portico's depth from wall face to column centreline is the same wall-face-to-outer-support-line measurement as a galerie or gallery, so gallery_depth_ft applies. Tests the absolute 8'0" clear-minimum floor; the preferred 10'0"-14'0" range and the <6'0" stage-flat threshold restate the same measurement and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Clear intercolumniation between 2.25 and 3.0 column diameters. The centre pair may open to 3.5 diameters to frame the entrance; no other bay may.

test.note: Tests the general-bay range. The centre-pair-may-open-to-3.5 exception stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12 behind the portico, and where a balustrade is used it must be a minimum 30 in. high with balusters spaced no more than 4 in. clear, so it reads as railing rather than as ornament.

test.note: Balustrade height (>=30in) and baluster clear spacing (<=4in) have no matching vocabulary variable and stay prose.

exemplars.name: Whitehall (Henry M. Flagler House)
exemplars.note: Carrere & Hastings. Marble-faced classical block with a colossal entrance portico; the type at its most emphatic and most public.

exemplars.name: Nemours
exemplars.note: Carrere & Hastings, Louis XVI classicism on an American plan - the point at which Neoclassical Revival and French academic classicism become the same office practice.

exemplars.name: Longue Vue House
exemplars.note: William and Geoffrey Platt. Late, restrained, and unusually intelligent about siting; demonstrates the style surviving well past its supposed end.

exemplars.name: Court of Honor, World's Columbian Exposition
exemplars.note: Burnham, Hunt, McKim, Post and others. Temporary, demolished, and the single most consequential built object in this branch of the taxonomy.

mid-atlantic-georgian.name: Mid-Atlantic Georgian

revival_periods.note: The Philadelphia and Annapolis houses became the schoolbook models for the American Georgian Revival, particularly through the White Pine Series monographs and the 1930s Annapolis surveys.

geography.hearth: Philadelphia and its Schuylkill and Germantown country seats, with a second concentration at Annapolis

lineage.note: Philadelphia's country seats are the most literally Palladian buildings in the colonies — pedimented central pavilion, Venetian window over the door, symmetrical flanking dependencies — because their owners had the books and, in several cases, had been to England.

description.short: The masonry Georgian of the Delaware Valley and the Chesapeake head: schist, limestone or brick with a moulded belt course, a pent eave on earlier work, and a shallow pedimented pavilion on the best.
description.long:
The Mid-Atlantic is the only American region where the Georgian house is normally built of stone, and that fact organizes everything else about it. Philadelphia sits on Wissahickon schist, a mica-flecked grey stone that quarries in beds and takes a dressed face; the Chester and Lancaster valleys sit on limestone; Delaware and the Maryland shore build in brick. Colonial masons in this region were unusually good — many were Scots, Irish or German — and the Quaker commercial economy could pay them. The result is a Georgian that expresses its wall rather than its trim.

Two horizontal devices are the region's signature. The first is the belt course: a moulded projecting band of brick or stone at the second-floor line, running the full facade, standing out an inch and a half to two and a half inches. It does something practical, throwing water off the wall face at the floor joint, and it does something compositional, dividing the elevation into two clearly proportioned registers. The second is the pent roof — a shallow shed thirty to forty-two inches deep, unsupported by posts, running across the facade or the gable at the second-floor line — which is a Delaware Valley speciality of the period before about 1770 and appears nowhere else in Georgian America in this form. Where a pent roof survives, the house is almost certainly pre-Revolutionary and almost certainly within eighty miles of Philadelphia.

Window heads are masonry and say so. Philadelphia uses a flat gauged arch of rubbed brick with a projecting keystone; stone houses use a dressed lintel, sometimes with a moulded cap. Chimneys are at or within the gable ends, often paired and joined above the roof. Roof pitch runs eight to ten in twelve, between the Northern and the Chesapeake norms. Ceilings are ten to eleven feet — a full foot above New England, a foot below the low country. Plans are double-pile from early on, thirty-four to forty feet deep, which is the region's other structural advantage: a stone wall carries a deeper house than a frame one does without complaint.

At the top of the range the Mid-Atlantic produced the most literally Palladian houses in British North America. Mount Pleasant, built 1762–65 on the Schuylkill for the privateer John Macpherson, has a pedimented centre pavilion, a Venetian window over the doorway, rubble walls stuccoed and scored to imitate ashlar with real brick quoins, and two symmetrical dependencies flanking the forecourt. Cliveden at Germantown has a pedimented and pilastered centre with urns on the roof. And at Annapolis, William Buckland's Hammond-Harwood House of 1774 lifts its door surround, rusticated blocks and all, directly out of Gibbs's A Book of Architecture of 1728 and executes it in southern pine painted to read as stone — pattern-book transmission caught in the act, in a building that still stands.

What one notices standing in front of one is the weight. Two feet of schist with a belt course and a keystoned arch is a serious wall, and the classical apparatus laid on it is thin by comparison: a doorway, a cornice, and nothing else. The house is convincing because the material is doing most of the talking.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing masonry: Wissahickon schist or local limestone laid coursed ashlar on the front and rubble elsewhere, or brick in Flemish bond over a moulded water table
A projecting moulded belt course at the second-floor line, standing 1.5–2.5 in proud and running the full facade
Pent roof on work before c. 1770 — an unsupported shed 30–42 in deep at the second-floor line, across the facade or the gable
Chimneys at or within the gable ends, frequently paired and joined above the roof
Masonry window heads: flat gauged brick arch with projecting keystone, or a dressed stone lintel; not a wood architrave
Roof pitch 8:12 to 10:12, side-gable or hipped, with a modillion or dentil cornice
Double-pile centre-passage plan 34–40 ft deep with ceilings of 10–11 ft; on the best houses a pedimented centre pavilion and a Venetian window over the door
diagnostic_tells: A pent roof — a floating shed band across the facade with nothing holding it up — is regionally unique and effectively conclusive
A belt course at the second-floor line, present in some form on nearly all good work
Keystoned flat brick arches over the openings, with rubbed and gauged voussoirs
Coursed ashlar on the entrance elevation and rubble on the sides, on stone houses
A Venetian (Palladian) window over the doorway on the most ambitious examples — rare in New England, rare in Virginia, common here

distinguished_from.difference: Cladding, chimney and head all differ: masonry with a belt course versus wood clapboard or rusticated board; gable-end chimneys versus interior chimneys inboard of the ridge; keystoned gauged brick arches or stone lintels versus flat wood architraves. Roof pitch is a step shallower (8:12–10:12 against 9:12–11:12), and ceilings a foot higher (10–11 ft against 8 ft 6 in – 9 ft 6 in).

Both are masonry with gable-end chimneys, but the Chesapeake house stays single-pile far longer (18–22 ft deep against 34–40 ft), pushes its dependencies out as detached buildings rather than attaching a service ell, uses segmental gauged arches and glazed-header Flemish bond, and runs a shallower roof at 7:12–9:12, often hipped. The pent roof and the belt course are Delaware Valley, not Chesapeake.

Same stone, same counties, same steepish roof, and the two converge after 1780. The test is plan and alignment: Georgian gives a centre passage, aligned windows floor to floor, a symmetrical rear elevation and a classical doorway; the German house gives an asymmetric three-room plan, unaligned windows and a plain door with a hood.

proportional_system.governing_logic: A pattern-book order (Gibbs, Swan, Langley) governs the doorway, cornice and pavilion; the masonry coursing and the belt course govern the horizontal registers.
typical_ratios: Facade 44–56 ft, five bays; depth 34–40 ft double-pile
Belt course at the second-floor line, projecting 1.5–2.5 in, 2–3 brick courses or a 6–9 in stone band deep
Window opening height:width 1.9:1 to 2.1:1; second-floor 82–88% of first-floor height
Ceilings 10–11 ft first floor, 9–10 ft second
Flat gauged arch rise 4–6 in over the opening, keystone 6–9 in wide
Roof rise:run 8:12 to 10:12; centre pavilion projection 12–24 in
Passage 11–14 ft wide
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five bays, with the centre bay taken by the doorway and, on Palladian examples, by a projecting pedimented pavilion one bay wide breaking forward 12–24 in with a Venetian window above.

massing_affinities.note: The double-pile masonry Georgian block; the region's default.
Main block with hyphens and dependencies, as at Mount Pleasant and Whitehall.
The more modest farmhouse version.
The Philadelphia and Annapolis town house on a narrow lot.
Maryland Eastern Shore growth pattern, stepping down from the main block.

constraints.statement: The wall is load-bearing masonry — 18–24 in of coursed stone or 13–18 in of brick — with openings expressing the full reveal depth. Frame construction with masonry veneer is a different building and shows it at every jamb.

test.note: Union of the two material-specific ranges (18-24in stone, 13-18in brick), which are contiguous at 18in with no gap. This tests thickness-is-consistent-with-at-least-one-material; it cannot by itself tell which material's own range was actually used.

constraints.statement: A belt course at the second-floor line, projecting 1.5–2.5 in and 6–9 in deep, running the full width of the facade. This is the region's non-negotiable horizontal, and its absence pushes the elevation toward the Chesapeake.

test.note: Tests the belt course's projection. Its depth (6-9in) is the statement's other dimension and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 8:12 to 10:12, with chimneys at or within the gable end walls. Interior chimneys set inboard of the ridge belong to New England.

constraints.statement: Window heads are masonry: flat gauged brick arches with a 4–6 in rise and a 6–9 in keystone, or dressed stone lintels. A wood architrave head on a stone or brick wall is incorrect.

constraints.statement: Pent roof only on work before c. 1770: 30–42 in projection at the second-floor line, 25–35 degree pitch, unposted, returning 12–24 in at the corners. Sash 9/6 to c. 1765, 6/6 after; shutter leaf width equals half the clear opening.

exemplars.name: Stenton
exemplars.note: James Logan's brick country seat, built 1723–30; the earliest fully Georgian house in the region and among the plainest — a wall with almost no trim on it.

exemplars.name: Mount Pleasant
exemplars.note: Built 1762–65 for John Macpherson. Rubble stuccoed and scored to imitate ashlar with brick quoins, a pedimented centre pavilion, a Venetian window over the door and two flanking dependencies.

exemplars.name: Cliveden
exemplars.note: Built 1763–67 for Benjamin Chew in Wissahickon schist, with a pedimented and pilastered centre and urns on the roof ridge; the site of the Battle of Germantown in 1777.

exemplars.name: Hammond-Harwood House
exemplars.note: William Buckland's last work. The rusticated Gibbs door surround and the oeil-de-boeuf windows in the pediment are taken directly from Gibbs's A Book of Architecture (1728), executed in southern pine to read as stone.

new-england-georgian.name: New England Georgian

revival_periods.note: Sketched by McKim, Mead & White and their contemporaries on the 1877 Colonial tour of Marblehead, Salem and Portsmouth; the New England Georgian house is the direct model for most of what Americans now call 'Colonial'.

regions: coastal New Hampshire and southern Maine
geography.hearth: the merchant ports — Boston, Salem, Marblehead, Newport, Portsmouth — where shipping fortunes and imported books arrived in the same hulls

lineage.note: The frame, the clapboard skin, the steep roof and the cold-climate habits are inherited unchanged; only the plan, the chimney arrangement and the trim are new.

description.short: The Georgian grammar executed in wood by shipwrights' carpenters: clapboard or rusticated board walls, paired chimneys set inboard of the ridge, steep Northern roof pitches and the most elaborately carved doorways in colonial America.
description.long:
New England Georgian is the tradition's answer to a specific problem: how to build a stone architecture out of pine. There is very little building stone in eastern Massachusetts, brick was expensive and cold, and the region had a surplus of extraordinarily skilled ship's joiners. The answer was to translate the whole classical apparatus into wood and then, on the most ambitious houses, to disguise the wood as stone. Boards are cut to a bevelled edge, laid flush, scored to imitate ashlar coursing, and painted with sand thrown into the wet paint so the surface takes the light like cut stone. The Isaac Royall House at Medford and the Jeremiah Lee Mansion at Marblehead both do this; so, later, does Mount Vernon. Nothing else in colonial America is quite so confident a piece of make-believe, and it works, at thirty feet, completely.

The chimney arrangement is the fastest way to tell a New England Georgian house from any of its Southern cousins. Northern winters make an exterior chimney a heat leak, so the stacks stay inside the envelope: two of them, symmetrically placed, rising through the roof slope five to twelve feet in from the gable ends and flanking the ridge, or on smaller houses a single central stack pierced by a passage running past it. Southern Georgian puts its chimneys at the gable walls and frequently outside them entirely. That one difference tracks the climate exactly, and it changes the roofline, the plan and the room layout with it.

The roof stays steep by Georgian standards — nine to eleven in twelve, against seven to nine in the Chesapeake — because snow load and the First Period habit both push it up, and it terminates in a boxed modillion cornice that returns a full twelve to twenty-four inches across each gable end. That full return, meeting a corner pilaster or a heavy corner board, is the second reliable tell. Windows sit in a plain flat architrave five to six inches wide with a simple crown moulding, without keystones or gauged arches, because there is no masonry to arch. Ceilings run eight and a half to nine and a half feet, distinctly lower than the ten to twelve of Virginia — again the climate, and the cost of heating a room.

Everything the house has to spend goes on the doorway. Engaged pilasters or three-quarter columns carrying a full entablature and a triangular, segmental or scroll (swan's neck) pediment, the whole thing three to five feet wide and carved in pine at a scale no English house of the same rank would have attempted in stone. There is no fanlight and no sidelight before about 1780; where you see one, the house is Federal or has been improved.

Inside, the passage is panelled floor to ceiling, the stair has three turned balusters to a tread with a moulded and ramped handrail, and the best room's chimney breast is a full architectural composition — bolection-moulded panels, a pilastered overmantel, and a cornice that agrees with every other cornice in the room because they were all taken from the same plate.

defining_characteristics: Wood construction: clapboard at 4–5 in exposure, or flush boarding, or boarding rusticated and sanded to imitate ashlar on the principal elevation
Chimneys interior and paired, rising through the roof slope 5–12 ft in from the gable ends and flanking the ridge — never on the exterior of a gable wall
Steep Northern roof pitch, 9:12 to 11:12, side-gable, gambrel or hipped, with a boxed modillion or dentil cornice
Full cornice returns of 12–24 in across each gable end, meeting corner pilasters or heavy corner boards of 6–12 in
Flat wood architrave window trim, 5–6 in wide with a crown moulding, without keystone, gauged arch or masonry lintel
A heavily carved entrance frontispiece — pilasters or engaged columns carrying an entablature and a triangular, segmental or scroll pediment — with no fanlight or sidelights before c. 1780
Double-pile centre-passage plan 32–38 ft deep, with ceilings of 8 ft 6 in – 9 ft 6 in
diagnostic_tells: Two chimneys emerging from the roof slope well inboard of the gable ends — the single fastest discriminator against every Southern Georgian variant
A wooden wall imitating stone: scored flush boarding, sometimes with sand in the paint, and wooden quoins at the corners
Full deep cornice returns, not the clipped triangular 'pork chop' of later work
A big pedimented doorway with no fanlight
Roof visibly steeper than a Virginia or Charleston Georgian house of the same size

distinguished_from.difference: Five explicit differences, all measurable: cladding (wood versus Flemish-bond brick with glazed headers); chimney position (interior, inboard of the ridge, versus gable-end or exterior); roof pitch (9:12–11:12 versus 7:12–9:12, and gable versus hip); window head (flat wood architrave versus segmental or flat gauged brick arch); and plan depth (double-pile 32–38 ft with an attached service ell versus single-pile 18–22 ft with detached dependencies). Ceiling heights differ too — 8 ft 6 in – 9 ft 6 in against 10–12 ft.

The First Period house has one enormous central chimney, a 12:12-or-steeper roof, window heads jammed under the eave and no classical order. Many New England Georgian houses are First Period frames re-clad; read the chimney count and the passage, not the doorway.

Revival versions use muntins under 3/4 in or applied grilles, generic stock mouldings rather than a coherent order, shutters narrower than half the opening, a fanlight on a nominally 1750 house, and an attached garage. Trim identical on all four elevations is a revival tell; colonial houses spend on the front.

proportional_system.governing_logic: A pattern-book order — most often Doric or Ionic from Gibbs or Langley — supplies the doorway and cornice module; the five-bay facade is then divided arithmetically.
typical_ratios: Facade 42–52 ft wide, five bays; depth 32–38 ft double-pile
Window opening height:width 1.9:1 to 2.1:1; second-floor windows 82–88% of first-floor height
Pier between windows 0.7 to 1.0 times the window width
Ceilings 8 ft 6 in – 9 ft 6 in first floor, 8 ft 0 in – 8 ft 9 in second
Passage 10–13 ft wide; cornice 20–30 in overall height
Roof rise:run 9:12 to 11:12
Corner pilaster 10–16 in wide; corner board 6–10 in
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five bays, even and unaccented, the centre distinguished only by the doorway; on the largest houses a shallow pedimented centre pavilion projecting 12–24 in.

massing_affinities.note: The double-pile Georgian block, four rooms per floor about a central passage.
The more modest inland version.
Gambrel-roofed Georgian houses are frequent in Rhode Island and coastal Massachusetts.
Urban lots in Boston, Salem and Portsmouth.
The connected New England farmstead — big house, little house, back house, barn — grows off the Georgian block.

constraints.statement: Chimneys interior, paired, set 5–12 ft in from the gable end walls and flanking the ridge. Exterior gable-end chimneys are a Southern device and are climatically wrong here — they lose the stack's stored heat to the outside.
Roof pitch 9:12 to 11:12. Below 8:12 the house reads Chesapeake or Federal; above 12:12 it reads First Period.
Cornice returns 12–24 in deep across the gable, carrying the full cornice profile including modillions or dentils. A clipped triangular return is a twentieth-century economy and is forbidden.

exemplars.name: Isaac Royall House
exemplars.note: Built out from a late 17th-century Usher core in the 1730s and raised to three storeys in the 1740s. The west facade is rusticated to simulate ashlar; the east has aproned windows, a modillion cornice and wooden quoining. The surviving slave quarters make it the most historically important Georgian house in New England.

exemplars.name: Vassall-Craigie-Longfellow House
exemplars.note: Wood construction with a giant order of Ionic pilasters and a pedimented centre pavilion — the classical apparatus in pine at full scale.

exemplars.name: Jeremiah Lee Mansion
exemplars.note: Three storeys of rusticated wood scored to imitate stone, with a projecting pedimented pavilion and a two-storey stair hall; among the most ambitious wooden houses in colonial America.

exemplars.name: Lady Pepperrell House
exemplars.note: A restrained late-Georgian block with a giant order of pilasters and a pedimented doorway; the type at its most disciplined.

greek-revival-american.name: Greek Revival

revival_periods.note: The Columbian Exposition returns the colossal portico to American building, now at institutional and banking scale, in stone or terracotta over steel.
Greek Revival is quietly absorbed into the market category 'Colonial', producing the two-storey pedimented entry porch that is proportionally neither.

geography.hearth: Philadelphia, then upstate New York and the Western Reserve

lineage.note: THE canonical reference edge in this taxonomy. No American builder had any line of transmission from Athens: no craftsman, no apprenticeship, no continuous trade, not even a surviving Greek building any of them had seen. What crossed was measured drawings - Stuart and Revett's Antiquities of Athens (1762-1830) - reproduced at fourth hand in carpenters' handbooks. This is quotation of an ancestor the style never descended from, and modelling it as descent would be false.

The actual mechanism, and it is embarrassingly literal. Asher Benjamin published The Country Builder's Assistant (1797) and The American Builder's Companion (1806) as Federal manuals, then reissued the same enterprise as The Architect, or Practical House Carpenter (1830) with Grecian plates. Same author, same audience, same trade, same moulding planes - a new set of profiles. Minard Lafever's Modern Builder's Guide (1833) and Beauties of Modern Architecture (1835) completed the retooling. The transmission is the pattern book and the carpenter who owned it.

And it is a proportional revolt before it is an ornamental one. Federal had thinned American classicism until it was a membrane: 7/8-inch muntins, 4-inch cornices, columns at ten and eleven diameters, ornament glued on as composition castings. Greek Revival answers with mass - baseless Doric at six diameters, an entablature a quarter as deep as the column is tall, trim boards six to twelve inches wide. Adamesque delicacy came to look effete and, worse, English.

The professional channel, distinct from the carpenter channel. Benjamin Henry Latrobe trained in England inside the British Greek Revival and brought it to Philadelphia with the Bank of Pennsylvania (1798-1801); his pupils William Strickland and, through Strickland, Thomas U. Walter carried it into the American profession. Every high-style American Grecian building descends through this line rather than from the handbooks.

Explicit in the period literature: Greek is claimed as the purer, earlier, freer source and Roman as its imperial corruption. This is also a quiet argument against Jefferson, whose Roman republic is displaced by an older Greek one.

description.short: The first American national style: a Greek temple, known only from measured drawings and carpenters' handbooks, pressed into service as farmhouse, bank, courthouse and plantation seat across two-thirds of a continent between 1825 and 1860.
description.long:
Greek Revival is the node this taxonomy exists to model correctly, because it is the clearest case in the whole of American building where what a style claims and where it comes from are two entirely different things. What it claims is Athens. What it descends from is Asher Benjamin's pattern book, and the descent is documented down to the individual plate. Formally the style is a set of substitutions performed on the Federal house: the elliptical fanlight becomes a rectangular transom; the slender colonnette becomes a baseless Doric column six diameters tall; the four-inch cornice becomes an entablature a quarter as deep as the column is high; the wall's corner boards swell into pilasters; the attic storey is lit through small windows cut into the frieze itself; and the roof is often rotated so its gable faces the street as a pediment. The result is a building that has more in common with a Greek temple in its silhouette than in any other respect, since it is generally made of white-painted pine over a braced frame and heated by cast-iron stoves.

The distinction between reference and descent is the substance of the node, so state it plainly. No American builder in 1835 had a line of transmission from Greek practice. There was no craft continuity, no apprenticeship lineage, no surviving Greek building on the continent, and until well into the nineteenth century almost no American had seen one in person; Greece itself was under Ottoman rule and effectively closed. What crossed the Atlantic was paper: James Stuart and Nicholas Revett's Antiquities of Athens, published in volumes from 1762, measured on site and engraved - and then abridged, simplified and re-engraved in the handbooks that a rural carpenter could actually afford. The style therefore quotes an ancestor it never descended from. Its real ancestor is the one it was reacting against. Asher Benjamin, who taught two generations of New England housewrights how to build Federal, published The Architect, or Practical House Carpenter in 1830 with the Grecian orders in it, and the same men who had been running Adamesque beads went out and ran Doric mouldings the following season. Minard Lafever's Modern Builder's Guide (1833) and The Beauties of Modern Architecture (1835) did the same for New York and the whole territory its canal system opened. Parallel to the handbooks ran a professional line - Latrobe out of the English Greek Revival, then Strickland, then Walter - which produced the banks and the marble porticoes. Two channels, one style, and neither of them touches Greece.

The conditions that made it national were political, economic and technological at once, and they arrived together. Politically: the Greek War of Independence (1821-32) made Greece a live cause in American newspapers at the exact moment when a young republic wanted a founding image that was neither English nor royal, and the natural rhetorical move - we are the new Athens - could be built. Economically: the Erie Canal opened in 1825, the Western Reserve and the Old Northwest filled with New England and New York settlers, and the cotton boom capitalised the Lower South, so an enormous quantity of building happened in one generation with money and without inherited local traditions. Technologically: the water-powered sash and blind mill, cheap machine-cut nails, and after 1833 the balloon frame made it possible for a small crew to raise a broad flat-trimmed wooden building fast; wide trim in clear pine was cheap, and white lead paint over it read at a quarter mile as marble. This is the first American style to be genuinely continental, and it is also the first whose spread is explained better by transport infrastructure than by taste.

What is it like to stand before one. Weight is the first fact - the reverse of Federal in every dimension. The eave line no longer runs as a thin shadow but sits as a horizontal band a foot and a half deep, and everything under it feels held down. If there is a portico it goes the full height of the block, so the columns commit the whole building rather than decorating its door, and standing between them you are inside a room without walls, on a stone or wood platform raised three or four steps above the grade. The wall itself has almost no incident: broad flat pilasters at the corners, wide plain casings, and a door assembly that is a rectangle inside a rectangle, transom above and sidelights beside, all under a heavy flat entablature. In the frieze, if you look, there are small horizontal windows, and they are the tell that the attic is habitable - the most quietly ingenious detail in the whole American kit, since it lets a full storey exist without disturbing a pediment. Inside, the rooms are taller than Federal rooms and much plainer: heavy symmetrical architraves with corner blocks, deep plain baseboards, black marble mantels of two square posts and a slab. It is a serious, slightly humourless, extremely durable architecture, and the reason it looks like the default image of an American house is that for thirty-five years it very nearly was.

defining_characteristics: Full-height portico, pilastered antae, or a pedimented gable-front used as the governing facade gesture - column height equals the full height of the block it fronts
Greek orders only: baseless fluted Doric, Greek Ionic, or the Tower-of-the-Winds Corinthian; no Roman arches, no domes, no Composite
Deep entablature, one quarter to one fifth of column height, carried as a continuous horizontal band around the building
Low roof pitch (4:12 to 6:12) so that a gable reads as a pediment, with the cornice returning or running level across the gable base
Rectangular transom over the entrance with flanking sidelights within a pilastered surround; elliptical fanlights eliminated
Broad, flat, unmoulded trim: corner pilasters, wide window casings, plain frieze board - ornament by profile and mass, not by relief carving
Frieze-band attic windows where an upper half-storey is habitable
diagnostic_tells: Small horizontal windows set into the frieze board directly under the eave: no other American style does this, and it settles the identification instantly

Greek Revival versus Colonial Revival portico at fifty feet - Greek Revival columns run the full facade height and carry a deep entablature; the Colonial Revival entry porch is one storey against a two-storey wall and has a thin cornice
Doric columns without bases, sitting directly on the porch deck; a base under a Doric column means Roman, which means Jeffersonian or a later revival
Door transom rectangular, not elliptical - the single fastest Federal/Greek Revival discriminator on a plain house
The house turned gable-end to the road, so the pediment faces the traveller; a Federal or Georgian house of the same size faces the road broadside
Cornice returns clipped short on the gable ends of a vernacular example - the cheapest possible gesture toward a pediment, and everywhere in the Northeast

distinguished_from.difference: A proportional inversion before an ornamental one. Federal attenuates - columns at 10-11 diameters, cornices at 1/25 of facade height, muntins under 7/8 inch. Greek Revival thickens - columns at 6-7 diameters, entablature at 1/4 to 1/5 of column height, trim boards 6-12 inches wide. If the trim looks heavy and the transom is rectangular, it is Greek Revival even in the absence of a single column.

Both build porticoes, but the vocabularies are mutually exclusive. Jefferson's classicism is Roman: bases under the columns, arches, domes, semicircular windows. Greek Revival forbids all four. Jeffersonian buildings argue from measured Roman antiquity via Palladio; Greek Revival argues from Stuart and Revett and reaches ten thousand carpenters who never heard of either.

The 1893-1940 revival uses colossal orders on masses of a size no antebellum builder attempted, in stone or terracotta over steel frames, with plate glass and Roman as often as Greek detail. Scale and material give it away; so does the fact that its columns are usually round-tapered mill-made shafts rather than built-up staves.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Greek orders with the module equal to the lower column diameter, taken at second or third hand from Stuart and Revett through Benjamin and Lafever. Because the source is a handbook rather than a building, the proportions are executed accurately at the level of the order and freely at the level of the building - a temple front applied to a domestic plan that owes nothing to Greece.
typical_ratios: Greek Doric column 5.5-7 lower diameters tall (Parthenon Doric is 5.5; American handbook Doric commonly 6-7)
Greek Ionic 8.5-9.5 diameters; Tower-of-the-Winds Corinthian about 10
Entablature depth 1/4 to 1/5 of column height - the single most diagnostic ratio in the style
Entablature subdivision architrave : frieze : cornice approximately 3 : 3 : 2
Pediment height 1/4.5 to 1/5.5 of its span (roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12)
Trim board widths: corner pilasters 8-14 inches, window casing 4-6 inches, frieze board 10-20 inches
Column height equals full facade height of the block it fronts, without exception in canonical work
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even intercolumniation of 2.25-2.75 diameters across the portico, set by the order and then imposed on the wall behind; on gable-front vernacular houses the rhythm is a simple 2 or 3 bay front with a side-hall door in the end bay, and the asymmetry of that door is tolerated because the pediment supplies the symmetry.

massing_affinities.note: The definitive American solution: keep the temple block pure and put the bedrooms and kitchen in lower recessed flankers.
The style's largest demographic contribution - rotating the ordinary house ninety degrees so its gable becomes a pediment, at no extra cost.
The inherited Georgian-Federal box, re-trimmed.
The Upland South and Midwest workhorse under Grecian trim.
New York, Brooklyn and Philadelphia rows of the 1830s-40s: brownstone or brick fronts with heavy Grecian door enframements.

constraints.statement: Portico column height must equal the full height of the facade it fronts, measured from porch deck to the underside of the main entablature. A two-storey block with one-storey columns is not Greek Revival; it is Colonial Revival or a later hybrid. Columns must be 5.5-7 lower diameters for Doric, 8.5-9.5 for Ionic.

Entablature depth must be 1/4 to 1/5 of column height, subdivided architrave : frieze : cornice at approximately 3 : 3 : 2. A cornice thinner than 1/8 of column height reads as Federal or Colonial Revival regardless of the columns below it.

test.note: 1/4 to 1/5 of column height. The 3:3:2 architrave:frieze:cornice subdivision and the under-1/8-reads-as-Federal clause stay prose.

constraints.statement: Where an upper half-storey is habitable it must be lit by frieze-band windows set within the entablature, no taller than one third of the frieze depth and aligned with the bays below. Dormers on the principal roof slope are forbidden; a frieze window and a dormer must never appear on the same elevation.

test.note: Tests the 'dormers forbidden on the principal roof slope' clause. Frieze-band window height relative to frieze depth (max one third), bay alignment, and the frieze-window/dormer mutual exclusion on one elevation are left as prose -- no vocabulary variable expresses frieze depth or per-elevation window/dormer co-occurrence.

constraints.statement: Greek vocabulary is exclusive: no round-headed arches, no domes, no elliptical fanlights, no columns with bases under a Doric order, no Composite capitals. The entrance must be a rectangular opening with a rectangular transom, sidelights optional, inside a pilastered surround.

Main roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12 so that any gable reads as a pediment (height 1/4.5 to 1/5.5 of span). Where no full pediment is built, the cornice must return at least 12 inches onto the gable end. Pitches above 8:12 push the building toward Gothic Revival.

test.note: Tests the 4:12-6:12 roof-pitch range. The pediment-height ratio and the 12in cornice-return-length rule (for a house with no full pediment) have no matching vocabulary variables and stay prose.

exemplars.name: Andalusia
exemplars.note: Thomas Ustick Walter's Doric temple front added to a 1794 house built for John Craig, acquired by Nicholas Biddle c. 1814 and turned to face the Delaware. The manifesto building of the American Greek Revival, by the man who later built the U.S. Capitol dome.

exemplars.name: Rose Hill Mansion
exemplars.location: Geneva (town of Fayette), Seneca County, New York
exemplars.note: Hexastyle Ionic portico with fully pedimented gable and Ionic colonnades on the flanking single-storey wings; builders working directly from Lafever's plates. National Historic Landmark.

exemplars.name: Berry Hill
exemplars.note: Begun 1842; architect John Evans Johnson, builder Josiah Dabbs. Octastyle Doric portico with an entablature six and a half feet deep, correctly detailed with triglyphs, metopes and guttae, plus matching tetrastyle Doric dependencies.

exemplars.name: Oak Alley
exemplars.note: Begun 1837. A peripteral colonnade of 28 stuccoed brick Doric columns on all four sides - the Greek temple hybridised with the Creole gallery house, and structurally a shading device before it is a quotation.

sources: Talbot Hamlin, Greek Revival Architecture in America (1944)
Roger G. Kennedy, Greek Revival America (1989)
Asher Benjamin, The Architect, or Practical House Carpenter (1830)
Minard Lafever, The Beauties of Modern Architecture (1835)
James Stuart and Nicholas Revett, The Antiquities of Athens (1762-1830)

proportion_packs.note: The single most consequential choice in this batch. Benjamin's Doric of The Practical House Carpenter (Boston, 1830), Example No. 3, is encoded as a STANDALONE order with overlay_of deliberately null, not as a delta on Vignola -- Benjamin says so himself in his preface, quoted in the pack: the Doric is the one order where 'the Greek and Roman creeds' are irreconcilable, so treating it as a Vignola overlay 'would be fiction' (docs/open-questions.md item 11). This pack's column stands 14 semidiameter-modules, i.e. 7 diameters -- the upper end of the style's own stated 'Greek Doric column 5.5-7 lower diameters' -- and it is architecturally the right choice specifically because this is Greek Revival, not Federal: Benjamin's OTHER 1816 Roman Doric (9 diameters, in the American Builder's Companion) is a legitimate delta on Vignola but is explicitly not what built this style, per the pack's own authority note.

A DELIBERATE SUBSTITUTION, STATED PLAINLY. This corpus gives Benjamin's Doric standalone Greek-order treatment but not his Ionic or Corinthian -- his 1816 Ionic and Corinthian overlays are the Federal-era Roman orders and their own authority notes say outright that 'where a house is Greek Revival rather than Federal, this pack is the wrong one.' No Benjamin or dedicated Greek Ionic pack exists in this corpus, so plain Vignola is bound here as an honest general-reasoning stand-in rather than a fabricated Grecian citation: Vignola's Ionic column runs 9 diameters, which happens to fall inside the style's own stated Greek Ionic range of 8.5-9.5, so the proportions hold even though the source is Roman rather than Greek. Bound at all because the style names Greek Ionic as a legitimate alternate order alongside baseless Doric (defining_characteristics) and because greek-revival-southern-plantation's exemplars use it directly.

Bind the wall_section_greek_revival / casing_greek_revival family -- the cleanest, most direct fit in this whole batch. The pack's own comparison names the diagnostic: Greek Revival's baseboard runs 10 1/4 in in only two members (against Georgian's 6 7/8 in in three and Federal's 6 1/8 in in three) because 'the pedestal has been abandoned entirely,' which is exactly the heavier, plainer, corner-blocked interior the style file itself describes -- 'heavy symmetrical architraves with corner blocks, deep plain baseboards, black marble mantels of two square posts and a slab.'

Governs the entrance void beneath constraint c04's hard exclusion: rectangular transom only, no elliptical fanlight, sidelights optional, all inside a pilastered surround -- the single fastest Federal/Greek Revival discriminator the style names for itself. Ranked ahead of sash-light here, the reverse of the Federal ordering, because the diagnostic weight in this style sits on transom shape and frieze-window placement, not on muntin width.

Still governs the window module and muntin coordination, but it is demoted relative to opening-proportion because Greek Revival, unlike Federal, does not stake its identity on sash pattern -- the style file's own diagnostic_tells list frieze windows, transom shape and portico proportion, and never mentions muntin count.

Governs the full-height portico composition and the bay rhythm the portico sets for the wall behind it (intercolumniation 2.25-2.75 diameters, per the style's own proportional_system). On the gable-front vernacular form the pack's odd-bay-count logic gives way to the style's own tolerated asymmetric side-hall door, which the pediment is stated to resolve compositionally rather than by bay symmetry.

Bound, but its usual Georgian/Federal job -- diminishing upper-storey window height so the eye reads a hierarchy -- is largely absent here: Greek Revival unifies the whole facade height behind one continuous entablature rather than stepping it down, and the style's own typical_ratios give no diminution ratio at all (unlike federal-style's explicit 0.80-0.90 / 0.60-0.75). Bound chiefly for the ceiling-height figure, which this pack's own authority note names directly ('Greek Revival 10-12 ft'), and for the frieze-band attic storey, where a habitable half-storey is lit through the entablature rather than through a dormer (constraint c03).

Bound for rooms that are 'taller than Federal rooms and much plainer' but still formally proportioned by a pattern-book carpenter rather than accumulated by habit -- the style's own description language. Benjamin-corinthian and benjamin-tuscan were both considered for a third bound order (the style names a Tower-of-the-Winds Corinthian as a legitimate third Greek order) and deliberately not bound at this parent level, to keep the same primary/secondary discipline georgian-colonial-american uses; the Corinthian is promoted instead on greek-revival-southern-plantation, where the style text and the corpus's own applies_to cross-reference both name it explicitly.

jacobethan-revival.name: Jacobethan Revival

geography.hearth: the Northeast and Great Lakes industrial cities

lineage.note: The formal, masonry, symmetrical wing of the same import. Same offices and the same masonry-veneer technology; the difference is that this variant abandons half-timbering and the picturesque.
The prodigy houses - Hardwick, Longleat, Montacute - supply the mullioned and transomed window wall, the E- and H-plan, and the flat-arched entrance.
The shaped and curvilinear parapeted gable, strapwork, and the heavy classical porch grafted onto a Gothic body.
Perpendicular tracery, label mouldings and the four-centred arch, which the sixteenth-century originals had themselves inherited.
The academic apparatus - measured drawing, axial planning, a drafting room that could detail cut stone - that this variant depends on far more than picturesque Tudor Revival does.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The formal, symmetrical, masonry wing of the English revival, quoting Elizabethan and Jacobean prodigy houses: parapeted and curvilinear gables, mullioned and transomed window walls, strapwork, and an E- or H-plan.
description.long:
Jacobethan Revival is what American architects built when they wanted England without the cottage. The name, coined by John Betjeman for the historical hybrid it imitates, is exactly right: the source is the sixty-year band from about 1560 to 1620 when English building was structurally Gothic and ornamentally Renaissance, and neither system had won. The revival takes that ambiguity as its programme. A Jacobethan Revival building is masonry - limestone, or brick with stone dressings - with a broadly symmetrical E- or H-plan, gables that terminate in shaped curvilinear parapets or in straight parapets with copings, windows composed as continuous walls of glass in stone mullions and transoms, four-centred or flat-arched openings with label mouldings, and ornament in the strapwork register: interlaced flat bands, obelisks, and heraldic panels.

It arrives in America in the 1890s and takes hold most strongly in two places. The first is the estate market of the industrial Midwest and Northeast, where a generation of manufacturers wanted a house with an English name that did not look like a farmhouse. The second, and more consequential, is the campus. From roughly 1900, American universities adopted the Elizabethan-Jacobean and Perpendicular registers as their default - Princeton, Yale, Chicago, Duke, Washington University, hundreds of high schools - producing what is usually called Collegiate Gothic and which shares almost all of its detail with domestic Jacobethan Revival. The two markets shared masons, stone suppliers, and detail books.

The claim is scholarship married to institutional weight. Where picturesque Tudor Revival argues for the charm of the vernacular, Jacobethan argues for the authority of the great house - the entrance is on axis, the plan is legible, the ornament is heraldic rather than rustic, and the whole composition presumes a long gravel approach. It was bought by people who wanted to be seen as founders rather than as settlers, which is why it went so easily onto campuses that had themselves been founded by such people.

Standing before one, the surprise is the glass. A prodigy-house window wall is an enormous grid - eight, twelve, twenty lights across, divided by stone mullions two to four inches wide - and it produces a facade that is more transparent than any other historicist style attempts. The stone between the windows is reduced to piers; the gables above rise into shaped parapets against the sky; and on a grey afternoon the whole front reads as a dark lattice. The interiors are correspondingly bright and long, with linenfold panelling, a screens passage where the plan allows one, and plaster ceilings in strapwork patterns. It is a colder and more formal thing than Tudor Revival, and considerably more expensive.

defining_characteristics: Masonry construction - ashlar, or brick with stone dressings - with no half-timbering
Broadly symmetrical plan, most often E-shaped or H-shaped, with a centred entrance on axis
Parapeted gables, either straight with copings and finials or shaped in curvilinear Flemish-derived profiles
Mullioned and transomed windows composed as continuous glazed walls, with stone or cast-stone mullions
Four-centred (Tudor) arches and flat-headed openings with label mouldings or drip stones over them
Strapwork, heraldic panels, obelisk finials, and clustered chimney stacks as the ornamental register
diagnostic_tells: Parapeted gable - the wall carries up past the roof plane and is capped with coping stones. Tudor Revival gables end at the rake with a barge or a bargeboard.
Windows are mullioned bands rather than punched openings; the glass area on a principal elevation may exceed the stone.
No half-timbering anywhere. Its presence moves the building back to picturesque Tudor Revival.
The plan is symmetrical and the front door is on the centre line, which almost never happens in Tudor Revival.

Compared with a genuine Elizabethan prodigy house: the revival's mullions are cast stone rather than carved, its glass is plate rather than leaded quarries in wrought iron saddle bars, and it has corridors, which Hardwick does not.

distinguished_from.difference: The parent style is picturesque, asymmetrical, gabled with rakes rather than parapets, and depends on applied half-timbering and a massive chimney. Jacobethan Revival is symmetrical, all-masonry, parapeted, and depends on mullioned window walls and strapwork.

The original is a load-bearing stone building of 2-4 ft walls, with a hall-and-screens plan, no corridors, leaded quarry glazing in iron frames, and a long-gallery circulation. The revival is masonry-veneered or thin-walled ashlar with corridor planning, plate glass in cast-stone mullions, and central heating.

Chateauesque is French, has enormous steep hipped roofs with through-cornice dormers and turrets, and uses late Gothic crocketed ornament. Jacobethan is English, has parapeted gables and a lower roof largely hidden behind them, and uses flat strapwork.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The mullion grid. Proportion is set by the window bay - a repeating unit of light width plus mullion - which regulates the elevation horizontally, and by the gable parapet profile, which regulates it vertically. There is no classical order except at the entrance porch, where one is deliberately introduced as a quotation.
typical_ratios: Window light 18-24 in. wide, mullions 4-6 in., transoms at 1/2 and 3/4 of opening height
Glazed area on the principal elevation 35-55 percent - far higher than any other revival in this branch
Gable parapet rising 12-24 in. above the roof plane, with coping 6-9 in. thick
Shaped gable profile composed of 2-4 ogee or quadrant curves terminating in a semicircular or triangular cap
Chimney stacks clustered in groups of 2-4 shafts, each 18-24 in. square, rising 4-8 ft above the ridge
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Regular and grid-driven. Window bays repeat at a constant module across each range, and the projecting wings of the E or H repeat the same module, so that the whole elevation reads as one system - the opposite of Tudor Revival's deliberate irregularity.

massing_affinities.note: The prodigy-house parti - a centre range with projecting end wings, front and rear.
The E-plan with a recessed entrance court between projecting wings.
Late or eclectic examples that drift back toward the parent style.
Collegiate and institutional examples with a fully enclosed quadrangle.
A compact double-pile block cannot carry the plan-form that defines the variant.

constraints.statement: All gables on principal elevations must be parapeted: the wall carries a minimum 12 in. past the roof plane and is capped with coping not less than 6 in. thick. Raking eaves and bargeboards are forbidden in this variant.

test.note: Tests the minimum wall-past-roof-plane rise. Coping thickness (>=6in, no matching vocabulary variable) and the prohibition on raking eaves/bargeboards stay prose.

constraints.statement: Applied half-timbering is forbidden. The variant is defined by its absence; a single timbered panel returns the building to tudor-revival.

Principal windows must be mullioned and transomed in stone or cast stone, mullions 4-6 in. wide, lights 18-24 in. wide, with a minimum of three lights per opening on principal rooms. Single punched windows with wood casings void the variant.
Entrance on the centre line of the composition, within an ornamented porch or frontispiece not exceeding 1.5 bay widths, with a four-centred or flat arch under a label moulding.
Chimney stacks clustered in groups of two to four shafts, minimum 18 in. square each, rising not less than 4'0" above the adjacent ridge. Single plain stacks are permitted only on service ranges.

test.note: Shaft count per cluster (two to four) and individual shaft cross-section (18in square) have no matching vocabulary variable and stay prose.

exemplars.name: Salisbury House
exemplars.note: Built 1923-28 for Carl Weeks, modelled on the King's House at Salisbury, England. Tudor, Gothic and Carolean elements; incorporates salvaged English fabric.

exemplars.name: Cranbrook House
exemplars.note: Albert Kahn for George Booth. English Arts and Crafts inflected, and the beginning of the Cranbrook campus programme in the same register.

exemplars.name: Stan Hywet Hall
exemplars.note: Charles Sumner Schneider. Straddles this variant and picturesque Tudor Revival - its Haddon Hall long gallery and mullioned window walls belong here, its timbered ranges to the parent style.

exemplars.name: Agecroft Hall
exemplars.note: A genuine late-medieval and Tudor Lancashire house dismantled, shipped and reassembled with new work; the limit case for the variant's ambitions.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)
Mark Girouard, Robert Smythson and the Elizabethan Country House (1983)
Ralph Adams Cram, American Church Building of Today (1929), for the shared collegiate detail culture

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. This is the least asymmetrical node bound to facade-picturesque in the whole corpus - the style's own symmetry field reads 'near-symmetrical' and its bay_rhythm is 'Regular and grid-driven... the opposite of Tudor Revival's deliberate irregularity' - but it is bound here rather than to facade-classical because facade-classical's own applies_to does not extend to it, and because the governing_logic is explicitly not a bay-and-pier classical rhythm: 'Proportion is set by the window bay - a repeating unit of light width plus mullion - which regulates the elevation horizontally, and by the gable parapet profile, which regulates it vertically.' A mullion grid punctuated by parapeted gables is closer kin to facade-picturesque's datum-and-gable-treatment logic than to a pier-and-cornice classical front, even where the plan itself is symmetrical.

JUDGMENT BINDING for the entrance porch only, following the style's own proportional_system directly: 'There is no classical order except at the entrance porch, where one is deliberately introduced as a quotation.' The lineage record supplies the reasoning for which order: the jacobean ancestor edge (weight 1.0) describes 'the heavy classical porch grafted onto a Gothic body', and Doric is the sturdy, plain order this corpus consistently assigns to load-bearing and entrance-porch work elsewhere (see the Georgian template's Doric-for-the-everyday-order note). Not confirmed in vignola-doric's own applies_to for this node - a general typological choice, held at low precedence and marked optional because the style's own text frames it as a single deliberate quotation, not a governing order for the building.

north-german-hall-house.name: North German Hall House

revival_periods.note: Heimatschutz and Niedersachsenstil: the great gable and the Grootdor quoted on villas, schools and railway stations across northern Germany, with the hall itself replaced by a corridor.

geography.hearth: Lower Saxony, Westphalia and the Luneburg Heath

lineage.note: The hall house is built in Fachwerk and shares its jointing, its bay module and its infill practice entirely. The two are separable because one is a framing system and the other is a plan and section; they meet in almost every surviving example.

The Brabant and Drenthe hallehuis is the same building type across a modern border — the earliest dated frame of the type, at Best in North Brabant, is of 1262 — and the Low German and Low Countries farm traditions are one continuum rather than two.

description.short: A single vast three-aisled timber hall entered through a wagon door in the gable, in which people, cattle, harvest and hearth occupy one undivided smoke-filled volume.
description.long:
The Low German hall house is the most extreme integration of dwelling and farm in European building, and understanding it requires giving up the assumption that a house contains rooms. What it contains is a hall. Two rows of posts run the length of the building and divide it into three aisles: a wide central floor, the Diele, and two lower side aisles, the Kubbungen. The Diele is a threshing floor. The side aisles are cattle stalls and horse stalls, the animals standing with their heads turned inward so that they are fed, watered, milked and watched from the central floor. At the far end of the hall, at the point where the Diele stops, is the Flett — an open hearth on a raised clay pad with no chimney at all — and around and behind the Flett are the beds, built into the wall as cupboards, and the room where the family sat. There is no door and no partition between the farmer's bed and the cows. There was never meant to be.

That arrangement is not poverty; it is a heating and processing strategy of considerable sophistication. A dozen cattle produce several kilowatts of heat continuously through a north German winter, and the hall captures all of it. The open hearth is unchimneyed on purpose: smoke rises freely into the roof space, where it dries the grain stored on the loft over the Diele, cures the hams and sausages hung in the rafters, and impregnates the entire frame with creosote, which is why five-hundred-year-old hall-house frames are still sound and why the interiors are black. The great door in the gable, the Grootdor, is sized to admit a fully loaded harvest wagon so that the crop can be brought inside, driven the length of the hall, and threshed on the floor without ever being rained on. Everything the farm does happens under one roof between October and April.

The building is set out on bays — Fach — of about two and a half metres, fixed by the beams spanning between the aisle posts, and the house is a whole number of them. It grows by adding bays at the far end from the Grootdor, so a prosperous farm becomes very long: forty and even fifty metres by the eighteenth century, thirteen to fifteen wide, under a single reed-thatch roof at forty-five to fifty degrees whose eaves come down to about head height over the byre aisles. Only one elevation is ever composed — the gable containing the Grootdor, which carries the carved and inscribed lintel, the owner's and his wife's names, the date, a Bible verse, and often crossed horse-head finials at the ridge. The long flanks, forty metres of thatch and framed panel, are given nothing.

Standing inside is unlike standing in any other European domestic building. It is dark, and very tall, and the roof structure disappears into smoke above you. The floor underfoot is beaten clay. The air is warm and thick and smells of cattle, hay and woodsmoke. The bright rectangle of the open Grootdor at one end and the fire at the other define the axis of the entire building, and the family's life happens at the fire end, in the open, with the animals visible and audible thirty metres away down the hall. In the nineteenth century chimneys were inserted, partitions built, and the byre pushed out into separate buildings, and within two generations the type was gone — the reform improved the air and destroyed the architecture.

defining_characteristics: Three-aisled timber hall: two rows of posts defining a central working floor (Diele) between lower side aisles (Kubbungen)
Livestock stalled in the side aisles facing inward, unseparated from the living end of the same volume
Entry through a great wagon door (Grootdor) in the gable end, on the building's long axis
Open hearth (Flett) with no chimney; smoke rises into the roof to cure meat, dry grain and preserve the frame
House length a whole number of structural bays (Fach) of roughly 2.5 m, growing by addition at the hearth end
Reed thatch at 45-50 degrees, eaves carried down to about 1.5-2 m above grade over the byre aisles
One composed elevation only — the entrance gable, with a carved and inscribed lintel over the Grootdor
diagnostic_tells: An enormous door filling the lower half of a thatched gable, wide enough for a hay wagon
Crossed horse-head (Pferdekopfe) finials at the gable apex
A thatch eave you can touch, carried far below the internal ceiling height
A carved and dated lintel beam running the full width above the Grootdor, with the owners' names in Low German
Blackened, tar-hard timbers throughout the interior with no soot line — the whole frame was smoked, not just the hearth wall

distinguished_from.difference: Fachwerk describes how the wall is made. This node describes what the building is. A Hessian Fachwerk town house and a Luneburg hall house are the same carpentry serving completely different sections.

The New England connected farmstead links distinct buildings in a descending chain, each with its own roof and function. The hall house does not link anything: house, byre and barn are a single undivided volume under one ridge.
The Flemish langgevelhoeve is also a merged range, but is entered from the long side, is one aisle wide rather than three, and separates the dwelling from the byre with a real cross-wall.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Structural and agricultural. The bay (Fach) of about 2.5 m is set by the span of the transverse beams over the aisle posts; the width of the Diele is set by what a threshing team and a wagon need, about 4.5-6 m; the total width of 13-15 m is the Diele plus two byre aisles. Length is a variable and reads directly as the wealth of the farm.
typical_ratios: Bay (Fach) 2.2-2.8 m on centre
Diele width 4.5-6 m; total width 13-15 m; length 20-50 m
Aisle post height 3.5-4.5 m; eave height over the Kubbungen 1.5-2.0 m
Thatch pitch 45-50 degrees
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Absolutely regular internally — the post bays march the whole length of the building. Externally the rhythm is invisible on the flanks and irrelevant on the gable, where the Grootdor takes the whole centre.

massing_affinities.note: The limiting case of the connected farmstead: not a chain of linked buildings but a single merged volume. Included here to mark that the catalog skeleton covers both ends of that spectrum.
The interior is genuinely one cell, however large — this is the single-cell logic scaled to a farm.
The gable is the entrance and the only designed face.
Two equal rooms side by side under one roof is the antithesis of a three-aisled hall; the type cannot be produced this way.

constraints.statement: Bay (Fach) spacing 2.2-2.8 m on centre, fixed by the transverse beams over the aisle posts. Overall length must be a whole number of bays; growth is by adding a bay at the hearth end, never by stretching a bay.
The Diele must run unbroken from the Grootdor to the Flett. No cross wall, no stair and no partition may interrupt it; the type dies the moment one does.

Reed thatch at 45-50 degrees, carried over the byre aisles to an eave 1.5-2.0 m above grade. The low eave is structural, thermal and functional — it protects the framed wall, buries the byre in the roof, and cannot be raised without producing a different building.

test.note: Tests the low-eave-height clause, the constraint's own emphasis. The reed-thatch pitch range (45-50 degrees) stated in the same sentence stays prose.

constraints.statement: No masonry chimney in the original type. Introducing one, or a smoke hood, converts the building to the 19th-century reformed plan and requires the byre to be separated out.

test.note: Tests the no-masonry-chimney rule as chimney_count == 0. The smoke-hood alternative and the reformed-plan consequence are conditional prose, not part of the count test.

constraints.statement: Carving, lettering and finials belong exclusively to the entrance gable. Ornamenting the long flanks is not a stylistic error but a misreading of the type.

exemplars.name: Hall house at Best
exemplars.note: Frame dendro-dated to 1262; the earliest dated example of the type anywhere, still in use as a stable with the living end rebuilt c. 1640-1680.

exemplars.name: Dat ole Huus
exemplars.note: Museum-preserved Heath farmhouse, c. 1540; one of the least-altered surviving hall interiors with the Flett intact.

exemplars.name: Hof der Heidmark
exemplars.note: Dated hall house, now the core of an open-air museum farmstead.

exemplars.name: Museumsdorf Hosseringen
exemplars.note: Landwirtschaftsmuseum Luneburger Heide; relocated hall houses and farm buildings of the 17th-19th centuries with the bay structure legible.

sources: Schepers, Haus und Hof westfalischer Bauern
Bedal, Historische Hausforschung: Eine Einfuhrung
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World
Rudofsky, Architecture Without Architects

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to; the hall house is built in Fachwerk and its own lineage entry states the two share jointing and bay module entirely. The bay (Fach, ~2.5 m) fixing house length by whole-bay addition at the hearth end is the same generative logic the pack describes for growth by adding a bay rather than stretching one. Caveat, as with german-fachwerk: the pack's 16-20 ft default bay is calibrated to Anglo-American framing and is roughly double the hall house's own ~8 ft Fach; treat it as governing the building's growth-by-bay logic, not a literal transplanted dimension.

Applies only to the Flett end of the hall — the heated living space with its built-in beds — where the daylight- and hearth-reach logic this pack encodes is genuinely at work. The Diele (threshing floor) and Kubbungen (byre aisles) are not rooms in this pack's sense and are governed instead by this node's own agricultural-process constraints; the binding is deliberately scoped to the one part of the building the pack actually describes.

northern-european-vernacular.name: Northern European Vernacular

description.short: The continental traditions of timber frame, steep roof, and hard climate that arrived in America with Dutch, German, French, and Scandinavian settlers.
description.long:
Continental northern Europe produced building traditions shaped by long winters, abundant timber, and dense agricultural settlement rather than by treatise. Their logic is material and climatic before it is compositional: a roof pitched steeply enough to shed snow, a frame exposed and infilled because timber was the scarce and expensive part, a house and byre under one roof because a cow in the next room is a heat source.

These traditions reached North America through settlement rather than through books, which changes everything about how they behave. A pattern book transmits a style intact and abstract; a settler transmits what he can remember and build with the materials at hand. Dutch framing survives in the Hudson Valley as a gambrel roof and a particular way of hanging a door, German framing survives in Pennsylvania as a bank-set stone house with a forebay, and both lose their surface identity within two generations while keeping their structural habits.

For a design system this is instructive: the durable inheritance is rarely the ornament. It is the section, the roof pitch, the relationship to grade, and the position of the hearth.

defining_characteristics: Steep pitches and large roof volumes doing significant work in the section
Exposed structural framing as both economy and expression
House and agricultural function integrated rather than separated
Transmission by settlement and craft memory rather than by treatise
Strong grade relationships — banked, cellared, or raised — responding to slope and frost

tudor.name: Tudor

revival_periods.note: First as Jacobethan country-house pastiche, then as the dominant suburban idiom of the English-speaking world between the wars — the most successfully commercialised revival in history, and the least structurally honest.

geography.hearth: The court and its circle in the Thames valley and Home Counties, radiating from royal works at Hampton Court, Richmond and Nonsuch

lineage.note: Direct and unbroken. Tudor is late Perpendicular working for laymen instead of the Church: the same masons' lodges, the same four-centred arch, the same panel tracery, redirected by the dissolution of the monasteries after 1536 from abbey to country house.
Below the level of the great house, Tudor is a timber-framing style. The carpentry tradition supplies the roofs and the whole vocabulary of the smaller Tudor house.

Transmission is real but confined to ornament. Italian craftsmen worked physically in England — Torrigiano on Henry VII's tomb from 1512, Giovanni da Maiano's terracotta emperor roundels at Hampton Court in 1521 — but they brought motifs, not the system that generated them. No Tudor building is proportioned classically.

description.short: The last Gothic style in England and the first secular one: red brick, four-centred arches, gatehouse courtyards and extravagant chimney stacks, with Renaissance ornament stuck on like jewellery to a suit of armour.
description.long:
Tudor is the architecture of a new dynasty with a shaky claim, a nobility forbidden to build seriously fortified houses, and — after 1536 — an enormous transfer of monastic land into private hands. All three conditions show. The castle's apparatus survives as costume: battlements you cannot fight from, gatehouses that frame an approach rather than block one, moats crossed by permanent bridges. What replaces defence is display, and the display medium is brick, which in early Tudor England was still expensive and fashionable enough to be worth patterning with burnt headers into diaper lozenges across an entire elevation. The great chimney stacks — clustered octagonal or spiral shafts with moulded caps, standing far taller than any draught requires — are the period's signature, and they exist because a chimney in 1520 announced that your house had private heated chambers rather than one communal fire.

Structurally nothing has changed since 1450. The four-centred arch, the hood mould with carved label stops, the mullioned window with cusped lights, the arch-braced roof: this is Perpendicular practice. What is new is the plan's slow rotation toward symmetry. The medieval hall with its off-centre screens entry persists at the heart of the house, but the gatehouse range in front of it begins to be composed as a face — a centred arch, an oriel above it, flanking turrets — and once the front elevation is being composed as an image, the logic that will eventually destroy the hall has been admitted.
