Italian ornament arrives on that same front, brought by craftsmen imported through diplomatic channels, and sits on it as pure surface: a terracotta roundel of a Roman emperor set into a diapered brick wall over a Gothic arch, with no attempt to reconcile the three.

What Tudor was reacting against is best described as insecurity itself. Henry VII's building programme, and Wolsey's after it, were arguments for legitimacy made in brick. The dissolution then supplied both the sites and the material — thousands of tons of dressed stone from wrecked abbeys went straight into gentry houses, and the recycling is often visible in the masonry.

To stand in a Tudor courtyard is to be enclosed by warm, slightly irregular brick, dark with the burnt headers of the diaper pattern, under a skyline that is deliberately busy: crenellated parapets, gables, cupolas, and everywhere the chimneys, which give a Tudor roofscape its unmistakable vertical restlessness. The windows are wide and low, divided into many small leaded lights, and the glass is uneven enough to move as you move. Indoors, the great hall is still the largest room, still cold at the low end, still entered through the screens; but off the dais end there is now a warren of private chambers with linenfold panelling and small windows, and the future of the English house is in those rooms rather than in the hall.

defining_characteristics: The four-centred (Tudor) arch struck from four centres, used for doorways, fireplaces and window heads, and almost always set within a rectangular label mould with carved spandrels
Red brick as the fashionable material, laid in English bond and patterned with vitrified headers into diaper lozenges; stone dressings at openings, quoins and copings
Tall clustered chimney shafts — octagonal, spiral or moulded — standing well above the roofline as a deliberate compositional element
The gatehouse-and-courtyard plan, with the entrance range composed as a symmetrical face while the plan behind it remains medieval
Mullioned windows of many small leaded lights, wide rather than tall, with transoms in taller openings and hood moulds above
The great hall retained with dais, screens passage and open or moulded-beam roof, entered off-centre
Non-defensive military apparatus: crenellated parapets, corner turrets, gatehouse towers and moats used for effect
diagnostic_tells: Four-centred arch under a square label mould with carved or moulded spandrels — the single most reliable Tudor signature
Diaper patterning in dark burnt headers across a red brick field; the pattern is structural bond, not applied render, and can be read on the wall's raking sunlight
Chimney stacks with individually moulded and spiralled shafts rising from a shared moulded base — a chimney treated as sculpture
An oriel window directly over the entrance arch, corbelled out on moulded stone brackets, marking the great chamber inside
No classical order anywhere used structurally; where Renaissance ornament appears it is a roundel, a putto or a shell set into a Gothic surface

distinguished_from.difference: Tudor composes a gatehouse front and hides a medieval plan behind it; Elizabethan composes the whole house as a symmetrical block, uses classical orders on a frontispiece, glazes vastly more of the wall, and puts the hall on the entrance axis. If the facade has superimposed orders and more glass than wall, it is Elizabethan.

Same construction, different client and different programme. Gothic proper is ecclesiastical and manorial with no interest in the frontal composition; Tudor is secular, courtly, brick rather than stone in the lowlands, and beginning — only beginning — to think of the elevation as a picture.

The revival's half-timbering is applied to a stud or masonry wall rather than framed; its arches are cut from a single stone or moulded in cement instead of struck from four centres in voussoirs; its chimneys are veneer over a flue block. The revival also mixes Tudor with Jacobean and Cotswold sources freely, which no Tudor building does.

proportional_system.governing_logic: No governing system in the classical sense. Setting-out is by the geometry of the four-centred arch (two small radii at the springing, two long radii to the apex) and by the mullion light as a repeating unit; the rest is composed by eye against a symmetry axis established at the gatehouse.
typical_ratios: Four-centred arch rise to span roughly 1:3 to 1:4 — much flatter than any earlier Gothic arch
Mullion light width 400-500 mm, in leaded quarries of roughly 100 x 150 mm; window width is a whole number of lights
Window opening proportion horizontal overall, typically 1:1.5 to 1:3 width to height per light but 2:1 to 4:1 wide overall
Storey heights nearly equal; no graduated diminution, which is what most clearly separates Tudor from Georgian at a glance
Chimney shaft height above ridge 1.5 to 3 times the stack's own width
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and additive except across the composed entrance range, where a centred arch, flanking turrets and an oriel establish a local three-part symmetry that does not extend around the corner. Windows are placed where rooms need them.

massing_affinities.note: The E-plan and half-H are the standard gentry answer: hall range with projecting wings and a porch making the middle stroke of the E.
The great Tudor house is a courtyard house — a base court for service and an inner court for the family, as at Hampton Court.
The smaller timber-framed Tudor house after the hall is floored over and a lobby-entry stack inserted.
Jettied timber street ranges in Tudor towns, though brick Tudor rarely takes this form.

constraints.statement: Depressed arches must be true four-centred arches in voussoirs with the rise between 1:3 and 1:4 of the span. A flattened ellipse, a segmental arch, or a moulded one-piece head is forbidden.

test.note: 1:4 to 1:3 rise:span. The requirement that the arch be a true four-centred arch in voussoirs (not a flattened ellipse, segmental arch or moulded head) stays prose -- no arch-form-shape variable exists.

constraints.statement: Classical orders may not be used structurally. Renaissance ornament is permitted only as inset panels, roundels or cresting on an otherwise Gothic surface, and may not exceed roughly 5 percent of the elevation.

test.note: Tests the 5 percent coverage ceiling. Where classical ornament may appear (inset panels, roundels, cresting only, never structural) stays prose.

constraints.statement: Windows are divided by stone or oak mullions into lights of 400-500 mm with leaded glazing; no sash windows and no single-pane openings. Where a window exceeds about 1.4 m in height it takes a transom.
Chimney stacks must rise at least 1.5 times their own width above the ridge and be moulded or shafted. A flush or clipped stack destroys the roofscape on which the style depends.

test.note: Chimney rise expressed in inches over its own width, both in inches, to test the stated 1.5x ratio. 'Moulded or shafted' stays prose.

constraints.statement: Battlements, turrets and moats are permitted as display only where the composition is clearly non-defensive; arrow loops, machicolation and portcullis grooves are forbidden as false archaeology.

exemplars.name: Hampton Court Palace, Base Court and Clock Court
exemplars.note: Begun 1515 for Cardinal Wolsey and taken by Henry VIII in 1529; Great Hall 1532-35. Diapered brick, gatehouse ranges, Maiano's terracotta roundels of 1521, and the definitive Tudor chimneyscape.

exemplars.name: Layer Marney Tower
exemplars.note: Built c.1520-25 for Henry, first Lord Marney. An eight-storey brick gatehouse with terracotta cresting and window dressings — a gatehouse so far outgrowing its house that the house was never finished.

exemplars.name: Compton Wynyates
exemplars.note: Built for Sir William Compton in the early sixteenth century, incorporating salvaged material. The least regularised of the great Tudor houses: a courtyard plan of astonishing picturesque irregularity in warm pink brick.

exemplars.name: Sutton Place
exemplars.note: Built 1521-33 for Sir Richard Weston. An early courtyard house, later opened on one side, whose terracotta ornament and near-symmetrical entrance front mark the first serious English negotiation with Renaissance detail.

sources: Maurice Howard, The Early Tudor Country House: Architecture and Politics 1490-1550 (1987)
John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England (county volumes)
R. W. Brunskill, Brick Building in Britain (1990)

proportion_packs.note: tudor is named directly in timber-bay's applies_to, and the style's own lineage confirms why: it descends_from english-medieval-timber-frame at weight 0.6, and 'below the level of the great house, Tudor is a timber-framing style. The carpentry tradition supplies the roofs and the whole vocabulary of the smaller Tudor house.' No order pack is bound: c02 forbids classical orders being used structurally at all and caps applied Renaissance ornament at roughly 5 percent of the elevation as inset panels only, which is more restrictive than elizabethan and rules out even a cautious reference binding.

Judgment binding (not in applies_to). Scoped to the smaller, domestic-scale Tudor house — the hall-and-parlor type this style's own massing_affinities record as common 'after the hall is floored over and a lobby-entry stack inserted' — not to the courtyard great houses (Hampton Court, Compton Wynyates), whose halls and state rooms remain governed by the style's own figured ratios and lie well outside the pack's ordinary-room scale.

scandinavian-log-vernacular.name: Scandinavian Log Vernacular

revival_periods.note: Nordic National Romanticism and the dragestil — Norwegian and Swedish architects returning to laft construction and stave-church ornament for hotels, villas and pavilions.

Carl Larsson's Sundborn and the Swedish Falu-red-with-white-trim house become an international image of the Nordic home; the open-air museums (Skansen 1891, Norsk Folkemuseum 1894) institutionalise the type.
A continuous living trade: laft is still taught, licensed and built in Norway and Sweden, and hytte construction keeps the craft economically viable.

geography.hearth: Telemark, Numedal, Dalarna and Savo

description.short: The corner-notched horizontal log building of the Nordic forests, in which every dimension is set by the length of a trunk and the farm is a cluster of small single-purpose buildings rather than a single house.
description.long:
Nordic log building is the most complete example in Europe of an architecture generated by one material and one joint. The material is straight-grained slow-grown pine or spruce, effectively unlimited in the Scandinavian forest belt and available in lengths of six to nine metres. The joint is the corner notch — the laft or knut — cut so that each log locks the two it crosses, in a family of profiles (findal, dovetail, round, square) that are regional signatures as reliable as an accent. Everything else follows. A wall cannot be longer than a log, so the room is six to nine metres at most; a wall cannot be built without corners to lock it, so a long building needs cross-walls at intervals; and a green log wall shrinks across the grain, settling three to five per cent of its height over the first years, so every opening needs a settlement gap and the whole building is designed to move. Because a room cannot be made bigger, the tradition grows by multiplying rooms and buildings instead. This is the single sharpest difference between the Nordic farm and its German or Flemish equivalents at the same latitude. A Norwegian tun or a Swedish gard is not a house; it is a yard with eight, twelve or twenty separate log buildings around it, each doing one job: the stue for living, the loft or stabbur for storage and for the family's textiles and grain, raised on staddle-stones or posts against rats and damp and given the finest carving on the farm; the eldhus for baking and brewing, kept separate because it burns; the fjos for cattle, the stall for horses, the smie for the smith, the badstue for the sauna. Fire is one reason for the dispersal and the log-length constraint is the other, but the deepest reason is that the farm is a set of processes and a log building is cheap and quick to put up, so each process gets its own.

The interior evolution is a story about smoke. The earliest surviving type, the arestue, has an open hearth in the middle of the floor and a smoke hole (ljore) in the roof — the room is high, the smoke sits in a layer above head height, the meat hangs in it, and there is no chimney at all. From the fourteenth century in Sweden and the sixteenth in Norway the corner fireplace with a hood (peis) and a stone flue arrives, and the ceiling can come down; the room gets lower, warmer, cleaner, and darker, and the loft above it becomes usable. The plan formalises as the parstuga — two rooms flanking a central entry passage, one of them the everyday room and the other the finer, colder festroom — which is the type Sweden exported to America. Painting is late: Falu red, the iron-oxide by-product of the Falun copper mine, becomes cheap in the seventeenth century and standard on farm buildings by the eighteenth, with white lead trim at the windows, and that combination is now more strongly identified with Scandinavia than any structural feature.

This is also the direct ancestor of American log building, and the transmission is specific and documented. New Sweden, founded on the Delaware in 1638, was settled substantially by Finns from Savo-Karelia — forest colonists who had been moved into central Sweden and then shipped on — bringing corner-notched log construction to a continent where the English had none. The colony was small and short-lived, but the technique was picked up by Germans and by Scots-Irish moving down the Great Valley, and it became the substrate of Appalachian and Upland South building for the next two centuries. Terry Jordan and Matti Kaups made the strongest version of this argument in The American Backwoods Frontier in 1989; it has been contested, particularly on how much the German Palatine contribution has been understated, and the honest position is that Fenno-Scandian log craft is one of two or three converging sources rather than the sole one. The claim is recorded here because the Delaware transmission is the reason this node has American descendants at all.

To stand inside a Norwegian stue is to be in a small, wooden, extremely tight box. The logs are scrubbed pale and left bare; the ceiling is low enough to touch; the floor is wide pine boards; the corner fireplace is stone and takes up a fifth of the room. Light comes through two or three small windows and, on a February afternoon at sixty degrees north, there is not much of it. The building creaks and settles audibly in the cold. And thirty metres away across the snow, on posts, stands the loft — the best-built, best-carved, least-lived-in building on the property, holding the family's grain and its clothes.

defining_characteristics: Horizontally stacked, corner-notched log walls (laft, knuttimring), structurally self-sufficient with no frame
Every plan dimension bounded by log length — 6 to 9 m maximum wall without an intersecting cross-wall
The farm as a cluster of many small single-purpose buildings around a yard, not a single consolidated house
The raised storehouse (stabbur, loft) on posts or staddle-stones, given the farm's best carving and craftsmanship
Settlement detailing throughout: gaps above openings, sliding jambs, and no rigid element locked through the wall
Sill logs carried on stone pads well clear of grade, the bottom course treated as sacrificial
Sod (torvtak) or split-shingle roof on birch bark, at a pitch matched to the covering
Falu red with white trim from the 18th century onward, applied to the whole cluster or none of it
diagnostic_tells: Log ends projecting past the corner, notched and visible — the notch profile identifies the valley
A small storehouse standing on stone or timber posts with a projecting upper storey and carved gable boards
Turf growing on the roof, with a birch-bark layer visible at the eave and a log or board holding the sod at the edge
Doors and windows with a visible slip joint above the head
A farmyard with eight or more separate small buildings and no single large one

distinguished_from.difference: Same construction system, opposite settlement strategy. The chalet consolidates house, byre and hay into one tall building on a slope with a huge overhang and a gallery; the Nordic farm disperses into many small buildings around a flat yard with modest overhangs and no gallery. The chalet leaves timber bare; the Nordic farm paints it red.

The American descendant keeps the notch and the log-length constraint and loses almost everything else: the building cluster collapses to one or two pens, the sod roof becomes riven shakes, the loft disappears, and daubed chinking between widely-spaced logs replaces the tight-fitted scribed Nordic wall. The chinked wall is the diagnostic of the American branch.

Both are timber and both merge functions, but the hall house is a framed three-aisled volume containing everything, whereas the Nordic farm is solid-walled and refuses to contain anything more than one function per building.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The log, absolutely. Wall length is what a straight sound trunk gives — 6 to 9 m — and this alone fixes the plan of every building on the farm. Course height of 150-250 mm is the vertical module and every opening lands on it. Nothing about the proportion of a Nordic log building is chosen; it is the residue of what a tree is.
typical_ratios: Maximum wall length 6-9 m; room plan typically 4-7 m x 5-8 m
Log course height 150-250 mm; settlement allowance 3-5 percent of wall height
Sod roof pitch 22-30 degrees; shingle roof 35-45
Sill log 300 mm minimum clear of grade on stone pads
Loft/stabbur upper storey oversailing the lower by 300-600 mm
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: There is no bay rhythm. Openings are cut where the room needs them, few and small, and the wall reads as continuous horizontal coursing interrupted rather than as a rhythm of bays.

massing_affinities.note: The log pen — one room, one hearth, one door — is the type specimen and the unit everything else is assembled from.
The Swedish parstuga puts two rooms of equal size either side of a central entry passage; two pens under one roof, and the direct ancestor of the American double pen.
In the western Norwegian fjord farms buildings do connect end to end, though the cluster remains the norm.
The stabbur and the loft present a carved gable as their designed face.
Two pens with an open passage between them under a shared roof is a configuration the Nordic tradition also reaches, and is the plausible European precedent for the American type.

constraints.statement: No log wall may exceed about 9 m without an intersecting cross-wall to lock its corners. The building grows by adding pens, storeys or separate buildings; a wall cannot simply be made longer.

test.note: 9 m converted to 29.5 ft ('about 9 m' in the source -- an approximate stated ceiling, not an invented one).

constraints.statement: A settlement allowance of 3-5 percent of wall height is required above every door and window head, and no rigid element — post, chimney, stair stringer — may be fixed through the log wall without a slip joint. This is the single commonest failure in modern reproductions.

The sill log must sit on stone pads or a dry-laid stone footing at least 300 mm clear of grade, and is treated as a sacrificial course to be replaced. A log wall bearing directly on soil or on a continuous impermeable slab will fail from the bottom.

test.note: Tests the 300mm clearance above grade. That the sill sits on stone pads/footing specifically (rather than any raised base) and is treated as sacrificial are left as prose.

constraints.statement: Sod roofs require a pitch of 22-30 degrees over birch bark, with an edge log or board to retain the turf; below 22 degrees the roof stays saturated and above 30 the turf creeps. Split-shingle roofs go to 35-45 degrees.
Paint is post-1700 and belongs to the whole farm cluster or to none of it. A red-painted main house among unpainted outbuildings is a modern arrangement, not a traditional one.

exemplars.name: Raulandsstua
exemplars.note: From Sore Rauland, Numedal; c. 1240 and possibly the oldest surviving wooden dwelling in the world. An arestue with an open central hearth and a smoke hole, in the corner-notch profile named raulandslaft after it.

exemplars.name: Setesdal loft (Aamlid loft)
exemplars.note: 14th-17th century; a two-storey raised storehouse with an oversailing upper floor and carved gallery — the most elaborately built structure on a Norwegian farm.

exemplars.name: Alvrosgarden
exemplars.note: Relocated from Harjedalen; buildings of the 14th-18th centuries preserved as an intact farm cluster, showing the dispersal principle rather than a single house.

exemplars.name: C. A. Nothnagle Log House
exemplars.note: Traditionally dated c. 1638-1643 and associated with Finnish settlers of New Sweden; the dating is genuinely contested and later dates have been proposed. Cited as the evidence for the Delaware transmission, not as a securely dated building.

sources: Jordan & Kaups, The American Backwoods Frontier: An Ethnic and Ecological Interpretation (1989)
Berg, Norske tommerhus fra mellomalderen
Erixon, Svensk byggnadskultur
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to, and its own sources cite Scandinavian log building directly. The pack's 12-18 ft two-man handling band is exactly the constraint this node's own text gives as the reason no log wall exceeds 6-9 m, and the pack's wing_strategy rule — a household that needs more room builds another pen, never lengthens one — is precisely the mechanism this node describes for why a Norwegian tun disperses into many small single-purpose buildings rather than growing as one house.

Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to. The arestue/parstuga interior — small, low, lit from two or three small windows, warmed by one hearth or corner fireplace serving a bounded floor area — matches this pack's span/hearth/daylight-limited room model closely; log-module's own ceiling_height_rule and window_grouping_rule are this pack's wall-construction complement.

hudson-valley-dutch.name: Hudson Valley Dutch

revival_periods.note: The revival largely bypassed the steep-gabled stone house in favour of the New Jersey gambrel; the Hudson type survives more in preservation than in imitation.

regions: Albany and Rensselaer counties, New York
Greene and Columbia counties, New York
Dutchess and Orange counties, New York
geography.hearth: the limestone belt of Ulster County — Kingston, Hurley, New Paltz — and the Beverwijck (Albany) region upriver

lineage.note: The town houses of Kingston and Albany reproduce the Netherlandish parapeted street gable with vlechtingen brick tumbling and iron beam anchors almost without modification.

description.short: The one-and-a-half-storey stone house of the mid and upper Hudson: two to two-and-a-half feet of coursed limestone, a steep unbroken gable, gable-end hearths, and a plate you can touch.
description.long:
The Hudson Valley Dutch house is what happens when a timber-framing culture meets a valley full of workable stone. In Holland the H-bent frame with its wedged anchor beams was the whole structure and brick or plank merely infilled it; in Ulster County the settlers found bedded limestone that split into courses with almost no dressing, and within a generation the frame retreated indoors while the wall became the structure. What survives from the frame is the room — a bent-spacing rhythm of eighteen to twenty-two feet — and the anchor beams themselves, which continue to be built into stone houses purely as floor framing, their through-tenons still projecting past the posts because that is how a Dutch carpenter made a beam land.

The hearth is the other survival, and it is the one that surprises people. The jambless fireplace has no cheeks: the fire burns on a raised hearth against a flat plastered wall, and a hood of plaster on lath or of timber, sometimes trimmed with a valance of chintz or leather, hangs above it on iron rods. There is no chimney breast projecting into the room. It draws badly by English standards and radiates superbly, and it makes the fire an object in the room rather than a recess in it. Jean Hasbrouck's house at New Paltz retains the only original eighteenth-century example on Huguenot Street, and standing before it explains more about Dutch domestic life than any inventory.

The exterior logic is austere and rational. The wall is twenty to thirty inches thick, laid in wide beds of shell-lime mortar, dressed and coursed on the entrance elevation and left as rubble on the other three — a house with one good face, which tells you exactly how much of the building was for looking at. The plate sits seven to nine feet above the floor, so the roof, forty-five to fifty-five degrees and unbroken, is most of the elevation. Chimneys are at or inside the gable ends. Windows are small, casement and leaded in the seventeenth century, replaced by nine-over-nine sash in the eighteenth, and set with iron shutter pintles still visible in the stone. After about 1700 the eave begins to spring: the lower rafters run past the wall face on a shallow concave curve, throwing water eighteen to twenty-four inches clear of the masonry.

In the towns the same culture builds in brick with the gable to the street, stepped or spouted, its raking edge finished with mouse-tooth tumbling, and studded with wrought-iron beam anchors that sometimes spell out a date. Nothing about that elevation is American; it is Amsterdam, moved. To stand inside one of the rural houses is to be in a single low room lit from two sides, with the anchor beams overhead at seven and a half feet, a flat wall at one end where the fire is, and two feet of stone between you and a Hudson Valley January.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing coursed limestone or sandstone walls 20–30 in thick, dressed on the entrance elevation and rubble elsewhere
Steep unbroken side-gable roof at 45–55 degrees, springing from a plate 7–9 ft above the floor
Chimneys at or within the gable end walls, serving jambless fireplaces with suspended hoods
Exposed transverse anchor beams with projecting wedged through-tenons carrying the upper floor
Dutch doors divided horizontally, with the upper leaf glazed on later work
Wrought-iron beam anchors visible on the masonry gable, sometimes forming a date
A flared or 'spring' eave projecting 18–24 in on a concave sweep, on work after c. 1700
diagnostic_tells: A flat, unbroken chimney wall in the principal room with no projecting breast — the jambless fireplace, or its ghost
Coursed ashlar on one elevation, rubble on the other three
Anchor-beam tenons projecting through the posts, visible from below
Iron anchors and date irons on the gable masonry
Roof volume exceeding wall volume in the elevation, with second-floor windows either absent or set in the gable only

distinguished_from.difference: The Jersey branch uses a gambrel roof, red-brown Newark sandstone, and a pronounced concave spring eave that becomes a porch. The Hudson branch uses a steep straight gable, grey limestone, and a spring eave that is a water-shedding device rather than a shelter.

The revival is a gambrel house with a full-width shed dormer, a wood frame, symmetrical fenestration and a straight overhanging eave. The Hudson Dutch house has none of those things — no gambrel in its earliest and best work, no dormers, no symmetry obligation, and a stone wall thick enough to sit in the window reveal.

Both are thick-walled steep-roofed stone traditions. The German house has a central chimney serving a closed jamb stove and an asymmetric three-room plan; the Dutch house has gable-end hearths, open jambless fires and a one- or two-room plan.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The H-bent span carried over into masonry: rooms one bent deep, the house lengthened by adding bents along the ridge.
typical_ratios: Room depth 18–22 ft; overall 30–46 ft long × 20–24 ft deep
Wall thickness 20–30 in; wall height to plate 7–9 ft, giving 1:4 to 1:5 thickness to height
Roof rise:run 12:12 to 17:12 (45–55 degrees)
Spring eave projection 18–24 in with a sweep radius of 5–9 ft
Window opening 2 ft 6 in – 3 ft 2 in × 4 ft 0 in – 5 ft 0 in, glazed area under 10% of wall area
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Additive and unequal — two, three or five openings across the eave front, with the door placed by the plan rather than by the composition until Georgian symmetry arrives after 1750.

massing_affinities.note: Two rooms with gable hearths, no passage.
The one-bent house, expanded by adding bents.
Late eighteenth-century Hudson work adopts the gambrel from the south.
Post-1750 Anglicization behind an unchanged section.
The Kingston and Albany urban gable-to-street house.

constraints.statement: Wall not less than 20 in of coursed load-bearing stone; window and door reveals must express the full wall depth. Stone veneer over frame produces a different building and reads as such at every opening.
Wall plate 7 ft 0 in to 9 ft 0 in above the finished floor, and roof pitch 12:12 to 17:12. If the plate rises or the pitch drops, the roof stops dominating and the type dissolves.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch clause. Wall plate height (7-9ft) is the same statement's other numeric claim, already tested on the parent dutch-colonial-american node, and stays prose here.

constraints.statement: Chimneys at or within the gable end walls. A central stack is a New England device and is incompatible with the open one- or two-room Dutch plan.
Spring eave, where used, projects 18–24 in on a concave sweep, not as a straight overhang, and only on work of c. 1700 or later. Below 12 in it does no work; a straight soffit is not a spring eave.

Openings: leaded casement with iron pintles to c. 1720; nine-over-nine or nine-over-six sash thereafter. Total glazed area under 10% of wall area. Dormers, where present at all, are small individual gabled ones, never continuous.

test.note: Tests the glazed-area clause. The sash/casement-by-date clause is date-conditional (OQ 22, no date-conditional resolution exists yet) and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Pieter Bronck House
exemplars.note: Thick stone walls, steep straight gable, single open chambers on two floors — the type before the gambrel and before Anglicization.

exemplars.name: Jean Hasbrouck House
exemplars.location: Historic Huguenot Street, New Paltz, New York
exemplars.note: National Historic Landmark. Retains the only original 18th-century jambless fireplace on Huguenot Street; built by Huguenots in wholly Dutch technique.

exemplars.name: Abraham Hasbrouck House
exemplars.location: Historic Huguenot Street, New Paltz, New York
exemplars.note: Multi-phase stone house whose successive campaigns are legible in the masonry — a good demonstration of additive bent-by-bent growth.

exemplars.name: Dyckman Farmhouse
exemplars.note: Late example: fieldstone lower storey, frame above, gambrel roof with a sprung eave carried on posts as a porch — the moment the eave becomes a porch.

sources: Helen Wilkinson Reynolds, Dutch Houses in the Hudson Valley before 1776 (1929)
Roderic H. Blackburn and Ruth Piwonka, Remembrance of Patria: Dutch Arts and Culture in Colonial America (1988)
Rosalie Fellows Bailey, Pre-Revolutionary Dutch Houses and Families in Northern New Jersey and Southern New York (1936)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: The bent-spacing rhythm is explicitly what survives the shift from frame to masonry, per the style's own long description: 'What survives from the frame is the room — a bent-spacing rhythm of eighteen to twenty-two feet — and the anchor beams themselves, which continue to be built into stone houses purely as floor framing.' hudson-valley-dutch is named directly in timber-bay's own applies_to. The historic 18-22 ft room sits close enough to the pack's documented 16-20 ft English depth_and_pile band to use its rule directly, even though the framing culture it derives from (English box framing) is not the one that produced this variant's anchor-beam bents.

This is the stone-house variant proper — 20-30 in coursed limestone or sandstone, dressed and coursed on the entrance elevation, rubble on the other three — exactly the front/flank grading brick-course's own conflicts section describes for Westover and Carter's Grove. Bound at higher weight than the parent style's own binding because masonry is this variant's near-universal walling, not merely common. Where the openings are not dressed, read the pack's window_head_masonry rules as an upper bound on regularity rather than a description of what was built. hudson-valley-dutch is named directly in the pack's own applies_to.

hudson-valley-dutch is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. The hall-and-parlor plan with gable hearths and no passage is the pack's own paradigm case of a room sized by span, hearth reach and daylight rather than by ratio.

The style's own text gives the dated sequence directly — leaded casement to c. 1720, nine-over-nine or nine-over-six thereafter — which is exactly sash-light's light-count-from-glass-supply logic, and dates the surviving sash independently of the house. Bound for the light-count and muntin arithmetic only: this variant's own typical_ratios give window openings of roughly 1.4-1.7:1, well under sash-light's 1.85-2.6 measured Anglo-American band, and that divergence should be read as a real difference in vernacular Hudson Valley window shape rather than corrected toward the pack's figure.

This variant's own text places Georgian symmetry later and more reluctantly than its Jersey sibling: post-1750 Anglicization is listed only as 'possible' in the massing affinities, and the variant's own proportional_system still calls its bay rhythm 'additive and unequal... until Georgian symmetry arrives after 1750.' Bound optional and at low precedence for that late minority of Anglicized Hudson Valley houses only.

queen-anne-patterned-masonry.name: Queen Anne, Patterned Masonry

geography.hearth: The Atlantic seaboard cities, where brick was the ordinary urban material

lineage.note: The masonry expression of the parent, a small minority of the American population by McAlester's count but the one closest to the British original.

Closer to the source than any other American subtype. Shaw and Nesfield built in brick with rubbed and moulded work and terra cotta sunflower panels, and this is the American branch that actually kept the material.
Shares the urban masonry trades and the taste for rock-faced stone bases and heavy arches, but keeps the Queen Anne's articulated wall rather than adopting Richardsonian mass.

description.short: The urban masonry Queen Anne, in which the multi-texture rule of the parent style is satisfied by brick of contrasting colours, moulded and rubbed brickwork, terra cotta panels, and stone trim rather than by clapboard and cut shingle.
description.long:
This is the smallest of the American Queen Anne subtypes and the closest to the English original, which is a useful reminder that the American mainstream is the deviation and not the norm. Richard Norman Shaw's houses were brick, with rubbed and gauged work, moulded string courses, and panels of terra cotta ornament, and the small number of American architects and builders who worked in that material rather than in balloon-framed pine produced the most literally Shavian buildings in the country. They cluster where brick was the ordinary urban material and where a large body of skilled masons existed: Baltimore, Philadelphia, Boston, and the Great Lakes cities.

The technological substrate is different from the rest of this branch and it is worth stating exactly. The mechanised brickmaking of the 1870s and 1880s, stiff-mud extrusion and dry-press machines, produced brick in consistent sizes, hard bright colours, and, decisively, in moulded shapes: rope courses, bullnose returns, cove and ovolo profiles, and complete ornamental panels, all orderable from a catalogue. Architectural terra cotta from firms in Chicago, Boston, and Perth Amboy supplied sunflower, foliate, and panel ornament by the piece. The result is that the same decoupling of ornament from construction that produced the spindled porch also produced the moulded brick frieze; the material changed and the economic logic did not.

The subtype satisfies the parent style's hard rule, that a principal elevation must carry at least two distinct wall textures changing at a horizontal line, by material rather than by cladding. A typical elevation runs rock-faced brownstone or granite at the base, dark red pressed brick through the main storeys, a moulded brick or terra cotta frieze at the top, and cut shingle or half-timbering only in the gable if at all. Because masonry cannot be sawn on site, every ornamental decision has to be made at the order stage, which enforces a discipline the wooden subtypes never had, and the buildings are correspondingly tighter.

What it feels like is heavier and more urban than the rest of the style. The wall has actual thickness, the window reveals are deep enough to shadow, the ornament is integral to the material and will still be there in a century, and the colour is in the clay rather than in the paint. The chimney becomes the compositional star, corbelled, panelled, and carried high, because in a brick house the chimney is the one element where the mason can show what he can do. Where the wooden Queen Anne is a light box wrapped in decorated boards, this is a solid thing with the decoration cut into and built out of its own substance, and it ages in the opposite direction: the wooden version needs paint and the brick version needs nothing.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing or substantially masonry wall construction in pressed or moulded brick
Two or more masonry colours or materials on each principal elevation, with the change occurring at a horizontal course, belt, or storey line
Moulded, rubbed, or gauged brick and terra cotta panels used as the ornamental vocabulary in place of sawn and turned woodwork
The parent style's dominant mass, irregular massing, projecting bays or oriels, and non-rectangular ridge
Corbelled and panelled chimney stacks treated as major compositional elements
Segmental or flat brick arches with rubbed voussoirs over openings, and stone or terra cotta sills and lintels
Deep window reveals expressing the thickness of the wall
diagnostic_tells: Terra cotta or moulded brick panels set into a brick field, often with sunflower, foliate, or geometric motifs: the clearest single tell
Two brick colours in a designed relationship rather than in a repair patch, with the change on a horizontal line
Corbelled chimney caps projecting several inches and stacks carried high above the ridge
Compared with Richardsonian Romanesque: the wall is articulated into zones with belt courses and the arches are segmental or flat rather than full semicircles, and there is far more opening area
Compared with the wooden subtypes: there is no porch spindlework, and the porch, if any, is small and masonry-piered

distinguished_from.difference: Both are urban masonry of the same decade and the boundary is real. Richardsonian uses one material top to bottom, semicircular arches, few openings, and reads as mass; patterned masonry Queen Anne changes material at horizontal lines, uses segmental and flat arches, has a high opening ratio, and reads as an articulated wall.

The same style in the opposite material culture. Everything the wooden subtype achieves with lathe and jigsaw this subtype achieves with mould and kiln, and the constraints run differently as a result: masonry ornament must be specified before construction and cannot be improvised on site.

The closest American relative to the British parent, but still American in massing: bigger, more irregular, with a taller corner tower and a more emphatic dominant mass than Shaw's tighter, more Jacobean compositions.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by the parent's mass hierarchy and by the brick course. Because the module is a brick dimension, every belt, panel, and arch is set out in whole courses, which gives this subtype a dimensional discipline the wooden ones lack.
typical_ratios: Brick course height 2.5 to 3 in; all belts, panels, and arch rises set out in whole courses
Ornamental panel field not more than 25 percent of any elevation
Window reveal depth 4 to 9 in
Chimney stack rising 4 to 8 ft above the adjacent ridge, with a corbelled cap projecting 3 to 6 in
Opening area 35 to 50 percent of a principal elevation, notably higher than Richardsonian Romanesque
Dominant mass at least 1.5 times any subordinate mass, per the parent style
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular by room, as in the parent, but tightened by the coursing: heads and sills align across an elevation even where widths do not, because the mason set them out from the same course.

massing_affinities.note: The urban masonry Queen Anne row of Baltimore, Philadelphia, and Boston.
Round or polygonal brick tower with a conical slate cap.

constraints.statement: Not fewer than two masonry materials or brick colours shall appear on each principal elevation, with every change occurring on a horizontal course line. A vertical or diagonal material change is prohibited.

All ornament shall be moulded, rubbed, gauged, carved, or cast in the wall material itself. Applied sawn or turned wooden ornament is prohibited on masonry elevations; a spindled porch places the building in the spindlework subtype.

Chimney stacks shall rise 4 to 8 ft above the adjacent ridge and shall carry a corbelled or panelled cap projecting 3 to 6 in. In this subtype the chimney is a primary compositional element and may not be suppressed.

test.note: Tests the chimney-height-above-ridge range. The cap's corbelled/panelled form and its 3-6 in projection have no matching vocabulary variable (no chimney-cap-projection concept) and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Ornamental panels of moulded brick or terra cotta shall occupy not more than 25 percent of any elevation and shall be concentrated in frieze, spandrel, and gable positions.
Arches shall be segmental or flat with rubbed voussoirs. A full semicircular arch springing from a squat column moves the building toward Richardsonian Romanesque and should be classified there.

exemplars.name: James E. Hooper House
exemplars.note: Freestanding masonry Queen Anne in dark red brick with terra cotta, brownstone, and granite trim, a slate roof, and a projecting wooden oriel; now part of the Old Goucher College group.

exemplars.name: William C. Sharpless House
exemplars.note: Wissahickon schist with clapboard and shingle above and terra cotta decorative details, with a brick stable with stone quoining on the property; a Philadelphia demonstration of masonry-plus-texture.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Mark Girouard, Sweetness and Light: The Queen Anne Movement 1860-1900 (1977)
Michael Stratton, The Terracotta Revival (1993)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)

proportion_packs.note: Explicit in this pack's applies_to. Governs the massing hierarchy and the datum discipline exactly as for the parent style; the node's own proportional_system explicitly layers this pack's mass rules under a second, masonry-specific module (brick-course) rather than replacing them, which is the same layering facade-picturesque plus brick-course already produces for the corpus's other masonry-Victorian case.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to, and it is the node's own stated 'dimensional discipline the wooden ones lack': the node's typical_ratios give brick course height 2.5-3 in with belts, panels and arch rises set out in whole courses, which is brick-course's governing logic verbatim. Its window_head_masonry and belt_course rules cover the segmental and flat arches this variant requires (c05); its corbelled-cornice and moulded-water-table assemblies cover the chimney and base. What it does NOT cover is the terra cotta sunflower/foliate panel vocabulary itself (c04) — see report gaps.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to, but the node states an opening area of 35-50 percent of the elevation with deep reveals — real double-hung sash in real glass, on the same 1878-1908 timeline as the wooden Queen Anne subtypes, so the same late-cylinder/early-plate glass reasoning applies. The head-height rule is superseded here by brick-course's own window_head_masonry, which is why this binding is opening/secondary rather than primary.

JUDGMENT BINDING, for the reasoning given on the parent queen-anne-american node. A load-bearing brick townhouse still faces a joist-span limit on its floor framing, and this subtype is explicitly the urban, narrow-lot version of the style (townhouse-row is a common massing affinity), which if anything tightens room breadth toward this pack's measured band rather than loosening it.

california-mission-colonial.name: California Mission Colonial

revival_periods.note: Driven by railroad tourism, Charles Fletcher Lummis's Landmarks Club and the Ramona myth; the revival abstracted the shaped parapet gable and the arcade and discarded the quadrangle.
The richer successor, launched by Goodhue's Panama-California Exposition, drawing on Mexican and Andalusian sources the missions themselves never had.

regions: coastal California from San Diego to Sonoma
geography.hearth: the twenty-one Franciscan missions founded between San Diego (1769) and Sonoma (1823), plus their associated presidios and pueblos

lineage.note: Founded and supplied from Mexico. The Franciscans came from the College of San Fernando in Mexico City; the master masons, the tile, the bells and the plans came up from New Spain, and San Luis Rey's plan was drawn from a Mexican model.

description.short: The Franciscan mission quadrangle of Alta California: adobe walls under low half-round clay tile, arcaded corredors on square piers, and all the province's ornament spent on one church front.
description.long:
The California missions were not built as architecture. They were built as self-sufficient agricultural and manufacturing complexes with a church attached, by an indigenous labour force under a coercive system, at a rate of roughly one every two years for sixty-five years, under the direction of friars who were not architects and who had access to almost no skilled masons. Understanding that production system explains everything about how they look.

The organizing figure is the quadrangle: a closed square, one hundred and fifty to three hundred feet on a side, formed by ranges of single-loaded rooms one span deep — workshops, granaries, weaving rooms, the friars' quarters, the monjerío — with the church occupying one corner and its facade turned outward to the approach. The court is the only public space and the only safe one. The rooms face into it through an arcaded corredor ten to fourteen feet deep, and that corredor is the circulation system of the entire complex: there are no internal corridors anywhere, and one crosses the open air to move from any room to any other.

The arcade itself is the type's most legible element and the most consistently misread. These are square masonry piers, not columns — usually two and a half to four feet wide, carrying semicircular arches whose clear opening runs one and a half to two and a half times the pier width. There is no order, no base, no capital, and often no impost moulding. That squatness is not naivety; it is what unreinforced adobe and rubble can do. Above sits a low roof, three to five in twelve, of half-round clay tile — thatch until fires and the arrival of tile-makers around 1790 — with an eave of twelve to twenty inches and no gutter.

Ornament was rationed to the point of severity. Domestic and workshop ranges are entirely plain: whitewashed lime plaster over adobe, undulating, with no mouldings. Everything the mission could afford in the way of carving and colour went onto one surface — the church portada — and to the campanario, a pierced bell wall or a detached tower. Santa Barbara's church, built 1815–20 by the master mason José Antonio Ramírez, went further than any of the others: engaged Ionic columns and a neoclassical temple front flanked by twin campaniles, worked in local sandstone with famously crude mortar joints, a Vitruvian composition executed by people with no Vitruvian training. The tension in that facade — high classical ambition, frankly rough execution — is the most honest thing about the whole tradition.

To walk a mission corredor at four in the afternoon is to understand why the twentieth century could not stop imitating it: a hundred and fifty feet of deep shade, a warm rough wall on one side, an open sunlit court on the other, and the arch rhythm slow enough to walk in time with.

defining_characteristics: A closed or three-sided quadrangle 150–300 ft on a side, formed by ranges of single-loaded rooms one span deep, with the church at one corner
Arcaded corredor 10–14 ft deep on square masonry piers carrying semicircular arches, serving as all circulation
Adobe or rubble walls, 24–36 in in the ranges and 3–5 ft at the church, lime-plastered and whitewashed
Low-pitched roof, 3:12 to 5:12, of half-round clay tile (teja) after c. 1790, with a 12–20 in eave and no gutter
Campanario — a pierced bell wall — or a detached or engaged bell tower at the church
Ornament confined to the church portada and the campanario; all other surfaces plain whitewashed plaster
Buttresses or thickened piers wherever wall height exceeds roughly eight times wall thickness
diagnostic_tells: Square piers, not columns, under semicircular arches, with no capitals and often no imposts
The arcade faces the court and stops at the corners; the outer face of the quadrangle is largely blind
Tile roof with a shallow pitch and a very short eave — the roof reads as a lid, not as a shelter
Whitewashed plaster that visibly undulates over the adobe beneath it
One decorated surface in the entire complex, and it is the church door

distinguished_from.difference: The 1890s revival takes the shaped or curvilinear parapet gable — a feature of only a few mission facades — and makes it the signature, applies quatrefoil windows, builds arcades of thin piers on wood frame or brick with stucco, and abandons the quadrangle entirely. It also builds two and three storeys, which the adobe original could not.

Both build in adobe. New Mexico roofs flat on vigas behind a parapet with canales and uses no arch, no arcade and no tile; California pitches a tile roof at 3:12–5:12 and organizes everything around an arcaded court.

Monterey is the secular, Anglo-inflected California adobe of the 1830s and 40s: two storeys, a cantilevered wooden balcony, a shingle hip roof and double-hung sash. Mission work is single-storey, ecclesiastical or institutional, tile-roofed and arcaded.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The arcade bay — pier width to arch opening — sets the rhythm of the whole complex; wall thickness is set by height, and room depth by the available roof timber.
typical_ratios: Pier width 2 ft 6 in – 4 ft; arch clear opening 1.5 to 2.5 times the pier width
Arch springing 7–9 ft above the corredor floor; corredor depth 10–14 ft
Range room depth 15–20 ft, single-loaded
Wall thickness 24–36 in in the ranges, 36–60 in at the church; height not more than 8× thickness without buttressing
Roof pitch 3:12–5:12; eave projection 12–20 in
Quadrangle 150–300 ft square; church nave 25–35 ft clear, 100–180 ft long
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: A long, slow, uninterrupted arcade of identical bays, typically ten to twenty of them, with no accent, no centre and no termination other than the corner of the court.

massing_affinities.note: The closed mission quadrangle.
Missions whose fourth range was never completed, or asistencias.
The single arcaded range of an outlying rancho or asistencia.
The individual room of a range, which is the repeated unit of the whole thing.

constraints.statement: Arcade geometry: square masonry piers 2 ft 6 in – 4 ft wide carrying semicircular arches whose clear opening is 1.5 to 2.5 times the pier width. Slender piers or columns with capitals convert the arcade into a revival and are structurally impossible in adobe.

test.note: 2ft6in-4ft converted to inches. The arch-opening-to-pier-width ratio (1.5-2.5x) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 under half-round clay tile, with an eave projection of 12–20 in and no gutter. Pitches above 6:12 are foreign to the tradition.

test.note: Eave projection (12-20in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Adobe or rubble wall not less than 24 in in the ranges; where wall height exceeds eight times thickness, external buttresses are required at not more than 15 ft on centre.

test.note: The conditional buttress-spacing clause stays prose.

constraints.statement: Corredor depth not less than 10 ft. Below that it stops functioning as circulation and shade and becomes a covered walk.
Carved or moulded ornament permitted only at the church portada and the campanario. Distributing ornament across the ranges converts the complex into Spanish Colonial Revival.

exemplars.name: Mission San Luis Rey de Francia
exemplars.note: Founded 1798; the surviving cruciform church of 1811–15 and the largest of the mission quadrangles, sometimes called the King of the Missions.

exemplars.name: Mission Santa Barbara church
exemplars.note: Built 1815–20 by master mason José Antonio Ramírez after the 1812 earthquake destroyed the adobe predecessor. Twin campaniles flanking a temple front with engaged Ionic columns, in rough-hewn stone with crude joints; second tower 1831–33, both rebuilt after the 1925 earthquake, facade reconstructed 1950–53.

exemplars.name: Serra Chapel, Mission San Juan Capistrano
exemplars.note: The oldest standing building in California and the only surviving church in which Junípero Serra is known to have said Mass; the adjoining Great Stone Church of 1806 collapsed in the 1812 earthquake and stands as a ruin.

exemplars.name: Mission San Gabriel Arcángel
exemplars.note: Church completed 1805 with buttressed side walls and a detached campanario of six bells — the pierced bell wall in its clearest form.

sources: Rexford Newcomb, The Old Mission Churches and Historic Houses of California (1925)
Kurt Baer, Architecture of the California Missions (1958)
Harold Kirker, California's Architectural Frontier: Style and Tradition in the Nineteenth Century (1960)
David Gebhard and Robert Winter, An Architectural Guidebook to Los Angeles (rev. eds.)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: Applies to the range rooms only (workshops, granaries, cells -- 15-20 ft deep, single-loaded, per this node's own record), not to the church nave, which the pack's measured band (11-18 ft) does not reach and which this node records separately (25-35 ft clear). Within that scope the fit is real: room depth here is capped by the same beam-span physics room-vernacular reconstructs from Anglo-American evidence, even though the beam is a different species and the wall behind it is adobe or rubble rather than framed. As with the parent spanish-colonial-american node, no pack in this corpus governs the mass wall itself or the arcade -- see this node's own arcade geometry constraint (c01), which states real numbers (pier 2 ft 6 in - 4 ft, arch clear opening 1.5-2.5x pier) that exist in this node's own text because no proportion pack here derives them. A dedicated mass-wall/adobe module and an arcade/portal system are both missing from the corpus.

Bound only for the named exception this node itself records, not for the type: Mission Santa Barbara's church front (built 1815-20 by master mason Jose Antonio Ramirez) carries engaged Ionic columns and a neoclassical temple pediment in local sandstone -- 'a Vitruvian composition executed by people with no Vitruvian training,' in this node's own words. Vignola rather than a named overlay (Gibbs, Palladio, Chambers, Benjamin) because there is no documentary evidence connecting a specific pattern book to Ramirez's work, so the base order is the honest choice rather than inventing a source. This entry governs a single church facade among dozens of mission buildings and should not be read as describing the type.

renaissance-classical.name: Renaissance Classical

description.short: The fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Italian recovery of antique proportion, and its conversion by Palladio into a transmissible design method.
description.long:
The Renaissance did not merely imitate Rome; it measured it, theorized it, and then printed it. That last step is the decisive one. Alberti, Serlio, Vignola, and above all Palladio converted a body of ruins into a set of rules a builder in another country and another century could execute from a plate.

The Quattro Libri of 1570 is the direct ancestor of the pattern book, the plan book, and the parametric catalog. Anyone building a rules-based design system today is working in a tradition that begins here, and would do well to notice both what it achieved and where it went thin — Palladio's rules govern proportion beautifully and say almost nothing about how a house grows.

defining_characteristics: Antique proportion recovered by measurement rather than inherited by craft
The treatise as the primary medium of transmission
Harmonic and geometric room ratios governing plan as well as elevation
The villa as a complete diagram of dwelling, agriculture, and status

low-countries-vernacular.name: Low Countries Vernacular

description.short: Dutch and Flemish brick building — the gabled canal house, the farmhouse, and their remarkable export to the Hudson Valley and the Cape of Good Hope.
description.long:
The Low Countries developed a brick urbanism of extraordinary discipline: narrow deep lots, party walls, and an elaborated street gable carrying all the architectural expression. On the land, a farmhouse tradition of large roof volumes over combined house and byre.

The export history is the interesting part. Dutch settlement carried this material to two places with almost nothing else in common — the Hudson and Delaware valleys, where it produced the American Dutch Colonial and its gambrel, and the Cape, where it met French Huguenot craft and Southeast Asian labour to produce Cape Dutch, one of the most distinctive hybrid architectures in the world.

defining_characteristics: Brick as the default material, with the gable as the site of expression
Narrow deep urban lots with party-wall construction
Large roof volumes doing significant work in the section
Whitewashed lime render in the colonial branches
Export by settlement rather than by treatise

queen-anne-spindled.name: Queen Anne, Spindlework

geography.hearth: The millwork centres of the Great Lakes and their railroad distribution

lineage.note: By McAlester's count roughly half of all American Queen Anne houses fall in this subtype, making it the parent's default expression rather than a specialisation.
The porch as an open frame of posts and braces carries forward, but every member has been put on a lathe.
The sawn porch bracket and the chamfered post arrive from the earlier catalogue and never entirely leave.

description.short: The lathe-turned expression of the American Queen Anne, in which porches carry turned posts, spindle friezes, and pierced valances, and gables are filled with cut-shingle patterning, all of it purchased ready-made.
description.long:
The spindlework subtype is what most Americans mean when they say Victorian. It is the Queen Anne composition, one dominant mass, wrapping porch, textured wall, executed with the products of the wood-turning lathe: turned posts with a swell, turned balusters, and above all the spindle frieze, a run of small turned members hung in a band beneath the porch head like a fringe. Above the porch the gables are filled with cut shingles in fish-scale, diamond, or sawtooth courses, and there is often a sunburst or a panel of pierced boards at the apex.

The subtype exists because of a specific machine and a specific supply chain. The powered turning lathe with a copying attachment could reproduce a profiled baluster in seconds and identically; the shingle mill could cut a decorative butt as easily as a plain one; and the millwork catalogue sold both by the linear foot with a part number. The Eastlake label often attached to these houses is a historical accident and an injustice, since Charles Locke Eastlake, whose Hints on Household Taste appeared in 1868 and in American editions from 1872, was arguing for rectilinear, honestly jointed, structurally legible furniture and was appalled to find his name on the most lathe-happy houses ever built. The American reception of Eastlake is a compact case study in what happens when a design argument travels faster than its reasoning.

It is also, in this taxonomy, the branch where a kit-of-parts system will find the largest and best-documented parts catalogue in American history, and the place where the rules of combination matter most. The spindlework Queen Anne is the easiest style in the country to do badly, because the parts are cheap, plentiful, and mutually compatible in the trivial sense that they all bolt to a porch. What separates the Carson Mansion from a thousand forgettable contemporaries is not the quantity of the ornament but the fact that its masses are hierarchically ordered underneath it. Ornament cannot rescue a composition, and this subtype is the historical proof.

Up close the effect is of a building edged in lace. The spindle frieze is the most successful device: it is dense enough to read as a continuous band from the street, open enough to let light through, and it puts a fine-grained texture at exactly the height where a person standing on the sidewalk is looking. The turned posts are slender and their shadows are thin, so the porch feels light and airy despite being deep. In San Francisco, where the type is compressed onto a twenty-five foot lot and painted in three to five colours, the whole street becomes a single decorated surface, which is a genuinely urban achievement that the freestanding Midwestern examples never quite reach.

defining_characteristics: Turned porch posts with a pronounced swell, in place of classical columns or square piers
A spindle frieze or pierced valance suspended beneath the porch head, running the full length of the porch
Turned balusters and, frequently, a second turned spindle band at the porch rail
Cut-shingle patterning filling at least one principal gable, in fish-scale, diamond, or sawtooth coursing
Sawn brackets or knee braces at the head of every porch post
The parent style's dominant mass, wrapping porch, and multi-texture wall preserved beneath the ornament
Absence of classical detail: no column with entasis, no dentil or modillion cornice, no Palladian window
diagnostic_tells: The spindle frieze is the single tell. No other American subtype hangs a band of turned members beneath the porch head
Every ornamental member is round in section because it came off a lathe; Stick Style members are all flat and rectangular
Cut-shingle gable over clapboarded wall, with the change at the second-floor line
Where you find a classical column or a Palladian window on an otherwise Queen Anne house, you are in the free classic subtype instead
Colour: this is the subtype that the multi-colour paint schemes of the 1880s and the 1970s revival were built for, because the ornament needs a value contrast to read

distinguished_from.difference: The same massing with the opposite porch. Free classic substitutes Tuscan or Ionic columns, dentilled cornices, and Palladian windows for the lathe-turned vocabulary; the two subtypes are chronologically sequential, spindlework peaking in the 1880s and free classic after about 1890.
Both are wooden and porch-obsessed, but Stick Style ornament is flat, rectilinear, and pretends to be structure, while spindlework is round, turned, and makes no structural claim whatever.

Identical ornament catalogue, entirely different building underneath. If the massing is a plain folk type with no dominant mass and no wall projection, the house is Folk Victorian no matter how elaborate the porch.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by the parent's mass hierarchy, with a second finer rhythm supplied by the turned members of the porch. The turning profile is a catalogue constant, so the designer's real control is over post spacing and frieze depth.
typical_ratios: Porch post 5 to 8 in diameter at the swell, spaced 6 to 9 ft on centre
Spindle frieze depth 10 to 18 in, spindles 1.5 to 2.5 in diameter at 3 to 5 in on centre
Bracket or knee brace 12 to 24 in on the diagonal at every post head
Cut-shingle gable field not less than 60 percent of the gable area
Porch depth 7 to 10 ft; porch head height 8 to 9 ft above deck
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Two rhythms at once: an irregular window rhythm set by rooms, and a regular fine-grained spindle rhythm across the porch that does most of the perceptual work at street level.

massing_affinities.note: Round tower with a conical cap and a spindled porch running under it.
The San Francisco and Sacramento rows, where the whole subtype is compressed onto a narrow frontage.

constraints.statement: The porch shall carry turned posts and a spindle frieze or pierced valance running its full length, with spindles 1.5 to 2.5 in in diameter at 3 to 5 in on centre and a frieze depth of 10 to 18 in. A porch without a frieze does not satisfy this subtype.

Classical elements are prohibited: no column with entasis or classical capital, no dentil or modillion cornice, no Palladian or Venetian window. Any of these places the building in the free classic subtype.

Not fewer than one principal gable shall be filled with patterned cut shingles over not less than 60 percent of its field, with the texture change from the wall below occurring at a belt course or storey line.
One turned profile shall be used for all posts on a building and one for all balusters. Mixing catalogue profiles within a single porch is prohibited.
A sawn bracket or knee brace of 12 to 24 in on the diagonal shall occur at the head of every porch post, on both faces at corners.

exemplars.name: Carson Mansion
exemplars.note: Samuel and Joseph Cather Newsom, 1884-86. Redwood, and the maximum case of the subtype; ornamentally extreme but hierarchically ordered underneath, which is why it works.

exemplars.name: Haas-Lilienthal House
exemplars.note: Peter R. Schmidt. Redwood, on a narrow deep lot, with a circular corner tower and full spindlework porch; the best-preserved public example of the urban West Coast version.

exemplars.name: Rosson House
exemplars.note: A. P. Petit, 1894-95. Brick and wood with an octagonal turret; documented as Stick-Eastlake Queen Anne, and a good example of the subtype at the arid frontier of its distribution.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Charles Locke Eastlake, Hints on Household Taste in Furniture, Upholstery and Other Details (American ed. 1872)
Elizabeth Pomada and Michael Larsen, Painted Ladies: San Francisco's Resplendent Victorians (1978)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)

proportion_packs.note: Explicit in this pack's applies_to. This is the plainest fit of any Queen Anne variant: the node retains the parent's dominant-mass, wrapping-porch, and texture-change rules without modification, so the pack's dominance rule, datum rule and porch-sizing rule all apply directly, with the porch depth range (7-10 ft, this node) sitting inside the pack's own porch_type derivation.

JUDGMENT BINDING. This pack's applies_to lists queen-anne-american and queen-anne-free-classic but not this sibling variant explicitly, which reads as an omission rather than a deliberate exclusion: spindled Queen Anne is contemporaneous (1878-1908) and shares the same glass supply as the parent style, so the same 1/1 or 2/2 late-cylinder-glass reasoning applies.

JUDGMENT BINDING, for the same reasoning given on the parent queen-anne-american node: balloon-framed, un-treatised rooms governed by span and daylight rather than by proportion. No change from the parent's reasoning is needed since spindlework versus classical trim is a porch and gable question and has no bearing on room shape.

french-colonial-american.name: French Colonial American

revival_periods.note: Revived chiefly as the 'Louisiana raised cottage' inside the broader Colonial Revival and in the 1930s work of Richard Koch and the Historic American Buildings Survey in New Orleans.

regions: Illinois Country (Ste. Genevieve, Missouri; Cahokia and Prairie du Rocher, Illinois)
geography.hearth: the Lower Mississippi Valley — New Orleans and the German and Acadian coasts above it — with a northern outlier in the Illinois Country

lineage.note: Plan habits — room-to-room circulation without a corridor, the salle and chambre pairing, French doors as the standard opening — arrive with settlers from western France.
The roof is the clearest inheritance: the Norman truss, a steep hipped or double-pitched frame in heavy timber, and colombage walling with earth infill.

description.short: The one colonial tradition that solved a hot wet climate from first principles: a raised floor, a deep encircling gallery, a steep hipped roof, and a plan with no corridor and no room that does not cross-ventilate.
description.long:
French colonial building in North America is a hybrid before it is anything else. The frame is Norman — heavy hewn posts, mortised and pegged, sometimes set directly in the ground (poteaux-en-terre) and more often on a sill (poteaux-sur-sol), with the gaps filled by bousillage, a mud-and-Spanish-moss cob, or by soft brick, briquette-entre-poteaux, later stuccoed because the brick would not survive the weather. The plan is western French: rooms opening into one another through pairs of full-height casement doors, no corridor, no hall, circulation happening around the outside of the house rather than through the middle of it. But the gallery — the galerie, eight to twelve feet deep, running along the front and often around all four sides, its roof either a continuation of the main slope at a flatter pitch or a separate structure altogether — is not French. It arrives from the Caribbean, where French and Spanish builders had already spent a century learning the same lesson from the same climate, and it is the element that makes the whole thing work.

What it is solving is specific and severe. Ninety-five degrees, ninety percent humidity, sixty inches of rain, hurricanes, standing water, termites, and no mechanical cooling for two centuries. Every element answers something. The floor is raised — on low piers in the country, on a full masonry storey where flooding warranted — to get air under it and water out of it. The gallery keeps direct sun off the wall entirely, so the wall stays cool and the rain never touches it; the deep shade also makes the openings usable in a downpour. The roof is steep to throw water fast, and hipped so there is no gable to catch wind. The rooms are one deep and every one of them has openings on two opposite walls, so a breeze always has a path. There is no hall because a hall is a room with one door and no cross-breeze, and in this climate that is a dead room.

The interior consequence is a house that is essentially open. Twelve- and fourteen-foot ceilings, French doors down to the floor on both sides of every room, jalousie blinds to keep sun out while letting air in, and no privacy of the Anglo sort — one moves between rooms by passing through them, or steps out onto the gallery and re-enters somewhere else. The gallery is the real circulation and also the real living room; the interior is for sleeping and for weather.

Standing on a galerie in August, with twelve feet of shade overhead and the floor two feet up in the moving air, is a physical argument that is hard to refute. The Anglo-American builders who arrived after 1803 could not refute it either: within a generation they had bolted galleries onto their own houses, and the Southern porch — arguably the most consequential American architectural habit — descends more from this tradition than from any English source.

defining_characteristics: A galerie at least eight feet deep on the principal elevation, and commonly wrapping two to four sides, carried on light colonnettes or masonry piers
The floor raised clear of the ground — on low piers in the vernacular cottage, on a full masonry service storey in the plantation house
Colombage framing (poteaux-en-terre or poteaux-sur-sol) with bousillage or briquette-entre-poteaux infill, weatherboarded or stuccoed
Steep hipped or double-pitched roof, 40–50 degrees on the main mass, breaking to 20–30 degrees over the gallery
No interior corridor: rooms open directly into one another and onto the galerie through full-height French casement doors
Rear loggia flanked by cabinets — small enclosed corner rooms, one usually holding the stair
Ceilings of 11–14 feet and openings on opposite walls of every principal room
diagnostic_tells: A visible pitch break where the main roof meets the gallery roof — the single fastest tell of the whole tradition
French doors, not windows, as the standard opening: two leaves, glazed to the floor, with exterior louvred blinds
The rear elevation shows a recessed open loggia with a small square room at each end
Roof hipped on all four sides with no gable end anywhere
Exposed bousillage or brick-between-posts visible in the attic or where stucco has failed

distinguished_from.difference: The Anglo plantation house that replaces it after 1820 has a giant order of full-height columns supporting a pediment, a central hall running front to back, and a low pitched roof. French Creole galleries are two-tier and slender, the columns change material at the gallery floor, there is no pediment and no central hall.

Both are Latin colonial and both use galleries, but the Spanish tradition turns inward to a courtyard behind a closed street wall, builds in thick load-bearing adobe or rubble, and uses small openings. The French tradition turns outward to a gallery, frames in timber with light infill, and opens the wall almost completely.

Revival Louisiana houses put the gallery on but keep the Anglo centre hall behind it, align the windows, use double-hung sash instead of French doors, and rarely break the roof pitch. The absence of a corridor is the honest test.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The room as an independent, cross-ventilated cell — dimensioned by the reach of a breeze and the length of a hewn cypress beam, not by a facade module.
typical_ratios: Principal room 15–18 ft × 15–20 ft; house body two rooms wide and two deep, 36–44 ft × 30–40 ft
Galerie depth 8–12 ft; on the raised plantation house up to 14 ft
Ceiling 11–14 ft on the principal floor
Main roof 40–50 degrees; galerie slope 20–30 degrees; break at the outer wall plane
Raised floor 18–36 in on piers; 8–12 ft on a full masonry ground storey
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even-numbered and door-dominated. A four- or six-bay front of identical French doors, with no privileged centre, is normal — the absence of a single front door is itself the composition.

massing_affinities.note: The urban and small-farm expression, at or near grade.
The plantation expression, principal floor over a masonry service storey.
Where the gallery encircles rather than fronts.
The simplest two-room Illinois Country houses approximate it, though without the Anglo entry logic.
Related by geography and by Afro-Caribbean transmission but a later and separate type.

constraints.statement: No interior corridor in the principal floor plan. Every habitable room must have exterior openings on two opposite or adjacent walls for cross-ventilation.

test.note: Tests the no-corridor clause. 'Every habitable room must have exterior openings on two walls' is a per-room universal claim the vocabulary has no single variable for and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Galerie depth not less than 8 ft measured from wall face to column centreline; below 6 ft it stops shading the wall at midday and becomes decoration.

The main roof and the galerie roof meet at a pitch break at the exterior wall plane: 40–50 degrees above, 20–30 degrees over the gallery. A single continuous slope from ridge to gallery eave is a later Anglo simplification.

test.note: Tests the main-roof (ridge-side) pitch. The gallery-roof (eave-side) pitch, 20-30deg, is the same statement's second slope and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Finished floor raised not less than 18 in above grade on piers; in flood-prone parishes, above the base flood elevation. Slab-on-grade is incompatible with the type.
Openings are French casement doors, two leaves, 5 ft 6 in – 7 ft 0 in wide overall and full ceiling height less 12–18 in, with exterior louvred blinds whose leaf width equals half the opening.

test.note: Tests the door width clause. Height (full ceiling less 12-18in) and the louvred-blind leaf-width-equals-half-opening clause stay prose.

exemplars.name: Louis Bolduc House
exemplars.note: Poteaux-sur-sol with bousillage infill, steep hipped roof on hand-hewn Norman trusses, galleries on all four sides — the best-preserved Illinois Country house.

exemplars.name: Cahokia Courthouse
exemplars.note: Built as a dwelling in poteaux-en-terre — vertical logs set directly in the ground — and converted to a courthouse in 1793; one of very few surviving poteaux-en-terre buildings.

exemplars.name: Madame John's Legacy
exemplars.note: Rebuilt for Don Manuel de Lanzos immediately after the 1788 fire on an earlier c. 1730 site; raised on a brick basement, six-bay gallery on colonnettes, double-pitched roof over Norman trusses.

exemplars.name: Parlange Plantation House
exemplars.note: Traditionally dated c. 1750; some recent fabric analysis argues for c. 1830–40. Either way it is the canonical raised Creole plantation house — brick ground storey, bousillage above, encircling gallery, octagonal pigeonniers.

sources: Jay D. Edwards, 'The Origins of Creole Architecture', Winterthur Portfolio 29 (1994)
Jessie Poesch and Barbara SoRelle Bacot, eds., Louisiana Buildings, 1720–1940 (1997)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)
Charles E. Peterson, Colonial St. Louis: Building a Creole Capital (1949)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
