proportion_packs.note: This is the style's own governing_logic in the pack's own words: 'the room as an independent, cross-ventilated cell — dimensioned by the reach of a breeze and the length of a hewn cypress beam, not by a facade module' is close to a paraphrase of room-vernacular's own module description ('dimensioned by... the depth daylight will carry from one window wall'). french-colonial-american is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. Its daylight_strategy rule (room depth capped at about 2 to 2.25 times the window head height, falling to about 1.8x behind a porch) is the direct mechanism behind this style's hard no-corridor, cross-ventilation constraint, and its own conflict note — that 'an eight-foot porch across a south front costs the rooms behind it about four feet of usable depth,' answered historically by raising the storey — is a sourced explanation of why this style's ceilings run 11-14 ft rather than the 8 ft of a northern vernacular room.

French doors here run 5'6"-7'0" wide overall, at or above the 40 in threshold opening-proportion's own entry_door rule names as the point where its canonical 2:1 door proportion 'belongs and is magnificent' — Palladio's ratio was derived for wide leaves, not the narrow 3 ft leaf that forces most Anglo-American doors away from it. Bound in preference to sash-light, whose apparatus (light count from glass-market supply, muntin dating) is built for double-hung sash windows and has no purchase on a full-height glazed French casement door; opening-proportion's door-from-storey and single-head-datum logic transfers cleanly instead.

monterey-colonial.name: Monterey Colonial

revival_periods.note: A distinct and well-documented California revival of the interwar years, usually executed in stucco over frame with a tile or shingle gable roof and a posted rather than cantilevered balcony.

regions: Monterey and the Salinas Valley, California
geography.hearth: Monterey, capital of Mexican Alta California, 1834–1846, in the decade when New England merchant capital and Yankee carpenters arrived by ship

lineage.note: Containment and kit inheritance: the ground storey, the wall thickness and the plaster finish are Hispano-Californian.

Recorded as a co-parent of equal weight as well as a containment parent, because Monterey is a genuine hybrid rather than a regional inflection: the adobe wall, the lime plaster and the shaded exterior circulation are the Hispanic half of the parentage.

The Anglo half: braced-frame carpentry, a wood-shingled hip roof, milled architrave trim, double-hung six-over-six sash, an interior stair and an interior corridor — all brought by New England shipmasters and carpenters into a province that had none of them.

description.short: A genuine two-culture hybrid of Mexican and early American California — Hispanic adobe walls below, New England frame carpentry above, and a two-storey cantilevered wooden balcony running the length of the facade.
description.long:
Monterey Colonial has one of the narrowest windows in this entire taxonomy — roughly 1834 to 1850 — and it exists because of a specific commercial situation. After Mexican independence and the opening of the hide-and-tallow trade, New England merchants settled at Monterey, the capital of Alta California. They married into Californio families, they imported lumber, milled sash and hardware in the same ships that took hides east, and they brought house carpenters with them. What those carpenters built was not a New England house and not a Californio adobe. It was both, stacked.

The ground storey is Hispanic: adobe brick, twenty-four to thirty inches thick, lime-plastered and whitewashed, sitting on a stone footing, with the deep reveals and small openings the material demands. The upper storey is Anglo: a light braced timber frame, sometimes over a second course of adobe, sheathed and plastered or clapboarded, with walls perhaps six to eight inches thick. Because the upper wall is so much thinner, the wall plane visibly steps in at the second floor, and that step is a permanent record of the two building cultures meeting.

The defining element is the balcony, and its structure is the point. It is cantilevered — the second-floor joists simply run out past the wall five to seven feet and carry a deck and a plain square-baluster rail, with no posts reaching the ground. This is Anglo carpentry doing something the adobe tradition could not do, and it is the fastest and most reliable identification of the type. Where a two-storey California adobe has posts under its upper gallery, it belongs to the Hispanic tradition or to the twentieth-century revival; where the balcony floats, it is Monterey.

The roof follows the same logic: a low hip, four to five in twelve, covered not in clay tile but in redwood shingle, which arrived with the same ships and the same sawmills. Windows are double-hung six-over-six sash — the first in California — set in milled New England architraves four to five inches wide, punched into an adobe wall whose reveal is two feet deep. Inside, the Anglo half wins outright: an interior stair, an interior corridor, and rooms that are entered rather than passed through.

Thomas Oliver Larkin, the American consul, built the first of them at Monterey in 1835, though Casa Amesti of 1834 is at least contemporary and the priority is not entirely settled. The type spread quickly to Petaluma, Milpitas, Salinas and Los Angeles and then stopped almost as quickly, because the Gold Rush brought balloon framing, milled lumber in quantity and an Anglo population large enough to build whatever it liked. Standing under a Monterey balcony one sees, quite literally, two building cultures in section: two feet of mud below, three inches of Massachusetts pine above.

defining_characteristics: Two full storeys — the ground storey of 24–30 in adobe, the upper of light Anglo-American braced frame or thinner adobe
A continuous cantilevered balcony 5–7 ft deep on the long facade, carried on the projecting second-floor joists with no posts to grade
Plain square wooden balusters and a simple top rail, without turning or classical profile
Low hipped roof, 4:12 to 5:12, covered in redwood shingle rather than clay tile
Double-hung six-over-six sash in milled New England architrave trim, set in deep adobe reveals on the ground floor
A visible step-in of the wall plane at the second-floor line, 6–12 in, where the thin frame wall sits on the thick adobe one
Interior stair and an interior corridor — Anglo circulation grafted onto a Hispanic envelope
diagnostic_tells: The balcony floats: no posts, no brackets to the ground, the deck simply projecting from the wall
Shingle, not tile, on a low hip roof over an adobe building
Sash windows in a wall two feet thick — an unmistakable collision of two building cultures at every opening
The wall plane steps back at the second floor; sight up the corner and it is obvious
Milled American trim profiles on an adobe house of the 1830s

distinguished_from.difference: The 1925–55 revival is stucco over wood frame throughout, usually with a gable rather than a hip roof, clay tile rather than shingle, a balcony that is frequently posted or bracketed rather than cantilevered, and often only a partial balcony over the entrance. Wall thickness at the ground-floor reveal and the presence or absence of posts under the balcony settle it.

Mission work is single-storey, institutional, arcaded on square piers, tile-roofed and organized around a quadrangle. Monterey is domestic, two-storey, balconied, shingle-roofed and organized around an interior stair.

It shares the framing, the sash and the trim, but the ground storey is two feet of adobe, the roof is a 4:12 hip rather than a 12:12 gable, there is no central chimney, and the balcony is a device New England never built.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The cantilever capacity of a second-floor joist sets the balcony depth; the adobe wall below sets everything else.
typical_ratios: Balcony depth 5 ft 0 in – 7 ft 0 in, i.e. roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of the building depth
Ground-storey wall 24–30 in; upper-storey wall 6–10 in; wall plane step-in 6–12 in
Storey heights 9–11 ft ground, 8–10 ft upper
Roof rise:run 4:12 to 5:12, hipped, eave 12–24 in
Baluster 1.5–2 in square at 4–5 in on centre; rail 30–34 in above the deck
Sash 6/6, opening 2 ft 8 in – 3 ft 2 in × 5 ft – 5 ft 8 in, architrave 4–5 in wide
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five to seven regularly spaced openings on the balcony elevation, essentially a Georgian rhythm learned in New England and applied to an adobe wall, with the door centred.

massing_affinities.note: A linear block with a continuous upper gallery — the Monterey diagram.
The Anglo double-pile plan behind the balcony on the larger houses.
The corridor arrives with the Yankee carpenters.
Where an older Californio adobe wing survives and the Monterey block is added to it.

constraints.statement: The balcony must cantilever from the second-floor framing with no posts or columns reaching grade, at a depth of 5–7 ft. A posted upper gallery is either Hispanic-tradition or revival, and in either case is not this type.

test.note: The no-posts-to-grade clause is categorical and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Ground-storey wall not less than 24 in of adobe or equivalent mass masonry, with the upper-storey wall plane set back 6–12 in. Uniform wall thickness top to bottom removes the hybrid and produces a revival.

test.note: Ground-storey wall thickness (not less than 24in adobe) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof is a hip at 4:12 to 5:12 in wood shingle. Clay tile is a twentieth-century revival substitution; gable roofs belong to the revival, not to the 1830s original.

test.note: The hip-not-gable and wood-shingle-not-clay-tile clauses are categorical and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Openings are double-hung six-over-six sash in milled architrave trim 4–5 in wide, punched through a reveal expressing the full adobe wall depth. Casements and grilles belong to the earlier Hispanic layer.
Balcony rail of plain square balusters 1.5–2 in at 4–5 in on centre, 30–34 in high, with no turning, scrollwork or classical profile. Turned balusters are a revival marker.

exemplars.name: Larkin House
exemplars.note: Built by Thomas Oliver Larkin, United States consul; generally identified as the first house of the type and its clearest statement — adobe below, New England frame above, cantilevered balcony on two sides, shingle hip roof. National Historic Landmark.

exemplars.name: Casa Amesti
exemplars.note: Contemporary with or slightly earlier than the Larkin House; the question of priority between the two is not fully settled and the type is better dated c. 1834–35 than to a single building.

exemplars.name: Cooper-Molera Adobe
exemplars.note: Begun 1827 for Captain John Rogers Cooper, a New England shipmaster, and enlarged through the 1830s and 40s; shows the transition from Californio adobe to the Monterey type within one building.

exemplars.name: Rancho Petaluma Adobe
exemplars.note: Mariano Vallejo's ranch headquarters, the largest surviving Monterey-type building — a two-storey adobe with a continuous upper balcony around a courtyard.

sources: Harold Kirker, California's Architectural Frontier: Style and Tradition in the Nineteenth Century (1960)
Rexford Newcomb, Spanish-Colonial Architecture in the United States (1937)
David Gebhard, 'The Monterey Tradition: History Reordered', New Mexico Studies in the Fine Arts 7 (1982)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: This node's own bay_rhythm record states the case directly: 'five to seven regularly spaced openings on the balcony elevation, essentially a Georgian rhythm learned in New England and applied to an adobe wall, with the door centred.' That is facade-classical's own domain -- a designed, module-divided, roughly-symmetrical front -- arriving here by direct transmission (the Yankee ship carpenters who built these houses came from a New England Georgian building culture) rather than through a pattern book. Bound at the balcony/upper-storey rank only: the ground-floor adobe wall, with its deep undivided reveals, is not composed to this or any module in the corpus -- see the mass-wall gap noted on the parent spanish-colonial-american node, which still governs the lower storey here.

Directly attested: this node records double-hung six-over-six sash -- 'the first in California' -- in 'milled New England architrave trim 4-5 in wide,' which is sash-light's own window_surround_wood figure (module x 0.55, about 5 in) almost exactly, and 6/6 sash is exactly what this pack's dating rule predicts for glazing done in the 1830s-40s ('do not put 6/6 on one before about 1780'). This node is not in the pack's applies_to list, which is very likely an oversight given how precisely the internal evidence matches -- the Larkin House (1835) is the type's own name-giving exemplar for exactly this glazing.

Governs the Anglo half of the hybrid: storey heights of 9-11 ft ground over 8-10 ft upper are a ratio of roughly 0.85-0.95, inside this pack's own 0.78-0.92 measured band for graduated Anglo-American work. What it does NOT derive is the wall-plane step itself (24-30 in adobe below, 6-10 in frame above) -- that is a material change, not a storey-height ratio, and no pack in this corpus owns it; it is the same mass-wall gap noted on the parent node, here meeting a pack that does apply to the storey above it. This node is not in storey-graduation's applies_to list either, for the same likely reason as sash-light: the hybrid is narrow enough (sixteen years, 1834-1850) that the general applies_to sweep may simply have missed it.

Explicitly listed in this pack's own applies_to. Governs the Anglo-planned rooms behind the balcony -- 'an interior stair, an interior corridor, and rooms that are entered rather than passed through,' in this node's own words, which is exactly the framed-room logic room-vernacular reconstructs, as against the beam-strung Hispanic room logic still governing wherever an older Californio wing survives within the same building.

greek-classical.name: Greek Classical

revival_periods.note: The Grecian taste in Britain, France and Germany, made possible by Le Roy (1758) and Stuart & Revett's Antiquities of Athens (1762-1816). The first time since antiquity that European architects had measured drawings of actual Greek buildings.
The American Greek Revival, transmitted by carpenters' handbooks rather than by archaeology, and applied overwhelmingly to houses - a building type the Greeks never gave the temple front.

geography.hearth: The Peloponnese and Attica

description.short: The first Western architecture to treat proportion as an explicit, written, transmissible system, worked out in trabeated stone at the scale of a single civic building.
description.long:
Greek classical architecture is a very small vocabulary used with extraordinary discipline. There is essentially one building type that matters - a rectangular cella surrounded or fronted by columns, carrying a low-pitched gabled roof - and three graduated treatments of the column and the beam it carries. Everything else is refinement within that frame. What makes it the trunk of the entire Western classical tradition is not the shapes but the method: a module is chosen, conventionally the diameter of the column at its base, and every other dimension in the building is stated as a ratio to it. This is the moment architecture becomes a system that can be written down, argued about, and carried across a sea.

The conditions that produced it are unusually legible. Sixth-century Greek cities had surplus from colonisation, silver and trade, no monarch to spend it on a palace, and a civic religion whose buildings were treasuries and votive offerings rather than dwellings for a priesthood - so the money went into the outside of the building, which everybody could see, and almost none into the inside, which almost nobody entered. The technical substrate is equally specific: iron tools and quarry technique good enough to cut and finish marble, drums set with wooden dowels and no mortar at all, and no arch and no vault. Without arcuated construction the maximum practical stone lintel span is around five to six metres, which forces a dense colonnade, which in turn makes the colonnade the architectural subject. The Doric order is a carpentry system petrified: the triglyph is a beam end, the mutule is a rafter tail, the guttae are pegs. Nobody designed that; it fossilised.

It was reacting, in the loose way an emerging tradition reacts, against the Egyptian and Near Eastern monumental manner it had certainly seen - architecture as sheer mass, awe by weight, an interior of forests of columns in darkness. The Greek inversion is total. The temple is an exterior object, sited in the open, meant to be walked around and seen against sky and landscape. Its scale is calibrated to the human body rather than to a god's; a Doric column is tall enough to dominate you and short enough that you can read its whole height at a glance. Within the tradition itself the drift from Archaic to Classical is a steady loss of weight - the squat Paestum columns at roughly four diameters give way to the Parthenon's five and a half, and the flaring Archaic capital tightens to a taut, almost straight profile.

Standing in front of a good one, the thing that registers first is that nothing is straight. The stylobate crowns upward by six centimetres across thirty metres so it does not read as sagging. The columns lean inward by about one part in a hundred and fifty, so the building gathers rather than splays. Each shaft swells slightly in its lower half so it looks loaded rather than slack. The corner columns are thicker and set closer, because against bright sky a column is optically eaten away. None of these corrections is visible as a correction; what you perceive is simply that the building looks alert. Then the flutes do their work - twenty shallow channels with sharp arrises catching a moving line of light, so that a column reads as a cylinder of graded shadow rather than as a stone post, and the whole colonnade changes character between morning and afternoon. The marble is warm and faintly translucent at the surface. The interior, when you finally get inside, is dark, plain and beside the point.

defining_characteristics: Trabeated construction only - post and lintel in dressed stone, with no arch, no vault, and no mortar in the primary structure
All dimensions derived from a single module, conventionally the lower column diameter, so the building is a propagated ratio rather than a set of measurements
The order as a complete graduated system: shaft, capital and entablature vary together, and choosing Doric or Ionic determines a hundred subordinate dimensions
The exterior colonnade as the architectural subject, with the enclosed room subordinate and undecorated
Optical refinements as standard practice, not as virtuosity - stylobate curvature, entasis, column inclination, corner contraction
A low-pitched gable producing a triangular pediment whose height is roughly one ninth of its span
Frieze and pediment sculpture integrated into the structural members rather than applied to a blank field
diagnostic_tells: Doric columns stand directly on the stylobate with no base - if there is a moulded base under a Doric column, it is Roman or later, not Greek
The Doric frieze alternates triglyphs and metopes, and the triglyphs at the corner are pushed to the very edge of the frieze with the last two bays visibly contracted
The pediment is shallow: roughly 12 to 16 degrees, so the gable looks almost flat compared with any post-medieval revival
Column shafts are fluted with sharp arrises and no fillet between flutes in Doric (twenty flutes); Ionic has twenty-four flutes separated by flat fillets
The whole building sits on a stepped crepidoma with risers too tall to climb comfortably - it is a plinth, not a stair

distinguished_from.difference: Rome adds the arch, the vault and concrete, which frees the wall from the colonnade; Roman temples therefore stand on a high podium with a frontal stair and a deep single-ended porch, while Greek temples sit on an all-round stepped base and are peripteral. Roman Doric acquires a base and a smoother, more standardised profile; Greek Doric never has one.

The American revival applies the temple front to a dwelling, uses timber and stucco to imitate marble, flattens the entablature to a workable board dimension, and almost never contracts the corner bay or curves the stylobate. It is the silhouette of Greek architecture without the refinements that were the point.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Module = lower column diameter. Every plan and elevation dimension is stated as a multiple or fraction of it; in Doric the practical working unit on site is the triglyph-plus-metope, since the frieze must resolve exactly over the colonnade.
typical_ratios: Doric column height 4 to 6.5 lower diameters (Archaic Paestum ~4.3; Parthenon 5.48; late Hellenistic ~6.5) - the tradition steadily lightens
Ionic column height 9 to 9.5 diameters; Corinthian about 10
Doric entablature approximately 1/3 of column height; Ionic approximately 1/5
Peristyle count follows n_flank = 2 x n_front + 1 (6x13, 8x17) - the Parthenon's 8x17 is a deliberate enlargement of the 6x13 norm
Parthenon governing ratio 4:9, holding simultaneously for stylobate width:length, column diameter:axial spacing, and facade height:width
Tympanum height approximately 1/9 of the span measured across the cornice (the rule Vitruvius later records)
Stylobate upward curvature of roughly 1:500 to 1:650 of the span
Column inclination toward the centre of about 1:150
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Uniform intercolumniation with corner contraction. In Doric the frieze must place a triglyph over every column axis AND terminate with a triglyph flush at the corner, which is geometrically impossible at constant spacing, so the final one or two bays narrow by roughly half a triglyph width each. That contraction is the single most reliable proof of authentic Doric grammar.

massing_affinities.note: The Greek oikos is an inward-turning court house presenting a nearly blind wall to the street; the domestic architecture and the temple architecture share almost nothing.
The megaron - a single room with a porch - is the ancestor of the cella and survives as the irreducible unit.
Orthogonally planned colonies such as Olynthos and Priene built party-wall house blocks on a strict grid.
The pedimented colonnaded front is a public and religious type in Greek practice. Its use as the face of a dwelling is a nineteenth-century invention and should not be attributed to Greek precedent.

constraints.statement: Pediment slope must fall between 12 and 17 degrees (tympanum height 1/7 to 1/9 of span). Above 20 degrees the profile reads Roman or Renaissance; above 30 degrees it reads as a domestic gable with a pediment drawn on it.

test.note: A Greek pediment's rake continues the roof's own pitch, so roof_slope_deg tests it directly. The parenthetical tympanum-height-to-span ratio is a restatement of the same slope in a different form, not additional information, and the descriptive thresholds above 20 and 30 degrees are commentary rather than a separate rule.

constraints.statement: A Doric column may not be given a moulded base. Doric shaft meets stylobate directly; if a base is required by the design, the order must change to Ionic or the reference must change to Roman.
Clear span between column axes must not exceed roughly 6 m without introducing an arch, which is outside the style. Intercolumniation between 1.2 and 1.7 lower diameters of clear space.

test.note: Tests the intercolumniation clause. The 'clear span must not exceed roughly 6 m without an arch' clause stays prose (a conditional construction-method rule, not a bound on a single variable).

constraints.statement: Entasis: the shaft diminishes only above roughly the lower third of its height, with total diminution of 1/6 to 1/5 of the lower diameter and a maximum swell of 1.5 to 2 percent over the straight-line taper.
If a Doric frieze is used, corner contraction is mandatory; an uncontracted corner with a half-metope is a revivalist error, not a Greek option.

exemplars.name: Parthenon
exemplars.note: Built 447-432 BC, Iktinos and Kallikrates. Doric octastyle peripteral, 8x17. The densest concentration of optical refinements anywhere in the tradition.

exemplars.name: Temple of Hephaestus (Hephaisteion)
exemplars.note: c. 449-415 BC. The most completely preserved Doric temple standing; the reference specimen for entablature detail.

exemplars.name: Erechtheion
exemplars.note: 421-406 BC. The canonical Attic Ionic capital and the caryatid porch; also the clearest demonstration that Greek symmetry is per-elevation, not per-building.

exemplars.name: Temple of Apollo Epikourios
exemplars.note: c. 429-400 BC, attributed to Iktinos. Contains the earliest known Corinthian capital.

sources: Vitruvius, De architectura, Books III-IV
William Bell Dinsmoor, The Architecture of Ancient Greece (1950)
A. W. Lawrence, Greek Architecture, Pelican History of Art
J. J. Coulton, Ancient Greek Architects at Work (1977)
John Summerson, The Classical Language of Architecture (1963)

proportion_packs.note: The only order-system in the library that is actually baseless, which matters here because c02 makes a moulded Doric base a hard error and Vignola's Doric (and every overlay built on it) has one. Benjamin's own applies_to list names greek-classical directly, and his 1830 preface states the reason in his own words: the Doric is 'the one order' where Greek and Roman 'differ essentially,' and what is encoded here is drawn from Stuart and Revett's measured Temple of Theseus rather than from Vignola. That said, it is not a scholarly Attic encoding: Benjamin's own recommended Example No. 3 is a nineteenth-century American wood-construction compromise, not the archaeological figures. Column height is 7 diameters including the capital against this style's own stated Doric range of 4 to 6.5 diameters (Parthenon 5.48); entasis begins at the foot rather than at the lower third this style's c04 specifies; the annulets are changed to 'Roman character' because Benjamin judged the Greek ones 'too small and indistinct'; mutules are halved from one-per-metope-and-triglyph to one-per-triglyph-only. It is the closest thing in the library to a baseless Greek Doric, and it is still a Federal-Boston-carpentry object standing in for a fifth-century-BC Athenian one.

Judgment binding: greek-classical is not in vignola-ionic's own applies_to. Bound anyway because this style's own proportional_system states Ionic column height as 9 to 9.5 diameters, and Vignola's Ionic (later codified from Roman practice but tracking a genuinely Ionic lineage) sits at almost exactly 9 diameters -- the two figures were not reconciled on purpose, they simply agree. Unlike Doric, a moulded base is not a Greek/Roman fault line for Ionic -- the Erechtheion's own columns are based -- so vignola-ionic's base does not trip a hard constraint the way vignola-doric would. It remains a Roman-transmitted reading (Vignola 1562) rather than a direct encoding of the Erechtheion or the Temple of Apollo Epikourios, and no pack in the library encodes either building specifically.

raised-creole-plantation.name: Raised Creole Plantation House

revival_periods.note: Revived through the 1930s HABS campaigns in Louisiana and the restoration practice of Richard Koch; the 'Louisiana raised cottage' becomes a recognized suburban idiom in the Gulf South.

regions: the Mississippi River parishes above and below New Orleans
Pointe Coupee and the False River
geography.hearth: the sugar and indigo river parishes of lower Louisiana, where annual flooding made a masonry ground storey a condition of building at all

lineage.note: The double-pitched roof carried on hand-hewn Norman trusses, and the hipped envelope with no gable to catch wind, are the structural inheritance.

description.short: The Creole plan lifted a full storey onto a brick service floor and wrapped in a gallery eight to fourteen feet deep, with an exterior stair and a broad hipped roof that breaks pitch at the gallery.
description.long:
The raised Creole house is what the four-room Creole plan becomes when the client is wealthy, the site floods, and the household includes both a family and a large enslaved workforce whose labour has to be organized. Everything in it follows from lifting the living floor eight to twelve feet into the air. The ground storey becomes a thick-walled brick or stuccoed-brick service level — wine and provision storage, offices, work rooms — cool because it is massive and shaded, expendable because water will eventually get into it. The principal floor above sits above the flood, above the mosquitoes, and up in the moving air off the river, and it is reached not through the house but by an exterior stair rising to the gallery. There is no front door in the Anglo sense; there is a stair, a gallery, and a row of French doors.

The gallery is the building's real room. Eight to fourteen feet deep, running the full front and often all four sides, it is carried on square or round masonry piers at the ground storey and on slender turned or chamfered wooden colonnettes above. That change of material and slenderness at the gallery floor line is the type's most reliable single tell, and it is structurally honest: masonry where the load is greatest and where water will reach, light timber where neither applies. Between the columns the space is shaded all day, and it functions as circulation, as dining room, as sleeping porch, and as the household's connection to the plantation landscape.

Behind it the plan is Creole and unmodified: rooms opening into one another through French doors, no corridor, a rear loggia recessed between projecting cabinets, chimneys internal, ceilings twelve to fourteen feet. Walls above the masonry storey are colombage with bousillage or briquette infill under weatherboard. The roof is broad, hipped, forty to fifty degrees over the body, breaking to twenty or thirty degrees over the gallery and framed on Norman trusses with dormers set into the main slope.

What it is negotiating against, from 1803, is the Anglo-American plantation house, which will arrive with a central hall, a giant order of full-height columns, and a pedimented portico. That house is a temple; this one is a shed with an enormous porch, and it is a far better building for the climate. Standing on a raised gallery at Homeplace or Parlange in late afternoon, twelve feet up with the shade twelve feet deep and the river breeze coming through, one can see very clearly that the Greek Revival that displaced it was a cultural argument rather than an environmental one.

defining_characteristics: Principal floor raised 8–12 ft on a full masonry (brick or stuccoed brick) service storey
Gallery 8–14 ft deep on at least the principal elevation, commonly encircling, reached by an exterior stair
Columns changing material at the gallery floor: masonry piers below, slender turned or chamfered wooden colonnettes above
Broad hipped roof, 40–50 degrees over the body, breaking to 20–30 degrees over the gallery, framed on Norman trusses with dormers set in the main slope
No interior corridor: rooms open into one another and onto the gallery through full-height French casement doors
Rear loggia recessed between projecting cabinets, one containing the stair to the garret
Upper walls of colombage with bousillage or briquette-entre-poteaux infill; ceilings 12–14 ft
diagnostic_tells: The column change at the gallery floor line — heavy masonry below, thin wood above — visible from any angle
An exterior stair as the only way to the principal floor
A visible pitch break in the roof where the gallery begins
Dormers set into the main roof slope rather than above the gallery
Openings are doors, not windows, all the way round

distinguished_from.difference: The Anglo house that supersedes it has a giant order of full-height columns of a single material carrying an entablature and often a pediment, a central hall running through the house, and a low roof with no pitch break. The Creole house changes column material at the gallery floor, has no hall, no pediment and a strong pitch break.
Identical plan logic; the raised house lifts it onto a masonry service storey and adds an exterior stair, deeper galleries and taller ceilings. The cottage sits at or near grade on low piers.

Twentieth-century 'Louisiana raised cottages' keep the gallery and the raised floor but insert a central hall, substitute double-hung sash for French doors, use uniform columns top to bottom, and rarely break the roof pitch. The absence of a corridor is the honest test.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The gallery depth and the service-storey height are the governing dimensions; the room block is whatever fits behind and beneath them.
typical_ratios: Body 40–60 ft wide × 30–44 ft deep; with galleries, overall 60–80 ft wide
Principal floor 8–12 ft above grade; service storey ceiling 8–10 ft
Gallery depth 8–14 ft, typically 25–35% of the total building depth
Principal-floor ceiling 12–14 ft
Colonnette diameter 6–9 in; masonry pier 16–24 in square — a slenderness change of roughly 1:2.5
Body roof 40–50 degrees; gallery roof 20–30 degrees
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five to nine equal bays of French doors across the gallery, columns evenly spaced at 8–11 ft on centre, with no centre bay emphasis and no pediment.

massing_affinities.note: Where the gallery encircles all four sides.
The unraised parent plan.
Service wings occasionally extend to the rear, but the type resists the ell.

constraints.statement: Principal floor not less than 8 ft above grade on a full masonry service storey (absolute minimum 6 ft), reached by an exterior stair. A raised cottage on wooden piers with an enclosed underfloor is a different and lesser building.

test.note: 8ft is the stated target but 6ft (72in) is the constraint's actual hard floor ('absolute minimum 6 ft') -- tested at the true minimum.

constraints.statement: Gallery depth 8–14 ft on the principal elevation. Below 8 ft the gallery stops shading the wall and stops functioning as a room.

Column material and slenderness must change at the gallery floor line: masonry pier 16–24 in square below, wooden colonnette 6–9 in above. A single continuous order top to bottom converts the building into a Greek Revival plantation house.

test.note: Tests the masonry pier (below the gallery floor line). The wooden colonnette above (6-9in) is the statement's other member size and stays prose.

constraints.statement: No interior corridor on the principal floor; every principal room opens onto the gallery through French casement doors, and every room has openings on two walls.
Roof pitch break required at the gallery: 40–50 degrees over the body, 20–30 degrees over the gallery. Dormers, where used, sit in the main slope with their faces set back behind the gallery line.

test.note: Same convention as french-colonial-american: tests the main-body (ridge-side) pitch, not the gallery pitch.

exemplars.name: Homeplace Plantation House (Keller Homeplace)
exemplars.note: Built 1787–91. Stuccoed brick ground storey, cypress above, encircling gallery under a two-storey hip roof; designated a National Historic Landmark in 1970 as one of the finest French colonial raised cottages in the country.

exemplars.name: Parlange Plantation House
exemplars.note: Traditionally dated c. 1750; some fabric analysis argues for c. 1830–40, and the date should be treated as contested. Brick raised basement, bousillage of mud, moss and animal hair above, encircling gallery, octagonal pigeonniers.

exemplars.name: Madame John's Legacy
exemplars.note: Rebuilt for Don Manuel de Lanzos immediately after the 1788 fire on a site occupied since c. 1730; six-bay gallery on shaped colonnettes, brick basement, double-pitched roof over Norman trusses with two dormers.

exemplars.name: Destrehan Plantation
exemplars.note: Built 1787–90 as a raised Creole house and given Greek Revival columns in an 1840 remodelling — the two traditions visible in one building, and a useful case for teaching the distinction.

sources: Jay D. Edwards, 'The Origins of Creole Architecture', Winterthur Portfolio 29 (1994)
Jay D. Edwards and Nicolas Kariouk Pecquet du Bellay de Verton, A Creole Lexicon: Architecture, Landscape, People (2004)
Jessie Poesch and Barbara SoRelle Bacot, eds., Louisiana Buildings, 1720–1940 (1997)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: raised-creole-plantation is named directly in storey-graduation's own applies_to, and the pack's own 'GROUND STOREY UNDER A PIANO NOBILE' rule names 'raised Creole and raised cottage types' by name as one of its three worked cases — the single most directly-attested binding in this whole batch. The rule's inversion (ground storey markedly lower than the principal floor above it, ratio about 0.72) is exactly this variant's own section: an 8-10 ft masonry service storey under a 12-14 ft principal floor, reached by an exterior stair rather than an internal one.

raised-creole-plantation is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. Every opening is a French door, 'all the way round' per the style's own diagnostic tells, at full ceiling height less 12-18 in on a 12-14 ft ceiling — again within the wide-leaf band where the pack's 2:1 canonical ratio applies without adjustment, unlike a narrow Anglo-American door.

cape-cod-revival.name: Cape Cod Revival

revival_periods.note: Continuous production in New England and as a New Traditional and cottage-community type nationally.

geography.hearth: Boston and eastern Massachusetts

lineage.note: The small, frame, one-and-a-half-storey wing of the parent style, and the only one whose proportions were seriously studied.
The claimed ancestor, and one of the few in this branch whose dimensions the revival genuinely tried to reproduce rather than inflate.
The broader New England frame vocabulary - clapboard, small sash, massive central chimney - from which the Cape is a reduction.
Convergent from about 1938: the FHA-standard minimal house and the Cape Cod Revival cottage become nearly the same building, and the reciprocal claim is recorded on both nodes.

description.short: The small, steep-roofed, one-and-a-half-storey frame house that Royal Barry Wills and the FHA between them made the default American starter home from 1935 to 1960, and the one revival in this branch that shrank its model rather than inflating it.
description.long:
Cape Cod Revival is unusual in this family for treating its historical model as a discipline rather than as a costume. The eighteenth-century Cape is a very tightly reasoned building: a rectangular box a room and a half deep, one and a half storeys, a massive central chimney, a steep gable roof to shed snow, an eave line dropped almost onto the window heads to reduce wind exposure, and no ornament except a door surround. The revival keeps almost all of that. What it adds is a dormer or two, a cellar, plumbing, and a garage; what it changes is that the chimney stops being structural and starts being an emblem.

Royal Barry Wills is the reason it is a style rather than a survival. Working from a Boston office from 1925, Wills spent thirty years measuring, publishing, and refining the type, and he was explicit that the whole thing lived or died on proportion. His office standards are worth repeating because they are exactly the sort of enforceable number this taxonomy exists to record: roof pitch between 8:12 and 10:12; eaves set just above the second-floor window heads; sash with 24 to 36 lights; clapboards graduated from about 2 3/4 in. exposure at the water table to 4 1/4 in. near the eave, so that the wall appears to rise. In 1938 Life magazine paired four modern and four traditional architects against each other for real client families; in the $5,000-$6,000 bracket Wills was set against Frank Lloyd Wright, and the family chose Wills. That result is the clearest single piece of evidence about mid-century American taste that exists.

The economics finished what the design started. The FHA's mortgage-insurance underwriting after 1934 favoured exactly this footprint - small, detached, expandable, on a modest lot - and after 1945 the veterans' housing programmes and the merchant builders adopted it wholesale. Levitt & Sons built roughly seventeen thousand houses at Levittown, New York, between 1947 and 1951, and the first model was a Cape. That is the moment the American production home acquires its default vocabulary, and it is a Colonial Revival vocabulary.

A Cape Cod house is small in a way that reads as deliberate rather than as poor, and the reason is the eave. Because the eave line sits within a foot or so of the upper window heads, the wall is very short and the roof is very large, and the building crouches. There is no shadow line to speak of, no cornice, no projection; the whole thing is one taut skin with a door in the middle of it and a chimney coming out of the ridge. Inside, the ground floor is compact and low and the upper floor is all sloped ceiling and dormer, and the effect - the reason people keep buying them - is that a very small building feels finished rather than incomplete.

defining_characteristics: One-and-a-half storeys, rectangular in plan, with a steeply pitched side-gable roof
Eave line carried low, within roughly 12 in. of the second-floor window heads, producing a short wall and a dominant roof
Central chimney on the ridge, or paired end chimneys, expressed as mass
Symmetrical three- or five-bay front with a centred entrance and a modest pilastered or hooded door surround
Multi-light double-hung sash, 6/6 or 8/12, small in individual dimension relative to the wall
Minimal ornament: no cornice beyond a simple moulding, no corner boards beyond a plain board, no porch beyond a stoop
diagnostic_tells: Second-floor windows sit in dormers or in the gable ends, never in a full-height side wall. A full second storey makes it a Colonial Revival, not a Cape.
Roof pitch 8:12 to 10:12 with the eave nearly touching the upper window heads; a 6:12 roof with a tall wall is Minimal Traditional.
The chimney is on the ridge at or near the centre. A gable-end chimney is acceptable in pairs; an off-centre single stack is a builder's compromise.
No cornice, no returns, no frieze board. The presence of a modillioned cornice means the house has left this variant.

Against the eighteenth-century original: revival Capes have dormers (the originals rarely did), a full cellar, larger sash, and a chimney that no longer contains the cooking hearth and the structural core.

distinguished_from.difference: The original, c. 1690-1850, is a shingled or clapboarded box with a genuinely structural central chimney stack 6-8 ft square containing multiple hearths, almost never dormered, with tiny sash and no cellar stair to speak of. The revival keeps the silhouette and the proportional discipline but hollows out the chimney and cuts dormers into the roof.
This is the parent style at one and a half storeys with the ornament removed. A Cape that grows a full second floor, a cornice, and a portico has become general Colonial Revival.

Minimal Traditional, the FHA type of 1935-1950, has a low roof pitch of 4:12 to 6:12, a shallow eave, a tall wall, and no chimney of consequence. It is what a Cape becomes when the builder economises on roof framing.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Roof pitch against wall height. The type is generated by pulling the eave down to the upper window heads, which fixes the wall height, which fixes everything else. Wills's office treated graduated clapboard exposure as a second proportional device operating on the wall itself.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 8:12 to 10:12
Wall height from grade to eave 11-13 ft for the full one-and-a-half storeys
Eave soffit within 12 in. of the second-floor window heads
Overall footprint 24-28 ft deep by 32-40 ft wide - a plan proportion near 1:1.4
Sash of 24-36 lights total per window; graduated clapboard exposure from 2 3/4 in. at the water table to 4 1/4 in. near the eave
Door surround overall width not exceeding 5'6" for a 2'8"-3'0" leaf
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three bays on the half Cape and three-quarter Cape, five bays on the full Cape, at 7'6"-9'0" on centre. The rhythm is tighter than general Colonial Revival because the original framing bay is genuinely being reproduced.

massing_affinities.note: The variant is this massing; the half, three-quarter and full Cape are its three states.
The rear lean-to extension, which Wills used constantly to add a kitchen or family room without breaking the front.
Where the Cape grows to a full two storeys it stops being this variant and becomes plain Colonial Revival.
A gambrel over a Cape footprint is a Dutch Colonial Revival move, not a Cape one.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 8:12 to 10:12, and the eave soffit must sit not more than 12 in. above the second-floor window head line. A tall wall with a low roof is Minimal Traditional and is not this variant.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch range. The eave-soffit-to-second-floor-window-head offset (not more than 12in, matching window_head_to_cornice_offset_in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Maximum two full storeys of wall is forbidden: the front wall may not exceed 13'0" from grade to eave. All upper-floor light on the front and rear must come from dormers.

test.note: Tests the front-wall grade-to-eave cap. 'All upper-floor light on the front and rear must come from dormers' has no matching vocabulary variable for light source and stays prose.

constraints.statement: A masonry chimney is required, on the ridge at or near the centre or paired at the gable ends, minimum 3'0" x 3'0" in plan for a central stack and rising not less than 2'0" above the ridge.

test.note: Tests the ridge-rise minimum. Chimney position (ridge-centre vs. paired gable-end, expressible via chimney_position but not tested here) and the 3'0"x3'0" plan footprint (no matching vocabulary variable) stay prose -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Dormers, where used, must total not more than 50 percent of the roof length on any one slope, with their faces set back not less than 12 in. from the wall plane and their ridges not less than 18 in. below the main ridge.

Ornament is limited to the door surround, a simple 4-6 in. eave moulding, and 4-6 in. corner boards. Cornice returns, modillions, friezes, pediments over windows, and full-width porches are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the eave moulding width. The door surround (undimensioned), the corner-board width (also 4-6in but a distinct element with no vocabulary variable of its own), and the forbidden-ornament list stay prose.

exemplars.name: Royal Barry Wills House
exemplars.note: The architect's own house and the reference example for his office's Cape standards; later extended to the rear.

exemplars.name: Life magazine 'Eight Houses for Modern Living' Wills house
exemplars.note: Royal Barry Wills. The traditional entry chosen by the client family over Frank Lloyd Wright's modern design in the same income bracket.

exemplars.name: Levittown Cape Cod model
exemplars.note: Levitt & Sons. The first mass-produced model at Levittown, 1947-49, and the vehicle by which the type became the American postwar default.

exemplars.name: Webber House
exemplars.note: Harry Morton Ramsay. Included as a contemporaneous Boston-area point of comparison; see garrison-revival, where its overhang places it.

sources: Royal Barry Wills, Houses for Good Living (1940)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Richard Wills and Kevin Bone, At Home in New England: Royal Barry Wills Architects 1925 to Present (2013)
Barbara Kelly, Expanding the American Dream: Building and Rebuilding Levittown (1993)

proportion_packs.note: Governs the composed front as a whole: the odd bay count (three or five), the pier arithmetic, and the ranking of horizontals. Cape Cod Revival is the one node in this branch whose facade is nearly pure void-in-wall with almost no cornice to speak of, so this pack's bay-count and solid-to-void rules do the work that a heavier order would do elsewhere in the family; the pack's own three-horizontal ranking is deliberately not fully used here, since the style forbids a projecting cornice and works mostly off the water table and the head datum.

The rectangle of the door and window openings and, in particular, the single-head-datum rule, which is exactly what Wills's office standard is describing when it fixes the eave 'just above the second-floor window heads' -- there is only one head line on the front and the whole silhouette depends on it staying level and low.

Explicitly applicable and load-bearing here: the node's own hard constraints and typical ratios specify 6/6 or 8/12 sash with 24-36 lights total, and Wills's graduated clapboard exposure (2 3/4 in at the water table rising to 4 1/4 in near the eave) is exactly the kind of measured, dated device this pack exists to record.

The node's own bay_rhythm is explicit that 'the rhythm is tighter than general Colonial Revival because the original framing bay is genuinely being reproduced' (7'6"-9'0" bay, matching the pack's 16-20 ft frame-bay logic scaled to a one-and-a-half storey house). The pack's own closing note names Cape Cod Revival directly as the test case for this discipline: a correct-looking exterior wrapped around a plan no frame would produce is exactly the failure this pack is written to catch.

Interior trim only, and reduced in scale from the parent style's: a Cape's baseboard, chair rail and door casing are classical-family (raised panel doors, simple backband) rather than craftsman flat stock, but run thin and plain to suit an 11-13 ft ground-floor room rather than a high-style Georgian one. Exterior ornament is explicitly capped by the node's own hard constraint c05 -- door surround, a 4-6 in eave moulding, and corner boards only, with cornice returns, modillions and porches forbidden -- so this pack's exterior wall-section family (water table, belt, entablature) is not invoked; only the interior assemblies are.

Judgment binding: cape-cod-revival is not in this pack's own applies_to list, but the node's lineage names cape-cod-colonial -- which IS in that list -- as the ancestor whose dimensions 'the revival genuinely tried to reproduce rather than inflate,' and the whole point of the style, per its own description, is discipline rather than costume. The pack's daylight-limited, span-and-hearth-constrained 'ordinary room' logic fits a Cape's low storey (11-13 ft to the eave) far better than room-harmonic's Palladian saloons, which this variant's own text never invokes.

american-colonial.name: American Colonial

description.short: The first American architecture: four European building cultures transplanted to four different climates, each mutating within two generations.
description.long:
The colonial period is best read as a controlled experiment. English, Dutch, German, French, and Spanish settlers each brought a coherent building tradition and each met conditions their tradition had not anticipated — colder winters, hotter summers, different timber, no guild structure, and a labour economy in which skilled craft was scarce and land was not.

What survived the transplant is instructive and consistent: the section survived, the plan survived, the surface did not. Roof pitch, chimney position, ceiling height, and the relationship to grade persisted for centuries. Ornament vanished almost immediately and returned only when pattern books arrived in the 1730s.

The variant level is where this family becomes operationally useful. New England Georgian and Tidewater Georgian are the same style and different buildings, and the differences — cladding, chimney position, roof pitch, plan depth — are climatic and quantifiable.

defining_characteristics: Transplanted European traditions adapting to unanticipated climates
Structural and planning logic surviving where surface ornament did not
Scarcity of skilled craft producing simplification within a generation
Strong regional divergence within each national tradition
Pattern-book classicism arriving late and unevenly after about 1730

italian-baroque.name: Italian Baroque

revival_periods.note: The Baroque scenographic plan and giant coupled order return through the Ecole des Beaux-Arts and the City Beautiful movement, applied to stations, museums and civic centres.

geography.hearth: Rome

lineage.note: Unbroken workshop and treatise transmission through Michelangelo, Vignola and the Mannerists. Vignola's Regola of 1562 remains the working manual; the orders themselves are not renegotiated.

The Baroque wall is the precise inversion of the Palladian one: curved where Palladio is planar, accelerating where he is even, multi-planar in column projection where he keeps one plane, and broken in its pediments where he keeps them whole.
Imperial scale and the ceremonial axis are quoted directly - Bernini's colonnade is a Roman forum portico deployed for papal ceremony - but the structural means are masonry and stucco, not concrete.

description.short: The classical order retained intact while the wall it governs is bent, layered and accelerated, producing an architecture of continuous surface and controlled emotional effect.
description.long:
The Baroque is often described as classicism gone loose, which gets it exactly backwards. Borromini's mouldings are more precise than Bramante's, not less; the module is preserved to the millimetre. What changes is what the module is applied to. In the Renaissance the wall is a flat plane and the orders are a grid laid on it. In the Baroque the wall itself becomes a deformable surface - convex here, concave there, its plan generated by interlocking ovals, circles and triangles - and the orders are made to follow it around the curve. A single bay may contain a pilaster, a half-column, a three-quarter column and a free-standing column, each in a different plane, so that the facade is read as depth rather than as pattern. The building stops being a figure you look at and becomes a space you are inside of even when you are outdoors.

The conditions are Counter-Reformation and papal. The Council of Trent closed in 1563 having decided, against the Protestant position, that images, ceremony and sensory persuasion were legitimate instruments of faith. That is a design brief. The new orders - Jesuits, Oratorians, Theatines - needed churches for large congregations focused on preaching and on the sacrament, which means a single wide nave with side chapels rather than aisles, an unobstructed sightline to the altar, and a dome over the crossing to concentrate light exactly where the mystery happens. Papal Rome simultaneously had a city-planning problem: pilgrim routes between the seven basilicas, needing obelisks, fountains, straightened streets and axial termini. Sixtus V's replanning from 1585 is the point at which architecture starts designing the space between buildings, and this is arguably the Baroque's most durable export - it is what Haussmann, L'Enfant and the City Beautiful all inherit.

What it reacts against, within its own family, is the terminal stasis of High Renaissance and Palladian composition. A Palladian front is resolved and finished; there is nowhere for the eye to go, which is the point. The Baroque decides that resolution is a waste of the observer's attention, and organises everything as movement toward a climax: bays compress and columns multiply as they approach the axis, entablatures break forward over the centre, the pediment splits open to admit a sculptural event, and the composition finishes on the sky with a silhouette of figures rather than a cornice line.

Inside San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, on a corner site of about twenty by twelve metres, the experience is disorienting in a way you cannot immediately explain. The lower order is a continuous undulating colonnade with no flat wall anywhere; the entablature above it runs unbroken around every curve like a taut band; and then the coffered oval dome above appears to hang free, lit from a lantern you cannot quite see, its interlocking crosses, hexagons and octagons diminishing so aggressively that the dome reads as twice its true height. Nothing is applied. The geometry goes all the way through the building, and the sensation is of standing inside a solved equation that is still moving.

defining_characteristics: The wall treated as a continuous deformable surface, curved in plan, with the orders following it around convex and concave sweeps
Multiple planes of column projection within a single bay (pilaster, half, three-quarter, free-standing) to produce read depth
A rhythm that accelerates toward the axis - bays compress and articulation multiplies at the centre
Plan geometry generated from interlocking ovals, circles and triangles rather than from additive rectangular bays
Broken, segmental and scrolled pediments used as compositional openings for sculpture or light
Concealed and directed light: hidden lanterns, windows behind cornices, and openings sized to create a single dramatic gradient
The building composed with its urban void - piazza, obelisk, fountain and street axis designed as one work
diagnostic_tells: A facade whose plan line is curved - if you can see the wall bend, no earlier classical style will account for it
Entablature that breaks forward and back over each change of column plane rather than running as a single straight band
Giant order of two-plus storeys with a small subordinate order tucked beneath it in the same bay
Pediments split at the apex, or a segmental pediment nested inside a triangular one
The silhouette against the sky is populated - statues, urns, volutes, scrolled buttresses - rather than terminated by a horizontal cornice

distinguished_from.difference: Flat versus curved wall; even versus accelerating bay rhythm; single versus multiple planes of column projection; whole versus broken pediments; horizontal cornice termination versus a populated sky silhouette.

The French keep the wall flat and get their plasticity by projecting whole masses - pavilions and avant-corps - forward as blocks. If the plasticity comes from a curved wall surface it is Italian; if it comes from rectangular blocks stepping forward, it is French.

The Spanish variant concentrates all ornament into a dense retablo-like frontispiece surrounded by plain wall, and does not curve the wall in plan. Italian Baroque distributes plasticity across the whole surface.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The order is retained exactly as Vignola codified it (module = half the lower diameter, in 12 or 18 parts), but the governing geometry of the whole moves from the additive bay to a continuous figure - interlocking ovals, circles and equilateral triangles set out on the plan and then extruded as curved wall surface. Proportion is dynamic: the module stays fixed while the surface it governs deforms.
typical_ratios: Oval domes and plans with major:minor axis typically 3:2 to 5:3
San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane: plan traditionally analysed as two equilateral triangles on a shared base, with circles inscribed, within an oval - on a site of roughly 20 x 12 m
Giant order spanning two storeys, entablature 1/5 to 1/4 of column height, with a subordinate small order of about 0.4 the giant order's height
Column projection graded in four planes across a half-bay, each step 1/2 to 1 module
Church front width:height approximately 1:1 for the two-storey scheme, with the upper storey 0.6 to 0.7 the width of the lower and joined by volutes
Nave width:height typically 1:2 to 1:2.5; side chapel openings 1/2 to 2/3 of the nave bay width
Dome coffering diminishing 15 to 25 percent per ring to exaggerate apparent height
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Accelerating toward the centre: A-B-C-B-A, where C is narrower than B and B narrower than A, and where the density of articulation increases inversely with bay width. The entablature breaks forward at each escalation, so the horizontal reads as a sequence of steps rather than as a line.

massing_affinities.note: The Roman palazzo persists as the domestic and institutional type; the Baroque changes its face and its stair, not its skeleton.
Suburban villas and casini open a cour d'honneur toward the approach, which the Baroque then treats as a stage set.
Baroque Rome and Turin build long uniform street walls with a single palazzo swelling out of them at the axis.
Used, but with the pediment broken and the wings curved forward as quadrant colonnades rather than kept straight.

Baroque irregularity is always resolved about an axis. Irregularity for its own sake, composed for a moving viewpoint without a governing symmetry, belongs to the picturesque and is a different argument entirely.

constraints.statement: If the wall curves in plan, the entablature must curve with it as a continuous member; a straight entablature over a curved wall is a hard error.

Column projection must increase monotonically toward the axis within a bay - pilaster, then half, then three-quarter, then free-standing. Random alternation of planes is not Baroque layering, it is noise.
Bay widths must narrow toward the centre by 10 to 25 percent per step. An even bay rhythm with Baroque ornament applied is Mannerist or revivalist, not Baroque.

Oval and curved-wall plans require masonry or reinforced construction with wall thickness of at least 1/10 the clear span; the geometry is not achievable in light frame without losing the depth of reveal that makes it read.

test.note: Combines a section reading (wall_thickness_in) with a plan reading (room_clear_span_ft, converted to inches) to test the 1/10-of-span slenderness floor. 'Not achievable in light frame without losing the depth of reveal' is prose commentary on the same rule, not a second fact.

constraints.statement: Broken pediments must be broken FOR something - a cartouche, a statue, a window admitting light. An empty break is a decorative tic, not a Baroque device.

exemplars.name: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane
exemplars.note: Borromini; church built 1638-1641, dedicated 1646; facade begun in Borromini's last years and the upper stage completed after his death in 1667. The undulating wall and interlocking-geometry oval dome in their purest form.

exemplars.name: Sant'Ivo alla Sapienza
exemplars.note: Borromini, 1642-1660. Plan generated from two superimposed equilateral triangles; concave courtyard front and a spiral lantern.

exemplars.name: Sant'Andrea al Quirinale
exemplars.note: Bernini, 1658-1670. Transverse oval plan with the entrance on the short axis - the compression of the approach is the whole design.

exemplars.name: Piazza San Pietro colonnade
exemplars.note: Bernini, 1656-1667. Two quadrant colonnades of four ranks of Tuscan columns; architecture used to shape an urban void rather than an enclosure.

sources: Rudolf Wittkower, Art and Architecture in Italy 1600-1750, Pelican History of Art
Anthony Blunt, Borromini (1979)
Paolo Portoghesi, The Rome of Borromini: Architecture as Language (1968)
Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola, Regola delli cinque ordini d'architettura (1562)
Christian Norberg-Schulz, Baroque Architecture (1971)

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding: italian-baroque is not in vignola-composite's own applies_to. Bound anyway because this style's own proportional_system states the order 'is retained exactly as Vignola codified it' while only the wall around it deforms -- module fixed, surface dynamic. Composite is the richest of the five and the natural register for the giant order at San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane and Sant'Andrea al Quirinale, matching the brief's own steer toward a richer, more ornamented order for this style.

Judgment binding. Named directly: the Piazza San Pietro colonnade is 'two quadrant colonnades of four ranks of Tuscan columns' in this style's own exemplar note. Bernini's Doric-plain register for shaping urban void rather than enclosing a room.

Judgment binding. An alternate giant-order register, less ornate than Composite, for the church and palazzo fronts where the sculptural intensity is carried by broken pediments and multi-plane column projection (c02) rather than by the capital itself.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Wittkower's own study, which is room-harmonic's authority, is substantially a study of Italian High Renaissance and Baroque interiors, so the fit is closer here than the pack's Palladian phrasing suggests -- though it governs the individual room, not the oval, triangle-and-circle plan geometry that generates the whole building, which is outside anything a room-proportion pack in this library models.

dogtrot-vernacular.name: Dogtrot

revival_periods.note: The open central breezeway has had a substantial second life in Southern regional modernism - Fay Jones, Lake|Flato, Rural Studio - where it is used exactly as the original used it, as a shaded outdoor room that cools the volumes on either side.

geography.hearth: the Tennessee Valley and the southern Appalachian foothills

lineage.note: The dogtrot is a combinatorial move on the pen: two of them under one roof with a gap. Its notching, spans, chimneys and roof are inherited unchanged from the single-pen tradition.

description.short: Two log pens under one continuous roof with an open, unheated passage between them - the coolest place on a Southern farm in August, and the clearest case in American building of a room whose only programme is moving air.
description.long:
The dogtrot solves two problems with one move. The first is structural: a log pen cannot exceed the length of a log a small crew can lift, so a bigger house has to be more than one pen. The second is climatic: in the humid Upland and Deep South, a compact heated house is unbearable for four months of the year. Setting the two pens eight to twelve feet apart and running a single roof and a single floor across the gap solves both at once. The passage draws air by venturi effect between the two masses, its floor stays shaded all day, and it becomes the room where the household actually lives from May to September - where meals are eaten, work is done, tools are kept, and visitors are received. The rooms on either side keep their own gable-end chimneys and their own doors onto the passage. A loft over one or both pens sleeps children, and a rear shed usually appears within a decade.

The conditions are the same frontier conditions that produced the log tradition generally, with heat added. The form spreads with settlement from the Tennessee Valley through Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas and into east Texas between about 1790 and 1860, following the same Scots-Irish and German families who carried log construction down the Great Wagon Road. It appears across the whole social range, which is what makes it interesting: Jacob Wolf built a two-storey hewn-log dogtrot in 1829 at Norfork, Arkansas to serve as the county courthouse, and Sam Houston lived in one at Huntsville, Texas from 1847. It is not a poverty type. It is a climate type that happened to be cheap, and its persistence past the arrival of sawmills - dogtrots were built in frame well into the twentieth century - shows that people were choosing the passage, not merely tolerating it.

What the type reacts against, if anything, is the enclosed Anglo hall. Its nearest relative, the center-passage plan of the Chesapeake, does the same environmental job with a hall that has doors at both ends; the dogtrot simply removes the doors and the walls. It is worth noticing that the two solutions arrive from opposite directions at the same answer, and that the wealthier the builder, the more likely the passage is to be enclosed. That enclosure is in fact the single most common transformation in Southern vernacular architecture: a dogtrot gets its breezeway walled in, gains a front door and a stair, and becomes a center-passage house, which is why so many apparently ordinary Southern farmhouses have a strange room proportion and a pair of chimneys too far apart.

Standing in the passage on a July afternoon is the entire argument. The temperature drop between the yard and the breezeway is real and immediate, and the air is always moving even when the trees are still, because two masses of hot air on either side and a shaded gap between them make a pressure difference that does not need wind. The floor is worn smooth by traffic. Both pen doors stand open and you can see into two rooms at once, which gives the small house an unexpected spatial generosity. Overhead, one continuous roof structure runs across all three volumes, and looking up at the underside you see the whole logic of the type at a glance: two boxes, a gap, one roof, and the gap is the best part.

defining_characteristics: Two log (or later frame) pens under one continuous unbroken roof, separated by an open central passage
Passage open at both ends, unheated, and floored continuously with the pens
Each pen retains its own gable-end chimney and its own door onto the passage
Pens read as separate volumes under a shared roof rather than as one long building
Passage width 8-12 feet, roughly half to two-thirds of a pen's width
Single-pile section throughout so that every room ventilates across
Growth by rear shed, loft, or enclosure of the passage - the last of which converts the type
diagnostic_tells: One roof ridge running continuously over what are visibly three volumes, the middle one open
Chimneys at the two far gable ends and nothing in the middle - the widest chimney spacing of any American folk house of its size
Two front doors facing each other across the passage rather than facing the yard
In an enclosed example: a center hall with an odd floor level or an odd width, chimneys unusually far apart, and weatherboard seams where the passage walls were infilled
Loft openings visible in the passage gable, showing the passage was never intended to be a room

distinguished_from.difference: The double pen has its two rooms contiguous with a shared wall and two front doors on the same facade. The dogtrot separates them with an open passage. The gap is the entire type, and filling it converts one to the other.

Both are two rooms flanking a passage, and an enclosed dogtrot is physically indistinguishable from a center-passage house. The distinction is historical and evidential: an original center-passage house has a stair in the hall and a front door; a converted dogtrot has infill framing, mismatched floor levels, and chimneys spaced for two independent pens.

The parent variant covers single and contiguous double pens. The dogtrot is the specific configuration with an open passage, and it is far more common in the hotter parts of the Upland and Deep South than in the mountains proper.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Log length sets the pens; the passage is dimensioned by airflow and by the width a single roof structure can span between two pens without an intermediate bearing point. The three-part rhythm is a consequence of both.
typical_ratios: Each pen 16-20 feet by 14-18 feet
Passage 8-12 feet wide, typically 0.5-0.7 of a pen's width and never wider than a pen
Overall front length 40-52 feet across the three volumes
Wall height 8-10 log courses, 7-9 feet to the plate
Roof pitch 8:12 to 12:12, one unbroken ridge; eave overhang 24-36 inches
Front porch, where present, 6-8 feet deep across the full front
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: A three-part rhythm of pen-void-pen, in which the void is narrower than the solids. This is the only compositional rule the type has, and it is a strong one: a passage as wide as a pen reads as a breezeway between two buildings rather than as one house.

massing_affinities.note: The type and the massing are the same object.
The immediate sibling, and what a dogtrot becomes when the passage is enclosed.
The starting state: many dogtrots began as one pen and acquired the second pen and passage later.
The end state after enclosure - the single most common type-transformation in Southern vernacular building.

constraints.statement: The passage must be open at both ends, unheated, and unglazed. Screening is tolerable; enclosing it converts the building to a center-passage house and must be recorded as such rather than described as a dogtrot.

Passage width 8-12 feet and never greater than the width of a single pen (typically 0.5-0.7 of it). A passage as wide as or wider than a pen dissolves the composition into two separate buildings under a carport.

test.note: Tests the passage width range (8-12ft). The 'never wider than the pen it separates' relative clause is left as prose -- no vocabulary variable expresses pen width.

constraints.statement: One continuous unbroken ridge must run over both pens and the passage, with the passage floor continuous and at the same level as the pen floors. A break in the ridge, or a stepped floor, destroys the reading of a single house.

Each pen is limited to 16-20 feet between notched corners and carries its own gable-end chimney. A central chimney is impossible in this plan and a single chimney serving both pens indicates a saddlebag, which is a different type.

test.note: Tests that chimney_position excludes interior-central, capturing 'a central chimney is impossible in this plan'. The per-pen span limit (16-20ft between notched corners) has no matching vocabulary variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Orient the passage axis to the prevailing summer breeze - generally south to southwest in the Upland South - and keep it shaded at both ends. The passage is a cooling device before it is a circulation space, and a badly oriented one is merely a hole in the house.

exemplars.name: Jacob Wolf House
exemplars.note: A two-storey hewn-log dogtrot built to serve as the county courthouse; the oldest standing public structure in Arkansas, National Register 1973. Evidence that the type carried institutional as well as domestic use.

exemplars.name: Woodland (Sam Houston's home)
exemplars.location: Sam Houston State University campus, Huntsville, Walker County, Texas
exemplars.note: A classic dogtrot: rectangular log chambers flanking a central breezeway, brick chimneys at the ends, clapboarded over the logs, with a winding stair to the loft.

exemplars.name: Gaineswood (original core)
exemplars.note: Nathan Bryan Whitfield's Greek Revival mansion grew outward from an existing dogtrot log house between 1843 and 1861 - the type as substrate, and a useful demonstration that a folk plan can survive under any amount of applied classicism. Built in campaigns 1843-1861.

sources: Henry Glassie, 'The Types of the Southern Mountain Cabin', in Jan Brunvand, The Study of American Folklore (1968)
Terry G. Jordan, American Log Buildings: An Old World Heritage (1985)
Fred Kniffen, 'Folk Housing: Key to Diffusion', Annals of the Association of American Geographers 55 (1965)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Jacob Wolf House'

proportion_packs.note: The type IS a derived_rule of this pack, almost too neatly to need restating: log-module's circulation_parti rule computes a ten-foot passage bounded above by the plate log -- 'a passage wider than the module cannot be roofed continuously without a splice, so it does not happen' -- which is exactly this node's own hard constraint (c02, passage never as wide as the pen it separates) and its own governing_logic ('the passage is dimensioned by airflow and by the width a single roof structure can span between two pens'). Pen dimension, per-pen gable-end chimney, notch geometry and roof pitch all inherit unchanged from the single-pen tradition per the node's own lineage note, so no second pack is needed for them. Bound alone for the same reason as appalachian-log-house: the type has no applied proportional system. Its later frame-built examples -- the node notes dogtrots 'were built in frame well into the twentieth century' -- still carry log-module's dimensions, because, per the pack's own closing note, 'the module survives even where the log does not': the plan outlived the material by two or three generations, so log-module remains the right pack to bind even on a frame dogtrot.

craftsman.name: Craftsman

geography.hearth: Pasadena and Los Angeles, California, with the transmission apparatus centred on Eastwood, New York

lineage.note: Craftsman is the builder-vernacular settlement of the American reform movement: its ideology reduced to a set of executable moves.

Parent one of four. Morris supplies the ethic, Voysey the long low roof, the sweeping eave, the roughcast wall, and the horizontal band of casements. The transmission is textual: Stickley's The Craftsman reprinted British theory and British plates beside American plans.

Parent two of four. The Anglo-American chalet fashion of the 1850s-1870s, propagated by Downing and by the picturesque cottage books, is where the exposed purlin, the projecting gable-end beam, and the knee brace enter American practice. Craftsman inherits the chalet's habit of showing the roof's structure at the gable end and drops its jigsawn balustrade.

Parents three and four arrive together on this edge. The American shingle and bungalow substrate supplies the continuous skin, the wrapping porch, and the hearth-centred open plan; and it is through this Californian and eastern-seaboard channel that Japanese timber architecture reaches the style. The Japanese parent has no node in this graph because it lies outside the traditions modelled here, but it is a true fourth parent: the Centennial Exposition of 1876 and the Ho-o-den at the 1893 Columbian Exposition gave Charles and Henry Greene the exposed and shaped beam end, the layered horizontal roof, the deep sheltering eave, and the treatment of a timber member as an object to be finished on all four faces.
Explicitly and commercially: Craftsman plan books sold themselves against the 'gingerbread' house their buyers had grown up in.

description.short: The American Arts and Crafts programme reduced to a reproducible builder's grammar of low gable roofs, deep exposed eaves, battered porch piers and hearth-centred open plans, distributed nationally by Gustav Stickley's The Craftsman and by the plan-book and mail-order trade that copied it.
description.long:
Craftsman is a four-parent hybrid and unusually legible as one, because each parent contributed a different part of the building. From British Arts and Crafts, and specifically from Voysey by way of the illustrated press, come the long low roof, the sweeping eave, the roughcast or shingled wall treated as a continuous skin, and above all the ethical claim that a house should show how it is made. From the Swiss chalet fashion that ran through Anglo-American picturesque building between the 1850s and the 1870s come the specific members: the exposed purlin running through the gable, the projecting ridge beam, the knee brace under the eave, the gable-end truss displayed as a face.
