From Japanese timber architecture — encountered by American architects at the Centennial Exposition of 1876 and, decisively for Charles and Henry Greene, at the Ho-o-den of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition — come the shaped and rounded beam end, the layered horizontal roof planes, the eave deep enough to become a spatial element rather than a trim detail, and the discipline of finishing a timber on all four faces because all four will be seen. From the American Shingle Style and the bungalow tradition already at hand come the plan: an open hearth-centred living room, a wrapping porch, a low horizontal spread, and a single continuous wall surface.

The transmission mechanism deserves naming precisely, because it is the reason a style invented by a handful of Californian architects for wealthy clients became the default American house within a decade. Gustav Stickley's magazine The Craftsman, published from 1901 to 1916, printed measured floor plans, elevations, and construction details free to subscribers, alongside the reform theory that justified them. Stickley collected the plans as Craftsman Homes (1909) and More Craftsman Homes (1912). The mail-order house companies — Aladdin from 1906, Sears Modern Homes from 1908 — and a shelf of competing plan books by Henry L. Wilson, Radford, and the Los Angeles bungalow publishers then copied the grammar wholesale and sold it as a precut package with the nails counted. What happened next is the single most instructive fact in this branch of the graph: a style built on the principle that ornament must be made by hand at the site was successfully productized, shipped in a boxcar, and assembled by a homeowner. It was the first fully specified traditional kit of parts, and it worked, because the grammar was reducible to a small number of enforceable rules.

What Craftsman reacts against is the millwork catalog Queen Anne, and its argument is economic as much as aesthetic: the same money spent on turned spindles and sawn brackets buys, in a Craftsman house, a deeper porch, a bigger fireplace, and better wood. The rhetoric of the plan books is relentless on this point. It is also, quietly, a house designed for a household without servants — the kitchen moves closer to the dining space, the built-in buffet replaces the sideboard, and the back stair disappears.

Standing before one, the first thing to register is the shadow. The eave projects two and a half to three feet, and it does so on the rake as well as the eave, so the whole wall sits in a band of shade with the rafter tails and knee braces reading as dark strokes against it. The porch is not a threshold but a room, seven to nine feet deep, roofed by the main roof continuing down rather than by a shed tacked on beneath it, and carried on piers that visibly widen toward the ground. Inside, the ceiling is low and beamed, the trim is broad and flat and the colour of the wood it is made of, and the fireplace is not a feature of the room but the reason the room is shaped the way it is. The materials change as they go down the wall — shingle to clinker brick to river boulder — and each change happens where something structural changes. Nothing is painted white. Nothing is symmetrical. And nothing on the building is there that is not also doing something.

defining_characteristics: Low-pitched gabled roof, front- or side-facing, with eave and rake overhangs of 24 to 36 inches on all sides
Structural members left exposed and doing visible work: rafter tails, purlins running through the gable, knee braces, and beam ends
A porch of habitable depth framed under the primary roof — either the main roof continuing down or a gable subordinate to it — never a shed applied below the eave
Porch supports as square or battered piers standing on heavy masonry bases of stone, clinker brick, or river rock
Stacked natural materials expressing base, wall, and gable, with each transition at a structural line
Horizontally banded windows, characteristically double-hung with a divided upper sash over a single-light lower sash
Interior organized on a hearth, with beamed ceiling, plate rail, and built-in seating and cabinetry fixing the plan against rearrangement
One or one and a half storeys, with habitable roof space reached by a dormer rather than a full second floor
diagnostic_tells: Four-over-one or three-over-one double-hung sash — vertical muntins in the upper sash only. This single detail separates Craftsman from every neighbour in the graph.
Battered porch piers: the support is wider at the bottom than at the top, on a base wider still
Knee braces under the gable overhang, and rafter tails visible along the eave, both structurally continuous
The porch roof is geometrically part of the main roof, not a separate element pinned to the wall below it
River boulder, arroyo stone, or over-fired clinker brick used for chimney, porch base, and foundation — deliberately irregular masonry against regular woodwork

distinguished_from.difference: Prairie hides its structure behind clean soffits and continuous planes and uses a hipped roof and casement bands; Craftsman displays its structure and uses gables and double-hung sash. Prairie is smooth and abstract, Craftsman is textured and rustic.

The parent node is a movement covering furniture, printing, metalwork, and several architectural expressions including Prairie. Craftsman is one architectural expression of it, the one that became a national builder's vernacular.

Colonial Revival is symmetrical, painted, and classically detailed with real orders; Craftsman is asymmetrical, stained, and has no orders at all. Where they meet — a Craftsman body with a classical porch — the building belongs to neither and usually to a builder's catalog.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Two horizontal datums and one structural rhythm. The porch beam sets a low datum, the aligned window and door heads set a high datum, and the exposed rafters declare the framing bay at 16 or 24 inches on centre. Because the system is dimensional rather than ratio-derived, it is directly encodable: the rules are all absolute lengths, which is why the plan-book trade could transmit it without transmitting any theory.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 3:12 to 6:12
Eave and rake overhang 24 to 36 in, equal on all four sides
Porch depth 7 to 9 ft clear; porch width not less than 60 percent of the facade
Porch pier base width 24 to 36 in, tapering to 12 to 18 in at the beam
Wall plate 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft 0 in; window and door heads at 6 ft 8 in to 7 ft 0 in on a single datum
Upper sash divided into three or four vertical lights; lower sash undivided
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Openings gathered into groups of two or three between exposed posts, with wide unbroken wall between groups; the group spacing follows the framing bay, not a facade module.

massing_affinities.note: The default vessel; the great majority of surviving Craftsman houses are this skeleton.
A single raised sleeping room above the bungalow body, its own low hipped roof floating above the main one.
The urban narrow-lot answer; requires special care because the foursquare's verticality fights the style's horizontal reading.
Occurs in transitional houses of 1905-1912 where a builder reskinned a Queen Anne skeleton; the result is legible but rarely coherent.

constraints.statement: Eave and rake overhang shall be between 24 and 36 in, and shall be equal on eave and rake within 6 in. An overhang under 18 in disqualifies the node.

test.note: Tests the overhang range. The eave-to-rake equality tolerance (within 6 in) has no comparator vocabulary variable and stays prose; the 'under 18 in disqualifies' clause is subsumed by (and looser than) the tested lower bound of 24 in.

constraints.statement: The porch roof must be framed under the primary roof — either as a continuation of the main slope or as a subordinate gable tied into it. A shed roof applied to the wall below the main eave is forbidden.
Principal roof pitch between 3:12 and 6:12.
Porch supports must be square posts or battered piers on masonry bases not less than 24 in wide. Turned columns, fluted columns, and classical capitals are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the masonry base width. The prohibition on turned/fluted columns and classical capitals is a categorical list and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Divided lights occur in the upper sash only; the lower sash is a single light. Muntins are vertical, three or four per upper sash, and not less than 1 1/8 in wide.

test.note: Tests the minimum muntin width. The sash light pattern (divided upper sash only, three or four vertical muntins, single-light lower sash) is a categorical description with no fixed pattern id to test against and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Gamble House
exemplars.note: Greene and Greene, 1908-09. The style's upper limit, where the Japanese parent is most visible in the shaped beam ends and layered roofs.

exemplars.name: Robert R. Blacker House
exemplars.note: Greene and Greene. Larger and earlier than the Gamble, with the timber grammar at its most explicitly Japanese.

exemplars.name: Craftsman Farms (the Log House)
exemplars.note: Gustav Stickley's own house, 1908-1911 — the publisher of the style building outside its Californian idiom.

exemplars.name: Bungalow Heaven Landmark District
exemplars.note: More than 800 modest Craftsman houses built c. 1900-1930; designated 1989. The style as it was actually inhabited, at plan-book scale.

sources: Gustav Stickley, Craftsman Homes (1909) and More Craftsman Homes (1912)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Clay Lancaster, The American Bungalow, 1880-1930 (1985)
Robert Winter, The California Bungalow (1980)
Edward R. Bosley, Greene and Greene (2000)

proportion_packs.note: The exterior composer for a style whose own proportional_system is 'two horizontal datums and one structural rhythm' -- porch beam, aligned head height, exposed framing bay -- which is this pack's datum_stack assembly by another name, and whose roof_form rule (the dominant roof must cover at least half the elevation's width, or 'no roof is in charge') is the mechanism behind this node's own hard constraint that the porch roof must be framed under the primary roof rather than applied beneath the eave (c02). Given role 'primary' because, unlike the classical styles in this corpus, Craftsman's module really is compositional -- the low dominant roof, the eave shadow -- rather than a fixed board size; the board size is trim-craftsman's business and belongs to the interior.

The interior millwork system this style actually built to: the pack's own sources are Craftsman's own transmission apparatus (Stickley's Craftsman Homes, the Universal Millwork Catalog, the Sears and Aladdin trim schedules), so binding it here is closer to citing the style's primary sources than to applying an analogous system. Governs the picture rail as the room's datum, the three-board casing family (1x4 leg, 1x6 head, 1x8 base), and the explicit prohibition on a mitred casing or a sprung classical crown that the movement was founded to object to.

cotswold-vernacular.name: Cotswold Vernacular

revival_periods.note: Gimson and the Barnsleys settled at Sapperton from 1893 and learned the tradition from working Cotswold masons and wallers — one of the very few revivals that reacquired a craft rather than copying a look.
Exported to America and the English suburbs as the storybook cottage, with cement-rendered walls and swept synthetic 'thatch' or false-graded slate.

geography.hearth: The Jurassic oolitic limestone belt of Gloucestershire, west Oxfordshire, north Wiltshire and south Worcestershire

lineage.note: Direct craft survival. The mullion, the hood mould and the Perpendicular window head are still being cut by Cotswold masons in 1700, two centuries after the style ended everywhere else. The wool churches — Northleach, Chipping Campden, Cirencester — are the source, and the masons who built them worked on the houses next.
The four-centred doorhead, the label mould and the gabled manor front reach the Cotswold builder through the Tudor gentry house and are then repeated, unchanged, for a hundred and fifty years.

description.short: A limestone building culture in which walls, roof, gutters, gateposts and field boundaries all come out of the same quarry, and a Perpendicular Gothic window detail survives in working use until the eighteenth century.
description.long:
The Cotswolds sit on a belt of Jurassic oolitic limestone that is soft enough to cut with a saw when freshly quarried and hardens on exposure, and which splits along its bedding planes into thin flat slabs. Both properties matter. The first gave a whole district cheap dressed stone for mullions, jambs, kneelers and copings; the second gave it a roofing material — the Cotswold stone slate, quarried at Stonesfield and elsewhere and traditionally split by leaving the 'pendle' out over winter to let frost do the work. Almost every characteristic of the tradition follows from these two facts. Because stone slates are heavy and small, the roof must be pitched steeply, generally 50 to 55 degrees, and the slates must be graded — large courses at the eaves, diminishing to small at the ridge — which is both structurally sensible and the single most beautiful thing about a Cotswold roof.

The economy that paid for it was wool. Between roughly 1350 and 1550 the Cotswold fleece was the best in Europe, and the money went into churches, market halls, clothiers' houses and rows of weavers' cottages. When the trade declined, the district became poor and stayed poor, which is why so much survives: nobody could afford to rebuild in brick during the eighteenth century, and nobody had a reason to demolish in the nineteenth. The result is a landscape of buildings in one material, weathering to one range of colours — honey and gold in the north around Broadway and Stanton, greyer and cooler to the south around Tetbury.

The tradition is not reacting against anything; it is simply continuing. What makes it architecturally serious is its conservatism. A Cotswold house of 1680 still has ovolo-moulded stone mullions, a hood mould over the window, a steeply gabled dormer rising through the eaves with its face flush with the wall below, kneelers at the foot of each gable and a coping raised above the roof plane with a ball or ogee finial. That is a Perpendicular vocabulary being used, correctly and without irony, a century and a half after the Renaissance reached England. When Ernest Gimson and the Barnsley brothers moved to Sapperton in the 1890s they were not reviving a dead style; they were apprenticing themselves to masons who were still building this way, and it is that continuity which gives the Cotswold contribution to Arts and Crafts its unusual authority.

The experience is of weight and of light behaving oddly. Walls are 500 to 700 mm thick, so windows sit in deep reveals and rooms are dim near the walls and bright at the openings; the stone's surface is granular enough that in low sun the whole wall seems to hold light rather than reflect it. There are no eaves to speak of — the verge is closed with a coping laid tight over the slates — so the building has a hard, clean edge against the sky, and the mass reads as carved from a single block. Inside, the stone is cold to the hand at any season, and the deep window seat cut into the reveal is the warmest place in the room, which is exactly where anyone who lives in one of these houses will be found sitting.

defining_characteristics: Walls of coursed or random oolitic limestone rubble, 500-700 mm thick, in lime mortar, with dressed ashlar reserved for mullions, jambs, lintels, quoins, kneelers and copings
Roofs of Cotswold stone slate, graded from large courses at the eaves to small at the ridge, at a pitch of 48-55 degrees
Stone-mullioned windows, ovolo- or cavetto-moulded, of two to five lights, with a hood mould or drip over the head and iron casements with leaded lights
Gabled dormers rising through the eaves with their faces flush with the wall below, so that they read as gables of the wall rather than as boxes on the roof
Gables finished with kneelers at the foot and a coping raised above the roof plane, frequently with a ball, ogee or finial at the apex
Massive stone chimney stacks, generally on the gable ends, with moulded caps and rising well above the ridge
Little or no eaves overhang, and no barge boards: the roof edge is closed with stone and the mass reads as unbroken
diagnostic_tells: Graded stone slates diminishing course by course from eaves to ridge — visible from a hundred metres and impossible to fake convincingly with a uniform slate
Wall dormers whose front face is continuous with the wall below, breaking the eaves line, rather than dormers set back on the roof slope
Kneeler stones at the base of every gable and a coping standing proud of the slates, so gables have a raised stone edge instead of a timber barge board
Ovolo-moulded stone mullions with a hood mould above, still in use on buildings of 1680 and later — a Perpendicular detail running two centuries past its own period
Everything in the district is the same stone: house, boundary wall, gatepost, barn, church, and the dry stone field walls running up the hill behind

distinguished_from.difference: Same social level, different geology. The lowland cottage is timber frame, cob or clay lump under thatch, with low eaves, small casements in shallow wooden frames and a soft, swept silhouette. The Cotswold house is stone with dressed stone openings under a hard graded slate roof, and it has crisp edges everywhere the cottage has rounded ones.

The revival takes the picture and drops the geology: cement render or thin stone veneer over frame, uniform machine-cut slates or swept composition shingles imitating graded stone, dormers set back on the slope, and wall thicknesses of 150 mm where the original has 600.

Overlapping but not identical. Arts and Crafts is a self-conscious movement with named architects, an ethic and a national reach; Cotswold vernacular is an anonymous regional building practice. The Sapperton group is where the two genuinely meet, and their work should be classified by intent rather than by appearance.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Material logic, not applied proportion. Wall thickness is set by rubble construction, roof pitch by the size and weight of the stone slate, opening width by the span of an available stone lintel, and window subdivision by the mullion light. Nothing is drawn; everything is set out on site.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 48-55 degrees, with 50 degrees the practical norm for stone slate
Wall thickness 500-700 mm, giving reveals of 250-450 mm at openings
Mullion light 300-450 mm wide by 600-900 mm high, in leaded quarries of roughly 100 x 150 mm
Window overall proportion horizontal: a three-light window is typically 1.5:1 to 2:1 wide to high
Storey height 2.1-2.6 m at ground, 1.9-2.3 m above, with an eaves height of 4.0-5.0 m for two storeys
Chimney height above ridge 0.9-1.5 m; stack width 900-1400 mm
Stone slate courses graded from 550-600 mm at the eaves to 150 mm at the ridge
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Additive and irregular. Openings are placed where rooms need them, and a facade acquires symmetry only when a gentry client asked for it — which in the Cotswolds happens from about 1620 and produces the characteristic gabled, near-symmetrical manor front.

massing_affinities.note: The two-cell house with a lobby-entry stack, the standard yeoman and weaver's plan through the whole period.
The gabled Cotswold manor — Owlpen, Snowshill, Chastleton — is an E- or half-H plan in stone.
Weavers' terraces such as Arlington Row, party-walled and continuous along the street or the stream.
Descending ranges from house to byre are common in the smaller upland farmsteads.
The one-cell cottage, usually later subdivided or extended.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch not less than 48 degrees where stone slate is used, and the structure must be sized for a dead load of roughly 100-140 kg per square metre — three to four times a modern tile roof.

test.note: Tests the roof-pitch clause. The dead-load figure (100-140 kg/m2) has no matching structural-load variable in the vocabulary and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Slate courses must be graded from large at the eaves to small at the ridge. A uniform course size destroys the roof and with it the whole reading of the building.
Openings are spanned by a stone lintel or a relieving arch and are therefore limited to roughly 1.8 m clear; wider openings must be subdivided by structural mullions, not by glazing bars.

test.note: 1.8 m converted to 5.9 ft ('roughly 1.8 m' in the source). The requirement to subdivide wider openings with structural mullions stays prose.

constraints.statement: No barge boards and no eaves overhang beyond about 75 mm. Gables are closed with kneelers and a raised coping; verges are bedded in mortar.

test.note: Tests the eaves-overhang ceiling. The no-barge-boards rule and the kneeler/coping/mortar-bedded-verge detailing are categorical and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Lime mortar and limewash only. Cement pointing and impermeable render trap moisture in a rubble wall and will spall the stone within a generation.

exemplars.name: Arlington Row
exemplars.note: Built as a monastic wool store in 1380 and converted to weavers' cottages in the late seventeenth century. A party-walled terrace of steeply pitched graded stone slate roofs and wall dormers, the type's most photographed statement.

exemplars.name: Chipping Campden Market Hall
exemplars.note: Built in 1627 by Sir Baptist Hicks for the sale of cheese, butter and poultry. An open arcaded hall of local stone with a graded slate roof and gabled bays — the district's civic vocabulary in its clearest form.

exemplars.name: Owlpen Manor
exemplars.note: A gabled Cotswold manor developed between roughly 1450 and 1616 around a medieval hall, with mullioned and transomed windows, kneelered gables and a Great Chamber — the vernacular reaching gentry scale without changing its details.

exemplars.name: Snowshill Manor
exemplars.note: A late medieval and Tudor manor house whose principal facade was refronted around 1720 in Cotswold stone with sash windows — a useful demonstration of how the tradition absorbed Georgian fashion without changing material or roof.

sources: R. W. Brunskill, Traditional Buildings of Britain (1981)
Alec Clifton-Taylor, The Pattern of English Building (1962)
Edwin Gunn and others, Cotswold Stone Houses (Ancient Monuments Society and later editions)
Nikolaus Pevsner and David Verey, The Buildings of England: Gloucestershire (Cotswolds volume)
Mary Greensted, The Arts and Crafts Movement in the Cotswolds (1993)

proportion_packs.note: cotswold-vernacular is named directly in room-vernacular's applies_to. governing_logic states plainly that dimensions here come from 'material logic, not applied proportion,' which is exactly what room-vernacular reconstructs from measured Anglo-American and British vernacular fabric rather than from a treatise: room breadth capped by joist span, area by hearth reach, depth by daylight. The daylight-depth cap is especially apt here given the deep-set windows the pack's own text describes ('windows sit in deep reveals and rooms are dim near the walls').

cotswold-vernacular is named directly in timber-bay's applies_to, which is worth flagging as slightly counter-intuitive: this is a masonry wall tradition (500-700 mm coursed limestone rubble), not a framed one, so the bay module does not set the wall the way it does at english-medieval-timber-frame. It is bound anyway, low and optional, because the roof and floor carpentry inside a Cotswold house — common rafters, floor joists — is still cut and spaced by the same oak-bay logic as its timber-framed neighbours, and the pack's own applies_to already reflects that. Wall material and coursing are governed by the style's own text, not by this pack.

continental-baroque-neoclassical.name: Continental Baroque & Neoclassical

description.short: The French-led sequence from Baroque grandeur through Neoclassical restraint to the Beaux-Arts system that trained a generation of American architects.
description.long:
France took the Italian classical inheritance and made it a state apparatus: an academy, a curriculum, a hierarchy of building types, and a method of composition taught by competition. The Baroque phase pursued theatrical spatial effect; the Neoclassical reaction pursued archaeological correctness and structural honesty; the Beaux-Arts synthesis systematized both into a teachable design process built on parti, poché, and axial hierarchy.

For American residential architecture this family matters chiefly through the Ecole des Beaux-Arts, where Richardson, Hunt, and hundreds of others trained. The eclectic revivals of 1880–1940 are not naive antiquarianism; they are the product of a rigorous compositional education applied to borrowed vocabularies.

defining_characteristics: Composition taught as a formal discipline: parti, axis, hierarchy, poché
State and academy as patrons and standard-setters
Archaeological correctness as a competing value against expressive effect
Building types codified and ranked

appalachian-log-house.name: Appalachian Log House

revival_periods.note: Recovered twice: first by the Appalachian craft-revival settlement schools and the CCC-era park reconstructions of the 1930s, then by the second-home log industry, which reproduces the silhouette with milled round logs, cathedral ceilings and window walls that the structural system cannot honestly support.

geography.hearth: the Great Valley of Virginia and the southern Blue Ridge

lineage.note: The technique travelled south from the Pennsylvania backcountry down the Great Wagon Road with Scots-Irish and German families between about 1730 and 1780. The notching is German; the plan vocabulary the Scots-Irish applied to it is Anglo.

description.short: The hewn-log single or double pen of the southern mountains: half-dovetail notched oak or chestnut, a stone gable-end chimney, a loft under a steep riven-shingle roof, and an expansion grammar that produced every named Upland South folk house type.
description.long:
The Appalachian log house is the most persistent and best-documented expression of American log building, partly because the technique survived here into the twentieth century and partly because the National Park Service preserved several hundred examples when it emptied the Smokies in the 1930s. The canonical form is a single pen roughly eighteen by twenty feet: walls of eight to ten courses of hewn oak, poplar or chestnut, half-dovetail notched at the corners so every joint sheds water outward, chinked with split-wood spalls and clay or lime, floored in riven puncheon or sawn boards, and covered by a steep roof of hand-split shingles on pole rafters. A stone chimney stands at one gable end, usually outside the wall line, and a loft reached by a corner stair or ladder sleeps the children. One door, one or two very small windows. That is the whole house, and for a great many families in 1830 it was the whole house for a lifetime.

What makes it a design system rather than a hut is the expansion grammar, which is unusually explicit. Because the pen cannot exceed the length of a log two to four people can lift, every increase in size is a combinatorial move on pens: a second pen against the first with a shared chimney (saddlebag); a second pen with its own end chimney and its own front door (double pen); two pens with an open roofed passage between them (dogtrot); a second storey of logs above the first; a rear shed or ell in frame. Henry Glassie's typology of the southern mountain cabin is essentially a grammar of these moves, and it is directly usable as a generative rule set: given a pen and a family, the possible next states are enumerable. This is the property that makes the node valuable to a kit-of-parts system, and it is why the constraint list here is about spans and notches rather than about mouldings.

The conditions are those of settlement in a landscape with abundant hardwood, no roads worth the name, no cash and no sawmills. Scots-Irish and German families moving south from Pennsylvania after 1730 into the Great Valley and then into the coves and hollows of the Blue Ridge and the Cumberlands found a place where timber was the only surplus material and where every alternative building system required something they could not obtain. Log building requires an axe, a broadaxe, a froe, an auger and neighbours. It also produced a house that was warm - a nine-inch solid hardwood wall has enough thermal mass to ride out a mountain night on a banked fire - and that could be built between clearing in spring and frost in autumn. The isolation that made the technique necessary is also what kept it alive for a century after the lowlands had gone to frame, and what made it, by the 1890s, a marker of poverty in the eyes of everybody outside the mountains and a marker of self-sufficiency to everybody inside them.

Standing inside one at Cades Cove or Little Greenbrier, the sensory facts are the wall and the silence. The hewn faces carry the scallop of the broadaxe, and low sun rakes across them so the whole surface reads as a shallow relief. The chinking is a bright band between dark courses and it is the only light-coloured thing in the room. Sound goes nowhere. The single window is small enough that on an overcast day the fire is the light source, and the room organises itself around the hearth in a way that no evenly-lit room ever does. Outside, the eave hangs out two or three feet to keep water off the chinking, the chimney stands proud of the gable in field stone laid without mortar above the firebox, and the roof line is steep because riven shingles will not shed at a low pitch. Nothing about the building is decorative and almost every visible feature is the direct expression of a constraint, which is why it survives being photographed so much better than most American architecture.

defining_characteristics: Single or double pen of hewn hardwood logs, half-dovetail or V-notched at the corners, walls 6-9 inches thick after hewing
Pen dimension 16-20 feet by 14-18 feet, set by log handling limits
Gable-end chimney of field stone, usually standing outside the wall plane, with a stone or clay-and-stick stack
Loft over the single ground-floor room, reached by a boxed corner stair or ladder, lit by a small gable opening
Steep roof (9:12 to 12:12) of riven shakes or shingles on pole rafters or purlins, with deep overhangs protecting the chinking
Very small window openings, cut after the wall was raised, set well clear of the notched corners
Growth by pen combination - saddlebag, double pen, dogtrot, two-storey, rear shed - never by lengthening a log wall
diagnostic_tells: Half-dovetail notching with the log ends sloping outward and downward - the southern mountain signature, distinct from the square notching of the Ozarks and the V-notch of Pennsylvania
Chimney standing entirely outside the gable wall, tapering in field stone
Eave overhang of 24-36 inches on a building with no other refinement whatever
Openings that stop at least two feet short of every corner
Round pole joists with bark intact carrying the loft floor

distinguished_from.difference: The dogtrot is a specific two-pen configuration with an open central passage, and it is common enough in the same region to be modelled separately. A single or contiguous double pen with no open passage belongs here.

Nordic work scribes round or squared logs to a tight chinkless fit, uses steeper roofs and often a full second storey of logs. Appalachian work hews two faces flat and relies on a 1-3 inch chinked gap, which is faster and requires less skill - a deliberate simplification, not a degradation.

The parent node covers the whole continental tradition including Pennsylvania, the Ozarks, Texas and the Old Northwest, whose notching, pitches and plan types differ. This variant is the southern mountain expression specifically.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Entirely material-determined. Log length sets plan dimension, log diameter sets course height, riven-shingle performance sets roof pitch, and the notch sets the corner. There is no applied proportional system and adding one falsifies the type.
typical_ratios: Pen 16-20 feet by 14-18 feet; a near-square plan is normal
Wall 8-10 courses, 7-9 feet to the plate; log course 8-14 inches
Hewn wall thickness 6-9 inches; chinking gap 1-3 inches recessed 1/2-1 inch behind the log face
Roof pitch 9:12 to 12:12; eave overhang 24-36 inches
Door 30-36 inches wide by 5.5-6.5 feet tall; original windows often under 4 square feet
Chimney breast 5-7 feet wide at the base, battering to 2-3 feet at the stack
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: None. Openings are placed by use and by the corner-clearance rule; the apparent front 'symmetry' of a double pen is an artefact of two identical pens, not a compositional decision.

massing_affinities.note: The single pen.
Two equal pens with two front doors and two end chimneys - the standard second stage.
Two-storey log I-houses occur where a family prospered without leaving the technique; they are almost always weatherboarded within a generation.
Where the two pens are deliberately unequal, giving the Anglo social gradient in log.

constraints.statement: No log wall may exceed 20 feet between notched corners; 16-18 feet is normal. Larger enclosures must be built as additional pens. This single rule generates every type in the family and must not be relaxed.

test.note: Tests the hard 20 ft ceiling. The 16-18 ft normal-range and 'built as additional pens' guidance stay prose.

constraints.statement: Corners must be half-dovetail or V-notched with the joint sloping outward to shed water, log ends projecting 2-6 inches beyond the joint. Square-notched corners require pegging and a deeper eave; saddle notching belongs to round-log work and to a different region.

Roof pitch 9:12 to 12:12 with eave and rake overhangs of at least 24 inches. Riven shingles will not shed below 9:12, and the overhang is what keeps water out of the chinking; a clipped eave destroys the wall within a decade.

test.note: Tests the 9:12-12:12 roof-pitch range. Eave/rake overhang (at least 24in) is also cleanly testable via eave_projection_in but is left as prose here since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Openings must stop at least 24 inches short of any notched corner and must be framed with pegged jambs against cut log ends. Glazed areas larger than about 12 square feet in a single log wall are structurally dishonest to the system.

Chimney at the gable end, outside the wall plane where possible, of laid field stone with a base 5-7 feet wide battering to a 2-3 foot stack. An interior or centred chimney consumes the only room the pen has.

test.note: Tests the gable-end-exterior chimney position ('where possible' softens this to a preference, reflected in the constraint's soft severity rather than in the test). Chimney base/stack width dimensions (5-7ft base, 2-3ft stack) have no vocabulary variable and stay prose.

exemplars.name: John Oliver Place
exemplars.location: Cades Cove, Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Blount County, Tennessee
exemplars.note: Built in the 1820s on the site of an 1818 cabin; the oldest surviving structure on the Cades Cove loop, a single pen with exterior stone chimney and loft.

exemplars.name: Walker Sisters Place
exemplars.location: Little Greenbrier, Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Sevier County, Tennessee
exemplars.note: Hewn logs with half-dovetail notching, stone-and-mud chimneys, and a circa-1838 McFalls cabin dismantled and reassembled as a kitchen wing in the 1870s - the expansion grammar documented in one building. National Register 1976.

exemplars.name: Carter Shields Cabin
exemplars.location: Cades Cove, Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Blount County, Tennessee
exemplars.note: Late nineteenth-century single-pen with a frame addition; useful as evidence that the technique was still current in the mountains sixty years after it had died in the lowlands.

sources: Henry Glassie, 'The Types of the Southern Mountain Cabin', in Jan Brunvand, The Study of American Folklore (1968)
Terry G. Jordan, American Log Buildings: An Old World Heritage (1985)
Michael Ann Williams, Homeplace: The Social Use and Meaning of the Folk Dwelling in Southwestern North Carolina (1991)
National Park Service, List of Classified Structures, Great Smoky Mountains National Park
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)

proportion_packs.note: The style's single generative fact -- no log wall exceeds 20 ft between notched corners -- is this pack's own module, and the node's own hard constraint (c01) restates it almost verbatim. Every other proportion in the house is a derived_rule of this one pack keyed to the half-dovetail/V-notch southern-mountain data specifically: pen dimension (log length less notch overhang and wall thickness), wall-log count to the plate, notch overhang and depth by type, gable-end chimney width, dogtrot passage width where present, and porch depth. Bound alone, with no facade, opening or trim pack: the node's own proportional_system says plainly that there is no applied proportional system here and that adding one falsifies the type, and log-module's own window_surround_wood rule states outright that 'there is no architrave, no backband and no casing on the outside of a log wall... applying a moulded surround is the commonest single error in log revival work' -- which makes binding opening-proportion or sash-light actively wrong here rather than merely unnecessary.

carpenter-gothic.name: Carpenter Gothic

geography.hearth: Hudson Valley and the Connecticut Valley

lineage.note: The wooden, small-budget, carpenter-executed expression of the parent style; quantitatively it is almost the whole of the parent's built population.
The frame, the plan, and the door and window stock come straight from the Greek Revival carpenter's kit; only the sawn ornament is new.
Cusping, tracery, and the lancet head are quoted at third hand, translated from stone into 1-inch pine board by a band saw.

description.short: Gothic Revival executed entirely in sawn softwood by ordinary carpenters, in which stone tracery becomes pierced board, the buttress becomes a batten, and the whole style is reduced to a purchasable set of profiles.
description.long:
Carpenter Gothic is the moment the Gothic Revival stops being an architect's argument and becomes a product. Downing and Davis supplied plates; the scroll saw supplied the labour; the railroad supplied distribution; and the result was that between roughly 1845 and 1885 a farmer in Iowa or a shipwright in Nova Scotia could buy a bargeboard, a finial, a drip mould, and a pointed sash, nail them to a perfectly ordinary frame house, and own a Gothic cottage. The style is defined less by a set of forms than by a translation rule: every element that was carved from stone in England is here cut from a plank, and the plank is nominally an inch thick, which sets the entire visual character.

The mechanism deserves to be stated exactly. A jig or scroll saw driven by a stationary steam engine, in general workshop use in American towns from the late 1830s, could follow a pierced curvilinear pattern through softwood board at a speed no hand-held fretsaw approached. Machine-cut nails, produced by the hundred million from the 1820s, made attaching that board to a light frame a matter of minutes. Balloon framing let a carpenter with no joinery training raise a wall of nailed studs and then hang whatever profile he liked on it. And the railroad meant the pattern did not have to be local. The American Gothic House in Eldon, Iowa, built in 1881-82, is the perfect specimen of the whole system: an utterly plain gable-front frame cottage with two pointed sash in the gable, and those windows are believed to have been ordered from a Sears catalogue. Grant Wood painted it in 1930 and made it the most reproduced building in the country.

What the mode was reacting against, and what it demonstrates, are two different things. It was reacting, at least in Downing's intention, against the white Greek Revival farmhouse and the doctrine that a house should look like a temple. What it demonstrates is the first full appearance of a condition that has never since gone away: ornament decoupled from structure and construction, produced elsewhere, chosen from a catalogue, and applied. Carpenter Gothic is the earliest American style where the parts list and the building are separable, and every judgement a contemporary kit-of-parts system has to make about which parts may be combined with which was first faced, and mostly not answered, by the carpenters of the 1850s.

The buildings themselves are thin and lively in a way that stone Gothic never is. Board-and-batten siding turns the whole wall into a set of shallow vertical shadow lines that shift as you move; the bargeboard, cut from a single plank, is only an inch deep, so at a raking evening light it reads as pure silhouette and lace against the sky, and at noon it nearly vanishes. There is no mass anywhere in the building. Inside, the ceilings are low, the pointed window in the gable lights a stair or an upstairs bedroom rather than anything grand, and the rooms are the ordinary rooms of an ordinary farmhouse. The whole style lives on the outer inch of the building, which is either its charm or its indictment depending on how much you require of architecture.

defining_characteristics: Light wood frame construction, with every ornamental element sawn from nominal 1 in board stock
Steeply pitched gables, 12:12 or greater, usually with a central gable over the entrance on a symmetrical body
Pierced and cusped bargeboard applied to the rake, the single indispensable element
Pointed, lancet, or ogee-headed sash, generally confined to the principal gable
Vertical board-and-batten siding, or, in later and cheaper examples, plain clapboard with Gothic trim
Turned or chamfered porch posts with sawn brackets and a pierced valance
No masonry ornament of any kind; a Carpenter Gothic building with a carved stone label mould is misidentified
diagnostic_tells: Ornament is flat. Sight along the wall: everything projects less than about two inches, because everything came off a plank

A central gable rising through the eave line of an otherwise symmetrical two-storey farmhouse is the commonest American Carpenter Gothic composition, and separates it from the irregular architect-designed villa
Pointed sash in the gable but square-headed sash everywhere else: the owner bought one Gothic window
Bargeboard patterns repeat on a short module (12 to 24 in) because they were cut from a template
If the vertical siding stops and clapboard begins at a storey line, the house is later and cheaper; true Downing practice runs battens unbroken from water table to eave

distinguished_from.difference: Same parent style, opposite economics. The villa is architect-designed, genuinely irregular in plan, and composed for silhouette from several viewpoints; Carpenter Gothic is a builder's symmetrical box with sawn ornament applied to one or two elevations.

The same operation performed twenty to forty years later with a different catalogue. Folk Victorian applies Italianate brackets and Queen Anne spindlework to a plain folk house; Carpenter Gothic applies pointed sash and bargeboards. Where a house has both, date it by the porch.

The British parent is a masonry tradition with real archaeological scholarship behind it and Pugin's insistence on structural truth; Carpenter Gothic is the exact thing Pugin condemned, an applied scenery of Gothic profiles over a frame that owes nothing to Gothic construction.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by stock lumber and by the saw. Board widths, plank thickness, and pattern-template repeat set every ornamental dimension; the body of the house keeps the symmetrical Greek Revival proportions the carpenter already knew.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 12:12 to 16:12 on the principal and central gables
Bargeboard depth 10 to 18 in, cut from 1 to 1.5 in stock, with pattern repeat 12 to 24 in
Battens 2 to 3 in wide at 12 to 16 in on centre over 8 to 12 in boards
Pointed window head included angle 60 to 75 degrees
Porch post 4x4 to 6x6 chamfered, with sawn brackets 12 to 20 in on the diagonal
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Regular three or five bay body inherited from the Greek Revival farmhouse, interrupted once by the central gable. The irregularity is ornamental, not planimetric.

massing_affinities.note: The two-storey single-pile farmhouse with a central Gothic gable is the most numerous American Carpenter Gothic form.
A hipped roof gives the bargeboard nowhere to go.

constraints.statement: All ornament shall be sawn or turned from wood and shall project not more than 3 in from its ground plane. Cast stone, carved stone, terra cotta, and moulded masonry ornament are forbidden in this variant.

test.note: Tests the projection ceiling. 'Sawn or turned from wood' and the forbidden cast-stone/carved-stone/terra-cotta/moulded-masonry materials are a material-category fact with no matching vocabulary variable and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Principal gable pitch shall be not less than 12:12, and the bargeboard shall run the full rake with a verge overhang of 12 to 24 in so it is read against shadow.

test.note: Tests the gable-pitch minimum. The bargeboard's full-rake run and 12-24 in verge overhang are a separate numeric/qualitative fact the schema's single test object can't also carry, and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Where board-and-batten is used, boards shall be 8 to 12 in wide with 2 to 3 in battens at 12 to 16 in on centre, running unbroken from water table to eave on every elevation that receives them. Mixing board-and-batten and clapboard on one elevation is prohibited.
Pointed or ogee window heads shall be limited to the principal gable, the entrance, and the stair, and to not more than three openings per building. Beyond that the house reads as a chapel.

Bargeboard pattern repeat shall not exceed 24 in, and the same pattern shall be used on every gable of the building. Two different bargeboard patterns on one house is a twentieth-century restoration error.

exemplars.name: Roseland Cottage
exemplars.note: Joseph Collins Wells for Henry Chandler Bowen. Board-and-batten, elaborate bargeboards, and the original saturated pink body colour.

exemplars.name: Henry Delamater House
exemplars.note: Alexander Jackson Davis. Board-and-batten wood frame; an architect-designed cottage that became the template thousands of carpenters copied.

exemplars.name: American Gothic House (Dibble House)
exemplars.note: Built 1881-82. A plain frame cottage with two Gothic sash in the gable, believed bought from a catalogue; the purest demonstration of ornament shipped by rail. Painted by Grant Wood in 1930.

sources: Andrew Jackson Downing, The Architecture of Country Houses (1850)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: Technology and the Picturesque (1978)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the composed elevation as a hierarchy of masses even though Carpenter Gothic is usually a builder's symmetrical box rather than a genuinely irregular villa plan: the two-storey gable-front body is the single dominant mass, and the central gable rising through the eave line (the style's own commonest American composition, per its diagnostic tells) is the one subordinate accent the pack's mass hierarchy needs to register. Read this pack's numbers at the plain end of its range - the composition here is a builder's box wearing ornament, not an architect's irregular massing.

Judgment binding: carpenter-gothic itself is not in this pack's own applies_to list, only its parent gothic-revival-american is. Bound anyway because the style's own lineage record states the door and window stock 'comes straight from the Greek Revival carpenter's kit; only the sawn ornament is new,' and the diagnostic tell is explicit - 'pointed sash in the gable but square-headed sash everywhere else: the owner bought one Gothic window.' That everywhere-else sash is an ordinary Greek-Revival-kit double-hung window and this pack's glass-light module governs it correctly. It does not govern the pointed or ogee gable sash itself, which is a real gap in the library (see report).

Judgment binding: not in the pack's own applies_to. The style's own description could not be plainer about it - 'the rooms are the ordinary rooms of an ordinary farmhouse,' low-ceilinged and small-windowed by later standards. This is exactly the reconstructed 14 ft joist-span room the pack records, not a treatise-derived harmonic shape; room-harmonic would misdescribe a style whose whole point is that the ornament is bought and the house underneath it is unchanged.

andalusian-courtyard-vernacular.name: Andalusian Courtyard Vernacular

revival_periods.note: The Andalusian strain of American Spanish revival — George Washington Smith in Santa Barbara, Addison Mizner in Palm Beach — drawn directly from Byne and Stapley's photographs of Cordoban and Sevillian patios.
Supplies the arcaded patio, the tile stair, the wrought grille and the fountain.
The domestic half of the revival is Andalusian vernacular rather than Spanish monumental architecture.

geography.hearth: Cordoba and Seville

lineage.note: Direct and continuous: the casa-patio of Cordoba is the domestic architecture of al-Andalus, inhabited and rebuilt without interruption after 1236. The court, the zaguan, the water, the whitewash and the blind street wall are not quotations; the houses were never abandoned.

The Roman peristyle house at Italica and Corduba is the same diagram, and southern Spain is the one part of Europe where it never stopped being built. The Islamic court house is a development of the Roman one on the same ground, not a replacement of it.
The tile dado, the brick arcade, the carved plaster over the zaguan arch and the timber gallery ceilings are Mudejar work, and the trades that produced them served both palaces and ordinary houses.

description.short: The whitewashed, plant-filled patio house of Cordoba and Seville: a blind street wall, one controlled entry, and an entire domestic life turned inward around a court that is the household's principal room for eight months of the year.
description.long:
The Andalusian casa-patio is the longest continuously inhabited house diagram in Europe, and its logic is entirely climatic. Cordoba is one of the hottest cities in Europe: forty degrees is a normal July afternoon and forty-five is not rare. A house here has three problems — to keep the sun off the fabric, to hold the night's coolness through the day, and to move air after dark — and the courtyard solves all three simultaneously. Deep in proportion to its width, it is in shade for most of the day, so the ranges around it are looking into cool air rather than at a hot wall. Its floor and its planting are watered daily, so evaporation drops the temperature within it by several degrees below the street. And at night, when the air above the city cools faster than the fabric, the court fills with cold air that sinks and sits, providing a reservoir the house draws on all morning. This is a passive-cooling machine that predates the word by two thousand years and outperforms most contemporary attempts at one.

The consequences run all the way through the building. Wall thickness of five to seven hundred millimetres in brick, rubble or tapia gives the thermal lag. The whitewash — cal, lime, renewed by every household every spring — is a performance layer before it is an aesthetic: it reflects roughly eighty per cent of incident solar radiation, it is vapour-open so the wall can dry, and it is mildly antiseptic. The ranges are one room deep so that every room can be cross-ventilated between court and street window. The street wall is nearly blind, and what openings it has are small, high, and grilled with wrought-iron rejas that project from the face so a person can lean out without opening anything. And the entry is a zaguan: a covered passage from the street to the court, closed at the street by a heavy door and at the court by a cancela, a light iron gate. The cancela is one of the great small devices in domestic architecture. Through it, from the street, a passerby can see the whole patio — the plants, the well-head, the tiled floor — and cannot enter. The house shows itself and stays shut.

The social range of the type is very wide and it is worth insisting on. The same diagram produces the palace of a Cordoban noble with a dozen courts, the two-storey house of a merchant, the single-court house of an artisan, and the corral de vecinos, in which twenty families each occupy one or two rooms around a shared patio with a communal well, sink and privy. The corral is the courtyard house as tenement, and it is where the tradition of the patio as a collectively made and collectively watered social space — the thing celebrated every May in the Fiesta de los Patios in Cordoba, inscribed by UNESCO in 2012 — actually comes from. It is not a rich person's amenity that trickled down; it is a poor person's shared room.

Walking through a zaguan in August is one of the great architectural experiences available anywhere. The street is white, glaring, and about thirty-eight degrees. You step into a dark, cool, vaulted passage two metres wide; the temperature drops five or six degrees in two paces and the sound of the street cuts off. At the far end is a rectangle of green and blue: geraniums and jasmine in painted pots hung ten deep on the walls, a stone well-head, wet tiled paving, a fig or an orange tree, and light coming down from above and bouncing off whitewash so that the whole space is filled with a soft glare with no visible source. Then you notice that all the rooms of the house open onto it and that there is no corridor anywhere in the building.

defining_characteristics: One or more courts as the organising void; the house is entered from the court, not from internal corridors
Blind or near-blind street elevation with small, high, iron-grilled (reja) openings
A zaguan — covered entry passage — with a heavy street door and a light iron cancela at the court end
Massive walls of brick, rubble or tapia, 500-700 mm, lime-rendered and annually limewashed
Single-pile ranges around the court, cross-ventilated between court and street
Water and planting required in the court: a well-head, fountain or pila, and potted plants hung on the walls
Court floor and gallery in glazed or unglazed tile, with a tiled dado on the surrounding walls
Curved canal tile roof at a low pitch, or a flat azotea terrace; no deep eaves, because the court does the shading
diagnostic_tells: A patio fully visible from the street through an iron gate, and completely inaccessible
Whitewash carried over every surface including the wall base, with a coloured (usually ochre or blue) skirting band 800-1000 mm high
Wrought-iron window grilles that bow outward from the wall face rather than sitting flush
Plant pots fixed to the courtyard walls in banks, at heights that require a watering cane
Rooms with a door to the court and a small high window to the street, and no other openings

distinguished_from.difference: The palace tradition has epigraphy, muqarnas, stratified surface programmes and a designed sequence of courts. The vernacular casa-patio keeps the diagram and the climate logic and drops the entire ornamental apparatus, replacing it with whitewash, tile and plants.
The mas is outward-facing, orientation-driven and rural, with a working yard rather than a domestic court. Both are thick-walled Mediterranean masonry; the plan diagrams are opposites.

The hacienda uses the same court but at agricultural scale and with a continuous arcaded corredor as the circulation. The Andalusian house is urban, party-walled, and its gallery is usually only on one or two sides.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The patio, dimensioned for shade at latitude 37 degrees north. Court width is set between 0.8 and 1.2 times the height of the enclosing ranges; room depth is set by the span of a timber joist, 3.5-5 m; storey height by what a masonry wall of that thickness carries comfortably. Nothing here is compositional — the whole proportional system is a shading calculation and a joist span.
typical_ratios: Patio 3.5-7 m across; width 0.8-1.2 times enclosing wall height
Court plan roughly 1:1 to 1:1.4
Room depth 3.5-5 m clear; wall thickness 500-700 mm
Roof pitch 20-30 degrees in canal tile, or flat azotea
Street openings under 8 percent of street wall area
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Court arcades of three to five bays a side on marble, stone or brick columns, evenly spaced. The street elevation has no rhythm worth the name and is not meant to.

massing_affinities.note: Four ranges around a court with a blind exterior — the type itself.
These are party-walled urban houses in continuous blocks; the block, not the house, is the unit of the street.
Three ranges with the fourth held by a wall, common on irregular medieval plots.
In the corral de vecinos an open gallery runs the full upper storey around the court and serves as the access to every dwelling.

constraints.statement: Patio width between 0.8 and 1.2 times the height of the enclosing ranges, and between 3.5 and 7 m across, at 36-38 degrees north. Outside that band it stops working: wider and it is an unshaded yard, narrower and it is a lightwell with no usable floor.

test.note: 3.5-7 m converted to 11.5-23 ft. The 0.8-1.2x-enclosing-range-height ratio clause stays prose (no enclosing-range-height variable exists independent of facade_height_ft, which would be a stretch for a courtyard's own surrounding walls).

constraints.statement: Walls 500-700 mm of brick, rubble or tapia, lime-rendered and limewashed. Cement render is prohibited — it traps moisture in a mass wall and destroys both the wall and the vapour-open behaviour the whitewash provides.

test.note: Tests the wall-thickness range. The material specification (brick, rubble or tapia), the lime-render/limewash finish, and the cement-render prohibition are categorical and stay prose.

constraints.statement: One controlled entry only, through a zaguan, with a heavy door at the street and a cancela at the court. A second street entrance, or a court entered directly off the pavement, breaks the type.
Roofs are canal tile at 20-30 degrees or flat azotea. Deep projecting eaves are not used and should not be added; shading is done by the court, not by the roof.
The court must carry planting and water. A paved, unplanted, dry patio is a lightwell, and the difference is not decorative — the evaporative cooling is a functional requirement of the type.

exemplars.name: Palacio de Viana
exemplars.note: 14th-century origins, largely 16th-19th century; twelve courts of successive dates in one property, effectively a museum of the type at every social level.

exemplars.name: Corral del Conde
exemplars.note: 16th century; the best-preserved corral de vecinos in Seville — communal courtyard housing showing the diagram at its poorest and most collective.

exemplars.name: Patios of the Barrio de San Basilio (Alcazar Viejo)
exemplars.note: 16th-19th century houses, still inhabited and still watered daily; the core of the Fiesta de los Patios, inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2012.

exemplars.name: Casa de Pilatos
exemplars.note: Begun 1483, largely 1519-1539; the aristocratic upper limit of the type, where the vernacular patio meets Mudejar tile and Italian marble.

sources: Byne & Stapley, Spanish Gardens and Patios (1924)
Chueca Goitia, Invariantes castizos de la arquitectura espanola
Rudofsky, Architecture Without Architects
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World

proportion_packs.note: The node's own governing_logic states 'Nothing here is compositional - the whole proportional system is a shading calculation and a joist span,' with room depth set to 3.5-5 m clear by the timber joist. That is room-vernacular's own generative logic (span, hearth-reach and single-sided daylight intersecting in roughly the same neighbourhood) rather than a proportioned or harmonic one, and the node is named directly in the pack's applies_to. No facade or order pack is bound: the street elevation 'has no rhythm worth the name and is not meant to,' and the only columns in the type are the plain, unornamented court arcade - there is no entablature and no classical order to invoke.

english-georgian.name: English Georgian

revival_periods.note: Neo-Georgian in Britain and Colonial Revival in America, both drawing on the same measured drawings and the same surviving pattern books.
The living New Traditional practice, in which Georgian remains the default reference for a well-mannered house in the English-speaking world.

geography.hearth: London and Bath, and from there by book to every county town and every British colony

lineage.note: Descent by book. Georgian is Palladian rule applied to ordinary construction through the builders' manuals: Gibbs's Book of Architecture (1728) and Rules for Drawing (1732), Batty Langley's Treasury of Designs (1740), William Halfpenny's Practical Architecture (c.1724), Abraham Swan's British Architect (1745), and Isaac Ware's Complete Body of Architecture (1756).

The carcass is a Queen Anne carcass: the compact double-pile brick box, the sash window, the hipped roof and dormer, the London building acts of 1667 and 1707, and the trade practices that came out of the post-Fire rebuilding.

Contested and deliberately weighted low. The sash window and the flat-fronted parapeted brick house are sometimes credited to Dutch practice arriving with the Anglo-Dutch court after 1688; H. J. Louw's research concludes the sash was developed in England, with the earliest survivors at Ham House and Palace House in the 1670s, and no inventor identifiable. The edge records a plausible channel, not a settled fact.

description.short: The most transmissible traditional style ever devised: a symmetrical brick or stone box of vertically aligned sash windows, graduated storey heights and a single elaborated doorcase, buildable anywhere from a printed plate by a builder who had never seen a classical building.
description.long:
Georgian is what happens when an aristocratic theory becomes a builder's default. Everything Burlington and Campbell established for the Whig country house — bilateral symmetry, an ordered wall, a fixed set of room ratios, ornament restricted to licensed positions — was stripped of its portico and its piano nobile and sold to the building trade in shilling parts. The pattern books did this work. James Gibbs's Book of Architecture of 1728 was explicitly written, in his own words, for gentlemen in remote parts of the country with no access to able architects; Batty Langley's Treasury of Designs of 1740 gave the carpenter full-size profiles he could set out with dividers; Abraham Swan's British Architect of 1745 solved the stair, which is the hardest thing in a small classical house; William Halfpenny and Isaac Ware supplied everything else. A joiner in Norwich or Norfolk, Virginia could produce a correct Doric doorcase from a plate without understanding the theory behind it — and the theory survived the loss of understanding, which is the single most important fact about this style and the reason it is the founding case study for any kit-of-parts system.

The conditions were legal, financial and material. The London Building Acts made Georgian as much as taste did: the 1667 Act following the Fire set four rates of house and prohibited timber facades; the 1707 Act banned the projecting wooden eaves cornice and required a parapet; the 1709 Act required window frames to be recessed at least four inches behind the face of the wall, which is why a Georgian window sits in a deep reveal and a mock-Georgian one does not; the 1774 Act codified the rates into a system that produced the terraces of Bloomsbury and the New Town of Edinburgh. Behind the Acts stood the leasehold building system, in which a landowner let ground on a 99-year lease to speculating builders who put up shells to a standard section, which is why Georgian streets are so consistent and Georgian back elevations so casual. Brick was cheap and improving, plate glass was not, and a sash divided into six or twelve panes was the economical answer to both.

What Georgian was reacting against is less a style than a condition: the irregularity and unruliness of the seventeenth-century town. Its virtues are urban virtues — a continuous cornice line, a repeated bay, a party wall, a shared palette, a facade that behaves. Individual expression is confined to the door, which is why the Georgian doorcase carries such an extravagant share of the design attention: fluted pilasters or engaged columns, a pediment or a fanlight of increasing delicacy as the century goes on, six raised panels, and a semicircular fan of glazing bars whose pattern is the one place a speculator's builder was allowed to be personal.

Standing in a Georgian street is a lesson in what repetition can do that variety cannot. No single house is remarkable; the wall of them is. The proportion that makes it work is the graduation of storey heights — ground floor tallest, first floor slightly less, second floor markedly less, attic squat — which makes the whole elevation appear to sit down on the pavement rather than float. Inside, the plan is a double-pile box around a stair hall, rooms of resolvable ratio, a chair rail at the height of a chair back, a cornice, a six-panel door, and a window whose sill you can sit on because the wall is a foot and a half thick. It is the most reproducible good house ever designed, and after three hundred years the reproduction has still not exhausted it.

defining_characteristics: Strict bilateral symmetry of the principal elevation, with an odd number of bays (3, 5 or 7) and the entrance centred — or, in the town house, deliberately displaced to one side over a side-hall plan
Vertical alignment of openings between storeys, with no window out of column, and graduated storey heights diminishing upward
Double-hung sash windows in deep reveals, of 6-over-6, 9-over-9 or 12-over-12 lights, with glazing bars thinning progressively from about 32 mm around 1720 to 16 mm by 1800
Brick in Flemish bond, or ashlar in the stone counties, with gauged brick flat arches or stone lintels over the openings
Ornament restricted to the doorcase, the cornice or parapet, and the window heads; the wall surface itself is left plain
A crowning modillion or dentil cornice in the country, or a plain parapet with concealed gutter in town, above a low-pitched hipped or side-gabled roof
A plan of resolvable proportion — double-pile with a central or side stair hall — that generates the facade rather than being fitted behind it
diagnostic_tells: Storey heights that visibly diminish upward: the first-floor window is shorter than the ground-floor window and the second-floor window shorter again. Equal window heights on all floors is the fastest way to spot a fake
Sash boxes set back at least 100 mm from the face of the brickwork, throwing a deep shadow at every opening; from 1709 in London the boxes are also concealed behind the reveal
A doorcase carrying the entire ornamental budget of the house — pilasters or columns, entablature and pediment, and after about 1760 a radiating fanlight — on a facade otherwise devoid of ornament
Gauged brick flat arches in rubbed and cut brick over the openings, with fine joints of lime putty barely a millimetre wide against the 6-10 mm joints of the field brickwork

Against Adam: Georgian mouldings are chunky and shadowed, Adam's are thin, flat and low-relief. Against Regency: Georgian shows its brick, Regency covers it in stucco and adds bows, iron balconies and wide bracketed eaves

distinguished_from.difference: Georgian is Palladianism without the ceremony. No piano nobile, no external stair, no portico, entrance at grade, brick instead of ashlar, and a doorcase where the villa had a temple front. Every proportional rule survives; the aristocratic apparatus does not.

Adam is a decorative revolution inside a Georgian envelope. The box, the sashes and the plan are Georgian; the mouldings are flattened, the ornament becomes low-relief fans, paterae, husks and honeysuckle in delicate colour, and the room shapes acquire apses, niches and screens of columns. At fifty feet, Adam is a Georgian house that has been thinned.

Regency renders the brick in stucco and scores it to imitate ashlar, bows the front, hangs cast-iron balconies with tented canopies, extends the eaves on brackets or drops them behind a shallow parapet, and takes its detail from Greece rather than Rome. Georgian shows its material; Regency conceals it.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Palladian ratios transmitted through builders' manuals and disciplined by the London Building Acts' rates of house. The working modules are the storey height, the bay width and the brick course; the orders appear only at the doorcase and the cornice, where the module is the column diameter.
typical_ratios: Sash opening 1.6:1 to 2:1 height to width; a 6-over-6 sash of roughly 900 x 1650 mm is the workhorse dimension
Storey graduation: ground floor exceeds first floor by 10-20 percent; second floor 0.7-0.8 of the first; attic or garret 0.5-0.6 of the first
Pier (solid) to void ratio on the elevation between 1:1 and 1.5:1 — wall must dominate glass
Bay spacing 2.6-3.6 m centre to centre, equal across the facade
Wall thickness at the ground floor one and a half bricks (330 mm) or more, giving a reveal of 100-150 mm at every opening
Doorcase opening 1.9:1 to 2.2:1 height to width, with a fanlight adding 0.4-0.5 of the door height above
Room ratios 1:1, 1:1.25, 1:1.33, 1:1.5 or 1:2, with ceiling heights of 3.0-3.6 m on the principal floor
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: An even metronome. Bays are identical in width and spacing, the centre marked only by the door and occasionally by a slight projection or a pediment. Any variation of spacing across a Georgian front is a mistake, and any variation of window size within a storey is a worse one.

massing_affinities.note: The double-pile centre-hall box is the Georgian house in its purest form; the symmetry is generated by the plan rather than applied to it.
The terrace is where Georgian does its most consequential work, and where the individual house is subordinated to the street wall.
The standard urban plan behind the terrace facade: stair and passage to one side, front and back rooms lit from the two short ends.
The country house version, with hyphens and flanking dependencies inherited directly from the Palladian generation.
A colonial and American adaptation rather than a British one; the mansard and gambrel are rare in British Georgian before the 1860s.

constraints.statement: Sash proportion between 1.6:1 and 2:1 height to width. Anything squarer reads as a modern opening with muntins applied; anything taller belongs to a piano nobile.
Ground-floor storey height must exceed the first floor by 10-20 percent, and each storey above must diminish. Equal storey heights are forbidden.

test.note: States the ground-to-first-floor pair. 'Every storey above diminishes' is the same variable applied storey-pair by storey-pair further up and stays prose beyond the first pair.

constraints.statement: Window frames set back not less than 100 mm from the external face of the wall, following the London Act of 1709. A frame flush with the cladding face is the single commonest failure of modern Georgian work.

test.note: London Building Act of 1709.

constraints.statement: Openings must align vertically between storeys without exception, and the solid-to-void ratio must not fall below 1:1. Wall dominates glass.

test.note: Tests the solid-dominates-void clause. 'Openings must align vertically between storeys without exception' has no numeric tolerance stated and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Applied ornament is confined to the doorcase, the crowning cornice or parapet, the window heads and, in grander work, a string course. Pilasters, quoins and pediments elsewhere on the wall require justification from a specific plate.

exemplars.name: Bedford Square
exemplars.note: Built 1775-83 by Thomas Leverton and others for the Bedford estate. The most complete surviving Georgian square in London, with palace-fronted terraces, Coade stone doorcases and the whole grammar of the leasehold building system visible in one place.

exemplars.name: Queen Square
exemplars.note: Built 1728-36 by John Wood the Elder. The north side is composed as a single Palladian palace front of seven bays plus wings, which established that a terrace of separate houses could be treated as one building.

exemplars.name: Fairfax House
exemplars.note: Remodelled 1755-62 by John Carr for Viscount Fairfax. A complete Georgian town house with its plasterwork by Giuseppe Cortese and its plan, stair and joinery intact — the provincial pattern-book classicism of the middle of the century at its best.

exemplars.name: Merrion Square
exemplars.note: Laid out from 1762 and built over four decades. Dublin Georgian, with its granite steps, iron area railings, elaborate radiating fanlights and famously coloured doors, is the largest surviving body of the style anywhere.

sources: Dan Cruickshank and Peter Wyld, Georgian Buildings of Britain and Ireland (1975)
John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)
John Summerson, Georgian London (1945)
James Gibbs, A Book of Architecture (1728)
Batty Langley, The City and Country Builder's and Workman's Treasury of Designs (1740)

proportion_packs.note: Bound at the trunk-style level in preference to Gibbs, deliberately. Gibbs's Book of Architecture (1728) is real and cited in this node's own sources, but its documented reach in this corpus is overwhelmingly through its EXPORT -- it is the book American Georgian owns and derives its own gibbs-ionic/gibbs-doric binding from. Chambers's Treatise on Civil Architecture (1759) is the later, more systematic and more purely metropolitan authority: Chambers was Comptroller of the King's Works and taught proportion at the newly founded Royal Academy from 1768, spanning the same decades (1760s-1800) in which most of England's surviving high-Georgian fabric -- Bedford Square, Charlotte Square -- was actually built. Binding Chambers here keeps the trunk style's own module distinct from its American descendant's, and lets the two English-Georgian variant nodes carry the Gibbs-derived thread of the lineage instead, where the record is more specific.

The everyday order: porches, secondary doorcases, and the plainer end of the 3-5-7 bay range the node's own defining characteristics describe. Graded below Ionic exactly as the American template grades Gibbs's two orders -- rank governs choice of order here as there.

The interior moulding family behind the chair rail, cornice and six-panel door this node names throughout. Its wall-section assembly and nineteen-part division apply directly; bind this family only, not the Federal or Greek Revival sections in the same pack, which belong to later and different styles even where they share a Georgian ancestor.

Dates the glazing bars this node calls out explicitly -- 'thinning progressively from about 32 mm around 1720 to 16 mm by 1800' -- and carries the muntin section and the deep-reveal setback the London Acts required. The measured counterpart to opening-proportion below.

Governs the sash ratio (1.6:1 to 2:1), the vertical alignment of openings between storeys 'without exception', and the 100 mm minimum window setback the 1709 London Building Act imposed and this node's own hard constraint c03 tests directly.

Governs the even Georgian metronome -- identical bay width and spacing, the centre marked only by the door -- and the solid-to-void discipline (wall must dominate glass, ratio not below 1:1) that the node's own hard constraint c04 tests.

Governs the diminishing storey heights this node names as its central diagnostic tell: ground floor exceeding first by 10-20 percent, second floor 0.7-0.8 of the first, attic 0.5-0.6 -- the graduation that 'makes the whole elevation appear to sit down on the pavement rather than float,' and whose absence (equal storey heights) the node calls 'the fastest way to spot a fake.'

The Flemish-bond wall and the gauged flat brick arch this node names; bound optional at the trunk level because the style also builds in ashlar in the stone counties, and promoted to primary in the brick-specific American descendants.

Governs the resolvable room ratios (1:1, 1:1.25, 1:1.33, 1:1.5, 1:2) and the ceiling heights (3.0-3.6 m) this node's own proportional_system states directly, generated from the plan outward rather than fitted behind the facade.

american-arts-and-crafts.name: American Arts and Crafts

description.short: Craftsman, bungalow, and Prairie — the American translation of the British reform argument into a mass-market house that millions actually bought.
description.long:
Britain produced the philosophy and a few hundred houses for wealthy clients. America produced hundreds of thousands of houses and shipped them by catalog. Gustav Stickley's *The Craftsman* magazine ran from 1901 to 1916 and distributed plans directly to readers; Sears, Aladdin, and dozens of plan services did the rest.

The result is the only moment in American history when a reform movement grounded in material honesty and craft became the default choice of ordinary buyers. It ended for economic reasons — the bungalow's exposed structure and heavy timber were expensive, and the Depression killed it — not because anyone argued it down.

defining_characteristics: Structure expressed rather than concealed: rafter tails, brackets, beams, joinery
Low horizontal massing with very deep eave overhangs
The porch under the primary roof as an outdoor room
Open planning around a hearth, replacing the formal parlor
Mass distribution by magazine and mail-order catalog

spanish-plateresque.name: Spanish Plateresque

revival_periods.note: Spanish neo-Plateresque, used for university and civic buildings at home and for Spanish pavilions abroad.

Arrives in California and Florida as the 'Churrigueresque' portada — the ornamental-panel-against-plain-wall device, which is Plateresque in origin, generally misattributed. Goodhue's California Building at San Diego, 1915, is the hinge.

geography.hearth: Salamanca, Toledo and Valladolid

lineage.note: The ornamental vocabulary — grotesques, candelieri, medallions, balusters, putti, shell niches — arrives with Italian craftsmen working in Spain from the 1490s and with engraved sheets, and is handled with real technical understanding. What does not arrive is the Italian sense that ornament should be regulated by an order.
