Underneath a Plateresque facade the building is very often Mudejar: brick construction, a par y nudillo or artesonado timber ceiling, tile paving and dado, and a carpentry trade unchanged since the 14th century. The two coexist in the same buildings continuously and the kit genuinely blends.

Columns, pilasters, entablatures and arches appear as a quoted surface repertoire framing the registers of a retablo facade. They are never used structurally and never regulate the building; this is quotation, not descent.

description.short: A Spanish ornamental system in which Italian Renaissance detail is compressed into a bounded, altarpiece-like panel of extraordinary density set against an otherwise blank ashlar wall.
description.long:
Plateresque is usually explained by its name — from platero, silversmith, so 'in the manner of a silversmith' — and the name is misleading. The style is not fine or small-scale in the way metalwork is; it is the exact opposite of small-scale, because its whole effect depends on a very large area of absolutely plain golden ashlar against which a very small area of hallucinatory carving detonates. The right analogy is not the silversmith's bench. It is the retablo, the carved and gilded altarpiece that stands behind a Spanish altar: a bounded rectangular field, divided into horizontal registers by cornices and vertically by columns or balusters, filled edge to edge with figures, medallions, heraldry and grotesque, and framed by a hard moulding that stops the whole thing dead. Plateresque takes that object off the sanctuary wall and puts it on the outside of the building, and the proportional system of the facade is retablo proportion, not classical proportion.

This is why Plateresque behaves so strangely by Italian standards. A Florentine palazzo facade is regulated throughout: string courses, window rhythm, cornice, and quoins are all part of one system, and ornament is distributed. A Salamanca facade has a plain wall with three or four small windows placed where the rooms need them, and then a single vertical explosion three or four registers tall around the door, which has almost no relationship to the fenestration behind it. Spain had received the Italian repertoire as a set of motifs rather than as a discipline, and — more importantly — Spain already had a late-Gothic Isabelline habit of doing exactly this, concentrating carving on a portada and leaving the wall alone. The Italian motifs simply replaced the Gothic ones inside a Spanish compositional habit that did not change.

The moment is short and the reasons for its end are documented. Plateresque belongs to the first half of the sixteenth century, the boom decades of Castilian confidence, university foundation and American silver, and it is essentially over by 1560. What kills it is the arrival of a genuinely disciplined classicism under Philip II — Juan Bautista de Toledo and Juan de Herrera at the Escorial from 1563 — which brings the Vitruvian regulation Spain had previously declined, and which produces a reaction so severe that estilo desornamentado, the 'unornamented style', becomes the court manner within a decade. Spanish architecture swings from the most decorated surface in Europe to the barest, in one generation, on the same peninsula.

Standing in front of a Plateresque facade in low sun is an experience of pure relief-depth. The Salamanca stone is a soft golden sandstone that carves like cheese and hardens on exposure, so the undercutting is extreme — five and six centimetres deep in places — and the shadow does the work. From across the plaza the portada reads as a dark textured rectangle. From ten metres you begin to resolve the registers. From two metres it dissolves into a legible programme of heraldry, portrait medallions, saints and inscriptions that a literate sixteenth-century Spaniard was expected to read like a page. And two metres to the left of it, the wall is empty.

defining_characteristics: Ornament confined to a bounded field — portada, window surround, patio arcade, cresting — with the great majority of the wall left plain ashlar
Retablo composition: the ornamental panel divided into two to five stacked horizontal registers by cornices and framed by a hard vertical border
Italian Renaissance motif vocabulary — grotesques, candelieri, medallions, putti, shell niches, balusters — executed in deeply undercut relief
Heraldry as a compositionally load-bearing element, usually anchoring the upper register
Classical columns and pilasters used as framing devices only; they never carry a real entablature across the whole facade
Arcaded patio on slender columns with basket or Corinthianising capitals, and a carved or wrought balustrade above
Mudejar construction and carpentry behind the classicising skin — brick walls, artesonado ceilings, tile floors
diagnostic_tells: A wall that is more than half empty, with all the carving in one vertical strip around the door
Relief so deeply undercut that at midday the portada reads black
Coats of arms of a size that makes no compositional sense unless you understand they are the point
Scallop-shell niches and roundel portrait medallions used as repeating units within a register
A cresting (cresteria) of pierced stonework or pinnacles running along the parapet, unrelated to any roof behind it

distinguished_from.difference: A century and a half later, and further gone. Churrigueresque uses the estipite — an inverted-obelisk pilaster — as its module, breaks and doubles every cornice, and dissolves the framing members into the ornament. Plateresque keeps its frames crisp and its registers legible.

Italian work regulates the whole facade by an order and distributes ornament across it. Plateresque leaves the facade unregulated and concentrates ornament in one panel. The motifs are shared; the compositional method is opposite.

Mudejar is brick, geometric, non-figural and produced by a continuous Islamic craft. Plateresque is stone, figural, humanist and quoted from Italy. They occupy the same buildings routinely, which is why they need distinguishing rather than merging.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Retablo, not order. The module is the ornamental panel and its frame: total portada width sets the register heights, and the columns or balusters within it are dimensioned to fill their register rather than to any canonical ratio of diameter to height. The plain wall around it has no proportional system at all — its openings are placed by the rooms behind them.
typical_ratios: Portada width to height roughly 1:2 to 1:3, in two to five registers
Ornamented area 15-40 percent of the principal elevation; plain ashlar the remainder
Relief depth 40-80 mm on the principal field, undercut
Patio arcade column slenderness 7-9 diameters
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: A single dominant vertical portada, symmetrical about its own axis, flanked by blank wall. The window rhythm of the building is independent of it and frequently in conflict with it, and the conflict is not resolved.

massing_affinities.note: The colegio, convento and palace are all fully enclosed arcaded patios; the portada is the one point where the block addresses the street.
Three-sided courts in smaller palaces and hospitals.
The cross-plan hospitals of Enrique Egas (Santa Cruz, Toledo; Santiago) are effectively an H or a Greek cross with courts in the angles.
Urban palaces sit in continuous blocks, but the style is almost never applied at row-house scale.

constraints.statement: Ornament must be confined to a bounded field with a hard frame. At least 60 percent of any principal elevation must remain plain ashlar. Distributing the ornament destroys the style outright.

Columns and pilasters frame registers; they must not carry a continuous entablature across the facade. If a real order regulates the whole wall, the building has become Italian Renaissance or Herreran, not Plateresque.
The portada is applied dressed stone carried on the wall behind, typically 300-600 mm deep. It is not a structural frontispiece and must not be modelled as one.

test.note: Tests the applied-portada-depth range, the same reading as churrigueresque.c04. 'Not a structural frontispiece and must not be modelled as one' stays prose.

constraints.statement: Heraldry is required and must anchor the composition, normally in the upper register. A Plateresque portada with no arms is missing the reason it was paid for.

Where the interior carpentry is Mudejar — artesonado, par y nudillo, tile dado — it must be allowed to remain so. Coffering a Plateresque building in the Italian manner is a common revival error and a historical falsification.

exemplars.name: Hospital de Santa Cruz
exemplars.note: 1504-1515, Enrique Egas; the transitional building, with a Gothic cross plan, a Plateresque portada and a Renaissance patio.

exemplars.name: Universidad de Salamanca, principal facade
exemplars.note: c. 1512-1529; the canonical retablo facade, three registers of villamayor sandstone against a plain wall, with the medallion of the Catholic Monarchs at its centre.

exemplars.name: Convento de San Esteban
exemplars.note: Facade begun 1524 by Juan de Alava, completed 1610; a Plateresque portada at cathedral scale under a Gothic-vaulted church.

exemplars.name: Ayuntamiento de Sevilla
exemplars.note: 1527-1564, Diego de Riano; the fullest civic application, with grotesque pilasters and medallion friezes over the Plaza de San Francisco front.

sources: Kubler & Soria, Art and Architecture in Spain and Portugal and their American Dominions 1500-1800
Marias, El largo siglo XVI: los usos artisticos del renacimiento espanol
Chueca Goitia, Historia de la arquitectura espanola: Edad Moderna
Bevan, History of Spanish Architecture

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding, bound narrowly. spanish-plateresque is not in vignola-tuscan's own applies_to, and this style's own proportional_system is explicit that the portada is retablo, 'not order' -- so this is NOT bound for the ornamental panel, which no order pack in the library should be forced onto. It covers only the patio arcade's column shafts: this style's own typical_ratios give 'patio arcade column slenderness 7-9 diameters,' which brackets Vignola's Tuscan column at 7 diameters closely. It does not cover the capitals, which this style's own text calls 'basket or Corinthianising' inventions rather than correct Tuscan capitals -- shaft proportion only.

Judgment binding, same reasoning and same doubt as the equivalent binding on churrigueresque. Not in room-harmonic's own applies_to, but its parent family 'spanish-classical' is. This style's own text gives slightly more support than churrigueresque's does: the proportional_system states outright that the plain wall's 'openings are placed by the rooms behind them,' i.e. the building genuinely has ordinary rooms following an ordinary logic independent of the portada -- this pack is offered as the best available (not a good) account of what that ordinary logic might be, for a style contemporary with the early Italian Renaissance whose vocabulary it explicitly imports (lineage edge to italian-renaissance, weight 0.4).

french-baroque.name: French Baroque

revival_periods.note: Napoleon III's New Louvre (1852-57) makes the pavilion-and-mansard silhouette an international fashion within a decade.
The Grand Manner plan - enfilade, cour d'honneur, axial approach - returned to America through Ecole-trained architects and the City Beautiful movement.

geography.hearth: Paris and the Ile-de-France

lineage.note: Continuous professional and craft descent - Lescot to de Brosse to Mansart is an unbroken chain of Paris masons and royal building offices. The corps de logis, the cour d'honneur, the pavilion and the tall roof all survive; what changes is that they are finally brought under proportional control.

France explicitly refuses the Roman Baroque's deformed wall. Bernini was brought to Paris in 1665 to design the Louvre east front and his scheme - curved, plastic, Roman - was rejected in favour of Perrault's flat, coupled-column colonnade. That rejection is the founding act of French classicism as a distinct thing.

The orders, the treatise habit and the palazzo cornice come from Italy, but by the seventeenth century the French are re-deriving them from Vitruvius and from their own measurement rather than from Italian practice - hence Perrault's 1683 Ordonnance, which corrects Vitruvius.

description.short: The French absorption of the classical order into a national manner of flat walls, projecting rectangular pavilions, tall roofs and absolute axial control, invented for and by the seventeenth-century French state.
description.long:
French Baroque - the French themselves prefer classicisme - is the point at which France stops importing architecture and starts exporting it. The formal move that defines it is a refusal. Where the Roman Baroque gets its drama by bending the wall, the French get theirs by moving whole rectangular masses forward and back: a central avant-corps, two end pavilions, plain recessed curtain walls between, each block with its own roof and its own crowning. The wall stays flat, the mouldings stay orthogonal, the orders stay correct, and the plasticity is delivered at the scale of the building rather than the scale of the surface. When Bernini came to Paris in 1665 with a scheme for the Louvre full of convex sweeps, he was politely paid off and sent home, and Claude Perrault's flat colonnade of paired Corinthian columns was built instead. Everything French about French architecture for the next two hundred and fifty years is in that decision.

The conditions are absolutist and bureaucratic. Richelieu and then Colbert built a centralised state that needed architecture as an instrument: the Academie royale d'architecture is founded in 1671, which means for the first time in Europe there is a state body that certifies what correct proportion is and teaches it. Colbert also organised the supply chain - royal quarries, the Gobelins manufactory for furnishings, standardised drawing conventions - so that a building could be designed in Paris and executed in the provinces to specification. Versailles is the fully developed instrument: not a house but a machine for holding several thousand courtiers in visible hierarchical relation to one man, with the plan itself doing the political work through the enfilade, the order of rooms, and the calibrated right of entry to each.

What the style reacted against internally was the chaotic verticality of the previous century. Mansart's generation suppresses the turrets, disciplines the dormer, brings the roof down and folds it - the brisee or mansard roof, with a steep lower slope and a shallow upper one, keeping the habitable attic French building needed while cutting the silhouette's height nearly in half. The wall stops being a field of ornamented travees and becomes a proportioned classical elevation with a rusticated ground storey, a piano nobile, and an attic. The vertical travee does not die; it is simply subordinated, which is why French classical facades keep a rhythmic regularity that Italian ones do not need.

Approaching Vaux-le-Vicomte along the axis, the building does something no Italian building does: it gets its effect from being seen whole, at distance, across a controlled void, with the garden reading as the building's continuation rather than as its setting. The centre swells forward and rises into an oval domed salon; the corner pavilions anchor the ends; the slate roofs are dark and enormous and take the whole composition up into a silhouette. Then inside, the shock is horizontal - the enfilade, five or seven doorways aligned exactly on one axis so that you can see through the entire depth of the house at once, the openings framing each other in diminishing rectangles. That single device is the French Baroque's most durable invention. It costs nothing, requires only that the wall openings agree, and it makes a building of ordinary rooms feel like an ordered world.

defining_characteristics: Plasticity by projection of whole rectangular masses - avant-corps and end pavilions - on a wall that remains flat and orthogonal
Hierarchy of blocks: corps de logis, ailes, pavillons, each a distinct step in height, roof and articulation
The brisee or mansard roof, steep below and shallow above, preserving the habitable attic while cutting the silhouette
The enfilade: doorways aligned on a single axis through five to nine rooms, with the axis extended into the garden
Correct, academically certified orders - frequently a giant order spanning the two principal storeys, or coupled columns
Rusticated or channelled ground storey supporting a piano nobile and terminated by a full entablature and balustrade
The building composed with an axial approach, a cour d'honneur and a formal garden as one continuous work
diagnostic_tells: Three or five distinct roof masses on one building - end pavilions and a centre, each with its own hipped or mansard roof and its own ridge
Coupled columns (pairs set half a diameter to a diameter apart) rather than evenly spaced single columns
A flat wall with a deep shadow line at the centre because the avant-corps steps forward as a block, not because the wall curves
Segmental-headed or square-headed dormers set into the lower mansard slope with full stone surrounds, evenly spaced
Tall French windows running to the floor, with the sill line suppressed on the piano nobile

distinguished_from.difference: The Italians curve the wall; the French move blocks. If the plan line of the facade is a straight line broken by rectangular projections, it is French. If the plan line itself bends, it is Italian.

Neoclassicism strips the sculptural relief, suppresses the mansard in favour of a low roof hidden behind a balustrade, leaves the column shafts unfluted or sparsely fluted, and reduces the entablature. Where the Baroque piles up incident at the centre, Neoclassicism holds an even, unaccented plane.

The nineteenth-century revival keeps the pavilion-and-mansard silhouette but multiplies the ornament, uses iron structure and much larger sheets of glass, and applies the mansard to buildings - townhouses, hotels, city halls - that have nothing to do with the Grand Manner plan behind it.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Academically codified orders (Claude Perrault's Ordonnance of 1683; Francois Blondel's Cours d'architecture, 1675-1683) applied to a flat wall, with composition proceeding by hierarchy of rectangular masses. The plan is generated on a dominant axis with cross-axes, and the elevation is an expression of that hierarchy rather than an independent design.
typical_ratios: Giant order spanning the two principal storeys; entablature 1/5 to 1/4 of column height
Coupled columns set 0.5 to 1.0 lower diameters apart, with the paired unit spaced 3 to 4 diameters from the next pair
Avant-corps projection 1/8 to 1/6 of its own width; end pavilion projection similar, plus 1 to 2 m of additional height
Storey heights rez-de-chaussee : piano nobile : attic approximately 1 : 1.15 : 0.6
Mansard roof: lower slope 65 to 75 degrees, upper slope 20 to 30 degrees, break point at 0.6 to 0.7 of total roof height
Total roof height 0.35 to 0.5 of the wall height below the cornice - roughly half what the previous century used
Enfilade doors 0.9 to 1.2 m wide aligned within 25 mm across five to nine rooms
Cour d'honneur width 1.0 to 1.5 times the corps de logis length; garden principal axis 5 to 20 times the building's depth
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: 1-3-1 or 3-5-3 across a symmetrical front: end pavilions and a centre pavilion, both projecting and both raised, joined by plain recessed curtain bays of uniform spacing. The rhythm does not accelerate as in Italy; it steps.

massing_affinities.note: The cour d'honneur between the entree and the corps de logis, with the garden on the opposite face - entre cour et jardin is the defining French diagram.
Mansart's brisee roof gives a full habitable storey inside the roof; the hotel particulier depends on it.
Corps de logis with subordinate wings and terminal pavilions is the same hierarchy, arrived at independently and executed at far larger scale.
The Place des Vosges (1605-12) and its successors put uniform classical fronts on a continuous party-wall terrace - the French invention of the designed urban square.
Irregular massing composed for a moving viewpoint negates the axial control that is the point of the style.

constraints.statement: The facade plan line must be straight; projections must be rectangular blocks. Any curvature of the wall surface in plan moves the building out of French classicism and into the Italian Baroque.
Every projecting pavilion must carry its own roof mass, terminated independently. A projecting avant-corps running under a continuous ridge is a nineteenth-century simplification.

Mansard lower slope between 65 and 75 degrees, upper slope between 20 and 30 degrees, with the break at 0.6 to 0.7 of total roof height. Outside that range the roof reads as a Victorian mansard block.

test.note: Tests the lower mansard slope. The upper slope (20-30 degrees, expressible via roof_slope_upper_deg) and the break-point fraction (0.6-0.7 of total roof height) are additional independent numeric clauses and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Enfilade door openings must be aligned within 25 mm across the whole run and set at least 400 mm from any internal corner, which constrains room dimensions and wall thicknesses upstream of the plan.

The principal axis must be extended into the landscape - a court on one side, a formal garden or allee on the other. A French Baroque block set down without its axis is a facade exercise, not the type.

exemplars.name: Chateau de Maisons (Maisons-Laffitte)
exemplars.note: Francois Mansart, 1630-1651. The purest statement of the style before Versailles: three pavilions, a flat wall, superimposed correct orders, and stone cut to a tolerance that has never been bettered in France.

exemplars.name: Chateau de Vaux-le-Vicomte
exemplars.note: Built 1658-1661 for Nicolas Fouquet; Louis Le Vau architect, Charles Le Brun decorator, Andre Le Notre gardens. The first complete integration of building, interior and landscape on one axis - and the template Louis XIV then took to Versailles by hiring the same three men.

exemplars.name: Louvre east front (Colonnade)
exemplars.note: 1667-1674; Claude Perrault with Louis Le Vau and Charles Le Brun, after Bernini's Roman Baroque scheme was rejected in 1665. Coupled Corinthian columns on a rusticated base - the manifesto of the flat French wall.

exemplars.name: Palace of Versailles, garden front
exemplars.note: Le Vau's envelope 1668-1670, extended by Jules Hardouin-Mansart from 1678; Galerie des Glaces 1678-1684. Roughly 400 m of facade held to a single three-part vertical division.

sources: Anthony Blunt, Art and Architecture in France 1500-1700, Pelican History of Art
Anthony Blunt, Francois Mansart and the Origins of French Classical Architecture (1941)
Claude Perrault, Ordonnance des cinq especes de colonnes selon la methode des anciens (1683)
Jean-Marie Perouse de Montclos, Histoire de l'architecture francaise: de la Renaissance a la Revolution (1989)
Robin Middleton and David Watkin, Neoclassical and 19th Century Architecture (1980)

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding: french-baroque is not in vignola-corinthian's own applies_to. Bound as primary anyway because the style's own named manifesto exemplar is explicit about the order -- the Louvre east front is 'coupled Corinthian columns on a rusticated base... the manifesto of the flat French wall,' Perrault's own Ordonnance built to correct Vitruvius rather than to follow Vignola, but Corinthian is the order in both.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The richest of the five, for the giant-order register the style's own proportional_system describes spanning the two principal storeys at Versailles and Vaux-le-Vicomte.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the individual room; the enfilade's alignment discipline (c04) is the thing this pack does not reach, since it governs a single room's shape and height, not a sequence of rooms agreeing on axis.

Judgment binding: not in facade-classical's own applies_to. Bound narrowly for the 'plain recessed curtain bays of uniform spacing' this style's own bay_rhythm names between the projecting pavilions -- not for the pavilion projection itself, which is a stepped-mass composition (c01, c02) that no pack in this library models; the order packs and this style's own constraints carry that part.

Judgment binding: not in this pack's own applies_to. Bound narrowly for the enfilade door -- this style's own typical_ratios give doors '0.9 to 1.2 m wide,' which brackets Palladio's own 3 ft (0.91 m) default almost exactly. Does NOT cover the style's tall floor-length French window (fenetre a la francaise, sill line suppressed on the piano nobile), which is a genuine local departure this pack's sill-datum assumptions do not model -- flagged rather than forced.

folk-victorian.name: Folk Victorian

geography.hearth: No hearth; the style appears wherever a railroad and a millwork catalogue arrive together

lineage.note: The substrate. Plan, massing, framing, roof pitch, chimney position, and room sizes are all inherited unchanged from the folk house; nothing about the massing is Victorian.

Real transmission, but of parts only: turned posts, spindle friezes, cut shingles, and sunburst gable panels arrive from the Queen Anne vocabulary by catalogue, stripped of the compositional rules that governed them.
The earlier catalogue layer: sawn eave brackets, porch brackets, and chamfered posts, which is why the earliest Folk Victorian houses are bracketed rather than spindled.
The oldest layer of applied millwork on the folk house: pierced bargeboard and the single pointed gable sash.

description.short: The ordinary American folk house of the late nineteenth century wearing factory-made Victorian ornament, in which a plain gable-front-and-wing, I-house, or pyramidal cottage receives a spindled porch, sawn brackets, and a decorated gable ordered from a catalogue and delivered by rail.
description.long:
Folk Victorian is the most numerous Victorian building type in America and the most consistently patronised in the literature, where it is often filed as a residue, a Queen Anne that could not afford to be one. That reading is exactly backwards. Folk Victorian is not a degraded style; it is a different and clearer phenomenon, and it is the single most important node in this branch for anybody building a kit-of-parts platform, because it is the first mass demonstration of what happens when ornament is fully decoupled from structure, composition, and place, and sold as a separate product.

The mechanism is exact and datable. Steam-powered lathes, jigsaws, and moulders in the millwork factories of Michigan, Wisconsin, Indiana, and later the Pacific Northwest could turn out porch posts, balusters, spindle friezes, brackets, and cut shingles at a unit cost no local carpenter could approach. The railroad network, which passed 93,000 miles by 1880 and 160,000 by 1890, put nearly every American town within a day of a freight depot. And the illustrated millwork catalogue, from firms such as the Chicago houses that later fed Sears and Montgomery Ward, turned architectural ornament into a mail-order commodity with part numbers and prices. A farmer in Georgia or Kansas could keep the house his father would have built, unchanged in plan, framing, pitch, and hearth position, and buy a front porch that made it modern. That is precisely what several hundred thousand of them did.

The result is a coherent building type with a hard internal rule that the fashionable styles do not have: the massing stays folk, and the ornament stays on the porch, the cornice, and the gable. There is no tower, no polygonal bay above the first floor, no wraparound, no dominant mass, no texture layering. The wall stays plain and one material. That restraint is not timidity; it is the natural consequence of buying ornament rather than designing a building, and it produces houses that are, at their best, better proportioned than the elaborate Queen Annes down the street, because the folk massing had been refined by two centuries of use while the Queen Anne massing had to be invented fresh by a builder who had seen a picture.

Standing in front of one is a quiet experience and a slightly moving one. The house is a plain gabled box or an L with a steep enough roof to shed snow or rain, sited square to the road, with a porch across the front that is the entire architecture. The spindle frieze catches the light and makes a lace edge along the top of the porch; the turned posts throw thin shadows; the gable has one decorated panel; everything else is siding. On a hot afternoon the porch is where the household actually is. The lesson the type teaches a design system is uncomfortable and worth keeping: the parts these people bought were good parts, correctly proportioned to their job, and the houses work because the parts were confined to the places where a porch and a cornice and a gable had always been. The failures of the period, and of the century since, come from putting purchased parts where nothing had ever been.

defining_characteristics: Massing inherited unchanged from a folk house type: gable-front, gable-front-and-wing, I-house, hall-and-parlor, or pyramidal cottage
A full-width or L-shaped one-storey porch as the principal architectural event of the building
Turned or chamfered porch posts with sawn brackets, and usually a spindle frieze or pierced valance at the porch head
Applied sawn ornament confined to porch, cornice, and gable, all of it factory-produced and catalogue-ordered
A single wall cladding, generally clapboard or drop siding, unbroken and untextured on every elevation
Symmetrical or simply organised fenestration, one or two windows per room, with plain surrounds
No tower, no dominant mass, no wraparound porch, and no upper-storey polygonal bay
diagnostic_tells: Simple massing plus fancy porch is the whole diagnosis: if you can describe the footprint in one sentence and the porch takes three, it is Folk Victorian
The ornament stops where the porch stops; walk to the side elevation and it is a plain farmhouse
Roof pitch and plan are those of the local vernacular of thirty years earlier, not of any fashionable style
Compared with Queen Anne: no tower, no bay above the first floor, no texture change, no wall projection, and the ridge is a simple rectangle or L
Porch posts are turned in a repeating catalogue profile, and the same profile will appear on other houses in the same county because they came off the same order

distinguished_from.difference: The definitive pair. Queen Anne requires a dominant mass, two wall textures, wall projections, and an irregular ridge; Folk Victorian forbids all four and keeps a folk footprint. The confusion arises because they share an identical ornament catalogue, so identification must be made from the massing and never from the trim.

The undecorated substrate, and a separate family in this taxonomy. Folk Victorian is that family's building with catalogue ornament added; strip the porch and the cornice brackets and what remains is a plain folk house. The distinction is exactly one purchase order.

The same operation performed a generation earlier with the Gothic catalogue: bargeboards and pointed sash rather than spindles and turned posts. Where both appear, date the house by the porch, which is nearly always the later purchase.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Two systems, deliberately unreconciled. The body is governed by folk framing practice, which is to say by the dimensions a carpenter's tradition had settled on: room sizes of 12 to 16 ft, storey heights of 8 to 10 ft, and pitches set by climate. The ornament is governed by catalogue stock dimensions. The type works because the two never argue, since the ornament is confined to zones the folk house already had.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 6:12 to 12:12, following local vernacular practice rather than style
Porch depth 6 to 8 ft, running the full width of the principal elevation or the full length of the L
Porch post 4x4 to 6x6 nominal, turned with a swell of 5 to 7 in diameter
Spindle frieze depth 8 to 16 in, spindles 1.25 to 2 in diameter at 3 to 5 in on centre
Ornament stock thickness 0.75 to 1.25 in throughout; nothing on the building is thicker
Storey height 8 to 10 ft, notably lower than any fashionable style of the period
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Regular and simple, inherited from the folk type: three or five bays on an I-house, two or three on a gable front, one or two per face on a pyramidal cottage. The porch posts establish an independent and usually finer rhythm across the front.

massing_affinities.note: The most common Folk Victorian form in the Midwest and South, with the porch in the reentrant angle.
Two storeys, one room deep, three or five bays, with a full-width spindled porch.
The narrow-lot town version, and the most easily catalogued.
A genuinely irregular cross-gable composition has left the type; classify as Queen Anne instead.

constraints.statement: Massing shall remain a recognised folk type: not more than two primary volumes, a rectangular or L-shaped ridge, no tower, no wraparound porch, and no polygonal bay above the first floor. Any of these converts the building to Queen Anne and it must then satisfy that style's dominant-mass rule.

Applied ornament shall be confined to the porch, the eave and cornice, and the gable field. Wall surfaces between these zones shall carry one cladding material, unbroken and untextured, on every elevation including the rear.

A porch of 6 to 8 ft depth shall run the full width of the principal elevation, or the full length of both faces of the reentrant angle in an L. A partial or entrance-only porch does not satisfy the type.

test.note: Tests the stated porch-depth range (gallery_depth_ft's own note names 'posted porch' as one of the measurements it covers). Whether the porch runs the full principal-elevation width, or the full length of both L reentrant-angle faces, is a plan-extent fact with no matching vocabulary variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: All sawn and turned ornament shall be dimensionally consistent with millwork stock: members not more than 1.25 in thick, spindles not more than 2 in in diameter, and one turned profile used throughout the building. Two different post profiles on one porch is a later replacement, not a design.

Ornament shall be applied only where the folk type already had an element to decorate: a porch, an eave, a gable, a door surround. Introducing an ornamented feature the underlying type never had is the characteristic failure of both the 1890s cheap builder and the modern imitation.

exemplars.name: James and Clara Butler House
exemplars.note: A one-storey side-gabled Georgian-plan cottage with chamfered porch posts, scrollwork, and scrolled bargeboards in the gable ends; the folk plan is entirely intact behind the ornament.

exemplars.name: Lizzie Garrard House
exemplars.note: One-and-a-half-storey frame house with a projecting front gable, cut shingles in the gable end, bargeboard, and a wraparound porch with turned posts, balusters, and a delicate spindlework valance.

exemplars.name: American Gothic House (Dibble House)
exemplars.note: Usually classed as Carpenter Gothic, and cited here as the boundary case and the clearest single illustration of the type's mechanism: a plain folk cottage whose only architecture is a pair of Gothic sash believed to have been ordered from a catalogue.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Alan Gowans, The Comfortable House: North American Suburban Architecture 1890-1930 (1986)
Henry Glassie, Folk Housing in Middle Virginia (1975)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)

proportion_packs.note: Folk Victorian is explicitly in this pack's applies_to, but the node's own constraints (c01, c02) narrow what it is licensed to do here: no dominant-mass hierarchy, no wall projection, no texture layering. What carries over is the datum discipline — the two continuous horizontals (water table, head line) that hold a plain gabled box and its porch together as one composition — and the porch-as-counterweight logic, since the porch is 'the entire architecture' of this type. The dominance rule, the wing-strategy rule and the multi-texture rules in this pack are effectively inert on a Folk Victorian body and should not be invoked; only the datum and porch-sizing rules do real work.

The node states plain surrounds and one or two windows per room on an inherited folk plan — this is the classical opening-proportion pack's territory (single head datum per storey, sill constant) applied modestly, not facade-picturesque's grouped picturesque openings, since the wall between the porch and the eave is explicitly described as unbroken and untextured with regular fenestration.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to. Folk Victorian sash date to 1870-1925 and would run 2/2 or 1/1 by the sash-light pack's own chronology (large panes available after 1870), which is consistent with the type's plain, catalog-glazed windows.

Folk Victorian is listed in both trim-craftsman's and trim-classical's applies_to, and the two are mutually exclusive at this role per the corpus rule. Trim-craftsman is chosen: the node's own substrate is american-farmhouse-vernacular, a plain-framed carpenter's house, and its ornament philosophy — factory-turned parts confined to a few zones, everywhere else left plain — is the same economic logic trim-craftsman is built from (a board is a board; the room does not generate the trim). Trim-classical's room-as-an-order derivation, calibrated to an 11-13 ft parlor with a full pedestal and entablature, has no purchase on an 8-10 ft farmhouse room with no dado. This is a judgment choice between two applies_to-sanctioned options, not a default.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to, and it is the correct system on its own terms: the node states plan, framing, roof pitch, chimney position, and room sizes are 'all inherited unchanged from the folk house,' which is exactly the span-hearth-daylight-constrained room this pack describes, not a treatise-proportioned one.

JUDGMENT BINDING, though the pack's own applies_to already lists folk-victorian. Bound optional and last because it covers only the minority of Folk Victorian porches whose posts are chamfered rather than turned — a chamfered square post is a simplified, carpenter-built stand-in for a Doric column, and Benjamin's 1816 Companion is the American pattern book that vernacular builders of this generation actually had in hand. It does not cover the majority spindled-and-bracketed porch, which has no order at all and no dedicated pack in this library (see report gaps).

english-gothic.name: English Gothic

revival_periods.note: Rococo 'Gothick' — Strawberry Hill and the picturesque castellated house. Antiquarian in mood, wholly Georgian in construction.
The archaeological revival after Pugin's Contrasts, which claimed structural and moral descent rather than mere quotation.

geography.hearth: Canterbury, where William of Sens brought Ile-de-France practice to the choir rebuilding of 1174

lineage.note: Unbroken transmission through the same masons' lodges and the same quarries. The Transitional work of the 1170s-1190s shows the two systems in the same building, often in the same bay.

description.short: Four centuries of pointed-arched masonry in which the English worked out how to concentrate structure into piers and buttresses so that the wall between them could become window, and which in domestic use produced the open-roofed great hall.
description.long:
English Gothic begins as an import and becomes the most self-contained regional Gothic in Europe. William of Sens brought French practice to Canterbury in 1174; within fifty years the English had bent it toward their own preferences — long low buildings rather than tall ones, elaborate rib patterns rather than structural daring, and a fixation on the surface pattern of tracery that culminates in Perpendicular, a style with no Continental parallel. The three conventional phases (Early English c.1180-1275, Decorated c.1275-1375, Perpendicular c.1375-1540) are Thomas Rickman's 1817 coinage, not a medieval self-description, but they track real changes in window tracery closely enough to be worth keeping.

The domestic story is separate from the ecclesiastical one and matters more here. Once a landholding class felt safe enough to come down to the ground, the first-floor hall gave way to the ground-floor open hall: a single tall volume open to a carpented roof, with a dais at the upper end for the lord's table, a screens passage at the lower end separating hall from buttery, pantry and kitchen, and a central open hearth until wall fireplaces and chimney stacks became general in the fifteenth century. That plan — dais, hall, screens, service — is the single most consequential diagram in British domestic architecture. The H-plan and E-plan manor, Tudor and Jacobean great houses, and the persistent English habit of entering a house off-centre through a passage rather than on axis all descend directly from it.

The conditions were wool money, monastic and collegiate patronage, and a masons' lodge system that moved skilled men between cathedral, castle and manor sites. The Black Death of 1348-49 is the hinge: it destroyed the labour supply, ended the enormous Decorated projects, and pushed the trade toward the repeatable, panel-based Perpendicular window, which could be cut from templates with less carving per foot. Perpendicular is often described as the style of a diminished age. It is more accurately the style of a labour shortage, and its rectilinear economy is the first standardised architectural system in England — a fact worth holding onto, because it is the same logic the pattern book would later apply to classicism.

A medieval great hall is one of the few interiors that still reliably silences people who walk into it. The volume is far taller than any domestic need requires; the roof is the whole show, an arch-braced or hammerbeam structure whose members are the size of ship timbers and whose joinery is visible from the floor; the light comes sideways and high from traceried windows, so the upper air is bright and the floor is dim. Entering through the screens passage rather than into the middle of the room means you arrive at the low end, in shadow, looking up the length of the room toward the dais. That was the point. The plan is a machine for producing a social gradient out of nothing but a sequence of thresholds and a fall of light.

defining_characteristics: The pointed arch used structurally throughout, freeing rise from span and allowing bays of unequal width to spring to a common height
Structure concentrated in piers, buttresses and ribs so that infill wall can be reduced to traceried window
Window tracery as the governing decorative system — plate, then geometric bar, then flowing curvilinear, then rectilinear panel
Deep stepped or flying buttresses with weathered offsets, expressing the line of thrust externally
In domestic work, the ground-floor open hall with dais end, screens passage at the low end, and service rooms beyond
Carpented open roofs (arch-braced, crown-post, hammerbeam) treated as the principal architectural display of the interior
Moulded and shafted openings with hood moulds and label stops shedding water clear of the reveal
diagnostic_tells: Pointed arch plus tracery plus a hood mould with carved label stops — the combination is decisive and appears nowhere else
Buttresses that step back and weather as they rise, rather than the flat pilaster strips of Norman work
In a house: an off-centre entrance leading into a passage across the low end of a tall room, with two or three service doorways in the wall opposite
Perpendicular window mullions running unbroken from sill to arch head and crossed by horizontal transoms, dividing the light into rectangular panels
Roof carpentry left exposed and moulded, with no ceiling — a plastered ceiling in a hall means it was floored over later, usually in the sixteenth or seventeenth century

distinguished_from.difference: Pointed versus round arch, and behind that a complete inversion of where material goes. Norman spreads stone evenly through a thick wall; Gothic gathers it into piers and buttresses and spends the savings on glass.

The original is a continuous building practice with no theory of itself; the revival is a theory in search of a practice. A medieval hall has a chimney where the fire is; a revival hall has a chimney where a medieval hall would have had one. The revival is also built with Georgian-descended trades, sawn timber and, after 1840, industrial glass.

Tudor is late Perpendicular domesticated and secularised — the same masons, the same four-centred arch, but a symmetrical-ish gatehouse front, brick instead of stone in the lowland counties, and Italianate ornament arriving as surface decoration on a wholly Gothic frame.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Geometric setting-out from the square and its diagonal (ad quadratum) and from the equilateral triangle (ad triangulum), worked out full size on a tracing floor rather than calculated. The pointed arch's freedom from a fixed rise:span ratio is what makes the whole system possible.
typical_ratios: Equilateral arch: rise equals span (centres struck at the springing points) — the Early English default
Lancet openings 4:1 to 6:1 height to width; Perpendicular windows 2:1 to 3:1 overall
Great hall: width 7.5-9.0 m, length 1.5 to 2 times width, wall-plate height roughly equal to width
Pier width to bay span roughly 1:4 to 1:6, against 1:2 to 1:3 in Norman work
Buttress projection 1/4 to 1/2 of its own width at the base, diminishing by weathered offsets
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Regular structural bays set by the roof trusses or vault ribs, 3.5-5.0 m apart in domestic work, with the hall usually of three or four bays plus a screens bay. Openings sit centred in their bay; the bay, not the facade, is the unit of composition.

massing_affinities.note: The developed manorial diagram: hall range in the centre, family solar wing at the dais end, service and kitchen wing beyond the screens.
The unaisled open hall before wings accrete — the base condition from which everything else grows.
Collegiate, monastic and larger castle plans, where ranges close a quadrangle around the hall.
Descending ranges from hall to service are common, though the medieval version steps by function rather than by generation.

constraints.statement: Arch heads are pointed. Where a depressed head is used it must be a true four-centred arch struck from four centres, not a flattened ellipse, and it belongs only to work after roughly 1400.
A traceried window requires a hood mould or a weathered label above it. Tracery set flush in a wall with no drip is a modern detail and will fail in a British rain.
Entry to a hall is through a screens passage at the low end, never centrally on the long side and never at the dais end. This is the load-bearing rule of the whole domestic plan.
Hall wall-plate height not less than the hall's clear width; a hall wider than it is tall is a room, not a hall.

test.note: Tests 'wall-plate height not less than the hall's clear width' using room_clear_span_ft as the hall's clear-span measurement -- an open medieval hall roof is exactly the beam/truss-clear-span case that variable describes. Direction at-least with threshold 0 expresses the difference must be non-negative.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch not less than 45 degrees, and 50-55 degrees where the covering is stone slate or thatch; the open roof must be framed to be seen from below.

test.note: Tests the universal floor (45deg). The stricter 50-55deg floor for stone slate or thatch is material-conditional and stays prose; 'framed to be seen from below' is qualitative and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Stokesay Castle
exemplars.note: Licence to crenellate granted 1291 to the wool merchant Laurence of Ludlow. A fortified manor whose great hall, with its cruck-braced roof and tall traceried windows, survives almost unaltered.

exemplars.name: Penshurst Place, Barons Hall
exemplars.note: Built for Sir John de Pulteney. The most complete surviving fourteenth-century domestic hall: central octagonal hearth, chestnut arch-braced roof, dais, and screens passage all intact.

exemplars.name: Westminster Hall roof
exemplars.note: Hugh Herland's hammerbeam roof of 1393-99 spanning 20.7 m without intermediate support — the largest medieval timber roof in Northern Europe and the technical summit of the tradition.

exemplars.name: Great Chalfield Manor
exemplars.note: Built c.1465-80 for Thomas Tropenell. A late-Perpendicular manor with the hall range flanked by gabled wings — the H-plan arriving in its finished domestic form.

sources: John Harvey, The Perpendicular Style 1330-1485 (1978)
Margaret Wood, The English Mediaeval House (1965)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England (county volumes)
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)
R. W. Brunskill, Traditional Buildings of Britain (1981)

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding: english-gothic is not in room-vernacular's applies_to, and its governing space — the great hall, 7.5-9.0 m wide, wall-plate height at least equal to that width — is a different order of scale from the pack's 14 ft (4.3 m) ordinary-room module entirely. Bound narrowly and scoped to the SUBSIDIARY spaces only (solar, chambers off the dais end, service rooms beyond the screens), which are genuinely closer to the pack's 9-14 ft chamber range; the hall itself remains governed by this style's own proportional_system (ad quadratum/ad triangulum setting-out and c04's wall-plate-to-span rule), which the library has no dedicated pack for. See gaps.

second-empire.name: Second Empire

revival_periods.note: The mansard returns as a commercial and apartment device in the late twentieth century, detached from the style entirely and usually applied as a partial screen; the constraint below exists to exclude it.

geography.hearth: New York, Boston, and Washington

lineage.note: The decisive edge. In America Second Empire is Italianate with a mansard: same plan, same bracketed cornice, same arched windows, same builders, same catalogues. Hundreds of Italianate houses were literally converted by adding a mansard storey.

The claimed ancestry. Visconti and Lefuel's New Louvre of 1852-57 under Napoleon III was published worldwide and gave the style its name and its pavilion-plus-mansard formula; no French building practice crossed to America with it.
Through Mansart's seventeenth-century roof form itself, and through the pavilion massing of the chateau, both quoted rather than inherited.
Genuine blending in the institutional and urban work: symmetrical palazzo bodies with academic cornices, then crowned by a mansard.

description.short: The mansard-roofed style of the 1860s and 1870s, in which an Italianate body is crowned by a full habitable storey of steep slate roof with dormers, and which was fashionable rather than revivalist because its source was contemporary Paris.
description.long:
Second Empire is the only style in this branch that was not a revival. Gothic, Italianate, Renaissance, and Egyptian all claimed a distant ancestor; Second Empire copied what was being built in Paris that decade. Napoleon III's rebuilding of the city and Visconti and Lefuel's New Louvre of 1852-57 were the most publicised construction projects on earth, illustrated in every architectural periodical, and Americans adopted the result as a mark of being current rather than of being cultivated. That distinction shows in where the style went: government buildings, city halls, hotels, and the houses of the newly rich, rather than the country cottages of the Downing programme. Its American nickname, the General Grant style, records exactly how thoroughly it became the official manner of the Reconstruction era.

Structurally, the mansard is a superb piece of engineering opportunism and the reason the style spread so fast. A roof with a near-vertical lower slope converts an attic into a full storey with usable headroom at the perimeter, which under nineteenth-century assessment practice was often taxed and regulated as a roof rather than as a floor. Combine that with the technology already in place, balloon framing that made complex roof geometry cheap, slate delivered by rail from Vermont and Pennsylvania quarries, machine-pressed metal cresting, and mass-produced dormer sash and bracketed cornices, and you have a way to add a whole storey to a house at roof prices. American Second Empire is, at bottom, an economic argument wearing a French hat.

What it was reacting to was the picturesque itself, or rather its sentimentality. Downing had died in 1852, and the generation that came up in the 1860s wanted urbanity, worldliness, and visible expense rather than moral instruction from a vine-covered veranda. Second Empire keeps the picturesque tools, the projecting pavilion, the tower, the asymmetrical wing, but it uses them for grandeur rather than for feeling, and it reintroduces symmetry, hierarchy, and the pavilion system that the cottage styles had abandoned. The Victorian conviction that architecture forms character survives, but the character it now proposes to form is civic and ambitious rather than domestic and pious.

The physical experience is dominated by the roof, which is the point. A mansard is the only roof form that reads simultaneously as a wall and as a crown; because the lower slope is nearly vertical and dormered, the building appears to have one more storey than its cornice admits, and because the slate is patterned in bands of fish-scale and diamond in coloured courses, the top of the building is the most decorated part of it. The silhouette against the sky is emphatic: cresting, finials, and dormer pediments all working at the roofline. Inside, the top floor is the surprise, a set of rooms with sloped ceilings and deep dormer reveals that feel like the best rooms in the house to any child who has ever been given one.

defining_characteristics: A mansard roof, dual-pitched with a steep lower slope of 65 to 80 degrees, forming a full habitable storey on all elevations
Dormers in the lower slope, one per bay, aligned with the openings below
A moulded and bracketed cornice at the curb line where wall meets roof, and usually a second cornice at the roof deck
Italianate substrate: arched or segmental window heads, tall narrow paired windows, quoins, string courses
Projecting central or end pavilions, frequently with a taller mansard of its own or with a tower
Decorative slate patterning, iron cresting, and finials at the roof, making the top the most ornamented zone
Symmetrical or near-symmetrical principal facade, in contrast to the picturesque styles it descends from
diagnostic_tells: If it is bracketed and arched and there is a mansard, it is Second Empire; if it is bracketed and arched and there is not, it is Italianate. There is no third possibility
The mansard runs all the way around; a mansard only on the street front is a twentieth-century commercial device, not this style
Dormer count equals bay count, and the dormers line up with the windows below
The tower, where present, has a steeper and taller mansard than the main roof, usually concave or with a distinct convex bell
Coloured and patterned slate in horizontal bands is nearly diagnostic; no other American style patterns its roof this consistently

distinguished_from.difference: The parent and the nearest neighbour. Only the roof differs, but it differs totally: a suppressed low hip that the cornice conceals versus a dominant habitable mansard storey that the cornice supports.

Chateauesque (1880-1910) is masonry, uses steep hipped roofs with elaborate dormers breaking the cornice line, and works from sixteenth-century Loire precedent. Second Empire is a mansard, contemporary rather than archaeological, and usually wood or brick.
Second Empire frequently takes a Renaissance Revival body wholesale. The mansard converts a wall terminated by a cornice into a mass crowned by a roof, which is the opposite compositional intention.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by the roof storey and the pavilion hierarchy. The mansard height sets the crown, and the central or end pavilions establish an A-B-A or A-B-C-B-A rhythm inherited from French practice. Below the curb cornice, the Italianate bracket module still governs.
typical_ratios: Mansard lower slope 65 to 80 degrees from horizontal; upper deck slope 2:12 to 4:12
Mansard storey height 0.8 to 1.0 times the storey below
Dormer width 0.55 to 0.75 of the bay width; dormer height 0.7 to 0.85 of the mansard lower slope height
Central pavilion projection 24 to 48 in, width 0.25 to 0.4 of the facade
Curb cornice projection 18 to 30 in with brackets at 24 to 48 in on centre
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Regular and pavilioned. The wall marches in equal bays and is punctuated by a projecting pavilion at the centre, at the ends, or at both, each pavilion taking a taller mansard.

massing_affinities.note: The towered Second Empire villa, with the tower mansard steeper than the main roof.
The mansarded brownstone row; often an Italianate row raised by a storey after the fact.
Late and looser examples, where the mansard has to negotiate an irregular plan.

constraints.statement: The mansard shall be continuous on all elevations of the mass it crowns, including rear and side elevations. A mansard applied to the street front only, or returned less than the full depth of the building, is prohibited.
The lower mansard slope shall be between 65 and 80 degrees from horizontal, and the upper slope shall not exceed 4:12 and shall not be visible from any point at eye height 40 ft from the building.

test.note: Tests the lower mansard slope, the pair-position match for roof_slope_lower_deg/roof_slope_upper_deg. The upper slope is stated in rise-per-12 (not degrees, so roof_slope_upper_deg's degree units don't apply without an unstated conversion) and the 40 ft eye-height visibility condition has no matching variable -- both stay prose.

constraints.statement: Dormers shall be provided one per structural bay and shall be centred on the openings of the storey below within 6 in. Dormer count and spacing shall not be varied independently of the fenestration.

test.note: Tests 'one dormer per structural bay' as dormer count minus bay count equalling zero. The further requirement that each dormer centre on the opening below within 6 in has no matching vocabulary variable (opening_vertical_alignment_in is a vertical storey-to-storey measure, not a dormer-to-window horizontal one) and stays prose.

constraints.statement: The curb cornice shall carry brackets at 24 to 48 in on centre at the same module as any porch or bay cornice on the building, preserving the Italianate rhythm the style inherits.

Where a tower is used, its mansard shall be steeper than the main mansard by at least 5 degrees and shall rise not less than one full storey above the main curb line, so that the hierarchy of crowns is unambiguous.

exemplars.name: Terrace Hill
exemplars.note: William W. Boyington, 1866-69, for Benjamin F. Allen. Mansard roof, paired narrow windows, bracketed eaves, and a tower; now the Iowa governor's residence.

exemplars.name: Eisenhower Executive Office Building (State, War and Navy Building)
exemplars.note: Alfred B. Mullett, 1871-88. Granite, ten acres of floor, and the most complete institutional Second Empire building in the United States.

exemplars.name: Philadelphia City Hall
exemplars.note: John McArthur Jr., 1871-1901. The largest masonry load-bearing building in the country and the late civic apotheosis of the style.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)
Leland Roth, A Concise History of American Architecture (1979)
Lawrence Wodehouse, American Architects from the Civil War to the First World War (1976)

proportion_packs.note: Explicit in this pack's applies_to. Second Empire is mansard-defined rather than order-defined — the style has no bound classical order in this library and none is forced here — but below the curb cornice the body is an Italianate-descended, near-symmetrical, bay-rhythmed wall (the node's own proportional_system: 'below the curb cornice, the Italianate bracket module still governs'), which is exactly facade-classical's territory: bay count, pier width, solid-to-void, cornice projection.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to, and the node states its own mansard-storey-height rule (0.8-1.0 of the storey below) as a direct extension of this pack's general diminution logic — the mansard is read as one more graduated storey in the stack, not as an unrelated roof form. Governs the ordinary storey diminution below the mansard and the sill/head datum discipline the dormers must key into.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to. Governs the rectangle of each opening and, critically, the single-head-datum-per-storey rule that the node's own hard constraint (c03) depends on: dormers must centre on the openings of the storey below within 6 in, which presumes the storey already has one disciplined head line for the dormers to agree with.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to, and its window_proportion authority_note names Second Empire directly (2.2-2.6 height:width, the tall end of the Anglo-American range) alongside Italianate. Governs light count and muntin section for the tall narrow paired sash the node's defining_characteristics call for.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to. Governs interior baseboard, cornice and casing; the node's Italianate-derived body and academic civic ambitions (city halls, hotels) place it with the formal classical interior tradition rather than a carpenter's trim family, and storey-graduation's own ceiling-height notes record 10-14 ft Italianate ceilings, which is inside this pack's well-calibrated 11-13 ft band rather than its low-ceiling failure zone.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to, but Second Empire's placement in facade-classical, trim-classical, opening-proportion, sash-light and storey-graduation together — the same set of formal-classical packs bound to georgian-colonial-american and colonial-revival — argues for a designed, treatise-adjacent room over room-vernacular's span-constrained folk room. Second Empire houses were civic and upper-class buildings (city halls, hotels, 'houses of the newly rich'), not vernacular construction, and the style's tall Italianate-derived ceilings (10-14 ft) are squarely in room-harmonic's working range rather than room-vernacular's 7-9 ft band.

new-jersey-dutch-gambrel.name: New Jersey Dutch Gambrel

revival_periods.note: This is the variant the revival actually copied — and immediately falsified, by replacing the sprung eave with a straight overhang and cutting a full-width shed dormer into the roof.

regions: Passaic and Hudson counties, New Jersey
Somerset and Middlesex counties, New Jersey
geography.hearth: the Hackensack and Passaic valleys of Bergen County, on the red sandstone of the Newark Basin

lineage.note: The Bergen population was heavily Flemish and Walloon, and the sprung eave has better parallels in the southern Low Countries than in Holland proper.

description.short: The Bergen County sandstone house: a low gambrel-roofed block whose lower roof slope sweeps out past the wall on a concave curve, shading the front and eventually becoming a porch.
description.long:
This is a house made of one geological accident and one roof idea. The accident is the Newark Basin sandstone — a red-brown stone that quarries in beds, dresses easily, and lies directly under the Hackensack and Passaic valleys. Bergen builders used it for everything, and used it with a very particular economy: dressed, squared and coursed on the entrance elevation, coursed rubble on the two ends, and whatever came out of the ground on the back. Walk around one of these houses and the quality of the masonry degrades with each turn. That is not carelessness; it is an exact allocation of skilled labour to the surface that will be seen.

The roof idea is the gambrel with a sprung eave, and it deserves careful description because almost everything built in its name since 1890 has got it wrong. A Bergen gambrel has a steep lower slope, sixty to seventy-two degrees, and a shallow upper one, eighteen to thirty degrees, which converts a low masonry wall into a full upper storey without building the wall any higher — an enormous economy when the wall is two feet of hand-laid stone. Then the lower slope does not stop at the wall. It continues past it on a concave sweep, projecting eighteen to thirty-six inches, flattening as it goes, so that the eave line is a curve rather than an angle. This throws rain clear of an unrendered stone wall and puts the summer sun off the openings entirely. In the middle of the eighteenth century somebody put posts under the sprung eave and extended it to eight or ten feet, and the full-width Dutch porch was born — the direct ancestor of a habit that would eventually cover the entire United States.

The plan behind it stays simple and stays Dutch for a long time: one or two rooms deep, gable-end chimneys, no passage, low ceilings at seven and a half to eight and a half feet, a Dutch door with a transom, and after about 1760 a five-bay front with the door in the middle because the neighbours were English. The interior keeps anchor beams and, on early work, jambless hearths.

What it feels like is low, broad and sheltering — the opposite of the Hudson Valley house's vertical roof. You approach across a shaded band of ground under the sprung eave; the wall is warm red stone with white mortar; and the roof, which is most of what you see, curves down to meet you at head height and then stops. The Colonial Revival spent forty years trying to reproduce that feeling with a shed dormer and a straight soffit, and never once managed it, because the curve was the whole thing.

defining_characteristics: Gambrel roof with a steep lower slope (60–72 degrees) and a shallow upper slope (18–30 degrees), the break at 55–70% of the half-span
A sprung (flared) eave: the lower slope continues past the wall face on a concave sweep, projecting 18–36 in, later carried on posts as a full-width porch
Load-bearing red-brown Newark Basin sandstone, dressed and coursed on the entrance elevation only, rubble elsewhere
Low wall: plate 7 ft 6 in – 9 ft 0 in above the floor, so the gambrel does the work a second storey would otherwise do
Chimneys at the gable ends, one or both, serving hearths in each principal room
Three- or five-bay eave-front elevation with a Dutch door, transom-lit after c. 1760
No dormers on the original front slope
diagnostic_tells: The eave is a curve, not an angle — sight along the roof edge and the concave sweep is unmistakable
Masonry quality drops with each elevation as you walk around the house
Gambrel with no dormer at all; if there is a continuous dormer the building postdates 1890
Red-brown stone with wide white lime joints, laid in courses of unequal height
The porch, where present, is an extension of the roof plane rather than a separate structure with its own pitch

distinguished_from.difference: The most instructive pairing in the whole Dutch branch. The revival keeps the gambrel and discards everything that made it work: it cuts a full-width shed dormer into the front slope (which no colonial Jersey Dutch house has), replaces the concave sprung eave with a straight overhanging soffit, frames in wood with a veneer or shingle skin, and imposes symmetry on every elevation. Test the eave profile and the dormer; either one settles it.
Steep straight gable versus gambrel; grey limestone versus red sandstone; a water-shedding sprung eave of 18–24 in versus a sheltering one of 24–36 in that becomes a porch.

Both are Mid-Atlantic stone houses with five-bay fronts after 1760. The Georgian house has a centre passage, aligned windows on all elevations, a classical door surround and a gable roof at 8:12–10:12; the Jersey Dutch house has a gambrel, a sprung eave, no passage and a plain door under a transom.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The gambrel geometry: the break point is chosen so that the upper floor gains full headroom at the knee wall without raising the masonry.
typical_ratios: Overall 30–46 ft × 22–30 ft; one or two rooms deep
Lower slope 60–72 degrees; upper slope 18–30 degrees; break at 55–70% of the half-span
Plate 7 ft 6 in – 9 ft 0 in; ridge 20–24 ft above grade
Sprung eave projection 24–36 in, sweep radius 4–8 ft; posted porch 8–10 ft deep
Wall thickness 20–28 in; ceiling 7 ft 6 in – 8 ft 6 in
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three bays early, five after c. 1760, with the door centred once symmetry arrives; window widths equal and piers wider than the openings.

massing_affinities.note: The plan under the gambrel before Anglicization.
The post-1760 Bergen house with a centre hall behind a Dutch section.
Growth by adding a kitchen wing along the ridge line.

constraints.statement: Gambrel geometry: lower slope 60–72 degrees, upper slope 18–30 degrees, break at 55–70% of the half-span. The two slopes must differ by at least 30 degrees or the roof reads as a modern barn profile.

test.note: This variant states the differentiation itself as the enforceable rule ('must differ by at least 30 degrees'), unlike the parent dutch-colonial-american's softer version -- so the difference expression is the more faithful test here, not the raw range.

constraints.statement: The eave must spring — a concave sweep projecting 24–36 in beyond the wall face, with a sweep radius of 4–8 ft. A straight overhang of any depth is not this type.

test.note: The sweep radius (4-8ft) is the same statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: No continuous shed dormer on any roof slope. This is the diagnostic marker of Dutch Colonial Revival and is absent from every colonial Bergen house.

Dressed and coursed sandstone confined to the entrance elevation; coursed rubble at the ends; random rubble at the rear. Uniform ashlar on all four sides is a later or wealthier building and reads as such.
Where the sprung eave is posted to form a porch, depth 8–10 ft with posts 8–10 ft on centre; the porch roof is the continued roof plane, not a separate structure with its own pitch.

test.note: A posted porch under the sprung eave is the same depth concept as a galerie/piazza.

exemplars.name: Steuben House (Zabriskie House)
exemplars.location: Historic New Bridge Landing, River Edge, New Jersey
exemplars.note: Kinderkamack Ridge sandstone, dressed on the two road-facing sides and coursed rubble elsewhere; enlarged c. 1765 when the fashionable gambrel roof was added.

exemplars.name: Hopper-Goetschius House
exemplars.location: 363 East Saddle River Road, Upper Saddle River, New Jersey
exemplars.note: Listed on the National Register within the Early Stone Houses of Bergen County multiple property submission — the single best documentary group for this variant.

exemplars.name: Dyckman Farmhouse
exemplars.note: Just outside New Jersey but structurally of this family: fieldstone below, frame above, gambrel with a sprung eave carried on posts.

sources: Helen Wilkinson Reynolds, Dutch Houses in the Hudson Valley before 1776 (1929)
Roderic H. Blackburn and Ruth Piwonka, Remembrance of Patria: Dutch Arts and Culture in Colonial America (1988)
Rosalie Fellows Bailey, Pre-Revolutionary Dutch Houses and Families in Northern New Jersey and Southern New York (1936)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
New Jersey SHPO, Early Stone Houses of Bergen County Multiple Property Documentation Form (1983)

proportion_packs.note: Bound on inheritance from the parent dutch-colonial-american rather than on this variant's own text, which foregrounds the gambrel roof geometry (the break point set so the upper floor gains full headroom without raising the masonry) rather than the framing bay as its stated governing_logic — no pack among the 36 models gambrel break-point geometry or the curvature of a sprung eave, and that gap is reported rather than papered over. The plan module this variant records — 22-30 ft deep, one or two rooms — is consistent with the wider Dutch H-bent bay rhythm, but new-jersey-dutch-gambrel is not itself named in timber-bay's own applies_to (unlike the parent and the Hudson Valley variant), so this binding is an extension of the family's logic rather than a separately attested one.

new-jersey-dutch-gambrel is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. One or two rooms deep, gable-end chimneys, no passage until Anglicization — the plan is constrained by span, hearth and daylight exactly as the pack describes, not proportioned by ratio.

Unlike its Hudson Valley sibling, this variant's own proportional_system already classifies its symmetry as 'near-symmetrical' rather than 'additive-vernacular,' and states plainly that the door centres 'once symmetry arrives' after c. 1760 on a five-bay front — which covers most of the variant's later floruit (1730-1820). Bound at facade role rather than merely optional for that reason, while still noting the pack's odd-bay/single-entrance model describes only the post-1760 Anglicized form; earlier Bergen sandstone houses (e.g. the Steuben House's 1752 core) are three-bay and not yet composed to this discipline. brick-course was considered and rejected: the style's own diagnostic tells state the stone is 'laid in courses of unequal height,' which contradicts the pack's core premise of a fixed mason's-gauge-rod coursing, unlike the tighter-coursed Hudson Valley sibling.

dutch-colonial-revival.name: Dutch Colonial Revival

geography.hearth: the Hudson Valley, northern New Jersey, and the New York suburbs

lineage.note: A roof-defined variant. Everything below the eave is standard Colonial Revival; the gambrel and the sweeping eave are the whole difference.
The claimed ancestor, and a genuinely misread one: the revival takes the gambrel from Hudson Valley and New Jersey barns and houses and makes it a full second storey, which the originals never did.
Source of the flared, kicked eave - the 'Dutch kick' - and of the deep stone-walled ground floor in the better examples.
The 1880s Newport and Long Island offices used the gambrel as a Shingle Style move before it was called Dutch anything; that is the actual line of transmission.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The gambrel-roofed variant of Colonial Revival, in which a Hudson Valley barn profile is stretched to enclose a full second storey and becomes, between 1910 and 1930, the most economically efficient two-storey house in the American suburb.
description.long:
Dutch Colonial Revival is a roof with a house under it. Its necessary condition is the gambrel: a two-slope roof, steep below and shallow above, running either side-to-side or front-to-back, with the lower slope pierced by a long shed dormer or a row of gabled ones, and very often flaring outward at the eave in the characteristic Dutch kick. Below that roof it is an ordinary Colonial Revival house - symmetrical or near-symmetrical, clapboard or shingle over frame, double-hung sash, a classical entry, shutters - and it inherits its entire kit from the parent style.

What made it ubiquitous was arithmetic. A gambrel encloses roughly 15 to 20 percent more usable floor area within the same roof volume than a simple gable of comparable ridge height, which meant a builder could sell a two-storey house while framing and heating a storey and a half. Between 1910 and 1930 that made it the default in the mail-order catalogs - Sears, Aladdin, Bennett - and in the streetcar suburbs of every Northeastern city. The style also carried a small, specific social advantage: for buyers in New York, New Jersey and the Hudson Valley, Dutch descent was old, prestigious, and comfortably distinct from the New England Yankee claim being made by everybody else.

The historical misreading is worth naming precisely, because it governs the proportions. Actual Dutch colonial building in the Hudson Valley and New Jersey was mostly one-and-a-half storeys of stone or brick, with a low, broadly spreading gambrel or a steep straight gable, a deeply overhanging flared eave often carried on an extended rafter over a porch, and an interior of two or three rooms without a centre passage. The revival raises the wall, shrinks the overhang, adds a centre-passage plan and a full second floor, and puts a 24-foot shed dormer in a roof whose original virtue was its unbroken sweep. The result is efficient and likeable and is not Dutch.

Standing in front of one, the roof dominates completely - it is usually more than half of what you see - and it gives the house a low, settled, sheltering look that a straight gable never does. The flare at the eave, where it is present, is the detail that separates the good examples from the merely serviceable: it softens the whole silhouette and throws a curved shadow onto the wall. Inside, the second floor is the interesting condition, because the walls kick in at about five feet and the ceiling follows the upper slope, producing rooms with sloped shoulders that children have always liked and adults have always found slightly cramped.

defining_characteristics: Gambrel roof - two pitches per side, steep below and shallow above - as the primary and defining massing element
The lower slope pierced by a long shed dormer or a row of dormers, providing full-height second-floor accommodation
Flared or kicked eave at the base of the lower slope in the better examples, projecting well beyond the wall face
Colonial Revival wall and openings below the eave: clapboard or shingle, double-hung multi-light sash, aligned bays, shutters
Classical entry with pilastered surround, transom or fanlight, frequently under a small pedimented or hooded porch
Chimney at a gable end or breaking through the gambrel slope
diagnostic_tells: A gambrel with a full-length shed dormer is Dutch Colonial Revival essentially by definition; almost nothing else in American housing produces that profile.
Look for the eave kick: a 12-24 in. flare below the lower slope. Its presence marks an architect or a good builder; its absence marks a catalog house.
The lower slope is steep - 20:12 to 24:12 - and the upper is shallow - 6:12 to 9:12. If both slopes are near-equal the roof is a mansard and the building is Second Empire.

Compared with genuine Dutch colonial buildings: the originals are one-and-a-half storeys of stone with an unbroken roof sweep and no centre passage; the revival is two full storeys of frame with a 20 ft dormer in it.

distinguished_from.difference: The original is a low masonry building of one and a half storeys with a broad unbroken gambrel or steep gable, a deeply projecting flared eave frequently sheltering a porch, and a two- or three-room plan without a centre hall.
