The revival doubles the storey count, cuts a shed dormer into the defining roof, and imposes a symmetrical centre-passage plan.
This is the parent style with a gambrel roof. If the roof is a simple gable or hip, it is Colonial Revival unqualified.

A mansard has four slopes with a flat deck on top and dormers set within the steep lower slope; the gambrel has two slopes per side and comes to a ridge. Second Empire is also masonry, bracketed, and Victorian in its detail.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Roof geometry. The gambrel is set out from the second-floor plate: the lower slope must be steep enough to give 7'0" headroom at 3'0" in from the wall, and the break point is placed to keep the upper slope shallow enough to look like a barn rather than a house.
typical_ratios: Lower slope 20:12 to 24:12; upper slope 6:12 to 9:12
Break point at 55-65 percent of the total roof height above the eave
Eave kick projecting 12-24 in. beyond the wall with the flare beginning 18-30 in. up the slope
Shed dormer face set back 18-36 in. from the wall plane and running 50-75 percent of the roof length
Wall height to eave 9-12 ft (one storey plus knee wall); roof height eave to ridge 12-16 ft
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even, three or five bays at 9'0"-11'0" on centre, with the entrance centred in the classic case and set to one side on the narrow-lot version. Dormer windows should align with the openings below.

massing_affinities.note: The variant is this massing. Everything else is a deviation.
The plan beneath is a standard centre-passage double pile; only the roof differs.
Narrow-lot suburban version with the entrance to one side and a front-facing gambrel.
A gambrel over a Cape footprint occurs but loses the variant's floor-area logic.

constraints.statement: Gambrel lower slope 20:12 to 24:12, upper slope 6:12 to 9:12, with the break at 55-65 percent of roof height. Slopes closer than 8:12 apart produce a mansard and void the variant.
The lower slope must genuinely enclose habitable second-floor area: minimum 7'0" clear headroom at a point 3'0" horizontally in from the exterior wall plane. A gambrel over an attic is decoration.

A full-length shed dormer face must be set back not less than 18 in. from the wall plane below and its ridge must sit not less than 24 in. below the main ridge. A dormer flush with the wall converts the roof to a clipped gable.
Where an eave kick is used it must project 12-24 in. past the wall, flare continuously across the full elevation, and return at the gable ends. A kick on the front only is forbidden.

test.note: Tests the kick's horizontal projection past the wall. Continuity across the full elevation and the return at gable ends are qualitative and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Shutters, where used, follow the parent style's rule: half the sash width each, full sash height, on offset pintles with holdbacks. Shutters are not permitted on dormer windows.

test.note: Hardware (offset pintles, holdbacks) and the dormer-window prohibition are qualitative and stay prose.

exemplars.name: William E. Curtis House
exemplars.location: 808 East Curtis Street, Seminole Heights, Tampa, Florida
exemplars.note: Gambrel-roofed Dutch Colonial Revival, NRHP 1987; evidence of how far outside the Hudson Valley the variant travelled.

exemplars.name: 57 Stone Street
exemplars.note: C. P. H. Gilbert. Urban Dutch Revival with a stepped gable, quoting the Netherlands rather than the Hudson Valley - the style's other branch.

exemplars.name: West End Collegiate Church and School
exemplars.location: West End Avenue at 77th Street, New York, New York
exemplars.note: Robert W. Gibson, after the Vleeshal at Haarlem. The institutional case that gave the Dutch reference its New York prestige. Cornerstone 1891, dedicated 20 November 1892.

exemplars.name: Wallabout Market
exemplars.note: William Tubby, 1894-96. A whole market district in Dutch Revival stepped-gable brick; demolished, but the largest commitment ever made to the idiom.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
William B. Rhoads, The Colonial Revival (1977)
Rosalie Fellows Bailey, Pre-Revolutionary Dutch Houses and Families in Northern New Jersey and Southern New York (1936)
John Milnes Baker, American House Styles: A Concise Guide (1994)

proportion_packs.note: JUDGMENT BINDING: dutch-colonial-revival is not in gibbs-ionic's own applies_to list. Bound because the node's own lineage states plainly that it is 'a roof-defined variant. Everything below the eave is standard Colonial Revival,' and colonial-revival itself binds gibbs-ionic as primary for the classical entry vocabulary. The gambrel is the whole distinction; the entrance, where classical, follows the parent style's Gibbs-derived surround.
JUDGMENT BINDING, inherited from colonial-revival on the same 'kit is the parent style's' basis as the primary order above.

JUDGMENT BINDING: not in the pack's applies_to list, but the node's own bay_rhythm is explicit -- 'even, three or five bays at 9'0"-11'0" on centre, with the entrance centred in the classic case' -- which is this pack's own arithmetic, inherited unchanged from colonial-revival for everything below the eave. Symmetry is recorded as 'near-symmetrical' rather than strict-bilateral, reflecting that the narrow-lot version sets the entrance to one side.

JUDGMENT BINDING, inherited: the node's own constraint c05 states the shutter rule follows 'the parent style's rule' verbatim, which is this pack's territory (shutter leaf = half the sash width), and the whole opening vocabulary below the eave is stated to be unchanged from colonial-revival.
JUDGMENT BINDING, inherited for the same reason: sash below the eave is ordinary Colonial Revival double-hung multi-light work, per the node's own defining_characteristics.

JUDGMENT BINDING, inherited: interior trim is not addressed separately in the node's own text, and 'everything below the eave is standard Colonial Revival' is read here to include the interior finish family as well as the wall.

JUDGMENT BINDING: dutch-colonial-american, the claimed historical ancestor, IS in this pack's applies_to list directly, and the node's own description states the type's economic logic in framing terms -- 'a gambrel encloses roughly 15 to 20 percent more usable floor area within the same roof volume than a simple gable of comparable ridge height.' The gambrel's own geometry (lower/upper slope, break point, eave kick) is fully specified by the node's own constraints and needs no separate pack; this binding covers only the underlying wall bay.

JUDGMENT BINDING, inherited: the plan below the roof is 'a standard centre-passage double pile' per the node's own massing_affinities, identical to the colonial-revival plan that binds room-harmonic. Not room-vernacular, despite dutch-colonial-american's presence in that pack's applies_to list, because the node is explicit that the plan is NOT the vernacular original's -- it 'imposes a symmetrical centre-passage plan' the original never had.

greek-revival-southern-plantation.name: Southern Plantation Greek Revival

revival_periods.note: The colossal-order colonnade returns as the standard dress of Southern banks, courthouses and the 'Gone With the Wind' image of the plantation house - an image largely constructed after 1900 and substantially inaccurate to what most plantations looked like.
Two-storey columned porticoes on suburban houses throughout the South, at a fraction of the original ceiling heights and none of the ventilation logic.

geography.hearth: the Lower Mississippi Valley and the Alabama Black Belt

lineage.note: The plan discipline - through-passage, single-pile where possible, tall ceilings, detached kitchen - comes from here unchanged; only the trim and the porch scale up.

In Louisiana and the Gulf the colonnade is grafted onto the Creole raised plantation house with its peripheral gallery, giving the peripteral colonnade that has no precedent in Greek or Anglo practice. Oak Alley is a gallery house wearing a temple.
Through professional architects - Nichols in North Carolina and Alabama, Gallier and Dakin in New Orleans, Walter's pupils - who carried British Greek Revival practice south.

description.short: The colossal colonnade as a shading machine: Greek orders wrapped around a Southern single-pile plan with twelve-foot ceilings and floor-length openings, built on cotton and sugar wealth and on the labour of enslaved people between 1830 and the Civil War.
description.long:
The Southern plantation Greek Revival is the version of the style in which the columns are doing real work. A Northern temple front is a facade; here the colonnade runs the full width of the house and frequently all the way around it, standing eight to twelve feet clear of the wall, two storeys tall, shading every opening on every elevation for most of the day. Behind it the plan is Southern rather than Greek: a central through-passage open at both ends, rooms one deep so they ventilate across, ceilings of eleven to fourteen feet, and windows carried down to the floor so they can be used as doors onto the gallery. The Greek apparatus - baseless Doric or Ionic shafts, deep entablature, low pedimented or hipped roof - is laid over a diagram that the Gulf had already worked out in the Creole raised plantation house and the Anglo South had worked out in the passage plan. The most spectacular examples are hybrids: Oak Alley's twenty-eight stuccoed brick columns on all four sides is a peripteral Greek temple in silhouette and a Caribbean gallery house in function, and neither reading is the whole truth.

The conditions were cotton, sugar, and slavery, in that order and inseparably. The 1793 cotton gin, the opening of the Black Belt and the Mississippi Delta to plantation agriculture in the 1820s and 1830s after Indian removal, and the sugar boom in south Louisiana produced a concentration of agricultural capital that had no equivalent in the North, and it arrived in exactly the decades when the Greek Revival was the available fashion. These houses were built by enslaved carpenters, brickmakers and plasterers - Gaineswood's owner explicitly used enslaved craftsmen, Oak Alley's brick was made and laid on site by enslaved people - and the columns were made possible by that labour in the same direct sense that a Roman temple was made possible by its own. A kit-of-parts system that reproduces this variant is reproducing a form whose scale was set by unpaid labour, and the honest way to handle that is to say so in the record rather than to launder it into 'Southern charm'. The professional channel ran through architects who moved south with the money: William Nichols, James Gallier, Charles and James Dakin, Minard Lafever's plates in every builder's hands.

What it reacted against was the Southern Federal house of its parents - not a rejection of the plan, which it kept almost intact, but of the plan's modesty of display. Where a Federal Virginia house put a slim one-storey portico at its door, this variant puts six two-storey columns across the whole front, and where the Federal house was one storey plus attic in the Gulf, this one is raised and doubled. The competitive display is explicit in the period record. So is the discomfort about it: the colonnade also solved a genuine problem, and the fact that it worked is why the type outlived the fashion by fifty years in the Gulf.

Standing under the gallery of one of these at four in the afternoon in August is the clearest possible argument for the type. The temperature under the colonnade is measurably lower than in the sun; the floor-length windows on both sides of the passage are open, and the air moves through the house continuously; the ceiling is fourteen feet up so the heat that does accumulate is above you. From a distance the house reads as a white block with a dark colonnade cut into it, and the strongest visual fact is the depth of shadow - Southern Greek Revival is a style about shade in the way that Northern Greek Revival is a style about snow-shadow on white boards. Inside, the rooms are enormous, plainly trimmed, and dark by design, with plaster ceiling medallions and heavy Grecian architraves as the only ornament, and the whole house is arranged so that the servants who made it work moved along back stairs and detached dependencies out of sight.

defining_characteristics: Colossal two-storey colonnade running the full width of the principal facade, and frequently peripteral (all four sides)
Colonnade set 8-12 feet clear of the wall so that it functions as a gallery and shades every opening behind it
Central through-passage open at both ends, with rooms one deep wherever the plan permits
Ceiling heights of 11-14 feet on the principal floor, with windows carried to the floor to serve as doors onto the gallery
Greek orders only - baseless Doric, Greek Ionic, Tower-of-the-Winds Corinthian - executed in stuccoed brick, built-up wood, or plastered timber
Low hipped or shallow-pedimented roof, often with a belvedere or roof monitor for stack ventilation
Detached kitchen and service dependencies; no service function in the main block
diagnostic_tells: Columns on more than one elevation - a Northern Greek Revival house never wraps its colonnade
Floor-length windows (triple-hung or jib) opening onto a gallery, unmistakable from outside by the sill line running down to the deck
Stuccoed and whitewashed brick columns rather than built-up wood staves, particularly in the Gulf
Belvedere, cupola or roof monitor over the stair, present for ventilation rather than for view
Gallery depth of 8 feet or more, which reads in shadow: the facade behind the columns is in darkness at midday

distinguished_from.difference: The Northern portico is a frontal composition on a compact heated plan with small windows; the Southern colonnade is a peripheral shading device on a thin, tall, cross-ventilated plan with floor-length openings. Depth of gallery and ceiling height separate them before ornament does.

The Creole raised plantation house has a peripheral gallery, a hall-less plan entered directly from the gallery, and a masonry base under a lighter upper storey. When a Greek colonnade is applied to that diagram the result belongs here; when there is no Greek order and no interior hall, it is Creole.

The 1893-1940 revival reproduces the colonnade at institutional scale with steel behind it, plate glass, Roman as often as Greek orders, and 9-foot ceilings. If the columns are colossal but the windows are ordinary in height, it is a revival.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Greek orders sized by module as in the parent style, but with overall dimensions governed by the gallery: column spacing is set by the bay of the house behind, and gallery depth by the shading angle required at the site's latitude in summer.
typical_ratios: Doric columns 6-7 lower diameters, Ionic 8.5-9.5; two full storeys, commonly 20-26 feet tall
Entablature depth 1/4 to 1/5 of column height
Gallery depth 8-14 feet; column spacing 9-14 feet on centre
Principal-floor ceiling 12-14 feet, upper floor 11-13 feet
Window opening 1:2.8 to 1:3.5 width to height where floor-length
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12, hipped or low-pedimented
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even hexastyle or octastyle colonnade across the front, continuing at the same spacing around the flanks in peripteral examples; the wall behind is bayed to match, and the entrance occupies the centre bay with a rectangular transom and sidelights.

massing_affinities.note: The main block behind the colonnade, though frequently thinned to single-pile for ventilation.
The Gulf hybrid, in which the colonnade is the gallery and the house is a core inserted into it.
In the lower Mississippi, the colonnade sits on a raised masonry base for flood and damp.
Berry Hill, where the dependencies get their own tetrastyle Doric porticoes.

constraints.statement: Colonnade columns must run the full height of the block (both storeys), 6-7 diameters for Doric and 8.5-9.5 for Ionic, carrying an entablature 1/4 to 1/5 of column height. A one-storey porch on a two-storey house is a different and lesser type.

test.note: 1/4 to 1/5 of column height, order-independent. The order-specific column-diameter ranges (6-7 for Doric, 8.5-9.5 for Ionic) stay prose since which order applies isn't itself a tested variable.

constraints.statement: Gallery depth minimum 8 feet (10-12 typical), sufficient to shade the full window height on the principal facade at the summer solstice for the building's latitude. A colonnade shallower than 8 feet is ornament, not a climate device, and the plan behind it must then be re-justified.

test.note: Tests the 8ft minimum gallery depth. The solstice-shading sufficiency claim (which depends on latitude and sun angle) and the 'ornament vs climate device' re-justification clause are left as prose.

constraints.statement: Principal-floor ceiling height minimum 12 feet, with openings on two opposite walls of every principal room and a through-passage operable at both ends. Windows on the gallery elevations must be floor-length or triple-hung so they function as doors.

test.note: Tests the 12ft principal-floor ceiling-height minimum. The cross-ventilation clause (openings on two opposite walls), the operable through-passage, and the floor-length/triple-hung window requirement on gallery elevations are left as prose -- no vocabulary variable captures per-room opening placement or sash type.

constraints.statement: Greek vocabulary is exclusive: no arches, no domes, no bases under Doric columns, no elliptical fanlights. A belvedere or monitor is permitted and should be detailed with the same entablature profile as the main order.

Kitchen and service functions belong in detached dependencies or a rear ell, never in the main block. Any contemporary reconstruction of this variant should record in its documentation that the type's scale was made possible by enslaved labour; the historical record is part of the kit.

exemplars.name: Oak Alley
exemplars.note: Begun 1837, probably designed by Joseph Pilie; a free-standing colonnade of 28 stuccoed brick Doric columns on all four sides, 16-inch walls, brick made and laid on site by enslaved people.

exemplars.name: Rosedown
exemplars.location: St. Francisville, West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana
exemplars.note: Built November 1834 to May 1835 of cypress and cedar milled on site; five-bay two-storey gallery on smooth Doric columns, with Doric-porticoed brick wings added 1845. Transitional Federal-to-Greek and useful for dating the shift precisely.

exemplars.name: Berry Hill
exemplars.note: Begun 1842; John Evans Johnson, architect. Octastyle Doric portico with a six-and-a-half-foot entablature correctly detailed with triglyphs, metopes and guttae, and matching tetrastyle Doric dependencies.

exemplars.name: Gaineswood
exemplars.note: Built 1843-1861 by Nathan Bryan Whitfield, who grew the house outward from an existing dogtrot log house using enslaved craftsmen and Lafever's plates. National Historic Landmark; the most elaborately Grecian interior in the South. Built in campaigns 1843-1861.

sources: Talbot Hamlin, Greek Revival Architecture in America (1944)
Roger G. Kennedy, Greek Revival America (1989)
Minard Lafever, The Beauties of Modern Architecture (1835)
Mills Lane, Architecture of the Old South (series, 1984-96)
Jay D. Edwards, 'The Complex Origins of the American Domestic Piazza-Veranda-Gallery', Material Culture 21 (1989)

proportion_packs.note: Berry Hill's octastyle portico is 'correctly detailed with triglyphs, metopes and guttae' at 7-diameter proportions per this pack, and Oak Alley's 28 stuccoed brick columns are the same order at plantation scale -- both named exemplars of this variant. Standalone Greek Doric per Benjamin's own 1830 preface, encoded outside the Vignola-overlay system for the reason docs/open-questions.md item 11 gives: the Doric is the one order Benjamin says Greek and Roman practice cannot reconcile.

This is the one Greek Revival node in the batch where the corpus's own applies_to cross-reference names vignola-ionic directly, not just an architectural inference -- Greek Ionic is one of this variant's three named orders (defining_characteristics: 'baseless Doric, Greek Ionic, Tower-of-the-Winds Corinthian'). No dedicated Benjamin/Greek Ionic pack exists in this corpus, so plain Vignola stands in; its 9-diameter column sits inside the style's own stated 8.5-9.5 range.

The third named order -- 'Tower-of-the-Winds Corinthian about 10' diameters per the parent style's typical_ratios -- and, like vignola-ionic, this is the one Greek Revival variant whose applies_to cross-reference actually lists it. Bound here rather than at the parent or the Northern variant because this is the only one of the three Greek Revival nodes in this batch where the style's own text names all three Greek orders explicitly rather than defaulting to Doric-with-occasional-Ionic.

The wall_section_greek_revival / casing_greek_revival family, for the 'plainly trimmed... heavy Grecian architraves' interiors behind the colonnade -- the same family as the rest of the Greek Revival cluster, executed here in stuccoed brick, built-up wood or plastered timber per the style's own material list.

Governs the width:height ratio the style states directly (1:2.8 to 1:3.5 for floor-length openings) and the rectangular-transom entrance (constraint c04). It does NOT capture the triple-hung or jib mechanism that lets these openings 'function as doors' onto the gallery (constraint c03) -- no vocabulary in any of the 36 packs expresses sash-as-door operability, which is a genuine gap distinct from the ordinary opening-proportion coverage.

Governs the colossal colonnade's composition and the bay spacing it sets for the wall behind (9-14 ft on centre, per the style's own ratios), continuing at the same spacing around the flanks in peripteral examples like Oak Alley. The pack does not model gallery depth as a shading function of solar geometry (constraint c02's 8 ft minimum, sized to the site's latitude) -- that is a climatic calculation outside any of the 36 packs' scope, carried as prose in the style file's own test.

Genuinely useful here where it is not for the other two Greek Revival nodes: this variant's own ratios (principal floor 12-14 ft, upper floor 11-13 ft) are a real diminishing pair, roughly 0.85-0.93, close to this pack's core 0.85 second-storey rule -- unlike the Northern and parent nodes, where the entablature runs level across an undifferentiated block.

Listed directly in this pack's applies_to cross-reference. Bound for rooms that are 'enormous, plainly trimmed' but still composed to the 11-14 ft ceiling heights and passage proportions the style states as hard constraints, not accumulated vernacular space.

arts-and-crafts-american.name: American Arts and Crafts

geography.hearth: Boston and Chicago as intellectual centres; Stickley's workshops at Eastwood, New York, as the transmission point

lineage.note: Ruskin and Morris arrive as text and as furniture before they arrive as buildings. The Boston Society of Arts and Crafts (1897), Elbert Hubbard's Roycroft (1895) and Gustav Stickley's United Crafts (1898) are all deliberate transplants of an English reform programme.
The American formal substrate: the continuous unornamented skin, the open living hall organized on a hearth, and the horizontal spread of the plan are inherited directly, not imported.
Richardson's insistence that material be shown doing its work, and his base-shaft-cap masonry hierarchy, pass into the movement through the Shingle Style and through Sullivan's office.
The specific target is machine-sawn applied ornament sold by the linear foot from a millwork catalog. The reform is not anti-decoration; it is a demand that decoration be produced by construction.

description.short: The American branch of the Arts and Crafts reform, which held that ornament must arise from construction and that a house, its furniture, and its site are a single commission, and which reorganized the middle-class plan around an open hearth-centred living room.
description.long:
American Arts and Crafts is a reform movement before it is a style, and this matters for how the node behaves in a graph: its defining content is a rule about where ornament may come from. Ornament must be produced by the act of building — by the joint, the bracket, the rafter end, the change of material at a structural transition — and not applied to a surface after the fact. Everything the movement looks like follows from that rule. Wood is left unpainted or matte-stained so that the grain and the joinery remain legible. Porch supports are battered piers on heavy bases because that is what a compressive member honestly looks like. Windows group into bands because they are openings between structural posts rather than punched holes in a decorated wall. The movement's American originality lies in its scale: where William Morris built for wealthy patrons, Stickley, Hubbard, and the Chicago and Pasadena architects built for a salaried professional class, and then published the result.

The conditions that produced it are specific and largely economic. The scroll saw, the moulding machine, and the national millwork catalog had, by the 1880s, made ornament cheaper than plainness, and the visible result was a generation of houses wearing decoration that no one had made and no one could account for. The Panic of 1893 discredited the display culture attached to it. At the same moment the domestic servant supply collapsed for middle-class households, which quietly rewrote the plan: the formal parlour, the back stair, and the segregated dining room became liabilities, and the open living room with built-in cabinetry, a hearth, and a plate rail became the answer — fewer rooms, fewer surfaces to dust, fewer pieces of furniture to move. The mail-order catalog and the mass magazine, the very instruments of the ornament glut, then became the movement's own distribution system. Stickley's The Craftsman (1901-1916) is the pivotal case: a magazine that printed Morris and Ruskin alongside measured plans a local carpenter could execute, which is to say a magazine that converted an ideology into a buildable specification.

What it reacts against is therefore not the Victorian era in general but a particular industrial dishonesty: the imitation of handwork by machine. The movement's American compromise, and it is an intelligent one, is to accept the machine where the machine does honest work — dimensional lumber, plate glass, cast hardware — and to reserve the hand for the joint and the finish. Greene and Greene push this to its limit in Pasadena, where the pegged scarf joints and rounded timber ends of the Gamble House are simultaneously a display of craft and a demonstration of how a stick of wood terminates. Stickley pushes it in the opposite direction, toward reproducibility, and it is Stickley's direction that produces a national vernacular.

To stand in one of these rooms is to be in a space that is lower and darker than a Victorian room and considerably calmer. The ceiling is beamed and near, often eight and a half feet. Light arrives filtered through art glass in rectilinear geometry and does not glare. The wood is brown and matte and absorbs rather than reflects. The hearth is the largest object in the room and everything is arranged with reference to it, including built-in seating that cannot be moved, which is the movement's most radical and least remarked act: the plan is fixed against redecoration. Outside, the eaves are wide enough that the wall is in shadow for most of the day, and the shadow is what gives a plain wall its interest. This last point is the one the twentieth century will spend the next fifty years forgetting.

defining_characteristics: Ornament produced by construction — exposed joinery, rafter tails, purlins, brackets, and material transitions — rather than applied to a finished surface
The hearth as the generative centre of the plan, with an open living room replacing the parlour and built-in cabinetry replacing movable furniture
Materials left in their own colour and texture: unpainted or matte-stained wood, clinker brick, river rock, stucco, matte tile
Horizontal emphasis established by low broad roofs, wide eaves, and continuous window and trim bands
House, interior fittings, furniture, and garden conceived as one commission under one grammar
Absence of applied classical orders and of machine-sawn Victorian ornament
diagnostic_tells: Exposed rafter tails and knee braces that continue the actual framing rather than being screwed on
Battered (tapered) porch piers standing on heavy masonry bases at least two feet wide
Wide flat unpainted trim, a plate rail at door head height, and bookcases built into the wall flanking the fireplace
Art glass in rectilinear, non-floral geometry, usually confined to upper sash and cabinet doors
Two or three natural materials stacked base-to-top on one elevation (stone base, shingle middle, stucco gable) with each change occurring at a structural line

distinguished_from.difference: Queen Anne ornament is sawn, turned, and applied to the surface; Arts and Crafts ornament is the structure itself left visible. If a bracket would fall off without changing anything, it is Queen Anne.
Colonial Revival restores bilateral symmetry, applied classical orders, and painted trim — all three of which American Arts and Crafts explicitly rejects.

Prairie abstracts and suppresses structural evidence into continuous planes; Arts and Crafts insists on displaying it. A clean soffit with no visible rafter is Prairie; a rafter tail is Arts and Crafts.

proportional_system.governing_logic: No canonical module. Proportion is set by two datums and one structural rhythm: the horizontal line of the porch beam, the aligned head height of all doors and windows, and the spacing of the stud or timber bay that the exposed members declare. The system is dimensional rather than ratio-based, which is why it scales badly upward — an Arts and Crafts house of more than two storeys loses its logic.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12
Eave and rake overhang 24 to 36 inches
Wall plate 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft 0 in at the principal floor
Window and door heads aligned at a single datum, 6 ft 8 in to 7 ft 0 in above finish floor
Porch depth 7 to 9 ft — deep enough to furnish
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Windows grouped into ribbons of two to four units between structural posts rather than isolated as punched openings; the group, not the sash, is the compositional unit.

massing_affinities.note: The single-storey hearth-centred bungalow is the movement's most-built vessel.
The 'Craftsman foursquare' — the movement's grammar applied to an efficient two-storey urban box on a narrow lot.
Shared with the Prairie branch; the pinwheel plan is common ancestry, not a distinguishing trait.

constraints.statement: Exposed rafter tails must correspond to actual rafters at 16 to 24 in on centre and project 24 to 36 in beyond the wall plane. Decorative tails applied to a boxed eave are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the projection beyond the wall plane. The 16-24in on-centre rafter spacing has no vocabulary variable (rafter spacing is not named) and stays prose, as does the prohibition on decorative (non-structural) tails.

constraints.statement: Principal roof pitch between 4:12 and 6:12. Pitches above 8:12 belong to the Tudor and Storybook families and break the horizontal reading.

Applied classical orders — fluted or turned columns, pedimented door surrounds, dentil courses — are forbidden. Porch supports must be square posts or battered piers on masonry bases not less than 24 in wide.

test.note: Tests the masonry base width. The prohibition on applied classical orders (columns, pedimented surrounds, dentil courses) is a categorical list with no vocabulary variable enumerating forbidden ornament and stays prose.

constraints.statement: All window and door heads on a given storey align to one datum, tolerance zero. Transoms and clerestories may sit above that datum only where the wall plate is raised for the whole bay.

test.note: Tests the zero-tolerance datum rule. The transom/clerestory exception (permitted above the datum only where the wall plate is raised for the whole bay) stays prose.

constraints.statement: No more than three wall materials per elevation, each change occurring at a structural line (water table, belt, plate) and returning fully around any corner it meets.

test.note: Tests the material-count ceiling. Where changes must occur (a structural line) and the corner-return requirement stay prose.

exemplars.name: Gamble House
exemplars.note: Greene and Greene. The movement's high-craft limit case: every joint, hardware piece, rug, and light fitting designed under one commission.

exemplars.name: Craftsman Farms (the Log House)
exemplars.note: Gustav Stickley's own house, built 1908-1911. The theorist of The Craftsman building for himself in chestnut logs and fieldstone.

exemplars.name: Roycroft Campus
exemplars.note: Elbert Hubbard's craft colony, built out c. 1897-1915. The American attempt at a Morris-style guild settlement, and the commercial engine that sold the idea nationally.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Wendy Kaplan (ed.), 'The Art That Is Life': The Arts and Crafts Movement in America, 1875-1920 (1987)
Clay Lancaster, The American Bungalow, 1880-1930 (1985)
Alan Gowans, The Comfortable House: North American Suburban Architecture 1890-1930 (1986)
Edward R. Bosley, Greene and Greene (2000)

proportion_packs.note: The movement's own governing rule -- ornament must be produced by construction, never applied after the fact -- is this pack's whole argument restated from the furniture side: 'there is no pedestal, no column and no entablature... the module is a board... the room does not generate the trim; the lumber yard does.' Bound as the interior counterpart to the node's own hard constraint (c03) forbidding applied classical orders. The pack's own applies_to list names this node directly, and its sources -- Stickley's Craftsman magazine among them -- are the movement's own transmission mechanism, not an analogous system borrowed from elsewhere.

Governs the 'balanced-asymmetrical' composition the node's own proportional_system describes only qualitatively (two datums and a structural rhythm, 'dimensional rather than ratio-based'): this pack's window_grouping_rule (openings gathered in groups of two to four between structural posts, adjacent groups differing in count) is precisely the node's own diagnostic that windows 'group into ribbons... the group, not the sash, is the compositional unit,' and its continuous-datum rule (water table and head line unbroken through every mass) is what makes the node's stacked base-shingle-stucco material hierarchy -- a defining characteristic -- read as one wall rather than three. Not given the top role: the movement genuinely has no module of its own at this level of generality, which the node's own proportional_system says outright, so no pack here stands in as an order-equivalent 'primary.'

romantic-revivals.name: Romantic Revivals

description.short: Gothic, Italianate, and their companions — the moment when American architecture abandoned classical symmetry for association, irregularity, and moral argument.
description.long:
Andrew Jackson Downing's argument, made in books that sold enormously between 1842 and 1852, was that a house shapes the character of the family inside it, that the classical box was inappropriate to domestic life, and that irregular, picturesque, vine-covered houses in Gothic or Italian dress would produce better people. It is the first fully articulated American theory of domestic architecture, and it is a moral theory.

The enabling condition was technological. Balloon framing, machine-cut nails, and the steam scroll saw arrived in the 1830s and 1840s and made complex irregular massing and elaborate sawn ornament affordable for the first time in history. Downing supplied the argument; the sawmill supplied the means.

defining_characteristics: Irregular, asymmetrical massing composed for picturesque effect
Historical association as the source of architectural meaning
Balloon framing and machine-cut ornament as the enabling technology
An explicit moral claim that domestic architecture forms character
Vertical emphasis and steep rooflines replacing the classical horizontal

dutch-colonial-american.name: Dutch Colonial American

revival_periods.note: The revival fixed on the gambrel roof and the full-width shed dormer — a combination that almost never occurs in the colonial original — and made it the second most common American suburban house type of the 1920s.

regions: Rockland and Westchester counties, New York
geography.hearth: New Netherland — the Hudson corridor from Nieuw Amsterdam to Beverwijck (Albany), with a second core in the Hackensack and Passaic valleys

lineage.note: The urban expression — parapeted gable to the street, mouse-tooth (vlechtingen) brick tumbling, iron beam anchors and date irons — is transplanted almost intact to Nieuw Amsterdam, Kingston and Albany.

Much of the rural framing tradition, including the H-bent anchor-beam frame and the flared eave, is Flemish and Brabantine rather than Hollandish; a large share of the settlers came from the southern Low Countries.

description.short: The building culture of New Netherland — anchor-beam framing, jambless fireplaces, and steep unbroken gables in stone and brick — which outlived Dutch rule by a century and a half and then was misremembered by its own revival.
description.long:
The Dutch lost New Netherland in 1664 and kept building it until about 1800. That gap is the most interesting fact about this style: it survived not as a political culture but as a set of carpentry habits and a language of domestic comfort transmitted inside families, in a region where English law and Dutch construction coexisted for five generations. What was transmitted was not a look. It was a frame — the H-bent, a pair of posts with a transverse anchor beam tenoned through them and secured with a projecting wedged tenon — and a hearth, the jambless fireplace, which has no side cheeks at all: the fire sits on a raised hearth against a flat wall and a plastered or timber hood hangs above it on iron rods, so that the fire is a piece of furniture in the room rather than a hole in a wall. Anyone who has stood in front of one understands immediately why the Dutch kept them and why the English thought them wasteful. They radiate into the room instead of drawing everything up the flue, and they smoke.

The walls follow the geology. In the Hudson Valley the settlers found workable limestone and sandstone and laid it in wide beds of shell-lime mortar, walls twenty to thirty inches thick, sometimes with the entrance facade coursed and squared and the other three sides left as rubble — a house with one good face, which tells you what the elevation was for. In the Hackensack Valley it is the red-brown Newark sandstone. In the towns it is brick, laid in cross bond, with the gable turned to the street and stepped or spouted in the manner of Amsterdam. The rural roof begins steep and straight, forty-five to fifty-five degrees, sprung from a low plate seven to nine feet above the floor, so that the roof is most of what you see. The gambrel — two slopes, a steep lower and a shallow upper — is an eighteenth-century arrival that lets you get a full upper storey out of a low wall, and it spreads through New Jersey and the lower Hudson after about 1720.

The deep flared eave, the so-called spring eave, is the tradition's signature and its most misunderstood element. It is not a porch and it did not begin as one: it is the lower rafter run continued past the wall face on a curve, projecting eighteen to thirty-six inches, throwing water clear of an unfired stone wall and shading the summer sun off the openings. Only later, in the eighteenth century, does someone put posts under it and discover a porch. That accidental porch is the most quietly influential detail in American domestic architecture — the ancestor of a national habit.

What the style negotiated against was English fashion, and it lost slowly and gracefully. By 1750 a Bergen County house has a Dutch frame, a Dutch eave, and a Georgian five-bay front with a centre door. Nothing about that is a compromise; it is exactly what a builder does when the plan and the section still work and only the face has to change.

defining_characteristics: H-bent anchor-beam framing, the transverse beams exposed and their projecting tenons visible in the room, on frame houses; twenty- to thirty-inch load-bearing stone or brick on masonry houses
The jambless fireplace — an open hearth against a flat wall with a suspended hood, no side jambs — as the domestic centre before c. 1750
Chimneys at or in the gable ends, never a single central stack of the New England kind
Steep straight gable (45–55 degrees) in the seventeenth century; the broad gambrel with a steep lower slope and shallow upper slope from c. 1720
A flared or 'spring' eave, projecting 18–36 in on a concave sweep beyond the wall plane, on eighteenth-century work
A low wall plate — 7 to 9 feet above the floor — so that the roof carries most of the visual mass of the building
Dutch (horizontally divided) doors, wrought-iron beam anchors on masonry gables, and casement or nine-over-nine sash
diagnostic_tells: A jambless fireplace, or the flat unbroken chimney breast that remains after one has been rebuilt, is decisive and occurs in no other American tradition
Exposed transverse anchor beams with wedged through-tenons projecting past the post
Wrought-iron wall anchors on a masonry gable, sometimes forming a date
Dressed and coursed stone on the entrance elevation only, with rubble on the other three
Low eave: the second-floor window sits partly within the roof, or there is no second-floor window at all

distinguished_from.difference: The revival is defined by a gambrel roof with a full-width shed dormer, symmetrical fenestration on all elevations, wood framing with a brick or shingle skin, and an eave that overhangs straight rather than springing on a curve. The colonial original almost never has a shed dormer; where it has dormers at all they are small individual gabled ones. If the dormer runs the length of the roof, it is a house built after 1900.

Chimney position separates them instantly: one enormous central stack in New England, gable-end stacks in New Netherland. New England covers its frame in clapboard and hides the joinery; the Dutch house exposes its anchor beams and builds in stone where stone exists.

Both build in thick stone with steep roofs, but the German house is organized around an asymmetric three-room Flurküchenhaus plan with a central chimney serving a closed jamb stove, while the Dutch house is a one- or two-room open plan with gable hearths and an open jambless fire.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The H-bent frame bay — a pair of posts with an anchor beam — repeated along the length of the house at 8 to 12 feet on centre; masonry houses inherit the same rhythm without needing it.
typical_ratios: Room depth 18–22 ft (one bent span); overall length 30–48 ft as bents are added
Wall plate 7 ft 0 in – 9 ft 0 in above the floor; total wall height to eave rarely exceeds 11 ft on a one-and-a-half-storey house
Masonry wall thickness 20–30 in, roughly 1:5 to 1:7 of wall height
Gambrel: lower slope 60–72 degrees, upper 18–30 degrees, break at 55–70% of the half-span
Spring eave projection 18–36 in beyond the wall face
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Additive along the ridge. Three-bay and five-bay fronts both occur; the door is centred on five-bay work after c. 1730 and off-centre before.

massing_affinities.note: Two rooms, gable hearths, no passage — the standard rural New Netherland plan.
The one-bent starting house, expanded by adding bents along the ridge.
The eighteenth-century form that the revival later seized on.
Post-1750 Anglicization of the plan behind a still-Dutch section.
The urban gable-to-street house of Nieuw Amsterdam, Kingston and Albany.

constraints.statement: Chimneys sit at or within the gable end walls. A single central stack is a New England device and destroys the Dutch plan, which depends on an open one- or two-room volume.
Wall plate 7 ft 0 in – 9 ft 0 in above the finished floor. If the plate rises above 10 ft the roof stops governing the elevation and the building reads Georgian.

Gambrel geometry: lower slope 60–72 degrees, upper slope 18–30 degrees, break point at 55–70% of the half-span. A gambrel whose two slopes differ by less than 30 degrees reads as a twentieth-century barn-roof house.

test.note: Tests the lower (eave-side) gambrel slope. The upper slope (18-30deg) and the break point (55-70% of half-span) are the same statement's other numeric claims and stay prose -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Full-width shed dormers are forbidden. They are the diagnostic signature of Dutch Colonial Revival, not of any colonial Dutch building.
Load-bearing stone walls 20–30 in thick, laid in lime mortar with wide joints; dressed and coursed on the entrance elevation, rubble elsewhere. Thin stone veneer over frame is a different building.

exemplars.name: Pieter Wyckoff House
exemplars.note: Occupied by the Wyckoffs from about 1652 and generally called the oldest house in New York City, though much of the standing fabric is later; the small kitchen wing preserves the earliest work.

exemplars.name: Pieter Bronck House
exemplars.note: Thick stone walls, steep straight gable, single open chambers on two floors — the rural Hudson type before the gambrel.

exemplars.name: Jean Hasbrouck House
exemplars.location: Historic Huguenot Street, New Paltz, New York
exemplars.note: National Historic Landmark; retains the only original eighteenth-century jambless fireplace on Huguenot Street. Built by Huguenot settlers using wholly Dutch construction — a useful reminder that this is a building culture, not an ethnicity.

exemplars.name: Steuben House (Zabriskie House)
exemplars.location: Historic New Bridge Landing, River Edge, New Jersey
exemplars.note: Bergen sandstone, enlarged c. 1765 when the fashionable gambrel roof was added.

sources: Helen Wilkinson Reynolds, Dutch Houses in the Hudson Valley before 1776 (1929)
Roderic H. Blackburn and Ruth Piwonka, Remembrance of Patria: Dutch Arts and Culture in Colonial America (1988)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)

proportion_packs.note: Supplies the base module of the whole rural tradition. The style's own governing_logic names it directly: the H-bent frame bay repeated along the ridge at 8-12 ft on centre. Even after the frame retreats into masonry on the Hudson Valley stone houses, the bent-spacing rhythm survives as the room module (18-22 ft), which is why the pack is bound here rather than replaced by a masonry-only system. Bound at the style's own 8-12 ft bay rather than the pack's documented 16-20 ft English box-frame band; no source explains why the Dutch H-bent runs shorter than the English bay, and that gap is worth stating rather than silently reconciling. dutch-colonial-american is named directly in timber-bay's own applies_to.

Governs the masonry houses, which are over half the surviving fabric by the style's own account of walls following the geology (Hudson Valley limestone, Hackensack red sandstone). Its corner_quoin and reveal_masonry rules (wall thickness in whole wythes) apply directly to a 20-30 in load-bearing wall, and its front-elevation/flank grading is the same hierarchy the style itself describes: dressed and coursed at the entrance, rubble on the other three sides. Bound secondary rather than primary because the earliest frame-and-plaster settlement work, before the geology was exploited, sits outside its scope, and because rubble stone coursing is looser than the pack's rod-based rigor assumes. dutch-colonial-american is named directly in brick-course's own applies_to.

The hall-and-parlor and single-cell plans are additive and function-constrained rooms exactly as this pack describes, not treatise-proportioned ones — the style's own text records no ratio ambition anywhere in the plan. dutch-colonial-american is named directly in the pack's own applies_to.

Governs the dated glazing sequence the style's own defining_characteristics name outright — casement to nine-over-nine sash — using the same glasshouse-supply arithmetic as any other Anglo-American tradition, since Dutch builders bought glass on the same market. Bound for its light-count and muntin-dating logic only: the measured window openings this family actually built (see the Hudson Valley sibling's own typical_ratios, roughly 1.4-1.7:1) run markedly squarer than sash-light's own 1.85-2.6 measured band or opening-proportion's Palladian 2.17:1, and that divergence is stated rather than absorbed. opening-proportion was considered and rejected for this reason.

Governs only the Anglicized late phase the style's own text names directly: 'By 1750 a Bergen County house has a Dutch frame, a Dutch eave, and a Georgian five-bay front with a centre door.' Bound optional and low because most of the period this node covers (1625-1750) is explicitly additive-vernacular with an off-centre door, and the pack's odd-bay/single-entrance-hierarchy invariants only start to hold once English fashion has taken over the elevation while the Dutch section underneath is unchanged.

colonial-iberian-americas.name: Colonial Iberian Americas

description.short: Three centuries of Spanish building in the Americas, where Iberian plans met indigenous labour, adobe, and a continent of new conditions.
description.long:
Spanish colonial building in the Americas is a translation problem worked out at scale over three hundred years: European plan diagrams executed by indigenous craftsmen in local materials, under a Church that wanted magnificence and a Crown that would not pay for it.

What emerged — massive plain walls, courtyards, arcaded corridors, tile roofs, and ornament concentrated at the portal — is the direct ancestor of the American Southwest's regional architecture, and by way of Mission Revival and Spanish Colonial Revival, of a substantial fraction of everything built in California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida since 1915.

defining_characteristics: European plan diagrams executed in local material by local labour
Courtyard and arcaded corredor as the organizing spatial devices
Massive adobe or rubble walls, plain except at the portal
Low-pitched clay tile roofs and long horizontal parapets
A genuinely new regional language rather than a diluted European one

spanish-colonial-revival.name: Spanish Colonial Revival

geography.hearth: San Diego and Santa Barbara, California

lineage.note: The nominal claimed ancestor, though the revival takes far more from Spain and Mexico than from anything built in Spanish North America.
The decisive ornamental reference. Goodhue's 1915 exposition buildings put Mexican and Spanish Baroque relief on the entrance and everything follows from that.
The domestic core: whitewashed courtyard house, patio, reja, tiled stair. See andalusian-spanish-revival.
Church facades, portales, and the specific colour and tile culture that Goodhue and Sylvester Baxter documented in Mexico from 1901.
Horseshoe and cusped arches, azulejo panels, pierced plaster grilles as an ornamental register.
Brick and tile geometry, artesonado ceilings, and the Spanish tradition of Islamic craft under Christian patronage.
The real line of practice. Same builders, same stucco-over-frame technology, same clay tile suppliers, same regionalist argument - enriched and then displaced.
The exposition-planning apparatus and academic drafting culture, though Goodhue himself never attended the Ecole and came out of Gothicist office practice with Cram.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The style launched by Bertram Goodhue's 1915 Panama-California Exposition in San Diego, which replaced Mission Revival's austerity with the full Spanish and Latin American repertoire: elaborately carved entrances against blank walls, wrought iron, decorative tile, low-pitched red tile roofs, and freely asymmetrical massing.
description.long:
Spanish Colonial Revival is Mission Revival's successor and its refutation. Where Mission Revival had argued that California's proper architecture was plain, symmetrical and Franciscan, Spanish Colonial Revival argued that it was rich, irregular, and drawn from four centuries of building across Spain, Mexico and the Spanish Americas. The change happened at a single site. For the 1915 Panama-California Exposition in San Diego, Bertram Grosvenor Goodhue - working against the Olmsted brothers' preference for a low Mission scheme - designed a Churrigueresque set piece at the California Quadrangle, with a facade of Mexican Baroque relief exploding out of an otherwise plain wall. It was decisive within two years. The style then found its domestic language in Santa Barbara, especially in the work of George Washington Smith, and after the 1925 earthquake destroyed much of that city's commercial core it became municipal policy there.

The formal system is precise despite its apparent looseness. Walls are stucco, off-white to warm ochre, with visible mass at reveals. Roofs are low-pitched, 3:12 to 5:12, in red barrel tile with minimal or no overhang, and - this is the key departure from Mission Revival - they are broken into multiple planes at multiple heights, with gables, sheds and hips meeting at varied levels to describe a building that appears to have grown. Ornament is concentrated absolutely: the entrance receives a carved or cast surround, sometimes with twisted columns and a broken pediment, and the twenty feet of wall either side of it receives nothing at all. Wrought iron does the secondary work - window grilles, balconettes, gates, stair rails - and glazed tile the tertiary, on stair risers, fountain basins, and window reveals. Windows are casements or multi-light double-hung, deeply recessed, and often arched at principal openings only.

What made it sell was the same thing that made Mediterranean Revival sell in Florida: it converted a hot, dry, recently-settled place into somewhere with a past. The Southern California land boom of the 1920s needed exactly that, and the style could scale from a Montecito estate to a four-unit bungalow court without losing its identity, because its identity lived in three or four moves rather than in a proportional system. That scalability is why it became, and remains, the default vocabulary of the American Southwest, and why every production builder from Phoenix to Orlando still sells a degraded version of it.

The experience turns on the relation between blankness and incident. You walk along a long, hot, pale wall that offers nothing - no base, no cornice, no rhythm - and then arrive at a door around which somebody has spent an entire ornament budget: carved stone or cast plaster, a heavy panelled leaf, a tiled reveal, an iron lantern. Inside, the rooms are dim, tall, white, and cool, with a beamed ceiling and a tiled floor, and they open onto a patio where a fountain is running. It is a style of extreme contrasts, and its failures are all failures of contrast - stucco boxes with a little ornament spread evenly everywhere, which is precisely what the tract-house version does.

defining_characteristics: Stucco wall of expressed mass, off-white to warm earth tones, with openings recessed at least 6 in. into it
Low-pitched roof, 3:12 to 5:12, in red clay barrel or mission tile, with minimal or no eave overhang
Roof broken into multiple planes at multiple heights - gables, hips and sheds - describing an accreted, asymmetrical mass
Ornament concentrated at the principal entrance (carved, cast or moulded surround, often Churrigueresque) against otherwise blank wall
Wrought iron as the primary secondary material: window grilles, balconettes, gates, rails, lanterns
Asymmetrical massing organised around at least one outdoor room - patio, courtyard, or walled garden
Deeply recessed windows, arched at principal openings, with decorative tile at reveals, stairs, or fountains
diagnostic_tells: Ornament is concentrated in one place and absent everywhere else. Evenly distributed ornament means a later imitation.
Roof planes meet at different heights and the ridges do not align. Mission Revival keeps a single roof line and a symmetrical front; Mediterranean Revival keeps a uniform hip.
No curvilinear shaped parapet. If there is one, the building is Mission Revival, or a hybrid.
Eave overhang under 12 in. with a closed soffit or a plastered edge, versus Mission Revival's 24-42 in. of exposed rafter tail.
Wrought iron somewhere - even one balconette or window grille. Mission Revival almost never uses it.

Against the historical original: actual Spanish colonial building in North America used 2-4 ft adobe walls, tiny unglazed openings, dirt or brick floors and almost no worked ornament outside of church facades. The revival puts church-scale ornament on a house.

distinguished_from.difference: The critical pair. Mission Revival (c. 1890-1920) is austere, symmetrical, ornamented almost nowhere, defined by a curvilinear parapet and a heavy pier arcade, with wide overhanging eaves on exposed rafters, and quotes only the California missions. Spanish Colonial Revival (c. 1915-1940) is asymmetrical, multi-planed in roof, concentrates elaborate ornament at the entrance, uses iron and tile freely, has minimal overhang, and draws on Spain, Mexico and Latin America generally. Mission Revival precedes it and is largely displaced by it after 1915.

Mediterranean Revival is more formal and more Italian: near-axial planning, a uniform low hipped roof at one level, arcaded loggias as the organising element, and Renaissance rather than Baroque ornament. Spanish Colonial Revival is picturesque, varies its roof heights, and takes its ornamental cues from the Spanish Baroque.

The original, built 1600-1840, is load-bearing adobe or rubble with walls 2-4 ft thick, minimal openings, hand-formed tile, and ornament confined to churches. The revival is stucco over wood frame, generously glazed, and applies ecclesiastical ornament to domestic buildings.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Mass and incident. No module and no order; proportion is controlled by wall thickness at reveals, by the height differences between adjoining roof planes, and by the size of the single ornamented entrance relative to the blank wall around it.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12; eave overhang 0-12 in.; adjacent roof planes differing in height by not less than 2'0"
Wall reveal at openings 6-12 in., splayed or returned in stucco without applied casing
Entrance surround 5-8 ft wide overall for a 3'0" x 7'0" leaf, with at least 12 ft of unornamented wall each side
Window proportion 1:1.8 to 1:2.6, arched openings springing at 2/3 of total height
Solid to void ratio 5:1 to 8:1 on street elevations; the blank wall is the point
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Deliberately irregular. Openings are placed by internal need and grouped in twos and threes, with long blank runs between; vertical alignment between storeys is neither expected nor desirable. Any regular repeating bay rhythm pushes the building toward Mediterranean Revival.

massing_affinities.note: The defining domestic skeleton: an L or U of ranges around a patio, one side open to a garden or wall.
Larger estate examples where volumes step and turn to describe apparent accretion.
Bungalow courts, apartment courts, and hotels; the fully enclosed patio type.
Where a portal or covered walk runs the length of a range; strong in the Monterey and hacienda variants.
A symmetrical double-pile block fights the style's asymmetry; if built this way the result usually reads as Mediterranean Revival.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 in clay barrel or mission tile, with eave overhang not exceeding 12 in. and no exposed dimensional rafter tails. Adjacent roof planes on the primary elevation must differ in eave or ridge height by not less than 2'0".

test.note: Eave overhang (<=12in, matching eave_projection_in but not tested here), tile material, and the adjacent-roof-planes-differ-by->=2'0" clause (no matching vocabulary variable for a cross-roof-plane height differential) stay prose -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Wall thickness must be expressed at every opening with a minimum 6 in. reveal from stucco face to frame, jambs returned or splayed in stucco with no applied wood casing. Flush windows in a thin stucco skin void the style.

test.note: Jamb finishing method (returned or splayed, no applied wood casing) is qualitative and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Ornament must be concentrated. Not more than two elevations may carry worked ornament, and the principal entrance surround must be the single most elaborate element on the building, with a minimum 12'0" run of unornamented wall on each side of it.
Wrought iron is required somewhere on the primary elevation - grille, balconette, gate, or lantern bracket - in members not less than 1/2 in. square. Cast aluminium substitutes are forbidden.

Native to IECC zones 1-3B. Flat parapet-drained roofs, deep unflashed reveals and low-slope tile all fail under freeze-thaw; north of zone 4 the assemblies must be genuinely redetailed rather than imitated.

exemplars.name: California Quadrangle, Panama-California Exposition
exemplars.note: Bertram Grosvenor Goodhue. The founding event of the style: Churrigueresque relief on an otherwise plain wall, over an arcaded quadrangle.

exemplars.name: Casa del Herrero
exemplars.note: George Washington Smith, with later library by Lutah Maria Riggs. Widely held to be the finest surviving example in the United States; Andalusian in register.

exemplars.name: Santa Barbara County Courthouse
exemplars.note: William Mooser III. The civic monument of the style, built under the post-1925 earthquake design ordinance.

exemplars.name: Adamson House
exemplars.note: Stiles O. Clements. Notable for the most complete surviving programme of Malibu Potteries decorative tile in situ.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
David Gebhard, George Washington Smith 1876-1930: The Spanish Colonial Revival in California (1964)
Rexford Newcomb, The Spanish House for America (1927)
City of Los Angeles, SurveyLA Citywide Historic Context Statement: Mediterranean and Indigenous Revival Architecture, 1893-1948
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)

proportion_packs.note: This style states its own bay rhythm as 'deliberately irregular... vertical alignment between storeys is neither expected nor desirable' and its own massing_affinities record massed-picturesque as 'common... where volumes step and turn to describe apparent accretion' -- precisely the dominant-mass-plus-subordinate-masses composition facade-picturesque was built to check. Bind the same general invariants as on andalusian-spanish-revival (dominance ratio, lever-arm balance, two continuous datums, window-proportion-count cap, window-grouping-rule) for the same reason, and exclude the pack's datum_stack member heights, which assume a shingled or clapboarded wood-frame wall this style does not have. This style's own entrance-ornament rule (c03: not more than two elevations carry worked ornament, the principal surround the single most elaborate element on the building, with 12 ft of blank wall on each side) IS this style's own dominance rule, stated in its own vocabulary, and should be read as controlling over the bound pack wherever the two might seem to disagree.

Bound for the daylight-depth rule, on the same reasoning as andalusian-spanish-revival: the courtyard-organized plan, with its single-pile ranges opening onto a patio, is exactly the condition the pack's daylight physics describes, and that physics is period-agnostic by the pack's own account. Do not carry over the hearth-reach, joist-span or frontage-driven room-count rules -- none of the three physical constraints those rules recover from Anglo-American vernacular fabric (span, hearth, and the folk-house catalogue built from tiling a frontage with rooms) describes a stucco courtyard house organized around a patio rather than a passage.

mission-revival.name: Mission Revival

geography.hearth: California; disseminated nationally by the Santa Fe and Southern Pacific railroads

lineage.note: The claimed ancestor. In 1890 the Franciscan missions were roofless ruins; the revival quotes a silhouette from photographs of buildings nobody had maintained for fifty years.
The broader colonial Hispanic reference invoked rhetorically, though Mission Revival takes very little from it beyond adobe massing.

Real transmission. The arcade as a compositional element, the massive unornamented wall and the round arch reach California through Richardson's followers, including A. Page Brown's own office training at McKim, Mead & White.
Professional training and the exposition-building apparatus that produced the California Building at Chicago in 1893.
The habit of a continuous unbroken skin over a simplified mass, transferred from shingle to stucco.
Explicitly a regionalist revolt against imported Eastern wooden eclecticism, argued as such in the Californian press of the 1890s.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: California's first self-consciously regional style, built c. 1890-1920 from the silhouette of the ruined Franciscan missions: smooth stucco, a curvilinear shaped parapet, an arcaded porch, and almost no ornament at all.
description.long:
Mission Revival is defined by subtraction. Its necessary elements are a smooth unbroken stucco or plaster wall; a curvilinear or stepped shaped parapet, the espadana, rising above the roof line at the entrance or the gable end; a red clay tile roof of low pitch, often with wide overhanging eaves on exposed rafters; a porch or veranda carried on large square piers with round arches between them; and a near-total absence of applied ornament. Where the missions had a bell wall, the revival gives itself a bell wall; where the missions had a quatrefoil window, the revival puts one over the door. That is the entire vocabulary, and its poverty is deliberate - the style was an argument that California should stop importing Eastern spindlework.

The catalyst was A. Page Brown's California Building at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, which assembled domed bell towers, scalloped parapets, tile roofs and stucco walls into a state pavilion that read instantly as Californian to a national audience of over twenty million. Within two years the vocabulary was official policy for two organisations that mattered enormously: the Santa Fe and Southern Pacific railroads, which built depots, hotels and Harvey Houses in it from Los Angeles to Kansas, and the California school and municipal building programmes. The railroads are the reason Mission Revival is found in Illinois and Texas, and they are also why it is remembered as a public style; the residential examples are numerous but modest.

The claim being made was regional identity, and it was made by people mostly uninterested in the actual Hispanic and Indigenous history of the buildings they were quoting. Charles Fletcher Lummis and the mission-restoration movement, the promotional campaigns built on Helen Hunt Jackson's 1884 novel Ramona, and the Southern California tourist economy together produced a sanitised Franciscan pastoral in which the missions were picturesque, benign and safely past. Mission Revival is the architectural form of that story. Understanding it as a marketing programme as much as a design movement explains its otherwise puzzling thinness: it needed to be recognisable at forty miles an hour from a train window, not to be inhabited thoughtfully.

A good Mission Revival building is bright, plain, and slightly severe. The wall is one uninterrupted pale surface with no belt courses, no quoins, no cornice, and windows cut simply into it. The parapet curves up over the entrance like a gesture and then stops. Under the arcade the light is sharp and the shadows are black, and the piers are heavy enough that walking through them feels like passing through a wall rather than a colonnade. There is nothing to look at closely, which is the difference between this and everything that follows it. After 1915 that plainness stopped being read as authentic and started being read as crude, and the style was largely displaced within five years by the far richer Spanish Colonial Revival.

defining_characteristics: Smooth stucco or plaster wall surface, unbroken by belt course, quoin, or cornice
Curvilinear, scalloped, or stepped shaped parapet (espadana) rising above the roof line, usually over the entrance or at a gable end
Low-pitched red clay tile roof, frequently with wide overhanging eaves and exposed rafter tails
Arcaded porch or veranda on heavy square or rectangular piers with round arches between them
Minimal to absent applied ornament; where ornament occurs it is a single quatrefoil window, a small bell tower, or a tile-capped parapet coping
Simple, blocky, largely rectilinear massing with openings cut plainly into the wall
diagnostic_tells: The shaped parapet is the whole diagnosis. A curvilinear or stepped parapet on smooth stucco is Mission Revival and almost nothing else.
No ornament at the entrance. If there is a carved or cast surround around the front door, the building is Spanish Colonial Revival, not Mission Revival.
Wide overhanging eaves with exposed rafter tails - Spanish Colonial Revival usually has minimal overhang and closed eaves.
Composition is symmetrical or simply rectilinear; Spanish Colonial Revival breaks into asymmetrical masses at varied heights.

Compared with the actual missions: the revival has thin stucco over frame rather than 3-5 ft adobe, machine tile rather than hand-formed, glazed windows in quantity, and parapets whose curves are smoother and shallower than any Franciscan mason ever produced.

distinguished_from.difference: The single most frequently confused pair in American architecture. Mission Revival (c. 1890-1920) is earlier, plainer, symmetrical, defined by the curvilinear parapet and the arcade, with almost no ornament, and quotes only the California missions. Spanish Colonial Revival (c. 1915-1940) is later, asymmetrical, ornamented at the entrance with carved or cast Churrigueresque detail, uses wrought iron and decorative tile freely, and draws on the whole Spanish and Latin American repertoire. Mission Revival was largely displaced by it after the 1915 San Diego exposition.

The original is adobe or rubble masonry 3-5 ft thick, built 1769-1834 by Indigenous labour under Franciscan direction, with hand-formed tile, tiny openings and no glazing. The revival is stucco over wood frame with normal fenestration; it takes the silhouette and nothing else.

Pueblo Revival has flat roofs, battered earth-coloured walls, projecting vigas and stepped massing, and takes New Mexican rather than Californian sources. Mission Revival has a pitched tile roof and a curvilinear parapet.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Silhouette and wall plane. There is no order and no module; proportion is set by the arcade bay and by the parapet profile, which is drawn as a freehand curve rather than constructed geometrically.
typical_ratios: Arcade piers 18-30 in. wide with clear spans 6-9 ft, giving a pier-to-span ratio near 1:3.5
Shaped parapet rises 3-8 ft above the adjacent eave and spans 1/3 to the full width of the elevation it caps
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12; eave overhang 24-42 in. with rafter tails at 24-32 in. on centre
Wall openings 1:1.6 to 1:2.2, cut plainly with a 3-6 in. reveal and no applied casing
Solid to void ratio 5:1 or greater; the wall is meant to dominate
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even and repetitive under the arcade, arbitrary above it. The arcade sets a regular rhythm at the ground; upper openings are placed by convenience and rarely align, because the wall is conceived as a continuous mass.

massing_affinities.note: The two-storey residential version - a simple double-pile block with a parapet over the entry and an arcaded porch.
The most common Mission Revival house form: a hipped stucco cube with a tile roof, an arcaded porch and a shaped parapet.
Institutional, hotel and school examples where an arcade wraps a patio.
Where a continuous arcaded gallery runs the length of the building, as at railway depots.
Large hotel and civic examples; the mission quadrangle taken literally.

constraints.statement: At least one curvilinear, scalloped, or stepped parapet must rise a minimum of 3'0" above the adjacent eave or roof line, capped with tile or a shaped coping. Without it the building is not Mission Revival.

test.note: Parapet shape (curvilinear, scalloped, or stepped) and coping material are categorical/qualitative and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Applied ornament is limited to: parapet coping, one quatrefoil or circular window, tile vents, and a simple moulded string at the parapet base. Carved or cast entrance surrounds, twisted columns, and Churrigueresque relief are forbidden - they convert the building to spanish-colonial-revival.

Arcade piers 18-30 in. wide with clear spans of 6'0"-9'0" and semicircular arches springing at not less than 7'0" above the porch floor. Slender turned or classical columns are forbidden; the arcade must read as wall pierced, not as posts.

test.note: Clear span (6'0"-9'0", no matching vocabulary variable -- an arcade-clear-span variable distinct from room_clear_span_ft is missing) and springing height (>=7'0") stay prose.

constraints.statement: Stucco must run in one continuous plane from grade to parapet with no belt course, quoin, water table, or cornice. Any horizontal articulation of the wall breaks the style.
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 in clay tile, with eave overhang 24-42 in. on exposed rafter tails where the eave is expressed at all. Asphalt shingle is forbidden.

test.note: Eave overhang (24-42in, matching eave_projection_in but not tested here) and the asphalt-shingle prohibition stay prose -- one test per constraint.

exemplars.name: California Building, World's Columbian Exposition
exemplars.note: A. Page Brown. The founding building of the style; domed bell towers, scalloped parapets, tile roofs, stucco walls. Temporary, demolished.

exemplars.name: Mission Inn, Mission Wing
exemplars.note: Arthur Burnett Benton, 1902-03, with arcaded walls added 1908. The purest large Mission Revival composition before the hotel's later wings drift into other idioms.

exemplars.name: Santa Fe Depot
exemplars.note: Bakewell & Brown. Built for the Panama-California Exposition year; the railroad case at full scale, twin domed towers and a long arcaded front.

exemplars.name: Powers House
exemplars.note: Arthur L. Haley. A documented residential example of the type, in the SurveyLA Mediterranean and Indigenous Revival context.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Karen J. Weitze, California's Mission Revival (1984)
David Gebhard and Robert Winter, An Architectural Guidebook to Los Angeles (rev. eds.)
City of Los Angeles, SurveyLA Citywide Historic Context Statement: Mediterranean and Indigenous Revival Architecture, 1893-1948

proportion_packs.note: Anticipated in the pack's own applies_to list, which already names mission-revival directly. This style's floruit (1893-1920) fully overlaps the Craftsman movement's, the two shared clients, carpenters and mail-order catalogues on the West Coast, and this style's own governing_logic ('no order and no module') rules out any trim family derived from a classical entablature -- which is exactly what distinguishes trim-craftsman from trim-classical in the first place. Bind for interior door and window casing, base and picture-rail logic only. This style's exterior is explicitly 'stucco... unbroken by belt course, quoin, or cornice' (c04), so nothing in this pack's exterior-adjacent members should be read as licensing applied exterior trim of any kind.

Not in the pack's own applies_to list, and bound here on general rather than documented grounds: the daylight-depth rule is stated by the pack itself as physics rather than period custom, and it governs the plain, minimally glazed rooms behind this style's arcaded porch (solid:void 5:1 or greater, 'the wall is meant to dominate') the same way it governs any single-loaded room. Bind narrowly for that rule; the hearth-count and frontage arithmetic do not describe a foursquare hipped stucco cube with an arcaded porch and no chimney-driven plan logic.

greek-revival-upland-vernacular.name: Upland Vernacular Greek Revival

revival_periods.note: The contemporary market's 'modern farmhouse' takes its silhouette from exactly this stratum - plain gable, wide flat trim, no ornament - while omitting the proportional rules that made the plainness legible.

geography.hearth: East Tennessee and the Kentucky Bluegrass

lineage.note: The center-passage plan, the gable-end chimneys and the tall single-pile section arrive from here; the Grecian trim is a change of profile on an unchanged house.

Extremely common and routinely missed: an existing log house is weatherboarded, given a Grecian doorway, corner pilasters and a frieze board, and thereafter reads as a frame Greek Revival house. Many 'Greek Revival' I-houses in the uplands have logs inside their walls.

description.short: The Greek Revival reduced to its cheapest legible signals - a heavy doorway, wide corner boards, a frieze under the eave - applied to the ordinary two-storey single-pile farmhouse of the Upland South and the Ohio Valley, frequently over a log core.
description.long:
This is the Greek Revival as most Americans actually encountered it, and it is almost entirely a matter of trim. The house underneath is the one the region was already building: two storeys tall, one room deep, a central passage running front to back, chimneys at both gable ends, a porch across the front. What the Grecian moment adds is a set of boards. The corner boards widen from four inches to ten or twelve and acquire a cap, so they read as pilasters. A frieze board a foot deep runs under the eave, and the cornice returns are clipped across the gable base. The door surround becomes a rectangular transom with sidelights inside broad flat pilasters carrying a heavy flat entablature - copied, usually badly and always confidently, from a plate in Benjamin or Lafever that a local carpenter owned or had seen. Nothing else changes. The plan does not change, the framing does not change, the chimneys do not move. This is the mechanism by which a national style becomes a vernacular one: it arrives as a set of profiles that can be run with planes a carpenter already owns, and it costs the price of wider boards.
