The conditions are those of a cash-poor but land-rich agricultural society reaching a modest surplus at exactly the moment the style was available. The Upland South and the Ohio Valley filled with Scots-Irish, German and Virginia migrant families between 1780 and 1830; by the 1840s the successful among them were replacing log houses with frame or brick ones, or - just as often - encasing the log house they already had. Water-powered sawmills on every creek supplied the wide boards; itinerant carpenters carried the handbooks; and the whole transformation could be accomplished a piece at a time. The result is a landscape where the same house form runs from a two-room log pen to a full brick I-house with a Grecian doorway, and the Greek Revival content of any given example is a fair measure of how good the last twenty years had been.

What it reacts against is not Federal - most of these builders never built a Federal house - but plainness itself, and the reaction is careful and cheap. There is no portico on the ordinary example, because a portico costs columns; there is a shed or hip porch on square or chamfered posts, and where a builder could afford it those posts get a bevel and a cap that gesture at an order. The most interesting quality of the stratum is its discipline: because there is no ornament to hide behind, the proportions have to carry the building, and the good ones are good almost entirely because the frieze depth, the trim widths and the roof pitch are right. The bad ones fail for exactly the same reason, which is the argument for encoding the ratios rather than the mouldings.

Standing in front of one, on a ridge road in East Tennessee or on a Bluegrass turnpike, the first impression is of a very tall, very thin house. The I-house is two storeys and one room deep, so from the gable end it is a slab, and the eave assembly is the only heavy thing on it. The doorway is where all the money went and it is out of scale in a way that is entirely satisfying: a fifteen-hundred-square-foot farmhouse with an entrance surround that would look correct on a courthouse. Inside, the passage runs straight through with a door at each end, the stair goes up one wall, the rooms are twelve feet square with plain heavy architraves and a mantel of two flat pilasters and a shelf, and everything is painted or whitewashed. In August, with both passage doors open, the house works exactly as the dogtrot works, which is the point: the same climate logic runs from the log pens through this stratum and up into the plantation houses, and only the amount of trim changes.

defining_characteristics: Greek Revival present as trim profile only: wide corner pilaster boards, deep plain frieze, clipped cornice returns, heavy flat door surround
Underlying plan unchanged from regional practice - two-storey single-pile with central passage, or double-pen, or hall-and-parlor
Rectangular-transom entrance with sidelights in a broad pilastered surround, disproportionately grand relative to the house
Gable-end chimneys, frequently exterior, retained from the region's earlier practice
Front porch on plain square or chamfered posts rather than a classical portico
Roof pitch dropped to 5:12-7:12 from the steeper pitches of the log and Federal-era work it replaces
Frequent log or hewn-timber core concealed inside a weatherboarded frame wall
diagnostic_tells: A courthouse-scale doorway on a farmhouse-scale building - the surest sign of the stratum
Corner boards 10-12 inches wide with a simple capital, and no columns anywhere on the building
Two-storey, one-room-deep silhouette (I-house) with a heavy eave band - it is a facade from the road and a wall from the side
Porch posts chamfered with a lamb's-tongue stop instead of turned or classical columns
Weatherboard that steps oddly around a thicker wall zone, or window jambs unusually deep: there are logs inside

distinguished_from.difference: A matter of two orders of magnitude in cost and of the presence or absence of an actual order. The plantation variant has a colossal colonnade, 12-14 foot ceilings and a detached kitchen; this stratum has trim boards, 9-10 foot ceilings, a rear kitchen ell and no columns.

The Northern variant turns the gable to the road and builds compactly with a side-hall plan; the Upland variant keeps the broadside I-house with a central passage open at both ends, because it is solving for summer heat rather than for winter.

Direct descendant and often indistinguishable on a bad day. The Greek Revival stratum keeps the classical trim discipline - continuous frieze, pilastered corners, entablature over the door. Once the frieze becomes a plain fascia and the doorway loses its entablature, the building has crossed into the un-styled farmhouse.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Classical proportion carried entirely by board width and eave depth, with no orders present. The frieze-to-storey-height and trim-width ratios are what make the building legible as classical; when they are wrong the house simply looks like a plain box, which is exactly what happened after 1875.
typical_ratios: Frieze board 10-16 inches on a two-storey house; total eave assembly 14-22 inches
Corner pilaster boards 10-12 inches wide, projecting 1-1.5 inches, with a 2-3 inch cap
Door surround: pilasters 6-9 inches wide, entablature 12-18 inches deep, opening 4.5-6 feet wide overall with sidelights
Ceiling heights 9-10.5 feet ground, 8.5-9.5 upper
I-house depth 16-20 feet single-pile; passage 8-12 feet wide
Roof pitch 5:12 to 7:12; cornice returns 10-18 inches
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three or five even bays broadside to the road with the door centred on the passage; the rhythm is the plan's, not the style's, and the trim simply marks it.

massing_affinities.note: Two storeys, one room deep, three to five bays - the definitive Upland South statement of arrival, and the substrate this variant dresses.
Where Northern settlement reached the Ohio Valley the upright-and-wing appears with the same Grecian trim.
The two-door, two-room house with Grecian corner boards - the cheapest possible expression of the stratum.
Dogtrots were routinely weatherboarded and given Grecian doorways at both ends of the passage in the 1840s-50s.

constraints.statement: A continuous frieze board of at least 10 inches (14-16 on a two-storey house) must run under the eave on all elevations, with corner pilaster boards no less than 10 inches wide. Below these widths the classical reading collapses and the building is simply a plain farmhouse.

test.note: Tests the frieze/eave trim board width floor (10in minimum; 14-16in on a two-storey house is a further refinement left as prose). Corner pilaster board width (also 10in minimum) has no separate vocabulary variable and stays prose too.

constraints.statement: Entrance must be a rectangular opening with a rectangular transom, sidelights optional, inside flat pilasters carrying a flat entablature at least 12 inches deep. Elliptical fanlights, arched openings and applied Adamesque ornament are forbidden.

Where a central passage is used it must be operable at both ends and the main block must remain single-pile (16-20 feet deep). Doubling the depth without adding cross-ventilation converts a working summer plan into a dark box.

test.note: Tests the single-pile depth range (16-20ft). The passage-operable-at-both-ends clause is left as prose -- no vocabulary variable expresses passage door operability.

constraints.statement: Free-standing classical columns are out of character; porch supports are square or chamfered posts 4x4 to 6x6, chamfer stopped 12-18 inches from deck and soffit. If columns are wanted, the building belongs to a different variant.

Where a log core is encased, the weatherboard must be furred out to a consistent plane and window jambs detailed for a wall 8-12 inches thick; the deep reveal is a legitimate and legible feature, not a defect to be concealed.

test.note: Tests the wall-thickness range where a log core is encased. The furring-consistency requirement is left as prose.

exemplars.name: DeVault-Massengill House
exemplars.note: Built by Isaac DeVault; upland East Tennessee Greek Revival on a farm whose earlier circa-1769 log house survives on the same property - the whole log-to-Grecian sequence in one place.

exemplars.name: Swaim House
exemplars.note: Circa 1840s; a plain Greek Revival farmhouse in the Middle Tennessee uplands, listed on the National Register in 1984. Ordinary in the way this stratum is ordinary, which is why it is worth recording.

sources: Henry Glassie, Folk Housing in Middle Virginia (1975)
Talbot Hamlin, Greek Revival Architecture in America (1944)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
Asher Benjamin, The Architect, or Practical House Carpenter (1830)
Tennessee Historical Commission National Register nomination files

proportion_packs.note: Bind the wall_section_greek_revival / casing_greek_revival family for the 'plain heavy architraves and a mantel of two flat pilasters and a shelf' the style's own description gives its interiors. NO ORDER PACK IS BOUND ON THIS NODE, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight -- see the report. This entry only covers the interior wall trim; the exterior frieze-board and corner-pilaster system that is this style's actual proportional identity (governing_logic: 'classical proportion carried entirely by board width and eave depth, with no orders present') has no dedicated pack anywhere in the 36. That is a genuine, acknowledged gap, not something this binding claims to solve.

Governs the doorway the style calls 'a courthouse-scale doorway on a farmhouse-scale building -- the surest sign of the stratum' and its own diagnostic tell. Constraint c02 (rectangular transom, sidelights optional, entablature at least 12 in deep, no ellipses or arches) is the style's hard rule layered on top of this pack's general door-sizing logic.
The window-glazing module. Bound but genuinely secondary here -- this style's own diagnostic_tells are all about board width and doorway scale, and sash pattern is not named among them at all.

The one Greek Revival node in this batch that gets room-vernacular rather than room-harmonic, and the corpus's own applies_to cross-reference lists it here specifically -- correctly, since the style's own governing_logic states the underlying plan (I-house, double-pen, dogtrot) is unchanged regional practice that predates the Grecian trim moment entirely: '12 feet square with plain heavy architraves,' composed by inherited habit rather than by a pattern-book room-generating ratio.

Bound for the frequent and 'routinely missed' log core this style hybridizes with -- an existing log pen weatherboarded and given Grecian trim, per the style's own lineage note and constraint c05 (encased log core, wall 8-12 in thick, furred to a consistent plane). The corpus's own applies_to cross-reference lists this node for log-module directly.

The frame (non-log) construction mode -- the weatherboarded I-house or double-pen built new in frame rather than encasing an existing log pen. Bound optional and below log-module because the style's own long description treats the log-to-frame sequence as the more distinctive and more often overlooked case.

mediterranean-revival.name: Mediterranean Revival

geography.hearth: Palm Beach and Miami, Florida; Santa Barbara, California

lineage.note: The claimed ancestor: the Tuscan and Ligurian villa with loggia, terrace and tile roof, known through photographs and Italian garden books.
The Spanish half of the mix - patio, reja, tiled fountain - which Mizner in particular collected in person.
Horseshoe arches, azulejo tilework and pierced screens as an occasional exotic register.
The direct professional parent. Same cornice, same tile roof, same arcaded ground floor - loosened, warmed, and turned outward to a garden.
Ecole-derived planning by axis and enfilade, which is what holds an apparently rambling Mediterranean Revival plan together.

Contemporary and reticulate. On the West Coast the same buildings are called Spanish Colonial Revival; on the Gulf and in Florida, Mediterranean Revival. The difference is real but it is one of formality and reference breadth, not of chronology.

description.short: The resort and estate style of the American subtropics, in which a symmetrical or lightly asymmetrical stuccoed block with a low tile roof opens through loggias and arcades onto terraces and courtyards, mixing Italian villa formality with Spanish and Moorish detail.
description.long:
Mediterranean Revival is what happens when the American palazzo moves to a warm climate and discovers the outdoor room. Its necessary features are stucco walls of expressed thickness, a low-pitched clay tile roof of consistent hipped geometry, round-arched openings gathered into loggias and arcades, and an organisation in which the terrace, the courtyard and the covered gallery are treated as rooms rather than as leftovers. Ornament concentrates at the entrance, at window surrounds, and at balconies; the rest of the wall is left blank and hot. Where Italian Renaissance Revival treats the wall as a plane to be composed, Mediterranean Revival treats it as a thick mass to be cut through.

The conditions were the Florida and California land booms. Between 1918 and 1926 Palm Beach, Boca Raton, Coral Gables, Sarasota and Miami were developed at extraordinary speed by promoters who needed an architectural identity that would sell a subtropical location to Northern money. Addison Mizner - untrained, well-travelled, and a genuine collector of Spanish and Italian fragments - supplied it at the Everglades Club in 1919 and then repeated it across Palm Beach for a decade, importing tile, ironwork and doors by the shipload and, when supply ran out, manufacturing them himself at his own Boca Raton works. The same demand in California produced Santa Barbara's post-earthquake rebuilding after 1925. In both places the style was as much a real-estate instrument as an architectural one; George Merrick's Coral Gables and the Mizner Development Corporation both wrote it into their deed restrictions.

What the style claimed was leisure and antiquity at once. A Northern industrialist wintering in Florida did not want a house that reminded him of Cleveland; he wanted one that said his money had been in the family long enough to have a villa. The Mediterranean reference did that work without the pretension of a chateau and, crucially, without the Anglo-Protestant severity of Colonial Revival. It also worked climatically in a way none of the Northern revivals did: thick shaded walls, deep loggias, cross-ventilated rooms and vaulted porches are functional responses to heat, and the style is the first American revival whose imagery and performance point the same direction.

Standing in one, the memorable thing is the sequence of light. You approach a blank, glaring, pale wall with a single elaborated door in it; you pass through into a cool, dark, thick-walled vestibule; and then the house opens sideways into a loggia and a courtyard where the light comes down filtered through arches and planting onto tile and water. The interior stays dim, the exterior stays bright, and the loggia is the room where the two are negotiated. This is a genuinely Mediterranean spatial idea, correctly imported, and it is the reason the style still performs well in Florida and Southern California ninety years later.

defining_characteristics: Stucco wall of expressed mass, with openings cut deep into it rather than set flush in it
Low-pitched hipped roof, 3:12 to 5:12, in barrel or pan-and-cover clay tile, with a shallow overhang or none
Loggias, arcades and covered galleries treated as primary rooms, opening the plan to terrace and courtyard
Round-arched openings, usually arcaded in threes or fives, with the arch springing well above head height
Ornament concentrated at the entrance and at selected windows and balconies, against otherwise blank stucco
Iron - grilles, balconettes, gates, railings - as the principal secondary material, with glazed tile as the third
diagnostic_tells: Wall reveals are deep: 6 in. minimum and often 12-18 in., so every window sits in a visible shadow box. This single measurement separates a real example from a stucco-clad frame house at fifty feet.
The roof is hipped, low, and continuous around the whole building; Spanish Colonial Revival breaks its roof into varied planes at varied heights and often uses gables.
Composition is broadly symmetrical or axial even when the plan rambles - the entrance sits on an axis that continues through the house to a garden feature.
Cornices and eaves are minimal or absent; where present they are a simple moulded band, never the modillioned overhang of Italian Renaissance Revival.
Look for the loggia. A Mediterranean Revival house without a covered outdoor room of at least 200 sq ft is a stucco box with tile on it.

distinguished_from.difference: Italian Renaissance Revival is a formal symmetrical block with diminishing storeys and a heavy modillioned cornice, composed as a plane. Mediterranean Revival lowers the cornice to nothing, thickens the wall, breaks the plan open to courtyards, and admits Spanish and Moorish ornament.

Spanish Colonial Revival is more asymmetrical, more picturesque, more consciously Spanish and Latin American in its sources, and freely varies roof heights and planes. Mediterranean Revival is more formal, more Italian, keeps a uniform roof line and a near-axial plan, and tends to larger and grander programmes.

Mission Revival is spare, uses curvilinear parapets and almost no applied ornament, and quotes California mission churches specifically. Mediterranean Revival is ornamented, has no parapets of that kind, and quotes the Italian and Spanish villa.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Wall mass and the arcade. Proportion is governed by the arcade module - pier width to clear span - and by expressed wall thickness; a nominal classical order appears only at the entrance surround.
typical_ratios: Arcade clear span 6-9 ft with piers 1/3 to 1/2 of the span in width; arch springing at 2/3 of total opening height
Loggia depth 10-16 ft, never less than 8 ft
Wall reveal 6-18 in.; window jamb splayed or returned in stucco with no applied casing
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12; eave overhang 0-18 in.
Solid to void ratio on principal elevations between 4:1 and 6:1 - the wall dominates
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Arcade-driven. Openings gather into arcaded groups of three or five with wide plain wall between groups; upper-storey openings are fewer and smaller than lower and need not align, since the wall is understood as mass rather than as frame.

massing_affinities.note: The defining skeleton: a main range with wings enclosing a patio open on one side.
Large estate and hotel examples with a fully enclosed cortile.
The compact suburban version - a symmetrical stuccoed block with an arcaded entrance loggia.
Where a continuous two-storey gallery replaces the courtyard, common on narrow Florida lots.
Rambling seaside examples; as this dominates, the building shades into spanish-colonial-revival.

constraints.statement: Wall thickness must be expressed at every opening with a minimum 6 in. reveal from the outer stucco face to the window or door frame, achieved by a returned or splayed jamb. Windows set flush to a thin stucco skin void the style regardless of any other detail.

test.note: Jamb construction method (returned or splayed) is qualitative and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 in clay tile, hipped, with eave overhang not exceeding 18 in. and no exposed dimensional rafter tails. Gables facing a principal elevation are forbidden; that move belongs to spanish-colonial-revival.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch range. Eave overhang (<=18in, matching eave_projection_in but not tested here), hipped form, exposed-rafter-tail prohibition, and the front-gable prohibition stay prose -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: At least one covered outdoor room - loggia, arcade, or gallery - of not less than 200 sq ft and not less than 8'0" clear depth must open off a principal interior room. A Mediterranean Revival house without one is incomplete.

test.note: Tests the clear depth minimum. The 200 sq ft area minimum (no matching vocabulary variable -- the corpus has no building- or room-area variable at all) and 'must open off a principal interior room' stay prose.

constraints.statement: Arcade piers between 1/3 and 1/2 of the clear span in width; arches semicircular or segmental with the springing not below 2/3 of the total opening height. Flattened arches spanning more than 9 ft read as commercial.
Native to IECC zones 1-3. Above zone 4, unvented low-slope tile roofs and uninsulated mass-wall reveals fail; either build the mass genuinely or do not use the style.

exemplars.name: Vizcaya
exemplars.note: F. Burrall Hoffman with Paul Chalfin and Diego Suarez. Veneto villa parti around a cortile with sea-facing terraces; the earliest fully achieved American example.

exemplars.name: Everglades Club
exemplars.note: Addison Mizner for Paris Singer. The building that established Palm Beach's identity and Mizner's career; 1918-19.

exemplars.name: Ca' d'Zan
exemplars.note: Dwight James Baum for John and Mable Ringling, 1924-26. Venetian Gothic, Italian Renaissance, Moorish and Spanish elements over a bayfront terrace.

exemplars.name: Greenacres (Harold Lloyd Estate)
exemplars.note: Sumner Spaulding. The California case: uniform hipped tile roof lines, near-axial symmetry, formal gardens extending from the house.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
David Gebhard, George Washington Smith 1876-1930: The Spanish Colonial Revival in California (1964)
Donald W. Curl, Mizner's Florida: American Resort Architecture (1984)
City of Los Angeles, SurveyLA Citywide Historic Context Statement: Mediterranean and Indigenous Revival Architecture, 1893-1948

proportion_packs.note: The required loggia (min. 8 ft clear depth, >=200 sq ft, opening off a principal room) is a covered outdoor room read on the same daylight logic as an interior one: at the pack's lower 1.8x multiplier -- used 'wherever there is a porch, a deep eave, a verandah... because all four lower the effective head' -- an 8-9 ft head loggia caps the interior room it opens off at a shallower daylit depth than an unshaded wall would, which is exactly the mechanism this style's arcade-and-terrace sequence depends on. Bind for that daylight-depth logic and for the general two-sided-lighting argument on courtyard-facing ranges; the pack's hearth-count and joist-span derivations do not describe a stucco or tile-floored house with no dogtrot or hall-and-parlor ancestry.

This style's own governing_logic states plainly that 'a nominal classical order appears only at the entrance surround' and that proportion is otherwise 'governed by the arcade module' -- which no pack in this corpus models; none of the 36 available packs derives an arcade's pier-to-span ratio or its arch-springing height (see the WP-4.1 report). Bound at low precedence and scoped narrowly to the punched window rectangles above the arcade, never the arcade itself, on the strength of this style's two inherits_kit=true lineage edges: descends_from italian-renaissance-revival at weight 0.9 (itself bound to this same pack) and descends_from beaux-arts-american at weight 0.8, whose 'ecole-derived planning by axis and enfilade... is what holds an apparently rambling plan together.' Use the pack's single-head-datum rule and its 5/6 per-storey window diminution for the upper-storey openings only, and defer entirely to this style's own reveal-depth (6-18in), roof-plane height-differential and solid:void (4:1-6:1) rules wherever the two conflict -- those are this style's genuinely sourced numbers, and this binding is a lineage-based judgment call rather than a documented Mediterranean Revival window-proportion source.

tuscan-vernacular.name: Tuscan Vernacular

revival_periods.note: The American Mediterranean Revival draws its stucco walls, low tile roofs and blank-wall discipline as much from the Tuscan farm as from the villa.

Mass restoration of abandoned poderi for residential and agriturismo use after the collapse of mezzadria, and a global 'Tuscan' idiom in speculative house-building that reproduces the finishes without the plan.

geography.hearth: The Chianti, Val d'Orcia, Val di Chiana and the Florentine and Sienese contado

lineage.note: Real but narrow descent: the coppo-and-embrice tile roof, the terracotta floor, the lime mortar, the rubble-and-brick wall and the villa rustica arrangement of stock below and living above are all Roman survivals in unbroken use. The order system is not inherited at all - there is no column in this tradition except in the loggia, and it arrives late.

description.short: The stone farmhouse of the central Italian sharecropping estate: an accretive, tower-marked, tile-roofed block housing one family and its animals on one podere, with no composed facade at all.
description.long:
The casa colonica is not a style in the sense that the other members of this family are; it is the physical residue of a contract. Under mezzadria, the sharecropping system that governed central Italian agriculture from roughly the thirteenth century until it was legally wound up in 1964, a landowner supplied land, house, stock and seed, and a peasant family supplied labour, and they split the harvest. The unit was the podere - as much land as one family could work, typically five to fifteen hectares - and each podere required exactly one house. That house had to accommodate a large extended family, its oxen, its pigs, its grain, its wine, its oil and its tools, in one building, on the boundary of an economy that had almost no cash in it. Every feature of the type follows from that: the stalla on the ground floor, where the animals' body heat rises through the terracotta into the living rooms above; the external stair, so the family's floor is reached without going through the stable; the granary in the roof space; the colombaia tower for pigeons, which supplied both meat and the most valuable fertiliser available before industrial nitrates.

What produced it technically is a set of hard local limits. There is good building stone almost everywhere in Tuscany but almost no long timber, so the room width is set by the chestnut or oak beam that can be cut and carried - about four to four and a half metres clear, five at the outside. The house therefore grows one four-metre cell at a time, and it grows sideways along the contour, because that is where the level ground is. Nobody drew it. A mason and the family added a bay when there was money and a reason, and the resulting building records its own history in the wall: changes of stone coursing, blocked openings, a straight vertical joint where a new cell was butted onto the old one, a roof that steps down where the added part was cheaper. There was a treatise attempt - Ferdinando Morozzi's Delle case de' contadini of 1770 - and a genuine reform programme, the Leopoldine farms built under Grand Duke Pietro Leopoldo from the 1770s to drain and settle the Val di Chiana, which regularised the type into a symmetrical block with a central colombaia. But even the Leopoldine are the same building with the arithmetic tidied.

It reacts against nothing, which is the honest thing to say about it, and this is precisely what makes it valuable in a kit-of-parts system. The casa colonica is a control case: architecture generated purely by climate, span, material and use, without a client who cares how it looks from a distance. Its virtues - the deep reveal, the small window, the thermal mass, the shaded loggia on the south, the aia threshing floor set to catch the wind - are not aesthetic decisions and cannot be reproduced by imitating the finishes.

Standing at one in July, the first thing you notice is that the wall is cold. Half a metre and more of rubble limestone with lime render, small openings, and internal shutters rather than glass mean the interior sits fifteen degrees below the yard at three in the afternoon and gives the heat back after dark. The openings are placed by what is behind them, so the facade has a door, a window, and then a blank stretch, and the rhythm is meaningless as composition and completely legible as plan. The tile roof overhangs by half a metre on projecting courses of coppi, so there is a hard shadow line at the eave and a line of terracotta glowing against the wall. There is a fig tree, an oak, and a flat swept area of brick or beaten earth for threshing. And somewhere on the block there is a tower two storeys taller than everything else, with pigeon holes in it, which from a distance reads as gravity and status and is in fact a fertiliser factory.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing rubble stone or mixed stone-and-brick walls 500-700 mm thick, lime-rendered or left as coursed stone, with the mass doing the thermal work
Animals stabled on the ground floor and the family living above, with the stalla's heat used deliberately
External stair or external landing giving direct access to the upper living floor without passing through the working ground floor
Additive growth in cells of roughly 4-4.5 m, set by the available timber beam span, extended along the contour rather than composed
Colombaia (dovecote tower) rising one to two storeys above the main roof, originally freestanding and later absorbed into the block
Shallow-pitched roof of coppi and embrici with a projecting corbelled tile eave (gronda) of 300-600 mm
Small, few, deeply reveal openings placed by internal need rather than by facade rhythm, with external shutters and no ornament
An aia - a swept, paved or beaten threshing floor - as an outdoor room of the house, with shade trees on the south side
diagnostic_tells: Ground-floor openings are wide and low with segmental brick heads (cart and stall doors), while upper-floor openings are small and vertical - the two storeys have visibly different logics
A straight vertical joint in the masonry where an added cell butts the original; the roof usually steps at the same line
Openings that do not stack: a window on the upper floor sitting over solid wall below is normal here and is a hard error in any composed classical style
A tower with rows of small square pigeon holes near its top, and a projecting tile course under them
Brick used only for arches, quoins, eaves courses and window heads, with rubble stone everywhere else - brick is the expensive material, spent only where geometry demands it

distinguished_from.difference: The villa is the same building regularised, given a compact near-cubic block, a hipped roof, a loggia, a bracketed eave and a symmetrical or balanced front. It is where the landowner stayed; the casa colonica is where the tenant lived. If the openings stack and the front is balanced, it is the villa; if the openings are placed by the plan, it is the farm.

The revival reproduces the stucco, tile and arch but drops the mass (stud wall with a render coat), the small aperture ratio, the additive plan and the working ground floor. Thin walls with large windows under a barrel-tile roof are the revival, not the vernacular.

The Andalusian type turns inward around a patio with a whitewashed, water-cooled court and a blind street face. The Tuscan farm turns outward onto its own land, has no courtyard, and gets its cooling from wall mass and shutters rather than from evaporation and enclosure.

proportional_system.governing_logic: None imposed. The generator is the clear span of a locally available chestnut or oak beam, which fixes the room width; the stall height fixes the ground storey; the family's need and the year's harvest fix how many cells get built. Growth is by repetition of the cell, not by subdivision of a whole.
typical_ratios: Room clear span 4.0-4.5 m, 5.0 m maximum; rooms near-square or up to 1:1.5
Wall thickness 500-700 mm at ground, reducing to 400-500 mm above
Storey heights approximately 2.4-3.0 m for the stalla and 2.8-3.2 m for the living floor
Aperture area 5-10 percent of wall area, with window proportions roughly 1:1.3 to 1:1.8 and reveals 400-600 mm deep
Roof pitch 18-27 degrees (4:12 to 6:12), appropriate to coppi-and-embrici tile laid without underlayment
Eave overhang 300-600 mm on two or three corbelled courses of tile and brick
Colombaia tower height 1.3-1.8 times the eave height of the block it stands on; tower plan 3-4 m square
Loggia, where present, of two to four arches with pier width 0.4-0.6 of the clear opening
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Additive and irregular. Openings are placed by what is behind them, so a wall may carry a door, a window, and a long blank in unequal spacing, and upper openings need not align with lower ones. Where regularity appears - notably in the Leopoldine farms of the late eighteenth century - it is an administrative reform imposed from above, not a vernacular instinct.

massing_affinities.note: Used here as a skeleton only: house, stall, barn and shed joined in a stepping additive chain. The Tuscan reason is accretion and contour, not a New England winter, but the geometry is the same.
The tower is a colombaia, a working dovecote and not a belvedere, and it usually sits at the angle of the block or over the entry rather than being composed against the mass.
Larger fattoria complexes close a working corte on three sides, with the aia occupying the open fourth.
The irreducible single-cell house with a stall below survives on poorer poderi and in upland Tuscany.

The irregularity is a byproduct of accretion, never a composition. Deliberately irregular massing designed for a viewpoint is a nineteenth-century picturesque idea and reads immediately as false here.

constraints.statement: No clear span above 5.0 m without either a masonry vault or an intermediate wall. Wide open-plan rooms are structurally impossible in the type and destroy its plan logic.

test.note: Tests the general clear-span ceiling. The 'without either a masonry vault or an intermediate wall' exception is a conditional escape clause with no matching vocabulary variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Aperture area must not exceed 12 percent of any wall area, and reveals must be at least 350 mm deep. The type's summer performance depends on small openings in high-mass walls; large glazing converts it into a greenhouse.

test.note: Tests the aperture-area ceiling. 'Reveals must be at least 350 mm deep' (maps to reveal_depth_in, section scope) is a second numeric fact in the same sentence, left as prose for the single-test limit.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch between 4:12 and 6:12. Steeper reads as northern European; shallower will not shed water under coppi-and-embrici tile laid dry.
Openings must not be forced into a symmetrical rhythm. Vertical alignment between storeys is permitted only where a structural pier requires it; imposed symmetry converts the building into a villa.
Brick appears only at arches, quoins, window and door heads, and eaves courses. Brick used as a general facing material is a later or urban condition, not this one.

exemplars.name: Leopoldine farmhouses of the Val di Chiana
exemplars.location: Val di Chiana, Arezzo and Siena provinces, Tuscany, Italy
exemplars.note: Built from the 1770s onward under Grand Duke Pietro Leopoldo's land-reclamation programme; several hundred survive. A symmetrical, regularised casa colonica with a central colombaia over the entrance - the type at its most codified.

exemplars.name: Villa Medicea di Cafaggiolo
exemplars.note: Michelozzo's reconstruction of an existing fortified farm for Cosimo de' Medici, 1452, keeping the crenellated entrance tower and battlemented wings. Included here because it preserves, at the moment of transition, the working farm block with tower from which the villa type was extracted.

exemplars.name: Podere and fattoria complexes of the Val d'Orcia
exemplars.location: Val d'Orcia, Siena province, Tuscany, Italy
exemplars.note: The mezzadria landscape of dispersed single-family poderi inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape in 2004; individual houses are undated but the settlement pattern is documented from the fifteenth century.

sources: Ferdinando Morozzi, Delle case de' contadini: trattato architettonico (Florence, 1770)
Renato Biasutti, La casa rurale nella Toscana, CNR Ricerche sulle dimore rurali in Italia (1938)
Emilio Sereni, Storia del paesaggio agrario italiano (1961)
Bernard Rudofsky, Architecture Without Architects (1964)
Paul Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World (1997)

proportion_packs.note: The node's own proportional_system could almost be this pack's abstract restated for Tuscany: 'None imposed. The generator is the clear span of a locally available chestnut or oak beam, which fixes the room width... Growth is by repetition of the cell, not by subdivision of a whole.' That is the exact intersection of span, hearth and daylight room-vernacular is built from, and tuscan-vernacular is named directly in its applies_to. No other pack in the library applies: massing_affinities explicitly marks massed-picturesque 'forbidden' ('the irregularity is a byproduct of accretion, never a composition'), the lineage note states the order system 'is not inherited at all', and the facade has, in the node's own words, 'no composed facade at all' - so no facade or order pack is bound.

beaux-arts-american.name: American Beaux-Arts

geography.hearth: New York City and Newport, Rhode Island

lineage.note: Direct and literal transmission. Hunt entered the Ecole in 1846; by 1900 several hundred Americans had followed, and the American profession simply is the Ecole's method applied to American programmes.
Louis XV and Louis XVI models supply most of the domestic vocabulary - Petit Trianon, Grand Trianon, the Parisian hotel particulier.
Imperial scale, the triumphal arch motif, coffered vaults and the Composite order, mediated through Ecole restoration studies of Roman ruins.
The palazzo wall and the stacked order, shared with italian-renaissance-revival, which is its restrained sibling.
Villa parti and the rhythm of the Palladian bay, largely as filtered through French academic teaching.
The 1893 Exposition was a deliberate national repudiation of Richardsonian weight and of Victorian eclecticism in favour of white, axial, correct classicism.

description.short: The high academic classicism of the American Gilded Age: monumental, richly sculptural, and rigorously planned on Ecole des Beaux-Arts principles of axis and hierarchy, built for the largest fortunes and the greatest public commissions between 1885 and 1930.
description.long:
American Beaux-Arts is less a style than a method that produced one. What Americans acquired at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris was not a set of shapes but a way of designing: begin with the parti, organise the plan on one or more axes, arrange spaces in a hierarchy from vestibule to principal room, express that hierarchy on the elevation, and render the result with enough authority to sell it. Richard Morris Hunt was the first American admitted, in 1846; Charles McKim, Louis Sullivan, John Carrere, Thomas Hastings, Whitney Warren and hundreds more followed. When the American economy after 1880 produced fortunes without precedent, this method was the only one available that could organise a hundred-room house or a railway terminal, and it took the commissions.

The formal signature is richness under discipline. Masonry, usually limestone or marble, with a rusticated base and a smooth upper wall. A full classical order at monumental scale, frequently paired or coupled, and frequently engaged rather than free. Deep entablatures and heavy projecting cornices, balustraded parapets, quoins, and a facade wall broken by pavilions - the ends and the centre advanced, the intervals recessed. Sculptural ornament in quantity: swags, cartouches, keystone masks, garlanded panels, figures on the skyline. Symmetry is absolute, and interior circulation is grand and processional, with the stair treated as a public event.

The 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago is the pivot. Burnham's coordination of Hunt, McKim, Post, Peabody and others produced the Court of Honor - uniform cornice line, white plaster surfaces, colossal orders, a lagoon on axis - and was seen by roughly a quarter of the American population. It converted a professional method into a national style within eighteen months and launched the City Beautiful movement, which carried it into every state capitol, courthouse, library and station for the next thirty years. It also gave the culture a name for itself: the American Renaissance, which is what its practitioners believed they were staging.

What a Beaux-Arts house is like to stand in is the answer to a question its clients were asking about themselves. The approach is axial and takes longer than it needs to. The vestibule is compressed and dark; the hall beyond it is enormous, top-lit or lit from a courtyard, with a stair rising in one flight and returning in two. Every material is the real one - marble, bronze, oak, plaster run in situ - and the ornament is executed by people who were very good at it, at a density that would be oppressive if the rooms were smaller. It is architecture as argument, and the argument is that the United States had arrived. The Depression and the income tax ended it more completely than any change of taste; the buildings survive, and almost nobody can afford to build another.

defining_characteristics: Symmetrical monumental masonry composition with a rusticated base, smooth upper wall, and advanced end and centre pavilions
Colossal or monumental classical order, frequently paired or coupled, correctly detailed and often engaged with the wall
Deep entablature and heavily projecting cornice, usually surmounted by a balustrade or an attic storey
Abundant sculptural ornament - swags, cartouches, garlands, keystone masks, and free-standing figures on the skyline
Plan organised on a dominant axis with a processional sequence from entrance to principal room, and a ceremonial stair
Genuine and costly materials worked by hand: cut limestone or marble, bronze, plaster run in place
diagnostic_tells: Paired or coupled columns and pilasters. Neoclassical Revival uses single columns; pairing is the fastest Beaux-Arts marker.
The skyline is populated - balustrades, urns, statuary, attic cartouches. Neoclassical Revival stops at the cornice.
Facade relief: the wall advances and recedes in pavilions of 18-36 in. Colonial and Neoclassical Revival keep the wall flat.
Rusticated ground storey with vermiculated or banded joints, under a smooth ashlar upper wall.
If it is wood, it is not Beaux-Arts. The style presumes cut stone and the masons to work it.

distinguished_from.difference: Neoclassical Revival is the same grammar with the sculpture, the pairing, the rustication and the pavilion relief removed - which is what made it buildable in wood in a county seat. Beaux-Arts is what the same offices did when the budget was unlimited.

Italian Renaissance Revival is deliberately flat, planar and restrained, with a single heavy cornice and no sculpture; it is the sober alternative chosen by clients who found Beaux-Arts vulgar. The two are contemporaneous and often by the same architects.

Chateauesque is vertical, French Renaissance and late Gothic in ornament, and dominated by an enormous steep roof. Beaux-Arts is horizontal, Roman and French neoclassical in ornament, and terminates in a balustrade or attic rather than a roof.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The classical order with a module of one column diameter, deployed under Ecole compositional discipline: axis, hierarchy, poche, and the marche - the designed sequence of movement through the plan. Elevation proportion follows plan hierarchy rather than the reverse.
typical_ratios: Base : principal storey : attic roughly 1 : 2 : 0.7 in height
Entablature 1/4 to 1/5 of column height; cornice projection equal to or greater than entablature depth
Coupled columns spaced 1.0-1.5 diameters clear between the pair, 3-4 diameters between pairs
Pavilion projection 18-36 in. from the recessed wall plane
Principal room clear height 16-22 ft; ceremonial stair rising 9-12 ft in a single first flight
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: A-B-B-B-A pavilion rhythm: advanced end bays and an advanced centre, with a regular intermediate rhythm between. The centre bay is always the widest and always contains the entrance.

massing_affinities.note: At mansion scale - a symmetrical double-pile block with a monumental order and pavilions.
Where a portico dominates the centre block and lower wings extend either side.
Estate examples with hyphens and dependencies; the American villa parti at full budget.
The hotel particulier plan - a cour d'honneur entered through a screen, with the corps de logis at the rear.
Institutional and club programmes with a full enclosed court.

constraints.statement: Orders must be executed to a published canon with entasis, correct capital, base and entablature. Entablature depth 1/5 to 1/4 of column height, cornice projection not less than the entablature depth. An order without a full entablature is void.

test.note: 1/5 to 1/4 of column height. Entasis, correct capital/base, and the cornice-projection-not-less-than-entablature-depth clause stay prose.

constraints.statement: Wall must be, or must fully express, cut stone: minimum 12 in. reveal at openings, jambs returned in the same material as the face, arches with true voussoirs and keystones, and a rusticated base of not less than one full storey with joints 3/4 to 1-1/2 in. deep.

test.note: Tests the minimum reveal depth at openings. Jamb material match, true voussoirs/keystones at arches, and the rusticated base (one full storey, joints 3/4-1-1/2in deep -- no matching vocabulary variable for joint depth) stay prose.

constraints.statement: The primary facade must be modelled in depth: end and centre pavilions advanced not less than 18 in. from the intermediate wall plane. A flat facade with applied ornament is Neoclassical Revival, not Beaux-Arts.

test.note: Tests the pavilion-advance minimum. 'A flat facade with applied ornament is Neoclassical Revival, not Beaux-Arts' is definitional prose, not a second numeric claim.

constraints.statement: The composition must terminate above the cornice - balustrade, attic storey, or sculptural group - to a height of not less than 1/8 of the wall height. A cornice that simply stops leaves the style unfinished.

Do not attempt below roughly 10,000 sq ft or in any material other than stone, terra cotta, or full-thickness cast masonry. Every reduction available - flat wall, single columns, no sculpture, wood construction - produces Neoclassical Revival, which is a legitimate style; a reduced Beaux-Arts is not.

exemplars.name: Marble House
exemplars.note: Richard Morris Hunt for William K. Vanderbilt, after the Petit Trianon. 500,000 cubic feet of marble; the American Beaux-Arts house in its purest state.

exemplars.name: Rosecliff
exemplars.note: Stanford White of McKim, Mead & White, after the Grand Trianon at Versailles. Terra cotta rather than marble, and the better building for it.

exemplars.name: New York Public Library, Stephen A. Schwarzman Building
exemplars.note: Carrere & Hastings, 1897-1911. The Ecole plan method - axis, hierarchy, marche - applied to a public programme at the highest level achieved in America.

exemplars.name: Court of Honor, World's Columbian Exposition
exemplars.note: Burnham with Hunt, McKim, Post, Peabody and others. Temporary and demolished, and the origin point of both this style and neoclassical-revival.

sources: Richard Guy Wilson, The American Renaissance 1876-1917 (1979)
Arthur Drexler, ed., The Architecture of the Ecole des Beaux-Arts (1977)
Leland M. Roth, McKim, Mead & White, Architects (1983)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)

proportion_packs.note: The style's own lineage record names this order directly: 'Imperial scale, the triumphal arch motif, coffered vaults and the Composite order, mediated through Ecole restoration studies of Roman ruins' (lineage edge to roman-classical, weight 0.8). Composite is also the richest of the five and the one whose Ionic-volute-over-Corinthian-acanthus capital reads correctly at the coupled, monumental scale the constraints demand (entablature 1/5-1/4 of column height, cornice projection not less than entablature depth). Bound plain Vignola rather than an overlay because vignola-composite's own applies_to already names beaux-arts-american, whereas none of the Chambers or Gibbs overlays extend this far into the eclectic-revivals branch - Chambers stops at the English Georgian family and Gibbs at colonial domestic work. A plain, unmediated classical reading is also the more honest one for a style whose module is 'one column diameter' with no intervening English pattern-book filter.

The domestic register, for the Newport houses rather than the civic ones: the Petit Trianon (Marble House) and the Grand Trianon (Rosecliff) that Hunt and White quoted directly are both Corinthian-ordered buildings, and vignola-corinthian's own applies_to list already names beaux-arts-american alongside beaux-arts-french. Grade the two orders by programme rather than by rank the way the Georgian template grades Ionic over Doric: Composite for the coupled monumental order and the triumphal-arch register, Corinthian for the single-family mansion quoting a French royal model.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The ceremonial stair hall and principal rooms are the one place in this whole batch where trim-classical's derivation - the wall read as pedestal:column:entablature - is not a compromise but an understatement, since real Beaux-Arts interiors ran marble, bronze and run-in-place plaster rather than painted millwork. Bind the family for the proportional discipline it encodes and expect every profile to be executed richer than the pack's own painted-joinery defaults.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the void before the order and the stone surround are applied to it - door height taken from the storey, the head datum discipline - though a Beaux-Arts opening is frequently a full aedicule or an arched Roman opening rather than the plain Palladian rectangle the pack defaults to; treat the derived ratios as the starting rectangle the surround is then built onto.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the elevation as a composition, but a Beaux-Arts front pushes every one of its numbers to the permissive edge of the band: the centre bay is not merely widened but advanced as a full pavilion (constraint c03, 18 in minimum), the cornice is not the boxed domestic member the pack's default describes but a full entablature-derived cornice at monumental scale, and the composition typically adds a balustraded attic the pack does not itself model (constraint c04). Bind it for the bay-count and solid-to-void discipline and let the order packs and the style's own constraints carry what it understates.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the vertical diminution the style's proportional_system states directly - base:principal storey:attic roughly 1:2:0.7 - which is steeper than the pack's own domestic default (0.85 then 0.80 compounding) and closer to its outer range; a Beaux-Arts attic storey is genuinely subordinate, not merely shorter.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The Ecole plan method is Palladian room-shape discipline turned into a whole-building organising principle - axis, hierarchy, poche, marche - so this pack governs the individual rooms (16-22 ft principal-room clear height per the style's own proportional_system) while the plan-level hierarchy itself is outside what any proportion pack in this corpus models.

english-georgian-country-house.name: English Georgian Country House

revival_periods.note: The Edwardian neo-Georgian country house of Lutyens's classical phase, Reginald Blomfield and Detmar Blow, and its American cousin in the Colonial Revival estate.

geography.hearth: The prosperous agricultural counties — Norfolk, Yorkshire, the Thames valley — and the offices of John Carr in York, James Paine and Sir Robert Taylor

lineage.note: The free-standing rural expression of the parent style: same proportional system, same sash, same pattern-book detail, released from the party wall and the building acts and given four elevations, a park and a service wing.

Closer to the Palladian source than the town house ever is. The five-part scheme, the pedimented centre, the Venetian window and the piano nobile survive here in reduced and affordable form, transmitted through Gibbs, Ware and Robert Morris's Select Architecture (1755).

description.short: The compact classical box in a park: five or seven bays, hipped roof, pedimented or slightly advanced centre, service wing pushed to one side, and a plan of resolvable rooms around a hall and stair.
description.long:
Between the Palladian palaces of the 1730s and the picturesque villas of the 1800s there is a fifty-year period in which England built several thousand medium-sized classical country houses of remarkable consistency, and this is the type that most people now mean by 'a Georgian house'. It is not a prodigy house. Its client is a country gentleman, a successful lawyer, a Yorkshire clothier or a nabob home from Bengal, with perhaps two to five thousand acres and no ambition to entertain the Court. Its architect is a competent regional professional — John Carr in Yorkshire, James Paine in the Midlands, Sir Robert Taylor around London — or, more often, a builder working from Gibbs and Ware with a gentleman amateur looking over his shoulder.

The formula is compact and repeatable. A rectangular block, two or two and a half storeys over a low basement, five or seven bays wide and two rooms deep, hipped in slate or lead behind a modest parapet or under a modillion cornice. The centre three bays are advanced 300 to 600 mm and often pedimented; the entrance sits at grade or up a short flight, with a Doric or Ionic doorcase from a plate; a string course marks the first floor; the corners may take rusticated quoins. Inside, an entrance hall on axis leads to a saloon or stair hall behind, with the principal rooms — dining room, drawing room, library — arranged around them in Palladio's approved ratios, and the service accommodation pushed into a basement, a subordinate wing or a detached court linked by a passage. That last decision is the one that separates this type from its Palladian parent: the Georgian country house keeps the symmetry of the main block absolutely and lets the service wing be as asymmetrical as it needs to be, usually screened by trees.

The conditions were agricultural improvement, enclosure, colonial and mercantile money, and above all a transport system good enough to move Portland stone, Welsh slate and London-trained plasterers into a Yorkshire field. Behind that stood the landscape park. Capability Brown's practice from the 1750s onward removed the formal garden, brought grass up to the walls, and made the house an object standing in an idealised pasture — which is why a Georgian country house is designed to be seen in the round at a quarter of a mile, with four composed elevations and a roofline that resolves from any angle. It is also why the offices are hidden: the park's fiction is that the house is not a place of work.

Standing in front of one on a grey afternoon, what registers is calm and correctness rather than drama. The house sits on the ground rather than rising from it, the graduated storeys settle the composition downward, and the eye finds nothing to argue with. Inside, the plan is legible within four steps of the front door — hall, stair, principal rooms left and right — and the rooms are the right size for their use in a way that later, larger houses rarely manage. That legibility is the type's real achievement, and it is why the same plan is still being drawn, in Surrey and in Connecticut, three hundred years later.

defining_characteristics: A free-standing rectangular double-pile block of five or seven bays, two to two and a half storeys over a semi-basement, composed to be seen in the round
Absolute bilateral symmetry of the main block, with the entrance centred and the service accommodation displaced into a basement, a subordinate wing or a detached service court
A centre of three bays advanced 300-600 mm and marked by a pediment, a doorcase, or both, against otherwise plain walling
Low-pitched hipped roof in slate or lead behind a parapet or under a modillion cornice, with chimneys grouped symmetrically at the ends
Entrance at or near grade, with the principal rooms on the ground and first floors rather than on a raised piano nobile
An entrance hall and stair hall on axis, with principal rooms of Palladian ratio disposed around them
The park setting: grass to the walls, no formal forecourt, and the service court screened by planting
diagnostic_tells: Five or seven bays with a three-bay centre advanced by a few hundred millimetres and topped by a pediment — the standard signature, and instantly distinguishable from the flat continuous front of a terrace
A service wing that is symmetrical about nothing, joined to a main block that is symmetrical about everything
Storey heights diminishing upward from the ground floor, which is the opposite of the town house's arrangement and identifies the building as rural at a glance
A Venetian window on the stair landing or in the centre of a side elevation — the one Palladian survival that persists to the end of the century
Quoins, string course, plinth and modillion cornice as the only wall ornament, with the doorcase carrying the rest

distinguished_from.difference: Free-standing versus party-walled; four composed elevations versus one; entrance centred versus displaced; principal rooms on the ground floor versus the first floor; storey heights diminishing upward versus peaking at the first floor.

The same grammar without the ceremony or the budget. No portico, no external stair to a piano nobile, no colonnaded hyphens, ashlar replaced by good brick in most counties, and the room ratios followed by habit rather than checked against a plate.

Regency renders in stucco, bows the front, brings the windows to the floor with iron balconies, and extends the eaves on brackets. The Georgian country house shows its brick or stone and keeps its openings punched neatly in the wall.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Palladian ratios applied through the builders' manuals, with the bay and the storey height as working modules and the orders confined to the doorcase, the cornice and any Venetian window. Composition is governed by the requirement that all four elevations resolve.
typical_ratios: Facade 5 or 7 bays; overall front length to height (ground to cornice) roughly 1.6:1 to 2.2:1
Storey graduation: ground floor exceeds first by 10-20 percent, second floor 0.7-0.8 of the first, attic 0.5-0.6
Sash proportion 1.7:1 to 2:1, in 12-over-12 lights before about 1770 and 6-over-6 after
Centre projection 300-600 mm over three bays; pediment height 0.2-0.25 of its own width
Roof pitch 25-35 degrees, hipped, with ridge concealed or nearly so from ground level at 30 m distance
Principal rooms 1:1, 1:1.25, 1:1.33 or 1:1.5 in plan, ceiling heights 3.3-4.0 m on the principal floor
Service wing ridge at least 25 percent below the main block ridge
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: An even metronome of equal bays with a three-bay accented centre. Side and rear elevations keep the same bay module and the same window heads, which is why the type reads as a solid rather than as a front with a back.

massing_affinities.note: The double-pile block around a hall and stair is the type's basic figure; the symmetry is generated by the plan.
The main block with hyphens and dependencies, inherited from the Palladian generation and reduced to an affordable scale.
The service and stable court behind or beside the block, deliberately screened from the park front.
At the smaller end, where a parsonage or a gentleman farmer's house accretes service and farm buildings in a descending line.
The type is defined by standing free and being seen in the round.

constraints.statement: The main block is strictly symmetrical about the entrance axis on the principal front, including chimney positions. Asymmetry is permitted only in the service wing, which must be visually subordinate and set back.
Ground-floor storey height exceeds the first floor by 10-20 percent, and every storey above diminishes. Sash proportion 1.7:1 to 2:1.

test.note: Same variable and test as english-georgian's storey-height constraint -- this variant restates the parent's rule. The sash-proportion clause (1.7:1-2:1) in the same statement stays prose.

constraints.statement: All four elevations use the same bay module, window head and cornice. A composed front with a plain or randomly fenestrated back is forbidden in a house designed to stand in a park.

Service wing ridge at least 25 percent below the main block ridge, and its eaves line demonstrably lower. A service wing that matches the house in height destroys the hierarchy on which the composition depends.
Wall ornament limited to plinth, string course, quoins and crowning cornice, plus one accented centre. Pilasters or a portico require a Palladian rather than a Georgian classification.

exemplars.name: Basildon Park
exemplars.note: Built 1776-83 by John Carr of York for Sir Francis Sykes, on an East India Company fortune. Bath stone, a pedimented centre with an Ionic portico, and flanking pavilions joined by short links — the type at its most polished.

exemplars.name: Danson House
exemplars.note: Built 1762-66 by Sir Robert Taylor for the slave-trade merchant John Boyd. A compact three-storey villa of near-cubic proportion with canted bays — Taylor's characteristic reduction of the Palladian villa to a suburban scale.

exemplars.name: Nostell Priory
exemplars.note: Begun 1733 to designs by Colonel James Moyser and executed by James Paine, with later interiors by Robert Adam from 1766. A main block with corner pavilions showing the transition from Palladian scheme to Georgian practice.

exemplars.name: Hagley Hall
exemplars.note: Built 1754-60 by Sanderson Miller, a gentleman amateur, for the first Lord Lyttelton. A four-square block with corner towers and Rococo plasterwork inside, and a good demonstration of how far a well-read amateur could get with pattern books.

sources: Dan Cruickshank and Peter Wyld, Georgian Buildings of Britain and Ireland (1975)
John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)
Isaac Ware, A Complete Body of Architecture (1756)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England (county volumes)

proportion_packs.note: This node's own lineage note names the transmission explicitly -- 'the five-part scheme, the pedimented centre, the Venetian window and the piano nobile survive here in reduced and affordable form, transmitted through Gibbs, Ware and Robert Morris's Select Architecture (1755)' -- and Ware's Complete Body of Architecture (1756) is in its sources list directly. This is the one node in the trunk where Gibbs is bound not against the American-export reading but on the strength of its own stated documentary lineage: the doorcase, cornice and Ionic or Doric portico of a Carr or Paine house are drawn from exactly the plates the American colonies also owned, at the same date, for the same reason.

The plainer order of the subordinate wing and the service court -- graded below the Ionic of the main block's pedimented centre exactly as the node's own hard constraint c04 requires the service wing to be subordinate in height.

Governs the centre-of-three-bays advanced 300-600 mm and the requirement, tested by this node's own hard constraint c03, that all four elevations share one bay module, window head and cornice -- the park-house discipline of being 'seen in the round' that a terrace or a townhouse never has to meet.

Governs the sash ratio (1.7:1 to 2:1) and the storey-diminishing window heights this node's hard constraint c02 restates from the trunk style, applied here to a facade entered at grade rather than up an external stair.
12-over-12 lights before about 1770, 6-over-6 after, per this node's own typical_ratios -- the same dating ladder as the trunk style, running the full length of the type's 1720-1830 span.

Ground floor exceeding first by 10-20 percent, second floor 0.7-0.8, attic 0.5-0.6 -- restated verbatim from the trunk style in this node's own hard constraint c02, and the diagnostic this node names as identifying a house as rural 'at a glance' against the townhouse's inverted arrangement.

Bound optional rather than primary, matching the node's own account: 'ashlar replaced by good brick in most counties' -- the type is built in whichever local material the county affords, Bath stone at Basildon Park, brick everywhere the stone is not local.

The entrance-hall-and-stair-hall sequence this node describes, with principal rooms of Palladian ratio disposed around them at full Georgian moulding richness -- the country house's larger rooms and taller ceilings (3.3-4.0 m against the trunk style's 3.0-3.6 m) sit within this pack's calibrated range rather than at its edge.

Governs the principal rooms this node states directly as 1:1, 1:1.25, 1:1.33 or 1:1.5 in plan -- the Palladian ratio set followed, per the node's own description, 'by habit rather than checked against a plate,' which is exactly the difference between this node and its Palladian parent.

The Palladian residue this node names as making it 'closer to the Palladian source than the town house ever is': the Venetian window on the stair landing or side elevation, the persisting piano-nobile echo in a house entered at grade. Bound low and optional -- this is a surviving motif inherited from english-palladian, not the governing order of the main elevation, which stays Gibbs's.

mediterranean-vernacular.name: Mediterranean Vernacular

description.short: The unwritten farmhouse and villa building of the Italian countryside, whose plain massing and tile roofs supplied the twentieth century with an entire romantic idiom.
description.long:
Alongside the treatise tradition ran a peasant one: stone or stuccoed masonry, low-pitched clay tile roofs, small deep-set openings, buildings that grew by accretion around a courtyard or along a slope. It has no theorists and no dates, and it produced the visual material that Italianate, Italian Renaissance Revival, and Mediterranean Revival all quarried.

The irony is instructive. The high tradition was designed to be copied and largely was not, outside of professional circles; the vernacular was never designed to be copied at all and became the most imitated Italian architecture in America.

defining_characteristics: Massive stuccoed or stone walls with deep reveals
Low-pitched clay tile roofs with modest overhang and exposed rafters
Accretive growth around courts and along contours
Ornament almost entirely absent, concentrated where it is unavoidable

iberian-islamic.name: Iberian Islamic

description.short: Eight centuries of Islamic building in Iberia and its continuation as Mudejar craft under Christian rule.
description.long:
Al-Andalus produced an architecture organized around the courtyard, water, shade, and geometric surface — a set of moves for hot-dry climates that has never been improved on. Its influence on Spanish building did not end with the Reconquest; Muslim craftsmen continued working for Christian patrons for centuries, a tradition called Mudejar.

That continuity is a transmission edge, not an imitation. The same guilds, the same masons, the same techniques — only the patron changed. It is the clearest case in the taxonomy of a craft tradition outliving the culture that produced it, and a caution against reading architectural lineage off political history.

defining_characteristics: Courtyard and water as the organizing elements of the plan
Blind or minimally-opened street elevation
Geometric surface ornament in tile, brick, and carved plaster
Horseshoe and multifoil arches, intricate timber ceilings
Craft continuity across a political and religious rupture

french-neoclassical.name: French Neoclassical

revival_periods.note: The American full-height-portico revival, launched by the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, takes its authority from the French academic tradition even where its immediate models are English.

geography.hearth: Paris

lineage.note: Continuous institutional descent through the Academie royale d'architecture and the Blondel school. The plan types - hotel entre cour et jardin, the enfilade, the corps de logis with pavilions - and the stonecutting practice pass through untouched; Gabriel is Mansart's grammar with the adjectives removed.

Directed at the Rococo interior and at Baroque surface plasticity specifically: Cochin's polemics from 1754, Laugier's Essai of 1753 demanding that the column be structural and the pediment express a real roof. The target is ornament without structural warrant, not the Grand Manner plan.
Re-quotation from newly excavated evidence rather than from Renaissance intermediaries - Herculaneum from 1738, Pompeii from 1748, Piranesi's Antichita Romane 1756, Robert Adam's Spalatro 1764.

Le Roy's Ruines des plus beaux monuments de la Grece (1758) and Stuart and Revett's Antiquities of Athens (from 1762) put measured Greek buildings in French hands for the first time; the resulting taste for baseless Doric and severe unfluted shafts is a direct consequence.

description.short: The reduction of French classicism to geometric primary volumes, archaeologically correct detail used sparingly, and an ethic that every classical member must be justified by structure.
description.long:
French Neoclassicism is the tradition's first attempt at intellectual housekeeping. The argument, made most sharply by the Abbe Laugier in 1753, is that architecture had accumulated members that no longer meant anything: pilasters that support nothing, pediments over no roof, engaged columns embedded in walls that do not need them. Laugier's primitive hut - four trunks, four beams, two rafters - proposes that only the column, the entablature and the pediment are legitimate, and that everything else is arbitrary. This was never fully buildable, but as a critical instrument it was devastating, and its effect is visible everywhere: French Neoclassical buildings use fewer classical members, place them further apart, and make them do real work.

Two other conditions matter as much as the theory. The first is archaeology. Herculaneum from 1738 and Pompeii from 1748 delivered actual Roman domestic interiors, and Le Roy in 1758 and Stuart and Revett from 1762 delivered measured Greek temples. For two hundred years Europe had derived antiquity from Vitruvius plus the ruins of imperial Rome; now it had evidence of a plainer, sterner, earlier antiquity, and it turned out the Renaissance had been wrong about a great deal. The second is economic and institutional: eighteenth-century France was building a new class of public buildings - theatres, hospitals, mints, customs barriers, exchanges - for which no traditional type existed, and in which the design problem was function and circulation rather than status. Soufflot's Sainte-Genevieve is the pivotal object because it takes the structural ambition of Gothic - slender supports, minimal masonry, maximum light - and executes it in a wholly classical vocabulary, using iron cramps hidden inside the piers. The critics who attacked it for structural imprudence were arguing about statics, not taste, which tells you what had changed.

The reaction against the Rococo was specifically a reaction against the interior. Louis XV interiors are boiserie, asymmetrical rocaille cartouches, dissolving corners, no order at all. The Louis XVI answer is rectilinear panelling, straight fluted pilasters, Vitruvian scroll and guilloche in narrow bands, and corners that are corners. But nothing in the plan changed. The hotel particulier of 1780 has the same court-and-garden arrangement, the same enfilade, and the same social choreography as the hotel of 1680; the revolution was confined to the surface, which is exactly what you would expect from a reform driven by critics rather than by clients.

The Petit Trianon is the thing to stand in front of. It is a stone cube about twenty-three metres on a side, three storeys, five bays, with four free-standing Corinthian columns on the garden face and pilasters on two others - and the fourth face has neither. There is no ornament anywhere except the capitals, a balustrade and a single stringcourse. The roof is invisible. The effect, once your eye stops looking for incident, is of extraordinary calm and of the wall being a real, thick, cool, load-bearing thing, with each window cut cleanly into it and given exactly enough moulding to declare itself an opening. The building's whole argument is that if the proportions are right, nothing else is needed - and it is one of the few buildings that wins that argument outright.

defining_characteristics: Primary geometric volumes - cube, cylinder, hemisphere - legible as whole solids, with the roof suppressed behind a balustrade or parapet
Ornament reduced to a small number of correctly measured members, separated by large areas of plain wall
Free-standing columns carrying a real entablature in preference to engaged columns and pilasters
Even, unaccented bay rhythm across the whole front, with the centre marked by a portico or a slight projection but no change of rhythm
Archaeologically derived detail - Greek key, Vitruvian scroll, guilloche, paterae, husk garlands - used in narrow disciplined bands
Rustication confined to the ground storey with fine joints, or eliminated altogether
Straight lines and right angles reasserted at every scale, particularly in interiors, against Rococo curvature
diagnostic_tells: No visible roof: a balustrade or blocking course runs along the cornice line and the low hipped roof behind it is invisible from the ground
Column shafts unfluted, or fluted only in the upper two-thirds, and set widely apart with plain wall between
Windows cut into the wall as clean rectangles with a flat architrave, no aedicular surround, and no keystone drama
A giant portico of four or six free-standing columns applied to an otherwise entirely plain block
Interior corners are square and panelling is rectilinear - the immediate tell separating Louis XVI from Louis XV

distinguished_from.difference: The Baroque works by hierarchy of projecting blocks and heavy sculptural relief at the centre; Neoclassicism holds a single plane, suppresses relief, and distributes the emphasis evenly. The mansard roof is Baroque; the invisible roof behind a balustrade is Neoclassical.

Beaux-Arts reinstates the sculptural richness, the coupled columns, the strong centrepiece and the visible attic or mansard, and works at a much larger scale. Neoclassicism is subtractive; Beaux-Arts is additive.

The American Greek Revival is a timber-and-stucco vernacular of temple fronts on houses, using Doric and Ionic almost exclusively and pattern-book profiles. French Neoclassicism is masonry, prefers Corinthian and Ionic, is applied to public and urban buildings, and derives its detail from measured survey rather than from a handbook.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Archaeological correctness of the individual member combined with geometric primitivism of the whole. The building is resolved into a small number of primary solids; the order is then applied at full correct proportion, sparingly, and is expected to be structurally justified. Jacques-Francois Blondel's Cours d'architecture (1771-1777) supplies the codified profiles.
typical_ratios: Principal block approaching a cube: plan 1:1 to 1:1.3, height 0.8 to 1.0 of plan width (Petit Trianon is 23 m square)
Wall to void ratio high: window aperture area 12 to 20 percent of elevation area, with pier width 1 to 1.5 times opening width
Corinthian and Ionic column height 9.5 to 10 diameters; shafts unfluted or fluted only above 1/3 height
Entablature reduced to 1/5 of column height, against the Baroque 1/4
Low hipped roof at 5:12 to 8:12 concealed behind a balustrade of height 1/12 to 1/16 of the wall height
Rustication, where used, confined to the ground storey with joints 10 to 20 mm wide and no rock face
Window proportions rationalised by storey: ground 1:1.6, piano nobile 1:2 to 1:2.2, attic 1:1 to 1:1.2
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even, unaccented and repetitive. The centre is marked by a portico or by a projection of one to three bays with no change in the spacing itself. Uniformity is the argument: Gabriel's two Place de la Concorde palaces (1755-1775) repeat a single colonnaded bay across two separate buildings so that the square, not the building, is the composition.

massing_affinities.note: The compact near-cubic double-pile block around a central hall or vestibule - the Petit Trianon and the whole maison de plaisance type.
The Parisian immeuble and the terraced hotel front; uniform bays, a plain stone wall and an invisible roof are what make a continuous street wall possible.
The hotel particulier entre cour et jardin survives unchanged from the Baroque; only its dress is renovated.
The full free-standing portico on a plain block, with subordinate flanking ranges, is the standing type for public buildings.
Neoclassicism actively suppresses the mansard in favour of a low roof behind a balustrade. A mansard indicates either a survival from the previous century or the nineteenth-century revival.

constraints.statement: The roof must not be visible from a normal standing viewpoint at the building line. Pitch 5:12 to 8:12, hipped, concealed behind a balustrade or blocking course at least 1/16 the wall height.

test.note: Tests the pitch range. 'Not visible from a normal standing viewpoint' is qualitative, and the balustrade/blocking-course height (at least 1/16 the wall height, expressible via parapet_height_in and facade_height_ft) is a second independent clause -- both stay prose.

constraints.statement: A pediment may appear only where a real roof or a real portico is behind it. Applying a pediment over a flat-roofed projection is the exact practice Laugier's critique was aimed at.
Plain wall must dominate: aperture area must not exceed 25 percent of any principal elevation, and every opening must be separated from the next by at least its own width.

test.note: Tests the aperture-area ceiling. 'Every opening separated from the next by at least its own width' is a relative, self-referential rule with no fixed vocabulary threshold and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Ornament is banded, not scattered. Enrichment may occur only in continuous horizontal bands (frieze, string, sill course) or within a single framed panel; free-floating swags and cartouches on open wall belong to the Baroque.
