Where free-standing columns are used internally, they must carry the vault or floor above them and be spaced at 2.25 to 3 diameters. Decorative free-standing columns supporting nothing invert the style's founding argument.

test.note: Tests the spacing clause. That the columns must carry a real vault or floor above them (not be decorative) stays prose -- no structural-load-bearing variable exists.

exemplars.name: Petit Trianon
exemplars.note: Ange-Jacques Gabriel, 1762-1768. A 23 m cube with four differently articulated faces responding to four different ground conditions; the reference object for the style's economy of means.

exemplars.name: Pantheon (church of Sainte-Genevieve)
exemplars.note: Jacques-Germain Soufflot, foundations 1758, completed 1790 by Rondelet. Corinthian portico on a Greek-cross plan with slender piers and hidden iron cramps - Gothic structural ambition in a Roman vocabulary.

exemplars.name: Place de la Concorde, twin palaces
exemplars.note: Ange-Jacques Gabriel, 1755-1775. Two identical colonnaded fronts framing the Rue Royale; the buildings are designed as the walls of an urban room.

exemplars.name: Hotel de Salm (Palais de la Legion d'Honneur)
exemplars.note: Pierre Rousseau, 1782-1787. The garden-front rotunda and the low balustraded silhouette that Jefferson admired in person and drew on at Monticello.

sources: Marc-Antoine Laugier, Essai sur l'architecture (1753; 2nd ed. 1755)
Jacques-Francois Blondel, Cours d'architecture (1771-1777)
Robin Middleton and David Watkin, Neoclassical and 19th Century Architecture (1980)
Emil Kaufmann, Architecture in the Age of Reason (1955)
James Stevens Curl, Classical Architecture (2001)

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding: french-neoclassical is not in vignola-corinthian's own applies_to. Bound as primary because this style's own typical_ratios name Corinthian and Ionic as the preferred pair (column height 9.5-10 diameters), and both named exemplars use it: the Petit Trianon's 'four free-standing Corinthian columns on the garden face' and Sainte-Genevieve's 'Corinthian portico on a Greek-cross plan.'

Judgment binding, same reasoning. The second of the style's own named pair; Vignola's Ionic column height (about 9 diameters) sits inside the style's own stated 9.5-10 diameter band for the two orders together.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the even, unaccented bay rhythm this style's own bay_rhythm field describes -- 'no change in the spacing itself' even where the centre is marked by a portico.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the clean rectangular opening this style's own diagnostic_tells describe -- 'a flat architrave, no aedicular surround, no keystone drama' -- which is closer to the pack's own plain-rectangle default than the aedicular Beaux-Arts reading is.
Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the individual room within the primary geometric solid the whole building is resolved into.

german-pennsylvania-colonial.name: German Pennsylvania Colonial

revival_periods.note: Revived mainly as the 'Pennsylvania farmhouse' — fieldstone, pent eave, six-over-six sash — within the broader Colonial Revival rather than as a distinct named revival.

geography.hearth: the limestone country of Lancaster, Berks, Lebanon and Montgomery counties, Pennsylvania, settled from the Rhenish Palatinate and Switzerland after 1710

lineage.note: The framing tradition arrives intact and is built in Pennsylvania for a generation — the Golden Plough Tavern at York is half-timbered exactly as a Palatine house would be — before stone and log displace it.
Secondary: the habit of housing family, stock and crop under one steep roof survives in the Pennsylvania forebay bank barn more than in the dwelling.

Horizontal log construction reached the Delaware from New Sweden; the Germans adopted it, added V- and dovetail-notching and their own three-room plan, and made it the substrate of backcountry American building all the way to the Ozarks.
After about 1770 the Continental plan is progressively regularized behind a symmetrical five-bay Anglo front — the same house, wearing a different face.

description.short: The Continental stone and log house of the Palatine and Swiss migration: a three-room asymmetric plan around a central chimney serving a closed iron stove, built into a hillside wherever the ground allowed.
description.long:
Pennsylvania German building is the one colonial tradition organized around a heating technology rather than around a fireplace. The Palatine settler brought the five-plate jamb stove — a cast-iron box open only to the back, fed through a hole in the masonry from the kitchen hearth on the other side of the wall. This single device restructures the plan. The kitchen, the Küche, becomes a large room containing the only open fire; the stove-room, the Stube, sits on the other side of the chimney wall and is heated without smoke, soot, draught, or the need for anyone to tend it from within; and the Kammer, the sleeping chamber, tucks in behind the Stube. Three rooms, not two; asymmetric, not paired; and the chimney is central not because of thermal mass — the English reason — but because it is a service wall between a wet room and a dry one. The Anglo world took two hundred years to arrive at the same idea and called it a mechanical core.

The second organizing idea is the ground. Where the English built on a level platform and dug a cellar, the German builder set the house across a slope so that the lower storey opens at grade on the downhill side and is buried on the uphill side. This yields a cool, frost-free service level — often built directly over a spring, its water running out through an arched opening — reached from outside without stairs, and a dry principal floor entered from the upper grade. Two front doors on two different levels is the result, and it is the most reliable single tell of the tradition. Nothing about it is picturesque; it is a refrigerator, a root cellar and a dairy obtained for the cost of moving earth.

The walls are squared limestone or sandstone laid in lime mortar, eighteen to thirty inches thick, with dressed quoins and unusually large corner stones, or else horizontal log with V-notched or full-dovetail corners and mud-and-straw chinking. The roof is steep, forty-five to fifty degrees, framed with a liegender Stuhl — a leaning-post truss that stands clear of the attic floor and leaves the loft usable for grain. Windows are small, irregularly placed, and set where the room wanted them rather than where the elevation did; glass was expensive and the frontier was not safe. A pent roof, a shallow shed thirty to forty inches deep running across the facade at the second-floor line, keeps water off the wall and off anyone standing at the door.

Standing inside, the surprise is the silence and the dryness. A stone house with two-foot walls and small openings has a stillness that a timber house does not; the Stube in winter, warmed by a stove and lit by two small deep-set windows, is one of the most comfortable rooms colonial America produced, and it does this without a fire in sight. The tradition was negotiating against nothing more exotic than English fashion and English land law, and it lost the elevation while keeping the section — which is the pattern of nearly every immigrant building culture in America.

defining_characteristics: Asymmetric three-room Flurküchenhaus plan — Küche, Stube, Kammer — arranged around a central chimney mass, with no through passage
Central chimney serving an open cooking hearth in the kitchen and a closed five-plate jamb stove fed through the wall into the stove-room
Load-bearing squared stone (or V-notched horizontal log) walls 18–30 in thick, with oversized dressed quoins
Steep gable roof, 45–50 degrees, framed with a liegender Stuhl leaning-post truss over a usable loft
Small, irregularly spaced openings placed by interior need rather than by facade composition, with deep reveals
Vaulted or barrel-arched masonry cellar, frequently over a spring
Pent roof — a shallow shed 30–42 in deep at the second-floor line — across the facade or the gable end on eighteenth-century work
diagnostic_tells: A pent roof band across the facade at the second-floor line, with no posts under it
Windows that do not line up floor to floor, in a house otherwise carefully built — the plan is winning the argument with the elevation
Very large squared quoin stones against smaller coursed wall stone
A door at the gable end entering the kitchen, plus a second door on the facade — two entrances of unequal status
Interior: a flat chimney wall in the stove-room with a small square iron-lined aperture, the ghost of a jamb stove

distinguished_from.difference: Both are masonry, five-bay, steep-roofed and Pennsylvanian, and after 1780 they converge. The test is the plan and the openings: Georgian gives you a centre passage, a symmetrical rear elevation, aligned windows floor to floor, and a classical door surround. The German house gives you an asymmetric three-room plan, unaligned windows and a plain door with a hood.

Both build thick stone with steep roofs. The Dutch house has gable-end hearths, an open jambless fire, exposed anchor beams and a low plate; the German house has a central chimney with a closed stove, a liegender Stuhl truss and a banked lower storey.

The twentieth-century 'Pennsylvania farmhouse' takes the fieldstone, the pent eave and the six-over-six sash and applies them to a symmetrical centre-hall plan with aligned windows, a fireplace in every room, thin veneer stone and an attached garage. Wall thickness at the window reveal settles it: two feet of real masonry, or four inches of veneer.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The three-room plan module: a kitchen bay of 16–20 ft and a stove-room/chamber bay of the same total width, divided roughly 2:1, with the chimney on the dividing wall.
typical_ratios: Overall 28–38 ft × 22–30 ft, i.e. close to 4:3
Küche occupies 45–55% of the plan; Stube and Kammer share the remainder, Stube the larger
Wall thickness 18–30 in at the ground storey, reducing 2–4 in at the upper floor
Ceiling 7 ft 0 in – 8 ft 6 in; loft usable to the collar of the liegender Stuhl
Window opening ratio near 1:1.6, and total glazed area under 8% of wall area on early work
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular on early work; a nominal three- or five-bay front emerges after 1770 but the door is often still off-centre because the chimney wall is.

massing_affinities.note: The nearest catalogued skeleton to the Flurküchenhaus, with the caveat that the German plan divides unequally and adds a third room.
The regularized post-1780 Pennsylvania farmhouse, sometimes with the distinctive paired central doors.
The log Einraumhaus of first settlement.
Anglicized late work.
Growth by attaching kitchen and summer-kitchen wings along the contour.

constraints.statement: The chimney mass sits on the partition between kitchen and stove-room, serving an open hearth on one side and a closed stove aperture on the other. Moving it to the gable ends dissolves the plan type.
Roof pitch 10:12 to 12:12 (40–50 degrees). Pennsylvania German work does not go below 9:12; a 6:12 roof on fieldstone is a twentieth-century invention.

Pent roof, where used, projects 30–42 in at the second-floor line at a pitch of 25–35 degrees, is unsupported by posts, and returns 12–24 in around the corner. It is a pre-1780 feature; on later work it reads as revival.

test.note: Tests the pent roof's projection. Pitch (25-35deg) and corner return (12-24in) are the statement's other numeric claims and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Load-bearing wall 18–30 in of squared stone, with quoins 1.5 to 2.5 times the height of the field coursing. Window and door reveals must show the full wall depth; a flush jamb reveals a veneer.

test.note: Tests the wall thickness. The quoin-to-coursing size ratio is a niche one-off comparison and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Openings by period: small casements with iron hardware to c. 1760; nine-over-six sash c. 1760–1800; six-over-six after. Glazed area under 8% of wall area before 1770, under 12% after.

exemplars.name: Hans Herr House (1719 Museum)
exemplars.location: West Lampeter Township, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: The oldest building in Lancaster County and the canonical American Flurküchenhaus: squared sandstone with oversized quoins, three-room plan, central chimney, high steep roof, small casement openings.

exemplars.name: Golden Plough Tavern
exemplars.note: Half-timbered Fachwerk with brick nogging, built as a Palatine builder would have built at home — the framing tradition before stone displaced it.

exemplars.name: Schifferstadt
exemplars.note: Built by Elias Bruner of the Palatinate. Retains the central wishbone chimney, liegender Stuhl truss, vaulted cellar, five-plate jamb stove and stone kitchen sink — the most legible surviving section of the type.

exemplars.name: Heinrich Zeller House (Fort Zeller)
exemplars.note: Limestone house banked over an everflowing spring that discharges through an arched cellar opening; narrow irregular windows.

sources: Sally McMurry and Nancy Van Dolsen, eds., Architecture and Landscape of the Pennsylvania Germans, 1720–1920 (2011)
Robert C. Bucher, 'The Continental Log House', Pennsylvania Folklife (1962)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)
Bernard L. Herman and Gabrielle Lanier, Everyday Architecture of the Mid-Atlantic (1997)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: The canonical construction — squared limestone or sandstone, 18-30 in, with oversized dressed quoins 1.5 to 2.5 times the height of the field coursing — is a direct match to brick-course's own corner_quoin rule that quoins must be laid up in whole-course multiples so long and short faces alternate. german-pennsylvania-colonial is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. Bound primary, not merely optional, because stone is this style's canonical and most-cited walling: Hans Herr House, Schifferstadt and Fort Zeller are all stone exemplars.

Governs the log Einraumhaus of first settlement, listed as a 'common' massing affinity (hall-single-cell) and explicit in the style's own lineage as a hybridization with Scandinavian log construction — 'the Germans adopted it, added V- and dovetail-notching and their own three-room plan.' german-pennsylvania-colonial is named directly in log-module's own applies_to. Bound optional and second because the style's canonical, most-documented built form is the stone Flurküchenhaus, not the log cabin, but the log phase is real, dated (first settlement, pre-stone) and should not be dropped.

german-pennsylvania-colonial is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. The style's own governing_logic is close to a paraphrase of this pack's argument: 'a kitchen bay of 16-20 ft and a stove-room/chamber bay of the same total width' — a plan sized by function (the jamb-stove wall, the hearth) rather than by a treatise ratio.

The style's own constraint c05 restates sash-light's dated light-count logic almost verbatim: 'small casements... to c.1760; nine-over-six sash c.1760-1800; six-over-six after.' Bound for that dating arithmetic only. The style's own typical_ratios give a window opening ratio 'near 1:1.6' — squarer than sash-light's 1.85-2.6 measured Anglo-American band, and consistent with the style's own diagnostic tell that openings are 'placed by interior need rather than by facade composition.' Do not read sash-light's ratio figure onto this style's windows. opening-proportion was considered and rejected for the same reason, more strongly: its Palladian door-and-window derivation assumes a composed elevation, and this style's own diagnostic tell is that 'windows that do not line up floor to floor, in a house otherwise carefully built' show 'the plan... winning the argument with the elevation.'

jacobean.name: Jacobean

revival_periods.note: Revived as the default English institutional and country-house manner of the nineteenth century, and exported to America as Jacobethan collegiate work.

geography.hearth: The Home Counties and East Anglia, where court patronage and Netherlandish craft traditions met

lineage.note: The same masons and joiners working for the same class under a new king; the break at 1603 is dynastic, not architectural, and the two styles overlap for a decade.

The shaped and scrolled gable and the heavy strapwork cartouche are Low Countries imports, carried by immigrant craftsmen and by Antwerp pattern sheets, and they take root most deeply in East Anglia where the immigrant communities settled.

Still known only through engravings and through Netherlandish reworkings of them. Inigo Jones's genuinely Palladian Queen's House, begun 1616, stands beside Jacobean work as a foreign object and is not part of this node.

description.short: Elizabethan composition thickened, curved and darkened under James I: shaped Dutch gables, columned porches, heavy strapwork, and interiors of carved oak and pendant plaster.
description.long:
Jacobean is a style of consolidation rather than invention. The prodigy-house programme continues — Hatfield, Audley End and Blickling are as large and as ruinously expensive as anything Elizabeth's courtiers built — but the nervous verticality of the 1580s settles into something heavier and more resolved. The silhouette stops being spiky and becomes curved: the Netherlandish shaped gable, with its scrolls and its little segmental or triangular pediment on top, arrives in force and becomes the period's most recognisable move. The frontispiece grows outward from a flat pilaster screen into a real columned porch, often of two orders with paired columns and a strapwork cartouche above.

The conditions are a peace dividend and a credit boom. James's accession ended the Spanish war and opened a period in which court office, monopolies and land speculation created fortunes rapidly and destroyed them almost as fast — Audley End nearly bankrupted the Earl of Suffolk, who was then convicted of embezzlement, and Hatfield was built by Robert Cecil while he was effectively running the country. Brick becomes the standard material for a great house in the lowland counties, with stone reserved for dressings, quoins and the porch, and the combination of red brick with pale stone dressings is the period's colour signature. Below the great-house level the same vocabulary migrates into what Summerson called Artisan Mannerism: London and provincial craftsmen assembling gables, pediments and pilasters into vigorous, incorrect compositions that carry the tradition to about 1660.

What Jacobean was reacting to is subtle: not Elizabethan taste, which it inherits wholesale, but the Elizabethan house's uninhabitability. Plans get more compact, glazing ratios come down from the Hardwick extreme, and the great chamber and gallery are joined by a proliferation of smaller private rooms and closets. The long gallery, top-lit and end-lit, becomes the centre of social life for a class that increasingly stayed indoors, and the dogleg or open-well great stair — broad, wooden, with heavily carved newels carrying obelisks or heraldic beasts — becomes the ceremonial armature of the house.

The Jacobean interior is the darkest in English domestic architecture and one of the most tactile. Oak panelling covers the walls to a moulded cornice; the plaster ceiling above is a dense field of ribs, pendants and modelled foliage, catching what light there is; the chimneypiece is a two-storey architectural event in coloured marbles and alabaster, with caryatids and strapwork, often the single most expensive object in the house. Rooms are warmer than their Elizabethan predecessors and much gloomier, and the effect of moving from a bright stair window into a panelled great chamber is a deliberate dimming — a compression of light and volume that reads as gravity, which is exactly what a Jacobean magnate wished to project.

defining_characteristics: Shaped and scrolled gables of Netherlandish derivation, usually capped by a small pediment, ranged symmetrically along a front or crowning end pavilions
A projecting entrance porch of one or two orders with paired columns, a strapwork cartouche or achievement of arms above, and a room over it
Red brick walling with contrasting pale stone dressings at quoins, mullions, copings and porch
Mullioned and transomed windows in flush grids, glazing ratio reduced from Elizabethan extremes to roughly 30-45 percent of the elevation
Symmetrical E-, H- or half-H plan with the long gallery on an upper floor and a compact double-pile core emerging
A broad open-well or dogleg oak stair with square newels carrying obelisks, finials or heraldic beasts, treated as the ceremonial spine of the house
Interiors of full-height oak panelling under enriched plaster ceilings with pendants, and multi-storey marble chimneypieces
diagnostic_tells: The shaped Dutch gable — concave and convex scrolls stepping up to a pediment — repeated across a front. Elizabethan gables are straight-sided and finialled; Jacobean gables curve
A columned porch standing proud of the wall plane with a chamber above it, rather than the flat applied frontispiece of Elizabethan work
Red brick with stone dressings as the default great-house material in the lowlands, where the Elizabethan default was ashlar or coursed stone
Strapwork that has thickened into deep, fleshy, three-dimensional cartouches and pendants rather than the flat interlaced bands of the 1580s
Carved newel posts rising well above the handrail and terminating in obelisks or beasts — a detail almost unique to this half-century

distinguished_from.difference: Curves versus spikes. Jacobean shapes its gables and projects its porch; Elizabethan crests its parapet and applies a flat frontispiece. Jacobean is more often brick, less glazed, heavier in ornament, and more compact in plan. The two overlap between 1600 and 1615 and cannot always be separated.

Both are heavy, but Baroque is correct and Jacobean is not. Baroque orders are proportioned to a module and used to model a whole mass; Jacobean orders are approximated from engravings, stacked, and applied to a porch. Baroque roofs are hipped behind balustrades; Jacobean roofs are gabled.

Shares the shaped gable and often the immigrant craftsmen, but the Dutch type is a narrow urban house whose gable is its whole street facade and whose plan is dictated by a canal-side lot. Jacobean deploys the same gable as a repeated incident along a wide country house front.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Bilateral symmetry about the porch axis, with the orders used approximately and by rule of thumb from Serlio and de Vries plates. The window grid supplies the module; the gable rhythm supplies the metre.
typical_ratios: Mullion light 450-550 mm; windows of two to five lights with one or two transoms
Glazed to solid ratio 30-45 percent of the principal elevation
Gable width 3.5-5.5 m, height to the pediment apex roughly 0.6-0.8 of the gable width
Porch column height 6 to 8 diameters — noticeably stubbier than any canonical order, and a reliable sign of the period
Storey heights roughly equal, or ground floor exceeding first by no more than 10 percent
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even and repetitive along the front, punctuated by projecting end wings and the central porch. The shaped gables establish a second, slower rhythm above the eaves line which may or may not align with the window bays — where it does not, the mismatch is characteristic rather than a fault.

massing_affinities.note: The E-plan with a central porch and the half-H are the standard Jacobean forms; Hatfield and Blickling are both variations on it.
Retained at the greatest scale, as at Audley End, which had two courts before its eighteenth-century reduction.
The compact double-pile block appears at the end of the period in Artisan Mannerist work and leads directly into the Restoration house.
Gabled brick street ranges in London and the provincial towns before the Fire of 1666 removed most of them.

constraints.statement: Where shaped gables occur they must be repeated in a symmetrical set of at least three, or paired on end pavilions. A single shaped gable on an otherwise plain front is a Victorian move.
The entrance porch projects from the wall plane by not less than 1.2 m and carries a room above it. A flat applied frontispiece belongs to Elizabethan.

test.note: Converted from the source's 1.2 m to in. Tests the porch-projection minimum. 'Carries a room above it' is a plan/programmatic fact, not a projection dimension, and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Brick walling requires stone or moulded-brick dressings at every opening, quoin and coping; unrelieved brick with no dressings reads as later vernacular.

Windows remain mullioned and transomed with leaded lights. Sash windows are forbidden; where they occur on a real Jacobean house they are an eighteenth-century alteration and should be modelled as such.
Glazing ratio 30-45 percent on principal elevations — above this the building reads Elizabethan, below it Tudor.

exemplars.name: Hatfield House
exemplars.note: Built 1607-12 for Robert Cecil, first Earl of Salisbury, with Robert Lyminge as chief craftsman. Brick with stone dressings, a stone-faced centre with a two-order loggia and clock tower, and the finest surviving Jacobean stair.

exemplars.name: Blickling Hall
exemplars.note: Built 1616-27 by Robert Lyminge for Sir Henry Hobart. Red brick with shaped gables and corner turrets, and a 37 m long gallery with a Jacobean plaster ceiling of exceptional density.

exemplars.name: Audley End House
exemplars.note: Built 1605-14 for Thomas Howard, first Earl of Suffolk, and originally of two great courts; reduced in the eighteenth century to roughly a third of its size. The scale that broke its builder.

exemplars.name: Chastleton House
exemplars.note: Built 1607-12 for Walter Jones, a wool merchant's grandson. Cotswold limestone rather than brick, with a compact symmetrical plan around a small court, and interiors — panelling, plaster, long gallery barrel ceiling — almost untouched since.

sources: John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)
Malcolm Airs, The Tudor and Jacobean Country House: A Building History (1995)
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England (county volumes)
Olive Cook, The English Country House: An Art and a Way of Life (1974)

proportion_packs.note: jacobean is named directly in timber-bay's applies_to. As with elizabethan, it governs the roof and floor carpentry and the smaller-house frame even though the great prodigy houses (Hatfield, Blickling, Audley End) are brick with stone dressings.

A cautious, low-precedence judgment binding, and the one order-pack binding in this entire British-traditions batch. jacobean sits at the genuine cusp: unlike elizabethan and tudor, this style's porch is real Renaissance ornament with real structural presence (c02: projects at least 1.2 m and carries a room above), not a flat applied frontispiece or an inset roundel, and its own text records real (if approximate) column proportions — 'porch column height 6 to 8 diameters.' Vignola's Tuscan, the plainest of the five canonical orders at seven diameters, is the nearest canonical reference point to that range and is the order this pack's own notes call 'the American default... whatever the pattern book calls them.' The binding is deliberately weak: distinguished_from english-baroque states outright that 'Jacobean orders are approximated from engravings, stacked, and applied to a porch' and are NOT proportioned to a module the way a correct order is, and the style's own figure (6-8D) sits at or below Vignola's canonical minimum, confirming the mismatch. Use this pack only as a rough comparative check on porch column scale — never as a governing derivation for the entablature, capital or pedestal, which should be drawn from the style's own approximate, Serlio-and-de-Vries-derived figures instead.

Judgment binding (not in applies_to). A somewhat better fit than at elizabethan: this style's own text records a shift toward 'a proliferation of smaller private rooms and closets' as the great chamber and gallery stop being the whole of social life, which tracks room-vernacular's ordinary-room band more closely than Elizabethan's state-room scale does. Still scoped away from the hall, gallery and great chamber, which remain governed by this style's own figured ratios.

roman-classical.name: Roman Classical

revival_periods.note: Recovery by measurement of standing ruins and by reading the rediscovered Vitruvius manuscript (Poggio Bracciolini, 1414).
Second, archaeologically better-informed recovery driven by the excavation of Herculaneum (1738) and Pompeii (1748) and by Piranesi's polemics.
Direct American adoption of specific Roman buildings as models for a republic; the Virginia State Capitol is the Maison Carree.

geography.hearth: Rome and Latium

lineage.note: Direct and self-conscious: Greek craftsmen worked in Rome, Greek buildings were looted and copied, and Vitruvius writes as a transmitter of Greek theory. Rome inherits the orders whole and changes their use rather than their grammar.

description.short: The Greek order system industrialised, freed from structure by the arch and concrete, and turned into an applied grid for articulating walls, vaults and cities across an empire.
description.long:
Roman classical architecture takes a system designed for one building type and makes it work for everything: temple, basilica, bath, theatre, aqueduct, warehouse, apartment block, house. The decisive technical change is that the Romans build with the arch, the barrel and groin vault, and above all with opus caementicium - a lime-and-pozzolana concrete poured into brick or rubble facing that behaves as a monolith. Once the wall is doing the work, the column is no longer required to hold anything up. It therefore becomes something new: an articulating device, applied to the face of an arcuated structure to give it scale, hierarchy and rhythm. The Colosseum bay - a pier with a half-column against it, spanned by an arch, repeated eighty times and stacked in three orders - is the single most consequential invention in the history of Western facade design, and every classical elevation from Alberti to McKim is descended from it.

The conditions are imperial and logistical. Rome had standing armies with engineering corps, an internal market for brick and lime, a road system, slave labour at industrial scale, and a political need to make provincial cities legible as Roman within a generation of conquest. Concrete is what makes that scalable: it does not require a guild of stonecutters, only a supervisor, formwork and an unskilled workforce. The result is a kit of parts in the literal sense - standardised column sizes quarried at Mons Claudianus or Proconnesus and shipped rough, standardised brick dimensions, a canonical set of five orders. Vitruvius, writing under Augustus, is not describing an art; he is writing a specification manual, and the reason the Renaissance could resurrect the whole tradition from a single surviving text is that the text was written to be a specification in the first place.

What Rome reacts against is the Greek limitation it inherited. A Greek temple has one interior and it is dark and small; a Greek building is an object to walk around. Rome inverts the priority: the great Roman spaces are interiors, and the exterior of the Pantheon is frankly ugly brick behind a stuck-on Greek porch. Roman architecture also abandons the Greek idea that all four sides matter. The Roman temple sits on a high podium, is approached by a stair only at the front, and is pseudoperipteral - real columns in the porch, engaged half-columns pretending to continue around the flanks. It has one face. This frontality, plus the podium, is precisely what makes the Roman temple adaptable as a facade for a courthouse or a bank two thousand years later, and the Greek temple not.

To stand inside the Pantheon is to understand what the arch bought. A sphere forty-three metres across is set inside a drum of the same diameter, the coffers of the dome step and diminish so that the surface reads as thinning as it rises, and a single nine-metre oculus admits a hard disc of sunlight that travels measurably across the wall over the course of an hour. There is no direct view of the sky except straight up. The space is not composed of parts you read in sequence, as a Greek temple is; it is one figure apprehended instantly and then slowly disbelieved. Outside, in the streets of Ostia or Pompeii, the same tradition produces something quite different and equally durable: four- and five-storey brick apartment blocks with shops at grade, a continuous street wall, and courtyard houses that turn a blank face outward and lavish everything on an interior peristyle.

defining_characteristics: Arcuated and vaulted structure in concrete or brick-faced concrete, with the orders applied to it rather than carrying it
The arch order - pier, engaged column or pilaster, entablature, arched opening - as the repeating unit of the facade
Frontality: a single principal face, a high podium, and access by a frontal stair rather than an all-round stepped base
Five codified orders including the Roman inventions of Tuscan and Composite, with all Doric variants given a base
Superimposition of orders in vertical sequence from heaviest below to lightest above
The interior as the primary architectural subject, with lit, vaulted, axially planned volumes
Dimensional standardisation of components - column shafts, brick, vault spans - allowing provincial construction by non-specialists
diagnostic_tells: Half-columns or pilasters engaged into a wall or pier that is itself doing the structural work - the giveaway that this is Roman and not Greek
Temple standing on a podium 2 to 4 m high with steps only on the entrance front, and engaged columns down the flanks
Roman Doric and Tuscan columns have bases; Greek Doric never does
Coffered vaults and domes, and the Composite capital (Ionic volutes on a Corinthian bell), neither of which exists in Greek work
Deep porch of two or three column ranks in front, with the cella pushed hard against the rear of the podium

distinguished_from.difference: Greek work is trabeated, peripteral, stands on an all-round crepidoma, has no arches or vaults, and lavishes attention on the exterior. Roman work is arcuated, pseudoperipteral, podium-mounted and frontal, and lavishes attention on the interior.

The Renaissance recovers the Roman vocabulary but not Roman concrete; its vaults are true masonry and its walls are load-bearing, so a Renaissance palazzo is thicker and more inert than the Roman work it imitates. The Renaissance also regularises what Rome did loosely - Roman detailing is far more varied and provincial than the Renaissance codification suggests.

Romanesque work reuses the round arch and often literal Roman spolia, but has lost the order as a proportional system: its capitals are cushion, scallop or figurative inventions rather than members of a graduated set, its arcades are dimensioned by the mason's rod rather than by a module, and its walls are thick load-bearing rubble rather than concrete monolith faced with brick.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Vitruvian module = half the lower column diameter, subdivided into 12 or 18 parts. But because the order no longer carries load, the real generator of a Roman elevation is the structural bay of the arcade, with the order laid over it as a grid; the two systems are reconciled by choosing an intercolumniation that suits the required arch span.
typical_ratios: Vitruvian intercolumniations: pycnostyle 1.5D, systyle 2D, eustyle 2.25D (central bay 3D), diastyle 3D, araeostyle 4D
Column height varies inversely with spacing: about 10 diameters at pycnostyle, 9.5 at eustyle, 8 at araeostyle
Canonical order heights as later codified by Vignola: Tuscan 7D, Doric 8D, Ionic 9D, Corinthian and Composite 10D
Entablature approximately 1/4 of column height; pedestal, where used, approximately 1/3
Tympanum height = 1/9 of the span across the corona (Vitruvius III.5.12)
Pantheon: interior diameter equals interior height, 43.3 m, so the section is a sphere resting on a cylinder; oculus 8.9 m
Roman temple plan typically 1:2 (Maison Carree 13.54 x 26.42 m) with the porch occupying roughly one third of the length
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Two coexisting rhythms. Trabeated fronts use uniform intercolumniation, often eustyle with a widened central bay. Arcuated fronts use a repeating pier-arch-pier bay, uniform along the whole run and stacked in superimposed orders, with the rhythm broken only at a gate or an axis.

massing_affinities.note: The domus - atrium and peristyle in sequence, blank to the street, wholly inward-lit.
The villa suburbana and villa maritima open the fourth side to a view or a garden.
The insula: party-wall blocks of two to five storeys with shops at grade, forming a continuous street wall.
Roman practice supplies the podium, the frontal stair and the deep pedimented porch that this skeleton depends on, though Rome applies it to public buildings rather than dwellings.
The great maritime villas do compose a dominant block with subordinate flanking ranges, but without the hyphen-and-flanker regularity the name implies.

constraints.statement: Any span above roughly 6 m must be arched or vaulted, not lintelled. A flat stone lintel spanning 8 m is not Roman; it is a modern steel beam with stone cladding.
Superimposed orders must ascend from heavier to lighter - Tuscan or Doric below, Ionic next, Corinthian or Composite above. Inverting this order is a hard error.

Where an order is applied to an arcade, the arch springing must align with a horizontal member of the applied order (impost or subordinate entablature), and the arch crown must clear the main entablature soffit by at least 1/2 module.
Temple podium height between 1/5 and 1/3 of the column height; below 1/6 the building loses the frontality that distinguishes it from Greek work.

Domestic Roman exteriors are plain to the point of blankness. Applying temple-front articulation to the street face of a house has no Roman precedent and should be flagged as a Renaissance or later move.

exemplars.name: Pantheon
exemplars.note: c. AD 113-125 under Hadrian, reusing Agrippa's inscription. Unreinforced concrete dome of 43.3 m, still the largest ever built.

exemplars.name: Maison Carree
exemplars.note: Dedicated c. AD 4-7 to Gaius and Lucius Caesar. Corinthian hexastyle pseudoperipteral on a 2.85 m podium; the most completely preserved Roman temple and Jefferson's direct model.

exemplars.name: Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheatre)
exemplars.note: AD 70-80. The canonical superimposed arch order: Tuscan, Ionic, Corinthian, with a Corinthian pilaster attic.

exemplars.name: House of the Vettii
exemplars.note: Final form after the earthquake of AD 62, buried AD 79. The best-preserved atrium-and-peristyle domus.

sources: Vitruvius, De architectura
J. B. Ward-Perkins, Roman Imperial Architecture, Pelican History of Art
Mark Wilson Jones, Principles of Roman Architecture (2000)
Frank Sear, Roman Architecture (1982)
John Summerson, The Classical Language of Architecture (1963)

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding: roman-classical is the antique source, so no pack's own applies_to names it -- the applies_to lists on all five order packs enumerate revival and descendant styles only. Bound anyway because Tuscan is named in this style's own defining_characteristics as one of 'the Roman inventions of Tuscan and Composite,' and it is the ground-storey order of the style's own paradigm case, the Colosseum, whose four-storey superimposition (Tuscan, Ionic, Corinthian, Corinthian-pilaster attic) is exactly the ascending sequence c02 makes a hard constraint.

Judgment binding, same reasoning as vignola-tuscan above. Bound because Roman Doric is explicitly distinguished from Greek in this style's own diagnostic_tells -- 'Roman Doric and Tuscan columns have bases; Greek Doric never does' -- so a based Doric is correct HERE in a way it is not for greek-classical. An alternative or intermediate base-storey register alongside Tuscan.

Judgment binding. The middle register of the Colosseum's superimposed triad, and of Vitruvian intercolumniation practice generally (pycnostyle through araeostyle), which this style's own proportional_system states directly.

Judgment binding. Both of this style's own named exemplars are Corinthian: the Pantheon's porch and the Maison Carree, 'Corinthian hexastyle pseudoperipteral.' The upper, richest register of the superimposition sequence c02 requires.

Judgment binding. Composite is the second Roman invention this style's defining_characteristics names outright, and vignola-composite's own authority note cites the Arch of Titus as its ancient case -- a genuinely Roman monument, not a Renaissance intermediary. Bound optional rather than secondary because Roman practice uses it selectively (triumphal arches, attic storeys) rather than as a standing register the way Corinthian or Ionic are used.

Judgment binding: roman-classical is not in this pack's applies_to, but the pack's own authority cites 'Vitruvius, De architectura Book IV ch. VI, for the Doric and Ionic doorway' directly -- a strand of genuinely Roman source material inside an otherwise Palladian pack, and the pack's own note records that Vitruvius's door ratio (2.18:1) and Palladio's (2.17:1) are checked against each other as an invariant. Governs the domus doorway and the Roman temple's single cella door; does not reach the deliberately different frontality of the podium-mounted temple facade itself.

Judgment binding, bound with real caveats. room-harmonic's own authority note credits Wittkower's demonstration that the seven room ratios recover 'the Greek theory of proportion' as transmitted through Vitruvius -- so the system's own intellectual lineage runs back through this style, even though the pack itself was written by Palladio in 1570. It covers the atrium-and-peristyle domus and the insula at best, at the scale of an ordinary room; it does not reach, and makes no claim to reach, the engineered interiors that are this style's real invention -- the Pantheon's sphere-in-a-cylinder or the great vaulted baths, which no pack in this library models.

jeffersonian-classicism.name: Jeffersonian Classicism

revival_periods.note: The City Beautiful and the American campus recover the Jeffersonian temple-and-lawn diagram wholesale; McKim, Mead & White's restoration of the Rotunda after the 1895 fire is the hinge.
'Jeffersonian' red brick with white trim and a tetrastyle portico becomes the default American institutional dress, usually with the ideological argument removed.

geography.hearth: Albemarle County, Virginia

lineage.note: The whole ideological point. Jefferson quotes the Maison Carree at Nimes for the Virginia Capitol and the Pantheon for the Rotunda, across seventeen centuries and an ocean, with no line of transmission whatever. A republic quoting a republic rather than a monarchy.

Palladio via the Leoni and Giacomo Leoni-derived English editions was Jefferson's 'bible', but he treated Palladio as a reliable transcriber of Roman antiquity rather than as a Venetian master to be imitated. The reference goes through Palladio to Rome, not to the Veneto.

The actual transmission: Virginia brickmasons, carpenters and joiners trained in the Tidewater Georgian trade built every Jeffersonian building. Monticello's Flemish bond, sash detail and interior joinery are Virginia Georgian craft executed to unfamiliar drawings.

Direct transmission, not quotation: Jefferson lived in Paris 1784-89, admired the Hotel de Salm to the point of remodelling Monticello around it, and collaborated with Charles-Louis Clerisseau, who drafted the Virginia Capitol model.
Explicitly and in writing. Jefferson called Williamsburg's buildings 'rude, mis-shapen piles' and set out to make the architecture of the new state unmistakably not English.
The Adamesque thinning that produced Federal is exactly what Jefferson refused: he wanted correct antique orders at correct antique weight, taken from measured plates, not fashionable attenuation.

description.short: Thomas Jefferson's Roman republicanism built in Virginia brick: correct antique orders taken directly from measured plates of Rome and from Palladio as their transcriber, deliberately bypassing the English intermediary that every other American builder was still working through.
description.long:
Jeffersonian Classicism is a small body of work by one amateur and his circle that changed what American public architecture was for. Formally it consists of a red brick body with white-painted wood or stuccoed trim, a portico of correct Roman orders scaled by module from published plates, a low pitched roof usually concealed behind a balustrade or a Chinese railing, and a plan built out of octagons, cubes and their halves. Its buildings look at first like well-made Georgian houses that have been rearranged by somebody with an unusual amount of geometry. Look longer and the Georgian conventions are all missing: no projecting frontispiece, no steep dormered roof, no fashionable Adam thinning of the orders, no visible service wing. Jefferson buried the dependencies in terraced L-shaped wings so that Monticello would read as a single-storey villa, which is both a compositional trick and an act of concealment about who did the work.

The conditions are unusually explicit, because the man wrote them down. The Revolution had produced a state that needed buildings and had no architectural language it could use without embarrassment: Georgian was the architecture of the Crown, and there was nothing else. Jefferson, in Paris as minister from 1784, solved the problem by going around England altogether. For the Virginia Capitol he chose the Maison Carree at Nimes, a first-century Roman temple, and had Charles-Louis Clerisseau draft the model; he substituted a Scamozzian Ionic for the original Corinthian because Virginia workmen could cut it. That decision - a modern legislature housed in a Roman temple, the first anywhere in the world - established the temple form as the American public building type and did so on an argument, not a fashion. The mechanism of transmission was books and one man's obsession: Palladio's Quattro Libri in English editions, Fréart de Chambray, Gibbs, Robert Morris, and later the measured antiquities of Desgodetz. The mechanism of execution was ordinary Virginia craft. Monticello was built and rebuilt for forty years by a rotating labour force that included enslaved brickmakers, carpenters and joiners - John Hemmings among them - working Georgian trade methods to non-Georgian drawings. Any honest account of this style has to hold both facts at once: it is the architecture of stated liberty, and it was built by people who did not have any.

What it reacts against is England, specifically and consciously. Jefferson's private verdict on Williamsburg - 'rude, mis-shapen piles' - is the founding statement of the style, and his choice of Rome over London is not aesthetic preference but constitutional argument: a republic should quote a republic. This is what separates the node from federal-style, which was busy importing Robert Adam's London fashion at the same moment and building beautifully with it. Federal is up-to-date; Jeffersonian is deliberately ancient. Federal thins the orders for elegance; Jefferson insisted on correct entasis and correct entablature depth because correctness was the point. It is also why the style barely propagates as domestic architecture: an argument does not scale into a builder's trade the way a plate of mouldings does. Its real inheritance runs through public buildings and campuses for the next century and a half.

Standing at Monticello's west front you understand the geometry before you understand the ornament. The dome sits on a low octagon and the whole house presents as one storey, which at the actual size of the building is a lie the eye accepts gratefully; the mezzanine windows are tucked under the entablature so that the second floor is invisible from outside. Inside, the rooms are octagons and half-octagons, and the light comes through triple-sash windows and skylights that make the plan feel larger and stranger than its footprint. At Poplar Forest the argument is purer still: an octagonal house around a twenty-foot cube of a dining room lit only from a skylight, so that at midday there is a column of light standing in the middle of the house. At the University of Virginia the diagram becomes urbanism - ten pavilions, each demonstrating a different correct order as a teaching specimen, joined by a colonnade and terminated by a half-scale Pantheon holding a library instead of an altar. It is the most complete piece of architectural reasoning produced in America, and it is made of the same brick as every tobacco warehouse in the county.

defining_characteristics: Orders taken from measured plates of Roman antiquity (or from Palladio as their transcriber) at correct antique proportion, never attenuated for fashion
Red brick laid in Flemish bond with white-painted wood or stuccoed trim; material palette essentially fixed
Temple-derived portico used as the governing gesture on public buildings and as a full-height entrance feature on houses
Plan geometry built from octagons, cubes, and their halves rather than from the rectangular Georgian room grid
Low roof pitch concealed behind balustrade, railing or parapet so the building reads as a single classical volume
Service and secondary storeys suppressed - dependencies terraced or sunk, mezzanines hidden behind the entablature - so the mass reads simpler than it is
Ideological intent: the classical form is chosen as a political argument about the form of government, and the choice bypasses English precedent on purpose
diagnostic_tells: A house that appears to be one storey but is demonstrably two, with small square mezzanine windows tucked directly under the cornice
Octagonal or semi-octagonal room projections in plan, visible as canted bays on the elevation
Portico entablature of correct Roman depth (roughly a fifth of column height) where a Federal house of the same date would have a thin cornice and no portico at all
Chinese-lattice roof railing or a balustrade concealing a nearly flat roof
Dependencies running out sideways at or below grade rather than as visible flanking wings above ground

distinguished_from.difference: Contemporaneous and opposite in method. Federal takes Adam's London fashion and thins the orders; Jefferson takes Rome directly and keeps them at antique weight. Federal's signature is the elliptical fanlight in a flat wall; Jefferson's is a correct portico and an octagon in plan. If the classicism looks archaeologically argued rather than fashionably light, it is Jeffersonian.

Both use full porticoes, but Jeffersonian orders are Roman (Tuscan, Doric with a base, Ionic, Corinthian, arches and domes permitted) while Greek Revival orders are Greek (baseless Doric, no arches, no domes). A dome or a round-headed arch rules out Greek Revival immediately.

The twentieth-century revival copies the temple front and the red brick but at institutional scale, with steel behind the brick, plate glass, and no interest in the geometry of the plan. Jeffersonian buildings are small, hand-built, and the octagons are real.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Classical orders with the module set as the lower column diameter, taken from published measured plates rather than from local practice; overall dimensioning by simple whole-number ratios and by the octagon, which Jefferson used as a room-generating figure rather than as a curiosity.
typical_ratios: Roman Doric 8 diameters, Ionic 9, Corinthian 10, with entablature 1/4 to 1/5 of column height
Intercolumniation 2.25-2.5 lower diameters (Palladian eustyle)
Cubic and near-cubic rooms: Poplar Forest's dining room is 20 x 20 x 20 feet
Octagonal rooms generated on a square, canted corners at 1/3 of the side
Roof pitch 3:12 or lower, concealed; parapet or railing at least 3 feet high
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even bay rhythm derived from the portico's intercolumniation and carried across the whole elevation; the portico sets the module and the walls obey it, rather than the portico being fitted to a pre-existing wall.

massing_affinities.note: But with the flanking dependencies terraced into the slope rather than raised as visible pavilions - Jefferson's characteristic inversion of the Palladian scheme.
Poplar Forest is the first octagonal house in America; the figure recurs as room shape throughout the style.
The underlying Virginia Georgian plan, geometrically disturbed.
Bremo and the pavilions at the University; the wings are colonnades rather than domestic ells.

constraints.statement: Orders must be executed at correct antique proportion: Roman Doric at 8 lower diameters, Ionic at 9, Corinthian at 10, with entablature depth 1/4 to 1/5 of column height. Attenuated columns above 10 diameters convert the building to Federal.

test.note: 1/4 to 1/5 of column height, order-independent. The order-specific diameter figures (Doric 8, Ionic 9, Corinthian 10) and the above-10-diameters-reads-as-Federal ceiling stay prose.

constraints.statement: Round-headed arches, domes and semicircular (Diocletian) windows are permitted and characteristic; the Greek baseless Doric column and the frieze-band attic window are forbidden. Roman and Greek vocabularies must not be mixed on one building.
Roof pitch must not exceed 4:12 and must be concealed behind a balustrade, Chinese railing or parapet at least 3 feet high. Dormers on a principal elevation are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the 4:12 roof-pitch ceiling. The concealment requirement (balustrade/railing/parapet at least 3ft high, testable via parapet_height_in) and the no-dormers-on-a-principal-elevation clause (testable via front_slope_dormer_count = 0) are also cleanly expressible but left as prose here since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Service dependencies must be terraced, sunk below the principal floor level, or run out as low L-wings whose roofs form usable terraces, so that the main block reads as a single volume. A visible two-storey service wing breaks the parti.

Material palette is fixed: red brick in Flemish bond with white-painted trim and, where used, stuccoed or sanded-paint columns imitating stone. Painted brick, stone facing, or contrasting trim colours fall outside the style.

exemplars.name: Virginia State Capitol
exemplars.note: Cornerstone 1785; occupied by the General Assembly 1788, finished later. Modelled on the Maison Carree at Nimes with Jefferson substituting Scamozzian Ionic for Corinthian. The first modern legislative building anywhere to take the form of a classical temple.

exemplars.name: Monticello
exemplars.note: Begun 1768, rebuilt from 1794 after Jefferson's return from France, substantially complete 1809. Octagonal dome, suppressed second storey, terraced L-shaped dependencies.

exemplars.name: Poplar Forest
exemplars.note: Begun 1806. Octagonal plan around a 20-foot cubic dining room lit by a skylight; probably the first octagonal house built in the United States.

exemplars.name: The Rotunda and Academical Village, University of Virginia
exemplars.note: Begun 1817. Ten pavilions each demonstrating a different correct order, joined by colonnades and terminated by a half-scale Pantheon housing the library rather than an altar.

sources: William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: The Colonial and Neoclassical Styles (1970)
Fiske Kimball, Thomas Jefferson, Architect (1916)
Andrea Palladio, I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura (1570), in the English editions Jefferson owned
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
Richard Guy Wilson, Thomas Jefferson's Academical Village (2009)

proportion_packs.note: PALLADIO OVER GIBBS OR BENJAMIN, AND THIS IS THE LOAD-BEARING CHOICE FOR THE WHOLE NODE. The style's own lineage explicitly makes Palladio -- via the English editions Jefferson called his 'bible' -- his source, and just as explicitly separates that from the Tidewater Georgian craft channel his masons and joiners actually came out of ('descends_from tidewater-georgian... Virginia brickmasons... trained in the Tidewater Georgian trade built every Jeffersonian building'). Both gibbs-ionic and benjamin-ionic are architecturally present in this corpus and gibbs-ionic is even listed in this node's own applies_to cross-reference, but binding either here would blur exactly the distinction the style file draws against english-georgian ('rude, mis-shapen piles') -- Jefferson's DESIGN authority is Palladio-as-transcriber-of-Rome, not the pattern-book tradition his craftsmen executed to. The fit is also numerically exact: this pack's column is 9 Palladian modules, i.e. 9 diameters, matching the style's own stated 'Ionic 9' precisely -- and it is the order of the Virginia Capitol, where Jefferson substituted a Scamozzian Ionic for the Maison Carree's original Corinthian because Virginia workmen could cut it.

The style's own stated 'Roman Doric 8 diameters' matches this pack's column exactly (16 semidiameter-modules = 8 diameters, identical to vignola-doric's figure since Palladio's Doric differs from Vignola's only in entasis and fluting, not in overall height). Demonstrated at the University of Virginia's Academical Village, where Doric is one of the ten orders the pavilions use as teaching specimens.

A THIRD ORDER IS BOUND HERE, UNLIKE ANY OTHER NODE IN THIS BATCH, because Jefferson's own practice genuinely deployed three correct Roman orders side by side as a stated pedagogical program at the University of Virginia, and because Corinthian was the Capitol's ORIGINAL order before Jefferson's Ionic substitution. Flagged honestly: the style states 'Corinthian 10' diameters but this pack's Palladian Corinthian column is 9.5 -- a half-diameter short of an exact match, the closest the corpus's 36 packs get, and left as a visible discrepancy rather than rounded away.

JUDGMENT CALL, STATED AS SUCH. None of the pack's three named families (wall_section_georgian / _federal / _greek_revival) is a clean fit for interiors built to correct antique weight rather than to any of those three American traditions. wall_section_georgian is bound as the closer analogue -- full relief, carved, NOT the flattened Federal composition-ornament family Jefferson explicitly rejected ('Federal thins the orders for elegance; Jefferson insisted on correct entasis and correct entablature depth because correctness was the point') -- but this is an approximation the pack was not built for, not a documented fit.

Governs door and window sizing generally, beneath constraint c02's hard co-occurrence rule: round-headed arches, domes and semicircular Diocletian windows are permitted and characteristic, while the Greek baseless Doric and frieze-band attic window are forbidden outright -- Roman and Greek vocabularies must never mix on one building. No pack among the 36 encodes Diocletian/lunette window geometry specifically; that stays prose in the style file, a genuine gap.

The glazing module, bound but genuinely minor here -- the style file names no sash pattern or muntin width at all among its diagnostic tells, unlike federal-style or new-england-federal, because triple-sash windows and skylights (Monticello, Poplar Forest) carry more of Jefferson's fenestration argument than muntin count does.

Governs the temple-front portico and the bay rhythm its intercolumniation sets for the wall behind (2.25-2.5 diameters, Palladian eustyle, per the style's own proportional_system) -- and this is arguably the single most apt use of this pack in the whole batch, since georgian-colonial-american's own binding of it cites 'Palladio Book I chs. XXI-XXVI' as its authority, and here that authority is not once-removed through Gibbs but the building's actual named source.

Governs the literal floor-to-floor ratios but does not model Jefferson's real trick -- the suppressed second storey, mezzanine windows tucked directly under the entablature so a demonstrably two-storey house 'reads as one storey' from outside (the style's own leading diagnostic tell). That is visual concealment, not proportional diminution, and no pack among the 36 addresses it; a genuine gap distinct from the ordinary storey-height coverage this pack does provide.

Bound for the cubic and near-cubic rooms the style states directly -- Poplar Forest's dining room is 20 x 20 x 20 ft -- which is exactly this pack's harmonic-ratio domain. It does NOT model the octagon-on-a-square construction that is Jefferson's own specific and most distinctive room-generating figure (Poplar Forest's plan, the Rotunda's flanking rooms); no pack among the 36 encodes octagonal room geometry by name, so the general harmonic-ratio machinery is the closest available fit and the octagon itself stays prose. A genuine, acknowledged gap.

The material palette is fixed rather than optional at the level of the building (constraint c05: red brick in Flemish bond with white-painted or stuccoed trim; painted brick, stone facing or contrasting trim colours fall outside the style), but the pack itself is bound at the same optional role the rest of this batch uses for masonry modules, consistent with the corpus's own applies_to cross-reference for this node.

beaux-arts-french.name: Beaux-Arts (French)

revival_periods.note: Not a revival so much as a transplant: Richard Morris Hunt entered the Ecole in 1846 and roughly 500 Americans followed before 1914, taking the method home wholesale.
The contemporary classical movement re-adopts Beaux-Arts composition and the poche-and-parti method explicitly, and several schools now teach the analytique again.

geography.hearth: The Ecole des Beaux-Arts, rue Bonaparte, Paris

lineage.note: Institutionally continuous: the Ecole is the reorganised successor to the Academie royale's teaching, the Prix de Rome runs unbroken, and Durand's and Blondel's compositional method is what the atelier system transmits.

The Grand Manner is deliberately reclaimed after 1850 - coupled columns, sculptural relief, the pavilion silhouette and the mansard all come back from Louis XIV, not from the Neoclassical generation that had suppressed them.
The scenographic plan, the ceremonial stair and the axial urban set-piece are quoted from Rome; Garnier's grand escalier is a Baroque theatre stage where the audience is the performance.
The palazzo elevation - graded rustication, superimposed orders, heavy crowning cornice - remains the default clothing for commercial and institutional blocks.

description.short: Composition taught as a transmissible method - parti, marche and poche - producing large, richly sculptural, axially planned public buildings whose elevations are direct projections of their plans.
description.long:
The Beaux-Arts is less a set of forms than a way of getting from a programme to a building, and it is the only such method the classical tradition ever fully institutionalised. A student in the atelier system received a programme, was locked in a cubicle for twelve hours to produce an esquisse - the parti, the fundamental diagram - and then spent weeks developing it without being allowed to change the diagram. The plan came first, always, laid out on a dominant axis with cross-axes, with major and minor spaces ranked by size and ceiling height, and with circulation - the marche, the sequence of movement - designed as an experience rather than as leftover corridor. The wall was drawn as poche, a thickened black mass carved out for stairs, closets, flues and lightwells, which is why Beaux-Arts buildings absorb their servicing invisibly. The elevation was then a projection of that hierarchy, and only at the end was the order chosen, according to caractere - the doctrine that a bank, an opera house and a hospital should each look like what they are.

The conditions are industrial and metropolitan. Nineteenth-century Paris needed building types that had never existed at that scale: railway termini, department stores, opera houses, exhibition halls, ministries, apartment blocks of six to eight storeys. It also acquired, under Haussmann from 1853, a state powerful enough to cut boulevards through a medieval city and impose a uniform cornice line on both sides. Behind the stone, everything had changed: rolled iron, then steel, then reinforced concrete, plus lifts, central heating and electric light. The Beaux-Arts settlement was to accept the new structure completely and to let the masonry envelope do a different job - to give a building scale, hierarchy, entrance and civic address. The Grand Palais of 1897-1900 is entirely explicit about this: a Classical stone shell wrapped around a 240-metre iron-and-glass barrel vault, with no attempt at reconciliation and no dishonesty either.

What it reacted against, quietly, was the thinness of its own Neoclassical parent. By 1850 the austere balustraded cube looked bloodless and, worse, insufficiently expressive for a Second Empire that wanted visible magnificence. So sculpture came back onto the wall - not scattered, but concentrated at the entrance, the centre and the skyline - and the mansard came back as an occupiable attic that also restored a silhouette. The result is often criticised as pastiche, and sometimes it is; but the compositional discipline underneath is real and independent of the dress, which is why the same method produced buildings as different as Garnier's Opera and Labrouste's iron-vaulted Bibliotheque Sainte-Genevieve.

What it feels like is arrival, staged. You come at the Palais Garnier along an axis cut for the purpose; the building presents a base you climb, an arcaded loggia, a giant order, and a skyline of gilt figures against the sky. Inside, the auditorium is smaller than you expect, because two-thirds of the building is circulation: a stair hall thirty metres high in coloured marbles with balconies at every level, arranged so that everyone ascending is on display to everyone already up. The plan does exactly what it was drawn to do. This is architecture designed around the truth that in a public building, the most important room is usually the one you pass through.

defining_characteristics: A plan generated first, on a dominant axis with cross-axes, with spaces ranked by size, height and position in the sequence
Poche: the wall drawn and built as a thickened inhabited mass absorbing stairs, services, closets and lightwells
The elevation as a direct projection of the plan's hierarchy - every important room reads on the outside
Three-part vertical composition: rusticated base, principal shaft of one or two storeys under a giant or coupled order, and a crowning attic or mansard
Sculpture concentrated at entrance, centrepiece and skyline rather than distributed over the wall
Caractere: the order and the degree of enrichment chosen to express the building's function and civic standing
Modern structure (iron, steel, reinforced concrete) accepted internally and clothed in a masonry envelope that supplies scale and address
diagnostic_tells: Coupled columns, usually of a giant order, marking a projecting central pavilion on a symmetrical front
A skyline populated with sculpture, quadrigae, cartouches and gilt attic figures above the main cornice
Deeply rusticated ground storey with heavy vermiculated or channelled blocks and segmental-arched openings
A grand exterior or interior stair treated as the principal architectural event, larger than any single room it serves
Enormous scale of the individual member - a keystone the size of a person, garlands two metres across - calibrated to the width of a boulevard rather than a street

distinguished_from.difference: Neoclassicism is subtractive, plane-dominant and unaccented, with the roof hidden and ornament rationed. Beaux-Arts is additive, sculptural and strongly centred, with a visible mansard or attic and enrichment concentrated at the accents.

The American branch works largely in limestone and terracotta on steel frames at greater height, favours the Roman Ionic and Corinthian over French Composite, and typically omits the mansard on commercial buildings. Its plans are Ecole plans; its budgets and its storey counts are not.

Second Empire as usually named is a silhouette style - mansard roof plus pavilions - applied to houses and small civic buildings. Beaux-Arts is a compositional method applied to large programmes; a house with a mansard is Second Empire, an opera house planned about a stair is Beaux-Arts.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Composition by method: parti (the plan diagram), marche (the designed sequence of movement), poche (the thickened, inhabited wall), and caractere (expressive appropriateness of the order). Proportion is hierarchical rather than modular - a room's ceiling height, its position on the axis and its degree of enrichment all encode its rank in the programme.
typical_ratios: Three-part vertical division base : shaft : attic approximately 1 : 2 : 0.5
Rusticated base one to two storeys, 0.25 to 0.35 of total wall height, with joints 25 to 50 mm
Giant order spanning two storeys; coupled columns set 0.5 to 1.0 diameters apart, pairs at 4 to 5 diameters on centre
Entablature 1/4 to 1/5 of column height; crowning cornice projection 1/14 to 1/18 of total facade height
Attic or mansard storey 0.5 to 0.7 of the principal storey height
Principal rooms in the plan set at whole-number multiples of the structural bay, with ceiling heights ranked 1 : 0.75 : 0.6 from major to minor
Grand stair: riser 140-155 mm, tread 340-400 mm, landing every 9 to 11 risers, clear width 1/3 to 1/2 the width of the hall containing it
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Strongly hierarchical and closed at both ends: a dominant centre pavilion, subordinate end pavilions, and a plain connecting rhythm between - commonly 3-2-5-2-3 across a fifteen-bay front. Corners are always resolved with a pavilion, a quoined pier or a change of plane; a Beaux-Arts elevation never simply stops.

massing_affinities.note: The Haussmannian immeuble: six to eight storeys, a uniform cornice line imposed across the whole boulevard, and the block rather than the building as the compositional subject.
The mansard returns as a fully occupiable attic and as the device that gives an otherwise flat-topped block a silhouette.
Institutional and palatial programmes retain the cour d'honneur; the Ecole itself is planned this way.
The free-standing hotel particulier and the exported American mansion reduce to a double-pile block about a central hall and stair.
Irregularity is the antithesis of the parti. Any Beaux-Arts building that appears irregular is resolving a difficult site with a symmetrical figure hidden inside it.

constraints.statement: Every elevation must resolve into base, shaft and attic with distinct horizontal terminations. An undifferentiated wall of repeated identical storeys is not Beaux-Arts, whatever ornament is applied to it.

Sculpture and enrichment must be concentrated at compositional accents - entrance, centrepiece, corners, skyline - and the connecting bays must be comparatively plain. Even distribution of ornament destroys the hierarchy that carries the composition.

Wall thickness must be sufficient to accommodate poche: minimum 600 mm at the principal storeys where stairs, flues or closets are absorbed, and reveals of at least 200 mm at every window so that openings read as cut into mass.

test.note: Tests the minimum wall thickness for poche. The window reveal minimum (200 mm, expressible via reveal_depth_in) is a second independent numeric clause and is left as prose.

constraints.statement: Ornament scale must be calibrated to viewing distance: members read from across a boulevard (25-40 m) should be at least 1/40 of the facade height in their principal dimension. Domestic-scale enrichment on a civic facade reads as thin.

Caractere: the order and level of enrichment must match the programme. Corinthian and Composite with full sculpture for theatres, exhibition and ceremonial buildings; Doric or Tuscan with restrained enrichment for markets, barracks, warehouses and utilitarian programmes.

exemplars.name: Palais Garnier (Opera de Paris)
exemplars.note: Charles Garnier, competition won 1861, built 1861-1875, inaugurated 5 January 1875. The canonical demonstration of marche: the grand escalier and its foyers occupy more of the building than the auditorium.

exemplars.name: Grand Palais
exemplars.note: Henri Deglane, Albert Louvet, Albert Thomas and Charles Girault, 1897-1900, for the Exposition Universelle. A Classical stone envelope wrapped around a 240 m iron, steel and glass barrel vault.

exemplars.name: Petit Palais
exemplars.note: Charles Girault, 1897-1900. A trapezoidal site resolved into a symmetrical parti about a semicircular garden court - the method solving a hard site in the open.

exemplars.name: Gare d'Orsay (now Musee d'Orsay)
exemplars.note: Victor Laloux, 1898-1900. An academic stone hotel-and-station front concealing a 32 m clear-span iron train shed; the clearest single statement of the Beaux-Arts settlement with industrial structure.

sources: Julien Guadet, Elements et theorie de l'architecture (1901-1904)
Arthur Drexler (ed.), The Architecture of the Ecole des Beaux-Arts (1977)
David Van Zanten, Designing Paris: The Architecture of Duban, Labrouste, Duc, and Vaudoyer (1987)
Robin Middleton and David Watkin, Neoclassical and 19th Century Architecture (1980)
Jean-Nicolas-Louis Durand, Precis des lecons d'architecture (1802-1805)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The style's caractere doctrine (c05) names Composite directly for 'theatres, exhibition and ceremonial buildings' with full sculpture -- the giant-order register for the Palais Garnier, Grand Palais and Petit Palais register of this style.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. c05 names Corinthian alongside Composite for the same high-caractere programmes; the more restrained of the two richest orders, and the one this style shares directly with beaux-arts-american's own binding.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs bay division and solid-to-void, though this style pushes every one of the pack's own defaults to its permissive edge: c01's hard requirement that base, shaft and attic resolve with distinct terminations goes well beyond what facade-classical assumes for a domestic front, and the order packs and this style's own constraints carry what the system pack understates.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the void before the surround; a Beaux-Arts opening is often a full aedicule or arched Roman opening rather than the pack's default plain rectangle, so treat its derived ratios as the starting rectangle the surround is built onto.
Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the individual room within the Ecole's axial hierarchy of parti and marche, which is itself outside anything a room-proportion pack models.

Judgment binding: beaux-arts-french is not in storey-graduation's own applies_to (beaux-arts-american is, and carries the identical binding). Bound because this style's own proportional_system states the vertical division directly -- base:shaft:attic approximately 1:2:0.5 -- which is the same diminishing-upward logic the pack encodes, only steeper than its domestic default.

Judgment binding: beaux-arts-french is not in trim-classical's own applies_to (beaux-arts-american is). Bound for the same reason the American branch is: the pedestal:field:entablature wall division is the correct proportional grammar even though real Beaux-Arts interiors ran marble, bronze and run-in-place plaster rather than the pack's default painted joinery -- bind the discipline and expect it executed richer than the pack assumes.

charleston-single-house.name: Charleston Single House

revival_periods.note: Charleston's 1931 zoning ordinance - the first historic district in the United States - froze the type and then licensed a continuous stream of new single houses, so the form has never actually stopped being built on the peninsula.

geography.hearth: Charleston, South Carolina

lineage.note: Reclassified 2026-08-18 from a Federal variant to a folk-vernacular type. It originates c.1720, sixty years before Federal, and is still being built in the 1880s, forty years after Federal ends. It wears Georgian, Federal and Greek Revival dress in turn without changing its plan, section or orientation, which is the signature of a type rather than a style expression. Federal is now one of the several dresses it wore, not its parent.

Unbroken. The type is fully formed in Charleston by the 1730s-50s under Georgian trim; the Federal generation inherited the plan intact and changed only the mouldings, the sash and the column profiles.
Arriving through imported London joinery, printed plates, and Charleston's exceptionally direct trade with Britain.

description.short: A house one room wide turned end-on to the street, with a multi-storey piazza down its south or west flank behind a false street door - the most thoroughly climate-determined dwelling type in Anglo-America, wearing Federal trim over a plan that is essentially a machine for moving air.
description.long:
The Charleston single house is what happens when a narrow deep urban lot meets a subtropical climate and an English building culture that has no ready answer for either. Its solution is to rotate the house ninety degrees. The narrow gable end - two or three bays, typically twenty-two to twenty-six feet wide - addresses the street; the long five-bay flank runs back into the lot; and along that flank, on the south or west side, runs a piazza of two or three storeys, ten or twelve feet deep, open to the prevailing breeze and shading the wall behind it for the entire afternoon. Inside, the plan is one room on either side of a stair passage, one room deep, so that every habitable room has windows on two opposite walls. The famous move is the door: what looks from the sidewalk like the front door of the house is a false door, a gate in a screen wall, and it opens not into the house but onto the piazza. The real entrance is halfway along the piazza, at right angles to the street, and you are outdoors and in shade for the twenty feet between the two. Charleston invented a threshold sequence that is genuinely without parallel in American building.

Every dimension of the type is doing thermal work. The single-pile section guarantees cross ventilation. Ceiling heights of eleven to thirteen feet on the principal floor put the hot air above the occupants and let the tall sash exhaust it. The piazza takes the sun off the long wall so that the windows behind it can stay open in the rain, which in a climate with sixty inches of annual rainfall and afternoon thunderstorms all summer is not a small matter. The blind wall on the opposite flank - built to or near the lot line, often with almost no openings - is a fire wall and a privacy wall at once, a lesson learned expensively in the fires of 1740 and 1778.
