The kitchen sits in a detached building at the back of the lot to keep its heat and its fire risk out of the house, with quarters for enslaved domestic workers above it, and it is worth being exact about that: the walled garden, the detached dependency and the gated piazza are a system for regulating who can see whom, and the type's celebrated privacy was privacy from the street for some people and enclosure for others.

The economic conditions were rice, indigo and, from the 1790s, sea-island cotton, plus a mercantile port that was for a time the richest city in British North America. The urban condition was a peninsula between two rivers with no room to grow sideways, which produced deep narrow lots, sometimes taxed on frontage, and made the rotated house an economic necessity as well as a climatic one. When the Federal fashion arrived after the Revolution, Charleston's builders did not change the diagram at all; they replaced Georgian bolection mouldings with Adamesque reeding, cut elliptical fanlights into the piazza screen and the real front door, swapped heavy Doric piazza columns for slender Tuscan or Ionic ones, and thinned the sash. The Nathaniel Russell House, which is a double house rather than a single, shows what the same builders could do when the lot allowed; the single houses along Church, Tradd, Legare and Meeting show what they did the other ninety percent of the time.

Standing on Tradd Street the effect is of a wall of houses that are all facing away from you. You see gable ends, chimney stacks, and a rhythm of garden gates, and the street is defined by buildings that give it almost nothing - the reverse of a New England or Philadelphia street where every house presents its best face. Then you open a gate and the whole logic reverses: you are in a shaded outdoor room the length of a house, floored in heart pine, ceiled in beadboard, with a garden on your right and eleven-foot windows on your left standing open. The air moves. In August, in a city that is functionally tropical for four months, this is not a pleasant amenity but the entire reason the building exists, and it works so well that the type survived air conditioning and is still being built.

defining_characteristics: One room wide, turned so the narrow gable end faces the street; two or three bays to the street, five to the flank
One room deep on either side of a side stair passage - single-pile, so every room is cross-ventilated and lit from two sides
Multi-storey piazza running the full length of the south or west flank, open to the prevailing breeze
False street door opening onto the piazza rather than into the house; the true entrance is set back along the piazza
Opposite flank built at or near the lot line as a near-blind fire and privacy wall
Tall principal-floor ceilings with sash carried close to the ceiling line to exhaust hot air
Detached kitchen house and dependency at the rear of the lot, historically with quarters above
diagnostic_tells: A door in a garden wall or screen that sits in the street facade but opens sideways onto a porch - unmistakable and unique to the type
The street elevation is a gable end two or three bays wide, with the long piazza visible in perspective down the lot
Piazza consistently on the south or west flank across a whole street, regardless of which side of the street the house is on
Near-windowless flank wall on the north or east side, tight to the property line
Chimneys on the rear wall or the blind flank rather than symmetrically paired on the street gable

distinguished_from.difference: Same plan, same piazza, same false door. The Georgian version has heavier piazza columns (Doric or Tuscan at 7-8 diameters), muntins over an inch, projecting door frontispieces and steeper roofs; the Federal version thins the columns, cuts an elliptical fanlight, and drops the roof pitch.

A single house is single-pile - one room deep - which is the whole point. A double-pile side-hall townhouse of similar street width has four rooms per floor and no cross ventilation to the interior rooms; it belongs to a colder climate.

Both are Gulf and Lowcountry climate types with galleries and no interior corridors in the Creole case. The Creole cottage faces the street broadside with four openings and no hall; the single house turns its narrow end to the street and keeps an Anglo stair passage. The distinction is Anglo versus French-Caribbean plan descent.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Dimensioned by airflow and by the lot. Room depth is set by the distance daylight and cross-ventilation will carry, house width by the standard Charleston lot, and ceiling height by stack effect - the classical trim is applied afterward and changes none of it.
typical_ratios: Street facade width 22-26 feet (rarely over 28); house depth 45-60 feet, occasionally more
Room dimension 16-20 feet square; stair passage 8-12 feet wide
Piazza depth 8-12 feet (10 typical), running the full flank length
Ceiling heights: ground 10-11 feet, principal floor 12-13 feet, upper floor 10-11 feet
Window opening 1:2.4 to 1:2.8 width to height, head within 12-18 inches of ceiling
Piazza column spacing 8-10 feet, columns 8-10 diameters tall in Federal-era work
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three bays to the street with the entrance bay off-centre or absent entirely (the false door sits in the piazza screen); five even bays along the piazza flank, the true entrance occupying the second bay from the street.

massing_affinities.note: The type and the massing are the same object; this node supplies the style dress.
Deeper lots and later dates occasionally produce a double-pile version, at the direct cost of the cross-ventilation the type exists for.
Single houses stand free with a gap for the piazza; a party-walled row of them is a contradiction, though the street reads almost as continuously.
Where the piazza wraps the rear as well as the flank, the type approaches the Caribbean gallery house it is often compared to.

constraints.statement: The piazza must be on the south or west flank, minimum 8 feet deep (10-12 preferred), running the full length of the house. A piazza on the north or east flank, or shallower than 8 feet, fails as both shade device and outdoor room and voids the type.

test.note: Tests piazza orientation as 'within 45 degrees of southwest' (south-through-west, 180-270 degrees) per the statement's 'south or west flank' -- the canonical use case constraint_vocabulary.py's own note names for piazza_bearing_deg. The minimum piazza depth (8ft, 10-12 preferred) is also cleanly testable via gallery_depth_ft but is left as prose here since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Street frontage must not exceed 28 feet and the plan must remain single-pile: one room on each side of the stair passage, room depth 16-20 feet, with operable windows on two opposite walls of every principal room.

test.note: Tests street frontage width (28ft maximum) via facade_width_ft -- the narrow gable end that addresses the street. Room depth (16-20ft) and the cross-ventilation clause are left as prose since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: The street door must be a false door opening onto the piazza, with the true entrance set at least one bay back along the piazza. Deleting the false door and entering the house directly from the sidewalk destroys the type's threshold sequence and its privacy logic.

Principal-floor ceiling height minimum 11 feet (12-13 typical) with window heads within 18 inches of the ceiling, and sash operable top and bottom. Ceilings under 10 feet break the stack ventilation the section depends on.

test.note: Tests the 11ft minimum principal-floor ceiling height. Window-head-to-ceiling offset (18in maximum) and the top-and-bottom operable sash requirement are left as prose.

constraints.statement: The flank opposite the piazza sits at or within 3 feet of the property line and carries no more than token openings - it is a fire wall, a response to the Charleston fires of 1740 and 1778, and modern separation-distance rules reach the same answer.

test.note: Tests the property-line clearance on the flank opposite the piazza. The 'no more than token openings' clause is left as prose.

exemplars.name: Robert Pringle House
exemplars.note: Circa 1774; a canonical pre-Revolutionary single house whose Federal-era neighbours copy its section exactly.

exemplars.name: Timothy Ford House
exemplars.note: Built circa 1800-1806; the type at full Federal maturity, three storeys with a two-tier piazza.

exemplars.name: Charles Elliott House
exemplars.note: Circa 1759; among the earliest documented single houses, showing the plan fully resolved a generation before Federal trim arrives.

exemplars.name: Charles Graves House
exemplars.note: Late eighteenth century; normal single-house plan with a three-storey central stair hall, one room each side, and a two-storey west piazza on Tuscan columns.

sources: Bernard L. Herman, Town House: Architecture and Material Life in the Early American City, 1780-1830 (2005)
Gene Waddell, Charleston Architecture 1670-1860 (2003)
Kenneth Severens, Charleston: Antebellum Architecture and Civic Destiny (1988)
Jonathan Poston, The Buildings of Charleston: A Guide to the City's Architecture (1997)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)

proportion_packs.note: Governs the one thing every dress the type wears agrees on: tall principal-floor windows with heads carried close to the ceiling to exhaust hot air, and doors sized from the storey rather than from a stock schedule. The node's own hard constraint (c04, 11 ft minimum ceiling with heads within 18 in of it) is this pack's window_head_wood rule (head at ceiling height x 16/19) applied to an unusually tall Lowcountry storey. Bound because the type is genuinely classically detailed at the piazza and the entrance, not merely vernacular wearing borrowed trim: Charleston's direct trade with Britain put real pattern-book proportion into this plan from the 1730s on, which is exactly why the node was reclassified from a Federal variant to a folk-vernacular type rather than dropped from the classical family altogether.

Cited by the pack itself as a worked example: its piano-nobile rule ('ground storey under a piano nobile... English Georgian townhouses, Charleston single houses, raised Creole and raised cottage types') names this massing directly, and its climate conflict entry states outright that 'Charleston Georgian and New England Georgian have the same trim and sections a foot and a half apart' -- the reason to set ceiling height from climate before style. Governs the ground-floor service storey under the piazza where present and the diminishing floor-to-floor heights (13/11/10-11 ft per the node's own typical_ratios) that make the piazza-side elevation read as three storeys graduating rather than three storeys stacked.

The single house wears three different sash across its 170-year building span -- 12/12-to-9/6 Georgian giving way to thin Federal muntins with elliptical fanlights, then Greek Revival 6/6 -- and this pack is what derives the light pattern from the date rather than from taste, exactly as its own notes describe the sequence running everywhere in the Anglo-American world within a couple of decades of the glass technology, independent of style. Bound secondary to opening-proportion because the rectangle (proportion, head datum) is fixed by the type's climate logic first, and the light count is a period-dress question second.

Bound narrowly, for the piazza flank only, where the node's own typical_ratios describe a genuinely classical bay discipline -- five even bays, columns at 8-10 ft centres, the true entrance occupying the second bay -- that this pack's odd-bay and pier-width arithmetic was built to check. NOT bound for the street gable, which is two or three bays with an off-centre or absent entrance and a false door onto the piazza: that composition is climate- and privacy-driven, not classical, and forcing facade-classical's centred-entrance logic onto it would misdescribe the type's most distinctive move.

The piazza order, held at the base pack rather than committed to a specific historical overlay, because the node's own description gives the type three different period dresses for the same columns -- 'heavier piazza columns (Doric or Tuscan at 7-8 diameters)' under Georgian trim, thinning to 'slender Tuscan or Ionic' under Federal -- and Tuscan is the one constant across both. Binding a Gibbs or Palladio overlay here would assert a specific pattern-book commitment the type's own century and a half of continuous building does not support; the base Vignola proportion is the honest choice until a specific building's date and dress are known. Bound secondary and low precedence: the piazza's climate function (see opening-proportion, storey-graduation) generates the type, and the order dresses it rather than governing it.

moorish-andalusian.name: Moorish Andalusian

revival_periods.note: Neo-Mudejar in Spain and Moorish Revival across Europe and America — bullrings, synagogues, railway stations, casinos and pavilions. A costume revival with no craft continuity.
Arrives in American practice at two removes, via Mexico and via Andalusian folk architecture: the patio with a fountain, the azulejo dado, the horseshoe and cusped arch, the mirador.
The Mediterranean Revival's tile, arcade and inward court are Andalusian at their root.

geography.hearth: Cordoba, Seville and Granada

lineage.note: Umayyad Cordoba is built literally out of Rome: the Great Mosque's arcades stand on reused Roman and Visigothic columns and capitals, its two-tier arch is a solution to the fact that those shafts were too short, and the horseshoe arch itself is Visigothic in Iberia before it is Islamic. The Roman peristyle house is the direct ancestor of the Andalusian patio.

description.short: The architecture of eight centuries of Islamic Iberia: an inward-turned world of courtyards, water, arcades and stratified geometric surface built behind walls that give the street nothing.
description.long:
Moorish Andalusian architecture is the one major European tradition organised around a void rather than a mass. A Roman temple, a Gothic cathedral and a Georgian house are all objects to be seen; an Andalusian palace or house is a sequence of enclosed outdoor rooms with buildings around their edges, and the thing being designed is the court, the water in it, and the way light moves across it during the day. This reverses almost every habit an Anglo-European designer has. There is no facade in the ordinary sense: the exterior wall is high, blind, and made of rammed earth (tapia) or brick, and the entrance is a single door, often set off-axis and reached through a bent passage so that no one on the street can see in. Everything the building has to offer begins on the far side of that door.

The climate produced the diagram and the diagram is extremely good. Cordoba reaches forty-five degrees in July; the courtyard, deep in relation to its width, is in shade for most of the summer day, and the ranges around it are one room deep so that every room draws air across from the shaded court to the cooler back. Water is not decoration: a still sheet in a long basin cools by evaporation and doubles the perceived size of the court by reflection, and a moving thread in a channel does the same audibly. The Court of the Myrtles at the Alhambra is a slab of water thirty-four metres long with a hall at each end looking down its length — an air-conditioning device that also happens to be one of the most beautiful spaces in Europe. Wall thickness of six hundred to nine hundred millimetres in earth or brick gives a twelve-hour thermal lag, so the fabric is coolest in the afternoon.

The ornament follows a rule that is nearly always missed: it is stratified by height and by material, and the strata never blur. From the floor to about head height the wall is tile — alicatado, cut glazed mosaic in the Nasrid period, later flat azulejo — because that is the zone that gets touched, splashed and scrubbed, and because tile is cool. Above it, to the ceiling, is carved and moulded plaster, yeseria, worked wet and painted, which can be extraordinarily fine because it does not need to be durable at that height. Above that is wood: coffered and strapworked timber ceilings, artesonado, in cedar and pine. Three materials, three heights, three degrees of durability, three completely different kinds of pattern, and a horizontal band — usually an epigraphic frieze in Kufic or cursive Arabic — marking each transition. Once you see it, you cannot look at an Andalusian interior any other way.

What it is like to stand inside is difficult to overstate and easy to misdescribe as merely lush. It is dark, and cool, and the darkness is the point: the eye adjusts, and then the very fine plaster and the tile and the epigraphy resolve out of the gloom, and beyond the arcade the court is a rectangle of unbearable white light with water in it. Sound is water and birds. The geometry is never resolvable — the lacería interlace is generated from a repeating star polygon and continues past every frame, so the wall reads as a cut-out from an infinite pattern rather than a bounded composition, which is a theological position as much as a decorative one. And the whole thing is made of clay, plaster and cheap wood. There is almost no stone in the Alhambra. It is a poor building made unimaginably rich by labour.

defining_characteristics: Inward organisation around one or more courts; the exterior street wall is high, near-blind, and undesigned
A single controlled entry, often through a bent or dog-leg passage so the court is never visible from the street
Water as a required architectural element on the principal axis — still basin, channel, or fountain
Massive walls of tapia (rammed earth) or brick, 600-900 mm, giving a long thermal lag
Single-pile ranges around the court, cross-ventilated, reached from the court rather than from internal corridors
Ornament stratified by height and material: tile dado, carved plaster above, timber ceiling on top, with an epigraphic band at each transition
The horseshoe and later the cusped and muqarnas arch, springing on slender columns and carried in arcades rather than as isolated openings
Geometric interlace (laceria) generated from a repeating star polygon and cut by its frame rather than composed within it
diagnostic_tells: An arch whose curve continues below its springing line by a quarter to a third of the radius — the true horseshoe
A rectangular moulded frame (alfiz) enclosing an arch, so the arch never floats free on a wall
A hard horizontal line at 1.5-2.0 m where tile stops and carved plaster begins, on every wall in the room
Muqarnas — stalactite vaulting in plaster — filling the transition from a square room to a dome
Arcade columns of extreme slenderness (shaft height 8-12 diameters) carrying brick or plaster arches, not stone entablatures

distinguished_from.difference: Mudejar is this same craft continuing under Christian patronage after the reconquest of a given city. The buildings can be technically indistinguishable; the difference is who paid and what the building was for. A church tower built by Muslim masons in Teruel in 1315 is Mudejar; the Alhambra is not.

The vernacular casa-patio is the domestic residue of this tradition, continuously inhabited and rebuilt for five centuries after 1492. It keeps the court, the water, the whitewash and the blind street wall, and loses the epigraphy, the muqarnas and the stratified surface programme.
The 20th-century revival takes the arcade, the tile and the fountain and applies them to buildings that are outward-facing, double-pile and corridor-planned. It reverses the one thing that mattered.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Geometric generation from a square. Plan and surface alike are set out by rotating a square to produce root-2 and root-3 rectangles, and by subdividing an eight- or sixteen-pointed star into a repeating cell. There is no order and no absolute module: the setting-out is a compass-and-straightedge procedure, which is why a Nasrid pattern can be executed at any scale from a tile to a courtyard without any change in method.
typical_ratios: Court length to width roughly 1:1.5 to 1:2, with the principal hall at a short end on the long axis
Court width 0.6-1.0 times the height of the enclosing ranges at 37 degrees north
Column shaft slenderness 8-12 diameters
Horseshoe arch: curve continued 0.25-0.33 of the radius below the springing
Tile dado 1.5-2.0 m high
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Arcades of odd bay counts with a wider central bay marking the entry axis; on the short ends of a court, a portico of three or five bays with the centre emphasised by a taller arch or a projecting mirador.

massing_affinities.note: The court enclosed on all four sides, with a blind exterior — the fundamental diagram of the whole tradition.
Three ranges with the fourth side held by a wall, a portico or a garden edge; usual at smaller scale and on sloping sites.
The portico along the long sides of a court performs the gallery's function of shade, circulation and social space, though it faces inward rather than out.
The dense medina fabric of Cordoba, Seville and Granada is party-walled courtyard houses in continuous blocks.

constraints.statement: At 36-38 degrees north, court width must be between 0.6 and 1.0 times the height of the enclosing ranges. Wider and the court floor bakes through the afternoon; narrower and it becomes a lightwell that admits no winter sun.

test.note: Reuses facade_height_ft as a stand-in for 'height of the enclosing ranges' -- the height of the walls that face onto the court is the same wall height the elevation record already states for this building, flagged here as a reuse rather than a purpose-built variable.

constraints.statement: External walls of tapia or brick, 600-900 mm minimum. Openings in the outer street wall not to exceed 5 percent of its area and to be set high, above head height from the street.

test.note: Tests the street-wall opening-area ceiling. Wall thickness (600-900 mm minimum, maps to wall_thickness_in) and the opening-height requirement ('set high, above head height') are further facts in the same sentence, left as prose for the single-test limit.

constraints.statement: Surface ornament must be stratified: tile below roughly 2 m, carved plaster above, timber ceiling, with a horizontal band at each transition. A single material or pattern running floor to ceiling is prohibited.
The horseshoe arch must continue its curve below the springing line by a quarter to a third of its radius. Less than that and it is a round arch with a stylistic pretension.
Water is required on the principal axis of any court of consequence, still or moving. A dry court is a yard.

exemplars.name: Great Mosque of Cordoba
exemplars.note: Begun 785 under Abd al-Rahman I on reused Roman and Visigothic material; extended 833-988. The two-tier horseshoe arcade is the founding move of the tradition.

exemplars.name: Madinat al-Zahra
exemplars.note: Caliphal palace city begun 936 and destroyed c. 1010; excavated and partly reconstructed. The clearest evidence of the terraced palace-and-court diagram.

exemplars.name: Aljaferia
exemplars.note: Built 1065-1081 for the Banu Hud; the surviving Taifa palace, and the direct bridge to Aragonese Mudejar.

exemplars.name: Alhambra, Palacio de Comares and Palacio de los Leones
exemplars.note: Built 1333-1391 under Yusuf I and Muhammad V; the fully developed Nasrid court sequence with the Court of the Myrtles and the Court of the Lions.

sources: Barrucand & Bednorz, Moorish Architecture in Andalusia
Dodds (ed.), Al-Andalus: The Art of Islamic Spain
Grabar, The Alhambra
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World

english-classical.name: English Classical

description.short: Two centuries of English classicism, from Jones and Wren through the Palladian, Georgian, Adam, and Regency phases, transmitted worldwide by pattern book.
description.long:
This family is the single most consequential body of work in the taxonomy for American residential architecture. It establishes the terms — symmetry, bay rhythm, the double-hung sash, storey graduation, the classical entry surround — that American building has been arguing with for three hundred years.

Its historical significance is also methodological. The English carpenter's guide converted architectural design from a guild secret into a purchasable commodity. Gibbs, Langley, Swan, Salmon, and Halfpenny made it possible for a builder who had never seen a correct Ionic order to execute one. That achievement, and its characteristic failure mode — correct details at wrong scales — is the closest historical analogue to what a design platform now attempts.

defining_characteristics: Strict bilateral symmetry and vertically aligned bays
Storey heights graduated rather than equal
The double-hung sash as the governing opening type
Classical apparatus concentrated at the entry and cornice
Pattern-book transmission of correct detail to non-architect builders

rural-gothic-villa.name: Rural Gothic Villa

geography.hearth: Hudson Valley, New York

lineage.note: The architect-designed, large-budget expression of the parent, in which the plan is genuinely irregular rather than ornamentally so.
Direct: Davis and Upjohn worked from Loudon, from Pugin, and from English published villa designs, and Upjohn had trained in England.
Oriels, tracery, label moulds, and clustered stacks quoted from Tudor and Perpendicular domestic work; the plan and the structure owe nothing to it.

description.short: The full-dress Gothic Revival country house: an architect-composed, genuinely irregular villa of towers, oriels, clustered chimneys and unequal gables, sited to be read in silhouette against trees and sky.
description.long:
The Rural Gothic villa is the American picturesque at full budget, and it is where the movement's ideas were worked out before being cheapened for the mass market. Alexander Jackson Davis established the type at Glen Ellen in 1832 and perfected it at Lyndhurst in 1838; Richard Upjohn built the wooden version at Kingscote in 1839; Downing published, praised, and theorised them. The essential move is that the plan is irregular for real reasons, a library wing where the morning light is, a veranda where the river view is, a service ell turned away from the approach, and the elevation is then composed to make that irregularity look inevitable rather than accidental.

It sits at an interesting technological angle to the rest of this branch. Balloon framing and machine ornament are what made the cheap Carpenter Gothic cottage possible, but the villa often refuses both: Lyndhurst is marble, Kingscote is timber with hand-worked detail, and the ambition of these houses reaches back toward the craft economy the rest of the century was leaving. What the villa does share with its cheaper sibling is total dependence on the pattern book for distribution. Davis drew a few dozen villas; Downing printed them; and within fifteen years there were Rural Gothic villas from Maine to Michigan built by men who had never met either of them. The book, not the guild, is the transmission organ of the entire American picturesque, and that is the historically closest analogue to what a machine-readable design language is attempting.

Downing's moral case is at its most explicit here, and it should be read as a serious position and not as decoration. He held that the villa of a cultivated family ought to express individuality, domestic affection, and a settled relation to its landscape; that a symmetrical facade lies about a household, since no family lives symmetrically; that the veranda is a moral instrument because it mediates between the private hearth and the public sublime of the American landscape; and that a house built on these principles would improve the people in it and, by demonstration, the neighbours around it. He also, more shrewdly, argued that the villa should look as though it had grown, which supplied a permission structure for the additive plan that American families needed anyway.

The experience is one of continuous rearrangement. There is no single correct view of a Rural Gothic villa; move twenty feet along the drive and a different gable dominates, the tower swings behind a chimney stack, the oriel catches the light. The silhouette is doing all the work, and it was designed to be read at a distance through trees. Come inside and the drama collapses into intimacy: a low entrance hall, a stair with a moulded rail and pierced brackets, a library with a bay looking down the slope, dark woodwork, small panes, and a general sense of being pleasantly and deliberately enclosed. Davis understood that the picturesque house must be exciting outside and quiet inside, and the ones that fail usually fail by reversing that.

defining_characteristics: A genuinely irregular plan, with wings, ells, and bays generated by room use and orientation rather than by facade composition
Three or more gables of unequal width forming a hierarchical silhouette against the sky
Steep pitches of 12:12 or greater throughout, with the roof reading as the dominant mass
Clustered, diagonally set, or moulded chimney stacks carried well above the ridge and composed as part of the outline
Oriel or bay windows on the principal rooms, with label mouldings and tracery heads
A veranda, loggia, or cloister of substantial depth attached to at least one principal elevation
Ornament worked in the building's own material, whether stone, stucco, or timber, rather than sawn and applied
diagnostic_tells: The plan is irregular, not merely the ornament. Walk the building; if the footprint has fewer than six external corners it is a Carpenter Gothic cottage wearing villa clothes
No two gables are the same width; equal gables indicate a builder's composition
Chimneys are designed objects with expressed flues, octagonal or clustered shafts, and moulded caps
Tracery has real depth and profile, cut in stone or in thick timber, and casts a modelled shadow rather than a flat one
There is a designed approach: the drive arrives obliquely so the house is first seen as a corner composition, never head-on

distinguished_from.difference: Architect versus builder, irregular plan versus symmetrical body, ornament in the material versus ornament sawn from board. Cost separates them by an order of magnitude and it shows in the depth of every profile.

The same clients, architects, and picturesque theory, opposite geometry. The Italianate villa is low-pitched, wide-eaved and bracketed with a square campanile; the Gothic villa is steep, bargeboarded, and towered with an octagonal or buttressed turret.

Baronial derives from actual surviving Scottish tower houses and keeps crow-stepped gables, corbelled bartizans, and conical turrets; the Rural Gothic villa derives from English ecclesiastical and Tudor domestic sources filtered through Loudon and Downing.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Silhouette hierarchy. The design is fixed in outline first, against a horizon: one dominant gable, subordinate gables at distinct widths, tower or chimney group completing the profile. Elevations are resolved afterwards, and are permitted to disagree with one another.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 12:12 to 18:12
Dominant gable width 1.4 to 2.2 times the next largest gable; equal widths are a failure
Tower or turret rising 0.75 to 1.5 storeys above the main ridge
Chimney stacks 4 to 8 ft above the ridge, with each flue expressed as a separate shaft
Veranda depth 8 to 12 ft, at least 0.35 of the elevation length it serves
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Non-repeating. Openings are placed by room requirement; two windows on one elevation may differ in width, head height, and sill height without fault.

massing_affinities.note: In the Gothic case the tower is octagonal, buttressed, or battlemented rather than a square campanile.
Where the villa grows a service ell in the New England manner.
Too regular; it produces a Carpenter Gothic house rather than a villa.

constraints.statement: The composition shall present not fewer than three gables of distinct width, with the dominant gable at least 1.4 times the width of the next largest. Equal gables are forbidden.
All principal roof pitches shall be 12:12 or steeper, and every pitch on the building shall be within 2:12 of every other. Mixing a steep front gable with a shallow rear roof is prohibited.

test.note: Tests the pitch floor. 'Every pitch on the building within 2:12 of every other' is a spread-among-an-arbitrary-number-of-roof-planes fact -- the vocabulary's roof_slope_lower_deg/upper_deg only names a single two-plane roof's pair, not a general variance check -- and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Chimney stacks shall rise not less than 4 ft above the adjacent ridge and shall express each flue as a separate shaft or panel. A flush or capped-off stack destroys the silhouette the type depends on.

test.note: Tests the chimney-height minimum. 'Each flue expressed as a separate shaft or panel' has no matching variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: A veranda, loggia, or cloister not less than 8 ft deep shall be attached to at least one principal elevation, covering not less than 35 percent of that elevation's length.

test.note: Tests the veranda/loggia/cloister depth minimum. The requirement that it cover not less than 35 percent of that elevation's length is a coverage-percent fact with no matching variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Tracery, label mouldings, and hood moulds shall be worked in the wall material with a minimum relief of 2 in. Flat sawn-board substitutes place the building in the Carpenter Gothic variant instead.

test.note: Tests the relief minimum. 'Worked in the wall material' versus a flat sawn-board substitute is a material-category fact with no matching variable and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Lyndhurst
exemplars.note: Alexander Jackson Davis, 1838 for William Paulding, greatly enlarged 1864-65 for George Merritt. Tuckahoe marble; the type's defining American statement.

exemplars.name: Kingscote
exemplars.note: Richard Upjohn for George Noble Jones. The wooden cottage-villa; later dining room by Stanford White, 1880-81.

exemplars.name: William J. Rotch Gothic Cottage
exemplars.note: A. J. Davis. Published by Downing as Design XXIV, A Cottage-Villa in the Rural Gothic Style, and thereafter the most copied villa design in America.

sources: Andrew Jackson Downing, The Architecture of Country Houses (1850)
Amelia Peck (ed.), Alexander Jackson Davis, American Architect 1803-1892 (1992)
William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: Technology and the Picturesque (1978)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and the best-fitting node in the whole branch for it: the style's own governing_logic is silhouette hierarchy - 'the design is fixed in outline first, against a horizon: one dominant gable, subordinate gables at distinct widths, tower or chimney group completing the profile' - which is this pack's dominant-mass method stated almost verbatim. Constraint c01 (dominant gable at least 1.4x the next largest, equal gables forbidden) is this pack's subordination rule with the style's own numbers attached.

Judgment binding, and the least comfortable one in this batch: this is an architect-designed, real-budget villa, not a farmer's cottage, so room-vernacular's own authority note (measured from ordinary surviving vernacular building) is a stretch. Bound anyway, over room-harmonic, because the style's own text describes the actual room experience in ordinary rather than treatise terms - 'the rooms are low, small-windowed by later standards, and dim... a general sense of being pleasantly and deliberately enclosed' - with no harmonic ratio or musical-mean language anywhere in the node, and the node's own proportional_system states that elevations (and by extension rooms) 'are resolved afterwards, and are permitted to disagree with one another,' the opposite of a Palladian room-shape discipline. Flagged rather than asserted as confident.

egyptian-revival.name: Egyptian Revival

revival_periods.note: The Tutankhamun discovery of November 1922 produced a second and entirely different Egyptomania, absorbed into Art Deco and into cinema architecture rather than into a traditional building grammar.

geography.hearth: Philadelphia and New Haven

lineage.note: The same architects (Strickland, Haviland, Austin, Lafever), the same masons, the same archaeological method, the same trabeated discipline. Egyptian Revival is Greek Revival practice pointed at a different corpus of plates.
Only through the Roman appetite for Egyptian spolia and the obelisk, which reached the nineteenth century as an inherited funerary sign.
In the cemetery-gate debate of the 1840s the Egyptian mode was argued for and against precisely as the pagan alternative to the Christian pointed arch; the two competed for the same commissions.

description.short: A narrow, short-lived, and almost entirely institutional American style of battered walls, cavetto cornices, and lotus columns, adopted for prisons, cemeteries, medical colleges, and a handful of churches because it read as permanent, solemn, and pre-Christian.
description.long:
Egyptian Revival is the smallest node in this branch and the one that best exposes how nineteenth-century Americans actually chose styles: by association, deliberately and almost semiotically. Napoleon's savants published the Description de l'Egypte between 1809 and 1829 and Dominique-Vivant Denon's Voyage dans la Basse et la Haute Egypte appeared in 1802, and within a generation American architects had a picture book of a civilisation whose buildings were understood to be the oldest and most durable on earth. That association, permanence beyond memory, made the mode almost irresistible for two building types: the cemetery, where the client wants to promise that the dead will not be disturbed, and the prison, where the client wants to promise that the living will not escape. It was used for both, and almost never for a house.

The style is trabeated, frontal, and massive. Walls batter inward as they rise; every terminating edge is turned with a torus roll and crowned by a cavetto cornice; columns are bundled reeds or papyrus stalks with lotus or palm capitals, squat and closely spaced; openings are small and rectangular; the winged sun disk sits over the door. Because the sources were engravings of temples rather than of dwellings, there was no domestic vocabulary to borrow, and the mode never developed one. This is a structural fact about revivalism worth recording in a taxonomy: a revival can only supply the building types its source corpus documented.

Its technological position is the mirror image of the rest of this branch. Egyptian Revival is a masonry style in an era that was learning to build cheaply in light wood, and it is precisely that mismatch which confined it. You cannot batter a balloon-framed wall convincingly, you cannot saw a torus moulding from a plank, and a cavetto cornice is a mason's or a plasterer's problem, not a millwright's. Where Gothic and Italianate detail rode the scroll saw and the railroad into every county in America, Egyptian detail stayed where there were stonecutters and institutional budgets. The Egyptian Building in Richmond gets its effect from stuccoed brick and cast iron; the Grove Street gate in New Haven from Portland sandstone. Both are the work of trades that were already being priced out of ordinary building.

Standing in front of one is genuinely unlike standing in front of any other American building of the period. Because the walls lean back, the building appears to be receding from you and settling into the ground at the same time, and because the cornice curves outward rather than stepping outward, the top of the wall reads as a lip rather than as a crown. There is no entasis to sympathise with, no bracket rhythm to follow, no order to measure yourself against. The effect is deliberately inhuman in scale reference, and everyone who commissioned one understood that. It is the only American traditional style whose purpose is to make the viewer feel small and temporary.

defining_characteristics: Battered (inward-sloping) exterior walls, typically 1:12 to 1:20 from vertical
Cavetto (hollow curved) cornice with a torus roll moulding at every terminating edge
Columns of bundled-reed or papyrus form with lotus or palm capitals, squat in proportion and never fluted
Trabeated openings throughout: post and lintel, no arches of any kind
Battered pylon forms flanking the principal entrance
Winged sun disk, vulture, or uraeus ornament placed in the cavetto over the entry
Massive, unbroken, minimally fenestrated wall surface
diagnostic_tells: Walls that lean inward as they rise: no other nineteenth-century American style batters its walls
The cornice curves outward in a concave sweep rather than stepping out in mouldings; this alone identifies the style at a hundred yards
Columns are wider at the base than a Greek Doric and shorter, typically four to five diameters, and stand in antis between battered piers rather than in a projecting portico
The building will almost certainly be a cemetery gate, a prison, a medical or scientific institution, a synagogue, or a church; a domestic Egyptian Revival is vanishingly rare
Obelisks used as gateposts, terminals, or fence standards

distinguished_from.difference: Shared architects and shared archaeology, opposite geometry. Greek Revival walls are plumb, its columns are slender and fluted with entasis, and it terminates in a horizontal entablature and a pediment; Egyptian Revival batters its walls, squats its columns, and terminates in a cavetto with no pediment ever.
Both use heavy masonry and small openings, but Richardsonian is arcuated, rock-faced, and asymmetrical, and Egyptian Revival is trabeated, smooth-faced or stuccoed, and rigidly frontal.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Trabeated and archaeological. Proportions are copied from published plates of Dendera, Edfu, and Philae rather than derived from a module; the governing decisions are the wall batter and the column diameter, and the rest follows the source engraving.
typical_ratios: Wall batter 1:12 to 1:20 (roughly 3 to 5 degrees from vertical)
Column height 4 to 5.5 shaft diameters, the squattest proportion in any Western revival
Cavetto cornice height 0.8 to 1.2 times the torus roll diameter times six
Intercolumniation 1.5 to 2.5 diameters, notably tight
Window area not exceeding 20 percent of any elevation
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Frontal and centralised: a heavy pylon or portico at the centre, flanked by near-blank battered wall. The rhythm is A-B-A, never a repeating march of equal bays.

massing_affinities.note: In the Egyptian variant the centre is distyle in antis between battered piers rather than a pedimented portico.
The rare domestic or institutional block, battered on all four faces.
Picturesque irregularity is incompatible with a frontal, symmetrical, mass-dominated style.

constraints.statement: All principal exterior walls shall batter inward between 1:12 and 1:20 from base to cornice. A plumb-walled building with Egyptian ornament is not Egyptian Revival.

Every terminating horizontal edge shall be composed as torus roll below cavetto cornice, in that order and without intervening classical mouldings. Dentils, modillions, and egg-and-dart are forbidden anywhere on the building.
No arches. All openings shall be spanned by lintels. A single round or pointed arch voids the identification.

test.note: A zero-rise head over every opening is the geometric signature of a flat lintel span with no arch, so the statement's own 'no arches, all openings spanned by lintels' is captured using the existing arch-rise variable at zero rather than an arch-presence boolean the vocabulary doesn't have.

constraints.statement: Column shaft height shall be between 4 and 5.5 base diameters, with intercolumniation between 1.5 and 2.5 diameters. Shafts shall be reed-bundle or palm form and shall never carry classical fluting or entasis.

The winged sun disk shall appear once per elevation, in the cavetto directly over the principal entry. Repeating it along a frieze is a twentieth-century cinema convention, not a nineteenth-century one.

exemplars.name: Egyptian Building, Medical College of Virginia
exemplars.note: Thomas S. Stewart. Battered walls, distyle in antis porticoes with palm capitals, flanking obelisks joined by a cast-iron fence with hermai. The finest surviving American example and still in university use.

exemplars.name: Grove Street Cemetery Gateway
exemplars.note: Henry Austin, 1845-48. Red sandstone, two battered pylons with torus framing and cavetto cornice, about 48 ft wide by 25 ft high.

exemplars.name: Downtown Presbyterian Church
exemplars.note: William Strickland, designed 1848, sanctuary completed 1851. Lotus columns, winged sun disk, and a fully Egyptianised interior; the rare ecclesiastical case.

sources: Richard G. Carrott, The Egyptian Revival: Its Sources, Monuments and Meaning, 1808-1858 (1978)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)
James Stevens Curl, The Egyptian Revival (2005)
Society of Architectural Historians, SAH Archipedia entries for the Egyptian Building and Grove Street Cemetery Gate

mexican-colonial.name: Mexican Colonial

revival_periods.note: The Californian mission chain is the northern frontier of this tradition, and the first American revival draws on its simplified adobe-and-arcade version rather than on the Mexican core.
The main channel. After Goodhue's San Diego exposition of 1915 the estipite portada, the tiled dome, the patio and the arcaded corredor become a national American residential vocabulary.
The looser, more Italianate American variant borrows the arcade, the tile and the low-pitched clay roof.
Indirect: the New Mexican adobe churches and casas of the northern frontier, themselves a branch of this tradition crossed with Puebloan building, are what Pueblo Revival actually revives.

geography.hearth: Mexico City, Puebla and the Bajio

lineage.note: The 16th-century conventos import the retablo-portada composition directly: a bounded panel of ornament against a plain wall, executed by Spanish masters and by indigenous carvers working from prints, which produces the tequitqui manner in which European motifs are cut with pre-Hispanic relief conventions.

Seville was the only legal port to the Indies, and what shipped out of it was Andalusian craft: par y nudillo and artesonado timber ceilings, azulejo tile, brick construction and the alfiz. Mudejar carpentry was standard practice in New Spain for two centuries, and the Mexican ceiling is technically an Andalusian ceiling.
The 18th-century phase, which in New Spain outruns its Spanish source: Jeronimo de Balbas brings the estipite to Mexico City in 1718 and Lorenzo Rodriguez brings it outdoors in 1749.

The domestic type — patio, zaguan, blind street wall, whitewash, tile — is not a monumental import but the ordinary Andalusian house, carried by ordinary settlers and reproduced in every colonial town grid in Mexico.

description.short: Three centuries of building in New Spain, in which Andalusian craft, Italian-derived ornament and indigenous labour and masonry tradition met a seismic, high-altitude, resource-rich continent and produced something with no European equivalent.
description.long:
Mexican colonial architecture is habitually described as Spanish architecture built in America. It is not, and the differences begin in the first generation. The Spanish crown's building programme in New Spain was a mass-conversion programme, and mass conversion required a building type that did not exist in Europe: a walled precinct (the atrio) large enough to hold thousands of people outdoors, with a raised open chapel (capilla abierta) from which mass could be said to a crowd in the open air, and four posa chapels at the corners of the enclosure for processional stations. The church itself, single-naved and buttressed, sits at one side of this enclosure rather than on the street. Nothing in Spain looks like this. It is an invention of the 1530s and 1540s, made under pressure by Franciscan, Dominican and Augustinian friars with an indigenous congregation that would not fit inside a building, and it is the clearest evidence that New Spain was producing architecture rather than importing it.

The labour and much of the technical intelligence were indigenous, and the record is explicit about it. The great sixteenth-century conventos were built by Nahua, Otomi, Mixtec and Maya masons and carvers working under friars who were not architects, using pre-Hispanic construction organisation and pre-Hispanic quarrying and lime-burning. What came out is a relief convention now called tequitqui: European motifs — vine scroll, angels, the instruments of the Passion — cut flat, in even depth, with the ground worked as pattern rather than as background, which is exactly how Mesoamerican relief carving handled a surface. Two visual grammars occupy the same stone. Later the same synthesis appears in the poblano tile facades, in the plaster and gilt of the Puebla and Oaxaca church interiors, and in the extraordinary indigenous-built and indigenous-decorated churches at Tonantzintla and Acatepec.

The material and structural culture is a response to the ground. The Valley of Mexico is seismic, high (2240 m), with a huge diurnal temperature swing and, in the colonial period, a subsiding lakebed under the capital. The response is low, massive, and heavily buttressed: adobe or rubble walls six hundred to a thousand millimetres thick, single-storey where possible, two-storey only around a stiffening patio arcade; flat azotea roofs with parapets and stone canales on the altiplano, where there is little rain and where a flat roof is a usable terrace; and tezontle, the deep red-brown vesicular volcanic stone that is light, strong, and beautiful against the pale chiluca limestone used for the dressed portadas and window surrounds. That red-and-cream combination is Mexico City's signature and there is nothing like it in Spain. In the tierra caliente and along the Gulf, where it rains, the same plan is roofed in clay tile at twenty to thirty degrees with a deep overhang, and the arcaded corredor around the patio becomes the deepest and most important space in the house.

Walking into a Mexican colonial house is a sequence of thresholds. Off a hard, sunlit, dead-flat grid street there is a plain plastered wall and a single tall doorway, often with a carved chiluca surround and no other decoration on the block. Inside is the zaguan — high, dark, wide enough for a carriage, paved in stone — and beyond it the patio: an arcaded court with an orange tree, a fountain and a stone stair, all of the rooms opening onto the corredor around it, and light bouncing down off cream plaster into the shade. The rooms are tall, cool and dark, their ceilings either beamed with vigas or, in the finer houses, a Mudejar interlace of small timbers. Then you look up past the parapet and there is a volcano.

defining_characteristics: Patio-centred plan with a single controlled entry (zaguan) and a largely closed street elevation, on a gridded colonial town plan
Massive adobe, rubble or tezontle walls, 600-1000 mm, single-pile ranges around the court
Arcaded corredor on the patio carrying circulation and social life; rooms entered from it, not from corridors
Ornament confined to the portada, window surrounds and cornice, against a plain field wall of tezontle, plaster or ashlar
Mudejar carpentry — par y nudillo and artesonado ceilings — and Andalusian azulejo tile as standard trades, not exotic features
Flat azotea roofs with parapets and canales on the altiplano; low-pitched clay tile with deep overhangs in the wet and hot lowlands
Seismic response as a formal determinant: low profile, heavy buttressing, wide wall-to-opening ratio
The walled atrio with open chapel and posa chapels at religious sites — a New World type with no Spanish precedent
diagnostic_tells: Dark red-brown vesicular tezontle field walls framed and trimmed in pale chiluca limestone
A church set within a large walled forecourt with a raised open-air chapel, rather than on the street line
Buttresses on a single-naved church that are visibly oversized for the vault they carry
Flat-relief carving in which the background is worked as pattern rather than left as ground (tequitqui)
Glazed tile applied over whole facade fields in Puebla, in contrast to Andalusia where tile stays at dado height

distinguished_from.difference: Churrigueresque is one ornamental phase, roughly 1730-1790, within this tradition. Mexican Colonial covers three centuries of plans, walls, roofs and construction practice, the great majority of which is entirely plain.

The Mexican house descends directly from the Andalusian one and then diverges: bigger lots on a regular grid, a continuous arcaded corredor rather than a partial gallery, flat azotea roofs at altitude, and seismic wall thicknesses. And it has an indigenous labour and carving tradition inside it that Andalusia does not.

The 20th-century American revival takes the portada, the tile, the arcade and the low tile roof and applies them to double-pile, corridor-planned, stud-framed houses that face outward to a lawn. The revival keeps the ornament and reverses the plan.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The arcade bay and the viga. The patio corredor bay of 2.5-3.5 m is set by the span of a stone arch on a monolithic shaft; room depth of 5-6 m is set by the span of the roof beams. Where a building has two storeys, the lower arcade order is heavier and the upper lighter. Facade composition is governed by the portada — a bounded ornamental panel inherited from Plateresque — rather than by any order regulating the wall.
typical_ratios: Patio arcade bay 2.5-3.5 m; column slenderness 7-10 diameters
Room depth 5-6 m clear; wall thickness 600-1000 mm
Church nave width 8-12 m, single-naved, with buttresses at 4-6 m centres
Tile roof pitch 20-30 degrees with 700-1000 mm overhang; azotea flat with a 600-900 mm parapet
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even, unaccented arcade rhythm on the patio, five to nine bays a side. On the street, a plain wall with a few tall openings and one emphasised doorway; the portada does not relate to the fenestration and is not expected to.

massing_affinities.note: The urban casa, the convento and the colegio are all four-sided enclosed patios with blind or near-blind street walls.
Three-sided courts on smaller and irregular lots, and in the second service patio behind the first.
The corredor is a true gallery — circulation, shade and social space in one, and the deepest room in the building.
Colonial town grids produce continuous party-walled blocks, each house a courtyard within it.
The rural and working-class house of one adobe room with a portal in front of it, which is the vast majority of what was actually built.

constraints.statement: Adobe or rubble walls 600-1000 mm minimum. In seismic zones a two-storey building requires the patio arcade to act as a continuous stiffening ring, and no unbraced wall may run more than about 12 m without a buttress or cross-wall.

test.note: Tests the stated minimum ('600-1000 mm minimum' reads as a minimum, not a between-range -- 1000 mm is the typical upper figure, not a stated cap). The seismic patio-arcade stiffening-ring requirement and the 12 m unbraced-wall-run limit are separate structural facts in the same statement with no matching vocabulary variable (no named 'unbraced wall run length'); left as prose.

constraints.statement: On the altiplano above roughly 1800 m, roofs are flat azotea with parapets and stone canales; in the tierra caliente and on the Gulf and Pacific coasts, clay tile at 20-30 degrees with an overhang of at least 700 mm. Mixing the two on one building is a revival error.
Room depth must not exceed the viga span, about 6 m clear. Ranges are single-pile and the building grows by adding courts, never by thickening a range.

test.note: Tests the viga-span depth ceiling. 'Ranges are single-pile and the building grows by adding courts, never by thickening a range' is a compositional/growth rule, not a single numeric expression, and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Ornament is confined to the portada, the window and door surrounds and the cornice. The field wall between them stays plain tezontle, ashlar or lime plaster; an evenly ornamented elevation misreads the tradition.

At religious sites the church stands within a walled atrio, set back from the street, with a processional route around it. Placing a colonial-type church on the street line removes the element that most distinguishes New Spain from Spain.

exemplars.name: Casa de Montejo
exemplars.note: 1542-1549; the earliest surviving substantial domestic facade in Mexico, with a Plateresque portada carved by Maya masons — including the notorious conquistadores standing on severed heads.

exemplars.name: Convento de San Nicolas de Tolentino
exemplars.note: 1546-1573; Augustinian, with an intact walled atrio, one of the largest surviving open chapels, and a fully frescoed stair.

exemplars.name: Casa del Dean
exemplars.note: c. 1580; the oldest surviving house in Puebla, with a Renaissance portada and two rooms of indigenous-painted mural cycles.

exemplars.name: Casa de los Azulejos
exemplars.note: 16th-century house whose facade was clad in Puebla talavera tile in 1737; the fullest surviving demonstration of tile used as a whole-facade field rather than as a dado.

sources: Kubler, Mexican Architecture of the Sixteenth Century (1948)
Kubler & Soria, Art and Architecture in Spain and Portugal and their American Dominions 1500-1800
Toussaint, Arte colonial en Mexico
Bunting, Early Architecture in New Mexico — for the northern frontier
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World

proportion_packs.note: JUDGMENT BINDING - mexican-colonial is not itself in room-vernacular's applies_to, but its own hard constraint c03 is nearly a restatement of the pack's core logic: 'Room depth must not exceed the viga span, about 6 m clear. Ranges are single-pile and the building grows by adding courts, never by thickening a range' - span-limited breadth and single-pile daylight depth are exactly what room-vernacular encodes, and 6 m (about 19-20 ft) sits at the outer edge of the pack's own 14-18 ft measured band, which is itself dominated by the same climate and material logic. The node's two closest kin are both explicitly in the pack's applies_to: andalusian-courtyard-vernacular, its direct antecedent ('the domestic type... is not a monumental import but the ordinary Andalusian house'), and mexican-hacienda, its direct rural descendant ('same walls, same vigas, same patio, same carpentry, same trades'). The binding is scoped to the ordinary courtyard house and convento range, not to the portada, which the node's own text says is governed by an inherited Plateresque ornamental panel rather than by any order or room system.

log-vernacular-american.name: American Log Vernacular

revival_periods.note: The Adirondack and National Park Service rustic traditions, the Rocky Mountain resort log house, and the modern milled-log kit industry are all revivals of this node's surfaces with none of its span constraints - modern kits use full-round logs of uniform diameter, which the original tradition almost never did outside the Nordic source.

geography.hearth: the Delaware Valley and southeastern Pennsylvania

lineage.note: The Finnish and Swedish settlers of New Sweden on the lower Delaware (from 1638) brought horizontal log construction to North America; the Finns in particular carried a fully developed forest-clearing and log-building culture. This is the earliest documented transmission, though its demographic weight relative to the German channel remains actively debated by Jordan, Kniffen and Glassie.

Stands here for the Germanic building culture of the Palatinate and Silesia, which carried Blockbau horizontal log craft alongside its half-timber framing. The very large Pennsylvania German migration after 1720 is the channel by which log building became the standard American frontier method; the notching vocabulary of the Upland South is substantially German rather than Nordic.

The immediate American ancestor. The Pennsylvania backcountry is where Nordic and German log practice fused with an Anglo plan vocabulary and then travelled south down the Great Wagon Road into Virginia, Carolina and Tennessee.

description.short: Horizontal hewn-log building as the standard American frontier construction from Pennsylvania to Texas - a Northern European craft transplanted, simplified, and married to Anglo room plans, whose dimensions are set almost entirely by how long a log two people can lift.
description.long:
American log building is a construction system that acquired a house grammar, and understanding it in that order explains everything about it. The unit is the pen: a rectangular enclosure of horizontal logs, hewn flat on two faces with a broadaxe, notched at the corners so the courses interlock without a single nail, chinked between the courses with split wood and clay or lime mortar, and roofed with riven shingles on light poles. The pen's dimensions are not chosen; they are dictated. A hewn log of white oak, poplar or chestnut long enough for a wall is heavy, and the practical limit for two to four people with a cant hook and a pair of skid poles is roughly sixteen to twenty feet. That single number generates the entire type family. A house bigger than one pen is not a bigger pen; it is two pens - side by side (double pen), side by side with a gap (dogtrot), stacked (two-storey), or one behind the other (saddlebag with a shared central chimney). Every named Upland South folk house type is a combination of pens, and the combination rules are the style.

The transmission is genuinely contested and worth stating honestly rather than tidily. Horizontal log construction has no Anglo precedent - English and Welsh settlers built timber frames, and the 'log cabin' as an English colonial form is a nineteenth-century invention of political myth. Two Northern European channels supplied it. The Finns and Swedes of New Sweden on the lower Delaware from 1638 brought a mature Nordic log culture; the C. A. Nothnagle Log House in Gibbstown, New Jersey and the Lower Swedish Cabin at Drexel Hill, Pennsylvania are its claimed survivors, though both carry dates (circa 1638-1700) that are traditional rather than dendrochronologically settled. The far larger channel is German: the Palatine and Rhineland migration into Pennsylvania after 1720 brought Blockbau practice, and it is German notching and German proportions that dominate the Upland South. The Scots-Irish, who did most of the actual settling of Appalachia, learned log building in Pennsylvania from their German neighbours and carried it down the Great Wagon Road; they contributed the plan types, not the technique. Anyone who tells the story with one origin is simplifying.

The economic logic is brutal and complete. On a forested frontier, timber is the one abundant material and cash is the scarce one. A log pen requires an axe, a froe, a broadaxe, an auger, and labour; it requires no sawmill, no nails, no lime kiln, no glass. It can be raised by a neighbourhood in days. It is also, and this matters for how the type is read, almost always intended as a first house: the Upland South pattern is a log pen followed within a generation by weatherboarding, a frame or brick addition, or an entirely new house with the pen demoted to kitchen. Log building persisted longest exactly where cash never arrived, which is why the surviving concentrations are in the mountains and why the form became a symbol of poverty and then, by a peculiar American inversion, of virtue.

Inside a good hewn-log room the experience is of a very still, very dark, very solid space. The walls are eight to ten courses of hewn oak, each course a foot or so deep, and the surfaces are flat and axe-scalloped rather than round; the light comes from one or two small openings and from the fire. Sound is dead - a foot of solid wood absorbs everything - and the temperature swings slowly, which is the actual thermal argument for the material. Overhead the joists are round poles with the bark still on, and the loft above them is reached by a ladder or a boxed corner stair, and is where the children slept. The chinking is the maintenance problem and the visual signature both: a two-inch band of white lime between dark logs, repointed every few years for a century, so that the wall records its own upkeep.

defining_characteristics: Horizontal logs, hewn flat on interior and exterior faces, laid in courses and interlocked at the corners by notching rather than by fasteners
Corner notching as the structural joint - V-notch, half-dovetail, full dovetail, square or saddle notch - each with a distinct regional and ethnic distribution
Pen dimensions limited by log length: 16-20 feet on the long wall is the practical maximum
Growth by pen addition rather than by enlarging the pen: double pen, saddlebag, dogtrot, two-storey, or rear ell
Chinking and daubing between courses as an integral and continually maintained part of the wall
Riven shingle or shake roof on light pole rafters or purlins, with no ridge beam required
Chimney at the gable end, exterior or partly exterior, of stone, or of stick-and-clay in the poorest work
diagnostic_tells: Logs hewn flat on two faces rather than left round - the mark of the historic tradition, and the fastest way to distinguish it from a twentieth-century milled-log kit
Corner notching visible at the pen ends, with log ends projecting a few inches beyond the joint
Wall length that stops abruptly at 16-20 feet and starts again as a second pen: the type never spans further
Openings cut after the wall was raised, with sawn jambs pegged to the log ends and no header over the opening
Loft floor of round pole joists with bark, visible from below in unceiled work

distinguished_from.difference: The Nordic source uses full-round or scribe-fitted logs with tight, chinkless joints, steeper roofs, and often no chinking at all. The American tradition hews the faces flat and relies on chinking - a simplification made because hewing is faster than scribing and clay is free.

The Appalachian variant is this style's most persistent and best-documented regional expression; the parent node covers the whole continental spread including Pennsylvania, the Ozarks and Texas, where notching vocabularies and roof pitches differ.

The Pennsylvania German house is often log but is organised on a Continental three-room Flurkuchenhaus plan with a central chimney and an off-centre door. Where the plan is Anglo - hall, hall-and-parlor, double pen with two front doors - the building belongs here.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Dimensioned by material handling, not by any system of proportion. Log length sets plan width, log diameter sets course height, and the number of courses a crew will lift sets wall height. Everything else follows from the pen.
typical_ratios: Pen 16-20 feet long by 14-18 feet deep; a square-ish pen is the norm and is a consequence of log length in both directions
Wall height 8-10 log courses, roughly 7-9 feet to the plate per storey
Log course depth 8-14 inches hewn; hewn wall thickness 6-9 inches
Chinking gap 1-3 inches
Roof pitch 8:12 to 12:12 for riven shingles; lower pitches fail with hand-split roofing
Door opening 30-36 inches wide, 5.5-6.5 feet tall; windows small, often under 3 square feet in early work
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: There is no bay rhythm. Openings are cut where they are needed, subject to the rule that a notched corner cannot be weakened, so windows and doors sit at least two feet from any corner.

massing_affinities.note: The single pen; the irreducible unit from which the rest of the family is built.
Two equal pens, two front doors, two end chimneys - the standard way to make a bigger house out of a limited log length.
Two pens with an open passage between them; see dogtrot-vernacular.
Two-storey log I-houses are frequent in the Upland South and are usually weatherboarded early, which is why they are so often misidentified as frame.

constraints.statement: No log wall may exceed 20 feet between notched corners; 16-18 feet is the practical norm. A larger enclosure must be built as a second pen or as a pen plus a framed addition, never as a longer log run.

test.note: Tests the hard 20 ft ceiling; the 16-18 ft practical-norm figure and the second-pen guidance stay prose.

constraints.statement: Corner joints must be notched (V, half-dovetail, full dovetail, square or saddle) and, except in saddle notching, must slope outward to shed water. Butted and spiked corners are outside the tradition and fail at the joint within a generation.

Log faces are hewn flat on interior and exterior; wall thickness 6-9 inches after hewing, chinking gap 1-3 inches, chinking recessed 1/2 to 1 inch behind the log face so water sheds off the log rather than sitting on the joint.

test.note: Tests the hewn wall-thickness range. Chinking gap (1-3in) and chinking recess depth (1/2-1in) are left as prose -- no vocabulary variable expresses either.

constraints.statement: Eave overhang at least 18 inches (24-36 preferred) on all elevations to keep water off the chinking; roof pitch 8:12 to 12:12 where riven shingles or shakes are used. Boxed soffits and clipped eaves destroy the wall.

test.note: Tests the 18in minimum eave overhang. Roof pitch (8:12-12:12, where riven shingles/shakes are used) is also cleanly testable via roof_pitch_rise_per_12 but is left as prose here since the schema allows one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Openings must stop at least 24 inches short of any notched corner, and their jambs must be pegged or spiked to the cut log ends. Corner windows and full-height glazed walls are structurally impossible in this system.

exemplars.name: C. A. Nothnagle Log House
exemplars.location: Gibbstown, Greenwich Township, Gloucester County, New Jersey
exemplars.note: Traditionally dated circa 1638-1643 and claimed as the oldest log house in North America. The date is traditional, not dendrochronologically established, and later dates have been argued; the building is nonetheless the standard reference for the New Sweden log transmission.

exemplars.name: Lower Swedish Cabin
exemplars.location: Creek Road, Drexel Hill, Upper Darby Township, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: Likely built between 1640 and 1650 by New Sweden settlers, restored and archaeologically excavated 1989; listed on the National Register 1982. Same dating caveat as Nothnagle.

exemplars.name: John Oliver Place
exemplars.location: Cades Cove, Great Smoky Mountains National Park, Blount County, Tennessee
exemplars.note: Built in the 1820s, replacing a 1818 cabin on the same site; the oldest surviving structure on the Cades Cove loop and a textbook single-pen with an exterior gable-end chimney.

exemplars.name: Jacob Wolf House
exemplars.note: A two-storey hewn-log dogtrot built as a courthouse - the oldest standing public structure in Arkansas, and evidence that the system was used well beyond domestic building. National Register 1973.

sources: Terry G. Jordan, American Log Buildings: An Old World Heritage (1985)
Henry Glassie, 'The Types of the Southern Mountain Cabin', in Jan Brunvand, The Study of American Folklore (1968)
Fred Kniffen and Henry Glassie, 'Building in Wood in the Eastern United States: A Time-Place Perspective', Geographical Review 56 (1966)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
C. A. Weslager, The Log Cabin in America (1969)

proportion_packs.note: Same relationship as its Appalachian variant, at the parent style's continental scope: pen dimension, notch geometry (V, half-dovetail, full-dovetail, square and saddle, each with its own regional and ethnic distribution), wall thickness after hewing, chinking, roof pitch and the whole combinatorial expansion grammar -- double pen, dogtrot, saddlebag, two-storey, rear ell -- are all derived_rules of this one module, and the node's own hard constraint (c01) restates the pack's 20 ft ceiling directly.

Bound secondary, at low precedence, for the wider massing range this parent style covers beyond the single- and double-pen combinatorics that log-module alone fully specifies: the hall-and-parlor affinity (common here) is a genuinely unequal two-room type whose social logic -- the parlor overtaking the hall in status through the eighteenth century, hence the off-centre door -- is room-vernacular's public_private_gradient rule and has no equivalent in log-module. Also carries the loft/chamber ceiling-height figure (7 ft 6 in) for the documented two-storey log I-houses. Not given a higher role: log-module's own interior-of-the-pen dimension is the more specific and better-attested number for this style's core single-pen and double-pen forms, and where the two packs disagree log-module should win.

minimal-traditional.name: Minimal Traditional

geography.hearth: No design hearth. The style was standardized in Washington by the Federal Housing Administration's underwriting manuals and built simultaneously in every American metropolitan area.

lineage.note: The silhouette, the double-hung sash, the shutter, and the centred or near-centred entry survive; the proportional system, the trim profiles, and the applied orders do not. This is the most consequential partial inheritance in the American branch.

The quoted silhouette. The compact one-and-a-half storey box with a steep side gable was the FHA's most-published small house image, and the Levittown house of 1947 is a Cape reduced to its outline. It is a reference rather than a descent because the two styles are contemporaries converging in the same market rather than one transmitting practice to the other; the actual transmission of building practice runs through colonial-revival, and the reciprocal convergence is recorded on the cape-cod-revival node as a hybridization.

The vestigial front-facing entry gable with a prominent chimney beside it is a Tudor Revival move that outlived its own style, surviving as the single compositional event on thousands of otherwise plain elevations.

Not an aesthetic reaction but a cost reaction, and the more instructive for it. Every expensive element of the bungalow — the 30-inch overhang, the deep porch, the masonry piers, the built-in cabinetry, the 5-inch casing — is deleted in turn between 1930 and 1940, while the plan efficiency the bungalow pioneered is kept.

description.short: The smallest complete house the American mortgage system could underwrite: traditional in silhouette, symmetrical enough to be legible, and stripped of overhang, porch, profile depth, and every other element that cost money — the direct ancestor of the ranch and the moment the traditional kit of parts was cost-engineered out of the American house.
description.long:
Minimal Traditional is the most consequential and least discussed style in American housing. Between the middle of the 1930s and about 1950 it was built in the millions; it set the physical template for the postwar suburb; it established the dimensional habits — the shallow eave, the thin trim, the small opening, the eight-foot plate — that still govern American production housing ninety years later. It has no theorists, no manifesto, no monograph, and no architect's name attached to it. It has a federal agency instead. The house is a compact rectangle or shallow L of 750 to 1,300 square feet, one storey or one and a half, under a gable or hip of four to six in twelve. The eave and rake overhang is six to twelve inches and sometimes zero. There is no porch, only a stoop, occasionally under a small hood. The trim is a two-and-a-quarter-inch clamshell casing and a flat frieze board. The ornament consists of a chimney, a pair of shutters, and, if the budget allowed, a simple door surround. Everything else that a traditional house had was removed, deliberately, one line item at a time.

The machinery that produced it is documentable to an unusual degree, which is why this node earns a long entry. The National Housing Act of 1934 created the Federal Housing Administration to insure mortgages, and in doing so replaced the five-year balloon loan requiring fifty percent down with the amortized twenty- and later thirty-year loan requiring ten. That single change moved the binding constraint on a house from total price to monthly payment, and it moved design authority from the builder and the plan book to the underwriter. The FHA then wrote down what it would insure: Minimum Property Requirements, the underwriting manual, and a series of technical bulletins of which No. 4, Principles of Planning Small Houses (1936), is the crucial document — a national specification for the American house, complete with minimum room dimensions, circulation diagrams, and approved elevations. Because the appraisal determined the loan, and the appraisal rewarded conventional appearance and marketability, style became a risk category. Traditional silhouette was the safe collateral. This is the precise mechanism by which the traditional look survived the disappearance of traditional substance: the underwriter would insure a house that looked like a Colonial and would not insure one that looked experimental, but nothing in the underwriting manual required an eave, a porch, or a moulding with depth. The same apparatus, it must be said plainly, wrote redlining into the national housing map, and the Minimal Traditional landscape is inseparable from that fact.

The cost engineering itself follows a legible sequence, and any design system for production housing should study it, because the same sequence runs today. Overhang goes first: it consumes rafter length, sheathing, soffit material, fascia, flashing, gutter, and labour at height, and its benefit — shadow, weather protection of the wall, and a visible termination for the roof — is invisible on a spec sheet. The porch goes second, because it is conditioned-area-equivalent cost with no conditioned area. Trim profile depth goes third: a two-and-a-quarter-inch clamshell costs a third of a four-and-a-half-inch moulded casing and, unlike the casing, casts no shadow. Wall thickness, window size, and ceiling height follow. Wartime accelerated all of it: the Linda Vista defense project in San Diego put up three thousand houses in two hundred and fifty-nine days in 1941-43, and by 1947 Levitt was building a 750-square-foot Cape on a 60-by-100-foot lot in twenty-six sequenced operations, thirty a day. The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944 supplied the demand. What survived the process is exactly what cost nothing: proportion of the overall mass, placement of the openings, and the outline against the sky.

And here is the part that resists the lament. These are, at their best, decent little houses, and a street of them reads better than most of what has been built since.
