The plans are tight and workable, the rooms are small but correctly related, the massing is compact, and — critically — the kit was so short that consistency was almost unavoidable, so the street has a coherence that no amount of variety-seeking has since reproduced. Minimal Traditional is the proof that a coherent public realm can be made from an impoverished kit of parts provided the rules are few, consistent, and universally followed. Standing in front of one you feel the absence physically: the wall meets the sky at a knife edge with no shadow at all, the door sits in the plane of the wall with no reveal, the shutters are half the width of the window and could never have closed, and there is nowhere to stand out of the rain. But you also feel that nothing is pretending. The house is exactly as big as it is, and it does not have a two-storey entry, and the roof is one simple shape. Between this house and the neo-eclectic house of 1985 the money spent per square foot went up substantially and the quality of the street went down, which is the single most useful fact in this entire branch of the graph.

defining_characteristics: Compact rectangular or shallow-L massing of 750 to 1,300 sq ft, one storey or one and a half, with the long axis often perpendicular to the street
Moderate roof pitch of 4:12 to 6:12, gabled or hipped, with eave and rake overhang not exceeding 12 in and frequently under 6 in
Complete absence of a habitable porch; entry is a stoop, at most under a small hood or shallow entry gable
Ornament reduced to three items at most: a chimney, a pair of decorative shutters, and a simple door surround
Trim of minimal profile depth — flat frieze, narrow clamshell or ranch casing, no cornice return of any consequence
Small double-hung openings, six-over-six or two-over-two, sized and placed by interior requirement rather than by facade composition
Traditional silhouette retained as the only surviving carrier of style: the outline is Colonial or Cape, and nothing below the outline is
diagnostic_tells: A recognizably traditional shape with essentially no eave — the roof surface stops at the wall surface and the two meet without a shadow line
Shutters roughly half the width of the sash they flank, fixed flat to the wall
The front door lies in the plane of the wall with a reveal of an inch or less and no projecting surround
A single small gabled or hipped entry projection or bay as the only three-dimensional event on the whole elevation
One-and-a-half storey examples carrying an added shed dormer at the rear, from a later expansion of the attic

distinguished_from.difference: Cape Cod Revival keeps the full symmetrical five-bay facade, the heavier trim, the correct cornice with returns, and a genuine central chimney. Minimal Traditional keeps the box and deletes all four. The tell is the rake: a Cape Cod Revival has a moulded rake with a return at the eave; Minimal Traditional has a 1x6 board.

The ranch is longer than it is deep, sits lower, has a wider eave, opens its plan, and attaches its garage. Minimal Traditional is an upright compact block with a cellular plan and a detached garage at the rear of the lot, reached by a driveway beside the house.

The same size and often the same footprint, thirty years apart. The bungalow has a 30-inch eave, a full-width porch, exposed rafters, and built-in cabinetry; Minimal Traditional has none of them. If it is small and has a deep porch it is a bungalow; if it is small and has a stoop it is Minimal Traditional.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Economic, not proportional, and it is important to say so without apology because it is the true answer. The governing modules are the FHA minimum room dimension, the 16-inch stud bay, the 8-foot precut stud and the 8-foot ceiling that follows from it, the 4-by-8 sheet, and the maximum insurable loan amount. The facade is a residual: openings are located by the rooms behind them and then nudged toward apparent balance. Nothing is derived from a module of order, and the style's visual coherence comes not from any internal system but from the smallness and uniformity of its vocabulary.
typical_ratios: Overall footprint 24 x 32 ft to 26 x 40 ft
Roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12; eave and rake overhang 0 to 12 in
Wall plate 8 ft 0 in; window and door head 6 ft 8 in
Window openings 2 ft 8 in to 3 ft 0 in wide by 4 ft 2 in to 4 ft 10 in tall, roughly 1:1.6
Casing 2 1/4 in wide with a projection under 3/4 in
FHA minimum principal bedroom approximately 9 ft 6 in by 11 ft 0 in
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and plan-driven. Openings occur in ones and twos with no governing interval; the appearance of rhythm on the best examples is the result of a two-room-deep plan happening to produce even spacing.

massing_affinities.note: The one-and-a-half storey side-gabled box; the FHA's most-published and Levitt's chosen form.
The single-storey version with a projecting entry or living-room gable — the one compositional move the style allows itself.
The transitional form of 1948-1953: the same detailing stretched along the lot. Watching this massing displace cape-cod-massing in a subdivision's build-out sequence dates it to within two years.
The two-room single-storey core of the smallest wartime examples is literally this ancient skeleton, arrived at again by cost rather than by tradition.

constraints.statement: Eave and rake overhang shall not exceed 12 in. Where overhang exceeds 12 in the node is misassigned; classify as cape-cod-revival, colonial-revival, or ranch-style.

test.note: The statement gives one shared 12in ceiling for both eave and rake overhang; eave_projection_in stands in for the general overhang measurement since no separate rake-overhang variable exists in the vocabulary.

constraints.statement: Conditioned floor area 750 to 1,400 sq ft; roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12; one or one and a half storeys only.

test.note: Tests the roof-pitch clause. Conditioned floor area (750-1,400 sq ft) has no vocabulary variable (missing: floor_area_sqft) and stays prose; storey count ('one or one and a half storeys only') is separately expressible via the existing storey_count variable as one-of ["1","1.5"] but only one test object is permitted per constraint, so it also stays prose here.

constraints.statement: Decorative shutters, where used, must each be not less than 45 percent of the width of the window opening they flank, hinged at the jamb, and must be omitted entirely from ganged, bay, and non-rectangular windows. Half-width shutters are the single most common failure of this style's descendants and are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the minimum leaf-width ratio. Hinge position and the omission-from-ganged/bay/non-rectangular-window rule are categorical and stay prose.

constraints.statement: No full- or partial-width habitable porch. Entry cover projection not more than 3 ft; where a deeper covered space is wanted the node is not minimal-traditional.

test.note: Tests the entry-cover projection ceiling. 'No full- or partial-width habitable porch' is a qualitative prohibition and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Room dimensions follow FHA Minimum Property Requirements as a historical floor: principal bedroom not less than 9 ft 6 in by 11 ft 0 in, secondary bedroom not less than 8 ft 0 in by 10 ft 0 in, minimum one full bath.

exemplars.name: Linda Vista Defense Housing Project
exemplars.note: 3,000 houses and 750 dormitory units built in 259 days, 1941-43, at up to 40 completions a day, under a garden-city neighbourhood plan. The style's wartime proving ground.

exemplars.name: Levittown
exemplars.note: The 1947 Levitt Cape: roughly 750 sq ft on a 60 x 100 ft lot, built in 26 sequenced operations. Over 17,000 houses by 1951, sold to veterans under the GI Bill at about $8,000 with almost nothing down.

exemplars.name: Westlake, Daly City
exemplars.note: Henry Doelger's tract, begun in the late 1940s and built out through the 1950s. The West Coast counterpart, and the place where the style visibly shades into the ranch mid-subdivision. Construction begins 1949; the tract was annexed to Daly City in 1948.

sources: Federal Housing Administration, Principles of Planning Small Houses, Technical Bulletin No. 4 (1936)
Kenneth T. Jackson, Crabgrass Frontier: The Suburbanization of the United States (1985)
Gwendolyn Wright, Building the Dream: A Social History of Housing in America (1981)
Barbara Miller Lane, Houses for a New World: Builders and Buyers in American Suburbs, 1945-1965 (2015)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)

proportion_packs.note: The FHA minimum room dimensions this node's own constraint c05 states as a historical floor (principal bedroom not less than 9 ft 6 in x 11 ft 0 in, secondary not less than 8 ft 0 in x 10 ft 0 in) and its governing_logic's own claim ('nothing is derived from a module of order') land inside this pack's reconstructed vernacular band -- span-, hearth- (obsolete by this date, replaced by forced air) and daylight-limited rooms clustering at a 1.0-1.5 ratio -- rather than anywhere in the treatise literature this pack is deliberately the counterweight to. The FHA principal bedroom's 9 ft 6 in breadth sits below even this pack's own 11 ft floor for a principal room, which is itself the diagnostic: this is the vernacular room logic pushed one further notch toward the economic minimum, continuing exactly the deletion sequence the node's own lineage entry against craftsman describes.

The style's own defining_characteristics name '6/6 or 2/2' sash directly, which is precisely the light pattern this pack's derived rules emit for cheap, large, early-to-mid-20th-century glass, and the node's constraint c03 (shutter leaf not less than 45 percent of sash width, hinged at the jamb, forbidden on ganged/bay/non-rectangular windows) quotes this pack's own shutter rule almost verbatim. Bound ahead of opening-proportion per this pack's own stated precedence over that one where the two disagree.

Retained for the single-head-datum rule, which still organizes what compositional discipline the elevation has ('the appearance of rhythm on the best examples is the result of a two-room-deep plan happening to produce even spacing'). FLAGGED DEVIATION: the node's own typical_ratios give openings 2 ft 8 in-3 ft 0 in wide by 4 ft 2 in-4 ft 10 in tall -- roughly 1.5:1 to 1.8:1 -- markedly squarer than this pack's canonical 13:6 (2.167:1) and below its documented range floor of 1.75:1, a real measured consequence of the 6 ft 8 in head and 8 ft 0 in plate the governing_logic names. No pack in the library currently states this compressed ratio as its own default; worth flagging for WP-4.6.

Bound as the closest available system, not a close fit. The node's own casing -- 2 1/4 in wide, under 3/4 in projection -- is thinner than even this pack's stated economy floor ('below 3 1/2 in the family stops working, because the head casing has nowhere to overhang to'), so what Minimal Traditional actually built is a further reduction beyond what any pack in this library describes as the cheapest classical-adjacent system. Bound optional and low: the flat-stock, order-indifferent logic is directionally correct, but no pack currently states a system thin enough to describe a 2 1/4 in clamshell casing without extrapolating past its own documented range. Worth flagging for WP-4.6.

queen-anne-free-classic.name: Queen Anne, Free Classic

geography.hearth: Newport and Boston, spreading through the pattern press after 1890

lineage.note: The late phase of the parent, roughly a third of the American Queen Anne population by McAlester's count, and the bridge to the twentieth century.

The classical vocabulary of this subtype and the mature Colonial Revival style are the same body of material, and the Colonial Revival node descends from this one rather than the reverse; the inheritance is therefore carried by the descends_from edge to georgian-colonial-american.
Shaw's own free-classic manner, the half of his work Americans initially ignored, reasserts itself here; the term free classic is taken directly from British usage.

The actual source of the columns, dentils, swan-neck pediments, and Palladian windows: eighteenth-century American work, measured and republished from the late 1870s, and then produced as stock millwork. Retyped 2026-08-18. This edge reaches early New England building through the 1877 McKim, Mead, White and Bigelow sketching tour of Marblehead, Salem, Newburyport and Portsmouth, and the measured drawings and photographs that followed. That mechanism transmits appearance, not craft. Ruling applied consistently across shingle-style, queen-anne-free-classic and colonial-revival: drawings do not carry a kit. A revival detailed with true eighteenth-century assembly is a reconstruction, not a revival.

description.short: The Queen Anne after 1890, in which classical columns, Palladian windows, and dentilled cornices replace turned spindlework while the irregular massing, dominant mass, and wrapping porch of the parent style are retained.
description.long:
The free classic subtype is the American Queen Anne getting its classical education, and it is the hinge on which the entire American house swings from the nineteenth century into the twentieth. The chronology is tight and legible: the 1876 Centennial revived interest in early American building, McKim, Mead and White measured the New England colonial in 1877, the Colonial Revival became a national programme through the 1880s, and the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 in Chicago gave the classical case an overwhelming public demonstration. By 1895 the turned spindle looked provincial and the Tuscan column looked correct, and builders responded by swapping the porch and leaving the house alone.

The result is a specific and analytically clean condition, which is why it deserves its own node: a picturesque body with classical trim. The massing rules of the parent survive intact, one dominant mass, an irregular ridge, a wrapping porch, projecting bays, and are simply detailed with a different vocabulary. That combination is unstable, which is exactly what makes it interesting. Classical trim carries its own logic, of symmetry, of hierarchy, of a column bearing an entablature, and once a builder has bought Ionic columns he tends to want to line them up. Ten years of this pressure straightened the massing out, and the result is the Colonial Revival house, the foursquare, and eventually the whole twentieth-century American suburb. Free classic Queen Anne is the transitional fossil, and a taxonomy that omits it cannot explain how the country got from the Carson Mansion to a 1915 foursquare in eleven years.

Technologically nothing changed. The same mills that had been turning spindles retooled to produce turned Tuscan columns, dentil moulding by the linear foot, and stock Palladian window units, and shipped them from the same catalogues on the same railroads. This is worth noting precisely because it complicates the moralised story of Victorian excess giving way to classical restraint. The restraint was itself a purchase. What changed was not the mode of production but the fashion in parts, and a design platform should expect its own users to behave the same way, swapping vocabularies while the underlying generative rules stay put.

In front of one the tension is visible and often rather charming. The house is still restless, still turning a corner with a tower or a bay, still refusing to show you a symmetrical face, but the porch now has three fat Tuscan columns on a shingled or brick balustrade, the cornice has a proper run of dentils that returns on the gable rake, and there is one good Palladian window in the front gable doing the work that a spindle sunburst used to do. It looks like a house that has recently acquired opinions. The interior usually follows: the living hall becomes more formal, the openings get classical casings, and the plan starts to close back up into named rooms.

defining_characteristics: Classical porch supports: Tuscan, Doric, or Ionic columns, singly or in groups of two or three, often raised on a pedestal or a solid balustrade
A cornice carrying dentils or modillions, with the same cornice returning on the gable rake
Palladian, Venetian, or cottage windows used as the gable or stair feature
Retention of the parent's picturesque massing: one dominant mass, irregular ridge, projecting bays, and a porch that wraps a corner
Absence of turned spindlework and pierced valances anywhere on the building
Wall texture change retained, but usually reduced to shingle above and clapboard or brick below, with a proper belt course
Swan-neck or broken pediments, garlands, and swags used sparingly at the entrance
diagnostic_tells: Classical columns on an asymmetrical house is the whole diagnosis; if the facade were symmetrical it would be Colonial Revival
Dentils or modillions on a Queen Anne body, and critically, the cornice returning on the rake rather than running as a plain bargeboard
One Palladian window, placed in the principal gable or over the stair, and only one
Porch columns are grouped, two or three on a single pedestal, which is a free classic habit that classical Colonial Revival avoids
Date it late: this subtype starts around 1890 and outlives the spindlework version by a decade

distinguished_from.difference: Same massing, opposite trim, and sequential in time. Turned posts and a spindle frieze versus classical columns and a dentilled cornice; the two vocabularies effectively never appear on the same original building.

The co-parent, and the distinction is made in the massing, never in the trim. If the principal facade is symmetrical about the entrance and the ridge is a simple rectangle, it is Colonial Revival; if a dominant mass and an irregular ridge survive under the classical detail, it is free classic Queen Anne.

Both mix classical trim with picturesque massing in the same years and the same offices. Shingle Style suppresses trim into a continuous surface; free classic Queen Anne emphasises trim and keeps the wall articulated and layered.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Two systems in tension, which is the subtype's whole character. The massing follows the parent's mass hierarchy with no proportional rule; the trim follows classical proportion, since a Tuscan column has a fixed height-to-diameter ratio and a dentil course has a fixed module. Good examples let the classical rules govern locally and the picturesque rules govern globally.
typical_ratios: Column shaft height to diameter 7:1 to 9:1 for Tuscan, 8:1 to 9:1 for Ionic
Columns in groups of one to three on a pedestal 24 to 36 in high
Dentil block 2 to 3 in wide at 4 to 6 in on centre, dentil course depth 3 to 5 in
Palladian window: centre light 1.5 to 2 times the width of each side light, arch springing at the head of the side lights
Dominant mass at least 1.5 times any subordinate mass, per the parent style
Porch depth 8 to 10 ft, wrapping at least one corner
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular in the wall, regular in the porch. The porch colonnade introduces the first genuinely classical rhythm to appear on an American picturesque house, and it is usually the element that later straightens the whole composition out.

massing_affinities.note: The hipped-roof free classic cottage with a classical porch, extremely common after 1900.
The end of the road for this subtype; when the massing becomes a cube the style has become something else.

constraints.statement: Porch supports shall be classical columns of correct proportion, shaft height 7 to 9 diameters, used singly or in groups of two or three on a pedestal or solid balustrade. Turned spindlework, pierced valances, and lathe-turned posts are prohibited anywhere on the building.

The principal massing shall remain asymmetrical with one dominant mass exceeding every other by at least 50 percent, and the ridge shall be non-rectangular in plan. A symmetrical facade with classical trim is Colonial Revival and shall be classified there.
Where a dentil or modillion cornice is used it shall run continuously at the eave and shall return on the gable rake. A dentil course that stops at the corner is prohibited.
Not more than one Palladian, Venetian, or cottage window shall appear on the building, placed in the principal gable or at the stair. Repetition of the motif destroys its hierarchical function.
Wall texture change, where used, shall occur at a moulded belt course rather than at a plain butt joint, in keeping with the classical detailing of the rest of the building.

exemplars.name: Fuller House
exemplars.note: Queen Anne massing culminating in a turret, with an unusually early and complete free classic vocabulary: Palladian window, Tuscan columns on a wraparound gallery, and denticular moulding. Listed on the National Register in 1996.

exemplars.name: Rector House
exemplars.note: Built 1915-16 and documented as Free Classic Queen Anne; a late survival showing how long the subtype persisted in the interior South after the coasts had moved to Colonial Revival.

exemplars.name: William Watts Sherman House
exemplars.note: Cited only for its later alterations; the free-classic elements added in the 1880s to Richardson's original demonstrate the vocabulary shift happening on a single building.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Mark Girouard, Sweetness and Light: The Queen Anne Movement 1860-1900 (1977)
Vincent Scully, The Shingle Style and the Stick Style (1955; rev. ed. 1971)
William B. Rhoads, The Colonial Revival (1977)

proportion_packs.note: Explicit in this pack's applies_to and unchanged in principle from the parent style: the node's own hard constraint (c02) requires the dominant-mass, non-rectangular-ridge massing to survive under the classical trim, which is precisely what distinguishes this node from colonial-revival. The pack's dominance rule and datum rule still govern the body; only the porch, cornice and one gable window are classical.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to (no style-book overlay in this library lists queen-anne-free-classic at all, so any order chosen here is necessarily a judgment call). Tuscan is bound as the modal case because it is the commonest, cheapest catalog porch column of the 1890s-1910s and because the node's own typical_ratios (shaft height 7-9 diameters) sit almost exactly on Vignola's own Tuscan (7 diameters, column 14 semidiameters). No specific pattern-book transmission is documented for these stock millwork columns the way Gibbs is documented for colonial builders' inventories, so citing Vignola's base proportions directly is more honest than inventing a named source for a catalog product. The Fuller House exemplar (1905) is described as having 'Tuscan columns on a wraparound gallery,' which is the concrete case this binding covers.

JUDGMENT BINDING, bound optional and low because the node's own text names Tuscan, Doric or Ionic as alternatives without preferring one, and Ionic (8-9 diameters, matching the node's stated range) is the grander end of the same catalog phenomenon, appropriate where the porch columns are paired with the Palladian window this subtype's gable typically carries. Not primary because Tuscan is the more common case in the surviving stock.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to. Windows of 1890-1918 fall well within the pack's post-1870 large-pane band; the one-per-elevation Palladian or Venetian window this node requires (c04) takes its side-light module from the ordinary sash beside it, per this pack's transom_sidelight rule.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to — and notably NOT in trim-classical's, despite the exterior columns being classical. This is a real distinction worth preserving rather than overriding: the classical vocabulary here is exterior porch trim bought from a millwork catalog at the same moment the interior of an ordinary American house was moving toward flat-stock carpenter's trim, not a room-as-an-order derivation with a pedestal and entablature. Binding trim-classical instead would import a Federal/Georgian interior system this node's own lineage does not claim.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to, but this is the one Queen Anne variant where it is defensible over room-vernacular: the node's own text states the interior 'usually follows' the classical porch — 'the living hall becomes more formal, the openings get classical casings, and the plan starts to close back up into named rooms' — and colonial-revival, this node's explicit co-parent and successor, IS in room-harmonic's applies_to. The formalizing pressure the node describes is exactly the pressure that produces treatise-proportioned rooms rather than span-constrained ones.

german-fachwerk.name: German Fachwerk

revival_periods.note: Heimatstil and Altdeutsch revival; Fachwerk adopted as a national-romantic emblem and applied decoratively over masonry, which is where the false 'applied half-timbering' of the whole later revival world begins.
Reaches Anglo-America mainly through the English Tudor Revival, by which point the frame is a nailed-on pattern with no structural meaning.
Post-war reconstruction of bombed Fachwerk towns (Hildesheim, Frankfurt, Nuremberg) and a continuing living trade of Zimmerleute repairing and building new frames.

geography.hearth: Hesse, Franconia, Lower Saxony and the Middle Rhine

lineage.note: From the mid-16th century the Weser and Franconian carpenters carve rosettes, Vitruvian scroll, diamond points and dentil bands into the sill beams and console brackets, and letter Latin inscriptions across them. The vocabulary is quoted from printed sheets; the frame behind it is unchanged medieval carpentry.

description.short: The exposed load-bearing timber frame of central Germany, in which the pattern of posts, rails and braces on the wall is not decoration but a legible diagram of how the building stands up.
description.long:
Fachwerk is a solution to an inversion that most people get backwards. In medieval central Germany timber was not cheap and infill was: a straight, sound oak of structural size took a century to grow and had to be felled, hauled, hewn and jointed by a skilled trade, whereas clay, straw, riven laths and later brick were locally free and could be handled by anyone. The rational building therefore uses as little timber as possible and puts it exactly where the loads are, filling the gaps with the cheap stuff. The result is a wall made of framed panels — Fächer, hence Fachwerk — and the panel size, roughly 0.9 to 1.3 metres, is simply the interval at which posts have to stand to carry the storey above. Everything a visitor reads as picturesque pattern is a load path.

The technical history is one decisive change. The early frame is Ständerbau: single posts running from the ground sill to the eave through every storey, which requires timbers of great length and makes floors an insertion into a fixed cage. From roughly 1400 the trade shifts to Stockwerkbau, storey-by-storey framing, in which each floor is a complete self-contained frame standing on the one below. That change is what produces the German street as we know it. Because the floor beams of the upper storey run out past the frame below and carry the next frame on their ends, each storey can jetty forward two to four hundred millimetres. Jettying stiffens the joint, gains floor area over a taxed ground footprint, and shelters the wall beneath from rain — and, over four storeys on a narrow medieval street, it closes the sky. Where the beam ends project they are carved into Knaggen, brackets, and the sill beam that runs across them becomes the building's inscription band, carrying the owner's name, the date, and a verse from Luther's Bible.

Regional dialects are sharp enough to locate a building within fifty kilometres. Lower Saxon framing is close-studded, tall and vertical, with heavy carved sills and few braces on the face. Franconian framing signs itself with figures — the Wilder Mann, a man-shaped assembly of braces standing in a panel; the Andreaskreuz, the St Andrew's cross; the Mann and the Halber Mann. Alemannic framing in the south-west uses long, shallow, sweeping curved braces running through several panels. Middle German framing on the Rhine and in Hesse is squarer and more heavily painted, often in ox-blood red with white panels. None of these are ornamental choices in origin: they are different regional answers to how you triangulate a rectangular frame against wind, and they hardened into signatures.

To walk into a Fachwerk house is to be inside its structure with nothing intervening. The frame is exposed indoors as well as out; the beams are low, the ceiling is a grid of joists, and the floors are not level anywhere because a five-hundred-year-old oak frame has settled differentially at every joint. The rooms are small and warm and dark — small because a panel wall wants small openings, warm because the Stube was heated by a masonry stove fed from the passage so no smoke entered the room, and dark because the windows are a few paired casements in the middle of a wall of clay. What you feel is a building that is entirely legible: you can see, from a chair, exactly how every load in the room reaches the ground.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing timber frame fully exposed on the exterior, with non-structural infill panels (Gefach) of wattle-and-daub or brick nogging
Storey-by-storey (Stockwerk) framing above about 1400, each storey a complete frame standing on the one below
Jettied upper storeys carried on projecting floor beam ends, with carved brackets (Knaggen) beneath
A carved and inscribed sill beam (Schwelle) at each jetty carrying name, date and text
Visible triangulating braces — Andreaskreuz, Wilder Mann, curved Alemannic braces — as the regional signature
The frame stands on a masonry or brick plinth (Sockel) clear of the ground; timber never touches the earth
Steep tile or slate roof, 45-60 degrees, with the frame's ridge and eave lines expressed
diagnostic_tells: Every infill panel framed on all four sides — if a timber runs across a panel without a joint at each end, the frame is fake
Floor beam ends visibly projecting at each storey line, with a carved sill beam running across them
Braces meeting posts at real joints (mortice-and-tenon with a visible peg), not butted
Panels of daub or brick, whitewashed or ochre, sitting proud of or flush with the timber — never behind it
A masonry plinth of at least 300 mm between grade and the bottom sill

distinguished_from.difference: English framing is oak on oak but uses wider panels, square panelling in the west and close studding in the east, has far less carved and lettered sill decoration, and almost never develops the four-storey jettied street front. English work also whitewashes or limewashes the timber as often as it leaves it dark.

The Low German hall house is built in Fachwerk but is a plan type, not a framing system: three-aisled, gable-entered, house and byre in one undivided hall. Fachwerk is what it is made of; the hall house is what it is.

Revival half-timbering is applied to a sheathed frame or a masonry wall and carries no load. The diagnostic is panels that are not framed on four sides, braces that do not reach a joint, and timbers of uniform machined section.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Structural, entirely. The panel (Gefach) is the module: post spacing of about 0.9-1.3 m, set by what a floor beam of available section will span onto the wall plate. Storey height is set by the length of a post plus the depth of the beam. The whole facade is a grid of these panels, and any decoration is fitted into the grid rather than imposed on it.
typical_ratios: Panel width 0.9-1.3 m; panel height 0.8-1.6 m; panel proportion roughly 1:1 to 2:3
Timber section 120-200 mm square for posts, 180-280 mm deep for floor beams
Jetty projection 200-400 mm per storey
Roof pitch 45-60 degrees; storey heights diminishing upward by roughly 10-15 percent
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: A visible, countable grid. Openings are made by omitting a panel or a pair of panels, so window position is always a whole number of panels from a corner, and the fenestration can never float freely on the wall.

massing_affinities.note: The German market square and the Fachwerk street are party-walled or near-touching rows; the type is urban before it is rural.
In the towns the narrow taxed lot turns the gable to the square, with the frame's jetties stepping out on the way up.
The rural Fachwerk cottage and the smallest artisan houses.
The Franconian and Hessian courtyard farm strings house, barn and stable in framed ranges around a yard.
Larger Weser and Westphalian houses reach a two-wing plan, though the frame limits range depth.

constraints.statement: Every infill panel must be framed on all four sides by timber, and every brace must terminate in a joint at both ends. A timber that dies into a panel is ornament, not frame, and is prohibited.
The bottom sill must sit on a masonry or fired-brick plinth at least 300 mm above finished grade, with a drip. Timber in contact with earth is the single commonest cause of loss in surviving frames.

test.note: Tests the plinth-height clause. 'With a drip' (a detail requirement) stays prose.

constraints.statement: Jetty projection between 200 and 400 mm per storey, carried on the ends of the floor beams of the storey below. A jetty greater than about 400 mm requires a bracket (Knagge) at every beam end.

test.note: Tests the 200-400mm jetty range. The >400mm bracket (Knagge) requirement is a conditional follow-on rule and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch not less than 45 degrees for tile or slate. Eave overhang at least 400 mm to keep driving rain off the daub panels; the gable verge at least 250 mm.

test.note: Tests the roof-pitch clause. Two further numeric clauses in the same sentence -- eave overhang at least 400mm and gable verge at least 250mm -- are distinct overhang measurements the vocabulary does not separate from each other and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Carving, colour and lettering belong on the sill beam, the corner posts, the brackets and the door frame. The infill panels stay plain. Ornamenting the panel rather than the timber inverts the whole logic of the wall.

exemplars.name: Fachwerkmuseum im Standerbau, Wordgasse 3
exemplars.note: Dendro-dated to the mid-14th century; among the oldest surviving half-timbered houses in Germany and a rare surviving Standerbau (through-post) frame.

exemplars.name: Rathaus
exemplars.note: Built 1512-1516; the canonical late-Gothic Hessian jettied frame on a stone arcaded base.

exemplars.name: Rathaus
exemplars.note: Odenwald; jettied frame carried on oak posts over an open market floor.

exemplars.name: Knochenhaueramtshaus
exemplars.note: Butchers' guild house; destroyed by bombing in 1945 and reconstructed 1986-1989 to the original frame drawings. Cited with that caveat.

sources: Gerner, Fachwerk: Entwicklung, Instandsetzung, Neubau
Stiewe, Fachwerkhauser in Deutschland: Konstruktion, Gestalt und Nutzung
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World
Rudofsky, Architecture Without Architects

proportion_packs.note: Fachwerk is a genuine box-frame system and this node is listed directly in the pack's applies_to. The pack's depth_and_pile rule (16-22 ft clear, one joist span, no interior bearing wall) matches the hall-single-cell and linear-ell-farmhouse massing this style favors, and its wing_strategy rule (a rear or ell frame narrower and lower than the main one) matches the courtyard-farm growth pattern described here. Caveat: the pack's own module is calibrated to the English/Anglo-American bent-to-bent bay (16-20 ft), an order of magnitude coarser than Fachwerk's own Gefach panel (0.9-1.3 m / 3-4 ft, stated in this node's own proportional_system) — use it for the building's overall framing bay and depth, not for the individual panel grid, which none of the 36 packs cover.

The Stube and chamber rooms of a Fachwerk house are exactly the daylight- and span-limited vernacular room this pack models: small, low, lit from a panel wall that 'wants small openings.' The pack's hearth_position and daylight_strategy rules match this node's own account of a masonry-stove-heated Stube reached off a smoke-free passage.

italianate-american.name: Italianate (American)

geography.hearth: Delaware Valley and the Hudson Valley

lineage.note: Transmitted at two removes: the Roman campagna farmhouse observed by English painters and travellers, systematised by Charles Barry and J. C. Loudon, then reprinted by Downing. American builders never saw the source. Typed as reference, not descent: American builders never saw the source, so no construction practice was transmitted and the kit must not cascade.
The palazzo cornice, the quoin, and the arcaded window are quoted; the Renaissance proportional system is not carried over at all.
The campanile and the low hipped roof are lifted from Tuscan farm groups as a picturesque motif.
Direct practice inheritance. Same pattern books, same authors, same carpenters, same balloon frame, same commercial millwork supply; Downing published Gothic and Italian designs on facing pages.
Against the temple front, the rigid symmetry, and the low horizontal entablature, replaced by a wide shadowed eave and a plan free to grow.

description.short: The most-built American style of the mid-nineteenth century: a low-hipped, wide-eaved, heavily bracketed villa or townhouse whose round-arched windows and optional tower promised a Mediterranean life to people living through Ohio winters.
description.long:
Italianate is what happens when the picturesque argument wins and then needs a version that ordinary people can afford and that looks prosperous rather than pious. John Notman's Riverside at Burlington, New Jersey (1839) is the usual American starting point, and Downing's books carried the type outward, but the style's real career belongs to the two decades after 1850, when it became the default dress for everything from a Brooklyn brownstone row to an Iowa farmhouse to a cast-iron commercial block on Broadway. It outnumbers every other Victorian style in the American building stock, and it is the one whose parts a modern kit would need first.

The technological explanation is nearly complete. The bracket is the diagnostic element of the style, and the bracket exists because a steam-powered band saw could cut a scrolled profile from a plank in seconds and a railroad could ship a crate of identical brackets anywhere in the country. The same is true of the arched window head, the moulded hood, the turned porch post, and the cast-iron cresting. Before 1840 the ornamental content of an American house was limited by the hours of a skilled hand; after 1850 it was limited by the owner's freight bill. Italianate is the first style whose visual density is a purchasing decision rather than a craft decision, and this is precisely the condition that a kit-of-parts platform reproduces. That the style then multiplied brackets past the point of coherence is a warning worth heeding.

Culturally the style traded on a specific fantasy. The Italian villa in the Anglo-American imagination of the 1840s was the house of a cultivated gentleman of leisure with a library, a view, and a tolerance for irregularity; Downing praised the mode precisely because it permitted a plan to grow by addition without embarrassment, and because its campanile gave a house a vertical accent without the ecclesiastical baggage of a Gothic spire. It suited a merchant class that wanted to look landed without looking aristocratic, and it suited the fact that American families were adding rooms as they added money. The moral seriousness of the Gothic argument survives here in weakened form: architecture still shapes character, but the character it now shapes is worldly, cultivated, and comfortable.

What the style actually does to a body standing in front of it is manufacture shadow. The eave projects two or three feet, and the brackets under it cut that projection into a rhythm of dark and light that changes hour by hour; the window hoods repeat the trick in miniature; the whole facade is legible from a distance because it is drawn in shadow rather than in line. Inside, the tall narrow round-headed windows drop a column of light almost to the floor, the parlour ceilings run eleven to fourteen feet, and the effect is of vertical, dim, generous space, cool in an August afternoon and impossible to heat in January. The tower, where there is one, is usually a disappointment: a stair, a small room, and a view that justified the whole expense in the owner's mind.

defining_characteristics: Low-pitched hipped or shallow gabled roof, 3:12 to 5:12, with the roof visually suppressed
Wide projecting eave, 18 to 36 in, carried on paired or single sawn brackets
Tall narrow windows with round-arched or segmental heads, frequently paired, with projecting hoods or moulded surrounds
Horizontal emphasis throughout: string courses, quoins, and clapboard or rusticated masonry courses reading across the elevation
An asymmetrical or additive plan permitted but not required; the style works on a symmetrical box as readily as on an L
Ornament concentrated at the eave, the openings, and the porch, and manufactured rather than carved
Optional campanile or cupola as the vertical accent
diagnostic_tells: Brackets under a wide eave with a low roof: Italianate. Add a mansard over the same brackets and it is Second Empire, which is the single most common misidentification
Round or segmental window heads with hoods, versus the pointed heads of Gothic Revival and the flat lintels of Greek Revival

If the tower stands in the reentrant angle of an L and rises a full storey above the main cornice, it is an Italianate villa; a tower rising from the centre of a symmetrical front is more likely Second Empire or Renaissance Revival
Cast-iron or wooden porch posts with chamfered or turned shafts and scrolled brackets at the head, never classical columns with entasis
The roof is nearly invisible from the street; if you can read the roof shape from the sidewalk, reconsider the identification

distinguished_from.difference: Second Empire is Italianate plus a mansard roof, and often literally so: the same bracketed cornice, the same arched windows, the same plan. The mansard is the whole difference, and it converts the roof from a suppressed element into the dominant one.

Renaissance Revival is academically symmetrical, uses a modillioned or dentilled cornice rather than sawn brackets, alternates pediment types by storey, and diminishes floor heights upward on a rule. Italianate is looser, bracketed, and indifferent to the palazzo's proportional discipline.
Opposite geometry on shared parentage: horizontal versus vertical, round versus pointed, low roof versus steep roof, bracket versus bargeboard.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by the eave, not by a module. The bracket spacing establishes the only repeating rhythm in the building, and every other element is sized against the cornice depth. Where a tower exists, the tower height sets the vertical hierarchy.
typical_ratios: Eave projection 18 to 36 in; cornice fascia depth 1/2 to 2/3 of the projection
Bracket spacing 24 to 48 in on centre, with paired brackets at corners and at the ends of each bay
Window height to width 2.5:1 to 3:1, with paired windows read as a single opening
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12
Tower rises 1.0 to 1.5 storeys above the main cornice
First-floor ceiling 11 to 14 ft, diminishing 8 to 15 percent per storey above
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Regular bracket rhythm laid over a possibly irregular plan. The brackets march at constant spacing across projections and recesses alike, which is exactly what unifies an additive elevation.

massing_affinities.note: The full Italian villa: L-plan with the campanile at the inner angle.
The brownstone row, quantitatively the largest population of Italianate buildings in America.
Works only if the pitches stay low; a steep cross gable pulls the building toward Gothic Revival.
The bracketed cube, extremely common in the Midwest and the direct ancestor of the 1900s foursquare.

constraints.statement: Eave projection shall be between 18 and 36 in measured from the wall face, and brackets shall be spaced between 24 and 48 in on centre and shall be paired at every external corner. A bracket spacing greater than 48 in reads as ornament rather than as rhythm and fails the style.

test.note: Tests the eave-projection range. Bracket spacing (24-48 in on centre) and the paired-at-corners requirement have no matching bracket-spacing variable and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Principal roof pitch shall not exceed 5:12. The roof must be substantially concealed by the cornice when viewed from a point 40 ft from the facade at eye height.

test.note: Tests the pitch ceiling. The 40 ft eye-height cornice-concealment condition is a visibility fact with no matching variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Window heads on any single elevation shall be of one family only: round-arched, segmental, or flat with a moulded hood. Mixing round and pointed heads on one building is forbidden.

A tower or campanile shall be provided only where a stair, a hall, or a room occupies it at every level. A tower that is a hollow ornament is prohibited; this is the single most common failure in modern Italianate work.
Porch depth shall be not less than 7 ft where a veranda is used, and the porch cornice shall carry brackets at the same spacing as the main eave, or at exactly half that spacing.

test.note: Tests the veranda-depth minimum. The porch-cornice-bracket-spacing-matching-the-main-eave (or exactly half) clause has no matching bracket-spacing variable and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Edward King House
exemplars.note: Richard Upjohn, 1845-47. Downing published it in The Architecture of Country Houses as one of the most successful specimens of the Italian style in the United States, which made it the national template.

exemplars.name: Morse-Libby House (Victoria Mansion)
exemplars.note: Henry Austin, 1858-60. Brownstone Italianate villa with a tower and an intact Gustave Herter interior; the most completely preserved American example.

exemplars.name: Litchfield Villa
exemplars.note: Alexander Jackson Davis, 1854-57. Davis's most ambitious Italianate villa, and a demonstration that the same architect drove both branches of the picturesque.

sources: Andrew Jackson Downing, The Architecture of Country Houses (1850)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)
William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: Technology and the Picturesque (1978)

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding: the pack's own applies_to names the italianate-villa child directly but not this parent style. Bound anyway because the parent's own proportional_system states its symmetry as 'balanced-asymmetrical' and its bay_rhythm as 'a constant bracket rhythm laid over a possibly irregular plan' - this pack's dominant-mass-with-subordinate-accents method, with the bracket line standing in for the accent hierarchy. The style's other child, italianate-townhouse, instead binds facade-classical directly, since the party wall forces the symmetrical half of what this parent's own text says the style 'works... as readily' on either register of.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the glass-light module of the tall narrow round-arched sash that is the style's most consistent diagnostic tell across all three registers (villa, townhouse, farmhouse).

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the void before the arched or segmental head and hood are applied to it - door and window sizing taken from the storey - though the round or segmental arch itself, and the frequent paired-window treatment the style's own diagnostic tells single out, are beyond what the pack's default rectangle models and are carried by the style's own constraints instead (c01, c03).

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and a close numeric match: the style's own typical_ratios give 'first-floor ceiling 11 to 14 ft, diminishing 8 to 15 percent per storey above,' which sits inside this pack's general diminution model without needing the wider allowance the style's academically-diminished Renaissance Revival cousin requires.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, but bound at its plainest register: the style's own lineage record is explicit that although the palazzo cornice and the arcaded window are quoted from italian-renaissance, 'the Renaissance proportional system is not carried over at all.' Read this pack as supplying the general wall-as-pedestal-field-entablature division rather than a specific order's fully worked profile family - the style's real ornament is the sawn bracket, which this pack does not model (see report).

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and the style's own aka list ('Tuscan Villa Style') invites it directly - but bound low and optional rather than as a governing order, because the style's own diagnostic tells are explicit that porch posts are 'cast-iron or wooden... with chamfered or turned shafts and scrolled brackets at the head, never classical columns with entasis.' Where this pack is used at all it should govern incidental elements at the plain end of the classical apparatus - a quoined corner, a door surround - never the porch, which the style's own text rules out.

Judgment binding, chosen over room-harmonic for the same reason trim-classical is bound at its plainest register above: the style's own lineage record states the Renaissance proportional system was not carried over, and its own interior description (via the villa child's text) is of loose, generous, additive space - 'the plan is generous and slightly loose' - rather than rooms set out to Palladian ratios.

cape-cod-colonial.name: Cape Cod Colonial

revival_periods.note: Royal Barry Wills, who founded his Boston practice in 1925, made the Cape the single most-built American house form of the post-war years; the FHA minimum house of 1946–55 is essentially a Cape.

geography.hearth: Cape Cod and the outer Massachusetts coast, where the wind is the governing design load

lineage.note: The one-and-a-half-storey cottage with a low plate and a loft in the roof is the English yeoman cottage, simplified and stiffened against the North Atlantic.

description.short: A one-and-a-half-storey, low-eaved, central-chimney cottage built to present as little surface as possible to the wind, and grown one bay at a time as a family could afford it.
description.long:
The Cape is the most economical house New England ever produced, and every one of its features is a consequence of that. There is no second storey, so there is no second plate, no second floor frame and no stair worth the name — just a steep winder beside the chimney to a loft under the rafters. The eave sits eight to nine and a half feet above the floor, which puts the head of the first-floor window within a foot of the cornice and leaves nothing for a frieze. The roof runs forty to forty-five degrees, steep enough to shed snow and to make the loft habitable, shallow enough that it does not act as a sail. And the whole building hunkers: no raised basement, no water table of consequence, no projections, no overhangs beyond a four-to-six-inch rake. On the outer Cape, where the sand offers nothing to anchor to and the wind comes off open water, a house shaped like this is a house that is still there in a hundred years.

What makes the Cape genuinely interesting as a kit of parts is that it is a growth grammar rather than a single form, and the grammar is legible on the facade. A quarter Cape has a door and one window. A half Cape has a door at one end and two windows beside it. A three-quarter Cape adds a single window on the other side of the door. A full Cape has two windows each side of a centred door. Families built the half and added to it as money and children arrived, moving the door or reframing it toward the centre. The chimney stays put through all of this, which means that in a half or three-quarter Cape the chimney is not centred on the facade — and that off-centre stack is the honest signature of an unfinished growth sequence, not a mistake.

The name is not local. Timothy Dwight, president of Yale, coined 'Cape Cod house' after travelling the peninsula in 1800; the description was published posthumously in his Travels in New England and New York (1821–22). The people who built them called them houses.

Inside, the Cape is small, warm and unexpectedly good. Two rooms flank the stack on the ground floor with the entry porch between; ceilings run seven feet; the loft above is reached by the winder and lit by gable windows only. The rooms are square, the fireplaces are close, and everything is within a few steps of everything else. There is a reason the twentieth century could not leave it alone: the plan is close to irreducible, and a family of four fits into eight hundred square feet of it without friction.

defining_characteristics: One to one-and-a-half storeys with no full second floor; the upper rooms are within the roof volume
Eave 8 ft 0 in – 9 ft 6 in above finished floor, with the first-floor window head within 14 in of the cornice and no frieze
Central chimney on the ridge (full Cape) or off-centre where the house is a half or three-quarter Cape
Side-gable roof, 40–45 degrees, of wood shingle, with a shallow rake and no soffit overhang beyond about 6 in
Facade organized by the quarter / half / three-quarter / full growth grammar, with the door offset until the plan is complete
Wall of clapboard or, on the outer Cape, unpainted white-cedar shingle laid at 5–6 in exposure
No dormers, no porch, no projections; the gable ends are blind or carry one small window each
diagnostic_tells: Window heads almost touching the cornice — the single most reliable Cape tell, and the one the revival always gets wrong
A door that is not centred, with a chimney that is not centred either but in a different place
The entire house reads as roof: the wall is roughly one-third of the elevation height, the roof two-thirds
Rake trim of 4–6 in with a plain 6–12 in return at the corner, not a full modillion cornice return
No basement showing above grade; the sill sits within 18 in of the ground

distinguished_from.difference: The revival raises the eave to clear a full-height second-floor knee wall, adds a row of gabled or shed dormers on the front slope, uses an 8:12 to 10:12 pitch, gives the house a centred door with sidelights and a symmetrical five-bay front regardless of the plan behind it, and attaches a garage. Original Capes have no front dormers. If there are dormers on the street elevation, it is a twentieth-century house.
The saltbox is two full storeys at the front with an asymmetric roof; the Cape is one-and-a-half storeys with a symmetrical one. A Cape can have a rear lean-to and remain a Cape.
The 1935–50 minimal-traditional house shares the low eave and small footprint but has a shallower roof (4:12–6:12), no central chimney, a side or end chimney if any, and picture or paired windows.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The chimney stack plus two flanking rooms of a single frame bay each, with the roof sized to make the loft usable at the ridge.
typical_ratios: Full Cape 32–38 ft wide × 26–30 ft deep; half Cape 20–24 ft wide
Eave 8 ft 0 in – 9 ft 6 in; ridge 18–22 ft above grade
Wall:roof height ratio on the front elevation about 1:2
Ground-floor ceiling 6 ft 10 in – 7 ft 6 in; loft 6 ft 0 in – 7 ft 0 in at the ridge
Roof rise:run 9:12 to 12:12
Window opening 2 ft 8 in – 3 ft 2 in × 4 ft 4 in – 5 ft 0 in
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: One, two, three or four windows plus a door, in the growth sequence quarter–half–three-quarter–full. The rhythm is a record of household economics, not a composition.

massing_affinities.note: The full Cape plan: two rooms flanking the stack.
The half Cape, one room and a stack.
A Cape with a rear lean-to; the front eave stays low.

constraints.statement: Eave height 8 ft 0 in to 9 ft 6 in above finished first floor, and the head of the first-floor window not more than 14 in below the underside of the cornice. This single rule separates every real Cape from every revival Cape.

test.note: Tests the window-head-to-cornice clause. Eave height (8ft-9ft6in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: No dormers on the front (street) roof slope. Rear-slope dormers are a permissible later addition; front dormers are not part of the type.
Roof pitch 9:12 to 12:12. Below 8:12 the loft is unusable and the house reads as minimal-traditional; above 12:12 it reads as a First Period two-storey house cut down.
Rake and eave trim not more than 6 in wide, returning 6–12 in at the corner. Full modillion cornices and deep returns belong to Georgian work.

test.note: The corner-return dimension (6-12in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof and wall overhangs kept under 8 in on exposed coastal sites; shingle exposure 5–6 in; sill within 18 in of grade.

test.note: Tests the overhang clause. Shingle exposure and sill height are the statement's other numeric claims and stay prose.

exemplars.name: Atwood-Higgins House
exemplars.note: Built c. 1730 as a half house and expanded to a full Cape in the late 18th or early 19th century — the growth grammar preserved in one building. Now within Cape Cod National Seashore.

exemplars.name: Jabez Wilder House
exemplars.note: Documented by HABS; a bow-roof ('rainbow roof') Cape, the coastal variant in which the rafters are given a slight convex curve. Date is traditional and not independently confirmed.

exemplars.name: Dillingham House
exemplars.note: Among the earliest Cape-form dwellings on the peninsula; substantially enlarged in the 18th century, so the original half-house core must be read through later fabric.

sources: Abbott Lowell Cummings, The Framed Houses of Massachusetts Bay, 1625–1725 (1979)
J. Frederick Kelly, Early Domestic Architecture of Connecticut (1924)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)
Ernest Allen Connally, 'The Cape Cod House: An Introductory Study', Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians 19 (1960)

proportion_packs.note: The bay still generates the plan -- two rooms flanking the stack, the winder beside it -- but the storey is cut to one-and-a-half rather than two, which is a roof decision (see the massing entry), not a bay decision. The quarter/half/three-quarter/full growth grammar this node leads with is literally this pack's own resolution philosophy for material scarcity in practice: 'hold the bay at 16-20 ft and add bays rather than stretching one, which is what every historic plan type is a record of' (timber-bay's own material-availability conflict entry) -- a Cape is that principle built as a household's actual construction history, one bay added at a time as money allowed. No facade-system pack is bound: the door is deliberately off-centre until the growth sequence completes, which is the opposite of a composed front.

Roof pitch (9:12-12:12) follows the habitable-loft-versus-wind-load logic this node states directly, and it is a lower, steadier pitch than the two-storey types because the rafter is shorter over a smaller frame. The eave is this pack's near-zero default (6 in or less) -- and uniquely among the four New England nodes bound in this pass, the Cape KEEPS that flush eave through its whole 1700-1850 run rather than acquiring an 18th-century boxed cornice, which is exactly why 'window heads almost touching the cornice' survives as this node's single most reliable diagnostic tell (its own words) long after garrison and saltbox houses had picked up Georgian trim.

Governs the light-count date sequence across this node's unusually long 1700-1850 floruit, and its window_head_masonry rule (head at ~0.78-0.82 of storey) is the arithmetic behind this node's own hard constraint (c01): window head within 14 in of the cornice on an 8-9.5 ft eave.
Bound for the single head-datum rule only, as on the other three nodes in this family; the treatise's 13:6 window ratio is not this tradition's governing figure.

The hall-single-cell (half Cape) and hall-and-parlor (full Cape) room logic is identical to new-england-colonial's, and the pack's own room_adjacency_overrides note -- 'the whole Anglo-American folk-house catalogue is this arithmetic' -- is a direct statement of the growth grammar this node is organized around.

germanic-vernacular.name: Germanic Vernacular

description.short: The half-timbered Fachwerk town house and the great hall-house of the north German plain, and their descendants in Pennsylvania stone.
description.long:
German building culture is organized around the visible timber frame — an infilled skeleton whose geometry is the architecture — and around the integration of dwelling, storage, and livestock under a single very large roof. Both traits reflect a scarcity of good timber and an abundance of long winters.

In Pennsylvania this tradition met abundant limestone and reorganized itself: the frame went away, the massive wall arrived, and the bank house with its forebay carried the section logic of the German farm into an American landscape. The style disappeared within two generations; the section survived.

defining_characteristics: Expressed timber frame with infill panels as the primary wall system
House, byre, and storage integrated under one large roof
Very steep pitches sized to snow and to the roof's storage volume
Banked construction using slope for a sheltered lower level
Durable section logic surviving the loss of surface identity

scottish-baronial.name: Scottish Baronial

revival_periods.note: A late municipal and hotel phase — railway hotels, distilleries and civic buildings across Scotland — after the country-house market had moved on.

geography.hearth: The Borders and Aberdeenshire, spreading from Abbotsford and from the Aberdeen granite trade

lineage.note: The actual practice. William Atkinson at Abbotsford, William Burn and David Bryce after him were classically trained men running Regency and early Victorian offices; the plans, the construction, the sash windows behind the mullions and the servant-wing planning are all of their own century. Baronial is a costume worn by a Regency house.

Quoted twice over. The corbelled bartizan with a conical roof reached Scotland from France during the Auld Alliance and the sixteenth-century royal works, and the nineteenth-century revival then quoted the result while also going back to the Loire directly — Bryce's Fettes College of 1863-69 is explicitly a Loire chateau crossed with a Scots tower house.

Contemporaneous, same clients, same builders, overlapping detail. Baronial is what the Gothic Revival becomes north of the Tweed when it takes its motifs from Scottish tower houses instead of English parish churches.

description.short: The nineteenth-century revival of the Scottish tower house — crow-stepped gables, corbelled bartizans with conical roofs and harled or granite walls — composed picturesquely and built with entirely Victorian technology.
description.long:
The vocabulary is genuinely old and the buildings are not, and keeping those two facts apart is the whole discipline of this node. Between roughly 1540 and 1680 Scotland built several thousand tower houses and fortified lairds' houses whose upper works were remarkably inventive: corbel courses stepping the wall outward at the head, angle turrets carried on those corbels and roofed with little conical caps, crow-stepped gables to give a mason a foothold and a wind-resistant edge, harled rubble walls to shed driven rain, and small openings placed for defence and for warmth. Craigievar, completed in 1626, is the finished form. That tradition faded after 1700 and was over as a living practice long before the revival.

What brought it back was literature and monarchy. Walter Scott rebuilt Abbotsford between 1817 and 1824 with William Atkinson as his architect, assembling salvaged fragments and antiquarian details around what is in plan a comfortable Regency house, and the Waverley novels then made the Scottish past a saleable commodity across Europe. Victoria and Albert completed the transformation by building Balmoral in 1853-56 to William Smith of Aberdeen's designs, and thereafter every Scottish landowner, brewer, shipping magnate and jute manufacturer who wanted to look established built baronial. William Burn and his partner David Bryce industrialised it: Bryce alone produced well over a hundred houses in which a rigorous Victorian service plan — separate approach for the family, a servants' wing with a bell system, a business room next to the front door — is wrapped in turrets and crow-steps.

What it reacted against was the Georgian classical box, which in Scotland had been unusually good and unusually pervasive; the Baronial argument was that a Scottish house should look Scottish, and it was made at exactly the moment Scotland was losing the last of its institutional distinctiveness. Highland clearance and Highland romance are the same decades, which is uncomfortable and true, and the style's association with sporting estates comes directly from it.

Standing in front of a good baronial house is a study in how vertical incident works against mass. The wall is plain and hard — squared rubble or Aberdeen granite ashlar, sometimes harled — with small windows and no ornament for two storeys, and then everything happens at once at the top: corbel courses, turrets, crow-steps, chimney stacks, dormers breaking the wall head with carved pediments. The eye is pulled up and around a corner, and the composition never resolves into a single frontal view, which is the picturesque intent. Indoors the illusion drops immediately. The rooms are large, square, well-lit, plastered and comfortable, laid out with a Victorian sense of circulation, and the only genuinely medieval thing about them is the draught.

defining_characteristics: Crow-stepped (corbie-stepped) gables as the standard gable treatment, with the steps of squared stone and no barge board
Corbelled angle turrets (bartizans) carried out from the wall head on projecting corbel courses and capped with conical or ogee roofs
Walls of squared rubble, granite ashlar or harled rubble, plain and unornamented through the lower storeys
A dominant tower or stair tower, usually placed asymmetrically at a reentrant angle, rising above the general roofline with a caphouse
Ornament and incident concentrated entirely at the wall head: corbel tables, crenellated parapets with rounds, carved dormer pediments breaking the eaves
Steeply pitched slate roofs with tall corbelled chimney stacks
Picturesque asymmetrical massing composed to be read obliquely and in the round, over a rationally planned Victorian interior
diagnostic_tells: Crow-steps and a conical-roofed corbelled turret on the same building — the combination is diagnostic of Scotland and of nowhere else
A corbel course stepping the wall outward at the head, so the top of the building is wider than its base
Dormers rising through the eaves with carved and dated stone pediments, frequently initialled for the owner
Two plain storeys of unornamented wall below a wall head that is entirely ornament — a vertical distribution the English Gothic Revival never uses

Against the sixteenth-century originals: revival buildings have large plate-glass or two-pane sashes, regular floor levels, generous stairs and a service wing; a genuine tower house has tiny openings, a turnpike stair and no corridor anywhere

distinguished_from.difference: Different quoted source. Gothic Revival takes pointed arches, tracery, buttresses and bargeboards from English parish churches and manor houses; Baronial takes crow-steps, corbelling, bartizans and harling from Scottish tower houses, and almost never uses a pointed window. Where a house has both, it was designed after 1860 by someone working from photographs.

The chateau uses the conical-roofed turret at much larger scale on a symmetrical or courtyard plan, with elaborate dormers, carved stone panels and steep pavilion roofs. Baronial is smaller-boned, harder-surfaced, deliberately austere below the wall head, and asymmetrical by intent.

The American Hunt-Vanderbilt manner is Loire chateau at palace scale in fine limestone with lavish carving; Baronial is granite or harl, plain-walled, and Scottish in its motifs. Chateauesque is about wealth; Baronial is about ancestry, real or claimed.

proportional_system.governing_logic: None classical. Composition is picturesque — balance of masses read obliquely, with a dominant vertical accent — laid over a plan generated by Victorian circulation and service requirements. The tower's height against the main block is the only ratio that must be controlled.
typical_ratios: Tower height above the main ridge not less than one full storey (3.0-4.5 m)
Bartizan diameter 1.2-2.0 m, corbelled out 450-750 mm from the wall face, with a conical roof of 55-65 degrees
Crow-step tread 300-450 mm, rise 200-300 mm, cut in squared stone
Main roof pitch 45-55 degrees in slate
Window proportion 1.6:1 to 2:1 height to width, noticeably smaller in relation to wall area than any contemporary classical house — glazed area 10-16 percent of elevation
Wall thickness expressed at reveals of 300-450 mm
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Deliberately irregular. Openings are grouped by internal function and by the demands of the composition; the only regularity is within a single flat range of wall, and even there it is often broken by a dormer or turret placed for silhouette.

massing_affinities.note: The style's native massing — an agglomeration of blocks, towers and turrets composed for the oblique view.
The tower at the reentrant angle holding the stair, exactly the Italianate campanile diagram in a different costume.
The Z-plan and L-plan tower house, with a tower at diagonally opposite corners, is the historical Scottish version of this figure and the one the revival most often quotes.
Where a service court is enclosed behind the show front, as at Balmoral.

constraints.statement: Bartizans and turrets must be corbelled out on a visible course of projecting stones. A turret sitting on a bracket, a cantilevered slab, or nothing at all is the commonest and most immediately visible failure of the style.

Ornament is confined to the wall head — corbel table, parapet, dormer heads, chimney caps. The lower two storeys must remain plain walling. Distributing ornament evenly up the elevation destroys the composition.
Pointed arches, tracery and English bargeboards are forbidden; openings are square-headed or, rarely, semicircular. Gables are crow-stepped or plainly coped, never boarded.
Glazed area not to exceed roughly 16 percent of elevation, and the dominant tower must rise at least one full storey above the main ridge.

test.note: Tests the glazed-area ceiling. 'The dominant tower must rise at least one full storey above the main ridge' stays prose -- no vocabulary variable compares a tower's height to the main ridge.

constraints.statement: Harl or dense squared rubble in lime mortar, detailed for driven rain: deep reveals, weathered copes, and no exposed horizontal ledges. Cement harl on a rubble wall fails in this climate faster than anywhere else in Britain.

exemplars.name: Abbotsford House
exemplars.note: Built 1817-24 by William Atkinson for Sir Walter Scott, incorporating salvaged fragments and antiquarian details. The founding building of the style and the clearest case of a Regency plan in baronial dress.

exemplars.name: Balmoral Castle
exemplars.note: Built 1853-56 by William Smith of Aberdeen with Prince Albert closely involved. Granite ashlar, a dominant clock tower with bartizans, and the royal endorsement that turned a regional revival into a national style.

exemplars.name: Fettes College
exemplars.note: Built 1863-69 by David Bryce. Explicitly a Loire chateau crossed with the Scots tower house, and the fullest demonstration of Bryce's ability to hold a vast picturesque silhouette over a rational plan.

exemplars.name: The Glen
exemplars.note: Built 1855-58 by David Bryce for the Tennant family on chemical-industry money. A textbook Bryce composition of towers, turrets, crow-steps and corbelled dormers on a hillside site.

sources: Charles McKean, The Scottish Chateau: The Country House of Renaissance Scotland (2001)
Nikolaus Pevsner, John Gifford et al., The Buildings of Scotland (series)
Mark Girouard, The Victorian Country House (1971, rev. 1979)
Miles Glendinning, Ranald MacInnes and Aonghus MacKechnie, A History of Scottish Architecture (1996)
David Walker, 'David Bryce' in Seven Victorian Architects (ed. Jane Fawcett, 1976)

proportion_packs.note: scottish-baronial is named directly in facade-picturesque's applies_to. governing_logic states 'None classical. Composition is picturesque — balance of masses read obliquely, with a dominant vertical accent' and symmetry is recorded as 'picturesque-asymmetrical,' which is exactly the pack's dominant-mass, oblique-reading logic. The one addition this style makes that the generic pack does not encode is the concentration of all ornament at the wall head over plain lower storeys (c02) — a vertical distribution rule with no equivalent slot in the pack, noted as a gap below.

Judgment binding: not in room-vernacular's applies_to, and the text is explicit that behind the tower-house costume the rooms are 'large, square, well-lit, plastered and comfortable, laid out with a Victorian sense of circulation' — larger and more regular than the anonymous vernacular median this pack reconstructs. Bound anyway because governing_logic rules out any classical room system ('None classical') and no closer fit exists in the library; treat the module and ratio figures as a loose floor rather than a governing target for a Bryce-scale house.

french-vernacular.name: French Vernacular

description.short: Norman half-timber, provincial stone farmhouse, and the small manoir — the source material for French Eclectic and Norman Revival in America.
description.long:
French regional building spans two very different worlds: the timber-framed, steeply-roofed farmhouses of Normandy, close cousins to English and German framing, and the stone farmhouse and manor of the interior with its hipped roofs, segmental arches, and characteristic round tower housing a stair.

American architects encountered this material directly — many of them served in France in the First World War and came home with sketchbooks. French Eclectic and the Norman cottage of the 1920s are among the very few American revival styles with a first-hand observational basis rather than a photographic one.

defining_characteristics: Steeply pitched hipped or gambrel roofs, often flared at the eave
Stucco, stone, or half-timber walls with segmental-arched openings
The round stair tower as a compositional and functional device
Farm buildings arranged around a court
Direct observational transmission to America after 1918

palladian.name: Palladian

revival_periods.note: Burlington, Campbell and Kent; triggered by Campbell's Vitruvius Britannicus (1715) and Leoni's English edition of the Quattro Libri (1716-20). A revival made from a book, not from the buildings.
Jefferson worked from Giacomo Leoni's Palladio and from Gibbs; Monticello and the University of Virginia are Palladian by transmission through England.
The five-part plantation house of Virginia and Maryland is the Palladian villa diagram in brick and timber, arriving via English pattern books.

geography.hearth: Vicenza and the Venetian terraferma

lineage.note: Palladio is trained as a stonecutter in the Vicentine workshop tradition and formed by Trissino's humanist circle; the vocabulary, the treatise habit and the proportional method are all inherited whole.

Palladio measured Roman baths, temples and bridges in person and published the surveys in Book IV. But his signature move - putting a temple portico on a farmhouse - quotes a Roman form Rome never used domestically. He believed, wrongly, that ancient houses had porticoes.

The Palladian villa is a working farm. The barchesse are barns and cart sheds, the dovecote towers are dovecotes, and the plan responds to grain storage and estate management. Half its DNA is the Veneto agricultural building, not the treatise.

description.short: Andrea Palladio's synthesis of the Roman temple front with the working farm villa, generated from a plan of harmonically proportioned rooms and made globally transmissible by a single illustrated book.
description.long:
Palladianism is the most consequential act of packaging in architectural history. Palladio did roughly forty villas, a handful of palaces and three great Venetian churches, all within about a hundred kilometres of Vicenza, and then in 1570 published I quattro libri dell'architettura: his own designs drawn to scale, with dimensions, next to his surveys of Roman antiquity, next to a clean statement of the orders. A book crosses oceans; a guild does not. Within a century his manner is being built in England, and within two in Virginia, Bengal and St Petersburg, by people who have never seen a Palladio building and in most cases never left their own country. The style spreads as data.

The generative innovation is that the plan comes first. Palladio designs a set of rooms whose lengths and widths are drawn from seven approved shapes - the circle, the square, the square-and-a-third, the square-and-a-half, the square-and-two-thirds, the double square, and the square's diagonal - and whose heights are set by taking the arithmetic, geometric or harmonic mean of each room's own two dimensions. The rooms are then arranged in graded sizes about a cross axis, and the elevation is whatever falls out of that arrangement. This is why a Palladian villa can be shrunk, enlarged or built in brick instead of stone and still look right: the ratios are the design, and the material is not.

The conditions are agricultural and political. Sixteenth-century Venetian patricians were being squeezed out of the eastern Mediterranean trade by the Ottomans and by the Atlantic routes, and were reinvesting capital into reclaiming and farming the terraferma. They needed buildings that were simultaneously a farm headquarters and an assertion of Roman gravitas by men who had just become landlords. Palladio's answer is brilliant and slightly fraudulent: give the granary the pediment of a temple, run the barns out sideways as arcaded wings, build it in brick and stucco-over-brick because there is no good local building stone, and paint the interior with frescoes that cost a fraction of what marble would. The villa is a farm dressed as an antiquity, and everyone involved knew it.

Standing at the foot of the steps of the Rotonda, what registers is that the building has no back. Four identical porticoes face four directions, each with its own flight of steps, and the house rotates around a domed central hall rather than proceeding from front to rear.
