Inside, the effect of the mean-derived ceiling heights is that no room feels either squashed or hollow, and the sequence from small corner room to large hall reads as a graded scale rather than as a set of different rooms. At Maser, the opposite pleasure: you stand in a long, low, sun-struck court with barn arcades running out to sundial pavilions on either side, smelling of dust and stone, and the temple front in the middle is doing rhetorical work it has no structural business doing at all - and getting away with it.

defining_characteristics: A plan generated first, from a closed set of harmonic room ratios, with the elevation derived from it rather than composed independently
Room heights fixed by the arithmetic, geometric or harmonic mean of the room's own width and length
The temple front - a pedimented portico of engaged or free-standing columns - applied to a domestic building
Tripartite A-B-A composition with a dominant raised centre and subordinate flanking elements
Piano nobile raised on a rusticated or plain service basement, reached by an external flight of steps
Subordinate wings (barchesse) stepping down in both height and order, carrying real agricultural or service functions
Stucco over brick treated as a legitimate finish standing in for ashlar, with the proportions rather than the material carrying the argument
diagnostic_tells: A pediment over a house rather than over a church - the single fastest identifier
Steps up to the principal floor on the outside, with the ground storey treated as a plinth and given smaller, plainer openings
Flanking arcaded wings that are lower AND use a simpler order than the centre; if the wings match the centre in order and height, it is not Palladian
The serliana (Palladian window: arched centre light flanked by two square-headed lights on columns) used as a compositional event, not as a repeated window type
Interlocking pediments on church fronts - a tall narrow temple front for the nave overlapping a wider low one for the aisles

distinguished_from.difference: The earlier Renaissance composes an even, unaccented, planar wall with no centrepiece and reserves the temple front for churches. Palladio introduces a dominant centre, a projecting portico on a house, and a plan-first design method.

The English revival is drawn from the Quattro Libri woodcuts rather than from the buildings, so it corrects Palladio's improvisations into a stricter grammar, builds in Portland stone rather than stucco, drops the working farm wings, and adds a fully developed English service basement. It is more correct and less agricultural than Palladio.

Palladian composition is planar, additive and static: one plane of columns, whole pediments, bays that do not accelerate. The Baroque deforms the wall itself into curves, stacks columns in several planes within one bay, and breaks its pediments.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Two systems locked together. The plan is generated from a closed list of room ratios; the elevation from the orders, module = lower column diameter. The link between them is the rule for room height, which makes the section a function of the plan rather than an independent decision.
typical_ratios: The seven approved room shapes: circle; 1:1; 1:1.414 (diagonal of the square); 3:4; 2:3; 3:5; 1:2
Vaulted room height h = (w+l)/2 (arithmetic), h = sqrt(w*l) (geometric), or h = 2wl/(w+l) (harmonic)
Flat-ceilinged square rooms: height equal to width; oblong rooms: height equal to width for the smaller dimension
Villa front commonly tripartite 2:3:2 or 3:5:3 in bay widths across the principal block
Portico of four or six columns, Ionic or Corinthian, occupying 1/2 to 3/5 of the block width
Il Redentore: total facade height = 4/5 of total width; the central portion's width = 5/6 of its own height
Barchesse wing eave height 0.5 to 0.7 of the principal block's eave height
Pediment tympanum height 1/5 to 1/4 of its span - notably steeper than antique practice
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Tripartite with a dominant centre: A-B-A, where B is both wider and taller. A five- or seven-bay front carries the portico across the middle three or five bays; the flanking bays are plain and equal. Long wings then repeat a single uniform arcaded bay outward from the centre with no further accent.

massing_affinities.note: The eponym: dominant central block, low connecting hyphens, terminal pavilions. Hierarchy made dimensional.
The compressed version, where the hyphens vanish and the wings attach directly to the block.
The compact villa block - Rotonda, Foscari, Emo - is a double-pile square around a central hall, which is the same skeleton the Georgians later standardise.
The barchesse can close three sides of a working court, as at Maser and Badoer.
The Vicentine palazzi sit in a street wall, but Palladio treats each as a free-standing composition regardless.

constraints.statement: Every principal room must take its plan proportion from the approved set (1:1, 1:1.414, 3:4, 2:3, 3:5, 1:2, or circular) within 3 percent, and its ceiling height from the arithmetic, geometric or harmonic mean of its own width and length.
Flanking wings must be subordinate in BOTH height and order - lower eave line and a simpler order than the centre. Equal wings destroy the hierarchy that defines the composition.
Pediment tympanum height between 1/5 and 1/4 of span (approximately 22 to 27 degrees). Shallower reads as antique quotation; steeper reads as a domestic gable with trim on it.
The piano nobile must be raised at least 1.2 m above grade on a plain or rusticated base, with external steps. A Palladian portico landing at grade is a nineteenth-century compression, not the type.

test.note: Converted from the source's 1.2 m to in. Tests the piano-nobile-height minimum. 'On a plain or rusticated base, with external steps' is a construction/material detail and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Use the serliana at most once per elevation and only on axis or as a terminal event. Repeating it as a standard window is a Georgian and Colonial Revival habit, not a Palladian one.

exemplars.name: Villa La Rotonda (Villa Almerico Capra)
exemplars.note: Commissioned 1565-66, begun 1567, completed under Vincenzo Scamozzi by 1605. Four identical porticoes about a domed circular hall; the whole plan inscribed in a single circle.

exemplars.name: Villa Barbaro
exemplars.note: Dating disputed; commonly given as c. 1554-1560, with some scholarship pushing completion to 1570. Ionic temple front over a working farm, barchesse terminating in sundial pavilions, frescoes by Veronese.

exemplars.name: Palazzo Chiericati
exemplars.note: Begun 1550, completed only in 1680. A two-storey open loggia across the entire front - the Roman forum portico turned into a private house facade.

exemplars.name: Il Redentore
exemplars.note: Founded 1577 as a plague votive, consecrated 1592. The canonical interlocking-pediment temple front.

sources: Andrea Palladio, I quattro libri dell'architettura (Venice, 1570)
James S. Ackerman, Palladio (1966)
Rudolf Wittkower, Architectural Principles in the Age of Humanism (1949)
Robert Tavernor, Palladio and Palladianism (1991)
John Summerson, The Classical Language of Architecture (1963)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Palladio's own book is the source, so this is close to zero-derivation. The style's own proportional_system names the portico order as 'Ionic or Corinthian,' Ionic first, and the named exemplar Villa Barbaro at Maser carries 'an Ionic temple front over a working farm.'
Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The alternate, richer portico order this style's own proportional_system names alongside Ionic, for the more ceremonial fronts.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Bound for the barchesse and flanking wings specifically: c02 makes it a hard constraint that wings be subordinate in BOTH height and order to the centre, and Doric is the plain order that sits under an Ionic or Corinthian portico without competing with it.
Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the plain, uniform wing bays outward from the dominant centre that this style's own bay_rhythm describes.
Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and by the same author as the order packs above.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. This is the pack's own founding text: room-harmonic's worked example (a 12x6 room taking an 8 ft vault by the harmonic mean) is quoted verbatim from Palladio Book I ch. XXIII, and this style's own proportional_system states the identical governing_logic -- 'the plan is generated from a closed list of room ratios... the section a function of the plan.' The single tightest pack-to-node match in this entire batch.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the vertical relation of the raised piano nobile to the plinth-like service basement below it (c04's 1.2 m minimum), though the pack's own domestic-Georgian calibration describes a gentler diminution than the more emphatic base/piano-nobile contrast this style actually builds.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the interior wall as pedestal:field:entablature, the same general-rule division (Vignola's pedestal at one third, entablature at one quarter of the column) this style's orders and its plan-derived room heights both assume.

mudejar.name: Mudejar

revival_periods.note: Neo-Mudejar: adopted in Spain as a national style for bullrings, markets, schools and workers' housing, precisely because it was read as the one genuinely Spanish architecture. Craft revival in brick, but no continuity of the workforce.
Reaches America mainly through Mexico, where Mudejar carpentry and tile had been standard practice since the 16th century.

geography.hearth: Toledo and Aragon (Teruel, Zaragoza, Calatayud)

lineage.note: This is the edge that matters. Mudejar is not a Christian imitation of Islamic form; it is Islamic building practice continuing without interruption under changed patronage. The same masons, carpenters, plasterers and tilers, organised in the same guilds and often living in the same quarters, went on working after their cities were taken and were hired by Christian kings, bishops and Jewish communities because they were the best trades available. Modelling this as a 'references' edge would be a category error: nothing is being quoted, because nothing was ever lost.

description.short: Islamic building craft continuing under Christian and Jewish patronage in reconquered Spain — the same brick, plaster, tile and carpentry, applied to churches, synagogues and palaces for four centuries after the political power that produced it was gone.
description.long:
Mudejar is the most instructive node in this entire taxonomy, because it is the case that breaks the assumption that a style is a set of intentions held by patrons. The patrons here are Christian kings and bishops. The intentions are Christian. The building types are churches, monasteries, city halls and synagogues. And the architecture is Islamic, unambiguously and technically, because the people who knew how to build were Muslims who stayed — mudajjan, 'those permitted to remain' — and their sons and grandsons, who went on running the same workshops, using the same setting-out squares and the same brick bonds, for four hundred years. When Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085 he did not import a workforce. He inherited one, and it kept building.

What this produces is an architecture that looks like a hybrid but is technically a continuity with new programme requirements. A parish church in Teruel has a nave and an apse and an altar, because it is a church. It is built in brick because Aragon has no good stone and abundant clay, and it is ornamented by corbelling, offsetting and turning whole bricks — dogtooth bands (esquinillas), sunken panels, interlaced blind arcading — because that is what brick ornament is when you cannot afford carving. Its ceiling is an armadura de par y nudillo, a tie-beam and collar truss whose pitch is fixed by a wooden setting-out square (the cartabon) and whose underside is boarded and worked into an interlace of small timbers, because that is how Andalusian carpenters roofed a rectangular room. And its tower is a minaret: a square shaft with an inner stair wrapped around a core, exactly the Almohad type, with a bell in it instead of a muezzin.

The tradition survives the political conditions that created it by a very long way, and its end is a political act rather than an architectural one. Forced conversion after 1502 in Castile and 1526 in Aragon turned the Mudejares into Moriscos; the expulsions of 1609 to 1614 removed the last of the workforce. Within a generation the brick towers stop being built, the par y nudillo ceiling survives only as a provincial habit, and the tile trade at Triana in Seville reorganises itself around Italian majolica technique. The craft did not evolve into something else; it was deported.

To stand in a Mudejar interior is to experience a strange doubling. The plan tells you where you are — nave, crossing, chancel, altar — and the surfaces tell you somewhere else entirely. Above your head is a shallow timber trough of interlaced strapwork, gilded and painted, with no rib, no vault, no Gothic ambition at all; around you is a brick wall relieved by blind arcading and, at the level you can touch, glazed tile; and behind the altar the ornament goes non-figural and geometric at exactly the point where a French or Italian church would put a Virgin. It is a Christian building thinking in another language, and it is far more common in Spain than the Gothic that gets photographed.

defining_characteristics: Continuity of workforce and technique from Islamic Spain, applied to Christian and Jewish building programmes
Brick as the structural and the ornamental material, with decoration generated by offsetting, corbelling and turning whole bricks rather than by carving
Timber ceilings of the armadura de par y nudillo type — tie-beam and collar trusses, boarded and worked into interlaced strapwork (lazo)
Glazed tile (azulejo, alicatado) used as a dado, a paving and a band, in geometric non-figural patterns
The alfiz — a rectangular moulded frame enclosing an arch — as a required device on any opening of consequence
Towers of Almohad minaret type: square shaft, inner stair around a core, brick ornament in vertical panels
Carved plaster (yeseria) at door heads, window grilles and chapel arches, in geometric and vegetal patterns without figures
Latin-Christian plan and programme carried entirely by Islamic construction and surface
diagnostic_tells: Brick ornament made of whole bricks set on edge or on point — dogtooth, dentil and interlace bands — with no carved or moulded profile anywhere
A flat or shallowly pitched boarded timber ceiling with a geometric interlace of small applied timbers, in a building with a Christian plan
A square brick bell tower with the same panelled elevations on all four faces and no buttresses
An alfiz frame around a Gothic or round-headed arch — the two vocabularies stacked without any attempt to reconcile them
Geometric ornament that stops at a frame mid-pattern, in a church

distinguished_from.difference: Same craft, different patron and programme. If it is a mosque or a Nasrid palace it is Moorish Andalusian; if it is a church, a synagogue, a convent or a Christian palace built by the same trades after the reconquest of that city, it is Mudejar.

Plateresque is a Christian, humanist, Italian-derived ornamental system applied by patrons who knew exactly what they were quoting. Mudejar quotes nothing. The two overlap constantly in the same buildings — a Plateresque portada under a Mudejar artesonado ceiling is entirely normal in 16th-century Spain.

Mexico inherits Mudejar carpentry and tile wholesale through Seville, and 16th-century Mexican ceilings are Mudejar in technique. But the plans, the atrio, the open chapel and the labour force are New World, and the tradition there is a descendant rather than the thing itself.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The brick and the cartabon. Ornament is dimensioned in whole brick courses — a course plus joint of roughly 60-70 mm — so every band, offset and blind arch is a whole number of bricks and nothing can be resized without redrawing. Timber roofs are set out with the cartabon, a fixed wooden square that gives the rafter pitch and the collar position for the whole building; the commonest is the cartabon de armadura cuadrada, giving a pitch near 26.5 degrees.
typical_ratios: Brick course plus joint 60-70 mm; ornamental bands 3-9 courses deep
Par y nudillo roof pitch fixed by the cartabon, commonly 26.5 or 33.7 degrees
Tower shaft slenderness roughly 1:4 to 1:6, square in plan
Tile dado 1.2-2.0 m
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Vertical panelling on towers — each face divided into two or three tall recessed panels running most of the shaft height, subdivided by horizontal ornament bands. In naves, the rhythm is set by the diaphragm arches carrying the timber roof.

massing_affinities.note: The Mudejar palace and the convent cloister are both fully enclosed courts with single-pile ranges.
Three-sided courts in smaller palaces and in the alcazar apartments.
Urban Toledo and Zaragoza are party-walled brick courtyard houses in continuous blocks.
The Aragonese church tower gives a Mudejar ensemble a dominant vertical shaft, though it stands beside the body rather than growing out of it.

constraints.statement: Brick ornament must be generated by whole-brick offsets, rotations and corbels. Carved, moulded or cast brick profiles are prohibited: the entire visual character depends on the ornament being an arrangement of a standard unit.

Timber roofs are par y nudillo — tie beam, rafters and collar as one assembly, with the pitch fixed by a single cartabon for the whole building. The ceiling and the roof are the same object; a suspended ceiling below a separate roof is a different tradition.
Any arched opening of consequence must be enclosed by an alfiz. An arch that floats free on the wall is outside the grammar.

Surface ornament is geometric, vegetal and epigraphic. Figural imagery does not appear in Mudejar work even where the patron and the building are Christian; figures belong to the altarpiece, not to the fabric.

Brick walls 500-700 mm. External openings small and high; large openings face the patio. In Aragon, where winters are hard and summers reach 40 degrees, the thermal mass is doing both jobs and cannot be reduced.

test.note: Tests the wall-thickness range. 'External openings small and high; large openings face the patio' has no stated number and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Santa Maria la Blanca
exemplars.note: Built c. 1180-1200 as the principal synagogue of Toledo by Mudejar craftsmen for a Jewish congregation under Christian rule; converted to a church in the early 15th century. Horseshoe arcades on octagonal brick piers with carved plaster capitals.

exemplars.name: Torre de San Martin
exemplars.note: 1315-1316; brick tower of Almohad minaret type with glazed ceramic inlay. Part of the UNESCO 'Mudejar Architecture of Aragon' inscription.

exemplars.name: Alcazar of Seville, Palacio del Rey Don Pedro
exemplars.note: Built 1364-1366 for Pedro I of Castile by craftsmen sent from Toledo and from Nasrid Granada — a Christian king's palace built by Muslim workshops, and the single clearest demonstration of the transmission edge.

exemplars.name: Casa de Pilatos
exemplars.note: Begun 1483, largely 1519-1539; Mudejar tile, plaster and artesonado combined with Italian Renaissance marble in one building without any attempt at reconciliation.

sources: Borras Gualis, El arte mudejar
Pavon Maldonado, Arte mudejar: arte islamico en Espana
Kubler & Soria, Art and Architecture in Spain and Portugal and their American Dominions 1500-1800
Dodds (ed.), Al-Andalus: The Art of Islamic Spain

french-provincial-farmhouse.name: French Provincial Farmhouse

revival_periods.note: American French Eclectic and 'French Provincial': the steep hipped roof, symmetrical stuccoed or brick block, segmental-arched openings and shutters, drawn from the farmhouse and the small manoir together.
A continuous international market vernacular — the Provencal mas as a renovation and holiday-house type, which has kept the trade alive and also flattened it.

geography.hearth: Provence and the Rhone valley, with strong parallel regional traditions across rural France

lineage.note: The southern half of the type is straightforwardly Mediterranean: rubble limestone walls, canal tile at a low pitch, the genoise cornice, whitewashed or lime-rendered surfaces, and a Gallo-Roman continuity of practice that never broke. Retargeted from the family container to a style node so the cascade resolves to a real kit.

The northern and western half is timber-framed and steep-roofed, and shares carpentry, dispersal and roof logic with Normandy. 'French farmhouse' is a single node covering two genuinely different climatic solutions, and the lineage records both.

description.short: The thick-walled, shuttered, low-tiled rural house of southern and central France, whose plan and orientation are dictated by wind, sun and the storage of a crop rather than by any compositional idea.
description.long:
The mas is the type specimen, and it is best understood as a machine for surviving the mistral. In Provence the dominant wind is a cold, dry, violent northerly that blows for days at a stretch, and the mas answers it by presenting a nearly blind wall to the north-west — no door, one or two small high openings, sometimes a bank of earth or a stand of cypress planted specifically as a windbreak — and opening its entire life to the south-east. The long facade faces the morning sun; the windows there are large and shuttered; the terrace and the plane tree that shades it are there. A building rotated ninety degrees from that orientation is not a mas. It is a house that happens to look like one, and it will be uninhabitable for two months of the year.

The wall does the rest of the work. Rubble limestone or river cobble bedded in lime mortar, five hundred to seven hundred millimetres thick, rendered in lime that leaves the aggregate faintly visible, gives a thermal mass sufficient to run a twelve-hour lag between outdoor and indoor temperature — the house is coolest in the afternoon and gives its heat back at night. The roof is canal tile, the round Roman tile, laid at a genuinely low pitch of twenty-five to thirty-five degrees because there is no snow to shed and because a low pitch is stable under a wind that will strip a steep one. Where the wall meets the roof there is a genoise: two, three or four courses of the same canal tile corbelled out and bedded in mortar to throw water clear. The number of courses was, quite literally, a statement of the owner's standing.

In the north and west the same social type — a working farm belonging to a family that owns it — produces something climatically opposite. The Breton and Norman longere is a long, low, single-pile granite or framed range with a steep slate or thatched roof and a chimney at each gable. The Bressan farm is a timber frame on a brick plinth under a vast low-pitched hipped tile roof, with an external gallery on the first floor and, uniquely, a freestanding timber-and-daub chimney — the cheminee sarrasine — carried up through the roof as a separate structure. The Alsatian farm is a Fachwerk courtyard block indistinguishable in construction from its neighbours across the Rhine. Grouping these under one node is a deliberate simplification: what they share is a social and economic condition — the owner-worked farm, the ground floor given to a crop, the plan organised by storage and process — rather than a construction system.

What is consistent everywhere is that the ground floor is not primarily for living. It is for the crop: the cave and the cuverie in the south, the byre or the cider press in the north, the grain floor in Beauce. People live above it or beside it, and the stair up to them is often external. The interior of a mas is therefore a sequence of low, deep, cool, hard-surfaced rooms with small deep-reveal windows, thick lime-plastered walls, exposed beam ceilings, and a fireplace so large that its hood is a room in itself. In August, walking in from a white glaring courtyard, the drop in light and temperature in the first two metres is physical, and the shutters — not the glass, the shutters — are the thing doing it.

defining_characteristics: Massive load-bearing masonry walls of local rubble stone, 500-700 mm thick, lime-rendered or left rough
Orientation as a climatic instrument: near-blind north or north-west elevation, principal openings to the south or south-east
Low-pitched canal (Roman) tile roof, 25-35 degrees, terminated in a corbelled genoise cornice of two to four tile courses in the south; steep slate or tile with gable chimneys in the north and west
External timber shutters on every opening, doing the environmental work that glazing does not
Ground floor given over to production and storage — cave, cuverie, byre, press — with living quarters above or alongside
Additive growth: bays and ranges added end to end and around a working yard as the holding prospers
Openings small in area and deeply reveal-set, sized by the lintel or relieving arch available
diagnostic_tells: A long facade of openings on one side and an almost blank wall on the other, on the same building
Genoise: two to four courses of round tile corbelled out under the eave, with no fascia, gutter or soffit board
Round canal tiles at a pitch visibly lower than any northern European roof
Shutters that are solid boarded below and louvred above, hinged directly to the masonry reveal, not to a frame
Window and door openings of visibly different sizes and heights on one elevation — the fenestration follows the room, never a composition

distinguished_from.difference: Very close, and genuinely the same building culture across the Ligurian Sea. The Tuscan casa colonica is more often a compact two-storey block with a dovecote tower and an external stair to a first-floor loggia; the mas is longer, lower, more additive, and is defined by an orientation the Tuscan house does not need because it has no mistral.

The Andalusian house turns inward around a patio and gives the street a blank wall on every side. The mas turns outward on its sunny face and encloses a yard only for work.  Whitewash is universal in Andalusia and optional in Provence.

A manoir has a great hall, dressed stone openings, a stair turret and an architectural intent. A farmhouse of the same date and county has none of these; the difference is social, and it is visible in the window surrounds before anywhere else.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Structural and climatic. The bay is the span of a floor beam or roof purlin between masonry cross-walls, about 4.5-5.5 m; the wall thickness is set by the stability of rubble masonry at storey height; opening width is limited by the timber lintel or the stone relieving arch available. The composition of the elevation is a consequence of these and of the orientation, never a starting point.
typical_ratios: Wall thickness 500-700 mm; range depth 5.5-7 m clear
Structural bay 4.5-5.5 m between cross-walls
Roof pitch 25-35 degrees (canal tile, south), 40-55 (slate or flat tile, north)
Openings 8-15 percent of wall area on the sun face, under 5 percent on the mistral face
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and functional. Openings are placed by room and by use; the only regularity is that they line up vertically where a wall above must be carried, and even that is often abandoned.

massing_affinities.note: The type grows by extension at the gable and by ells into the yard, each addition a whole bay, roofs stepping as they go.
A prosperous farm closes three sides of a working cour, keeping the fourth open to the south.
The single-cell cabanon and the smallest holdings — one vaulted or beamed room with a hearth.
Fully enclosed in the largest Provencal and Languedoc bastides and in the Alsatian courtyard farm.

constraints.statement: In the Rhone valley and Provence, the north-west elevation must be effectively closed: openings not to exceed 5 percent of its wall area, none at ground level, and no principal entrance. Principal openings and outdoor living space face south to south-east.

test.note: Tests the north-west elevation's glazed-area ceiling. 'None at ground level', 'no principal entrance', and the south/south-east orientation of principal openings are the statement's other clauses and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Canal tile roofs at 25-35 degrees; below 22 degrees wind-driven rain lifts under the tile. The eave must be a corbelled genoise of at least two tile courses, projecting a minimum of 200 mm; a fascia-and-gutter eave is prohibited on southern work.

test.note: Tests the roof-pitch clause. The genoise eave (minimum two courses, 200mm projection) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose; the 22-degree figure is an illustrative failure point below the stated range, not an additional bound.

constraints.statement: Rubble masonry walls 500-700 mm thick. Openings not wider than 1.2 m without a stone relieving arch or a full-bearing timber lintel; a wide opening in a rubble wall requires dressed stone jambs.

test.note: Tests the wall-thickness range. The 1.2m opening-width-without-relieving-arch clause is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Every opening carries an external shutter, hinged to the masonry reveal. Shutters are the primary environmental control; a mas with fixed glazing and no shutters is a facade, not a building.
Ornament is essentially absent. Where money was spent it went into dressed stone at the door surround and into the number of genoise courses, not into applied decoration.

exemplars.name: Ferme de la Foret
exemplars.note: 17th century; a Bressan timber-framed farm with an external first-floor gallery and a cheminee sarrasine of timber and daub. Classee monument historique.

exemplars.name: Mas de la Pyramide
exemplars.note: A working mas cut into the face of the Roman quarry at Glanum and continuously occupied into the 20th century; the clearest demonstration of a Provencal farm built out of, and into, its own material source.

exemplars.name: Village de Poul-Fetan
exemplars.note: A restored Breton hamlet of 16th-19th century granite longeres with thatched roofs, preserved as a working ensemble.

exemplars.name: Ecomusee d'Alsace
exemplars.note: Some seventy relocated Alsatian rural buildings of the 15th-19th centuries, reassembled as a village; the largest single sample of the eastern French farm.

sources: Doyon & Hubrecht, L'Architecture rurale et bourgeoise en France
Trochet, Maisons paysannes en France et leur environnement
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World
Rudofsky, Architecture Without Architects

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to. This node's own text is close to a restatement of the pack's central finding: rooms are shaped by orientation, storage function and 'the room it lights' rather than by composition, and the ground floor is explicitly given to production (cave, cuverie, byre) rather than living — matching the pack's service_zone_strategy rule almost exactly.

Judgment bind: this node is not listed in the pack's applies_to, and it covers several regional constructions of which only the Bressan and Alsatian variants are genuinely timber-framed. Bound narrowly for those: this node's own structural bay (4.5-5.5 m / 15-18 ft, fixed by a floor beam or purlin span between cross-walls) sits inside the pack's documented 16-20 ft bay band almost exactly, and the pack's wing_strategy rule (an ell narrower and lower than the main frame) matches the additive growth by bays and ells described here. Does not apply to the Provencal or Breton stone variants, which have no frame.

french-eclectic.name: French Eclectic

geography.hearth: the Philadelphia Main Line and the Long Island North Shore

lineage.note: The principal claimed ancestor - the small provincial manor house of the Ile-de-France, Touraine and Normandy.
Source of the flared eave, the segmental dormer, the stucco-over-rubble wall and the informal L-plan.
The half-timbered and round-towered Norman register; where this dominates the result is french-normandy-revival.
The formal symmetrical subtype, quoting Louis XV and Louis XVI town and country houses rather than farm buildings.
The real descent. Delano & Aldrich, Carrere & Hastings, Trumbauer, Mellor Meigs & Howe - Ecole-derived offices with French plate books on the shelf.
Informal planning, grouped fenestration and the deliberate cultivation of the picturesque came through the same Anglo-American channel that produced Tudor Revival.
Same offices, same buyers, same masonry-veneer economics; the two styles share a kit almost entirely and differ in roof geometry and ornament.

description.short: The interwar American reading of the French provincial manor and farmhouse, distinguished from its English-derived neighbours by a tall hipped roof of near-equal pitch on all sides, flared at the eave, and by dormers that break the cornice line.
description.long:
French Eclectic is the quietest of the big interwar revivals and the hardest to name from memory, because its identity rests almost entirely on roof geometry. Where Tudor Revival organises itself around gables and Colonial Revival around a symmetrical facade, French Eclectic organises itself around a steep hipped roof - 12:12 and up - that runs at the same pitch on all four sides, comes down low, and very often flares outward at the eave in the characteristic bell curve of a French provincial roof. Under that roof the house may be symmetrical or rambling, brick or stone or stucco, three bays or nine. The roof is what makes it French.

The style has an unusually specific catalyst: the First World War. Between 1917 and 1919 something over a million American soldiers spent extended periods in the villages of northern France, and a great many of the young architects and draughtsmen among them came home with sketchbooks. That experience arrived in offices already primed by Ecole training and by a well-established American taste for French academic classicism, and it converted French building from an aristocratic reference - the chateau, which only Vanderbilts could afford - into a domestic one. The 1920s house market was the beneficiary. Publishers ran plate books of Normandy farm buildings; Mellor, Meigs & Howe in Philadelphia and Delano & Aldrich in New York built the high end; and by 1930 the suburban builder could produce a passable French Eclectic in brick veneer with a steep hip and two segmental dormers.

What the buyer was claiming is worth stating precisely, because it differs from the Tudor claim. Tudor asserts ancestry - English descent, old family, inherited land. French asserts cultivation - taste acquired rather than inherited, travel, education, an eye. This is why French Eclectic appears disproportionately among clients who were self-consciously modern: it flattered people who wanted to be understood as sophisticated rather than as old. It is also why the style tolerates so much variety. A house that claims taste can be symmetrical or informal without contradiction, whereas a house that claims lineage must be consistent.

In front of one, the roof does the work. It is large - often more than half the visible height of the building - and because the pitch is constant on every face, the building reads as a solid under a lid rather than as a set of gables. The flare at the eave softens the meeting of roof and wall and casts a long, low shadow, and the eye follows that line all the way round the house. Dormers push up through it, arched or segmental, with their own little hipped or eyebrow roofs. The wall below is usually calm: stucco or brick with quoins, tall casements often running to the floor, shutters that in the best examples actually work. The entrance is modest, sometimes only a stone surround and an arched door. The whole composition is less theatrical than Tudor and less insistent than Colonial, and it ages better than either.

defining_characteristics: Steeply pitched hipped roof, 12:12 or steeper, at substantially the same pitch on all faces, with the ridge short relative to the plan
Eave carried low and, in most examples, flared outward in a bell curve over the wall head
Dormers that break through the cornice line, most often arched or segmental-headed with hipped or eyebrow roofs
Massive masonry or stucco wall with quoins, water table, or other expression of thickness at reveals and corners
Tall casement windows, frequently paired and running near to the floor, with true divided lights and functional shutters
Absence of a dominant front-facing gable - the element that would immediately make the house read as English
diagnostic_tells: Hipped roof of equal pitch on all four sides with no front gable. One dominant cross-gable and the house is Tudor Revival, not French Eclectic.
The eave flare: a change of rafter angle in the bottom 18-30 in. of the roof, producing a visible upward curve. Nothing English does this.
Dormers cut through the wall head so that their cheeks are masonry continuous with the wall below, rather than sitting entirely on the roof slope.
Windows are casements, not double-hung, and their proportion is tall - 1:2.5 or better - with the head often segmental or round.
Chimneys are tall, slim and often stuccoed, placed at ridge ends; the massive corbelled brick stack of Tudor Revival is absent.

distinguished_from.difference: Chateauesque is aristocratic, load-bearing cut stone, and vertical, with turrets, cresting and late Gothic ornament on a Loire chateau model. French Eclectic is domestic, usually veneered or stuccoed, and takes the small manor and the farmhouse as its models, with almost no carved ornament.

Roof geometry decides it. Tudor Revival is gabled, English-referenced, and depends on half-timbering and a massive chimney; French Eclectic is hipped, French-referenced, flares its eave, and uses casements without applied timbering.

The original is a masonry building of two-foot walls with a plan generated by defensible parti and generations of accretion, small windows and interior circulation through rooms. The revival is a single-campaign house with a corridor plan, large glazing, and a roof that is imitated rather than framed to carry slate or thatch.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Roof-dominant. The hipped roof mass is designed first and the wall is sized to sit beneath it; wall thickness expression at reveals and quoins sets the secondary scale. No classical module except in the formal symmetrical subtype, where a nominal French order governs the entrance.
typical_ratios: Roof height eave to ridge 0.6 to 1.0 times wall height, so the roof reads as 40-50 percent of the elevation
Roof pitch 12:12 to 18:12, constant within 1:12 on all faces
Eave flare: rafter angle reduced by 15-25 degrees over the bottom 18-30 in. of slope
Casement leaf 18-24 in. wide by 54-84 in. high; paired openings 1:2.5 to 1:3 overall
Wall reveal at openings 5-8 in. in masonry examples
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even and calm in the symmetrical subtype - three, five or seven bays with a centred entrance - and loosely grouped in the informal subtype, where wings of differing height meet at right angles and each carries its own regular fenestration.

massing_affinities.note: The informal subtype: an L or a T of hipped volumes at differing heights, often with a round entrance tower at the junction.
The formal symmetrical subtype - a double-pile block with a centred entrance under a tall hip.
Estate examples with projecting wings enclosing a forecourt.
Where service ranges and stabling are pulled into the composition, as in a Norman farm court.
A dominant front-facing gable converts the house to Tudor Revival.

constraints.statement: Principal roof pitch not less than 12:12 and constant within 1:12 across all faces. No front-facing gable may occupy more than 25 percent of the primary elevation width; a dominant front gable voids the style.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch floor. 'Constant within 1:12 across all faces' and the front-gable-width cap (<=25% of primary elevation width, no matching vocabulary variable) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Dormers of the principal rank must be wall dormers whose cheeks continue the wall material and whose sills sit at or below the eave line. Roof-set dormers set entirely above the eave are permitted only as secondary attic lights.

Where an eave flare is used, the flare shall extend 18-30 in. up the slope with a rafter-angle reduction of 15-25 degrees, and shall be carried continuously around all hips. A flare on the front elevation only is forbidden.

Masonry or stucco walls must express thickness: minimum 5 in. reveal at window and door jambs, with quoins, water table, or a returned surround. Flush-set windows in a thin veneer wall read as builder-grade and break the style.

test.note: The quoins/water-table/returned-surround alternatives are categorical with no set threshold stated and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Windows shall be casements with true divided lights, minimum leaf proportion 1:2.5. Where shutters are used they must be board-and-batten or louvred, sized to cover the full opening, and hung on strap hinges with tiebacks.

test.note: Tests the minimum casement-leaf height:width proportion (reusing the corpus's general opening-proportion variable for a casement leaf rather than a double-hung sash). Shutter material and hardware (board-and-batten or louvred, strap hinges, tiebacks) stay prose.

exemplars.name: Oheka Castle
exemplars.note: Delano & Aldrich for Otto Kahn; begun 1914. French chateau parti executed in fireproof steel and concrete - the grand end from which the suburban version is reduced.

exemplars.name: Nemours
exemplars.note: Carrere & Hastings for Alfred I. du Pont, in the Louis XVI manner with gardens after the Petit Trianon. Precedes the suburban floruit and defines its formal subtype.

exemplars.name: The Elms
exemplars.note: Horace Trumbauer, after the Chateau d'Asnieres. Included as the academic French model that the interwar suburban style domesticates.

exemplars.name: French Village
exemplars.location: Chestnut Hill / Mount Airy, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: Robert Rodes McGoodwin, 1925-1928. A whole development of French provincial houses; the point at which the style becomes a suburban product. See also french-normandy-revival.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)
Robert A. M. Stern, Gregory Gilmartin and Thomas Mellins, New York 1930 (1987)
John Milnes Baker, American House Styles: A Concise Guide (1994)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The style's own proportional_system calls itself 'roof-dominant' with 'no classical module except in the formal symmetrical subtype', which is exactly the picturesque system's governing logic - a dominant mass (here, the hipped roof itself rather than a gable) that every other element is subordinate to. Applies across both the symmetrical and informal subtypes described in massing_affinities; even the 'near-symmetrical' formal subtype is a calm massed composition rather than a bay-rhythm classical front, and facade-classical's own applies_to list does not extend to this node.

JUDGMENT BINDING, held at low precedence and marked optional deliberately. The style's own proportional_system states 'a nominal French order governs the entrance' in the formal symmetrical subtype only - Nemours and the Louis XVI-derived estate end of the style. No order-system pack's applies_to names french-eclectic, so this is general typological reasoning rather than a documented fit: Ionic is chosen over Corinthian or Composite because the style's own description insists the entrance stays modest ('sometimes only a stone surround and an arched door'), and Ionic is the order the corpus elsewhere treats as the restrained, non-triumphal choice. Do not apply to the informal subtype, which the style explicitly describes as having 'almost no carved ornament'.

JUDGMENT BINDING for the formal symmetrical subtype only, paired with the order accent above. The lineage record gives this style a direct, weight-1.0 descent from beaux-arts-american ('Delano & Aldrich, Carrere & Hastings, Trumbauer, Mellor Meigs & Howe - Ecole-derived offices with French plate books on the shelf'), which is the strongest lineage weight in the whole node and stronger than the arts-and-crafts-british edge (weight 0.5) that would argue for trim-craftsman instead. Deliberately not bound as primary or as the sole trim pack: the informal subtype, hybridized with tudor-revival (weight 0.6) and descended from arts-and-crafts-british, plausibly wants trim-craftsman, and asserting one trim family as THE answer for a style with two named subtypes would overstate what the sources settle. Both are left at 'optional' rather than one being forced to 'interior'.

french-normandy-revival.name: French Normandy Revival

geography.hearth: Philadelphia's Chestnut Hill; Berkeley and Los Angeles, California

lineage.note: The picturesque, half-timbered, tower-centred wing of the parent style. Same offices and same roof logic; the difference is the tower and the timbering.
The claimed ancestor: the timber-framed and rubble farm buildings of Normandy, with their round dovecote and colombier towers.
The farm-court plan, the flared eave, and the segmental dormer.
The small manor register, invoked where the composition becomes formal enough to need one.

Genuinely blended. American half-timbering, steel casements, leaded glass and masonry veneer are shared wholesale with Tudor Revival; on many streets the two are separated only by the presence of a round tower.
Informal planning and the deliberate composition of irregular groups, transmitted through the same Anglo-American publishing channel that produced Tudor Revival.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The Norman farmhouse variant of French Eclectic, identified by a round or polygonal entrance tower with a conical roof set at the junction of two wings, combined with steep hipped roofs, half-timbering, and mixed brick, stone and stucco walls.
description.long:
French Normandy Revival is the one variant in this branch that can be identified from a moving car by a single element. The round entrance tower, capped with a conical roof and containing the front door and often a stair, sits in the inside corner where two wings meet, and it comes directly from the freestanding colombier - the dovecote tower - of the Norman farm court, which American architects and returning soldiers had photographed extensively and which they moved from the farmyard to the front door because it made a spectacular entrance.

Everything else follows the parent style. The roofs are steeply pitched hips, 12:12 and up, running at the same pitch on all faces, often flared at the eave. The walls mix materials with some freedom - brick, rubble stone, and stucco, with half-timbered panels in the gables and upper storeys, which is the point where this variant borrows heavily from Tudor Revival and where the two become genuinely difficult to separate. Windows are casements, tall and grouped. Dormers break the cornice line, arched or segmental. The plan is informal, usually an L or a shallow U, and where the composition is large it wants a walled forecourt.

Two developments define its American realisation. Robert Rodes McGoodwin's French Village at Chestnut Hill, built 1925-28 for George Woodward, is the East Coast case, executed in Wissahickon schist with real masonry and real restraint. William Raymond Yelland's Thornburg Village - universally called Normandy Village - at 1781-1851 Spruce Street in Berkeley, built in 1927 for the contractor Jack Thornburg, is the West Coast case and is considerably wilder: sagging ridges, hand-adzed timbers, carved corbels, and a deliberate air of medieval fantasy that shades into the Storybook manner then flourishing in Los Angeles. Between the two lies the whole range of the variant, from archaeology to theatre.

What it is like depends on which end you are at. At the Philadelphia end it is calm, grey, and heavy, and the tower reads as a legitimate piece of planning - you enter through it, turn, and arrive in a hall. At the Berkeley end the same tower is a stage set: the plaster is trowelled unevenly on purpose, the timbers have axe marks that were put there with an axe, and the whole group is theatrical in a way that is completely unembarrassed about itself. Both work. The failure mode is the middle - a suburban builder's box with a half-round clad turret glued to the front, which has neither the mass of the first nor the conviction of the second.

defining_characteristics: Round or polygonal entrance tower with a conical roof, set at the junction of two wings and containing the front door or a stair
Steeply pitched hipped roofs, 12:12 or steeper, at consistent pitch on all faces, frequently flared at the eave
Mixed wall materials - brick, rubble stone, and stucco - with half-timbered panels in gables and upper storeys
Casement windows, tall and grouped, with true divided or leaded lights
Dormers breaking the cornice line, arched or segmental-headed
Informal L- or U-shaped plan, ideally with a walled or partly enclosed entrance court
diagnostic_tells: The conical-roofed round tower at an inside corner is decisive; nothing else in American domestic architecture places one there.
Steep hipped roofs with no dominant front gable, plus half-timbering. Tudor Revival gives you the timbering with gables; the parent French Eclectic gives you the hips without timbering.
Wall material changes vertically and abruptly - stone below, stucco and timber above - at a floor line or a jetty.
Casements, not double-hung, and a segmental or round-headed dormer.

Against genuine Norman building: the original tower is a freestanding dovecote in a farm court and does not contain the house entrance; the original timber frame is structural and 4-8 in. thick; and the original farm is a group of buildings, not one house pretending to be a group.

distinguished_from.difference: The parent style is broader and usually calmer - it may be entirely symmetrical, is often all-masonry, and rarely uses half-timbering or a tower. This variant is the picturesque Norman end, defined by the conical entrance tower and by mixed timbered walls.

Roof geometry again. Tudor Revival is gabled and English-referenced; French Normandy Revival is hipped, flares its eave, uses casements, and puts a round tower at the entrance. The half-timbering and the masonry-veneer technology are shared, which is why the pair is so often confused.
The Cotswold variant is lower, all-stone, has no tower and no timbering, and rolls its eaves. The Norman variant is taller, mixes materials, uses timbering, and depends on the tower.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Roof-dominant, as in the parent style, with the tower as the compositional pivot: its diameter and height set the scale against which the two wings are judged, and its conical roof establishes the steepest pitch on the building.
typical_ratios: Tower diameter 9-14 ft; height to eave 1.1 to 1.4 times the adjacent wall height
Conical tower roof pitch 18:12 to 24:12 - steeper than the main roof by at least 4:12
Main roof pitch 12:12 to 16:12, constant on all faces; roof height 0.6-1.0 times wall height
Half-timber members 5-8 in. face width, spaced 16-30 in. clear, projecting at least 1 in. from the stucco plane
Casement leaf 16-22 in. wide by 40-56 in. high, grouped in twos and threes
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Additive and grouped. Each wing carries its own loose rhythm of casement clusters; the tower interrupts both and is the only element on the composition that resolves anything.

massing_affinities.note: Two or more hipped wings of unequal height meeting at a tower.
The suburban builder reduction - a simple block with a turret and one steep hip.
Larger examples where the composition becomes formal enough to read as a manor.
The Norman farm court taken literally, with service ranges pulled into the composition.

constraints.statement: A round or polygonal tower, minimum 9'0" in diameter, capped with a conical roof at 18:12 or steeper, must be present at the junction of two wings and must contain either the entrance or a stair. A tower applied flat to a facade, or one narrower than 9'0", voids the variant.

test.note: Tests the tower's own conical roof pitch. Tower diameter (min 9'0" -- no matching vocabulary variable, tower_diameter_ft is missing) and 'must contain either the entrance or a stair' stay prose.

constraints.statement: Main roof pitch 12:12 to 16:12, constant within 1:12 across all faces, hipped. The tower roof must exceed the main roof pitch by not less than 4:12.

test.note: Tests the main roof pitch range. 'Constant within 1:12 across all faces, hipped' and 'the tower roof must exceed the main roof pitch by not less than 4:12' (no separate tower-roof-pitch variable exists to compute the cross-roof differential against) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Where half-timbering is used it must describe a plausible frame under the parent Tudor rule: continuous verticals from sill to plate, horizontals terminating at posts, braces at 45 degrees or steeper, members 5-8 in. wide projecting not less than 1 in. from the infill plane.
Vertical material changes must occur at a floor line, a water table, or a jetty, with a minimum 4 in. horizontal offset. Stone below and stucco above stopping mid-storey is forbidden.
Windows shall be casements with true divided or leaded lights, leaves 16-22 in. wide, grouped in twos and threes. Double-hung sash on principal elevations is forbidden.

exemplars.name: Thornburg Village (Normandy Village)
exemplars.note: William Raymond Yelland for Jack Wood Thornburg. The West Coast case at its most theatrical - hand-adzed timbers, sagging ridges, carved corbels - and a Berkeley landmark.

exemplars.name: French Village
exemplars.location: Chestnut Hill / Mount Airy, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: Robert Rodes McGoodwin for George Woodward, 1925-28. The East Coast case in Wissahickon schist, archaeological rather than theatrical.

exemplars.name: Oheka Castle
exemplars.note: Delano & Aldrich, 1914-19. Included as the grand French precedent from which the suburban Norman version is derived, with the same steep hipped roofs and tower motifs at estate scale.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Arrol Gellner and Douglas Keister, Storybook Style: America's Whimsical Homes of the Twenties (2001)
David R. Contosta, Suburb in the City: Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, 1850-1990 (1992)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The style's own proportional_system names the tower explicitly as 'the compositional pivot: its diameter and height set the scale against which the two wings are judged' - a textbook statement of the picturesque dominant-mass logic, and the tower's conical roof at 18:12-24:12 against a main roof of 12:12-16:12 is close kin to facade-picturesque's own gable_treatment and roof_form derived_rules. No classical order anywhere in the defining characteristics or constraints; unlike chateauesque and beaux-arts-american, this variant's own lineage carries no Beaux-Arts weight (its Ecole descent is inherited only at second hand through the french-eclectic parent) and no order is bound here for that reason.

The variant's own hard constraint (c03) requires that half-timbering, where used, 'describe a plausible frame under the parent Tudor rule: continuous verticals from sill to plate, horizontals terminating at posts, braces at 45 degrees or steeper' - a real structural-frame logic, not applied decoration, which is exactly what timber-bay's bay-and-post reconstruction encodes. Genuine gap flagged honestly: timber-bay's own applies_to list does not yet name this node (it names norman-vernacular, german-fachwerk, tudor, elizabethan and jacobean, but not this revival or its parent french-eclectic) - bound anyway because the fit is structurally direct and the omission reads as an oversight in the pack's applies_to curation rather than a deliberate exclusion.

The lineage record carries real weight here: 'arts-and-crafts-british, descends_from, weight 0.6 - informal planning and the deliberate composition of irregular groups' and a hybridizes_with edge to tudor-revival at weight 0.7, which is itself bound to trim-craftsman in this corpus (see tudor-revival's own applies_to entry on that pack). Chosen over trim-classical because nothing in this variant's defining characteristics, diagnostic tells or constraints calls for a classical order or an entablature-derived interior - the register is rustic timber and stone throughout, at both the Chestnut Hill (restrained) and Berkeley (theatrical) ends the style's own description names.

prairie-school.name: Prairie School

geography.hearth: Oak Park and Chicago, Illinois

lineage.note: Shares the reform ethic, the hearth-centred open plan, the built-in furniture, the art glass, and the refusal of applied classical ornament. Wright exhibited and published within the movement's institutions.

Wright's formative years with J. L. Silsbee. The continuous unbroken skin, the pinwheel plan turning about a central chimney mass, and the horizontal spread are all Shingle Style inheritances stripped of their picturesque incident.
Through Sullivan's office: the low sheltering arch, the base-shaft-cap wall hierarchy, and the conviction that a wall's mass should be expressed in long horizontal courses.

Wright's stated programme in 'The Art and Craft of the Machine' (1901) and in the Ladies' Home Journal designs: eliminate the attic, the cellar stair, the porch spindle, the bric-a-brac, and the room-by-room subdivision of the ground floor.
The competing American answer to the same Victorian exhaustion. Prairie rejects the historicist route explicitly, which is what places it at the edge of this taxonomy.

description.short: The Chicago-centred style that answered the exhaustion of Victorian building by dissolving the house into horizontal planes gathered about a central chimney, and in doing so became the point at which the American tradition begins arguing with itself.
description.long:
Prairie School belongs in this graph and sits uneasily in it, and the honest thing is to say why. Every other node here inherits a grammar and modifies it. Prairie inherits a grammar and sets out to replace it with a first-principles derivation from site, plan, and material — the same intellectual move that modernism will make twenty years later, made here while the details are still being cut by Arts and Crafts craftsmen out of oak and art glass. It is traditional in its methods, its materials, its craft economy, and its plan lineage from the Shingle Style; it is anti-traditional in its refusal of any historical reference whatsoever. This is the point where the American tradition begins arguing with itself, and the argument is not settled: the Wasmuth Portfolio of 1910 carried these houses to Berlin, where they were read as a programme rather than a style, and the reading returned to America in the 1930s as the International Style, which then spent forty years dismantling everything else in this taxonomy. A design system that omits Prairie because it is inconvenient is falsifying its own history.

The conditions that produced it are Chicago's. A flat glaciated landscape with no vertical incident, which the style takes as an instruction rather than a deficiency. A rail commuter suburb — Oak Park, River Forest, Riverside — with deep lots and a professional clientele willing to be argued with. A local building economy fluent in plaster, in long thin Roman brick, in leaded glass, and in the wide-span steel and timber framing that Chicago commercial work had made routine. And a specific intellectual milieu: Sullivan's theory of an organic ornament generated from the building's own geometry, Hull House and its Arts and Crafts Society, and the conviction, widely shared in Chicago in 1900, that a democratic society ought to be able to produce a domestic architecture of its own. The transmission mechanism is worth naming as precisely as Stickley's magazine: in February and July 1901 the Ladies' Home Journal — then the largest-circulation magazine in the world — published Wright's 'A Home in a Prairie Town' and 'A Small House with Lots of Room in It' as buildable designs for its readers. The style reached the American public through a women's magazine before it reached the profession, and the plan-book trade promptly reduced it to the 'Prairie box': a foursquare with wide eaves and a belt course, which is how most Americans have actually seen it.

What it looks like follows from one decision: the house is composed of horizontal planes, and every vertical element is either suppressed or converted into a datum. The roof is low-pitched and hipped, its eaves projecting far enough — thirty inches to four feet — to throw the whole wall into shadow and to read as a floating plane. A continuous water table, a sill band, a lintel band, and the fascia draw four unbroken lines around the building. Windows become bands of casements set at the outer wall face so that the wall reads as a screen rather than as a mass with holes. Corners are dissolved with glass or turned by a projecting pier. The entry is displaced — around a corner, behind a wall, under a low overhang — so that arrival is a sequence rather than an announcement, and the front door is frequently invisible from the street. What holds all of this together is the chimney: the plan pinwheels about a masonry mass that is the heaviest, tallest, and most solid object in the composition, and the horizontal planes are understood as slabs slid past it.

To be inside one is a specific and still-startling experience of compression and release. Ceilings drop to seven feet at the entry and in the circulation zones and lift to nine and a half or more over the living space, and the change is felt in the body before it is noticed by the eye. Light is filtered through art glass whose geometry is derived from the plan, so the pattern on the floor at four in the afternoon is a projection of the building's own logic. There is nowhere to hang a picture and no place to put an inherited sideboard, which is the source of most contemporary complaints about these houses and also the point. Outside, at a hundred feet, the building appears to be pressed down into the ground and spreading; at twenty feet, it appears to be made entirely of edges. Neither reading resembles anything else built in America before it.

defining_characteristics: Dominant low-pitched hipped roof with eaves projecting 30 in to 48 in and reading as an unbroken floating plane
Horizontality asserted by continuous banding: water table, sill course, lintel course, and fascia drawn unbroken around the whole building
Windows as horizontal bands of casements, glazed in rectilinear art glass and set at the outer face of the wall
Plan pinwheeling about a massive central masonry chimney, which is the tallest and heaviest element of the composition
Suppressed or indirect entry — the front door is displaced from the principal elevation and often not visible from the street
Wall surfaces continuous and unornamented: stucco with wood banding, or long thin Roman brick in raked horizontal joints
Ceiling heights deliberately varied between compressed circulation and released living volume
No historical reference of any kind — no orders, no revival motifs, no applied period detail
diagnostic_tells: The eave soffit is clean: no rafter tails, no knee braces, no brackets. This is the fastest separation from Craftsman.
Roman brick — brick roughly twice as long and half as tall as standard — laid with raked horizontal and flush vertical joints so only the horizontal reads
Casement windows in continuous ribbons, with art glass in rectilinear geometry and no curves
The chimney is visibly the fattest object in the composition and the plan turns around it
You cannot find the front door from the sidewalk

distinguished_from.difference: Craftsman shows the structure — rafter tails, braces, piers, stacked rustic materials — and roofs in gables over double-hung sash. Prairie suppresses all structural evidence into planes and roofs in hips over casement bands. If you can count the rafters, it is not Prairie.
Same movement, opposite method. Arts and Crafts finds its expression in the evidence of the hand; Prairie finds it in geometry, and is content to have the machine execute it.

The ranch inherits Prairie's horizontal parti and low hipped roof but none of its hierarchy: the ranch is long because the lot is wide and the plan is single-loaded, not because horizontality is being composed. Prairie has a centre; the ranch has an extent.

proportional_system.governing_logic: A system of horizontal datums rather than a vertical module. Four continuous lines — water table, sill band, lintel band, fascia — are established first and every element is then sized to die into one of them. The secondary module is dimensional: the Roman brick course and the standard casement width of roughly 2 ft, from which window bands are built in multiples. Vertical proportion is handled by ceiling height differentiation, not by facade ratio.
typical_ratios: Hipped roof pitch 3:12 to 4:12
Eave overhang 30 to 48 in, uniform on all sides
Ceiling heights differentiated: 6 ft 10 in to 7 ft 4 in at compression, 9 ft 0 in to 10 ft 0 in at release
Window band length 3 to 8 casement units, each 1 ft 10 in to 2 ft 4 in wide
Lintel band to sill band dimension approximately equal to the fascia depth, so the three lines read as one family
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Continuous rather than bayed. The compositional unit is the band, subdivided by mullions at a regular casement module; solid wall occurs between bands, not between windows.

massing_affinities.note: The pinwheel of wings about a central chimney is the style's own skeleton and was largely invented for it.
The 'Prairie box' of the plan-book trade: a foursquare with wide hipped eaves, a belt course, and a hipped dormer. This is how the style reached most of the country.
Wright's Usonian houses of the later 1930s take this direction, and it is the formal channel by which Prairie horizontality reaches the postwar ranch.
Occurs as the 'Prairie bungalow' of Midwestern builders; correct in silhouette and usually wrong in the eave and the sash.

constraints.statement: Principal roof hipped at 3:12 to 4:12 with eave overhang not less than 30 in on every side. A gabled principal roof or an overhang under 24 in disqualifies the node.

test.note: Tests the pitch range. The eave overhang minimum (30 in, expressible via eave_projection_in), the hipped-not-gabled requirement (no roof-form vocabulary variable), and the 24 in disqualification threshold are left as prose.

constraints.statement: Exposed rafter tails, knee braces, applied brackets, shutters, and any classical or revival ornament are forbidden. The eave soffit is a continuous closed plane.
All window heads on a storey must die into a single continuous lintel band, and all sills into a single sill band; the bands must return around every corner without interruption.
The primary entry may not be centred on the principal street elevation, and should be approached at right angles to the direction of arrival.
The chimney mass must exceed the width of any other vertical element by at least 50 percent and must terminate above the highest roof plane.

test.note: Tests only that the chimney terminates above the highest roof plane (height above ridge > 0). The '50 percent wider than any other vertical element' clause needs a chimney-width variable not in the vocabulary and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Frederick C. Robie House
exemplars.note: Frank Lloyd Wright, designed 1908-09 and completed 1910. The style's limit case: cantilevered roof planes, a continuous glass band, and an entry hidden behind the chimney mass.

exemplars.name: Ward W. Willits House
exemplars.note: Wright's first fully resolved Prairie house; the cruciform pinwheel about a central hearth in its clearest form.

exemplars.name: Purcell-Cutts House
exemplars.note: Purcell and Elmslie. Demonstrates that the style was a school rather than one man, and carries Elmslie's Sullivanian ornament.

sources: H. Allen Brooks, The Prairie School: Frank Lloyd Wright and His Midwest Contemporaries (1972)
Frank Lloyd Wright, 'A Home in a Prairie Town', Ladies' Home Journal, February 1901
Frank Lloyd Wright, Ausgefuehrte Bauten und Entwuerfe (the Wasmuth Portfolio, 1910)
Vincent Scully, The Shingle Style and the Stick Style, rev. ed. (1971)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)

proportion_packs.note: This pack's own datum-band mechanism -- 'at least two horizontal lines must run through every mass on the elevation at one level and without a break... normally the water table and the first-floor head line' -- is Prairie's own stated governing logic restated almost word for word: this node's own hard constraint (c03) that every window head must die into one continuous lintel band and every sill into one continuous sill band, returning unbroken around every corner, is this pack's datum rule with a fourth band (the fascia) added on top. Given role 'primary' because Prairie genuinely has a module in this sense, even though it has none in the classical sense: the horizontal band, not a mass, is what everything is sized against. The dominant-mass and lever-arm rules are read here with the chimney -- this node's own 'tallest, heaviest element of the composition,' see c05 -- standing in for the picturesque tradition's dominant gable, an adaptation the pack's own wide, explicitly-judgment-marked tolerance bands accommodate.

Bound optional and low, with a real caveat the node itself supports: this node's own diagnostic tells state that Prairie suppresses structural evidence Craftsman displays, and its distinguished_from entry against craftsman is explicit that Prairie's soffit is clean where Craftsman's shows rafter tails and knee braces -- so this pack's exterior vocabulary (rafter tails, knee braces, exposed structure) does not belong here at all. What plausibly does is the interior catalog-millwork descendant: the 'Prairie box' foursquare that carried the style to most of the country by plan-book (a common massing affinity here) was very often built and trimmed by the same regional lumberyards that supplied Craftsman bungalows next door. It does NOT describe Wright's own architect-designed interiors, whose bespoke geometric oak trim and art-glass-derived ornament are a real gap in this pack set: no pack here owns a first-principles, non-catalog Prairie interior system, and none should be invented for one.

southern-federal.name: Southern Federal

revival_periods.note: The Colonial Williamsburg restoration and the country-house architects of the 1920s make the Chesapeake Federal five-part plan the standard American 'important house' diagram.
The two-tier portico and the fanlighted door migrate into the national suburban vocabulary, usually detached from the climate logic that produced them.

geography.hearth: Baltimore and the Virginia Piedmont

lineage.note: Direct craft continuity: Chesapeake brickmasons working Flemish bond with glazed headers, the five-part plan with flanking dependencies, and the through-passage plan, all carried unbroken across the Revolution.
Arriving as print, imported mantels, and Wellford composition ornament out of Philadelphia rather than as first-hand observation.

In Virginia the two overlap in the same building trade and the same decade; Piedmont Federal houses routinely borrow Jefferson's octagonal room ends, terraced dependencies and low concealed roofs without adopting his archaeological argument.

description.short: The Federal vocabulary applied to a Southern plan discipline that had already solved for heat: brick or frame, one room deep where it can be, high-ceilinged, porched, and organised around a through-passage that works as a ventilation device.
description.long:
Southern Federal is the same Adamesque surface treatment as its New England sibling laid over an entirely different set of plan priorities. The Chesapeake and Piedmont had spent a century learning that a house in a humid subtropical summer wants to be thin in section, tall in the ceiling, shaded on its openings, and open at both ends of its central passage. Federal ornament did nothing to disturb that, so the variant looks like a Tidewater Georgian house that has been re-trimmed: flat wall plane, elliptical fanlight, thin muntins, slender colonnettes, and behind it the through-passage plan, the tall first floor, the gable-end chimneys often set outside the wall entirely, and the porch. Where New England's Federal is closed and vertical, the Southern version spreads. Five-part plans with hyphens and dependencies are far more common here than in the North, because the household to be housed was larger and more stratified, and because the labour to build the wings was owned rather than hired.

The conditions were agricultural, and they were built on slavery, which needs saying plainly rather than in the euphemism of 'plantation economy'. Tobacco money in Maryland and Virginia, and after Whitney's gin in 1793 the beginning of cotton money further south, capitalised a generation of building between 1790 and 1830. The five-part parti - main block, low hyphens, flanking dependencies - is not a compositional preference but a diagram of a social order: kitchen, laundry, quarters and offices kept out of the main block for heat, smell, fire and hierarchy, while remaining connected under cover. The masons and carpenters who executed it were very often enslaved, and Chesapeake brickwork of this period is among the finest in North America. Materially the region gave brick and heart pine rather than the clear white pine of the North, so Southern Federal detail is generally executed in brick with wood or marble trim, and the wood mouldings are heavier in the same dimensions because heart pine will not run as crisply as white pine.

What it reacted against was Georgian heaviness, exactly as the North did, but also against the Tidewater's own steep-roofed, dormer-studded, tightly-massed colonial house. The Federal generation lowered the pitch, pulled the dormers off the principal roof, moved the chimneys out to the ends as exterior stacks that shed their heat outdoors, and raised the ceilings. It also, quietly, began raising the whole house on a basement so that the principal floor sat above the damp and caught more air. Where Jefferson was working in the same counties the two idioms interpenetrate, and there is no sharp line between a Piedmont Federal house with a canted bay and a minor Jeffersonian one.

The experience of one is of air and length. The passage runs straight through the house with a door at each end and a stair to one side, and in July, with both doors open, it is measurably the coolest place on the property - the same device the dogtrot uses in log a hundred miles west, executed in Flemish bond with a fanlight at either end. Ceilings are eleven or twelve feet, so the tall windows put daylight deep into rooms whose shutters are closed against the sun. From outside, the building sits low and long, its wings stepping down to either side, its brick a dark red-brown with lighter mortar joints thinner than a pencil, and the only concentrated ornament in the whole composition gathered around the door: a fan of leaded glass, sidelights, and a slim portico that would not keep the rain off anyone.

defining_characteristics: Federal ornamental vocabulary (elliptical fanlight, flat wall plane, attenuated colonnettes, applied composition ornament) over an inherited Chesapeake plan discipline
Central through-passage open at both ends, used as a cross-ventilation device as much as circulation
Tall principal-storey ceilings (10-13 feet) with windows extending close to the ceiling line
Gable-end chimneys, frequently exterior-end stacks standing proud of the wall to shed heat outside the envelope
Flemish-bond brick with thin joints as the prestige wall, frame with beaded weatherboard as the vernacular equivalent
Five-part composition with hyphens and flanking dependencies far more common than in Northern Federal
Porch or portico present as a working shading element rather than only as a doorway frame
diagnostic_tells: Exterior-end chimney stacks standing away from the gable wall - a Southern habit New England never adopted
One-room-deep main block with a through-passage, where a Northern Federal house of the same status would be double-pile
Ceiling heights visibly taller than Northern work at the same date, readable from outside in the window-to-storey proportion
Low flanking dependencies joined by hyphens, stepping down from the main block
Raised basement lifting the principal floor three to six feet above grade, with an exterior stair to the entrance

distinguished_from.difference: Identical ornament, opposite plan logic. New England builds compact, three storeys, double-pile, closed, no porch. The South builds long and thin with a through-passage, taller ceilings, exterior-end chimneys, and a porch. The tell is section, not trim.

Same brickwork, same five-part instinct, same passage. The Georgian version has a steeper roof with dormers on the principal slope, a projecting pedimented door frontispiece, heavy muntins, and a modillioned cornice with real projection. Federal flattens all four.

They overlap in Virginia and share workmen. Jefferson insists on correct antique orders, concealed roofs, and octagonal geometry as an argument; Southern Federal takes the same devices as fashion, keeps its roof visible, and uses Adam-thin colonnettes no Roman authority would license.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Adamesque classical proportion imposed on a plan whose dimensions are set by ventilation and by the practical span of a single-pile room, so that the section is climatically governed while the elevation is stylistically governed.
typical_ratios: Principal storey 10-13 feet floor to ceiling; upper storey 0.75-0.85 of it
Passage width 10-14 feet, roughly one third to one half of a flanking room's width
Single-pile room depth 16-20 feet, set by cross-ventilation rather than by framing limits
Window openings 1:2.2 to 1:2.5 width to height, taller than Northern Federal at the same width
Dependency ridge at least 4 feet below the main ridge; hyphen ridge below both
Roof pitch 6:12 to 9:12, generally without dormers on the principal slope
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five bays even on the main block, three on lesser houses; dependencies read as separate three-bay units and are never allowed to align their bay spacing with the main block, which would flatten the hierarchy.
