massing_affinities.note: The urban and highest-status version - Baltimore, Richmond, Alexandria.
The Chesapeake signature, and a social diagram before it is a compositional one.
The regional workhorse: one room deep so that every room is cross-ventilated and lit from two sides.
The Piedmont farmer's version, two storeys tall and one room deep with Federal trim at the door only.
Baltimore, Alexandria, Richmond's Church Hill.

constraints.statement: A central passage must be open at both ends with operable doors, and no room may be more than 20 feet deep without a second exterior wall. Filling in behind the passage to make a double-pile plan removes the variant's climatic reason for existing and must be a deliberate, argued decision.

test.note: Tests the 20ft maximum via plan_depth_ft, standing in for per-room depth on the assumption of the single-pile plan the variant depends on (room depth approximately equals overall plan depth minus the passage in a true single-pile). The passage-operable-at-both-ends clause is left as prose.

constraints.statement: Principal-storey ceiling height 10-13 feet, with window heads within 12-18 inches of the ceiling. Ceilings under 9 feet convert the building to a Northern Federal proportion regardless of trim.

test.note: Tests the 10-13ft ceiling-height range. The window-head-to-ceiling offset clause (12-18in) is left as prose -- window_head_to_cornice_offset_in measures head-to-exterior-cornice, a different reference line, not head-to-interior-ceiling.

constraints.statement: Flanking dependency ridges must sit at least 4 feet below the main ridge, and hyphens must be lower and shallower than both elements they join. Equal-height wings destroy the hierarchy that the parti exists to express.

Brick laid in Flemish bond with joints no wider than 3/8 inch; where a water table or belt course occurs it projects no more than 2 inches. Exterior-end chimney stacks must stand clear of the gable wall by at least 4 inches at the shoulder.

test.note: Tests the belt-course/water-table projection cap (2in). Flemish-bond joint width (3/8in) and the exterior-end-chimney standoff distance (4in) have no matching vocabulary variables -- chimney_inset_ft measures the opposite case, an interior chimney's inset from the gable, not an exterior chimney's standoff -- and stay prose.

constraints.statement: A porch is permitted and encouraged as a shading device, but a Federal porch is one storey and carried on colonnettes no more than 8 inches in diameter. A full-height two-storey portico converts the building to Greek Revival or Neoclassical.

exemplars.name: Homewood
exemplars.note: Begun 1801 for Charles Carroll Jr.; five-part Palladian plan with Adamesque detail throughout and the finest Federal joinery in Maryland.

exemplars.name: Woodlawn
exemplars.note: Built 1800-06 for Lawrence and Nelly Custis Lewis, attributed to William Thornton; five-part brick composition with a pedimented five-bay central block, and among the most copied early Virginia designs.

exemplars.name: Nathaniel Russell House
exemplars.note: The Lowcountry high point of the Southern Federal interior: cantilevered free-flying stair, oval drawing room, full-height polygonal garden bay.

exemplars.name: Levi Coffin House
exemplars.location: 113 U.S. 27, Fountain City, Wayne County, Indiana
exemplars.note: Late, plain, and built by Carolina Quaker emigrants - a two-storey Flemish-bond brick I-house with Federal trim, showing the variant migrating northwest with its builders a decade after it had died on the seaboard.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
Dell Upton, Architecture in the United States (1998)
Henry Glassie, Folk Housing in Middle Virginia (1975)
Mills Lane, Architecture of the Old South (series, 1984-96)
Virginia Department of Historic Resources register files

proportion_packs.note: The single order run throughout, matching the parent style's choice and the same reasoning: this pack's column stands 10 diameters, inside Federal's stated 9-11 diameter Adam-attenuated range. The style's own distinguished_from clause against jeffersonian-classicism names the diagnostic directly -- 'Adam-thin colonnettes no Roman authority would license' -- which is precisely what this Chambers-descended, carpenter-executed overlay is, as against the correct antique weight of Jefferson's Palladio-sourced orders next door in the same Virginia counties.

The wall_section_federal / casing_federal family, with a material caveat this variant's own description states directly: Southern Federal mouldings are executed in heart pine rather than the clear white pine of new-england-federal, and 'heart pine will not run as crisply,' so the same dimensions read heavier here even though the proportional family is identical.
The same ranking and reasoning as the parent style and new-england-federal: the sash module wins over opening-proportion where the two disagree, per sash-light's own stated rule.

Governs door and window sizing beneath constraint c05's porch rule (one storey, colonnettes no more than 8 in diameter; a full-height two-storey portico converts the building to Greek Revival or Neoclassical) -- the same threshold the parent style's fanlight co-occurrence rule states, applied here to a porch that is 'a working shading element' rather than only a doorway frame, per this variant's own description.

Governs the five-part composition with hyphens and dependencies -- far more common here than in New England, per the style's own defining_characteristics -- through the same reduced-projection discipline the whole Federal family imposes. Constraint c04 layers Chesapeake-specific figures on top: Flemish bond joints no wider than 3/8 in, belt course or water table projecting no more than 2 in.

The variant's own stated ratios -- principal storey 10-13 ft, upper storey 0.75-0.85 of it (constraint c02, hard: ceilings under 9 ft convert the building to Northern Federal proportion regardless of trim) -- are a steeper diminution than New England's, and are bound as the governing figures the pack's general mechanism executes.

Listed directly in this pack's applies_to cross-reference. Bound for the composed geometry the style's own exemplars name -- the Nathaniel Russell House's oval drawing room and cantilevered free-flying stair, the full-height polygonal garden bay -- proportioned rooms rather than accumulated ones.

PROMOTED ABOVE timber-bay here, the reverse of new-england-federal's ordering. This variant's own description names Flemish-bond brick with thin joints as 'the prestige wall, frame with beaded weatherboard as the vernacular equivalent' -- the masonry case is the style's own stated primary, not merely one option among equals.

The vernacular frame equivalent, per the style's own wording -- demoted below brick-course for this variant specifically, the inverse of new-england-federal's ranking. Present chiefly on the Piedmont farmer's I-house version, where the style's own massing_affinities note 'Federal trim at the door only.'

italian-renaissance.name: Italian Renaissance

revival_periods.note: The palazzo mode adopted for banks, clubs and city mansions in Britain and America, usually at brownstone rather than travertine scale.
The Beaux-Arts-trained American revival, this time with correct proportions and real stone, for country houses and institutions.

geography.hearth: Florence

lineage.note: Recovery rather than unbroken practice: architects measured standing ruins directly (Brunelleschi and Donatello in Rome c. 1402-04) and read the Vitruvius manuscript recovered by Poggio Bracciolini in 1414. Italian masonry craft, brickwork and tile roofing were, however, genuinely continuous, so the material substrate never lapsed even while the proportional system did.

The orders are attributed to Greek origin throughout the treatises, but no fifteenth- or sixteenth-century Italian architect had seen a Greek temple. The Greek ancestry is textual, mediated entirely by Vitruvius.

description.short: The deliberate reconstruction of the Roman proportional system as a written, teachable design method, applied for the first time to the private urban palace and the country villa.
description.long:
The Italian Renaissance is not a style that grew; it is a style that was reconstructed on purpose, by a small number of identifiable people, from physical evidence and one text. What they were after was not Roman shapes - those had never fully disappeared - but the rule that generated the shapes. Alberti's formulation of concinnitas, that a building is finished when nothing can be added, taken away or altered without making it worse, is the whole programme in a sentence, and it converts architecture from a craft judgement into an argument about number. The consequence is that Renaissance buildings can be discussed, drawn to scale, published and copied in a way that Gothic buildings could not, and this is why the tradition, once restarted, never stops again.

The conditions are commercial and urban. Fifteenth-century Florence, Venice, Milan and later papal Rome had banking and textile fortunes in private hands, a class of patrons who were neither feudal nor clerical, and a legal and political situation in which the private palace in the city was the main statement of family standing. That produces a new building type: a four-storey block on a tight urban site, defensible but not fortified, blank and rusticated at the base where the street is, with the family's floor above it. It also produces a new professional: the architect as an educated designer who does not lay stone, whose authority comes from drawing and from knowledge of antiquity rather than from apprenticeship in a lodge. Printing arrives at exactly the right moment. Serlio's illustrated books from 1537 turn the orders into a mail-order product, and the system leaves Italy in the hands of anyone who can buy a folio.

What it was reacting against is unmistakable if you stand in Florence: Gothic construction, which the Italians never loved and which they characterised as barbarous and northern. The Gothic wall is dematerialised, its structure exposed and expressive, its verticality unbounded, its ornament naturalistic and proliferating. The Renaissance answer is the opposite at every point - the wall reasserted as a flat, continuous, obviously solid plane; horizontality restated by string courses and terminated absolutely by a heavy cornice; ornament reduced to a fixed vocabulary of mouldings whose profiles can be specified. Brunelleschi's dome over Florence Cathedral is the pivot: Gothic in its ribbed double-shell structure, wholly un-Gothic in its serene hemispherical intention.

Standing in the Piazza Farnese, what you feel is weight held absolutely still. The palazzo is a single unbroken plane about thirty metres high; the rustication grades from rough quoins at the corners to smooth ashlar; the storey heights diminish upward so the building sits down rather than rises; the windows are identical, evenly spaced, and none of them is more important than any other; and then the cornice - Michelangelo's, deep enough to lay a body in - throws the entire facade into a single band of shadow and stops it dead against the sky. There is no centrepiece and no crescendo. The doorway is simply the one opening you can walk through. Inside, the cortile does the whole architectural argument in miniature: three superimposed arcades, one order per storey, and a well of hot Roman light dropped into the middle of a cold building.

defining_characteristics: Whole-number commensurable ratios governing plan and elevation together, derived from a module and defensible in argument
The wall reasserted as a flat, continuous, evidently solid plane, with the orders applied to it as pilasters rather than projecting from it
Horizontal termination: string courses at every storey and a single deep crowning cornice that ends the composition absolutely
Storey heights and rustication both grading from heavy at the base to light at the top
An even, additive, non-hierarchical bay rhythm with no centrepiece and no crescendo
The arcaded internal courtyard (cortile) as the organising void of the urban palace
A fixed, published vocabulary of mouldings and orders, transmissible by treatise independent of any craft lodge
diagnostic_tells: Every window on a facade is the same size and the same distance apart, including the ones next to the door
Rustication is graded by storey - heavy channelled or rock-faced below, progressively flatter above - and stops at a string course, never mid-wall
The cornice projection is enormous relative to the wall (roughly 1/12 to 1/15 of total facade height) and has no gable behind it; the roof is invisible from the street
Round-headed arches only, springing from an impost, with the arch rise exactly half the span - no segmental, pointed or elliptical arches
Pilasters are flat, shallow (projection about 1/6 of their width) and do not carry anything; the wall behind them is continuous

distinguished_from.difference: Palladio makes the plan the generator and puts a temple portico on a house; the earlier Renaissance keeps the temple front for churches and composes its palaces as even, unaccented, planar walls. If there is a projecting pedimented portico dominating a domestic front, it is Palladian, not quattrocento or High Renaissance.

The Baroque wall curves, the bays accelerate toward the centre, columns are stacked in several planes of projection within one bay, and pediments are broken or segmental. The Renaissance wall is flat, the bays are even, columns are in one plane, and pediments are whole.

The revival reproduces the palazzo silhouette at reduced scale, usually with a modern floor-to-floor height that makes the storeys equal rather than graded, and often with a visible roof. The absence of storey-height grading is the fastest tell.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Commensurable whole-number ratios propagated from a module through plan and elevation alike (Alberti's concinnitas). The unit of composition is the bay - a pilaster-framed panel containing one opening - not the column.
typical_ratios: Room and bay proportions 1:1, 3:4, 2:3, 3:5, 1:2, with the square and the double square dominant
Storey heights diminishing upward in the region of 10:9:8; Palazzo Farnese's principal storeys step down visibly
Crowning cornice projection roughly 1/12 to 1/15 of total facade height, with projection approximately equal to its own height
Pilaster projection about 1/6 to 1/8 of its width; entablature about 1/4 to 1/5 of the pilaster height
Arcade: arch rise exactly 1/2 the span (semicircular); pier width 1/3 to 1/2 the clear span
Window aperture 1:1.6 to 1:2 (w:h), with pier-to-opening ratio between 1:1 and 1:1.5
Cortile typically square or 3:4 in plan, with an odd number of bays per side
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even, additive and non-hierarchical: five to eleven identical bays across a front, with emphasis given only by centring the portal and, at most, by a slightly enlarged central window. The Renaissance palazzo has no centrepiece; the composition is a field, terminated by quoins and a cornice.

massing_affinities.note: The palazzo: rooms on all four sides of an arcaded cortile, blank rusticated street face, all significant light borrowed from the court.
The palazzetto sits in a continuous street wall and reads as a unit of the block, not as a free-standing object.
The villa suburbana opens its fourth side to garden and view once it leaves the city wall.
The dominant-centre-with-flanking-wings diagram exists before Palladio but without the hyphen discipline.
Irregular agglomeration composed for the moving eye is the precise negation of the Renaissance argument that a building is a single resolved figure.

constraints.statement: Storey heights must diminish upward by at least 8 percent per storey above the piano nobile. Equal-height storeys make the composition float and read as revival or as modern floor plate.
All arches are semicircular: rise = half span, within 2 percent. Segmental, elliptical, pointed and flat arches are outside the style except in service openings below the piano nobile.

test.note: Rise = half span within 2 percent, read as +/-2 percentage points around 0.5. Which arch forms are excluded (segmental, elliptical, pointed, flat except at service openings) stays prose.

constraints.statement: Crowning cornice must project between 1/12 and 1/16 of the total facade height, and its projection must be at least equal to its own vertical dimension, so that it throws the whole wall into shadow.

test.note: Tests the projection-to-facade-height ratio (1/16-1/12). 'Its projection must be at least equal to its own vertical dimension' needs a cornice-vertical-dimension variable -- only cornice_projection_in exists, not a separate cornice depth/height -- and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Rustication may change only at a string course or a storey line, never within a storey and never partway across an elevation.
No pedimented projecting portico on a domestic front; the temple front is reserved for churches until Palladio.

exemplars.name: Ospedale degli Innocenti
exemplars.note: Brunelleschi, begun 1419, completed 1445. The first fully proportioned Renaissance elevation: an arcade of nine bays in which the column height, arch span and bay depth are all the same dimension.

exemplars.name: Palazzo Rucellai
exemplars.location: Via della Vigna Nuova, Florence, Italy
exemplars.note: Traditionally 1446-1451, attributed to Alberti with Bernardo Rossellino executing. The first application of superimposed pilaster orders to a private palace facade - the Colosseum bay brought indoors to the city street.

exemplars.name: Tempietto, San Pietro in Montorio
exemplars.note: Bramante, c. 1502. A peripteral Tuscan drum under a hemispherical dome; the purest surviving demonstration that the Renaissance had fully recovered the ancient system.

exemplars.name: Palazzo Farnese
exemplars.note: 1517-1589; Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, cornice and upper cortile by Michelangelo from 1546. The reference palazzo for storey grading and cornice proportion.

sources: Leon Battista Alberti, De re aedificatoria (written c. 1452, printed 1485)
Sebastiano Serlio, Tutte l'opere d'architettura et prospettiva (1537-1575)
Rudolf Wittkower, Architectural Principles in the Age of Humanism (1949)
Peter Murray, The Architecture of the Italian Renaissance (1963)
John Summerson, The Classical Language of Architecture (1963)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Palladio is himself an Italian Renaissance architect writing from within this tradition rather than reviving it, which is about as close to zero-derivation as this corpus gets. Named directly by this style's own exemplar: the Tempietto is 'a peripteral Tuscan drum under a hemispherical dome' and 'the purest surviving demonstration that the Renaissance had fully recovered the ancient system.'

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The base-storey register of a superimposed cortile arcade -- 'three superimposed arcades, one order per storey,' as at Palazzo Farnese -- graded heavier below and lighter above, the same logic the style's own storey-height diminution constraint (c01) states for the wall around it.
Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The upper, richest register of the same cortile superimposition, and the order of the piano nobile where a single order is used rather than three stacked ones.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the even, additive, non-hierarchical bay rhythm this style's own bay_rhythm field states explicitly -- 'no centrepiece and no crescendo' -- and its cornice-projection band (1/12-1/16 of facade height) matches this style's own c03 constraint almost verbatim.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and by the same author as the order packs above. 'Every window on a facade is the same size and the same distance apart, including the ones next to the door' is this style's own diagnostic_tell, and it is precisely the rule Palladio's chapters on doors and windows state.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and by the same author. Governs the individual room to the seven approved shapes and the three means; the style's own proportional_system field states 'room and bay proportions 1:1, 3:4, 2:3, 3:5, 1:2' as the same set this pack encodes.

adam-style.name: Adam Style

revival_periods.note: Carried to America almost immediately by the Works in Architecture and by emigrant craftsmen; the Federal style is substantially an Adam derivative executed in wood.
Neo-Adam interiors become the standard grammar of the Edwardian and American country-house drawing room.

geography.hearth: London and Edinburgh, from the Adam brothers' office in the Adelphi

lineage.note: The envelope, the plan, the sash window, the brick and the trades are all Georgian. Adam almost never built a new shell where an existing one could be remodelled; a great deal of his most famous work is decoration inside somebody else's carcass.
Adam trained within the Palladian consensus and kept its plan discipline and its proportional habits even while attacking its ornament.

Stated in the Adams' own preface to the Works in Architecture (1773), which condemns the 'ponderous' compartment ceiling and the massive entablature of Kent and Burlington by name and proposes lightness, movement and variety in their place.

Adam's authority is archaeological but selective: Diocletian's palace at Split, which he surveyed in 1757 and published in 1764, and above all Roman domestic and bath interiors — the grotesque wall-painting of the Golden House rediscovered through Piranesi's circle. He quotes Roman interiors, not Roman structure.
The grotesque ornament reaches Adam as much through Raphael's Vatican loggie and their engraved copies as through antiquity itself.

description.short: A decorative revolution conducted inside the Georgian box: flattened, delicate, polychrome ornament and rooms shaped into apses, ovals and screened recesses, by an architect who designed everything down to the doorknob.
description.long:
Robert Adam returned from four years in Italy and Dalmatia in 1758 with a survey of Diocletian's palace, a portfolio of Roman interior ornament, and an accurate reading of the market. The Palladian generation had exhausted itself; its rooms were rectangular, its ceilings compartmented and heavy, its ornament derived from Roman temple exteriors applied indoors at a scale that suited nothing. Adam's proposal, argued in the preface to the Works in Architecture published with his brother James from 1773, was that interiors should follow Roman domestic precedent instead — lighter, flatter, more varied, more colourful — and that a building should exhibit what he called movement: rise and fall, advance and recess, convexity and concavity, so that a composition changes as you walk past it.

What he actually delivered was the first complete design system in British architecture. An Adam room is designed as a totality: the plaster ceiling, the carpet echoing the ceiling in reverse, the chimneypiece, the door furniture, the mirror frames, the sconces, the silverware. The vocabulary is small and endlessly recombined — fans, paterae, husk swags, anthemion, urns, griffins, arabesque candelabra, all in relief so shallow that it reads as drawing rather than sculpture, and coloured in pale green, lilac, pink and terracotta against white. The spatial vocabulary is equally consistent: apsed ends, screens of columns dividing a space without closing it, niches for statuary, oval and circular rooms, and a sequence of rooms deliberately varied in shape so that the movement doctrine operates in plan as well as elevation.

The economic context matters. Adam ran a large office as a business, took on speculative development at the Adelphi in 1768 which nearly ruined him, and licensed his manner through publication in a way no British architect had before. His ornament was also uniquely suited to the new industries: Coade artificial stone for exteriors from 1769, cast composition for interior enrichments, wallpaper, and Wedgwood's jasperware, which is Adam ornament in ceramic. This is why the style spread so fast and so far, and why the American Federal style is essentially Adam translated into carved and moulded wood by joiners working from the plates.

The experience of an Adam interior is peculiarly modern: it is light, precise and slightly cool, and it flatters the person moving through it rather than overawing them. Ceilings appear higher than they are because the ornament is drawn in pale colour rather than modelled in shadow; a screen of columns across the end of a library makes the room feel longer than its dimensions allow; the sequence from a square anteroom to an apsed drawing room to an oval boudoir is composed like music. Outside, the same house is often almost plain — Adam's exteriors are frequently a Georgian elevation with the mouldings thinned, a shallow relieving arch, and a Coade stone panel — which is exactly the point. This is a style that put nearly all of its intelligence indoors.

defining_characteristics: Room shapes deliberately varied in sequence: rectangles alternating with apsed, oval, circular and niched spaces, and columnar screens dividing without enclosing
Ornament in very low relief — 5 to 15 mm projection — drawn rather than modelled, in fans, paterae, husk swags, anthemion, urns, sphinxes and arabesque grotesques
Polychromy: ornament picked out in pale green, lilac, rose, straw and terracotta against white or off-white ground, replacing the white-and-gold or plain plaster of the Palladians
Total design of the interior, with ceiling, carpet, chimneypiece, furniture, mirrors and metalwork designed as one system by one office
Attenuated orders and thinned mouldings throughout, including thinner sash glazing bars and more delicate cornice profiles than Georgian practice
The 'movement' doctrine: elevations and plans composed with advance and recess, convex and concave, so the composition changes with the viewer's position
Radiating fanlights and delicate ironwork as the exterior signature of an otherwise restrained Georgian facade
diagnostic_tells: A radiating spider-web fanlight in fine lead or wrought iron over a six-panel door, far more elaborate and much thinner in section than a mid-Georgian fan
Low-relief plaster ceilings laid out as a geometric field of roundels, fans and octagons, colour-picked rather than left white — the inverse of the Palladian deep-coffered ceiling
A screen of two or four attenuated columns across the end of a room, defining a recess that is neither a separate room nor part of the main volume
Ornament repeating at small scale across every surface — the same honeysuckle in the frieze, the chair back, the fire grate and the carpet
Externally: a Georgian box whose mouldings have all been thinned, often with a shallow blind relieving arch linking the first-floor windows and a Coade stone panel or plaque

distinguished_from.difference: Same box, thinner everything. Georgian mouldings are chunky and cast strong shadows; Adam's are shallow and read as pattern. Georgian rooms are rectangles; Adam rooms are shaped. The exterior difference is small and the interior difference is total.

The declared enemy. Palladian interiors are heavy, rectangular, deeply coffered and derived from temple exteriors; Adam interiors are light, varied, shallow and derived from Roman domestic and bath decoration. Palladian rooms impose; Adam rooms accommodate.

Regency takes the thinning further but changes the source from Rome to Greece and then to anywhere — Egypt, India, China. Adam ornament is delicate, floral and polychrome; Regency ornament is sparse, linear and archaeologically Greek, and Regency exteriors go over to stucco, bows and iron balconies.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Georgian and Palladian proportion retained for the shell, with the orders attenuated beyond canonical limits and the interior organised by a sequence of contrasted room shapes rather than by a single module.
typical_ratios: Columns attenuated to 10-11 diameters where the canonical Ionic is 9 and Corinthian 9.5-10
Ornament relief depth 5-15 mm; cornice projection reduced to roughly 0.6 of Palladian practice at the same room height
Glazing bars 16-20 mm, against 25-32 mm in early Georgian work
Room sequence alternating 1:1, 1:1.5 and apsed or oval plans; apse depth 0.25-0.35 of room width
Ceiling height 3.0-4.2 m on the principal floor, with the frieze occupying 0.10-0.14 of wall height
Sash proportion 1.7:1 to 2:1, unchanged from Georgian
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Georgian evenness on the street front, modulated by shallow advance and recess: a slightly projecting centre of three bays, or an end pavilion brought forward 300-600 mm, so that the wall models itself in raking light without any change of bay spacing.

massing_affinities.note: The remodelled or newly built double-pile block, with the plan's interest concentrated in the shaping of individual rooms.
Adam's most consequential urban work — the Adelphi, Portman Square, Fitzroy Square and the design of Charlotte Square in Edinburgh in 1791 — treats the terrace as a single palace-fronted composition.
Retained at Kedleston, where Adam completed a Palladian five-part scheme and rebuilt its centre.
Adam's castle style — Culzean, Seton, Oxenfoord — wraps drums, battlements and turrets around a wholly classical plan, and is the direct link from this node to the picturesque family.

constraints.statement: Interior ornament relief must not exceed 20 mm projection. Deep, heavily modelled enrichment belongs to Palladian or Baroque work and reads as the wrong century immediately.

test.note: Source states the figure in millimetres; the vocabulary variable is named _in by convention but its unit here is the units field, mm, not inches.

constraints.statement: Ceiling, carpet, chimneypiece and joinery in a principal room must share one ornamental vocabulary. Mixing Adam plasterwork with a heavier moulding family is the standard failure mode of revival work.
Glazing bars not thicker than 20 mm, and cornice and architrave profiles reduced by roughly a third from mid-Georgian section. Adam is Georgian thinned; if it is not thinner it is not Adam.

test.note: Tests the glazing-bar clause only. The second clause -- cornice/architrave profiles reduced by roughly a third from mid-Georgian section -- has no recorded mid-Georgian baseline value to compare against in this corpus, so it stays prose.

constraints.statement: At least one principal room in the sequence must be shaped — apsed, oval, circular or screened — or the movement doctrine that defines the style is absent.
External modelling by advance and recess of 300-600 mm at the centre or ends, without changing bay spacing.

exemplars.name: Syon House interiors
exemplars.note: Remodelled 1762-69 for the first Duke of Northumberland inside a Jacobean shell. The Ante-Room with its twelve verd-antique columns from the Tiber and the apsed Long Gallery are the fullest demonstration of Adam's spatial doctrine.

exemplars.name: Osterley Park
exemplars.note: Remodelled 1761-80 for the Child banking family, again around an Elizabethan core. The Etruscan Dressing Room, painted throughout in the antique grotesque manner, is the most complete surviving Adam interior scheme.

exemplars.name: Kedleston Hall, Marble Hall and Saloon
exemplars.note: Adam took over from Matthew Brettingham and James Paine in 1760 and completed the south front and principal interiors 1759-65, including a triumphal-arch south elevation and a domed rotunda saloon.

exemplars.name: Home House, 20 Portman Square
exemplars.note: Built 1773-77 for Elizabeth, Countess of Home. A town house whose top-lit oval staircase and sequence of shaped rooms show what Adam could do within a terrace plot.

sources: Robert and James Adam, The Works in Architecture of Robert and James Adam (1773-78)
John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)
Eileen Harris, The Genius of Robert Adam: His Interiors (2001)
Damie Stillman, The Decorative Work of Robert Adam (1966)
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)

proportion_packs.note: The Georgian/Chambers Ionic is the shell order Adam remodels rather than replaces, and the retained baseline his own numbers are stated against: 'columns attenuated to 10-11 diameters where the canonical Ionic is 9'. This node's own proportional_system quotes that delta directly, but the attenuated order itself -- the actual entasis, capital and entablature of a column drawn a full diameter thinner than any published seventeenth- or eighteenth-century treatise permits -- is not one of this corpus's 36 packs. THE GAP: there is no dedicated Adam overlay. What is bound is the Chambers baseline (chosen over Gibbs because Chambers 1759 is Adam's own exact professional generation and rival -- both taught proportion in London in the 1760s-70s -- where Gibbs 1728-32 belongs to the generation Adam's own preface attacks) and the 10-11 diameter figure is carried as a judgment on top of it, not as an encoded member.

The order of Adam's grandest rooms -- the type is a rich-order screen or colonnade dividing a shaped space without enclosing it, of which Kedleston's alabaster-columned Marble Hall is the best-documented example in this node's own exemplars. Bound secondary and not primary because Adam's own preface treats Corinthian richness as the exception rather than the default register; most of his screens (Syon's Ante-Room among them) are the lighter Ionic.

Governs the retained Georgian metronome -- equal bays, vertical alignment, plain wall between doorcase and cornice -- to which Adam adds only shallow advance-and-recess modelling (300-600 mm at the centre or ends) without changing bay spacing. This is the 'movement' doctrine applied to a wall that is otherwise disciplined by the same rules as english-georgian.

Governs the sash void and the door; unchanged in ratio from Georgian practice (1.7:1 to 2:1) but crowned, after about 1770, by a radiating spider-web fanlight far finer in section than a mid-Georgian fan -- the exterior signature this node names as its fastest diagnostic tell.

Carries the glazing-bar figure the constraint tests directly: not thicker than 20 mm, against 25-32 mm in early Georgian work -- Adam thinned even the sash before Regency thinned it further to 12-18 mm.

Bound as the base family Adam's plasterers cut down from, not as a literal profile match. The pack's Georgian members run 5-15 mm deep is roughly Vignola-Chambers scale; Adam's constraint caps relief at 20 mm and the style's whole vocabulary -- fans, paterae, husk swags, low-relief drawing rather than modelled shadow -- is a different design language layered on the same wall divisions this pack derives. THE SECOND GAP: no 'trim-adam' pack exists among the 36, so the flattening itself (roughly a third off Palladian-Chambers section) is carried as the node's own stated ratio and not as an encoded profile family.

Supplies the base ratio set (1:1, 1:1.5, and the rest) that Adam's room SEQUENCE varies rather than abandons -- an apsed or oval room is still proportioned by a stated relation of length, breadth and height before it is shaped. THE THIRD GAP: the actual shaping doctrine -- apse, niche, columnar screen, the alternation of rectangular and curved rooms that IS the 'movement' argument -- has no corresponding system among the 36 packs. This entry governs the underlying ratio only; the shaping is unencoded and is this node's most significant real gap.

Retained without material change on the mostly-Georgian exterior: Adam almost never built a new shell where an existing one could be remodelled, so the storey-height diminution this pack governs is inherited fabric more often than new design.

The retained Georgian brick carcass, where Adam is building new rather than remodelling an existing Jacobean or Elizabethan shell (as at Syon and Osterley, both of which are older cores). Low precedence because Adam's own design attention is almost entirely indoors.

neo-eclectic.name: Neo-Eclectic

geography.hearth: No design hearth; the style was generated inside production builders' plan departments and merchandising groups and distributed through model-home parks

lineage.note: The real inheritance: the truss, the sheet-goods module, the attached street-facing garage, the eight-foot plate, and the production apparatus. Everything structural about a neo-eclectic house is a ranch grown to two storeys.
The deeper inheritance: the principle that the traditional look is a marketable surface applied to a cost-optimized shell, and the shallow eave that follows from it.

The definitional edge of this node. Colonial motifs are quoted — pediment, keystone, fanlight, dentil, shutter, Palladian window — with no transmission of the proportional system that generated them. The quotation is selected from an elevation menu after the plan is fixed, which is exactly what makes it a reference and not a descent.
The 'Tudor' elevation package: applied half-timbering in the front gable only, stucco panels, and a stone-veneered entry, over the same plan that carries the Colonial package.

The mansard roof of 1965-1980, used as a device for concealing a second storey or an apartment building's bulk. The most short-lived of the quoted grammars and the most obviously detached from its source.
The hipped 'French Country' package of the 1990s: steep hips, quoins, arched windows with keystones, and a stone-veneered entry mass.

description.short: The production-builder idiom of the late twentieth century, in which historical motifs were selected from an elevation menu and applied to a plan generated independently of them — the point at which the traditional grammar decoupled from its own logic.
description.long:
Neo-eclectic is the name for what American builders did between roughly 1965 and 2000, and the useful way to define it is procedural rather than visual. In every earlier style in this graph, the plan, the section, the structure, and the elevation were generated together, by one person or one tradition, out of one set of constraints. In the neo-eclectic house they were separated into different departments. The plan was generated first, from a marketable schedule of rooms and a target price per square foot, and optimized against the truss span, the setback envelope, and the mortgage. The elevation was then selected — genuinely selected, from a printed menu of three to six options labelled A through F, or Colonial, Traditional, French Country, Craftsman — and applied to the front of that plan. The other three elevations received vinyl. This is the decoupling, and every characteristic failure of the style follows from it mechanically rather than from anyone's bad taste.

The conditions that produced it were the consolidation of homebuilding and the disappearance of every institution that had previously transmitted proportional knowledge. Between 1960 and 1995 the industry shifted from tens of thousands of small builders to a smaller number of large regional and national ones — Ryan, Pulte, NVR, Toll — operating through merchandised model-home parks, whose economics reward visible difference between adjacent products. At the same time the transmission mechanisms died: no pattern book, no plan-book publisher, no trade magazine that taught proportion, no apprenticeship in the moulding profiles. What replaced them was the sales brochure and the appraisal comparable. Materials changed at the same moment and in the same direction: vinyl and aluminum cladding, injection-moulded polymer trim, thin brick and stone veneer on a wire-lath backing, fiberglass entry doors with moulded fanlight assemblies. Each is dimensionally shallow — a quarter-inch to three-quarters of an inch of relief where the original had three to six inches — and shallow trim cannot cast a shadow, which is the physical reason these buildings must resort to contrast and size for effect. Lot economics did the rest: rising land cost pushed the house to the front of the lot and the garage to the front of the house, and the two-car garage became a three-car garage in the 1990s.

The failure modes deserve naming precisely, and without contempt, because they are exactly the failures a rules-based generator exists to prevent, and naming them is the most useful thing this node can do. First, material return failure: brick or stone covers the front elevation and turns the corner by six to twelve inches before giving way to vinyl, which announces that the masonry is a face rather than a wall. Second, shutter failure: shutters half the width of the sash they nominally cover, screwed flat, applied to ganged, arched, or bay windows they could never have closed over. Third, head-height failure: window heads on one elevation at three or four different levels because each was set by the room behind it, so no horizontal datum organizes the wall. Fourth, gable proliferation: four to seven gables of similar width and identical pitch on one elevation, none dominant, so the eye cannot find a primary roof and the building has no top. Fifth, entry inflation: a two-storey entry element with a half-round or Palladian assembly, at one and a half to two times the scale the wall can carry, opening into a twenty-foot volume in a twelve-foot-wide space. Sixth, eave collapse: overhangs of six to twelve inches, leaving no shadow line, which forces every applied detail to grow in size and colour contrast to remain visible — this is why the ornament looks loud. Seventh, garage dominance: two or three doors occupying thirty-two to forty-eight feet of a fifty- to sixty-foot frontage, with the front door subordinate to them.

What should be said in fairness is that these are large, well-equipped, structurally sound houses that people wanted, that solved real problems of storage, bathroom count, and family life, and that are far better built than their critics assume. The failure is not of ambition or of workmanship; it is a failure of transmission. Every one of the seven failures above was prevented in earlier practice by a tacit rule that no one had to write down because the builder had learned it from the last builder. When the chain broke, the rules did not survive, because they had never been externalized. That is the whole argument for writing them down.

defining_characteristics: Motif selection performed independently of, and after, plan generation — the elevation is chosen from a menu applied to a fixed floor plan
Two or more unrelated historical grammars quoted on a single building, or one grammar quoted at incorrect scale
Masonry or stone applied to the street elevation only, with vinyl or panel siding on the remaining three
Multiple gables of near-equal width and identical pitch, with no dominant roof form
An entry element inflated in height and width relative to the wall that carries it, frequently rising through two storeys
Trim of minimal profile depth in extruded polymer, vinyl, or aluminum, compensating with size and colour contrast for the absence of shadow
A street frontage in which the garage doors are the largest architectural element
Shallow eave and rake overhang, typically 6 to 12 in
diagnostic_tells: Brick front with a 6-to-12-inch return onto the side elevation, then vinyl
Shutters at roughly half the width of the window, present on windows that are ganged or arched
A half-round or 'Palladian' window filling a gable, unrelated in width to anything below it
Three or more different window shapes — rectangular, arched, half-round, octagonal — on one elevation
A garage projecting forward of the front door plane (the snout house), with the entry recessed behind it
Roof planes meeting at valleys with no consistent eave line, so the fascia steps up and down across the facade

distinguished_from.difference: Colonial Revival composes to a proportional system: symmetrical bays, a governing head datum, correct entablature and door surround profiles with real projection, and masonry that wraps. Neo-eclectic quotes the same motifs without the system. The single fastest test is the corner: a Colonial Revival house is the same material on all four sides.

The same buyer, the same builders, and often the same decade — but governed by a form-based code that forbids precisely the moves listed in this node's constraints. The difference between them is not taste but enforcement.

Its structural parent. The ranch is single-storey, horizontal, and unornamented; neo-eclectic is two-storey, vertical in its entry, and heavily ornamented. Ranches that received applied shutters and cupolas after 1965 are transitional and should be assigned by storey count and roof complexity.

proportional_system.governing_logic: None operative, and it is more honest to record that than to invent one. The plan is generated from a marketable room schedule and a cost-per-square-foot target; the elevation is selected afterward. The only real modules are the 4-by-8 sheet, the 24-inch truss, the 16- or 18-foot garage door, the 8- or 9-foot plate, and the zoning setback envelope. Where classical proportion appears it appears as quotation at the wrong scale, because the element was sized to be seen from the street rather than derived from a module.
typical_ratios: Eave and rake overhang 6 to 12 in
Entry element 1.5 to 2 times the height of the adjacent wall opening; two-storey foyer volume in a plan 12 to 14 ft wide
Garage doors 32 to 48 ft of a 50 to 60 ft frontage — 55 to 80 percent, against the 33 percent that a coherent frontage tolerates
Applied shutter width 45 to 55 percent of the sash it flanks — half of correct
Trim profile projection 1/4 to 3/4 in, against 3 to 6 in in the sources quoted
Four to seven gables per principal elevation, pitches identical at 8:12 or 10:12
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Absent. Openings follow the plan behind them; apparent rhythm is coincidental and is usually broken by the garage bay at one end and the entry mass at the other.

massing_affinities.note: The two-storey multi-gabled mass is the style's default skeleton, arrived at by additive plan growth rather than by picturesque intent.
The single-storey and split-entry versions of the 1965-1985 period.
The 1965-1980 neo-mansard subtype, in both houses and small apartment buildings.
Occasionally used as the base for a 'Colonial' elevation package, and the one skeleton on which the style tends to behave.

constraints.statement: A masonry veneer must be applied to all elevations of the mass it clads, or terminate at an inside corner or a change of plane of not less than 24 in. A return of less than 24 in onto a side elevation is forbidden.

test.note: The statement's disjunction (veneer to all elevations, or terminate at an inside corner, or a plane change) is covered by its own unconditional floor -- any terminating plane change must be at least 24in -- so testing that floor doesn't falsely accept a case the statement would reject, matching the safe-shared-bound pattern.

constraints.statement: Decorative shutters shall each be not less than 45 percent of the width of the window opening, shall be hinged at the jamb, and are forbidden on ganged, arched, bay, and non-rectangular windows.

test.note: Hinge position and the omission-from-ganged/arched/bay/non-rectangular-window rule are categorical and stay prose.

constraints.statement: All window heads on a given storey of a given elevation shall align to one datum. Departures are permitted only where a change of roof plane or a change of wall plane of not less than 24 in separates them.

test.note: Tests the zero-tolerance datum rule. The roof/wall-plane-change exception (departures permitted only where a change of not less than 24 in separates them) stays prose.

constraints.statement: Maximum three gables per principal elevation. The dominant gable must exceed the next largest by not less than 25 percent in width, and secondary gables must be subordinate in ridge height.

test.note: Tests the maximum-three-gables ceiling. The dominant-gable width-excess and subordinate-ridge-height clauses stay prose (no width-comparison or ridge-hierarchy variable exists).

constraints.statement: Total garage door width not more than 33 percent of the street-facing facade; garage door plane set back not less than 4 ft behind the front door plane; three-car garages must be split or turned.

test.note: Tests the 4 ft setback-behind-front-door-plane clause. The 33 percent door-width ceiling and the three-car-split requirement stay prose.

exemplars.name: The Woodlands
exemplars.note: Opened October 1974 and built out over three decades; a large, well-planned master community whose houses show the full sequence of elevation packages from neo-Colonial through neo-Mediterranean.

exemplars.name: Weston (Indian Trace)
exemplars.note: Arvida; first homes completed 1984, incorporated as a city in 1996. A textbook late-century merchandised subdivision, and a useful control case because the planning is competent and the elevations still decouple from the plans.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013) — the Neoeclectic chapter
Dolores Hayden, Building Suburbia: Green Fields and Urban Growth, 1820-2000 (2003)
Andres Duany, Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk and Jeff Speck, Suburban Nation (2000)
Witold Rybczynski, Last Harvest: How a Cornfield Became New Daleville (2007)
Marianne Cusato and Brent Hull, Get Your House Right: Architectural Elements to Use and Avoid (2007)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to. This is the genuinely diagnostic binding in the whole assignment: the node's own hard constraints appear to be this pack's derived rules restated as enforcement against the style's own named failures. Constraint c04 (maximum three gables per elevation, dominant gable must exceed the next largest by not less than 25 percent) is this pack's dominance rule (module-area ratio floor of 1.35, 'below about 1.35 the two masses compete and the elevation has no subject') applied to gable count instead of elevation area; constraint c03 (one head datum per storey, departures only at a real plane change of 24 in or more) is this pack's datum rule stated as a zero-tolerance test. The node does not merely resemble this pack's subject matter, it appears to encode the pack's own dominance and datum rules as the corrective against the exact failure the long description names ('gable proliferation... none dominant, so the eye cannot find a primary roof'). Bound primary/facade accordingly, and consistent with the distinguished_from entry against new-urbanist-traditional: 'the code reads as an itemized prohibition of neo-eclectic practice.'

JUDGMENT BINDING: not in this pack's own applies_to list, and deliberately so -- the node exists to document that this pack's system is quoted rather than run. The long description and the typical_ratios both name the failure with the same figure: 'Trim profile projection 1/4 to 3/4 in, against 3 to 6 in in the sources quoted.' trim-classical is that source -- its casing-width rule (opening_width/6, six inches on a 36 in door) and backband projection are the 3-6 in figures the node cites as what Neo-Eclectic fails to deliver. Bound optional and at low precedence specifically so this node's package carries the named source of comparison rather than a governing system: the pack describes what the style is failing to be, not what it is.

JUDGMENT BINDING: not in this pack's own applies_to list. Bound because constraint c02 -- decorative shutters not less than 45 percent of sash width, hinged at the jamb, forbidden on ganged/arched/bay/non-rectangular windows -- quotes this pack's own shutter rule (leaf width = half the opening, less meeting clearance) as a prohibition against the exact failure the long description names: 'shutters half the width of the sash they nominally cover... applied to ganged, arched, or bay windows they could never have closed over.' As with trim-classical above, bound at low precedence as the named source of the violated rule rather than as a governing system for this node's own built fabric.

british-picturesque.name: British Picturesque & Revival

description.short: The deliberate composition of irregular, historically allusive buildings for visual and emotional effect — the intellectual origin of nearly all Anglo-American suburban architecture.
description.long:
The picturesque begins as a theory of landscape and becomes a theory of building: that irregularity, variety, and historical association are legitimate architectural aims, and that a house may be composed like a painting. Once accepted, it licenses Gothic Revival, Scottish Baronial, Old English, Queen Anne, and eventually the entire vocabulary of the freestanding suburban house.

This family is where the classical assumption that a building should be symmetrical is abandoned as a general rule. Everything that follows in America — the Victorian villa, the Shingle Style, the ranch — depends on that permission having been granted.

defining_characteristics: Asymmetry and irregular massing as deliberate compositional choices
Historical association valued as a source of architectural meaning
Silhouette and skyline treated as primary design material
Texture and material variety used to animate surface

british-arts-and-crafts.name: British Arts and Crafts

description.short: The reform movement that rejected industrial ornament in favour of honest material, visible craft, and the dignity of the vernacular cottage.
description.long:
Morris, Webb, Voysey, Lethaby, and Lutyens argued that the machine had corrupted both the object and the person who made it, and that architecture should return to local material, direct construction, and the modest forms of the rural cottage. The argument was moral before it was aesthetic.

It is the most philosophically explicit family in the taxonomy, and the one whose ideas travelled furthest — to Stickley's Craftsman in America, to the Deutscher Werkbund, and by an unexpected route into modernism, which kept the honesty-of-material argument while discarding the craft.

defining_characteristics: Material honesty: construction expressed rather than concealed
Local and traditional materials preferred to industrial substitutes
The vernacular cottage taken seriously as a model for serious architecture
Ornament arising from craft process rather than applied from a catalog
An explicit moral argument connecting how things are made to how people live

nordic-alpine-vernacular.name: Nordic & Alpine Vernacular

description.short: Log building and the deep-eaved chalet — timber traditions from regions with long winters, heavy snow, and abundant softwood.
description.long:
Horizontal log construction and the Alpine chalet share a logic: solid timber walls, very large roof overhangs, and elaborate carved detail concentrated on the gable and balcony where it can be seen and where the roof protects it.

Both reach America. Log building arrives with Finnish and Swedish settlers on the Delaware in 1638 and becomes the substrate of Appalachian building. The chalet arrives as a fashion in the 1850s through Downing and the pattern books, and its exposed rafter tails, brackets, and sawn balusters pass directly into the Craftsman bungalow half a century later.

defining_characteristics: Solid horizontal log or heavy timber walls rather than framed cavities
Very deep roof overhangs sheltering the wall and the balcony
Carved and sawn ornament concentrated at gable, bargeboard, and rail
Corner notching and joinery expressed as the primary detail
Span limited by available log length, setting room size directly

mexican-hacienda.name: Mexican Hacienda

revival_periods.note: The long low arcaded range around a courtyard, the tiled roof and the massive plastered wall are the hacienda's contribution to the American revival, distinct from the church-derived ornamental strain.
The arcaded courtyard house at estate scale in Florida, Texas and California.
Partial: the two-storey range with a continuous cantilevered upper balcony is the Californian offspring of the same arcade logic, crossed with Anglo framing.

geography.hearth: the Bajio, Hidalgo, Puebla and Yucatan

lineage.note: Direct and unambiguous: the hacienda is colonial building practice applied to a rural productive estate. Same walls, same vigas, same patio, same carpentry, same trades.

The Andalusian cortijo — a walled agricultural precinct with a casa, a chapel, granaries and workers' quarters around one or more working courts — is the direct organisational model, and many of the first encomenderos came from Andalusia and Extremadura where that model was standard.

Under the Porfiriato (1876-1911) many casas grandes were re-dressed in French neoclassical and Second Empire detail — mansard pavilions, pedimented window surrounds, cast-iron cresting — applied over an entirely unchanged colonial plan. Quotation from a fashionable elsewhere, with no transmission of practice.

description.short: The walled rural estate of New Spain and independent Mexico: a working precinct of casa grande, chapel, granaries and workers' quarters organised by arcaded corredores around one or more courts, sized by an economy of silver, sugar, pulque or henequen.
description.long:
A hacienda is not a house; it is a settlement with an owner's house in it, and the misunderstanding of that fact is why most reproductions of the type fail. The unit is the casco, the walled core of the estate, and inside it are the casa grande, the chapel, the trojes or granaries, the tinacal or the sugar mill or the desfibradora depending on what the estate produced, the stables, the workshops, the store, and the housing of the resident workforce, which on a large estate might be several hundred people bound to it by debt peonage. Around the casco lie the fields and the water rights, and the whole thing is enclosed by a wall with one or two controlled gates. Read as architecture it is a village with a hierarchy; read as an institution it is a self-contained economic and juridical world with the owner as its magistrate, and the walls are not ornamental.

The organising architectural element is the corredor. An arcade of eight, twelve, twenty bays, three to four metres deep, runs around the courts and along the fronts of the ranges, and it does everything: it is the circulation, since the rooms are single-pile and have no corridors; it is the shade, since the rooms behind it face into it rather than into the sun; it is the working floor for sorting, drying and repairing; and it is the social space, since the entire life of the estate happens under it. Everything else follows from repetition of that bay. Because the corredor is repetitive, and because the ranges behind it are one room deep, a hacienda grows by getting longer and by adding courts, never by getting deeper or taller. That gives the type its characteristic proportions: enormously long, one or at most two storeys, low, and horizontal against a horizontal landscape.

The construction is local by necessity. Adobe seven hundred to a thousand millimetres thick at the base in the highlands, or rubble and lime, or cut limestone in the Yucatan where the stone is at the surface; a stone or fired-brick socle a metre and a half high against rain splash and rising damp, which on an unrendered wall reads as a visible base band; vigas of local timber setting a room depth of five to six metres; flat azotea roofs on the dry altiplano and clay tile at low pitch where it rains. The walls are lime-plastered and colour-washed, and the colour is regional — the ochres and deep reds of the Bajio, the almagre red and cream of Yucatan. The ornament budget goes almost entirely to two places: the entrance gate, which carries the owner's arms and the estate's name, and the chapel, which is often the only vaulted, the only carved, and the only twin-towered thing on the property. The casa grande is distinguished from everything else by its height and by having the better arcade order, not by being decorated.

The end of the type is a date. The Revolution and the Constitution of 1917 established the legal basis for agrarian reform, and between 1917 and the Cardenas expropriations of the 1930s the hacienda system was dismantled; thousands of cascos were burned, abandoned or handed to ejidos, and the henequen haciendas of Yucatan were left standing empty when the sisal market collapsed. That is why the surviving examples are so often ruins or hotels rather than working estates. To walk into an abandoned casco at midday is a peculiar experience: a hundred metres of arcade with nothing under it, a chapel with a bell still hanging, a machine house with a rusted German engine in it, a courtyard of dust and one enormous tree, and the whole thing built to a scale that assumed several hundred people would be moving through it and that has been silent for a century.

defining_characteristics: A walled precinct (casco) with one or two controlled gates, containing house, chapel, production buildings and workers' housing
Continuous arcaded corredores, three to four metres deep and running eight to twenty bays, as the circulation, shade and social space
Single-pile ranges around one or more courts; the complex grows in length and in courts, never in depth
Massive adobe, rubble or cut-stone walls 700-1000 mm at the base on a raised stone or brick socle
Room depth fixed by the span of local timber vigas, 5-6 m clear
Flat azotea roofs with parapets and canales on the dry highlands; low-pitched clay tile with deep overhangs where it rains
The chapel as the only ornamented and often the only vaulted structure; the casa grande distinguished by height and arcade order rather than by decoration
Production buildings — trojes, tinacal, mill, desfibradora — as full architectural members of the composition
diagnostic_tells: An arcade of more than eight identical bays running in a straight line
A tall stone or brick base band 1.2-1.8 m high under a plastered adobe wall, unrendered and clearly a different material
A twin-belfry chapel facade standing inside a walled compound rather than on a street or plaza
A monumental gateway with a carved name and coat of arms, in a wall that is otherwise entirely blank for a hundred metres
Colour-washed lime plaster in strong regional colours — almagre red, ochre, indigo — with white trim at the arcade

distinguished_from.difference: The hacienda is the rural agricultural branch. It is longer, lower, far more repetitive, spends nothing on the domestic portada, and includes production buildings and workers' housing as part of the architecture.
The catalog skeleton describes the enclosed court; the hacienda is usually several of them plus a walled field of ancillary buildings. A single-court hacienda is a small one.

Both are whitewashed, thick-walled working farm precincts on colonial ground. The Cape homestead puts all its rhetoric into a central gable and a stoep and has no arcade; the hacienda has no gable at all and puts everything into an arcade.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The arcade bay and the viga span. The corredor bay of 3-4 m, repeated, sets the whole rhythm and length of the complex; the viga span of 5-6 m sets range depth absolutely; the walled rectangle of the casco, not any facade, is the compositional frame. Nothing is derived from an order, and no elevation is composed as a whole — the composition is a plan.
typical_ratios: Corredor bay 3-4 m; corredor depth 2.5-4 m; arcade runs of 8-20 bays
Range depth 5-6 m clear; wall thickness 700-1000 mm at base, tapering
Stone socle 1.2-1.8 m high
Court dimension 20-60 m across; tile roof pitch 20-30 degrees with 800-1200 mm overhang
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Relentlessly even. The uninterrupted repetition of the arcade bay over great length is the type's single most characteristic effect, and any attempt to accent, group or break it works against the building.

massing_affinities.note: One or more fully enclosed courts, with a blind or near-blind outer wall and a single gate.
The corredor is the building's real room; the ranges are a core inserted behind a gallery, exactly as the catalog describes.
Three-sided service and production courts behind or beside the principal one.
The smaller ranchos and the outlying estancias string house, store and stable in a linear chain with a continuous portal along the front.
Only where flooding or termites force a raised floor, which is rare in the highland heartland.

constraints.statement: Adobe or rubble walls 700-1000 mm at the base, carried on a stone or fired-brick socle at least 1.2 m high. Rain splash and rising damp destroy an adobe wall from the bottom; the socle is not optional and must read as a different material.

test.note: Tests the base wall-thickness range. The socle requirement ('carried on a stone or fired-brick socle at least 1.2 m high') is a second numeric fact in the same sentence -- it maps to water_table_height_in (at-least 1200 mm) but a single test object can only cover one clause; left as prose.

constraints.statement: Room depth must not exceed the viga span, about 6 m clear. Every range is single-pile and every room is entered from the corredor. Thickening a range to gain area destroys the ventilation and the circulation at once.

test.note: Tests the viga-span depth ceiling. 'Every range is single-pile and every room is entered from the corredor' is a categorical plan-organisation rule, not a single numeric expression, and stays prose.

constraints.statement: The corredor must be at least 2.5 m deep and must be continuous along the ranges it serves; it is the circulation as well as the shade. A discontinuous arcade forces internal corridors the type does not have.

test.note: Tests the minimum corredor depth. 'Must be continuous along the ranges it serves' has no matching vocabulary variable (corridor_present tests whether an interior corridor exists at all, a different concept) and stays prose.

constraints.statement: The casco is a walled precinct with one or two controlled gates and must include, at minimum, the casa grande, the chapel and at least one production building. A freestanding casa grande without its working precinct is not a hacienda.
The ornament budget goes to the gate and to the chapel. Carving, vaulting and twin belfries belong to the chapel; the casa grande asserts itself by height and by the order of its arcade.

exemplars.name: Hacienda de Santa Maria Regla
exemplars.note: c. 1762-1774; the silver-refining hacienda of Pedro Romero de Terreros, Conde de Regla, with courts of patio arches built for amalgamation work — the industrial hacienda at its largest.

exemplars.name: Hacienda San Gabriel de Barrera
exemplars.note: Late 17th to early 18th century; a mining hacienda with an intact casa grande, chapel and hacienda de beneficio.

exemplars.name: Hacienda Yaxcopoil
exemplars.note: Founded in the 17th century; the surviving buildings are largely of the 19th-century henequen era, including the machine house. The clearest surviving example of the industrialised late hacienda.

exemplars.name: Hacienda de Jaral de Berrio
exemplars.note: 18th century; one of the largest cascos in Mexico, with a fortified perimeter, a domed chapel and a Porfirian remodelling of the casa grande.

sources: Rendon Garcini, Haciendas de Mexico
Kubler & Soria, Art and Architecture in Spain and Portugal and their American Dominions 1500-1800
Toussaint, Arte colonial en Mexico
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World

proportion_packs.note: The node's own governing_logic states 'The arcade bay and the viga span... Nothing is derived from an order, and no elevation is composed as a whole - the composition is a plan,' with range depth fixed at 5-6 m clear by the viga span - almost the pack's own 14-18 ft measured room-breadth band restated in Mexican terms. mexican-hacienda is named directly in room-vernacular's applies_to. facade-picturesque was considered and rejected: the hacienda's bay_rhythm is explicitly 'relentlessly even' with 'any attempt to accent, group or break it' working against the building, which contradicts facade-picturesque's dominance-and-grouping logic outright, and the node is not in that pack's applies_to either. No order pack applies - there is no order in the composition, only a repeated arcade bay.

iberian-vernacular.name: Iberian Vernacular

description.short: The whitewashed courtyard house of southern Spain — thick walls, small openings, deep shade, and a patio that does the work of a room.
description.long:
The Andalusian house is the Islamic courtyard diagram sustained in ordinary building for a thousand years: a blank whitewashed street wall, a controlled entry, and an interior court planted and often fitted with water. The climate logic is exact — thermal mass, night flushing, shaded transitional space, minimized solar gain on the envelope.

This is the most technically relevant traditional inheritance available for the American Sun Belt, and it is almost entirely unexploited by production builders there, who instead build Midwestern houses with more insulation.

defining_characteristics: Blank whitewashed street elevation and one controlled entry
Interior patio as the principal living space for much of the year
Very thick lime-rendered masonry with deep reveals
Small high openings and generous shaded galleries
Water and planting as architectural rather than decorative elements

american-farmhouse-vernacular.name: American Farmhouse Vernacular

revival_periods.note: The contemporary 'modern farmhouse' is an imitation of this node specifically - board-and-batten, standing seam, simple gable, black windows - and it imitates the surfaces while inverting the proportions, the window sizes and the wing hierarchy that made the original coherent.
The Depression-era and FHA minimal house is this type stripped further, and is arguably a continuation rather than a revival.

geography.hearth: no single hearth; the type is the residue of national settlement

lineage.note: The direct ancestor of the form. The gable-front and the gable-front-and-wing are Greek Revival inventions; the farmhouse is what remained after the frieze board thinned to a fascia and the pilasters shrank to corner boards. Its proportions are Grecian proportions with the money taken out.

In the Upland South, the Midwest and the Plains the farmhouse frequently replaces or encases a log pen, and inherits the pen's plan logic (single-pile rooms, additive growth, gable-end chimneys) directly.

The residual symmetry - three or five even bays, a centred door, vertically aligned openings - is Georgian discipline surviving two centuries of dilution, which is why even the plainest farmhouse still reads as ordered.

Downing's Cottage Residences (1842) and The Architecture of Country Houses (1850) put a pointed gable window and a bargeboard into the farmer's vocabulary as an available catalogue item. The farmhouse quotes Gothic Revival at the gable and nowhere else, and descends from none of it.

description.short: The un-styled American workhorse: a gable-front-and-wing or two-storey single-pile house with minimal trim and whatever ornament the local mill happened to stock, built in enormous numbers between 1830 and 1920 and now the substrate the 'modern farmhouse' market imitates.
description.long:
Calling this a residual category is the standard mistake, and it gets the causality backwards. The American farmhouse is not what is left over when style is subtracted; it is a coherent building culture with its own rules, and those rules are about growth, hierarchy and cost rather than about ornament. The two dominant configurations are the gable-front-and-wing - a taller gable-fronted block with a lower side-gabled wing and the porch tucked into the reentrant corner - and the I-house, two storeys tall, one room deep, three to five bays, with a rear kitchen ell. Both are additive: they assume the house will grow, they establish which mass is dominant before the first addition, and they place the entry in the sheltered inside corner where it will still make sense after the third ell has been built. That is a design system. It is simply one whose parameters are ridge height, wing setback and porch depth rather than order, entablature and portico.

The conditions that produced it are the industrialisation of building supply, and they are worth being precise about because they explain the trim. Between 1830 and 1870 the circular sawmill, the machine-cut nail, the balloon frame and the water-powered planing and moulding mill converted lumber from a craft product into a catalogue product. After 1870 the railroad delivered that catalogue anywhere: sash, doors, brackets, spindles, porch posts, bargeboards, all mill-run and shipped. A farmer building in 1885 was not choosing a style; he was choosing a plan he had known all his life and then choosing from a millwork list. What he bought is a fair index of what he could afford - one jigsawn gable ornament, or a run of turned porch posts, or nothing - and the ornament therefore sits in exactly the places that are visible from the road and cheap to install: the porch, the gable peak, the door. The Dibble House at Eldon, Iowa, which Grant Wood painted in 1930, is the perfect specimen precisely because it is a plain board-and-batten farmhouse with a single pointed Gothic window in the gable, probably ordered from a catalogue. That one window is the entire style content of the building, and Wood understood that it was the point.

What it reacts against is nothing, and that is its most misunderstood quality. It is not a rejection of high style; it is high style's residue and its distribution network, arriving in the countryside a generation late and pared to what a two-man crew could raise. But it does encode an argument, and it is an economic one: never spend on what cannot be seen from the road, never build a room you do not need yet, never build a wing that competes with the main block. The failure mode of the twenty-first-century imitation is exactly the violation of that last rule - contemporary 'modern farmhouses' routinely put the wing at the same ridge height as the main block, wrap the porch on three sides, and glaze the walls at a ratio no heated farmhouse could have afforded, producing a building that quotes the surfaces of frugality at enormous cost.

Standing in the dooryard of a real one you are struck first by how little there is. Clapboard or board-and-batten, white or unpainted, a plain fascia, a 6/6 or 2/2 sash with a four-inch casing, a stone or brick chimney, and a porch. The mass does the work: a two-storey block, a lower wing stepping down, a still lower ell behind it, and finally a summer kitchen and a shed - the whole economic history of a family legible in a descending ridge line. The porch is the social apparatus, six to eight feet deep, facing the drive rather than the road, and it is where the house actually lived. Inside, the rooms are small, the ceilings nine feet, the stair steep and boxed, the woodwork a plain four-inch casing with a bevel, and the kitchen is enormous because that is where everyone was. It is unglamorous, extremely legible, and it is the most-built American house of the nineteenth century - which is the argument for treating it as a first-class node rather than as a leftover.

defining_characteristics: Additive massing with an explicit hierarchy: a dominant block, a lower wing, and successively lower ells, with ridge heights stepping down monotonically
Entry in the sheltered reentrant corner of the L (gable-front-and-wing) or centred on the passage (I-house), and a porch that shelters it
Minimal trim: plain corner boards, plain fascia, 4-5 inch window casings; no continuous entablature, no pilasters, no columns
Ornament restricted to the porch, the gable peak and the door surround, drawn from whatever the mill or catalogue supplied
Single-pile or shallow room depth carried well into the twentieth century so rooms light and ventilate from two sides
Plan and elevation retain Georgian-derived alignment - openings stack vertically and bays are evenly spaced - without any classical apparatus
Designed to grow: the first-built block anticipates the ell, and the ell anticipates the shed
diagnostic_tells: Descending ridge line across three or four attached volumes - the family's economic history in silhouette
Porch in the inside corner of the L rather than across the gable front, and facing the farm drive rather than the public road
Exactly one piece of ornament on an otherwise plain building: a jigsawn gable bracket, a pointed window, a run of turned posts
2/2 sash after about 1870 (cheap large glass) where the same house form of 1845 would have 6/6
Corner boards 4-6 inches and a plain fascia where a Greek Revival house of the same massing has 10-12 inch pilasters and a 14-inch frieze - this is the single test that separates the two

distinguished_from.difference: Same massings, and the farmhouse descends directly from it. The Greek Revival stratum keeps the trim discipline - continuous deep frieze, wide pilastered corners, an entablature over the door. When those thin to a fascia, corner boards and a plain casing, the building has become a farmhouse.

Folk Victorian is this same house with spindlework porch detailing and jigsawn trim applied in quantity. One catalogue ornament is a farmhouse; a full spindle frieze, turned posts with brackets and a decorated gable is Folk Victorian. The line is one of quantity, and it is genuinely fuzzy.

The contemporary imitation equalises what the original made hierarchical: wing ridges level with the main block, wrap-around porches, wall-to-wall glazing, and 9-10 foot ceilings throughout. It also uses black window frames and large fixed lights that no mill of the period produced. The tell is that nothing steps down.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Massing hierarchy rather than ornament: the ratios that matter are ridge height between volumes, wing setback, porch depth and window-to-wall ratio. Classical proportion survives only as inherited habit in bay spacing and opening alignment.
typical_ratios: Wing ridge 3-8 feet below the main ridge; each successive ell lower again
Wing front plane set back 2-8 feet behind the main block's front plane
Porch depth 6-8 feet, ceiling 8-9 feet, posts 4x4 to 6x6
Window-to-wall ratio 10-15 percent on principal elevations - low by modern standards and central to the look
Ceiling heights 8.5-9.5 feet ground, 8-9 upper
Roof pitch 6:12 to 10:12; main block 1.5-2 storeys, wing 1-1.5
Trim: corner boards 4-6 inches, fascia 6-8 inches, window casing 4-5 inches
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three to five even bays on the main block with vertically aligned openings; the wing carries its own independent two or three bay rhythm and is not required to align with the block, which is what keeps the composition additive rather than monumental.

massing_affinities.note: Arguably the most-built American house form of the nineteenth century, and the type specimen for this node.
The prosperity statement of the farming Midwest and Upland South: tall, thin, and visible across open land.
In northern New England the additive logic goes all the way to the barn: big house, little house, back house, barn.
The prosperous plain farmhouse, symmetrical and double-pile, with no style content whatever.
The Southern single-storey equivalent.
