constraints.statement: Wing and ell ridges must step down monotonically from the main block by at least 3 feet each, and each attached volume must be set back from the plane of the one before it. Equal ridge heights or a flush front plane produce a building with two fronts and no hierarchy - the defining failure of contemporary imitations.

Trim budget is capped and must read as a budget: corner boards 4-6 inches, fascia 6-8 inches, window casing 4-5 inches, with no continuous frieze and no pilasters. Applied ornament is limited to a single location - porch, gable peak, or door - not distributed across all three.

test.note: Tests the fascia width range (6-8in), deliberately much narrower than greek-revival-upland-vernacular's frieze-board floor (10in+) using the same rake_trim_width_in variable -- exactly the trim-budget distinction the two nodes are drawing. Corner-board width (4-6in), window-casing width (4-5in) and the single-ornament-location rule are left as prose.

constraints.statement: Entry belongs in the reentrant corner of an L-plan, sheltered by a porch at least 6 feet deep. Placing the door in the gable front of an L produces two competing front doors and no entry hierarchy.

test.note: Tests the minimum porch depth (6ft) via gallery_depth_ft, reused per its documented generic porch/gallery-depth definition. The reentrant-corner entry-placement rule is categorical and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Window-to-wall ratio on principal elevations should not exceed 18 percent; the historic range is 10-15 percent. The type's proportional character depends on wall dominating opening, and its thermal performance depends on the same thing.

Sash is 6/6 or 2/2 double-hung with muntins 7/8 to 1-1/8 inch; 2/2 only after about 1870, when cheap large glass reached rural suppliers. Single large fixed lights and undivided sash are out of period.

test.note: Tests the muntin-width range. Sash light pattern (6/6 vs 2/2) and its date-conditional rule (2/2 only after c.1870) are left as prose -- the date condition is blocked on open question 22, which has no constraint-side resolution mechanism yet.

exemplars.name: American Gothic House (Dibble House)
exemplars.note: Built 1881-82 by local carpenters Bussy and Herald; 504 square feet, board-and-batten, with two catalogue Gothic windows in the gable as the building's entire ornamental content. The specimen case for 'whatever the mill offered'. National Register 1974.

exemplars.name: Jarrell Plantation farmhouse
exemplars.location: 711 Jarrell Plantation Road, Juliette, Jones County, Georgia
exemplars.note: Plain-style Georgia piedmont farmhouse of heart pine, with a second 1895 house on the same site by the next generation - two dated points on the same vernacular line. Georgia state historic site; National Register 1973.

exemplars.name: Seeley Farmhouse
exemplars.location: 2 Freeman's Bridge Road, Glenville, Schenectady County, New York
exemplars.note: L-shaped, with a two-storey pedimented centre and one-and-a-half-storey flanking wings; the transitional case where the Greek Revival trim discipline is fading into plain farmhouse practice. National Register 1978.

exemplars.name: Levi Coffin House
exemplars.location: 113 U.S. 27, Fountain City, Wayne County, Indiana
exemplars.note: A brick I-house with a two-storey rear wing - the prosperous, disciplined end of the farmhouse spectrum, built by Quaker emigrants and reduced to trim-only classicism. National Historic Landmark.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013), 'Folk Houses' and 'National Folk'
Henry Glassie, Folk Housing in Middle Virginia (1975)
Fred Kniffen, 'Folk Housing: Key to Diffusion', Annals of the Association of American Geographers 55 (1965)
Thomas C. Hubka, Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn (1984)
Andrew Jackson Downing, The Architecture of Country Houses (1850)

proportion_packs.note: The type's own hard constraint -- wing and ell ridges must step down monotonically by at least 3 ft, with each volume set back from the plane before it, 'the defining failure of contemporary imitations' -- is this pack's dominance-and-subordination rule stated independently and reached the same way: a subordinate mass must read as subordinate, in height, in setback, or both, or the composition has no argument. Bound too for the datum rule: the water table and head-casing line are the only lines this plain a building has to hold it together across the wing and the ell, and losing them is exactly how a correctly-massed farmhouse still reads as a pile of boxes. Not bound for its order-derived vocabulary (belt-course mouldings, a shaped cornice) -- the farmhouse has none.

Governs the single-pile depth -- the type's defining plan trait, carried into the twentieth century after every wealthier neighbour had gone double-pile -- and the wing/ell logic directly: an ell is a shorter, lower frame leaning on the main block's rear plate exactly as the pack's wing_strategy rule describes, and its corollary that a rear addition drawn at the main block's full depth 'is a 20th-century move and it destroys the type' is precisely the diagnostic the node's own distinguished_from entry gives for the 'modern farmhouse' imitation (wing ridges level with the main block). Used here as a planning grid rather than a literal structural bent: most surviving farmhouses are balloon- or platform-framed, not heavy-timber, but the bay discipline the pack argues for surviving the change in technique is exactly what this type's partitions and window centrelines still show.

The farmhouse's small, additive rooms -- 8.5-9.5 ft ceilings, single-pile depth kept well into the twentieth century for two-side daylight and ventilation -- are exactly what this pack reconstructs from measured Anglo-American vernacular fabric, and its room-count rule (hall-and-parlor, double-pen, center-passage and i-house as the small number of ways a room breadth tiles a frontage) explains this node's own massing affinities directly. Preferred over room-harmonic because nothing about this type is proportioned to a treatise ratio; its rooms are constrained by span, hearth reach and daylight exactly as the pack describes.

Bound optional, not primary, because log construction is regional and generational rather than universal to the type: in the Upland South, the Midwest and the Plains the farmhouse 'frequently replaces or encases a log pen' per the node's own lineage entry (weight 0.4), inheriting the pen's single-pile rooms and gable-end chimneys directly, while in New England and the Mid-Atlantic the type is frame from the start. Promote to primary on any regional child node that is documented log-under-weatherboard.

Bound optional and only for the type's late tail (c. 1900-1920), where the same rural lumberyards and mail-order catalogs that supplied Craftsman bungalow trim also supplied farmhouse trim packages, and the flat-stock, indifferent-to-opening-size logic genuinely describes a plain 4-5 in farmhouse window casing about as well as it describes a bungalow one. It does NOT describe the type's more central and much longer-lived trim logic -- a Greek Revival entablature thinned to a fascia and pilasters shrunk to corner boards -- which the node's own hard constraint (c02) states as a budget rather than a system. No pack in this set owns that thinning-of-an-order-until-only-the-budget-survives logic; it is a real gap, worth naming for WP-4.6.

english-baroque.name: English Baroque

revival_periods.note: Edwardian Baroque — the imperial manner of town halls, insurance offices and Whitehall, sometimes called Wrenaissance. Domestic only at the largest scale.

geography.hearth: London after the Fire of 1666, and the great Yorkshire and Northumberland commissions of Vanbrugh and Hawksmoor

lineage.note: The trade base is continuous. Wren's masons, bricklayers and joiners were trained in the Artisan Mannerist workshops of the 1630s-50s, and the London brick house of the 1670s is a Jacobean carcass with a classical cornice.

Through Inigo Jones and the Office of Works. Jones's Palladian drawings and buildings passed to John Webb and thence into the institutional memory of the royal works that Wren inherited as Surveyor in 1669.

Wren's only foreign journey was to Paris in 1665, where he studied the Louvre works, met Bernini and saw his Louvre designs, and absorbed the French planning of the hotel and the chateau. French practice, not Italian, is the proximate source of the English Baroque plan.

Quoted without descent, and this is the sharpest case of the distinction in the whole British branch. Neither Wren, Hawksmoor nor Vanbrugh ever went to Italy; Borromini and Bernini reached them through engravings and through Paris. The result is an English Baroque that is inventive precisely because it was working from second-hand evidence.
The orders, the triumphal arch motif and the Roman bath plan, known through Palladio's and Serlio's reconstructions rather than from the ruins.

description.short: England's brief, heavy, self-invented Baroque: giant orders, banded rustication and sculpted skylines composed for shadow and mass, by three men who had never seen Rome.
description.long:
English Baroque exists because of a fire, a war and a shortage of information. The Fire of 1666 handed Christopher Wren fifty-one City churches and a cathedral, and with them the authority to invent an English classicism from a standing start; the peace and prosperity following 1688 paid for the great houses; and the fact that none of its three principal figures — Wren, Nicholas Hawksmoor and John Vanbrugh — ever travelled to Italy meant they were reconstructing the Baroque from prints, from Palladio's plates and from one visit to Paris. Not knowing the rules exactly is why Hawksmoor could invent details that no Italian would have permitted and that are, on their own terms, better.

The style's whole subject is mass and shadow. Openings are cut deep and keyed with exaggerated voussoirs; walls are banded with rustication that runs across pilasters as if the building were being quarried rather than assembled; the giant order rises through two storeys so that the elevation is scaled to the whole block instead of to its floors; roofs are hipped and hidden behind balustrades so that the mass reads as a single geometric solid, and then the skyline is loaded with urns, statues, cupolas and chimneys treated as pedestals. At Blenheim and Castle Howard the composition extends outward into quadrant colonnades, courts and flanking service blocks, producing an approach sequence a quarter of a mile long. This is architecture as statecraft, and the two greatest examples were literally paid for by the nation as war trophies.

What it was reacting against was the flat, gabled, insular Jacobean manner, and what it produced in reaction was itself so extravagant that a counter-reaction followed within a decade. Colen Campbell's Vitruvius Britannicus of 1715 attacked the 'affected and licentious' Italians by name, Lord Burlington bought Palladio's and Jones's drawings, and by 1730 the giant order had been legislated out of English taste. Baroque's domestic legacy survives instead in the ordinary Restoration and Queen Anne house, which is where most of this node's usable kit lives: a compact double-pile brick box with a hipped roof, dormers, a bold modillion cornice, tall segmental- or flat-arched sash windows, and a carved wood or stone door hood on scrolled brackets. That house is the immediate parent of the Georgian house and of American colonial building.

Standing at the foot of Vanbrugh's north front at Seaton Delaval is an experience closer to standing under a cliff than in front of a house. The rustication is so heavy and the shadows so deep that the wall stops reading as a surface at all; the giant Doric columns are banded, which makes them look compressed under their own load; and everything is scaled about a third larger than the human body expects. Inside, the compensation is spatial drama — halls rising through two or three storeys, stairs turning around top-lit voids — and it is the last time English domestic architecture was allowed to be theatrical without apologising for it.

defining_characteristics: The giant (colossal) order embracing two or more storeys, in pilaster or engaged column form, scaling the elevation to the block rather than to the floor
Mass and shadow as the compositional subject: deep reveals, heavy banded rustication, boldly keyed arches, strongly projecting cornices
Hipped roofs concealed behind a balustraded parapet so that the volume reads as a geometric solid
A sculpted skyline of urns, statuary, cupolas and chimney stacks treated as pedestals
Extended composition beyond the block: forecourts, quadrant colonnades or curved wings, and flanking service pavilions
Double-height entrance hall and a dramatised stair as the interior climax
In the ordinary house, the compact double-pile brick box with hipped roof, dormers, modillion cornice, tall sashes and a carved door hood on scrolled brackets
diagnostic_tells: A giant order running through two storeys — the single detail that Palladianism abolished after 1715, and therefore the fastest way to date a facade to before 1730
Rustication banded across pilasters and columns as well as walls, so that the vertical members appear to be built of the same courses as the field
Keystones enlarged out of all proportion and often carried up into the string course above
Balustraded parapet with urns, concealing the roof entirely, on a building whose plan is nonetheless English and double-pile
A door hood of carved wood or stone on large scrolled console brackets over a six-panel door — the Queen Anne town house signature

distinguished_from.difference: Palladianism is the direct, explicit reaction. It abolishes the giant order in favour of a single portico on a rusticated basement, flattens the wall, halves the ornament, and derives every dimension from Palladio's published rules. Where Baroque models mass, Palladianism composes a diagram. If the facade is doing something Palladio never published, it is Baroque.

Georgian is the domesticated, ruled, repeatable descendant. The Queen Anne house of 1700 and the Georgian house of 1760 share a plan and a construction, but Georgian has graduated storey heights, thinner glazing bars, a flat-arched or gauged-brick window head instead of a keyed segmental one, and no giant order under any circumstances.

Both are heavy, but Jacobean orders are approximate and applied to a porch while Baroque orders are proportioned to a module and used to organise the whole mass. Jacobean gables; Baroque parapets. Jacobean mullions; Baroque sashes.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The classical orders with the module taken as the lower column diameter (or half-diameter), used correctly but freely — proportions are deliberately stretched or compressed for effect, which is precisely the licence Palladianism withdrew.
typical_ratios: Giant order height 2 to 2.5 storeys, column height 8-10 diameters depending on order
Entablature depth 1/4 to 1/5 of column height; cornice projection roughly equal to its own depth
Rusticated basement 0.5 to 0.75 the height of the principal storey above it
Sash proportion 1.8:1 to 2.1:1 height to width, in 12-over-12 or 9-over-9 lights with glazing bars 25-32 mm wide
Main block to wing ridge height ratio not less than 1.3:1
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Emphatically hierarchical rather than even: a dominant centre of three to five bays, subordinate flanking bays, and terminal pavilions, with bay spacing widening at the centre. Rhythm is A-B-B-A-B-B-A rather than the Georgian metronome.

massing_affinities.note: Main block, quadrant or straight hyphens, and flanking service pavilions — the diagram of Castle Howard and Blenheim, arriving in England through Baroque before Palladianism codified it.
The Restoration and Queen Anne double-pile house with hipped roof and central stair hall — the everyday form of the style and the direct ancestor of the Georgian box.
The great forecourt open to the approach, as at Blenheim.
Post-Fire London brick terraces, rebuilt to the 1667 Act's four rates of building — the origin of the English urban house as a regulated product.

constraints.statement: Where a giant order is used it must run a whole number of storeys and land on a continuous plinth or rusticated basement; it may not stop mid-storey or die into a string course.
Roofs are hipped and concealed behind a parapet or balustrade on principal elevations. A visible gable end on a Baroque front is forbidden.
Sash proportion 1.8:1 to 2.1:1 height to width, with glazing bars not thinner than 25 mm. Thin bars date the window to after 1780 and break the period.

test.note: Tests the sash proportion. The glazing-bar clause (not thinner than 25mm) is a second numeric claim in the same statement and stays prose-only here -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Rustication, if used, must be continuous around all faces of the mass it belongs to, including returns; rustication applied to a front elevation only is the commonest modern failure of the style.
Main block ridge or parapet height must exceed flanking wings by at least 30 percent; the hierarchy is the composition.

exemplars.name: Castle Howard
exemplars.note: Begun 1699 by John Vanbrugh with Nicholas Hawksmoor for the third Earl of Carlisle; main block substantially complete by 1712, dome 1706. The first English house to be conceived as landscape-scale theatre.

exemplars.name: Blenheim Palace
exemplars.note: Built 1705-22 by Vanbrugh and Hawksmoor as the nation's gift to the Duke of Marlborough after Blenheim (1704). Giant Corinthian order, colossal rusticated gate towers, and a great court reached across Vanbrugh's bridge.

exemplars.name: Seaton Delaval Hall
exemplars.note: Built 1719-28, Vanbrugh's last house. Banded giant Doric columns, a compressed central block between long service wings, and the most physically overbearing domestic elevation in England.

exemplars.name: Easton Neston
exemplars.note: Hawksmoor's only complete country house, c.1695-1702. A single compact block in fine ashlar with a giant Composite order — the style at its most disciplined and least theatrical.

sources: John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)
Kerry Downes, English Baroque Architecture (1966)
Kerry Downes, Hawksmoor (1959)
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England (county volumes)

proportion_packs.note: The giant order at its most consequential: Blenheim's own exemplar note here records a 'giant Corinthian order' on the nation's war-trophy house. Vignola rather than any of the overlay authorities, because none of the three -- Chambers 1759, Gibbs's own 1728/1732, Palladio via Ware 1738 -- existed, or existed in England, when Wren, Hawksmoor and Vanbrugh were working (floruit 1690-1730); the standing English order-book of their generation was Vignola's Regola of 1562, known in translation since the mid-seventeenth century and the source none of the three architects, none of whom had been to Italy, had any reason to depart from when reaching for a module. This is also the node's own stated logic: 'the classical orders... used correctly but freely, which is precisely the licence Palladianism withdrew' -- a free stretching of Vignola's rule, not a rule of its own.

The everyday order of the type this node calls out explicitly as its domestic legacy: 'the ordinary Restoration and Queen Anne house... a compact double-pile brick box with hipped roof, dormers, modillion cornice'. Bound here for Gibbs's own biography rather than his later export: Gibbs trained in Rome under Carlo Fontana, and his early masterpiece St Mary-le-Strand (1714-17) is genuinely Baroque -- this is Gibbs as a participant in this style's own moment, before A Book of Architecture (1728) turned him into the pattern-book author the American colonies would inherit. The giant order never appears on the ordinary house; this is its separate, smaller-order world.

Governs the interior mouldings of the ordinary house and, with real strain, the double-height hall and dramatised stair the node names as 'the interior climax'. The pack's own calibration is for rooms of 11-13 ft; a Baroque great hall rising two or three storeys through a top-lit void is well outside that range, and its cornice and entablature should be drawn at the room's own height rather than at the pack's default -- the same caution the Georgian template raises for rooms under 9 ft 6 in, mirrored here at the opposite extreme.

Governs the void beneath the style's real subject, which is what surrounds it: deep reveals, exaggerated keystones 'enlarged out of all proportion and often carried up into the string course above', and segmental- or flat-arched heads keyed boldly enough to read as mass rather than as an opening's frame.

Governs the composed elevation, but the bay rhythm it enforces must be read as this node's own hierarchical A-B-B-A-B-B-A -- a dominant centre of three to five bays with subordinate flanking bays and terminal pavilions, bay spacing widening at the centre -- rather than the even Georgian metronome the pack assumes by default. The giant order and the extended forecourt-and-wings composition (Blenheim, Castle Howard) are what the pack's water-table and cornice-projection rules are being asked to organise at an unusually large scale.

Bound for the double-height entrance hall and the dramatised top-lit stair void that the node names as the style's interior climax -- a room proportioned to impress rather than to the resolvable domestic ratios of the Georgian sequence that follows it.

renaissance-revival-american.name: Renaissance Revival (American)

revival_periods.note: The academic Beaux-Arts generation returns to the palazzo with measured drawings and archaeological discipline; that is a separate and better-informed node.

geography.hearth: Philadelphia and New York

lineage.note: The Florentine and Roman palazzo is the quoted model, arriving through Charles Barry's London clubs rather than through Italy. American architects worked from engravings.

Genuine blending, and the boundary is porous. The two share masons, brownstone, plan types, and clients; the difference is whether the cornice is academic or bracketed and whether the facade obeys a symmetry rule.
Actual transmission: the same masonry trades, the same ashlar and brownstone technique, the same disciplined regard for a correct profile.
The urban row and the raised parlour floor come forward unchanged from the Federal city house; only the dress is new.

description.short: The disciplined, symmetrical, astylar palazzo mode adopted for American libraries, clubs, banks, and merchant houses from the mid-1840s, in which correctness of profile replaced picturesque effect.
description.long:
Renaissance Revival is the one branch of the American romantic revivals that is not romantic. Where Gothic Revival and Italianate were sold as instruments of feeling, the palazzo mode was sold as evidence of judgement: it is symmetrical, astylar, flat-walled, and governed by rules that can be checked. John Notman's Athenaeum of Philadelphia, designed in 1845 and finished in 1847, is the canonical American beginning, and Trench and Snook's A. T. Stewart store at 280 Broadway in 1846 established the commercial version that would clothe American downtowns for forty years. The style's institutional character was not accidental. A library, a club, or a dry-goods palace wanted to say that it was solvent and permanent, and the fifteenth-century Florentine banking house was the most exact available symbol of exactly that.

The technological conditions here run the other way from the rest of this branch. Balloon framing and the scroll saw made picturesque wooden complexity cheap; the palazzo mode instead depended on the industrialisation of masonry. Steam-powered stone saws and planers made brownstone, a soft and easily worked Triassic sandstone quarried in the Connecticut Valley and northern New Jersey, dramatically cheaper to dress; the railroad delivered it to New York and Philadelphia by the bargeload; and cast iron let Daniel Badger and James Bogardus reproduce an entire palazzo elevation in bolted sections, arriving on site as a kit. That last fact deserves emphasis, because the cast-iron commercial front of the 1850s is the most literal kit-of-parts building system the nineteenth century produced: a catalogue of columns, arches, spandrels, and cornices, orderable by number, assembled in weeks. It worked, and it worked because the underlying grammar was rule-governed rather than pictorial.

What the style rejected was the Greek Revival's insistence on the temple as the only respectable form for a public building, and, more quietly, the picturesque claim that irregularity was morally superior. A palazzo has no portico, no pediment, and no columns; it has a wall, and the wall is organised by the diminishing rhythm of its openings and terminated by a single powerful cornice. This is a harder discipline than it looks, because with no orders to fall back on, the whole composition rests on the storey heights, the window surrounds, and the cornice depth. Nineteenth-century American practitioners got it right surprisingly often, because the rules were few and printable.

In front of one, the experience is of weight and address. The wall is flat and stays flat, so the eye finds the openings; the ground storey is rusticated and dark and the piano nobile above it is taller, brighter, and given the pedimented heads, so the building tells you where its important room is before you enter; the cornice is deep enough to throw the top of the wall into shade and stop the building cleanly against the sky. Inside a brownstone of this kind the sequence is stoop, low vestibule, then a tall bright double parlour with fourteen-foot ceilings and eleven-foot windows to the floor. The compression and release is the whole design, and it survives in every well-made New York rowhouse to this day.

defining_characteristics: Strict bilateral symmetry of the principal elevation, with a centred or clearly weighted entrance
Astylar composition: no columns, no portico, no pediment on the facade as a whole
Storey heights diminishing upward, with a rusticated or channelled ground storey and a taller piano nobile
Window heads differentiated by storey, typically pedimented or entablatured below and square-headed above
A single dominant crowning cornice, modillioned or dentilled, terminating the wall against the sky
Flat, uninterrupted wall plane articulated by string courses and quoins rather than by projection
Ashlar, brownstone, pressed brick, or cast iron; a wooden Renaissance Revival is a contradiction
diagnostic_tells: If the cornice is carried on modillions or dentils rather than on sawn scroll brackets, it is Renaissance Revival and not Italianate
Alternating triangular and segmental window pediments in a row is a Renaissance signature and appears in no other American style of the period
The ground floor is treated differently from the floors above (rustication, larger openings, darker stone); Italianate treats all floors alike
Facade symmetry is exact. If any part of the composition is picturesquely off-balance, it is Italianate
Quoins run the full height of the corner in an unbroken alternating rhythm; partial or decorative quoining indicates a later eclectic hand

distinguished_from.difference: The two overlap so heavily that many buildings are legitimately both. Decide on three tests: is the facade exactly symmetrical, is the cornice academic rather than bracketed, and do the storey heights diminish on a rule? Three yeses is Renaissance Revival.
Second Empire takes the same palazzo body and puts a mansard roof on it, which converts a terminated wall into a crowned mass. If the roof is a visible storey, it is Second Empire.
Beaux-Arts (1885-1920) is columned, sculptural, and archaeologically trained; mid-century Renaissance Revival is astylar, flat, and worked from engravings rather than from measured drawings.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Genuinely proportional, and the only style in this branch that is. The governing dimension is the storey height of the piano nobile; the ground storey, the upper storeys, and the cornice are all derived from it. The system is transmissible in a single table, which is why cast-iron founders could sell it by catalogue.
typical_ratios: Piano nobile height 1.15 to 1.35 times the storey above it
Crowning cornice depth 1/12 to 1/16 of total facade height
Window height to width 2:1 to 2.6:1 at the piano nobile, reducing to 1.6:1 at the attic storey
Rusticated base 0.8 to 1.0 times the piano nobile height
Pier to opening ratio on the facade between 1:1 and 1.5:1, wall always winning
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Strictly regular. Three, five, or seven bays at equal spacing, with the centre bay optionally widened by not more than 15 percent.

massing_affinities.note: The brownstone row is the style's native residential form.
The freestanding palazzo block, square in plan and symmetrical on all faces.
Picturesque irregularity destroys the only compositional rule the style has.

constraints.statement: The principal elevation shall be bilaterally symmetrical about the entrance axis. No projecting bay, tower, or wing may break the symmetry of the street front.
Floor-to-floor heights shall diminish monotonically upward, with each storey between 78 and 88 percent of the one below and the piano nobile at least 1.15 times the storey above it.

test.note: Statement gives each storey as 78-88 percent of the one below; re-expressed here as the equivalent diminish-percentage (100 minus that range = 12-22 percent) to match storey_height_diminish_pct's own convention (docs/constraints.md's english-georgian.c02 precedent). The separate 'piano nobile at least 1.15x the storey above it' comparison stays prose.

constraints.statement: The crowning cornice shall project between 1/12 and 1/16 of the total facade height and shall run unbroken across the full width of the facade, including across party walls in a row.

test.note: Tests the stated 1/16-to-1/12-of-facade-height cornice projection as a ratio (cornice_projection_in converted to feet by the /12 unit constant, over facade_height_ft). 'Runs unbroken across the full width, including across party walls in a row' has no matching variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Window head treatment shall change at each storey and shall be uniform within a storey. Where alternating pediments are used, the alternation shall begin and end with the same type so the row reads as closed.

Quoins, where used, shall run the full height of the corner from water table to cornice in an unbroken alternating rhythm with long faces of 18 to 30 in. Partial-height or purely decorative quoining is prohibited.

exemplars.name: Athenaeum of Philadelphia
exemplars.note: John Notman, designed 1845, completed 1847. A National Historic Landmark cited as one of the nation's first palazzo-facade buildings, and one of the first brownstone buildings in Philadelphia.

exemplars.name: A. T. Stewart Store (Marble Palace, later the Sun Building), 280 Broadway
exemplars.note: Joseph Trench and John B. Snook. The commercial palazzo that set the pattern for American downtowns; extant and a New York City landmark.

exemplars.name: Boston Athenaeum, 10 1/2 Beacon Street
exemplars.note: Edward Clarke Cabot; cornerstone 1847, opened 1849. Palladian-Renaissance sandstone front, enlarged 1913-14 by Bigelow and Wadsworth.

sources: Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: Technology and the Picturesque (1978)
Constance Greiff, John Notman, Architect (1979)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and the node's own text supports the choice directly - Palladio is named as the quoted model ('the Florentine and Roman palazzo is the quoted model'), and this is the branch's most literally classical node, the one place in the Romantic Revivals family where an order genuinely governs the moulding apparatus rather than merely decorating it. Governs the enrichment of the window aedicules, the door surround, and the crowning cornice's modillion/dentil profile - NOT a literal colonnade or portico, since the node's own defining_characteristics state the composition is astylar: 'no columns, no portico, no pediment on the facade as a whole.' The order supplies the profile family for what IS built (cornice, surrounds) without ever being expressed as a freestanding column.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The plainer alternative register for the same astylar moulding apparatus - a bank or a smaller merchant's house pitched at Corinthian rather than Composite richness. Bound as the base Vignola order rather than an overlay because no Palladio, Gibbs or Chambers Corinthian overlay in this library extends its own applies_to to renaissance-revival-american; only the Composite overlay does, which is itself evidence for grading Composite as the more richly documented register of the two.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and the node's own hard constraint (c01) restates the pack's governing rule almost exactly: the principal elevation must be bilaterally symmetrical about the entrance axis, with no projecting bay, tower or wing permitted to break it - the one Romantic Revivals node besides italianate-townhouse to bind this pack rather than facade-picturesque.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and the node's own hard constraint c02 gives the exact numbers this pack generalises: each storey between 78 and 88 percent of the one below, with the piano nobile at least 1.15 times the storey above it. The node's own proportional_system calls this 'the only style in this branch that is' genuinely proportional in the storey-height sense, which this pack is built to encode.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the storey-differentiated window head treatment the node's own c04 requires - pedimented or entablatured openings at the piano nobile, square heads above - and the door sizing beneath whatever surround the primary order supplies.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The double parlour behind the brownstone front is described in the node's own text as running fourteen-foot ceilings and eleven-foot windows to the floor - well inside this pack's calibrated range - and its pedestal:field:entablature division is the direct interior counterpart of the astylar exterior order bound above.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and the node's own text makes the strongest possible claim for it: 'the governing dimension is the storey height of the piano nobile... the system is transmissible in a single table' - Palladio's own harmonic-proportion language, restated almost verbatim as the style's proportional_system.

mid-century-traditional.name: Mid-Century Traditional

description.short: Minimal Traditional, Ranch, and their relatives — the era when the traditional kit of parts was systematically cost-engineered out of the American house.
description.long:
This family is the most important and least examined in the whole taxonomy for anyone building production housing. Minimal Traditional keeps the traditional silhouette and deletes everything else: no overhang, no cornice return, no depth of profile, sash reduced to the cheapest available. It was underwritten by FHA lending standards that rewarded minimum cost per square foot and had no way to value proportion.

The Ranch that follows is the first American house organized around the automobile, and it inherits an unsolved problem that every traditional style built today still carries: how to put two or three garage doors on a street elevation without destroying it. No historical style answers this, because none had to. It is the single largest gap in the traditional kit of parts and the place where a modern design system has to author something genuinely new rather than retrieve it.

defining_characteristics: Traditional silhouette retained while trim, overhang, and profile depth are deleted
Financing standards and cost per square foot as the governing design constraint
The automobile reorganizing plan, lot, and street elevation
Horizontal single-storey massing on wide suburban lots
An unresolved garage problem inherited by everything built since

shingle-style.name: Shingle Style

revival_periods.note: Named and rehabilitated by Vincent Scully in 1955, then revived in practice by Venturi, Charles Moore, Robert A. M. Stern, and the coastal New England custom house, where it remains in continuous production and is arguably the only Victorian style still genuinely alive.

geography.hearth: Newport, Rhode Island

lineage.note: The immediate American parent, and the two are inseparable before about 1882. Same architects, same clients, same irregular plans, same balloon frame; Shingle Style is what happens when a Queen Anne house stops articulating.

Direct and documented. Richard Norman Shaw's Old English work, with its tile-hung upper walls, sweeping roofs, and long horizontal window bands, reached Richardson and McKim, Mead and White through The Building News and Shaw's published perspectives; Leyswood of 1868 is the specific ancestor of the Watts Sherman House.

A co-parent in substance and the reason this node cannot sit on a single-parent tree: the 1877 sketching tour of Marblehead, Salem, Newburyport and Portsmouth by McKim, Mead, White and Bigelow put measured early New England building into the same office that was drawing Shaw. Direction note: the mature Colonial Revival style node descends from this one, so the graph carries no inheritance edge back the other way. What this node actually inherited was the antiquarian colonial interest of the 1870s, which is recorded here as the descends_from edge to new-england-colonial.

The load-bearing colonial edge, and the one that carries the kit. Practice transmission through those 1877 measured drawings and through surviving local carpentry: the gambrel, the lean-to, the massive central chimney, the unpainted weathered shingle, and the low broad entrance are taken from seventeenth and eighteenth-century fabric rather than from a style book. Retyped 2026-08-18. This edge reaches early New England building through the 1877 McKim, Mead, White and Bigelow sketching tour of Marblehead, Salem, Newburyport and Portsmouth, and the measured drawings and photographs that followed. That mechanism transmits appearance, not craft. Ruling applied consistently across shingle-style, queen-anne-free-classic and colonial-revival: drawings do not carry a kit. A revival detailed with true eighteenth-century assembly is a reconstruction, not a revival.

Richardson is literally the same author, and the transfer is a principle rather than a motif: the wall as a continuous unbroken surface stretched over a volume. Shingle Style is that idea executed in a light skin instead of in ashlar, frequently with a rock-faced stone base carried up under the shingle.

Shared sensibility about material honesty and the vernacular, arriving in parallel rather than by transmission; the American style is earlier than most of the British Arts and Crafts houses it resembles.

description.short: The one genuinely original American style of the nineteenth century: an irregular, freely planned house wrapped in a continuous unbroken skin of wooden shingles that runs across storey lines, around corners, and over the roof as a single surface.
description.long:
Shingle Style is this taxonomy's best argument that a single-parent tree cannot represent architectural descent, and it is worth stating why in the terms the graph uses. The style has at least four ancestors of comparable weight, and they arrive by different mechanisms. From the American Queen Anne it takes the irregular plan, the living hall, the corner tower, and the whole practice of balloon-framed picturesque composition, and that inheritance is so complete that the earliest examples, notably Richardson's Watts Sherman House at Newport of 1874-76, are legitimately classified as both. From Richard Norman Shaw's Old English manner in Britain it takes the sweeping roof, the tile-hung upper wall translated into shingle, and the long horizontal window band; that transmission is by publication, and it is documented in the drawings. From the emerging Colonial Revival it takes the gambrel, the lean-to section, the classical porch column, and the entire idea that early New England building is a usable resource; that transmission is by the 1877 McKim, Mead, White and Bigelow sketching tour of Marblehead, Salem, Newburyport and Portsmouth, which is the rare case of a stylistic parent with a date and an itinerary. And from Richardson's Romanesque it takes the principle that a wall should be one continuous surface, transposed from ashlar into shingle.

Assign any one of these as the parent and you lose something the buildings actually contain. Make it a child of Queen Anne and the Colonial gambrel and the Romanesque continuity become inexplicable decoration. Make it a child of Colonial Revival and the wildly irregular plans and the towers make no sense. Make it a child of Richardson and you lose the wooden lightness that is its whole substance. This is what reticulation means in practice: the node is the intersection of four traditions, each contributing a different layer, and a tree can only record the strongest edge. A directed acyclic graph with weighted, typed edges records all four and lets a kit-of-parts cascade draw the gambrel from one parent, the plan from another, and the surface doctrine from a third.

The technological conditions are the same as for Queen Anne and produce the opposite result, which is instructive. Shingle mills in Michigan, Maine, and the Pacific Northwest were by 1880 turning out sawn cedar and white pine shingles by the millions and shipping them anywhere by rail; the shingle was the cheapest cladding in America. Queen Anne builders used that cheapness to buy pattern, cutting shingles into fish-scale and diamond courses and stacking textures. The Shingle Style architects used the same cheapness to buy uniformity, running one plain butt across the entire building and eliminating corner boards, water tables, belt courses, and trim so nothing would interrupt it. The difference between the two styles is a decision about what to do with an industrial surplus, and it is exactly the decision a modern kit-of-parts platform will have to make, over and over, on behalf of its users.

What it feels like is the thing the imitations never get. A shingled wall has no visible joints, no trim, no shadow lines except the courses themselves, so the building reads as a solid carved from one substance, and the shingles silver unevenly with weather so the surface is alive and slightly mottled. Openings appear to be cut into the mass rather than framed into it. The roof comes down low, sometimes to the height of a person's shoulder at the eave, so the building crouches; the porch is a void scooped out of the volume rather than a structure added to it. Inside, the living hall opens through wide screens and inglenooks into every principal room, the stair is a piece of furniture, and there is a continuous flow of space that no European house of the period offers. It is the American house at its least anxious and its most confident, and it is not an accident that it is the one Victorian style still being built.

defining_characteristics: A continuous unbroken wooden shingle surface running across storey lines, around corners, and frequently over the roof as one material
Suppression of trim: no corner boards, minimal window casing, shallow eaves cut tight to the wall
Irregular, freely composed plan and massing, unified entirely by the skin rather than by articulation
A broad sheltering roof of large simple planes, often gambrel or a long sweeping gable, coming low to the ground
Porches and loggias read as voids carved out of the volume, not as attached structures
Horizontal window bands of multiple sash grouped under a single head, frequently with multi-light upper sash over single-light lower
A living hall with fireplace and stair as the organising interior space, with rooms opening into it through wide cased screens
diagnostic_tells: Run your eye along a corner: if the shingles wrap the corner with no corner board, it is Shingle Style. A corner board makes it Queen Anne
Eaves are shallow, 6 to 12 in, and cut tight; deep bracketed eaves belong to Italianate or Stick Style
Window trim is 2 to 3 in wide or absent, and openings look punched rather than framed
Shingle butts are plain and uniform; patterned fish-scale or diamond coursing over more than a small panel indicates Queen Anne
The roof is a few large simple planes, in contrast to the Queen Anne's multiplication of small gables
A rock-faced stone base carried up around the ground storey and then shingled above is a Richardson-derived signature

distinguished_from.difference: The closest sibling and the one it descends from. Queen Anne articulates and layers the wall into textured zones with visible trim; Shingle Style unifies it into one surface and deletes the trim. The corner board test settles nearly every case.

A co-parent, not a neighbour, and the boundary is real: Colonial Revival is symmetrical, trimmed, painted, and archaeologically referential; Shingle Style is asymmetrical, untrimmed, unpainted, and uses Colonial elements as material rather than as quotation. Where the plan becomes symmetrical and the shingles get painted white, the building has crossed over.

The same surface doctrine in a different material and weight class. Ashlar is the mass; shingle is a skin over a light frame. Where both appear on one building, which is common, the stone stops at the first floor.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by surface continuity and by the roof. There is no module and no bay system; the design is controlled by keeping one material unbroken over an irregular volume, and by making the roof large and simple enough to gather that volume into one shape.
typical_ratios: Shingle exposure 4 to 6 in, uniform across the entire building
Eave overhang 6 to 12 in; rake overhang 4 to 10 in
Window casing width 2 to 3 in, or omitted entirely
Roof plane area: the largest single plane not less than 40 percent of total roof area
Eave height at the lowest sweep 6 to 9 ft above grade
Porch column height to diameter 5:1 to 8:1 where classical, or shingled piers 16 to 24 in square
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Grouped rather than regular. Windows occur in bands of two to five under a common head, separated by long stretches of plain shingle. The rhythm belongs to the openings, not to a structural bay.

massing_affinities.note: The Colonial inheritance, and the reason so many Shingle Style houses have a gambrel that Queen Anne houses do not.
The long rear catslide, taken directly from seventeenth-century New England and used to bring the roof to the ground.
Round and shingled, absorbed into the mass rather than standing free.
The style requires a freely modelled volume and a wrapping surface; a party wall gives it neither.

constraints.statement: The shingle field shall be continuous across every storey line, corner, and change of plane on all elevations. No corner board, water table, belt course, frieze board, or storey band may interrupt it. This single rule is what separates the style from Queen Anne and it admits no exceptions.
Eave overhang shall not exceed 12 in and rake overhang shall not exceed 10 in, and both shall be closed tight to the wall plane with no exposed brackets, rafter tails, or purlin ends.

test.note: Tests the eave-overhang ceiling. Rake overhang (<=10 in, a separate stated figure) has no dedicated variable distinct from eave_projection_in and stays prose, along with the 'closed tight to the wall plane, no exposed brackets/rafter tails/purlin ends' clause.

constraints.statement: Window and door casing shall not exceed 3 in in width and shall not project more than 1 in from the shingle plane. Projecting hoods, crowns, pedimented heads, and moulded sills are prohibited.

test.note: Tests the casing-width ceiling. The casing's own projection (<=1 in from the shingle plane) has no matching vocabulary variable and stays prose, along with the prohibited-hood/crown/pediment/sill list.

constraints.statement: Shingle exposure shall be uniform at 4 to 6 in over the entire building. Decorative butt patterning, where used at all, shall not exceed 10 percent of total wall area and shall occur only within a single gable field.
Where a masonry base is used it shall be rock-faced, shall terminate at or below the first-floor window sill line, and shall be the only material change permitted on the elevation.

exemplars.name: Isaac Bell House
exemplars.note: McKim, Mead and White, 1881-83. Shingled walls over a brick base, bamboo-turned porch columns, an open living hall, and a Japanese-influenced lightness; the most complete surviving statement of the style.

exemplars.name: Mary Fiske Stoughton House
exemplars.note: H. H. Richardson, 1882-83. Shingles stretched over irregular volumes as a taut skin with minimal ornament; the building that demonstrated the surface doctrine in wood.

exemplars.name: William Watts Sherman House
exemplars.note: H. H. Richardson, 1874-76. The prototype, and simultaneously an American Queen Anne; contemporaries reported that builders could not find a name for it, which is the reticulation problem stated by the people who were there.

sources: Vincent Scully, The Shingle Style and the Stick Style (1955; rev. ed. 1971)
Vincent Scully, The Shingle Style Today, or The Historian's Revenge (1974)
Leland Roth, McKim, Mead and White, Architects (1983)
Jeffrey Karl Ochsner, H. H. Richardson: Complete Architectural Works (1982)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: Explicit in this pack's applies_to. The node's own proportional_system says plainly 'there is no module and no bay system... the design is controlled by keeping one material unbroken over an irregular volume,' which is close to a paraphrase of this pack's own self-description of itself as a system of constraints and starting points rather than a computed module. The pack's belt_course datum-count rule (at least two continuous horizontals) is the formal version of the node's own hard constraint (c01) that the shingle field itself must run continuous across every storey line and corner — in Shingle Style the shingle field largely replaces the trim-based datums the pack otherwise describes.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to. Governs the light count and muntin section of the horizontal window bands the node calls for (multi-light upper sash over single-light lower is a documented late-19th-century pattern this pack's diminishing-muntin-width rule tracks); the node's own casing-width ceiling (2-3 in, or omitted) is carried by this pack's window_surround_wood rule at the narrow end of its range.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to, and it is a strong fit: the node's hard constraint (c03) that casing shall not exceed 3 in and shall not project more than 1 in, with no hoods, crowns or pediments, describes trim-craftsman's flat-stock, minimally-profiled family far better than trim-classical's room-as-an-order pedestal-and-entablature system, which this node's suppressed-trim ethos explicitly rejects.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to. Bound because the node's own text states there is no module governing the design and the interior priority is spatial flow through the living hall rather than fixed ratios, which rules out room-harmonic's treatise proportions as firmly as the exterior rules out a bay system. The fit is approximate — architect-designed Newport houses were not vernacular cottages — but the physical constraints (joist span, daylight depth) still bound wood-frame construction regardless of who designed it, and no better system exists in this library for a non-treatise-proportioned room.

new-mexico-adobe.name: New Mexico Adobe

revival_periods.note: Codified in Santa Fe between 1912 and 1930 by Sylvanus Morley, Carlos Vierra and the Museum of New Mexico, and made mandatory by ordinance in 1957. Chris Wilson's The Myth of Santa Fe is the essential corrective: much of what is now taken as ancient is a twentieth-century construction.

regions: upper Rio Grande valley, New Mexico
Taos and the Sangre de Cristo foothills
geography.hearth: the upper Rio Grande — Puebloan coursed-earth building at Taos, Acoma and the Rio Grande pueblos predates Spanish arrival by six centuries and is the substrate on which the Spanish tradition was laid, largely by Puebloan hands

lineage.note: Everything Spanish in New Mexico came up the Camino Real from New Spain: the moulded adobe brick, the wooden form, the door and window frame, the corner fireplace, the plan diagram of the placita house.

description.short: Flat-roofed mud building on the upper Rio Grande, in which Spanish plan diagrams and moulded adobe brick were laid over a Puebloan earth-building tradition six centuries older, largely by Puebloan builders.
description.long:
It should be said plainly at the outset, because the popular account routinely omits it: the earth-wall building tradition of northern New Mexico is Puebloan first. When Oñate's colonists arrived in 1598 they found multi-storey, terraced, flat-roofed communal buildings at Taos, Acoma, Pecos and the Rio Grande pueblos, built of hand-puddled coursed earth on stone footings, roofed on peeled round beams with brush and packed earth above, plastered and re-plastered by women as a maintained annual practice. Taos Pueblo had already been standing for two hundred years. The Spanish contribution was real but specific: the moulded adobe brick and the wooden form that makes it, which turns an incremental hand-built wall into a modular one; the fired-earth-free lime whitewash; the door and shuttered window with a frame; the corner fireplace; the horno oven; and the plan diagrams of the placita house and the mission church. Almost all of that was executed by Puebloan labour, often coerced, and the resulting architecture belongs to both traditions in a way that neither an 'indigenous' nor a 'Spanish' label captures.

The physics are unforgiving and they set every dimension. Adobe has compressive strength and no tensile strength, so walls are thick — twenty-four to thirty-six inches — battered slightly, and kept low, rarely more than ten times their thickness in height. Openings are structurally expensive and were also glazing-expensive at the end of a thousand-mile supply line, so they stay small, under ten or twelve percent of wall area, deeply splayed inward to spread the light. The roof is flat because there is no framing timber long enough or plentiful enough to build a truss and because there is very little rain: peeled ponderosa vigas at two to two-and-a-half feet on centre, split cedar latillas laid herringbone or straight above them, brush, then eight to fourteen inches of earth graded a quarter-inch to the foot toward wooden canales that spit water clear of the wall. Room width is therefore locked to viga length — twelve to sixteen feet — and rooms cannot be aggregated into a block, only strung into files and folded around a placita.

The climate this serves has a diurnal swing of thirty to forty degrees and two hundred and eighty days of sun at seven thousand feet. Three feet of earth is a nearly ideal thermal battery for that regime: the wall absorbs all day and releases all night, and the interior temperature swings a few degrees while the outside swings forty. No twentieth-century assembly does this better, and several do it much worse.

Standing inside a real one — not a Pueblo Revival house, a real one — the first thing is the light. It comes through a small deep opening and hits a mud-plastered wall that has no flat plane and no sharp corner anywhere, so it diffuses into a warm, grainy glow with no glare. The second thing is the quiet: three feet of earth is an acoustic wall. The third is the corner fireplace, small, high, shallow, burning ocote upright, throwing heat into a room that is already holding yesterday's.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing adobe walls 24–36 in thick, laid in moulded sun-dried brick on a stone footing, slightly battered and finished in mud plaster
Flat roof on peeled round vigas at 24–30 in on centre, with latillas, brush and 8–14 in of earth above, drained by projecting wooden canales
Parapet 12–24 in above the roof surface on all sides, with no gable or eave anywhere
Room width limited to the viga span, 12–16 ft, with rooms strung in linear files and folded around a placita
Corner fireplace (fogón) — a Spanish-Puebloan hybrid — rather than a wall-centred hearth
Small openings, under 12% of wall area, deeply splayed inward
Portal on peeled posts with carved corbels (zapatas) carrying a beam, 8–12 ft deep, serving as the building's circulation
diagnostic_tells: Canales projecting through the parapet — a flat roof that visibly drains through the wall
No straight lines: mud plaster over adobe produces rounded arrises, undulating planes and no true corner
Room depth constant throughout the building, because it is the length of a beam
Corner fireplace with a small arched opening, set diagonally across the corner of the room
Portal posts with carved zapatas of a specific New Mexican profile, doing real structural work

distinguished_from.difference: The most consequential misidentification in the Southwest. Pueblo Revival is cement or synthetic stucco over wood frame or concrete block: walls six to twelve inches thick with sharp machine-true arrises, large windows, protruding 'vigas' that carry nothing and often stop at the wall face, two-storey plans the material could never support, and parapets with hard clean coping. Test any window reveal — a foot and a half of visible wall depth or four inches — and it is settled. Note also that the celebrated portal on the Palace of the Governors is itself a 1909–13 reconstruction.

California builds in adobe too but roofs in half-round clay tile at 3:12–5:12, uses semicircular arcades on square piers, and works at a mission-quadrangle scale. New Mexico has no tile, no arcade, no arch and no pitched roof: it has vigas, canales, parapets and posts.

The 1915–42 revival, drawn from Andalusia and Mexican Churrigueresque by way of Bertram Goodhue and San Diego, brings tile roofs, wrought iron, ornate cast plaster and towers — a vocabulary the Rio Grande never possessed at any date.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The viga sets the room and the wall thickness sets the height; nothing else is negotiable, and the composition is whatever those two constraints permit.
typical_ratios: Room clear width 12–16 ft (viga span), length 1.5–2.5 times the width
Wall thickness 24–36 in; wall height not more than 10× thickness, i.e. 8–11 ft
Ceiling 7 ft 6 in – 9 ft 0 in to the underside of the vigas
Window opening 2 ft – 3 ft wide × 3 ft – 4 ft high; glazed area 6–12% of wall area
Parapet 12–24 in above roof; roof fall 1/4 in per ft to canales
Portal depth 8–12 ft, posts at 6–9 ft on centre
Placita 30–60 ft across for a house
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Set by the portal posts. Wall openings are placed by the rooms behind them and routinely do not align with the posts — the two systems are independent and the tradition never reconciles them.

massing_affinities.note: The three-sided placita house, the standard rural and villa form.
The room-file growing along its own length before it turns a corner.
The closed placita of a defended hacienda such as the Martinez house at Taos.
The one-room adobe of first settlement.
Where the portal fronts a linear block that never encloses a court.

constraints.statement: Adobe wall thickness 24–36 in, with wall height not exceeding ten times thickness. Openings not exceeding 12% of wall area, with reveals expressing the full wall depth.

test.note: Tests thickness. Wall-height-to-thickness ratio (not exceeding 10x) and glazed area (not exceeding 12%) each have their own variable, already exercised elsewhere in this family, and stay prose here -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Room clear span limited to 16 ft — the practical viga length. Any wider room requires an intermediate bearing and is not of the tradition.
No pitched roof, no gable, no eave. The roof is flat behind a parapet of 12–24 in, drained at 1/4 in per ft through not fewer than one canale per roof plane, projecting 12–18 in beyond the wall face.

test.note: The no-pitch/no-gable/no-eave clauses are categorical and stay prose; canale drainage rate and projection are the statement's other numeric claims and also stay prose.

constraints.statement: Finish in mud plaster or lime wash only. Cement stucco on historic adobe traps moisture at the interface and destroys the wall from within; it is a preservation failure as well as a stylistic one.
Vigas project 12–24 in beyond the wall face and must actually carry the roof. Non-structural applied viga ends are the single clearest marker of Pueblo Revival.

test.note: Vigas are functionally the same kind of structural roof-member overhang the variable already covers elsewhere. 'Must actually carry the roof' is a structural-truth claim no plan measurement alone confirms and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Palacio de los Gobernadores (Palace of the Governors)
exemplars.note: Founded with the villa in 1610, with substantial construction c. 1618–25 and a rebuilding in 1731 after the Pueblo Revolt. The famous portal is a 1909–13 reconstruction by Jesse Nussbaum and is not colonial fabric.

exemplars.name: Taos Pueblo
exemplars.note: The Puebloan substrate, in continuous occupation for more than six centuries. Included here not as a Spanish colonial building but because the New Mexican adobe tradition is unintelligible without it.

exemplars.name: Mission San Esteban del Rey
exemplars.note: Built 1629–41 with adobe walls up to nine feet thick and roof timbers carried on foot some thirty miles from Mount Taylor; built by Acoma labour to a Franciscan plan.

exemplars.name: Hacienda de los Martínez
exemplars.note: A fully enclosed two-placita adobe hacienda with no exterior windows on the ground floor — the defended domestic type at full development.

sources: Bainbridge Bunting, Early Architecture in New Mexico (1976)
George Kubler, The Religious Architecture of New Mexico (1940)
Chris Wilson, The Myth of Santa Fe: Creating a Modern Regional Tradition (1997)
Peter Nabokov and Robert Easton, Native American Architecture (1989)
Boyd C. Pratt and Chris Wilson, The Architecture and Cultural Landscape of North Central New Mexico (1991)

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in this pack's own applies_to, and the fit is close: viga span limits room clear width to 12-16 ft here, against the pack's reconstructed 14-18 ft band, and the resulting long, narrow, strung-rather-than-stacked room is exactly what the pack's span/hearth/daylight logic predicts for a beam-limited vernacular tradition, even though the beam is a peeled ponderosa viga rather than a sawn joist and the wall behind it is adobe rather than frame. As on the parent spanish-colonial-american node, nothing else in this corpus governs: the wall itself (24-36 in thick, height not more than 10x thickness), the corner fogon, the portal on posts with carved zapatas, and the canale-drained parapet are all real, numbered constraints in this node's own record with no proportion pack behind any of them. A dedicated mass-wall/adobe module is missing from the corpus.

storybook-style.name: Storybook Style

geography.hearth: Los Angeles, California — specifically the film studio craft shops of Culver City and Hollywood

lineage.note: The immediate parent and the source of the swept eave, the catslide roof, the massive chimney, and the low arched door. Storybook takes each of these and exaggerates it past the point of plausibility, on purpose.
Supplies the half-timbering, the leaded casement, and the steep multiple gable. In Storybook the timbering ceases to correspond to any frame and becomes drawing.

Specifically its Norman register — the round tower with a conical roof, the stone-and-stucco mix, the flared eave and the farmhouse silhouette — which reached America through photographs brought back by servicemen in 1918-19 and through the shelter magazines of the 1920s, and which Storybook takes and exaggerates.

The claimed ancestry, and a precise instance of the references edge. No English cottage practice was transmitted: the actual sources were photographs, illustrated children's books, Arthur Rackham, and the studio plaster shop. What is imitated is a picture of a cottage, not a cottage.
Named as a reaction in this node's own description: against the archaeological seriousness of the period revivals it grew out of, and against the bungalow's earnest structural honesty.
Named as a reaction in this node's own description: against the archaeological seriousness of the period revivals it grew out of, and against the bungalow's earnest structural honesty.
Named as a reaction in this node's own description: against the archaeological seriousness of the period revivals it grew out of, and against the bungalow's earnest structural honesty.

description.short: A knowingly theatrical Los Angeles idiom of the 1920s in which the English and Norman cottage was rebuilt in studio plaster with its irregularities deliberately exaggerated — sagging ridges, rolled eaves, oversized chimneys, undersized doors — to make a house that performs a narrative.
description.long:
Storybook is the one node in this branch that is not trying to be authentic and does not think it should be. It is an architecture of deliberate caricature, produced by people whose day job was building convincing lies at twenty-four frames a second, and it is best understood as set design that was permitted to become permanent. Harry Oliver, who built the first canonical example, was a Hollywood art director; so were several of his imitators. The techniques are the studio's: lath and plaster shaped by hand to imitate weathered stone or slumping thatch, rolled and steamed shingle courses curled over the eave and around the gable end to fake a thatched roof, timbers distressed with adzes and chains, stucco troweled to look four hundred years old and stained accordingly. The moves are the studio's too: everything is scaled for legibility. The chimney is too large, the door is too small, the ridge sags, the eave undulates, the tower is too short for its cone. Each departure is on the order of ten to twenty percent from convention — enough to register as character, not so much as to read as failure.

What produced it is a specific coincidence of place and decade. Los Angeles in the 1920s had the largest concentration of skilled scenic plasterers, carpenters, and painters in the world, a population that had grown from about 577,000 to 1.2 million in ten years, an enormous speculative housing boom, and a cheap and completely plastic wall system — wood frame with wire lath and portland cement stucco — that could be shaped into any profile a modeller could sketch. It also had an audience trained by the movies to read buildings as characters. The parallel stream is quieter and just as important: Hugh Comstock, who was not a builder at all, put up a small cottage in Carmel-by-the-Sea in 1924 to house his wife's rag doll business, followed it with a second in 1925, and inadvertently produced the template for an entire seaside town's identity. The Carmel line is handmade and sincere where the Los Angeles line is professional and theatrical, and the two together define the style's range.

What it reacts against is the archaeological seriousness of the Period Revivals it grew out of. Tudor Revival and Cotswold Cottage Revival in the 1920s were policed by shelter magazines and by architects who had measured actual English buildings; Storybook cheerfully abandons the enterprise and admits that the client wants a feeling rather than a fact. It is also, less obviously, a reaction against the bungalow: after twenty years of the honest low horizontal Craftsman house, the market wanted verticality, romance, and a picture.

Standing before one, the effect is immediate and slightly unsettling: nothing is straight, and you become aware of how much of your reading of a house depends on the assumption that lines are level. The eave rolls. The ridge dips at the middle by four to six inches over its length. The wall bulges. The chimney occupies a third of the gable end and is battered and stepped and has more chimney pots than the flues require. The front door is six feet or so tall, board-and-strap with visible iron, set in an arched opening under a catslide roof that drops within seven feet of the ground. Windows are small, leaded, diamond-paned, and placed where a room needed them rather than where the elevation wanted them. Inside, the rooms are ordinary — this is a 1920s speculative house, with a normal plan and normal ceilings, and the enchantment is entirely a surface half an inch thick. That is the honest assessment, and it does not diminish the buildings: they are extremely good at what they set out to do, they are loved by everyone who lives near them, and they demonstrate something a rule-based system should take seriously, which is that deliberate, systematic, bounded deviation from a norm produces charm, while random deviation produces noise.

defining_characteristics: Deliberate distortion of geometry executed as designed intent: sagging ridge, undulating eave, out-of-plumb wall, irregular window placement
Steeply pitched roof, 12:12 or greater, with eaves rolled, swept, or curled over the rake to simulate thatch
A chimney oversized in width and height relative to the flue it contains, treated as the principal sculptural event
Wall surface as plastic material — troweled and modelled stucco, simulated or genuinely distressed masonry, timbering that follows no frame
Small leaded casements, diamond- or rectangular-paned, placed by internal need and never aligned to a facade datum
An entry composed as a set piece: low arched opening, board-and-strap door, catslide or hooded roof dropping close to the ground
Overall composition legible as a single picture from one viewpoint, usually the street corner
diagnostic_tells: Shingle courses rolled and curled around the eave and rake edge — the fake-thatch move, and the fastest positive identification
A roof that sweeps down to within 6 or 7 ft of the ground on one side (catslide) while the opposite eave stays high
Half-timbering that does not meet at the corners or align across a floor line
A round or polygonal turret whose conical roof is too tall and too steep for its diameter
A front door noticeably shorter than a person expects, in an opening arched at the head

distinguished_from.difference: Tudor Revival takes its English sources seriously and gets the timber framing, the brick bonds, and the window proportions right. Storybook knows they are wrong and makes them wronger. If the ridge is level and the timbering resolves at the corners, it is Tudor Revival.
The Cotswold type is built of real or convincing stone with genuine masonry coursing and restrained irregularity; Storybook simulates the same effects in plaster and pushes them past plausibility.

Normandy Revival keeps a sober farmhouse composition around its tower and stays symmetrical about it; Storybook uses the tower as one incident in a picturesque agglomeration and abandons any regulating geometry.

proportional_system.governing_logic: None in the conventional sense — the governing logic is pictorial and theatrical. Elements are scaled for narrative legibility from a single approach viewpoint, and the method is systematic bounded deviation: each element departs from its conventional dimension by roughly 10 to 25 percent, in a consistent direction (doors and windows down, chimneys and roofs up), so the whole composition reads as one exaggeration rather than a set of errors. This is encodable, and it is the only node in the branch where the rule is a rule about breaking rules.
typical_ratios: Principal roof pitch 12:12 to 18:12
Ridge deliberately deflected 3 to 6 in below level over its length
Eave line deviating from straight by 2 to 6 in
Entry door height 6 ft 0 in to 6 ft 6 in — 10 to 15 percent under convention
Chimney width 1.5 to 2.5 times the width required by its flues, and rising at least 4 ft above the ridge
Casement lights 6 to 10 in wide, in openings under 3 ft
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: None. Openings are placed by internal need and by pictorial balance; any perceived rhythm is accidental and should be disrupted.

massing_affinities.note: The agglomerated irregular mass with multiple roof directions is the style's home skeleton.
The commonest speculative version: an ordinary L-plan cottage with the whole apparatus applied to the street-facing gable.
Where a turret is present it converts the massing to this skeleton, usually with the tower shorter than the Italianate original.
The regular symmetrical box actively defeats the style; where it occurs the Storybook treatment is a veneer on an unwilling skeleton.

constraints.statement: Principal roof pitch not less than 12:12. Below 10:12 the style collapses into ordinary Period Revival.

test.note: 'Below 10:12 the style collapses into ordinary Period Revival' is the same variable's explanatory floor and stays prose (the enforced threshold is the stated 12:12, not the explanatory 10:12).

constraints.statement: A strictly symmetrical principal elevation is forbidden. At least three of the following must be present and deliberately irregular: ridge line, eave line, wall plane, window head heights, chimney profile.

Deviations from level, plumb, and convention shall lie between 5 and 25 percent of the nominal dimension, and shall be consistent in direction across the building. Deviation beyond 25 percent reads as damage rather than character.
The principal chimney must be the tallest and most massive element of the composition, not less than 1.5 times the width required by its flues, and must terminate at least 4 ft above the main ridge.

test.note: 'Tallest and most massive element of the composition' is a comparative claim and the flue-width multiplier (1.5x, no matching vocabulary variable for flue width) has no numeric support here; both stay prose.

constraints.statement: The idiom is coherent only at cottage scale. Applied to a house of more than roughly 2,500 sq ft or more than two full storeys, the exaggerations invert and read as bombast; use tudor-revival or french-eclectic instead.

exemplars.name: Spadena House (the Witch's House)
exemplars.note: Harry Oliver. Built 1921 in Culver City as offices and dressing rooms for Irvin Willat's film studio, moved to the corner of Walden Drive and Carmelita Avenue in Beverly Hills in 1926. The founding example, and literally a set.

exemplars.name: Hansel and Gretel Cottages
exemplars.note: Hugh Comstock, Hansel completed 1924 and Gretel 1925, built by hand by a man with no building training. The sincere, non-studio branch of the style and the origin of Carmel's cottage identity.

exemplars.name: Tam O'Shanter Inn
exemplars.note: Harry Oliver again, for the restaurateur Lawrence Frank. A commercial building in the domestic idiom, still operating; the style at its most confident.

sources: Arrol Gellner and Douglas Keister, Storybook Style: America's Whimsical Homes of the Twenties (2001)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Kevin Starr, Material Dreams: Southern California through the 1920s (1990)
Los Angeles Conservancy, survey files on the work of Harry Oliver

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in this pack's applies_to, and an unusually direct fit: the node's own proportional_system states its governing logic is 'systematic bounded deviation' from a norm, which is precisely how this pack frames its own ten judgment-marked rules -- constraints stated as hard bands with the exact number left to the designer's eye. The node's own hard constraint c02 (at least three of ridge/eave/wall-plane/window-heads/chimney deliberately irregular) is this pack's dominance-and-datum discipline pushed past its ordinary tolerance on purpose, which the node states outright is the point.

Explicitly listed. The node's own description is direct that the interior carries none of the style's claim -- 'the rooms are ordinary... this is a 1920s speculative house, with a normal plan and normal ceilings, and the enchantment is entirely a surface half an inch thick' -- which is exactly the ordinary Los Angeles bungalow-era catalog trim this pack records, ordered from the same millwork suppliers as any other 1920s spec house of the region.

JUDGMENT BINDING: storybook-style is not in this pack's applies_to list. Bound on the strength of the node's own description quoted above -- an ordinary plan and ceiling height behind the theatrical surface -- which is squarely this pack's 'what rooms actually measure' domain rather than room-harmonic's designed Palladian one. Bound at low precedence and deliberately thin: the node's own text is explicit that the room is not where this style's claim is made, and no proportional system should be dressed up as governing what the node itself calls ordinary.

tidewater-georgian.name: Tidewater Georgian

revival_periods.note: The Colonial Williamsburg reconstruction from 1926 made Tidewater Georgian the semi-official national image of 'colonial' and standardized a set of details — some of them conjectural — across thousands of later houses.

geography.hearth: the James, York, Rappahannock and Potomac river plantations, where the tobacco economy put wealth on navigable water and every great house had its own landing

lineage.note: The five-part composition of block, hyphen and dependency arrives through Campbell's Vitruvius Britannicus and Gibbs, and is realized here more completely than anywhere else in the colonies.

description.short: Brick laid in glazed-header Flemish bond, tall gable-end chimneys, a low hipped or gabled roof, and a plan one room deep with its service buildings pushed out into the yard as separate structures.
description.long:
Tidewater Georgian is a hot-climate architecture wearing English clothes, and every place it deviates from its English model is a place where the climate or the labour system won. Start with the plan. Virginia keeps the single-pile house — one room deep, eighteen to twenty-two feet — for two generations after New England and Philadelphia have gone double-pile, because a single-pile house with opposed windows ventilates and a double-pile one does not. The centre passage, ten to fourteen feet wide, runs straight through with a door at each end, both of them aligned, and in July both stand open: it is a breezeway with a stair in it, and Virginians used it as a room, dining and sitting there in summer. Ceilings go to ten, eleven and twelve feet, well above the Northern norm, because hot air has to go somewhere.

Then the dependencies.
