In New England the kitchen is attached at the back in an ell; in Virginia it is a separate brick building thirty or fifty feet away, along with the laundry, the dairy, the office and the quarters for the enslaved people who worked in them. This is partly fire, partly heat, and mostly the organization of a labour system on a plantation that was a village. At the top of the range it becomes a formal composition: main block, curved or straight hyphens, and symmetrical flanking dependencies — the five-part Palladian arrangement, of which Virginia and Maryland have more surviving examples than any other region.

The brickwork is the region's real achievement. Flemish bond on the entrance elevation, with headers dipped in a glaze that fires to a blue-grey sheen, laid in a chequer visible at two hundred yards; a moulded or bevelled water table two to three feet above grade; rubbed and gauged arches over the openings — segmental on early work, flat with a slight camber later — and moulded brick belt courses and ogee water tables where the mason was good. Westover's segmental heads and ogee water table are the standard by which the rest is judged.

Chimneys are at the gable ends, and they are tall. Whether interior-end, rising within the gable wall, or fully exterior with a stepped weathering, they clear the roof by six to ten feet and often stand in pairs joined by an arched curtain, as at Stratford Hall, where two clusters of stacks rise from the end blocks joined with arches and rails. Roof pitch drops to seven to nine in twelve, and the hipped roof is at least as common as the gable. Both are climate responses: a lower roof over a taller room, hipped to shed the wind.

Standing in the passage at Westover or Carter's Grove with both doors open, the building explains itself in about four seconds. The river is at one end of the axis and the approach at the other; the air moves; the room is twelve feet high and the walls are two feet of brick; and the working buildings — which is to say the buildings where the enslaved labour that produced all of it was performed — are visible outside through the far door. It is the most articulate and the most uncomfortable architecture in colonial America.

defining_characteristics: Brick laid in Flemish bond on the entrance elevation, commonly with glazed headers, over a moulded or bevelled water table 24–36 in above grade
Chimneys at the gable ends — interior-end or fully exterior — rising 6–10 ft clear of the roof, often paired and joined by an arched curtain
Low roof pitch, 7:12 to 9:12, hipped as often as gabled, with a modillion cornice and dormers
Gauged and rubbed brick window heads: segmental arches on early work, flat cambered arches later; not keystoned and not wood
Single-pile centre-passage plan 18–22 ft deep, retained long after other regions went double-pile; passage 10–14 ft with opposed aligned doors at both ends
Service functions in detached dependencies — kitchen, laundry, dairy, office, quarters — rather than in an attached ell, formalized at the top of the range into a five-part composition
Ceilings 10–12 ft on the principal floor
diagnostic_tells: Tall gable-end chimneys standing well clear of the roof, frequently paired and linked — visible from a mile away and conclusive against New England
Glazed-header Flemish bond producing a visible chequer across the front wall
Front and rear doors aligned on the passage axis, so the house can be seen straight through from the approach
A separate brick kitchen thirty to eighty feet from the house instead of a service ell
Segmental (curved) brick arches over the openings on pre-1750 work

distinguished_from.difference: The five discriminators, all measurable: cladding (glazed-header Flemish bond brick versus clapboard or rusticated board); chimney position (gable-end and often exterior versus interior, inboard of the ridge); roof pitch (7:12–9:12, often hipped, versus 9:12–11:12 gable); window head (segmental or cambered gauged brick arch versus flat wood architrave); and plan depth (single-pile 18–22 ft with detached dependencies versus double-pile 32–38 ft with an attached ell). Ceilings run 10–12 ft here against 8 ft 6 in – 9 ft 6 in in New England.

Both masonry, both gable-end chimneys. The Delaware Valley house is double-pile 34–40 ft deep, carries a belt course and often a pent roof, uses keystoned flat arches, and attaches its service wing. The Chesapeake house stays single-pile, has no pent roof, uses segmental arches and glazed headers, and detaches its dependencies entirely.

The nineteenth-century Southern plantation house adds a giant order of full-height columns and a pediment, uses six-over-six sash and heavy plain trim, and generally goes double-pile. Georgian Tidewater has no colossal portico except in a handful of late Palladian cases, and concentrates its ornament in brickwork and interior joinery.

proportional_system.governing_logic: A pattern-book order for the doorway and cornice, and the brick module — a 2 1/4 in brick with a 1/2 in bed joint, four courses to eleven inches — for everything horizontal.
typical_ratios: Facade 48–72 ft, five or seven bays; depth 18–22 ft single-pile, 32–36 ft double-pile
Passage 10–14 ft wide, roughly one-fifth to one-quarter of the facade
Ceilings 10–12 ft first floor, 9–11 ft second
Window opening height:width 2.0:1 to 2.2:1 — taller and narrower than the Northern norm
Water table 24–36 in above grade; belt course, where used, at the second-floor line
Roof rise:run 7:12 to 9:12; chimney 6–10 ft above the ridge
Five-part composition: hyphens 12–20 ft long, dependencies 60–75% of the main block's height
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five or seven bays, unaccented, the centre marked only by the doorway; on the largest houses a pedimented pavilion or a two-storey portico breaking forward 24–48 in.

massing_affinities.note: The defining Chesapeake plan and the reason the type ventilates.
Main block, hyphens, dependencies — Virginia and Maryland hold the densest surviving group in America.
The double-pile block on the largest houses such as Westover and Carter's Grove.
Stepped-down service ranges, particularly on the Maryland Eastern Shore.
Rare survival of Jacobean planning, as at Stratford Hall.

constraints.statement: Chimneys at the gable ends, interior-end or exterior, rising not less than 6 ft above the ridge. Interior chimneys set inboard of the ridge are a New England device and are wrong here on both stylistic and climatic grounds.

test.note: The interior-end-or-exterior position clause is categorical and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 7:12 to 9:12. Above 10:12 the elevation reads Northern; below 6:12 it reads Federal or Greek Revival.
Centre passage 10–14 ft wide with exterior doors at both ends, aligned on axis and both operable. This is a ventilation device, not a hallway; narrowing it below 9 ft defeats it.

Flemish bond on the entrance elevation, glazed headers optional but regionally characteristic; English or common bond elsewhere; moulded or bevelled water table 24–36 in above grade; segmental gauged arches with a 3–5 in rise before c. 1750, flat cambered arches after.

test.note: Tests the water table height. Bond pattern and the date-conditional arch-rise clause (OQ 22) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Kitchen and service functions in detached dependencies not less than 25 ft from the main block, not in an attached ell. Where formalized, hyphens 12–20 ft long and dependencies at 60–75% of the main block height.

test.note: Tests the categorical placement claim via the existing service_zone_position enum. Distance (25ft+) and hyphen-length figures stay prose.

exemplars.name: Westover
exemplars.note: Built by William Byrd III shortly after the 1749 fire destroyed the earlier house — a correction to the long-standing attribution to William Byrd II. Segmental window heads, ogee brick water table, steep hipped roof, tall paired chimneys; the Portland stone doorways were added c. 1767.

exemplars.name: Stratford Hall
exemplars.note: Built c. 1725–38. H-plan of two three-bay hip-roofed end blocks about a central great hall, raised on a high basement, with two clusters of chimney stacks joined by arches and rails; floor levels distinguished by brick of different colours and sizes in Flemish bond.

exemplars.name: Carter's Grove
exemplars.note: Built 1750–55 for Carter Burwell; among the finest surviving colonial Virginia interior joinery, and a legible five-part composition before its twentieth-century alteration.

exemplars.name: Gunston Hall
exemplars.note: Built 1755–59 for George Mason; the interiors are William Buckland's first American work, and the Palladian and Chinese Chippendale rooms are directly traceable to imported pattern books.

sources: Thomas Tileston Waterman, The Mansions of Virginia, 1706–1776 (1946)
Dell Upton, 'Vernacular Domestic Architecture in Eighteenth-Century Virginia', Winterthur Portfolio 17 (1982)
Cary Carson et al., 'Impermanent Architecture in the Southern American Colonies', Winterthur Portfolio 16 (1981)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Fiske Kimball, Domestic Architecture of the American Colonies and of the Early Republic (1922)

proportion_packs.note: PROMOTED to primary and effectively governing. A Tidewater house is set out on the mason's gauge rod: water table at ten courses, segmental arches with a rise of opening/8 before c. 1750 and flat cambered arches with a camber of opening/96 after, sills one course, quoins and chimney plans in whole bricks. The Flemish bond with glazed headers is the visible expression of the same module. Where a dimension in this kit disagrees with the coursing, the coursing wins.

Re-anchored at a taller principal storey. The Chesapeake principal floor is 10–12 ft against New England's 8 ft 6 in – 9 ft 6 in, so every dimension the pack derives from the storey — window head at 0.78, sill at 30 in, cornice at module/8 — moves up with it while the sill stays put. That divergence is the whole reason a Virginia window looks taller than a Massachusetts one of the same width.

DEMOTED. The canonical Tidewater house is brick and single-pile at 18–22 ft, which is one bay deep and therefore says nothing the brick module does not already say. Retained only for the frame houses of the middling planters, where it governs.

churrigueresque.name: Churrigueresque

revival_periods.note: Bertram Goodhue's California Building at the Panama-California Exposition, San Diego, 1915, is the single act that reintroduces the estipite portada to American practice and launches Spanish Colonial Revival nationally.
A thinner secondary transmission — the ornamented portada against plain stucco, without the estipite.

geography.hearth: Madrid, Salamanca and Andalusia; the fullest development in New Spain

lineage.note: The compositional habit is inherited whole: a bounded panel of extreme ornamental density against a plain wall, composed in stacked registers as a retablo. Churrigueresque is Plateresque's method carried to its limit with a new vocabulary.

Borrominian and Berninian devices — the broken and doubled cornice, the concave-convex plan, the solomonic shaft, the theatrical light source — reach Spain through prints and through Naples and Sicily, which were Spanish possessions with continuous exchange of craftsmen.
In New Spain especially, the substrate remains Mudejar: brick and tile construction, artesonado ceilings, and a plasterwork trade whose modelling technique is unbroken from Andalusia.

The orders are present and systematically dismantled. The estipite is a column that has stopped being a column; the entablature is broken at every vertical. The classical apparatus is quoted precisely in order to be seen collapsing.

description.short: The last and most extreme phase of Spanish Baroque, in which an ornamental portada built around the estipite pilaster is compressed against a plain wall until the classical orders visibly dissolve.
description.long:
Churrigueresque takes its name from the Churriguera family of Salamanca, which is unfair to them: Jose Benito de Churriguera's actual work is comparatively restrained, and the extreme phase belongs to Pedro de Ribera in Madrid, Narciso Tome at Toledo, the Arevalo workshop in Granada, and above all to Jeronimo de Balbas and Lorenzo Rodriguez in Mexico City. What the name reliably identifies is a specific device and a specific attitude. The device is the estipite: a pilaster whose shaft is not a shaft at all but a stack — an inverted truncated pyramid, then a cube, then a baluster, then a capital — so that the member gets narrower as it goes down and appears to be balancing rather than supporting. Once the estipite appears, it becomes the module of the whole composition; everything is set out from its width and from the count of blocks in its stack.

The attitude is harder to state and more important. Churrigueresque is not simply Baroque exuberance. It is a deliberate demonstration that the classical apparatus, having been received into Spain a century and a half late and never really believed in, can be taken apart in public. Cornices are broken, doubled, returned, and broken again at every vertical member. Entablatures never run. Niches are set into other niches. The ornament is not applied to a frame; it consumes the frame, and the moment at which a viewer stops being able to say where the architecture ends and the sculpture begins is the intended effect. Behind this sits the Spanish retablo tradition and, behind that, the Counter-Reformation conviction that a church interior should overwhelm rather than persuade.

In New Spain the style goes further than in Spain, for reasons that are economic and technical. Mexican silver paid for it; a large, skilled indigenous and mestizo carving workforce executed it, working in soft volcanic tezontle, in chiluca limestone, and in moulded and gilded plaster and wood; and the seismic realities of the Valley of Mexico encouraged a light, low-rise, heavily buttressed church with all its budget spent on two flat surfaces — the west front and the retablo behind the altar. The result — the Sagrario Metropolitano, Santa Prisca at Taxco, the Ocotlan sanctuary — is the most concentrated ornamental architecture produced anywhere in the eighteenth century, and it is Mexican work, not a provincial copy of a Spanish original.

What ends it is an administrative decision. The Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando, founded in 1752, campaigned against the style as barbarous, and from 1777 a royal order required Academy approval for church designs in Spain and its empire. Neoclassicism arrived by decree. Standing in front of a Churrigueresque portada today, the thing that surprises is how small the ornamented area actually is: a strip perhaps eight metres wide on a facade of forty, and the rest bare tezontle or bare stone. The density is entirely a function of the emptiness around it, and photographs, which crop to the portada, systematically misrepresent the buildings.

defining_characteristics: The estipite pilaster — inverted-obelisk shaft assembled from a truncated pyramid, cube, baluster and capital — as the governing member and module
Ornamental portada composed as a compressed retablo in stacked registers, bounded and framed against an otherwise plain wall
Cornices and entablatures broken, doubled and returned at every vertical; no straight uninterrupted horizontal crosses the composition
Extreme relief depth and undercutting, so that the composition reads as shadow at distance and as programme close up
Ornament concentrated at the west front, the transept portal, the sacristy and the retablo; nave and flank walls left plain
Sculpture, architecture and framing continuous — no legible boundary between the figures and the members that carry them
In New Spain, plain tezontle or ashlar field walls setting off dressed chiluca or moulded plaster ornament
diagnostic_tells: A pilaster that is narrower at the bottom than at the top and is visibly a stack of dissimilar blocks
A cornice that returns on itself three or four times across a single portada
Deep red-brown volcanic stone field with pale limestone ornament, in Mexican examples
Niche-pilasters — a niche with a figure cut into the body of the pilaster itself
A facade in which the ornamented strip occupies less than a quarter of the wall area

distinguished_from.difference: Plateresque keeps crisp frames, legible registers and recognisable classical members. Churrigueresque dissolves all three, and is defined by a member — the estipite — that Plateresque never uses.

Italian Baroque manipulates whole building masses, plans and vaults in curves and controls light spatially. Churrigueresque leaves the mass and plan almost untouched and does everything on two flat surfaces.

Churrigueresque is one ornamental phase within Mexican colonial building, roughly 1730-1790. Mexican Colonial as a node covers the plans, walls, patios, atrios and construction culture across three centuries, most of which is plain.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The estipite. Once present, its width sets the bay of the portada and the count of blocks in its shaft sets the register heights. There is no classical module: the entablature that would regulate the composition has been deliberately broken, so the only continuous dimension in the design is the estipite itself. The plain wall around the portada is dimensioned by structure and by seismic buttressing, not by composition.
typical_ratios: Portada width 15-30 percent of facade width; height two to four registers
Estipite slenderness roughly 1:8 to 1:11 overall, with the pyramidal base block 0.25-0.35 of shaft height
Relief depth 100-250 mm; niche recesses 300-600 mm
Ornamented area under 25 percent of the elevation
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three to five vertical divisions within the portada set by the estipites, with the central bay widest and holding the door and the principal niche. The rhythm exists only inside the frame; outside it there is none.

massing_affinities.note: The convento, colegio and seminario are enclosed arcaded courts; the ornament appears at the church front and the portería.
Three-sided courts in smaller foundations and in the sacristy ranges.
The larger palace commissions reach a two-wing plan around a principal patio.
Urban palaces in Madrid and Mexico City sit in continuous blocks with the whole budget at the portada.

constraints.statement: The estipite is definitional. A facade of this ornamental density using a normal column or a solomonic (barley-sugar) shaft is Salomonico Baroque, an earlier and different phase, not Churrigueresque.

The ornamented portada must be a bounded field against plain wall occupying no more than about a quarter of the elevation. Extending the ornament across the whole facade destroys the contrast the style is built on.
No straight uninterrupted entablature or cornice may cross the portada. Every horizontal is broken and returned at each vertical member.

The portada is applied dressed stone or moulded plaster on brick, carried on the wall behind, rarely more than 600 mm deep. In seismic regions the field wall must be buttressed and the church kept low; ornament is not permitted to drive the structure.

test.note: Tests the applied-portada-depth ceiling. The seismic buttressing/low-church clause is conditional and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Ornament belongs to the west front, the transept portal, the sacristy and the retablo. Nave walls, flanks and cloister ranges stay plain; a uniformly ornamented building is a revival misreading.

exemplars.name: Hospicio de San Fernando, portada (now Museo de Historia de Madrid)
exemplars.note: 1722-1726, Pedro de Ribera; the Madrid strain, ornament exploding out of an otherwise plain brick institutional block.

exemplars.name: El Transparente, Toledo Cathedral
exemplars.note: 1729-1732, Narciso Tome; sculpture, architecture and a cut roof-light fused into one object.

exemplars.name: Sacristy of the Cartuja
exemplars.note: 1732-1747, Luis de Arevalo and Luis Cabello; the most extreme surviving interior of the style anywhere.

exemplars.name: Sagrario Metropolitano
exemplars.note: 1749-1768, Lorenzo Rodriguez; the canonical estipite portada, chiluca limestone against tezontle, and the direct source for Goodhue in 1915.

sources: Kubler & Soria, Art and Architecture in Spain and Portugal and their American Dominions 1500-1800
Bonet Correa, Andalucia barroca
Toussaint, Arte colonial en Mexico
Bevan, History of Spanish Architecture

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding, bound narrowly and with real doubt. churrigueresque is not in room-harmonic's own applies_to, but its parent family 'spanish-classical' is, which is the only signal pointing this way at all. This style's own proportional_system states flatly that 'there is no classical module' and that the estipite is 'a column that has stopped being a column' -- so this pack is NOT bound for the portada, the church interior, or anything the ornamental programme touches. It is offered only as a weak, last-resort covering for the secular institutional rooms (cells, refectory, sacristy antechambers) of the convento, colegio and seminario that carry this style's canonical courtyard-full massing, on the theory that those ordinary rooms were sized by the period's general domestic habit rather than by the ornamental system next door. This is the thinnest binding in the whole batch and should be read as such.

english-cottage-vernacular.name: English Cottage Vernacular

revival_periods.note: The cottage orne and the model estate hamlet — Nash's Blaise Hamlet of 1811, Acland's Selworthy of 1828 — in which the cottage is composed for the picturesque eye by an architect for the first time.
Voysey's roughcast and long low eaves, Lutyens's Surrey tile-hanging and Baillie Scott's cottage plans all descend from close study of this tradition.
The suburban 'Tudorbethan' and American storybook cottage, which keeps the silhouette and discards every constructional reason for it.

geography.hearth: The lowland clay, chalk and cob districts — Devon, Dorset, Somerset, Hampshire, East Anglia and the south Midlands

lineage.note: The same carpentry tradition at the bottom of the social scale: cruck pairs, low box frames, wattle-and-daub panels and thatched roofs, built by the same village carpenters who framed the yeoman's house.

Sibling rather than ancestor. The two are the same building culture — same plan, same social class, same period — differentiated almost entirely by geology, and they meet and blend along the edge of the limestone belt.

description.short: The small house of the English labourer and husbandman: one and a half storeys of cob, rubble or timber frame under deep thatch, built low to the ground with a stack that is the largest thing in it.
description.long:
The English cottage is the least designed and most imitated building in the world. Its form is the residue of a set of hard constraints. Walls are whatever the ground provided within a few hundred metres: cob in Devon and Dorset, clay lump in Norfolk, flint and chalk on the downs, rubble in the west, timber frame with daub panels everywhere there was oak. Roofs are thatch, in wheat reed or water reed or combed straw, which demands a pitch of at least 45 and preferably 50 degrees and which insists on being a continuous surface — hence the swept eyebrow dormer, the rounded hip, the catslide down over a rear outshot, and the total absence of valleys and hard edges. Eaves are low, often only two metres above the ground, because a cob wall costs money by the course and because heat rises. Windows are small and few, because glass was expensive and a window tax existed from 1696 to 1851.

The social history is harsher than the picture suggests. Most surviving cottages are not labourers' houses at all but the houses of husbandmen, small freeholders and craftsmen — the genuinely poor lived in dwellings that have not survived, and the 1834 Poor Law and the nineteenth-century agricultural depression emptied much of the countryside. What did survive was upgraded during the Great Rebuilding of roughly 1570 to 1640, when a chimney stack was inserted into an open one-cell or two-cell house and a floor thrown across at the old wall-plate level, creating the classic lobby-entry plan: front door opening onto the face of the stack, hall to one side, parlour to the other, and a winder stair squeezed behind the fire.

The cottage was not reacting against anything until other people started looking at it. From the 1790s the picturesque movement turned it into an object of taste, and John Nash's Blaise Hamlet of 1811 — nine cottages arranged around a green, each with a different thatch, a different chimney and a deliberately crooked plan — is the moment the vernacular becomes a style. Everything from Arts and Crafts to the interwar suburb runs through that door. The distinction worth holding is between a cottage that is low because cob is expensive and a cottage that is low because low looks charming; the kit-of-parts consequences are entirely different.

The interior of a real one is small, dark and warm. The stack occupies perhaps a fifth of the ground floor and radiates for hours after the fire is out; ceilings are 2.0 to 2.2 metres and crossed by chamfered beams you will hit if you are tall; the walls are 450 to 600 mm of cob, limewashed, and every corner in the building is slightly rounded because cob does not do arrises. Windows are deep-set and let in less light than you expect, but the thatch is silent under rain in a way no other roof is, and the whole house holds temperature like a cave. It is a building that was made by the same hands that lived in it, and it feels like it.

defining_characteristics: One to one-and-a-half storeys with a low eaves height of 2.0-2.7 m, the upper rooms partly within the roof
Walls of locally available mass material — cob, clay lump, flint, chalk, rubble — or of low timber frame with daub panels, finished in limewash
Thatch, or in later and eastern examples plain clay tile, at a pitch of 45-55 degrees, treated as a continuous unbroken surface
Eyebrow or swept dormers formed within the thatch, and a catslide carried down over a rear outshot rather than a separate roof
A single dominant chimney stack — central lobby-entry or gable-end — of brick or stone, disproportionately large relative to the house
Small side-hung casement windows with leaded lights or timber glazing bars, set in deep reveals with few and irregular openings
An additive plan that grows by cell, outshot and lean-to rather than by any composed extension
diagnostic_tells: No hard edges anywhere: rounded eaves, swept dormers, rolled hips, and wall corners visibly curved because cob will not hold a sharp arris
Eaves low enough to touch, with the upper-floor windows sitting in the roof rather than in the wall
A stack that is out of scale with the building, standing well above a low ridge, often with the front door opening directly against its side
Openings placed by internal need and never in vertical alignment between floors — the opposite of every classical rule
Wall thickness of 450-600 mm showing at the reveals, with sills deep enough to sit on and window frames set well back

distinguished_from.difference: Geology decides. The Cotswold house has dressed stone mullions, kneelered gables, raised copings and a hard graded stone slate roof; the cottage has soft-edged cob or frame walls, timber casements and thatch. Cotswold work has crisp arrises everywhere the cottage is rounded.

The timber-frame node is the designed frame of a yeoman or merchant — close studding, jetties, moulded bressumers, a carpented open roof. The cottage uses the same joints with a quarter of the timber, no jetty, no display, and often no frame at all where cob or rubble does the work.

The twentieth-century imitation exaggerates every feature that was originally a constraint: the sweep of the eaves becomes a wave, the catslide reaches the ground, the chimney becomes a sculpture, and the walls are 150 mm of stud with render. Real cottages are irregular by accretion; storybook cottages are irregular by drawing.

proportional_system.governing_logic: None applied. Dimensions come from material limits — the bay of a cruck or box frame, the height a cob wall can be raised in a season of lifts, the pitch thatch requires, the span a floor joist will carry — and from the size of the family.
typical_ratios: Bay length 3.0-4.5 m; a cottage is one to three bays plus outshot
Eaves height 2.0-2.7 m; ridge height 5.5-7.0 m for one and a half storeys
Roof pitch 45-55 degrees, with 50 degrees typical under long straw or combed wheat reed
Wall thickness 450-600 mm in cob, 350-500 mm in rubble, 150 mm in a daub-panelled frame
Window opening 600-1000 mm wide by 700-1200 mm high, in leaded quarries or small timber lights
Glazed area 4-8 percent of floor area, against 15-20 percent in a Georgian house of the same date
Thatch depth 300-400 mm at the ridge, giving the eaves their characteristic soft thickness
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular. Openings are placed where the room needs light and never aligned between storeys; the only rhythm is the structural bay, which is often invisible from outside.

massing_affinities.note: The two-cell lobby-entry plan produced by the Great Rebuilding, with the stack backing onto the entry.
The one-cell cottage with a gable-end or corner hearth — the irreducible base of the whole tradition.
The catslide over a rear outshot is the English original of which the New England saltbox is the transplanted and formalised descendant.
The Devon and Dartmoor longhouse, with house and byre in a single range under one roof, sharing a cross passage.
Paired cottages under one roof with separate doors, a common estate and enclosure-era arrangement.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch not less than 45 degrees where thatch is used, and 50 degrees preferred; thatch must run as an unbroken surface with no valleys, no hard verges and no interruption by boxed dormers.

test.note: Tests the hard 45-degree minimum. The 50-degree preferred figure is advisory, not the hard bound, and the unbroken-surface/no-valleys/no-hard-verges/no-dormer requirements are categorical and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Cob and clay walls require a masonry or rubble plinth at least 450 mm above ground and a generous roof overhang at the eaves — the traditional formula of a good hat and a good pair of boots. Neither is optional.

test.note: Tests the plinth-height clause ('boots'). The eaves-overhang clause ('hat') gives no number -- 'generous' is not a stated threshold -- and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Lime mortar, lime render and limewash only. Cement render on a cob or rubble wall traps water and will collapse the wall from within.

Eaves height 2.0-2.7 m at the wall plate, and glazed area not more than about 10 percent of floor area. A cottage with tall eaves and large windows is a different building type wearing a thatched hat.

test.note: Tests the eaves-height clause. The glazed-area clause (not more than 10 percent of FLOOR area) has no matching vocabulary variable -- glazed_area_pct_wall exists but is glazed area over WALL area, a different denominator -- and stays prose.

constraints.statement: One chimney stack must dominate the composition, rising at least 1 m above the ridge. Multiple equal stacks belong to a farmhouse or a gentry house, not a cottage.

test.note: Tests the ridge-clearance clause for the dominant stack. The single-dominant-stack-versus-multiple-equal-stacks comparison stays prose.

exemplars.name: The Priest's House
exemplars.note: First recorded in 1308. Local lias stone roughly cut and squared with Ham stone dressings, thatched roof half-hipped to the east with a stepped coped gable west, and wattle-and-daub partitions inside — the small late-medieval house in near-complete survival.

exemplars.name: Anne Hathaway's Cottage
exemplars.note: The earliest part dates to 1463 as a single-storey three-room house; the upper part was built between 1610 and 1624. Timber frame with daub panels under long-straw thatch, and a textbook demonstration of the Great Rebuilding raising an open house into two storeys.

exemplars.name: Selworthy Green
exemplars.note: Rebuilt in 1828 by Sir Thomas Dyke Acland to house the aged of the Holnicote estate, in ochre-tinted limewashed cob under thatch. Composed for the picturesque eye in the manner of Blaise Hamlet, but built with entirely authentic local technique — the honest borderline case between vernacular and revival.

exemplars.name: Blaise Hamlet
exemplars.note: Nine cottages designed by John Nash around a green for John Scandrett Harford's estate pensioners. The moment the vernacular becomes a style, and the origin of every cottage orne and storybook cottage since.

sources: R. W. Brunskill, Illustrated Handbook of Vernacular Architecture (1970)
R. W. Brunskill, Traditional Buildings of Britain (1981)
Alec Clifton-Taylor, The Pattern of English Building (1962)
W. G. Hoskins, 'The Rebuilding of Rural England 1570-1640', Past and Present 4 (1953)
Eric Mercer, English Vernacular Houses (RCHME, 1975)

proportion_packs.note: english-cottage-vernacular is named directly in room-vernacular's applies_to, and the fit is close to definitive: governing_logic states 'None applied. Dimensions come from material limits,' which is precisely room-vernacular's reconstruction method, and the style's own low ceiling figures (2.0-2.2 m) and small, irregular openings track the pack's daylight-limited room closely. This is one of the source vernacular traditions the pack itself was reconstructed from.

english-cottage-vernacular is named directly in timber-bay's applies_to. Bound higher than the equivalent binding on cotswold-vernacular because this tradition genuinely is a timber-frame wall system in most of its range ('timber frame with daub panels everywhere there was oak'), not a masonry one — the bay module sets both the frame and, through the room-vernacular deduction, the room it encloses. Where the wall is cob, clay lump or flint rather than frame, this pack governs only the roof carpentry, as at cotswold-vernacular.

italianate-townhouse.name: Italianate Townhouse

geography.hearth: Manhattan and Brooklyn

lineage.note: The urban party-wall expression of the parent style; numerically the largest population of Italianate buildings in North America.
The astylar palazzo facade rules, the diminishing storey heights, and the brownstone technique come directly from the Notman and Trench and Snook generation.
The side-hall double-pile plan, the high stoop, the raised parlour floor, and the basement kitchen are inherited unchanged from the Greek Revival city house.
The underlying party-wall row, lot dimension, and vertical section come from the Federal city house and were never redesigned, only redressed.

description.short: The party-wall Italianate city house: a brownstone or brick row with a high stoop, a raised parlour floor of eleven-foot windows, arched heads with heavy hoods, and a bracketed cornice that runs continuously across the whole block.
description.long:
The Italianate townhouse is the most-built urban dwelling type in nineteenth-century America and probably the most successful piece of repeatable traditional design the country has produced. The plan is not Italian at all; it is the English and Federal side-hall double-pile row, unchanged since the 1790s, with a stair against the party wall, two parlours in file on the raised main floor, a kitchen in the basement, and bedrooms above. What changed in the 1850s was the dress: the flat Greek Revival lintel became a round or segmental arch with a projecting hood, the plain box cornice grew brackets, and the whole front was faced in the newly cheap chocolate-brown Triassic sandstone that gave the type its universal name.

The economics are precise and are the reason it worked. Steam-powered saws and planers at the Portland, Connecticut and Newark quarries made dressed brownstone cheap; the railroad and the coastal barge delivered it in quantity; and speculative builders erecting ten or twenty houses at once could order identical stoop rails, identical hoods, identical brackets, and identical newels for the whole run. The result is the specific and undervalued urbanism of the brownstone block: houses that are individually ordinary and collectively magnificent, because a single repeated cornice line and a single repeated stoop rhythm produce a street wall of extraordinary coherence. No architect designed that street. A parts catalogue and a party-wall constraint did.

This is the clearest nineteenth-century case of a kit of parts producing good urban form, and it is worth being exact about why. Three constraints did the work. The party wall fixed the width. The lot depth and the basement kitchen fixed the section, so every house had the same floor heights and therefore the same cornice line. And the builder bought one set of parts for the whole row, so the ornament was not merely compatible but identical. Coherence was a byproduct of constraint rather than of taste. When later builders relaxed any of the three, and especially when they varied cornice heights house to house, the street immediately stopped working.

Standing on such a block the eye reads a single dark bracketed line running the length of the street, punctuated at even intervals by the stoops projecting into the sidewalk like a row of gangplanks. The stoop is the type's social instrument: it lifts the parlour floor above the street's dirt and gaze, buys a full storey of light for the basement kitchen, and creates the half-public perch that has organised New York street life for a hundred and seventy years. Inside, the sequence is compression and release, a low dark vestibule and then a parlour eleven to fourteen feet tall with windows to the floor, and the depth of the double parlour makes a room longer than most people have ever lived in.

defining_characteristics: Party-wall row construction on a narrow deep lot, typically 16 to 25 ft wide
High stoop rising to a raised parlour floor over an exposed English basement
Side-hall double-pile plan with the stair against the party wall and parlours in file
Round-arched or segmental window heads with projecting moulded hoods or full architrave surrounds on the parlour floor
Diminishing storey heights above the parlour floor, expressed in window height
A bracketed cornice running continuously across party walls for the length of the row
Brownstone, pressed brick, or brick with brownstone trim; a flat unbroken wall plane apart from a shallow bay
diagnostic_tells: Arched window heads with hoods on the parlour floor and square heads above: the storey hierarchy is the fastest identification
The cornice line is continuous across the whole row; a break in cornice height means either a later infill or a different builder
Stoop of six to ten risers with cast-iron rails and newels, and an areaway with an iron fence at the sidewalk
Compare with Greek Revival rows: flat lintels, lower stoops, and a plain fascia cornice with no brackets
Compare with Second Empire rows: identical body, but a visible mansard storey above the cornice

distinguished_from.difference: Same style, opposite urban condition and opposite composition. The townhouse is symmetrical, party-walled, flat-fronted, towerless, and detailed in stone; the villa is asymmetrical, freestanding, towered, and detailed in sawn wood.

Heavily overlapping in the city, and many rows are honestly both. The Renaissance Revival row is astylar and academically proportioned with a modillioned cornice; the Italianate row substitutes sawn or moulded brackets and relaxes the proportional discipline.
The mansard is the whole difference. In New York and Brooklyn entire Italianate rows were later given mansard storeys; the body below is unchanged.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by the section, not by the plan. Lot width is fixed by the party wall, so the design problem is entirely vertical: stoop height, parlour height, and the diminishing storeys above, terminated by the cornice. This is why the type repeats so well.
typical_ratios: Lot width 16 to 25 ft, depth of house 40 to 55 ft
Stoop 6 to 10 risers, lifting the parlour floor 4 to 7 ft above sidewalk
Parlour floor-to-ceiling 11 to 14 ft, diminishing 10 to 15 percent per storey above
Parlour window height to width 3:1 to 3.5:1, sill within 12 in of the floor
Cornice projection 18 to 30 in with brackets at 24 to 36 in on centre
Facade window area 30 to 40 percent of the elevation; wall always dominant
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Two or three bays per house, unequal by design: the entrance bay is narrower than the parlour bays. Across a row, the resulting rhythm is A-B-B / A-B-B repeated, which is what gives a brownstone street its characteristic beat.

massing_affinities.note: The wider double-parlour house on a corner lot.
There is no elevation on which a tower can stand in a party-wall row.

constraints.statement: The main cornice shall be continuous in height, projection, and bracket module across every house in a row, aligning across party walls within 2 in. A row whose cornice line steps house to house has failed the type regardless of the quality of any individual facade.

The parlour floor shall be raised 4 to 7 ft above sidewalk level on a stoop of 6 to 10 risers, with an exposed basement storey below. A ground-level entrance converts the type into a later English-basement or Renaissance Revival row.

test.note: Tests the parlour-floor-above-sidewalk height range (units left in ft to match the statement, as elsewhere in the corpus). The stoop's 6-10 riser count and the exposed-basement-storey clause have no matching variables and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Floor-to-floor heights shall diminish monotonically above the parlour floor by 10 to 15 percent per storey, expressed in the window heights, which shall diminish in the same proportion.

test.note: States the diminishment for the storey immediately above the parlour floor. 'Monotonically' extended to every subsequent storey-pair, and the parallel window-height-diminishment clause, stay prose -- the same coverage the english-georgian.c02 precedent uses for this variable.

constraints.statement: Arched heads with projecting hoods shall be used on the parlour floor only; upper storeys take the same arch profile with a flush moulded surround, or square heads. Hoods on every storey read as coarse.
Facade projection beyond the building line shall not exceed 24 in and shall be limited to a single bay window or oriel. The value of the type is the flatness and continuity of the street wall.

test.note: Tests the projection ceiling. The restriction to a single bay window or oriel (as opposed to multiple projections) has no matching count/type variable and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Irad Hawley House (Salmagundi Club), 47 Fifth Avenue
exemplars.note: The last surviving single-family Italianate brownstone mansion on lower Fifth Avenue, in continuous use by the Salmagundi Club since 1917.

exemplars.name: Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace, 28 East 20th Street
exemplars.note: Original brownstone of 1848 demolished 1916 and reconstructed 1919-23 by Theodate Pope Riddle from photographs and the surviving adjoining twin; a documented reconstruction rather than an original fabric example, and cited here for the interior sequence.

exemplars.name: Brooklyn Heights Historic District brownstone rows (Willow, Hicks, and Remsen Streets)
exemplars.note: Speculative Italianate rows of roughly 1850-1870; New York City's first designated historic district, 1965. Cited as a block-scale exemplar because the type's achievement is collective rather than individual.

sources: Charles Lockwood, Bricks and Brownstone: The New York Row House 1783-1929 (1972)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Landmarks Preservation Commission, Brooklyn Heights Historic District Designation Report (1965)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and the node's own hard constraint (c01) states the case for it directly: the main cornice must be continuous in height, projection and bracket module across every house in a row, aligning within 2 in across party walls - a street-scale discipline this pack's single-bay module and pier-width rules are built to enforce. This is the one Italianate node in the batch whose composition is genuinely classical-regular rather than picturesque, which is why it binds this pack instead of facade-picturesque.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the glass-light module of the arched parlour-floor sash and the diminishing square-headed sash above it, tied to the same 10-15 percent diminution the node's own c03 requires.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the door and the storey-based sizing rule beneath the parlour-floor arched surround, which per the node's own diagnostic tells receives 'projecting moulded hoods or full architrave surrounds' while upper storeys drop to a flush surround or a square head - the storey-differentiated treatment this pack's head-datum-per-storey discipline expects.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and a direct numeric match to the node's own hard constraint c03: 'floor-to-floor heights shall diminish monotonically above the parlour floor by 10 to 15 percent per storey.' The section, not the plan, is the whole design problem here - the pack's storey module is the type's real governing dimension.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the double-parlour interior - the pack's pedestal:field:entablature wall division fits a parlour floor of 11-14 ft ceilings (the node's own figure) directly, and the row's shared millwork order (one set of parts bought for the whole speculative row, per the node's own long description) is exactly the kind of coherent, repeatable classical trim family this pack encodes.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Bound optional because the type's defining material is brownstone ashlar, which this pack does not govern; it applies on the pressed-brick or brick-with-brownstone-trim examples the node's own defining_characteristics also allow, where the coursing module sets window-head and belt-course lines the way it does on any American brick front of the period.

Judgment binding: not in the pack's own applies_to. The double parlour is a long fixed-width room set by the party wall rather than a room chosen to a harmonic shape, and the node's own governing_logic is explicit that 'lot width is fixed by the party wall, so the design problem is entirely vertical' - a measured, constraint-derived room in exactly the sense this pack (rather than room-harmonic's chosen ratios) records.

medieval-british.name: Medieval British

description.short: Norman masonry, English Gothic, and the timber-framed hall — the substrate every later British style either extended or rebelled against.
description.long:
The medieval inheritance in Britain is structural before it is stylistic: thick walls and round arches from Normandy, the pointed arch and its structural consequences from the twelfth century onward, and a parallel domestic tradition of oak framing that has almost nothing to do with either.

The domestic line matters most here. The open hall with its screens passage, the jettied upper floor, the cruck and box frame — these persist in ordinary building for centuries after the great churches stop being built, cross the Atlantic in the seventeenth century, and reappear as a fashion in the nineteenth.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing masonry and oak box framing as two parallel construction cultures
The hall with screens passage as the governing domestic diagram
Steep roofs, small openings, and prominent chimney stacks
Craft transmission by guild and apprenticeship rather than by book

eclectic-revivals.name: Eclectic Revivals

description.short: The period-revival era, in which professionally trained architects reproduced historical styles with increasing archaeological accuracy — and gave American suburbia its permanent vocabulary.
description.long:
Every style in this family claims a historical ancestor while descending from something else entirely: Beaux-Arts professional training, the measured-drawing and architectural-photography culture of the 1890s onward, and the millwork catalog. The gap between what these styles claim and where they actually come from is the most important fact about them, and the reason the taxonomy needs separate `references` and `descends_from` edges.

Accuracy increases sharply after about 1915, as measured drawings of colonial buildings circulate in portfolios like the White Pine Series. Early Colonial Revival is a free interpretation at exaggerated scale; late Colonial Revival is nearly a reproduction. A builder needs to know which one is being asked for, and the distinction is invisible if the taxonomy stops at the style name.

This is also where the contemporary American production-home vocabulary actually comes from. Almost every traditional plan sold today is a descendant of something in this family rather than of anything genuinely colonial.

defining_characteristics: Historical accuracy as an explicit and increasing professional value
Beaux-Arts compositional training applied to borrowed vocabularies
Photography, measured drawings, and portfolios as the transmission medium
Systematic departure from the model in scale, storey height, and bay width
The origin of nearly all current American traditional production housing

gothic-revival-american.name: Gothic Revival (American)

revival_periods.note: Collegiate and ecclesiastical Gothic continue in masonry under Cram, Goodhue, and Klauder long after the domestic mode dies; that stream is academic and archaeological, not picturesque, and is a different animal from the wooden Rural Gothic.

geography.hearth: Hudson Valley, New York

lineage.note: Real transmission, and entirely by print: Loudon's Encyclopaedia of Cottage, Farm and Villa Architecture (1833) reached Davis and Downing directly, and Pugin supplied the moral vocabulary. No craft lineage crossed the Atlantic with it.

The claimed ancestor. American builders quoted the label, the pointed arch, and the tracery silhouette while building in balloon-framed pine with sawn boards. Nothing about the structural system descends from English Gothic.
The actual building practice. The same carpenters, the same pattern-book habit, the same frame, the same millwork suppliers; only the plates changed.

Downing's explicit polemic: the white temple was cold, foreign, aristocratic, and a lie about how Americans lived. The Gothic cottage was to be warm, Christian, domestic, and honest about its irregular plan.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The first American style built for emotional and moral effect rather than for correctness, in which steep gables, bargeboards, and pointed windows were sawn out of pine by machine and sold as an argument about how a family should live.
description.long:
American Gothic Revival is a wooden style wearing a stone style's clothes, and its interest begins exactly there. In England the Gothic Revival could plausibly claim descent from surviving medieval fabric; in the United States there was nothing to descend from, so the style arrived as an idea in a book and had to be manufactured. Alexander Jackson Davis built the first serious example at Glen Ellen in 1832 and the canonical one at Lyndhurst in 1838; Andrew Jackson Downing, a nurseryman from Newburgh with no architectural training and an extraordinary prose gift, converted Davis's drawings into a mass-market program through Cottage Residences (1842) and The Architecture of Country Houses (1850). Within a decade the pointed gable and the sawn bargeboard were available to anyone in the country who could read a plate and hire a carpenter.

The enabling technology is the whole story, and it is worth stating as mechanism rather than as atmosphere. Balloon framing, developed in Chicago in the 1830s, replaced the mortised heavy timber frame with a cage of light sawn studs nailed together; machine-cut nails, cheap from about 1830, made nailing an economical substitute for joinery; the steam-powered scroll saw and the circular saw made a linear foot of pierced and cusped board cost pennies rather than a day of a joiner's life; and the railroad delivered that board, and the sash and the finials, from a mill in Albany to a village in Michigan. Before this convergence, an irregular plan with three unequal gables was punitively expensive, because every additional corner was a set of hand-cut joints. After it, irregularity was nearly free. Gothic Revival is the first style in history to be produced by cheap complexity, and every style downstream of it in this branch inherits that condition.

Downing's argument for all this was frankly moral and should not be softened into taste. He held that a house shapes the character of the people inside it, that the symmetrical classical box expressed a rigidity and a pride foreign to domestic affection, and that a house whose form follows the irregular facts of family life, whose vertical lines lift the eye, and whose veranda mediates between hearth and landscape, would make its inhabitants better. He wrote about the vine on the porch and the bay window in the parlour as instruments of moral improvement, and hundreds of thousands of Americans believed him. This conviction, that architecture forms character, is the load-bearing idea of the entire Victorian century in America, and it is the reason the styles that follow escalate rather than settle.

To stand before a good Rural Gothic cottage is to be worked on by verticals. Board-and-batten siding runs the eye up the wall without a single horizontal to rest on; the gable pitch is so steep that the roof reads as the dominant fact of the building; the bargeboard hangs from the verge like frozen lace and casts a moving shadow pattern across the wall all afternoon. Inside, the effect inverts. The rooms are low, small-windowed by later standards, and dim, the diamond-paned casement throws a lattice of light across the floor, and the deep veranda that looked so generous from the drive turns the parlour into a cave. It is a style that promises the landscape and then keeps you slightly withdrawn from it, which is a fair summary of what the American picturesque actually wanted.

defining_characteristics: Steeply pitched roof, 12:12 or greater, with the gable as the governing compositional element
Pointed or lancet openings in the principal gable, and label or drip mouldings over the heads
Sawn bargeboard or vergeboard applied to the rake, with a pierced repeating pattern
Vertical board-and-batten siding, or, in masonry examples, an insistently vertical fenestration rhythm
Irregular, additive plan generated by room use rather than by symmetry, with the elevation following the plan
Clustered or diagonally set chimney stacks carried well above the ridge
A veranda or porch treated as a permanent part of the composition rather than as an appendage
diagnostic_tells: If the roof pitch is steeper than 12:12 and the siding runs vertically, it is Gothic Revival and not Italianate, which is always low-pitched and horizontally sided
Bargeboard on the rake with no bracket under the eave: Gothic Revival. Brackets under a wide eave with no bargeboard: Italianate
A pointed window in the gable of an otherwise plain farmhouse is Carpenter Gothic, not Gothic Revival proper; look for whether the plan is irregular
Label mouldings that stop with square returns rather than continuing as a string course distinguish it from the Tudor Revival of the 1920s
Gothic Revival chimneys are tall, clustered, and expressive; Greek Revival chimneys are hidden in the gable end

distinguished_from.difference: Same carpenters, same frame, opposite argument. Greek Revival is symmetrical, horizontal, white, and low-pitched, with the entablature as the governing line; Gothic Revival is asymmetrical, vertical, coloured in earth tones on Downing's explicit instruction, and governed by the roof.

Both are Downing products published in the same books, and both use irregular massing, but Italianate is horizontal, low-pitched, round-arched, and bracketed, while Gothic Revival is vertical, steep, pointed, and bargeboarded. The two almost never mix on one building.

Tudor Revival (1890-1940) is masonry-minded, uses half-timbering and casement groups, and derives from measured English precedent; American Gothic Revival is wood-minded, uses board-and-batten and sawn ornament, and derives from a printed idea.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Not proportional. The composition is governed by silhouette hierarchy: a dominant gable, subordinate gables of unequal width, and a chimney group that completes the outline against the sky. Downing's own instruction was to judge the design in profile against the landscape before judging any elevation.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 12:12 to 18:12; below 12:12 the style fails
Window height to width 2.5:1 to 3.5:1, taller than any preceding American style
Verge overhang 12 to 24 in, deep enough to shadow the bargeboard
Principal gable width 1.4 to 2.0 times the width of the largest subordinate gable
Chimney height above ridge 3 to 6 ft
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and non-repeating. Bays are generated by rooms; a three-gable elevation may have three different bay widths and no two window heads at the same height.

massing_affinities.note: The workhorse of the Downing cottage: a steep gabled block with a lower wing and the veranda in the reentrant angle.
The villa scale, where the plan is genuinely irregular and the section varies.
The vernacular substrate that receives a central gable and a pointed window and becomes a Gothic Revival farmhouse.
Urban and masonry examples only; the symmetry works against the style.
Gothic Revival needs a silhouette, and a party-wall row denies it one.

constraints.statement: Principal roof pitch shall be not less than 12:12. Below this the gable ceases to dominate the composition and the building reads as Carpenter Gothic ornament applied to a folk box.

Bargeboard, where used, shall follow the full length of the rake from eave to apex without interruption, with a verge overhang of 12 to 24 in so that the board is read against shadow. A bargeboard applied only to the upper third of the rake is forbidden.

test.note: Reuses eave_projection_in for the bargeboard's verge overhang (the only overhang figure this statement states, and the same 'overhang beyond the wall face' concept the variable's own note already extends to a pent roof and viga ends). The full-length-of-rake-without-interruption clause has no matching variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Where vertical siding is used, boards shall be 8 to 12 in wide with battens 2 to 3 in wide at 12 to 16 in on centre, and the battens shall run unbroken from water table to eave. No horizontal belt course may cross the batten field.

Pointed and lancet heads shall be confined to the principal gable, the entry, and the stair window, and shall not exceed 30 percent of the openings on any elevation. Universal pointed heads produce a church, not a house.

Body colour shall be a landscape tone (fawn, drab, grey, straw) with trim two to three values darker, per Downing's explicit instruction in The Architecture of Country Houses. White is prohibited on the body; Downing regarded it as the principal aesthetic error of the American countryside.

exemplars.name: Lyndhurst
exemplars.note: Alexander Jackson Davis for William Paulding, 1838; nearly doubled for George Merritt in 1864-65, also by Davis. Marble, not wood, and therefore atypical, but it is the style's intellectual origin in America.

exemplars.name: Kingscote
exemplars.note: Richard Upjohn. A wooden Gothic cottage-villa; the 1880-81 dining room addition by Stanford White for McKim, Mead & White is a separate and later event.

exemplars.name: Roseland Cottage
exemplars.note: Joseph Collins Wells for Henry Chandler Bowen. Board-and-batten, still painted a saturated pink, which is itself evidence for Downing's colour argument.

exemplars.name: William J. Rotch Gothic Cottage
exemplars.note: A. J. Davis. Published by Downing in The Architecture of Country Houses as Design XXIV, A Cottage-Villa in the Rural Gothic Style, and thereby copied nationwide.

sources: Andrew Jackson Downing, The Architecture of Country Houses (1850)
Andrew Jackson Downing, Cottage Residences (1842)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: Technology and the Picturesque (1978)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. This is the style whose own governing_logic states plainly that it is 'not proportional' but governed by silhouette hierarchy - a dominant gable, subordinate gables of unequal width, a chimney group completing the outline - which is exactly this pack's dominant-mass-and-subordinate-accents method, read at the picturesque end of its range rather than the near-symmetrical end that governs its Italianate sibling.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the glass-light module and muntin section of the style's ordinary sash - the square-headed openings that make up the majority of any elevation, per the style's own constraint that pointed and lancet heads shall not exceed 30 percent of the openings on any elevation (c04). It does not reach the pointed, lancet or diamond-lattice-casement openings that carry the style's real identity, which fall outside every pack in this library - see report.

Judgment binding: not in the pack's own applies_to. The style spans a carpenter's cottage and an architect's villa, but its own interior description reads as ordinary and constrained rather than harmonically proportioned in either register - 'the rooms are low, small-windowed by later standards, and dim.' Bound at the parent because both children (carpenter-gothic and rural-gothic-villa) independently resolve to the same pack rather than to room-harmonic; see their own notes for the reasoning specific to each.

colonial-revival.name: Colonial Revival

geography.hearth: Newport and Boston

lineage.note: The claimed ancestor. Deliberately resurrected after a sixty-year gap, and known at first only through anecdote, ruin, and bad engraving.
Quoted for the seventeenth-century phase - overhangs, pendants, clustered chimneys - by architects who had never framed one.
Source of the fanlight, the elliptical entry, and the attenuated Adamesque colonnette that the revival uses far more freely than the Federal period did.
The actual line of practice. The same Newport and Boston offices, the same clients, the same draughtsmen; the plan loosens and the wall tightens, and the result is called Colonial.
Classical trim grafted onto Victorian massing is the immediate precursor; Colonial Revival is what happens when the massing finally submits to the trim.
Ecole training in composition, in the parti, and above all in the habit of measuring and redrawing precedent.
Explicitly framed by its promoters as a corrective to Victorian excess: order, whiteness, and ancestry against spindlework and polychromy.

description.short: The first and longest-running American revival, in which Beaux-Arts-trained offices and millwork catalogs recomposed a half-remembered Georgian and Federal vocabulary into houses larger, looser, and more emphatic than anything the colonies ever built.
description.long:
Colonial Revival is not Colonial, and the distance between the two is the whole point of the style. It begins in the 1880s as free invention: architects who had grown up with Queen Anne massing take a Georgian door surround, a modillioned cornice, and a Palladian window, and hang them on a cubic or rambling body that no eighteenth-century builder would recognize. Sash grows, ceilings rise, entrances swell to two or three times their historical size, and the elements are assembled by feel. After about 1915 the style changes character. Measured drawings begin to circulate in quantity - the White Pine Series of Architectural Monographs runs from 1915, the Georgian Period portfolios were already in the office, and by the 1930s Colonial Williamsburg supplies a whole vetted catalog of profiles - and the revival becomes correct. Early Colonial Revival is a free interpretation at exaggerated scale; late Colonial Revival is an accurate copy at exaggerated scale. For anyone specifying parts, that break around 1915 is the single most useful fact in the branch.

The conditions that produced it were only partly architectural. The 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia put a fabricated 'New England Kitchen' in front of ten million visitors and made the colonial past a consumable image. The following summer McKim, Mead, Bigelow and White toured the old towns of the New England coast sketching doorways, and the profession acquired a subject. Simultaneously architecture was professionalizing: the AIA, the first university programs, the Ecole-trained partner as a status good, and a drawing culture in which precedent circulated as photograph and measured plate rather than as a carpenter's memory. Underneath ran two economic engines - the millwork catalog, which made a correct Ionic pilaster a shipping-crate item, and the streetcar suburb, which needed a house type that read as established on a lot cleared eighteen months earlier. Underneath that ran anxiety. Between 1880 and 1920 immigration remade American cities, and a style that advertised descent from Anglo-Dutch settlers was doing legible social work for the people who bought it. The Colonial Revival house is, among other things, a claim about who belongs.

What the buyer was purchasing was continuity, and the purchase was sincere. A family three generations off the farm and one generation into salaried work could buy, for the price of a mortgage, a house that asserted an ancestry it did not have. This is why the style is so durable and why it survives every modernist attack: it is not a taste, it is a form of respectability. It also explains the style's peculiar tolerance for inaccuracy. Nobody minded that the entrance was too big, because the entrance was the argument. The parts that carry the claim - door surround, cornice, shutter, fanlight, small-paned sash - are elaborated far past their historical importance, while the parts that carry no claim - rear elevations, service wings, later additions - are left plain and are usually the most honestly built parts of the house.

Standing in front of a good one, the effect is of a house that is calmer than its neighbors and slightly too large for its own gestures. The wall is broad and quiet, painted white or clapboarded in a single tone, and the eye is pulled straight to the door, which is doing all the work: pilasters, an entablature, a pediment, and glass around three sides of the leaf. The windows are generous and regular and the second storey sits down firmly rather than floating. Inside, the plan is modern - a real entry hall, a stair that turns rather than winding around a chimney, radiators instead of a hearth in every room - and the trim is thinner and crisper than any hand-planed original, because it came off a shaper in Grand Rapids. The house feels less like a survival than like a very good memory of one, which is exactly what it is.

defining_characteristics: Symmetrical or near-symmetrical primary facade on an odd bay count, with the entrance centered and given the greatest architectural emphasis on the building
An entry assembly of pilasters or engaged columns with an entablature, pediment, or portico, plus fanlight and/or sidelights - larger and more elaborate than any colonial precedent
Double-hung sash in a regular repeating rhythm, multi-light in at least the upper unit, with vertical alignment maintained between storeys
Side-gable or hipped roof carrying a continuous classical cornice with modillions, dentils, or a plain bed moulding, returned at the rake
Machine-milled classical trim of catalog origin rather than site-shaped profiles, applied to a balloon- or platform-framed wall
Storey heights, plan depth, and overall bulk substantially exceeding the eighteenth-century models being quoted
diagnostic_tells: The entrance is the largest well-made element on the facade. On a genuine Georgian house it is among the smallest.
Sash runs 6/6, 8/8, or 6/1 with muntins 7/8 in. or wider in flat, uniform glass; eighteenth-century sash runs 9/9 or 12/12 with muntins nearer 5/8 in. and visibly irregular glass.
Cornice returns are short decorative stubs applied to the gable end rather than the full eaves carried around a framed roof.
Shutters are roughly half the width they would need to be to close, and are screwed flat to the siding without pintles or holdbacks.
Pre-1915 examples show oversized openings in undersized walls and freely invented detail; post-1915 examples reverse both, as measured drawings and Williamsburg profiles reach the office.
Anything with an attached garage, a sunroom wing, or a picture window is Colonial Revival by definition - the colonies had none of these.

distinguished_from.difference: The original is smaller in every dimension, has thinner glass in more and narrower lights, keeps its entry modest and its cornice shallow, and was framed and trimmed by hand on site. The revival is a machine-trimmed frame house wearing an amplified version of the original's face.

Free Classic keeps irregular Victorian massing, corner towers, and varied wall textures and merely swaps spindlework for classical columns. Colonial Revival disciplines the massing itself into a symmetrical box or a hipped block.
Neoclassical Revival puts a colossal portico of two-storey columns across the centre or the whole facade. Colonial Revival keeps its portico to one storey, or omits it entirely for a door surround.

proportional_system.governing_logic: A nominal classical order taken from a millwork catalog rather than derived from a module. The facade is set out by bay count and by the stock dimensions of purchasable trim; proportion is checked by eye against published plates rather than computed.
typical_ratios: Five bays wide by two storeys is the reference case; seven bays on large examples, three on the side-hall type
Storey heights 9'0"-10'0" first floor and 8'6"-9'0" second - roughly a foot more per floor than eighteenth-century practice
Window openings 3'0" x 5'6" to 3'4" x 6'0", about 15-20 percent greater in area than the Georgian originals they quote
Total cornice depth 12-18 in., near 1/20 of the wall height, against 8-12 in. on genuine colonial work
Wall area to opening area roughly 4:1 before 1915, tightening toward 5:1 or 6:1 afterwards
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Odd bay count with the centre bay widened for the entrance. Bays spaced 9'0"-11'0" on centre, noticeably wider than the 7'0"-8'0" rhythm set by hand-hewn eighteenth-century framing, which is why revival facades read as slack where originals read as taut.

massing_affinities.note: The default. Two rooms deep, centre passage, five bays, side-gable roof.
The urban and narrow-lot version; three bays with the entry to one side.
Characteristic of the free early phase, 1890-1915, when a hipped cube carried colonial trim.
Overlaps heavily with dutch-colonial-revival; see that node.
Post-1935 builder variant; see garrison-revival.
Reserved for large architect-designed examples on generous sites.

constraints.statement: The entry surround must be dimensioned for a door leaf of 3'0" x 6'8" to 3'0" x 7'0". Flanking pilasters not wider than 8 in.; a broken or swan's-neck pediment not wider than 6'0" overall; sidelights not wider than 12 in. each. A surround set out for an 8'0" leaf reads as commercial and voids the style.

test.note: Tests the door leaf width, which the statement states as a fixed 3'0" (unlike the leaf height, which is a 6'8"-7'0" range). Pilaster width (<=8in), pediment overall width (<=6'0", no matching vocabulary variable -- an entry-surround-width variable distinct from door_opening_width_ft is missing), and sidelight width (<=12in each) all lack vocabulary variables and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Shutters, where used, must each equal half the sash width and the full sash height, be hung on offset pintles with functioning holdbacks, and be capable of closing over the opening. Panels narrower than half the opening, or fixed flat to the wall, are forbidden.

test.note: Hardware (offset pintles, holdbacks) and functional closability are qualitative and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Second-storey window jambs must align with first-storey jambs within 2 in. of centreline, and head heights must be constant across each storey. Vertical misalignment is the fastest disqualifier in the whole style.

test.note: 'Head heights must be constant across each storey' is the statement's other clause and has no numeric tolerance stated; stays prose.

constraints.statement: A cornice return is permitted only where the eave carries a full classical cornice of at least 10 in. projection continuing around the corner. A return applied to a bare fascia is forbidden.

test.note: The conditional logic ('a return is permitted only where...') is a permission rule, not a second numeric fact, and stays prose.

constraints.statement: No garage door on the symmetrical primary facade. Place the garage on a subordinate wing whose face is set back at least 8'0" from the main block and whose ridge is at least 2'0" below the main ridge.

exemplars.name: H. A. C. Taylor House
exemplars.note: McKim, Mead & White. The canonical first fully realised Colonial Revival house; symmetrical cubic block, one-storey Ionic entry portico, flanking Palladian windows. Demolished 1952.

exemplars.name: Hill-Stead
exemplars.note: Theodate Pope Riddle with McKim, Mead & White. Free phase at its most confident: a colossal portico and a rambling plan under an ostensibly colonial skin.

exemplars.name: Governor's Palace (reconstruction)
exemplars.note: Perry, Shaw & Hepburn. Not a revival house but the instrument of the accuracy phase - it supplied the measured profiles that disciplined the style after 1930.

exemplars.name: Dr. Glenn R. Frye House
exemplars.note: Two-storey stone Colonial Revival with frame wing; a competent late-phase example of the type as built for professionals rather than magnates. NRHP 2009.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
William B. Rhoads, The Colonial Revival (1977)
Richard Guy Wilson, The Colonial Revival House (2004)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)
The White Pine Series of Architectural Monographs (1915-1940)

proportion_packs.note: Gibbs is the direct source: the node's own lineage records georgian-colonial-american as the claimed ancestor at weight 1.0, and Gibbs's A Book of Architecture is the specific text McKim, Mead, Bigelow and White were sketching from on their 1877 New England tour and that the White Pine Series and Colonial Williamsburg later disciplined into a documented catalog. IMPORTANT CAVEAT the node's own proportional_system states directly: unlike georgian-colonial-american, here 'the order is taken from a millwork catalog rather than derived from a module... proportion is checked by eye against published plates rather than computed.' Bound as primary because it still supplies the vocabulary for the entrance and cornice, but its governing rigor is real only in the post-1915 phase; pre-1915 work applies it freely and at exaggerated scale, per the node's own diagnostic tells.
The plainer everyday order, for the eave cornice and the many side-hall and foursquare examples that never carry a full Ionic frontispiece. Bound at the same reduced rigor as the primary order above.

Governs the composed elevation: the odd-bay rule the style keeps even where it invents freely, the ranking of horizontals, and the double-square check. The node's own constraint c03 (vertical alignment of storeys) and c04 (cornice returns require a full running cornice) are this pack's territory directly.

The door and window rectangle, and specifically the single-head-datum rule that the node's own hard constraint c03 restates as 'the fastest disqualifier in the whole style.' The node's c01 (entry surround dimensioned for a 3'0" x 6'8"-7'0" leaf, pilasters not wider than 8 in) is this pack's door_surround and entry_door slots read almost verbatim.

Governs the measured glazing pattern the node's diagnostic tells hinge on: 6/6, 8/8 or 6/1 sash with muntins 7/8 in. or wider, against the 9/9 or 12/12 with 5/8 in. muntins of the genuine original -- that comparison is exactly this pack's business.

The node's own typical_ratios state storey heights 'roughly a foot more per floor than eighteenth-century practice' (9'0"-10'0" first, 8'6"-9'0" second) -- a real but looser graduation than the parent style's, which this pack records as a band rather than a fixed ratio.

The interior wall-section family, run in the same profile family as the parent Georgian style but off a machine shaper rather than a hand plane -- the node's own description is explicit that the trim is 'thinner and crisper than any hand-planed original, because it came off a shaper in Grand Rapids.'

Primary on the masonry examples (the node's own exemplar, the Dr. Glenn R. Frye House, is two-storey stone) and absent on the far more numerous frame-and-clapboard ones, exactly as on georgian-colonial-american. Bound optional for that reason.

The node's own bay_rhythm states the diagnosis directly: bays run 9'0"-11'0" on centre against the 7'0"-8'0" of hand-hewn eighteenth-century framing, 'which is why revival facades read as slack where originals read as taut.' Bound low and optional because the style, unlike cape-cod-revival, does not try to reproduce the historical bay -- it is recorded here as the diagnostic of the very slackness the style is built from.

The node's own description states the plan is 'modern' -- a real entry hall, a stair that turns -- composed by a Beaux-Arts-trained office rather than accumulated, which is exactly the harmonic room-system's domain. Applies to the principal rooms of the high-style and post-1915 examples; the smaller catalog houses are proportioned more loosely, as the style's own 'checked by eye' proportional_system statement concedes.

octagon-house.name: Octagon House

geography.hearth: Fishkill, New York

lineage.note: Genuine blending. The octagon is a plan thesis with no ornamental vocabulary of its own, so nearly every built example wears Italianate dress: bracketed eaves, a cupola, round-arched windows, and a wrapping veranda.
The actual carpentry, trim profiles, and door and window stock of the earlier octagons are straight Greek Revival millwork; Fowler proposed a geometry, not a detail set.
Fowler's argument was explicitly against the rectangular house as wasteful of wall, of heat, and of steps, and against the classical box as an inherited habit nobody had audited.
