description.short: An eight-sided house type promoted by the phrenologist Orson Squire Fowler in A Home for All (1848) on the argument that an octagon encloses more floor area per foot of wall than a rectangle, and adopted by several thousand American builders before it died of its own geometry.
description.long:
The octagon house is the only node in this branch that was generated by an argument rather than by a use, and it is therefore the most instructive one for anybody building a design system. Orson Squire Fowler was a phrenologist, a lecturer, a publisher of self-improvement literature, and an enthusiast of the sort the 1840s produced in quantity. His book A Home for All, or the Gravel Wall and Octagon Mode of Building appeared in 1848 and was reissued and expanded through the 1850s. Its case was quantitative and, as far as it went, correct: a regular octagon encloses about 21 percent more floor area than a square of the same perimeter, so it uses less wall for the same house; it presents more of its surface to sun and breeze; interior travel distances are shorter; and, in Fowler's second enthusiasm, it could be built by unskilled hands in lime-and-gravel concrete rather than in framed timber or laid brick. Several thousand were built between 1850 and 1860, concentrated in New York, New England, the upper Midwest, and Northern California.

It could not grow, and the reason is worth being candid about. Every economy Fowler identified is real, and every one of them is purchased by a geometric cost he did not price. Furniture, stairs, beds, tables, and rugs are rectangular, and human beings arrange rooms rectangularly; an octagon delivers its saved area as eight triangular residues in the corners, which become closets, or awkward passages, or nothing. Roof framing over eight hips converges on a point that wants to be a cupola whether the plan wants one or not. Additions are effectively impossible, because there is no elevation to extend without destroying the figure, and the American house of the period grew constantly. Within a decade the type was finished, not because taste turned but because the argument was incomplete.

That failure mode is exactly the one a kit-of-parts platform derived from first principles is exposed to. Fowler optimised a single legible metric, wall length per unit of enclosed area, and treated everything he had not measured as free. The traditional styles surrounding him in this taxonomy were optimised by nothing at all, only by two centuries of selection under real constraints, and they encode dozens of unstated accommodations to furniture, expansion, framing, weather, and habit that no closed-form argument recovers. A design system should be able to generate the octagon, because the octagon is real, and should also be able to say why almost nobody wanted a second one.

Inside a good one the experience is genuinely strange and rather pleasant. Light arrives from three or four directions in every principal room, so the quality of illumination is soft and shadowless in a way rectangular rooms of the period never achieve; the central stair rises to a cupola that pulls hot air out of the whole house in August, which was Fowler's other genuinely good idea; and the wrapping veranda means there is always a shaded side. What you cannot do is put a sofa against a wall without thinking about it, and that turns out to be enough.

defining_characteristics: A regular or near-regular eight-sided plan as the whole of the building's parti
A central vertical core, either a stair or a chimney stack, serving all eight sectors
A low eight-hipped roof converging on a flat deck or a cupola
A veranda or piazza wrapping a majority of the faces
Rooms arranged radially around the core, with triangular residual spaces used as closets, stairs, or service
Applied ornament borrowed wholesale from the prevailing style of the moment, usually Italianate, since the type supplies none of its own
diagnostic_tells: Eight exterior walls; there is no near-miss identification available
A cupola or belvedere at the roof apex, present in the large majority of surviving examples because the eight hips demand a termination
Wall construction is frequently lime-and-gravel concrete, board-formed in lifts, per Fowler's second thesis; look for horizontal form lines under the stucco
The ornament will date the house rather than the type, and it will almost always be Italianate bracketwork
Veranda runs continuously across five or more faces, breaking only at the entry

distinguished_from.difference: Nearly all octagons are Italianate in dress, so the two are not alternatives. Italianate is a style, the octagon is a massing thesis; a taxonomy that treats them as competing labels will misfile every surviving example.

Both are 1840s pattern-book propositions sold with a reformist argument, but Downing argued from feeling and moral influence and Fowler argued from arithmetic. The Gothic cottage is irregular by conviction; the octagon is regular by calculation.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Purely geometric, and uniquely so in this branch: a regular octagon, with everything else derived from the side length. The design is closed-form, which is both its appeal and its limitation.
typical_ratios: Side length 12 to 20 ft, giving an inscribed diameter of about 29 to 48 ft
Wall height 1.0 to 1.4 times the side length per storey
Cupola width 0.25 to 0.35 of the inscribed diameter
Veranda depth 7 to 10 ft, uniform on every face it crosses
Roof pitch 4:12 to 7:12 on all eight hips
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: One or two openings per face, identically placed on every face, producing an eightfold rotational rhythm with a single break at the entry.

massing_affinities.note: The type is the massing; there is no other reading.
Only as the central cupola or belvedere, never as an offset asymmetric tower.
The square-cored octagon with canted corners is a common cheat that gives up most of the geometric claim.
The octagon cannot be added to; picturesque growth destroys the figure that justifies the type.

constraints.statement: The plan shall be a regular octagon with all eight sides equal within 5 percent, side length between 12 and 20 ft. Irregular or elongated octagons forfeit the wall-economy argument that is the type's only justification.

A central core, being either the principal stair or a stack of flues, shall be provided and shall serve all storeys. Without it the eight-hip roof has nothing to bear on and the plan has no organising element.

No single room shall occupy more than three of the eight sides, and each principal room shall have openings on at least two faces. This is what buys the cross-light and cross-ventilation the type exists for.
A veranda shall run continuously across not fewer than five faces at a uniform depth of 7 to 10 ft, breaking only at the entrance face.

test.note: Tests the veranda-depth range. Coverage across not fewer than five of the octagon's eight faces, breaking only at the entrance, is a face-count-coverage fact with no matching variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Additions are prohibited on the primary figure. Where more space is required, build a detached or breezeway-linked wing; extending one face of the octagon destroys the type.

exemplars.name: Armour-Stiner (Octagon) House
exemplars.note: Built 1859-60 for Paul J. Armour on Fowler's principles; the encircling dome added and enlarged by Joseph Stiner 1872-76. The only known fully domed octagonal house.

exemplars.name: Longwood
exemplars.note: Samuel Sloan, designed 1859, construction halted by the Civil War in 1861 and never resumed above the basement storey. The largest octagonal house in the United States, and an Oriental-Italianate hybrid rather than a Fowler house.

exemplars.name: McElroy Octagon House
exemplars.note: Built 1860-61 by William C. McElroy at Gough and Union Streets; concrete construction, four rooms per floor around a central winding stair.

sources: Orson Squire Fowler, A Home for All, or the Gravel Wall and Octagon Mode of Building (1848; expanded 1853)
Carl F. Schmidt, The Octagon Fad (1958)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and the one pack in the whole library that shares this style's actual intellectual method: both are closed-form geometric arguments rather than accumulated custom. Fowler's octagon and Palladio's seven room shapes are both derived from a single module by rule rather than measured from what building stock happens to contain, which is exactly the property the node's own text singles out ('the design is closed-form, which is both its appeal and its limitation'). Governs the individual room, with the important caveat the node's own text states plainly: the eight-sided plan delivers its saved area as triangular residues in the corners that neither this pack nor any rectangular room-shape system models.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the storey-based sizing of the one or two openings per face; the node's own bay_rhythm ('one or two openings per face, identically placed on every face') is a stricter, rotationally-repeated version of this pack's ordinary rhythm.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, though it governs the applied dress rather than the plan: the node's own text is explicit that the octagon 'supplies no ornamental vocabulary of its own' and that nearly every surviving example borrows its cornice, brackets and cupola wholesale from Italianate. Bound for that borrowed elevation treatment, not for the underlying geometry, which is strict-bilateral and eightfold-rotational rather than picturesque in the pack's own sense.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The earlier and plainer octagons carry Greek Revival millwork directly ('the actual carpentry, trim profiles, and door and window stock of the earlier octagons are straight Greek Revival millwork,' per the node's own lineage record), which this pack covers; the later Italianate-bracketed examples are dressed by whatever trim the borrowed style itself supplies.

queen-anne-british.name: Queen Anne (British)

revival_periods.note: The style's brick-and-white-paint grammar is absorbed into Edwardian neo-Georgian in Britain and into Colonial Revival in America, where its picturesque half becomes the American Queen Anne.

geography.hearth: Kensington, Chelsea and Bedford Park in London, and the Sussex and Surrey Weald for its country work

lineage.note: Direct office descent. Richard Norman Shaw, Philip Webb and William Morris all passed through G. E. Street's Gothic office, and Shaw and Nesfield were trained entirely in Gothic practice. The plan-driven asymmetry, the tall chimneys and the ethic of visible construction come straight from there.

And equally a rejection of it. By 1870 High Victorian Gothic looked grim, ecclesiastical and unlivable; Queen Anne answered with red brick, white paint, sunlight, sash windows and secular good humour. The same men made both arguments within a decade.

The name is a misnomer and everyone involved knew it. What the style actually quotes is the ordinary English brick house of roughly 1660-1720 — the Wren-era vicarage and merchant's house — for its sash windows, its rubbed-brick aprons, its hipped roofs and its white-painted joinery.

The shaped and scrolled gable, the tall narrow brick front and the moulded brick panel come from the Low Countries by way of the Anglo-Dutch houses of East Anglia and Kent. London's nickname for the result — Pont Street Dutch — is accurate.

Shaw's 'Old English' country work — tile-hanging, half-timbered gables, massive brick stacks, long catslide roofs — comes from close on-site study of Wealden farmhouses and cottages, and is the same investigation that produces Arts and Crafts a decade later.

description.short: The red-brick, white-painted, sunlit reaction against High Victorian Gothic: sash windows, shaped gables, tall thin chimneys and a picturesque plan, quoting an English brick vernacular that had nothing to do with Queen Anne.
description.long:
Queen Anne is the most cheerful style in British architecture and the most casually misnamed. It has almost no connection to the reign of Anne (1702-14); what its architects were actually after was the plain red-brick English house of the century between the Restoration and the Georgian codification — the sort of thing found in a cathedral close or a market town, with a hipped roof, white-painted sashes, rubbed brick over the windows and a garden. Richard Norman Shaw, W. Eden Nesfield, J. J. Stevenson and Philip Webb assembled that vocabulary in the late 1860s and 1870s and combined it, freely and without embarrassment, with Dutch shaped gables, Flemish moulded brick, sunflower and swag panels in terracotta, oriels, balconies, and — after the 1862 International Exhibition — a strong dose of Japanese detail.

The conditions were social as much as architectural. A new professional and artistic class — painters, writers, publishers, academics — wanted houses that were comfortable, well-lit, informally planned and inexpensive to run, and had no interest in the moral gloom of the Gothic Revival or the pomp of an Italianate stucco terrace. Shaw's studio-houses in Chelsea and Kensington were designed for exactly these clients, with north-lit double-height studios and rooms of irregular shape and size. Bedford Park in west London, begun in 1875 by Jonathan Carr with E. W. Godwin and then Shaw as architects, took the same idea to a whole suburb: modest brick houses with tile-hung gables, white-painted balconies and existing trees preserved between them. It is the first garden suburb, the direct ancestor of Hampstead, Letchworth and every leafy suburb in the English-speaking world, and it was widely mocked at the time.

What it reacted against is unusually easy to name: its own practitioners' previous work. The move from Gothic to Queen Anne is a move from ecclesiastical to domestic, from stone to brick, from dark to light, from moral argument to comfort, and from the pointed arch to the sash window. What it kept from Gothic was the important part — the plan drawn first, the massing following the plan, and construction left visible.

A Queen Anne house is a pleasure to be in, which cannot be said of most Victorian architecture. Brick is warm red and finely jointed, woodwork is white, and the windows are big, small-paned in the upper sash and clear below, so the light is abundant and the view is uninterrupted at eye level. Rooms vary in size and ceiling height as their use requires; there are inglenooks, window seats, and stairs that turn around a landing with a window on it. Outside, the composition is busy but not aggressive: gables of different shapes, a projecting bay, a balcony, tall thin chimneys, and everywhere the contrast of red brick against white paint that the whole English-speaking world has been copying ever since.

defining_characteristics: Red brick, finely jointed, with rubbed and cut brick ornament — aprons, panels, pilasters, sunflower and swag reliefs — and frequently terracotta enrichment
White-painted joinery throughout: sashes, balconies, balustrades, porches and eaves, in deliberate contrast to the brick
Sash windows with many small panes in the upper sash and one or two large panes below, often with margin lights and occasionally leaded
Shaped, scrolled or pedimented Dutch gables, and steep tile roofs with tall, thin, multiple chimney stacks
Picturesque asymmetrical composition generated by an informally planned interior, with oriels, bays, balconies and recessed porches
In country work ('Old English'), tile-hanging on upper storeys, half-timbered gables, catslide roofs and massive brick stacks drawn from Wealden farmhouses
Abundant daylight and a deliberate cheerfulness of colour and detail, in explicit contrast to High Victorian Gothic
diagnostic_tells: Red brick with white-painted woodwork as an absolute rule — the colour pairing is the style's fastest identification at any distance
A sash whose upper leaf is divided into six, eight or more small panes over a single-pane lower leaf: a Victorian window pretending to be a 1700 window and not quite managing it
Cut and rubbed brick sunflowers, swags and pilaster panels — the sunflower is practically the movement's trademark
Chimney stacks that are tall, thin and numerous, well out of proportion to the flues they carry, used as vertical accents in the composition
Tile-hanging on the upper storey over brick below, with the tile courses often shaped into fishscale or club patterns

distinguished_from.difference: Same architects, opposite mood. Gothic uses pointed arches, stone, structural polychromy and a moral argument; Queen Anne uses sash windows, red brick, white paint and a joke about the name. If the openings are square-headed with sashes and the woodwork is white, it is Queen Anne.

The American version keeps the asymmetry, the tall chimneys and the wraparound complexity but rebuilds it in balloon-framed timber with spindlework, patterned shingles, corner towers and full-width porches — features Shaw never used. British Queen Anne is a brick style; American Queen Anne is a wood one.

The quoted source, six generations earlier. A genuine Queen Anne house of 1710 has small-paned sashes top and bottom in a symmetrical facade, no shaped gables, no tile-hanging and no terracotta sunflowers, and its plan is a symmetrical double pile.

proportional_system.governing_logic: No applied system. Composition is picturesque and plan-driven, with proportion controlled locally: the sash, the gable and the chimney are each proportioned by precedent, and the elevation is assembled from them by eye.
typical_ratios: Sash proportion 1.7:1 to 2.2:1 height to width, upper leaf divided into 6-12 panes over a 1- or 2-pane lower leaf
Storey heights 3.0-3.6 m at ground, 2.9-3.3 m above — much less graduated than Georgian, since the composition no longer depends on it
Shaped gable width 3.0-4.5 m, apex height 0.8-1.1 of the gable width
Roof pitch 45-55 degrees in plain clay tile
Chimney stack width 450-900 mm, rising 1.5-3 m above the ridge — deliberately over-tall
Tile-hung upper storey over brick, with the change of material always at a floor level and marked by a slight oversail or a tile course
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular by intent. Windows are grouped in twos and threes where rooms need them, with wide blank brick between groups; gables and bays punctuate the front at uneven intervals, and a frontal symmetry, where it occurs, is local rather than overall.

massing_affinities.note: The Shavian country house — Cragside, Grim's Dyke — is a picturesque agglomeration composed for the oblique view.
The Bedford Park house and its countless suburban descendants: intersecting gabled volumes with a tile-hung upper storey.
The Kensington and Chelsea red-brick town house, in a terrace whose units are deliberately unlike one another — the anti-Georgian terrace.
The smaller Queen Anne rectory or dower house, symmetrical and hipped, quoting the 1700 house directly.
Nesfield and Shaw both used the gambrel and the jerkinhead, and it is one of the routes by which the form re-entered American practice.

constraints.statement: Brick must be red, finely jointed and finished with rubbed or cut brick at openings; external joinery must be painted white or off-white. Breaking the red-and-white pairing removes the style's primary identity.
Windows are square-headed sashes or casements. Pointed arches, tracery, buttresses and structural polychromy are forbidden — those belong to the style this one was formed against.
Where tile-hanging occurs it must begin at a floor level and be carried on a proper oversailing course, never start mid-storey. The material change is a construction event, not a decorative one.
Chimney stacks rise 1.5-3 m above the ridge and are grouped, thin and multiple. A single squat stack cannot carry the composition.

test.note: Converted from the source's 1.5-3 m (not a corpus unit) to ft to match chimney_height_above_ridge_ft. 'Grouped, thin and multiple' stays prose -- no vocabulary variable for chimney grouping or stack thinness.

constraints.statement: Entry must not be centred on a symmetrical front unless the whole building is a deliberate small-scale quotation of a 1700 house.

exemplars.name: Cragside
exemplars.note: Enlarged 1869-84 by Richard Norman Shaw for the armaments manufacturer William Armstrong. Old English at full stretch — half-timbered gables, immense stacks, a rambling hillside plan — and the first house in the world lit by hydroelectricity.

exemplars.name: Lowther Lodge
exemplars.note: Built 1873-75 by Shaw for William Lowther, now the Royal Geographical Society. Red brick, tall shaped gables, white sashes and rubbed-brick ornament: the style's arrival in the capital.

exemplars.name: Bedford Park
exemplars.note: Developed from 1875 by Jonathan Carr with E. W. Godwin and then Norman Shaw as architects. The first garden suburb, and the model for the entire Anglo-American leafy suburb that followed.

exemplars.name: Old Swan House
exemplars.note: Built 1875-77 by Shaw for the collector Wickham Flower. Three tall oriels on the first floor over a recessed ground storey, small-paned sashes throughout — the most refined statement of the urban manner.

sources: Mark Girouard, Sweetness and Light: The 'Queen Anne' Movement 1860-1900 (1977)
Andrew Saint, Richard Norman Shaw (1976, rev. 2010)
Mark Girouard, The Victorian Country House (1971, rev. 1979)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England: London volumes
Margaret Richardson, Architects of the Arts and Crafts Movement (1983)

proportion_packs.note: queen-anne-british is named directly in facade-picturesque's applies_to. This node's own text is explicit that the reading taken here is the picturesque one, not the 'restrained early Georgian classicism' some corpora use for British Queen Anne: governing_logic states 'No applied system. Composition is picturesque and plan-driven,' c05 forbids a centred entry except on a deliberate small-scale quotation of a 1700 house, and symmetry is recorded as 'picturesque-asymmetrical.' The pack's dominant-mass and datum-line logic — Shaw's asymmetrical Kensington and Bedford Park fronts are literally in its authority note — governs the gable, oriel, bay and porch composition directly.

Judgment binding (not in applies_to): no classical room system is appropriate given the explicit 'no applied system' text, and room-vernacular's daylight and hearth constraints are the only period-agnostic physical rules in the library that still bear on Shaw's plan-driven, irregularly sized rooms. Not a strong fit in scale — a Kensington studio-house room is not an anonymous cottage room — but the alternative, binding nothing, leaves the node with no room-scale governance at all.

Judgment binding (queen-anne-british is not in sash-light's applies_to). Bound narrowly for the sash construction mechanics — muntin proportion, the meeting-rail geometry, the shutter-leaf rule where shutters occur — since the style's own diagnostic tells describe a real sash window ('upper leaf divided into six, eight or more small panes over a single-pane lower leaf'). The pack's DATING scheme (12/12 to 6/6 by decade) does not apply here: this is a Victorian pane pattern quoting 1700 rather than a genuine 1700-1770 progression, and the note exists to flag that explicitly rather than let the dating rule misapply.

Judgment binding (queen-anne-british is not in brick-course's applies_to, whose native target is Georgian-era coursing). Bound low and optional because 'red brick, finely jointed, with rubbed and cut brick ornament' is a defining characteristic and c01 makes the red-and-white pairing a hard constraint, and Victorian imperial brick is close enough in dimension to Georgian brick that the coursing module transfers reasonably — but this is the pack's first documented use outside its native period and the fit should be treated as approximate rather than sourced.

stick-style.name: Stick Style

geography.hearth: Newport, Rhode Island

lineage.note: Direct. Downing's board-and-batten argument, that a wooden house should announce that it is wooden, is the exact premise the Stick Style takes to its conclusion; the vertical batten becomes an expressed structural grid.
Real transmission by print: Downing and Calvert Vaux published Swiss chalet designs, and the deep bracketed eave, exposed rafter, and applied gable truss come from that source.

Claimed rather than descended. The stickwork alludes to half-timbering but is thin applied board over sheathing and expresses no structural member; Scully's account of the style turns on precisely this.
The bracket and the porch post vocabulary are shared; many transitional houses are honestly both.

description.short: A short-lived wooden style of the 1860s and 1870s in which flat boards applied over the clapboard in horizontal, vertical, and diagonal bands claim to express the frame beneath, producing the most linear and least massive architecture America has built.
description.long:
The Stick Style is a specific idea carried out with unusual rigour: that a wooden building should be drawn on its own surface. Horizontal boards mark the floor lines, vertical boards mark the corners and the intervals between windows, diagonal boards fill the gable panels, and the whole elevation becomes a diagram of a frame. The diagram is a fiction. Behind the sticks is a balloon frame of two-by-four studs at sixteen inches, nailed and sheathed, which the applied boards neither reveal nor correspond to. Vincent Scully named and defined the style in 1955 and built his argument on exactly that tension, and the tension is the reason the style matters here: it is the first American attempt to make an industrial framing system legible as architecture, and it fails in an instructive way.

The enabling conditions are the same rupture that produced this whole branch, but the Stick Style responds to them more honestly than its neighbours. Balloon framing had by 1860 made the American house a nailed cage of light sawn members; machine-cut nails made the cage economic; the planing mill turned out flat surfaced board in any dimension by the thousand feet; and the railroad delivered it. Gothic Revival used that board to imitate stone tracery and Italianate used it to imitate palazzo brackets. The Stick Style used it to talk about the frame. That it talked about an imaginary frame rather than the real one is a genuine intellectual failure, but the ambition is the correct one, and it is the ambition the Craftsman movement would take up thirty years later with actual structural expression.

What it was reacting against was the mass-imitating tendency of everything around it, the wooden building pretending to be masonry. Its own aesthetic argument is that a wooden building should be light, linear, skeletal, and shadowed, and it commits to this so completely that Stick Style houses have almost no wall in the perceptual sense; they are a scaffold with infill. The style is also, unmistakably, a rich person's experiment: Richard Morris Hunt's Griswold House at Newport of 1864, Frank Furness's Physick House at Cape May of 1879. It never went mass-market, and one reason is that the stickwork has to be complete to make sense. A partial application does not read as a frame, it reads as trim, which is precisely what happened when builders tried it cheaply.

In front of one there is nothing to rest on. Every surface is subdivided by boards into panels, the eaves overhang far and are held on exposed brackets and rafter ends so the roof edge is a fringe of shadow, the porch is a lattice of posts and diagonal braces, and the whole building vibrates with line. In raking light it is extraordinary and slightly nervous; in flat noon light it can look like a house wearing a net. Inside the excitement stops abruptly: the plan is a conventional picturesque one with a hall, parlours, and a stair, and the exterior linear obsession barely enters the rooms.

defining_characteristics: Applied flat boards on the wall surface forming horizontal, vertical, and diagonal bands over clapboard or shingle infill
A gable truss or king-post ornament in every principal gable, applied rather than structural
Deep overhanging eaves on exposed brackets, purlins, or rafter tails
Steep gabled roofs with prominent cross gables and a vigorous irregular silhouette
Porches and verandas built as visible frames of posts, diagonal braces, and open rails rather than as trabeated classical structures
Wall surface subdivided into panels by the stickwork, with texture changing only at a stick band
Entirely rectilinear ornament: no turned spindles, no scrolled brackets, no curved members anywhere in the stickwork
diagnostic_tells: Straight lines only. If the applied woodwork curves, turns, or scrolls, the building has moved to Queen Anne or Eastlake
The stickwork is continuous and encircles the building; trim that stops at the front corner is Folk Victorian
Diagonals in the gable panels, forming a truss that carries nothing, is the single most reliable tell
Compared with Queen Anne, there is no dominant mass and no round tower; the Stick Style composition is a set of gables of comparable weight
The wall reads as flat panels, not as texture. Cut shingle patterning is a Queen Anne trait, not a Stick one

distinguished_from.difference: The nearest and most-confused neighbour. Stick Style is linear, rectilinear, panelised, and has no dominant mass; Queen Anne is volumetric, curvilinear, textured, and requires one mass to dominate. A spindled porch or a round tower rules out Stick Style entirely.
Descended from it and keeps its steep pitches and its wooden honesty argument, but replaces sawn pierced ornament with flat structural-looking board, and abandons pointed openings.

Exact opposites built by the same architects a decade apart, which is why Scully treated them as one book. Stick Style articulates the wall into panels of line; Shingle Style dissolves it into one continuous unbroken surface.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by the stick grid. The applied board layout establishes a rectangular field over the entire elevation, and openings, panels, and infill are sized within that grid. It is the closest thing in this branch to a modular system, though the module is decorative rather than structural.
typical_ratios: Stick boards 1x4 to 1x6 nominal, standing 3/4 to 1 in proud of the wall plane
Panel field 3 to 6 ft square between stick bands
Eave overhang 18 to 36 in on exposed brackets or rafter tails at 24 to 48 in on centre
Roof pitch 9:12 to 14:12
Porch post 5x5 to 8x8 with diagonal braces at 45 degrees, brace length 0.3 to 0.5 of post height
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: The stick grid supplies a regular rhythm across an irregular plan, as the Italianate bracket does, but it operates over the whole wall rather than only at the eave.

massing_affinities.note: Square and gabled, never round; a round tower moves the building to Queen Anne.
Some transitional 1870s houses carry both, but the mansard suppresses the gable trusses the style depends on.

constraints.statement: Stickwork shall be continuous: a horizontal band at every floor line and at the eave, vertical members at every corner and at each side of every opening group, and a diagonal or truss member in every gable field. Stickwork applied to the principal elevation only is prohibited.

All stickwork members shall be flat sawn boards 1x4 to 1x6 nominal, standing 3/4 to 1 in proud of the wall plane. No stickwork member may be turned, scrolled, chamfered on a curve, or otherwise non-rectilinear.

test.note: Reuses ornament_relief_in for stickwork's proud-of-the-wall-plane projection. The 1x4-1x6 nominal board width and the ban on turned/scrolled/curved members are cladding-dimension and member-shape facts with no matching variables and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Wall cladding shall change texture only at a stickwork band, and not more than two textures may occur on any one elevation. A texture change in the middle of a panel field is prohibited.

Eave overhang shall be 18 to 36 in and shall be carried on visible brackets, purlin ends, or rafter tails at 24 to 48 in on centre. A boxed eave with no visible support contradicts the style's entire premise.

test.note: Tests the eave-overhang range. The 24-48 in bracket/purlin/rafter-tail spacing has no matching variable and stays prose, along with the 'visible support, no boxed eave' clause.

constraints.statement: No single mass shall exceed any other by more than 30 percent in height or plan area. Stick Style composition is a balance of comparable gables; a dominant mass produces a Queen Anne house.

exemplars.name: John N. A. Griswold House (Newport Art Museum)
exemplars.note: Richard Morris Hunt; sources give the design and construction variously as 1862-64. Generally cited as the first fully developed American Stick Style building.

exemplars.name: Emlen Physick Estate
exemplars.note: Frank Furness. Oversized inverted corbelled chimneys, huge brackets, and a complete stickwork grid; the style at its most idiosyncratic. The Frank Furness attribution is traditional and not documented.

exemplars.name: Mark Twain House
exemplars.note: Edward Tuckerman Potter. Classified variously as Stick Style and as High Victorian Gothic; included with that caveat because its brick polychromy and applied timber banding show the boundary between the two.

sources: Vincent Scully, The Shingle Style and the Stick Style (1955; rev. ed. 1971)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)
Leland Roth, A Concise History of American Architecture (1979)

proportion_packs.note: Explicit in this pack's applies_to. The node's own proportional_system states the stick grid is 'the closest thing in this branch to a modular system, though the module is decorative rather than structural' — the pack's dominance rule and wing-strategy rule apply only loosely, since this node's own hard constraint (c05, soft) caps mass imbalance at 30 percent, well inside the pack's 1.35-2.5 dominance band rather than requiring it. What transfers directly is the datum discipline: the pack's two-continuous-horizontal rule matches this node's own requirement (c01) of a horizontal stick band at every floor line and at the eave, running unbroken around the building.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to. Governs light count and muntin section for the period's (1860-1895) double-hung sash; the stick grid governs the wall around the opening but not the glass within it, which this pack owns throughout the corpus.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to. An imperfect but defensible fit: the node's own hard constraint (c02) — flat sawn boards 1x4 to 1x6, standing 3/4 to 1 in proud, no turned or curved members — describes a squarer, more skeletal vocabulary than trim-craftsman's board-and-batten family, but both are carpentry-derived flat-stock systems rather than order-derived ones, and trim-craftsman is the only pack in the library built on that logic. Trim-classical's room-as-an-order derivation is the wrong family entirely for a style whose whole premise is a wooden building drawn on its own surface rather than dressed as an order.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to. Bound for the same reasoning as shingle-style and stick-style's other Victorian siblings: the node states plainly that 'the exterior linear obsession barely enters the rooms' and the plan behind the stickwork is 'a conventional picturesque one with a hall, parlours, and a stair' — an ordinary balloon-framed plan governed by span and daylight, not by a proportional treatise.

italian-villa-vernacular.name: Italian Villa Vernacular

revival_periods.note: The British Italianate villa: John Nash's Cronkhill (1802), Charles Barry's clubs and country houses, and J. C. Loudon's Encyclopaedia (1833) which put the type into the hands of every builder in the English-speaking world.

The American Italian Villa and Italianate, transmitted by A. J. Downing's Cottage Residences (1842) and The Architecture of Country Houses (1850); the bracketed eave and the campanile become national domestic property.
The second, better-informed American revival, this time with Beaux-Arts training and real trips to Italy behind it.

geography.hearth: The Florentine and Sienese hill country

lineage.note: The villa is genetically a farm. The casa padronale is the owner's wing of a working fattoria, and the earliest villas are literally converted fortified farms - Cafaggiolo, Careggi, La Petraia all keep their towers. The tile roof, the rendered mass wall, the deep reveal and the loggia all come from the farm unchanged.

The regularising influence: the arcaded loggia with real proportional arches, the string course, the graded opening, the aspiration to a compact block with a legible front. The villa takes the discipline without ever fully accepting the order system.

description.short: The Italian country house in its informal, non-treatise form: a compact rendered block with a low bracketed tile roof, an arcaded loggia and a belvedere or dovecote tower, balanced rather than symmetrical.
description.long:
This is the most influential Italian building type that no architect designed. It sits between the peasant farmhouse and the architect's villa, and it is what most Italian country houses actually are: a landowner's house on a working estate, regularised into a compact block, with a loggia to sit in, round-headed openings, a shallow hipped tile roof carried out on brackets, and very often a tower left over from a fortified predecessor or built as a dovecote and then enjoyed as a view. Nobody wrote a treatise about it. It reached the rest of the world through pictures - through the backgrounds of Italian landscape painting, through Claude and the Grand Tour, and then, decisively, through nineteenth-century pattern books. When Nash built Cronkhill in Shropshire in 1802 with a round tower and a bracketed eave, he was not quoting Palladio; he was quoting a painting of a Roman Campagna farm.

The conditions that produced it are the same agricultural economy that produced the casa colonica, seen from the other end of the contract. A fattoria - the estate headquarters administering a dozen or more poderi - needed an office, storage for the landlord's half of the harvest, a wine cellar, and rooms for a family who came out from the city in summer and at vintage. That is a farm building with better rooms in it, and its architecture is farm architecture with the arithmetic tidied: the openings brought into alignment, the block squared up, the loggia given proper arches, and the whole thing rendered and limewashed. The tower is the honest oddity. Sometimes it is genuinely defensive in origin, from the era of the casa-torre; sometimes it is a colombaia; and by the seventeenth century it is sometimes simply a belvedere, because standing above your own land in the evening is a pleasure people will pay for.

It is not reacting against anything - it predates the reaction - but it became useful in the nineteenth century precisely as a reaction. British and American architects wanted a classical vocabulary that could be composed asymmetrically, because the picturesque movement had made symmetry look stupid on a hillside, and because plans were getting more functionally specific and refusing to be forced into a rectangle. The Italian villa was the only classical thing available with an asymmetrical tower already in it. That single feature - the tower at the inner angle, off the axis, giving vertical accent without requiring a symmetrical answer on the other side - is why the type conquered the English-speaking world between 1840 and 1885 and why the American Italianate exists at all.

Standing in the loggia of one in September, the pleasures are specific and repeatable. The eave overhangs a metre on paired brackets, so the wall is in shadow and the terracotta of the underside of the tile glows orange with reflected light off the paving. The arcade frames the landscape into three or four equal pictures, and moving one step sideways swaps one picture for another. The wall is rendered and limewashed, warm ochre or a pale grey-pink, and it is not flat - the render follows the rubble under it, so the surface takes raking light in a way no modern flat render does. There is a stone bench built into the loggia wall because that is where people sit. And the tower, when you climb it, gives you the whole podere system laid out below: the vineyard rows, the cypress line up the drive, the dispersed farmhouses each on its own hill. The building is an instrument for looking at the property.

defining_characteristics: Compact, near-cubic principal block of two to three storeys under a single shallow hipped or low-gabled tile roof
Wide overhanging eave, 600-1200 mm, carried on paired or single brackets (modiglioni) with an exposed and often decorated soffit
A tower - belvedere, colombaia or a survival of a fortified predecessor - taller than the block and set off the main axis
An arcaded loggia of three to five semicircular arches, on the ground or upper floor, oriented for shade and view
Round-headed or square-headed openings with plain rendered or stone surrounds, graded in size by storey, and external shutters throughout
Rendered and limewashed mass masonry walls in warm earth colours, with no applied order and rarely a column outside the loggia
A balanced but not strictly symmetrical front, in which the tower and the loggia deliberately unbalance the composition
Deep integration with terraced ground - retaining walls, a raised terrace, an axial cypress approach - so the house and its platform read as one construction
diagnostic_tells: A low hipped roof with a wide bracketed eave over a plain rendered wall - the two together are near-conclusive
A square tower placed at the inner angle of an L or beside the entrance rather than on the centre line
Semicircular arches with the arch rise exactly half the span, springing from a simple impost band with no capital
Openings that align in columns but are graded in height by storey, with the top storey noticeably squarer and smaller
Chimneys with a tile cap on small piers - a little roof over the flue - which is a Tuscan detail with no northern equivalent

distinguished_from.difference: The farm is additive and its openings are placed by the plan; the villa is a compact block whose openings align and grade. The farm's tower is a dovecote at the corner of an accreted mass; the villa's tower is a composed element. The villa has a loggia designed for sitting in; the farm has a portico for working under.

The American Italianate is a timber-framed, machine-milled reproduction: sawn scroll brackets, deep cornice returns, arched window hoods in wood or cast iron, and a cupola rather than a real tower. Its walls are thin, its windows are twice as large in proportion, and its bracket spacing is set by the mill rather than by the rafter.

Palladio starts from harmonic room ratios and applies a temple portico; the villa vernacular has no portico, no pediment, no module and no order except in the loggia arcade. Where a Palladian villa is strictly symmetrical about a portico, this type is balanced about a tower that is off-axis on purpose.

proportional_system.governing_logic: A regularised farm building. Proportion is set by the storey height and the opening, not by a module, and there is usually no column in the composition except in the loggia arcade. The tower's height and position are judged against the mass of the block by eye, which is why the type reads as composed but never as calculated.
typical_ratios: Principal block plan 1:1 to 1:1.3; eave height 0.8 to 1.0 of the plan's shorter dimension
Tower height 1.3 to 1.8 times the block's eave height; tower plan 3.5-5 m square, 0.2 to 0.3 of the block's frontage
Roof pitch 14-23 degrees (3:12 to 5:12), hipped, in coppi and embrici
Eave overhang 600-1200 mm on brackets at 600-900 mm centres, bracket depth 0.5 to 0.75 of the overhang
Loggia arcade of three to five equal semicircular arches; clear span 2.0-3.0 m; pier width 0.35-0.5 of the clear span; impost height 0.55-0.65 of the total arch height
Window proportions 1:1.8 to 1:2.2 at the piano nobile, 1:1.3 to 1:1.5 at the top storey; aperture area 12-20 percent of wall
Storey heights diminishing upward roughly 10:9:7.5
Wall thickness 450-600 mm with reveals of 300-450 mm
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three to five bays, nominally even and tolerant of a single deviation where the plan demands it. The loggia occupies a run of two to four bays at one end or across the centre, and the tower deliberately breaks the rhythm at an angle or beside the entrance rather than on the axis.

massing_affinities.note: The type the massing catalog's Towered Villa is named after, arriving in the catalog by way of the nineteenth-century Italianate but originating here.
The compact double-pile block about a central hall or sala passante running through from front to back for cross-ventilation.
The fattoria closes a working court behind or beside the padronale block, with the family's rooms on the view side and the estate functions on the court.
Where the loggia wraps two or three sides, the block becomes a core inside a shaded perimeter - the same logic as the tropical gallery house, arrived at from the same climate problem.
On steep ground the living floor sits over a full masonry undercroft of cellar and cantina reached from the downhill side, with an external stair on the uphill.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch between 3:12 and 5:12, hipped, with an eave overhang of 600-1200 mm on brackets. A steep roof, a narrow eave, or an eave without brackets each individually break the type.

test.note: Tests the pitch range. The eave-overhang range (600-1200 mm, maps to eave_projection_in) and 'hipped'/'on brackets' are further facts in the same sentence, left as prose for the single-test limit.

constraints.statement: The tower must be off the centre line and must exceed the block's eave height by at least 30 percent. A tower centred on the facade converts the composition into a symmetrical villa; a tower below 1.2 times the eave height reads as a stair bulkhead.
All arches semicircular: rise = half span within 3 percent. Segmental and elliptical arches belong to the working farm; pointed and Tudor arches are outside the tradition entirely.

test.note: Rise = half span within 3 percent, read as +/-3 percentage points around 0.5. Which arch forms belong to the working farm vs. are excluded entirely stays prose.

constraints.statement: No pediment and no applied order on the exterior. Columns occur only in the loggia arcade, and there they are unfluted Tuscan or Doric carrying an impost, not an entablature.

The loggia must face between south-east and south-west in the northern hemisphere and must be at least 2.4 m deep so that the summer sun is excluded from the wall behind it while winter sun reaches the back wall.

test.note: Tests the south-east-to-south-west orientation band (135-225 degrees, 0=north). The 2.4 m minimum depth (maps to gallery_depth_ft) is a second numeric fact in the same sentence, left as prose for the single-test limit.

exemplars.name: Villa Medicea di Cafaggiolo
exemplars.note: Reconstructed by Michelozzo for Cosimo de' Medici in 1452 from an existing fortified farm, retaining a crenellated entrance tower, battlemented wings and a moat. The moment the working farm block with a tower becomes a house worth being seen in.

exemplars.name: Villa Medicea La Petraia
exemplars.note: A Brunelleschi-family palace of 1364, bought by Cosimo I in 1544 and transformed from 1588, traditionally under Buontalenti. The medieval tower is kept and made the centre of the composition - the clearest surviving demonstration of how the villa tower came to exist.

exemplars.name: Villa Medicea di Careggi
exemplars.note: Medici property from 1417; Michelozzo's remodelling for Cosimo de' Medici is conventionally dated to the 1450s. A fortified farm block cautiously opened up with loggias onto a garden - the villa emerging from the castello without discarding it.

sources: James S. Ackerman, The Villa: Form and Ideology of Country Houses (1990)
Georgina Masson, Italian Villas and Palaces (1959)
Edith Wharton, Italian Villas and Their Gardens (1904)
John Claudius Loudon, An Encyclopaedia of Cottage, Farm, and Villa Architecture (1833)
Emilio Sereni, Storia del paesaggio agrario italiano (1961)

proportion_packs.note: This is the type facade-picturesque's own literature points back to: Nash's Cronkhill (1802) is a direct quotation of this diagram, and the pack lists italian-villa-vernacular in its applies_to. The node's hard constraint that the tower must exceed the block's eave height by at least 30 percent and sit off the centre line (c02) is exactly the pack's dominance-and-lever-arm logic - one mass must clearly outrank the others, and a subordinate element earns its compositional weight by standing well clear of the visual centre rather than by size alone. Bound at facade role because the villa is 'balanced but not strictly symmetrical' by design, which is the pack's whole subject.

The node's own governing_logic states plainly that 'proportion is set by the storey height and the opening, not by a module' - no harmonic system, no order outside the loggia. That is room-vernacular's counter-treatise logic exactly: rooms sized by span, storey height and daylight rather than by a proportioned ratio. italian-villa-vernacular is named directly in the pack's applies_to.

tudor-revival.name: Tudor Revival

geography.hearth: the streetcar and rail suburbs of the Northeast and Midwest

lineage.note: The claimed ancestor, known to American architects almost entirely through photographs, Country Life, and a summer's sketching tour.
The half-timbered wall is quoted from genuine box-frame construction whose structural logic the revival almost never reproduces.
Stone-and-slate cottage register, drawn on for the smaller suburban examples; see cotswold-cottage-revival.

Real transmission. Shaw, Voysey, Lutyens and Baillie Scott were published in American journals monthly; the plan-forms, the sweeping roof, and the grouped casement come from there, not from the sixteenth century.
Composition, drafting culture, and the office structure that made a large picturesque house buildable on schedule.
The American carpenter's habit of picturesque massing and applied wall pattern, which Tudor Revival inherits and re-skins.
In the 1890s the two are barely separable; the same offices produced Tudor gables over shingled walls.
The Anglophile alternative for buyers who wanted lineage without American plainness - romance and shadow in place of white symmetry.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The dominant American picturesque revival of the interwar suburb, in which steeply pitched cross-gables, decorative half-timbering, and massive chimneys assemble a fantasy of English medieval building on a balloon-framed house with a two-car garage.
description.long:
Tudor Revival is the great counterweight to Colonial Revival, and it wins the 1920s. Its necessary conditions are a steep roof - 10:12 and up - with at least one prominent front-facing cross-gable, a massive and elaborated chimney placed on a visible face rather than hidden, tall narrow casement or multi-light double-hung windows grouped in bands, an entrance with a Tudor arch or a round-arched stone surround, and a wall of at least two materials, typically brick or stone below with stucco and applied timbering above. What it references is a two-hundred-year band of English building from roughly 1450 to 1650 that American architects had never touched. What it descends from is quite different: the British Arts and Crafts movement, published continuously in American journals from the 1890s; the picturesque massing habits of American Queen Anne; and the professional apparatus of the Beaux-Arts-trained office, which could get a complicated irregular building through working drawings and a general contractor.

Two material facts made the style possible. The first is the perfection of masonry veneer. Brick and stone tied back to a wood frame, rather than laid as a bearing wall, gave American builders the appearance of English mass at American labour rates, and it is the reason Tudor Revival could descend from millionaires' estates to $6,000 suburban houses within twenty-five years. The second is the millwork and metalwork catalog, which by 1925 supplied steel casements, leaded glass, strap hinges, and precast stone surrounds as stock items. The style's economics run exactly opposite to its imagery: the more it claims hand-craft, the more of it came out of a catalog.

The social claim being made was specific. If Colonial Revival argued descent from the American founders, Tudor Revival argued descent from the English, which for the professional class of Cleveland, Kansas City, Detroit and Toronto was the more prestigious of the two and carried none of the provincialism. It read as scholarship - the buyers of Stan Hywet or Meadow Brook Hall knew the names Compton Wynyates and Haddon Hall - and it read as antiquity, which mattered in cities that were forty years old. In the suburban version the same claim is compressed into one gable, one chimney, and forty running feet of applied board.

The experience of a Tudor Revival house is one of deliberate compression and release, inherited from Arts and Crafts planning rather than from anything medieval. The entrance is low, arched, and set in shadow beneath an overhanging storey; you duck slightly and then the living room opens tall, with a beamed or trussed ceiling and a fireplace scaled to burn logs the length of a man. Light comes sideways through leaded casements in bands rather than down through big windows, so the interior stays dim and the stained oak reads warm. Outside, the building never resolves into a single view: the gables are of different sizes, the chimney is off-axis, the roof sweeps down over a bay on one side and stops short on the other. That refusal to resolve is the point of the style, and it is the hardest thing to fake, which is why the cheap examples read as a symmetrical box wearing a costume.

defining_characteristics: Steeply pitched roof, 10:12 minimum and frequently 12:12 to 16:12, with one or more prominent front-facing cross-gables of unequal size
A massive, elaborated chimney placed on a visible elevation, often with corbelled or clustered stacks and decorative brick or stone patterning
Tall, narrow windows in grouped bands - casements or multi-light double-hung - with leaded, diamond, or small rectangular glazing
Entrance under a Tudor (four-centred) arch or a heavy round-arched masonry surround, usually recessed and often placed in a projecting gabled bay
Multi-material wall with a horizontal change of material between storeys, most often masonry below and stuccoed half-timbering above
Picturesque asymmetrical massing in which no elevation reads as symmetrical and the front door is not at the centre of the facade
diagnostic_tells: Half-timbering that describes no possible frame: timbers that stop mid-wall, do not meet at corners, or run past window heads without a lintel. Genuine box-frame timbering always resolves into posts, sills, plates and braces.

Timbering thickness is the giveaway - revival boards are 1 to 2 in. thick nailed to sheathing; real English frames are 4 to 8 in. members with the stucco or brick nogging set between them and behind their face.
A cross-gable whose rake meets the wall in a straight line without a return, and an entrance arch of cast stone with a visible mould seam.
Windows are grouped in threes and fours with a single continuous head; Colonial and Georgian revivals keep windows single and evenly spaced.

Compare with the historical Tudor original: real Tudor houses have almost no windows on the ground floor of the entrance range, tiny rooms, and no through-composition; the revival puts its biggest glass at the front and plans in open suites.

distinguished_from.difference: The original is a bearing structure - either a genuine timber box frame with infill, or stone walls carrying a roof - with small openings, low ceilings, no corridor circulation, and a plan generated by adding rooms over generations. The revival is a single-campaign wood frame with veneer, large grouped glazing, corridor circulation, and applied timbering that carries nothing.

Jacobethan Revival is the formal, masonry, symmetrical end of the same import - parapeted shaped gables, mullioned and transomed bay windows, strapwork, and an E- or H-plan. Tudor Revival is the picturesque, half-timbered, asymmetrical end. Both were built by the same architects, often on the same street.

The Cotswold cottage version is small, all-stone or stone-and-slate, has a rolled or swept eave, and generally omits half-timbering entirely. Tudor Revival is larger, taller, and depends on the timber pattern for its identity.

proportional_system.governing_logic: No classical module. Proportion is governed by the notional structural bay of the timber frame being imitated - roughly 8 to 12 ft between posts - and by roof geometry, since the steep pitch makes the gable triangle the dominant proportional figure on every elevation.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 10:12 to 16:12; the principal cross-gable steeper than the main roof, never shallower
Gable width to eave-to-ridge height approximately 1:0.7 - the triangle reads taller than half its base
Casement leaves 16-22 in. wide by 40-56 in. high, proportion between 1:2.2 and 1:2.8, grouped in 2, 3, or 4
Second-storey overhang (jetty) where used: 8-16 in., never more than the depth of a plausible joist
Chimney breadth at least 1/6 of the elevation it sits on; stack height at least 3 ft above the ridge
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Additive rather than rhythmic. Windows group into clusters separated by broad blank wall, and the clusters do not align between storeys. Any facade that produces an even, repeating bay spacing has left the style.

massing_affinities.note: The defining skeleton: an irregular assembly of gabled volumes of differing height and depth.
The suburban builder version - a simple block with one dominant front cross-gable.
Large estate examples; shades into jacobethan-revival as it becomes symmetrical.
Narrow-lot urban Tudor, common in Chicago and Toronto; the picturesque is reduced to the gable and the chimney.
A symmetrical double-pile block with Tudor trim is the failure mode of the style, not an expression of it.

constraints.statement: Applied half-timbering must describe a structurally plausible frame. Every vertical member must run continuously from a sill or plate to a plate above; every horizontal must terminate at a post; braces must run corner to corner at 45 degrees or steeper; no member may cross a window head without a continuous lintel member above it. Free-floating decorative boards are forbidden.

Timbering members shall be no less than 5 in. and no more than 10 in. in face width, with a minimum 1 in. projection from the stucco plane, and shall be spaced 16-30 in. clear between verticals. Wider spacing or thinner boards reads as trim rather than as frame.
Main roof pitch not less than 10:12. Where a subordinate cross-gable is introduced its pitch must equal or exceed the main roof pitch. Any Tudor Revival roof below 10:12 is void.

test.note: 'Where a subordinate cross-gable is introduced its pitch must equal or exceed the main roof pitch' is a relational rule between two roof planes with no distinct cross-gable-pitch variable to compare against and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Where masonry meets stucco on a wall plane, the material change must occur at a floor line or at a projecting jetty, with a minimum 4 in. horizontal offset or a water table. A material change stopping in mid-storey without an offset is forbidden.

The principal chimney must be expressed on an elevation visible from the approach, be no less than 3'0" wide in plan, and project at least 12 in. from the wall face. A Tudor Revival house with a flush or concealed flue is incoherent.

test.note: Tests the chimney's projection from the wall face, reusing the corpus's general wall-plane-projection variable for a chimney breast. The 3'0" minimum plan width (no matching vocabulary variable) and 'expressed on an elevation visible from the approach' stay prose.

exemplars.name: Stan Hywet Hall
exemplars.note: Charles Sumner Schneider with George B. Post & Sons. Composed after a 1912 study tour of Compton Wynyates, Ockwells Manor and Haddon Hall, and explicitly designed to suggest growth across centuries.

exemplars.name: Meadow Brook Hall
exemplars.note: William Kapp of Smith, Hinchman & Grylls. 88,000 sq ft; the late estate version at full budget, with genuinely varied stonework and a chimney programme of unusual quality.

exemplars.name: Cranbrook House
exemplars.note: Albert Kahn. Early and restrained; shows the Arts and Crafts descent more plainly than the Tudor reference.

exemplars.name: Agecroft Hall
exemplars.note: A genuine fifteenth-century Lancashire house dismantled, shipped and reassembled with substantial new work. Instructive as the limit case: the revival's ambition made literal.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Gavin Stamp and Andre Goulancourt, The English House 1860-1914 (1986)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)
John Milnes Baker, American House Styles: A Concise Guide (1994)

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in this pack's applies_to. The node's own proportional_system states directly that there is 'no classical module' and that the roof geometry and the gable triangle govern -- exactly this pack's domain of a dominant mass, subordinate masses ranked against it, and datums that hold an asymmetrical front together. The node's own bay_rhythm ('additive rather than rhythmic... any facade that produces an even, repeating bay spacing has left the style') is this pack's window-grouping-by-count rule stated in the node's own words.

Explicitly listed. Governs the interior register the node's own description names -- a 'beamed or trussed ceiling,' exposed structure treated honestly -- which is this pack's carpentry-derived, exposed-joinery family rather than the orders-derived classical one; the two packs are the deliberate contrast the trim-craftsman pack states of itself. The exterior half-timbering itself is fully governed by the node's own hard constraints (c01, c02) and is not restated here.

JUDGMENT BINDING: tudor-revival is not in this pack's applies_to list, but two of its strongest lineage references are -- english-medieval-timber-frame (weight 0.9, 'the half-timbered wall is quoted from genuine box-frame construction') and cotswold-vernacular (weight 0.6) -- and the node's own description of compression-and-release planning inherited from British Arts and Crafts practice (Shaw, Voysey, Lutyens, Baillie Scott) matches this pack's constrained, daylight-and-hearth-limited room far better than room-harmonic's Palladian one, which no source cited on this node ever invokes.

english-medieval-timber-frame.name: English Medieval Timber Frame

revival_periods.note: Half-timbering returns as applied decoration over a stud or masonry wall. Almost all Victorian and later 'black-and-white' work is non-structural, and the applied version arrives in America as Tudor Revival.

geography.hearth: The wooded lowland belt — Kent and Sussex Weald, East Anglia, the West Midlands, Cheshire and the Welsh Marches

lineage.note: The carpenters who framed a manorial hall roof and those who framed a cathedral roof were the same trade working from the same geometry. Moulded arch-braces, cusped wind-braces and crown-post capitals in houses are Gothic details executed by carpenters rather than borrowed from masons.

description.short: The native carpentry tradition of lowland Britain, in which a jointed frame of oak carries the whole building and the wall between the timbers is merely infill.
description.long:
This is the tradition that never came from anywhere. Masonry arrived with the Normans; timber framing was already here, continuous from Anglo-Saxon practice, and it simply kept going, absorbing Gothic taste at the level of moulding while never changing its structural logic. Two systems coexist. The cruck frame pairs curved blades rising from ground to ridge, each pair cut from a single tree split in half so the two blades are mirror images — a building conceived as a sequence of arches, dominant in the west and north. The box frame builds a rectilinear cage of sill, post, tie-beam and plate, braced diagonally, and is the ancestor of every later Anglo-American frame. Above both sits the carpented roof: crown-post and collar-purlin in the south-east, arch-braced collar trusses in the west, hammerbeams where money and ambition met.

What produced it was oak, and a very particular economy of oak. England had enough timber and not enough cash; a frame could be cut, jointed and numbered in a framing yard, then reared by a village in a day, whereas masonry needed quarries, carts, lime and a season of curing. Because the frame carries everything, the wall panels can be wattle and daub, brick nogging or lath and plaster without altering the structure, which is why the same house may show three different infills from three different centuries. The jetty — an upper floor cantilevered forward on projecting joists — is the tradition's most-argued detail; the honest structural account is that it lets the upper floor joists be shorter and stiffer while gaining floor area, and the honest social account is that it was also showing off, since a jetty costs timber and announces it.

The fifteenth-century Wealden house is the type's masterpiece and the clearest case of a plan producing a form. An open hall in the centre, two-storeyed bays at each end jettied forward, and one great hipped roof carried across all three on a deep sprocketed eave: from outside, a recessed centre under a continuous overhang, which reads as a single deliberate composition and is in fact a direct expression of the hall-and-crosswing plan. When wall fireplaces and chimney stacks became affordable in the sixteenth century — the 'Great Rebuilding' Hoskins identified between roughly 1570 and 1640 — the open hall was floored over, a stack was inserted in the screens passage, and thousands of these houses acquired the chambers upstairs that they still have.

Standing inside one is unlike any masonry interior. The room is defined by lines rather than surfaces: posts, braces and joists divide the space into a visible cage, and because oak moves as it dries, none of those lines is quite straight. Ceilings are low, sills are high, and the floor gives slightly. There is a strong sense of the building as an assembly of pieces that could in principle be taken apart — which is literally true, and many have been, dismantled and re-erected elsewhere with their carpenters' assembly marks still legible on the joints. That legibility is the tradition's deepest gift to a kit-of-parts system: every joint in a medieval frame was numbered before it was ever raised.

defining_characteristics: A jointed hardwood frame — cruck or box — carrying all vertical and lateral load, with wall panels as non-structural infill
Mortice-and-tenon joints secured by riven oak pegs; no metal fasteners in the primary frame
Structural bays of 3.0-5.0 m set by the length of available oak and expressed on the elevation as panel divisions
A carpented roof designed to be seen — crown-post, arch-braced collar or hammerbeam — over the open hall
Infill panels of wattle and daub, later brick nogging or plaster, sitting flush or slightly recessed behind the timber face
Jettied upper floors on projecting joists, with the jetty bressumer moulded and the joist ends exposed or boarded
Steep roof pitch (48-55 degrees) demanded by thatch, stone slate or plain clay tile
diagnostic_tells: Timbers of irregular section and slight curvature, wide panels in the south-east and small close studding in East Anglia — the closer the studs, the wealthier the builder, since close studding is a deliberate waste of oak
Carpenters' assembly marks (chiselled Roman numerals) at the joints, and empty peg holes where members have been reused from an earlier frame
A jetty that returns around a corner with a dragon beam set diagonally at 45 degrees — a detail that cannot be faked convincingly and is absent from all applied half-timbering
Wall panels that are not rectangles: curved braces cutting across the panel field, and quatrefoil or herringbone patterned panels in Cheshire and the Welsh Marches
A massive brick or stone stack inserted awkwardly into a frame it clearly post-dates, usually in the old screens passage — the signature of the Great Rebuilding

distinguished_from.difference: Tudor is a period and a taste that timber framing passed through, not an alternative to it. Tudor at the great-house scale is brick and stone with four-centred arches and symmetrical gatehouse fronts; timber framing is the underlying carpentry tradition of the same decades at every scale below that.

The cottage tradition is the same carpentry at the bottom of the social scale, and in the west it is often not carpentry at all but cob or rubble. Timber frame proper is a merchant's and yeoman's architecture with a designed frame; the cottage is what is left when the frame budget is a quarter of that.

Parallel rather than derived. Continental Fachwerk uses much closer studding with carved and painted sill beams, wall panels usually smaller and more decorated, and roofs framed with principal rafters and purlins rather than the English crown-post. English work leaves the oak to silver; the black-and-white paint scheme is largely a Victorian addition.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The structural bay of the frame. Everything — panel width, window width, jetty depth, roof truss spacing — is a division of a bay, and the bay is set by the length of sound oak a carpenter could get, roughly 4.5 m at the limit. There is no applied proportional theory of any kind.
typical_ratios: Bay length 3.0-5.0 m; hall of two bays, crosswings of one to two
Wall panel roughly square in the south-east (1.0-1.4 m), and 1:3 to 1:4 vertical in East Anglian close studding
Post section 200-300 mm square; tie beam 250-350 mm deep
Jetty projection 350-600 mm, roughly one third of the floor joist depth times four — never the exaggerated overhang of revival work
Roof pitch 48-55 degrees; eave height 2.1-2.7 m at the wall plate
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Visible and insistent: principal posts every 3.0-5.0 m carry the tie beams and truss, with secondary studs subdividing. Openings are cut within the panel field and never cross a principal post, so window widths are dictated by the frame rather than the other way round.

massing_affinities.note: The hall with jettied crosswings at both ends — the Wealden and half-H types are the tradition's central form.
The single-bay open hall, the irreducible unit before crosswings are added.
The post-Rebuilding condition, hall and parlour either side of an inserted lobby-entry stack.
Jettied timber street ranges in Lavenham, Shrewsbury, Chester and York, party-walled and gable-end or eaves-on to the street.
The jetty is precisely the ancestor of the American garrison overhang, which survived across the Atlantic as a decorative memory after the structural reason had gone.

constraints.statement: Timber positions must be structurally derivable: every vertical member reaches a sill or a beam, every brace resolves a corner, and no timber terminates in mid-panel. Applied patterning that does not correspond to a frame is forbidden.
Jetty projection 350-600 mm. Below 300 mm the shadow line fails to register; above 750 mm the building reads as twentieth-century Tudor Revival caricature.

test.note: 300mm and 750mm are the statement's illustrative failure points, not additional bounds -- the stated range is 350-600mm.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch not less than 45 degrees, and not less than 50 degrees under thatch. Infill panels must be set behind the timber face so that water is thrown clear of the joint, never proud of it.

test.note: Tests the universal floor (45deg). Thatch's stricter 50deg floor is material-conditional and stays prose, as does the infill-panel weathering clause.

constraints.statement: Openings are cut within a panel and may not interrupt a principal post or tie beam; window width is therefore a whole number of stud bays.
Where a masonry stack occurs in a frame of pre-1550 character it should read as an insertion — full-height, of different material, breaking the panel grid — because that is what it historically is.

exemplars.name: Alfriston Clergy House
exemplars.note: A fourteenth-century Wealden hall house, thatched, with its open hall and chalk-and-sour-milk floor intact; the first building bought by the National Trust, in 1896.

exemplars.name: Paycocke's House
exemplars.note: A cloth merchant's house with elaborate close studding, a richly carved jetty bressumer and moulded ceiling beams — timber framing used as conspicuous display of wool wealth.

exemplars.name: Little Moreton Hall
exemplars.note: North range 1504-08, west range 1546, south range with the Long Gallery c.1560-62. The West Midlands patterned-panel tradition at its most extravagant and least structurally disciplined; the gallery is visibly deforming the frame beneath it.

exemplars.name: Lavenham Guildhall of Corpus Christi
exemplars.note: East Anglian close studding at full strength, in a town where the wool trade collapsed early enough that nobody could afford to rebuild in brick.

sources: R. W. Brunskill, Timber Building in Britain (1985)
R. W. Brunskill, Traditional Buildings of Britain (1981)
Richard Harris, Discovering Timber-Framed Buildings (1978)
W. G. Hoskins, 'The Rebuilding of Rural England 1570-1640', Past and Present 4 (1953)
Margaret Wood, The English Mediaeval House (1965)

proportion_packs.note: english-medieval-timber-frame is named directly in timber-bay's applies_to, and it is effectively the pack's anchor node: the pack's own authority note is 'reconstructed by measurement from surviving English and Anglo-American box frames,' and this style's proportional_system states the bay IS the governing logic ('Everything — panel width, window width, jetty depth, roof truss spacing — is a division of a bay... There is no applied proportional theory of any kind'). The pack's jetty, depth-and-pile and window-grouping rules map directly onto this style's own defining characteristics.

english-medieval-timber-frame is named directly in room-vernacular's applies_to. The two packs are complementary by design (room-vernacular's own module note explicitly distinguishes the room from the bay that contains it), and this style's hall-and-parlor and hall-single-cell massing affinities are literally room-vernacular's own worked examples.

english-palladian.name: English Palladian

revival_periods.note: Returns as the reference standard for Edwardian and American country-house classicism, largely through the same books that established it in 1715.

geography.hearth: Lord Burlington's circle in London and at Chiswick, and the Whig country houses of Norfolk and Yorkshire

lineage.note: Transmission is textual and graphic rather than by apprenticeship: Giacomo Leoni's English edition of the Quattro Libri from 1716, Isaac Ware's more accurate translation of 1738, and the Palladio and Inigo Jones drawings Burlington bought in Italy in 1719 and published through William Kent in 1727. This is the founding case of pattern-book descent in Britain.

Explicit and polemical. Colen Campbell's preface to Vitruvius Britannicus (1715) attacks the 'affected and licentious' Italian moderns by name and proposes Jones and Palladio as the correction. The giant order, the broken pediment and the sculpted skyline are legislated out within fifteen years.

A reaction still inherits its trades. Campbell, Kent and Burlington built with masons, joiners and plasterers trained on Wren's and Vanbrugh's sites, and the carcass construction of a Palladian house is a Baroque house's carcass.

Claimed rather than descended. The temple portico applied to a dwelling rests on Palladio's belief that ancient houses were fronted like temples, which is now known to be wrong. The style's central motif is therefore an archaeological error, faithfully transmitted.

description.short: A rule-governed classicism imported from Vicenza by book and drawing, in which a temple portico stands on a rusticated basement and every dimension in the building can in principle be justified from a published plate.
description.long:
English Palladianism is the first architectural style in Britain to be launched deliberately, in print, as a programme. Three publications appear within a year of each other around 1715: Colen Campbell's Vitruvius Britannicus, Giacomo Leoni's English Palladio, and the political moment of the Hanoverian succession, which gave the Whig aristocracy both power and a motive to distinguish its taste from the Tory-Stuart Baroque. Richard Boyle, third Earl of Burlington, supplied the money, the drawings and the authority; William Kent supplied the interiors and, eventually, the garden that broke the geometry outdoors while the house held it indoors.

The system is unusually explicit. A rusticated basement of service rooms carries a piano nobile of state rooms, reached by an external stair; a portico or a pedimented centrepiece marks the axis; the wall surface is plain ashlar, and ornament is concentrated in a few licensed places — the aedicule window surrounds of the principal storey, a Venetian window in a projecting bay, a Diocletian window in the attic or wing. Room dimensions are taken from Palladio's list of approved shapes: the circle, the square, the square and a third, the square and a half, the double square and the diagonal of the square. This means that a Palladian plan can be checked, and could be executed by a competent provincial builder from a book without the designer ever visiting the site. That is not a side effect; it is the point. Palladianism is the moment English architecture became transmissible information, and the pattern-book industry that followed — Gibbs, Langley, Swan, Halfpenny, Morris — is its direct commercial consequence.

Against the Baroque it is an argument for restraint, correctness and legibility, and it wins so completely that by 1740 a giant order on a house looks provincial. The cost of the victory is that the style is difficult to inhabit.
