Holkham and Houghton are magnificent and cold; the piano nobile puts the family a full storey above the ground and the servants below it, which is socially exact and practically miserable; and Palladio's Veneto villas, designed for a hot climate with deep loggias and thin walls, needed serious adjustment for a wet one — hence the English preference for the closed portico, the sash window in place of the shutter, and the service basement in place of the barchessa.

What a Palladian house does to a body is regulate it. You approach on axis, climb an external stair that raises you deliberately above the ground, pass under a portico whose columns are spaced so that the intercolumniation frames the door, and enter a hall that is very often a cube. Rooms open into one another in enfilade along the front, so that the doors align and you can see through four rooms at once — the alignment is the ornament. Everything is quiet, pale and dimensionally resolved, and after an hour the effect is either serenity or a mild sense of being measured. Both reactions are period-appropriate.

defining_characteristics: A piano nobile of principal rooms raised over a rusticated service basement, reached by an external stair on the principal front
A temple portico or pedimented centrepiece of a single order, correctly proportioned, replacing the Baroque giant order
Plain ashlar or fine brick wall surfaces with ornament concentrated at licensed points: the centrepiece, the piano nobile window aedicules, the cornice
Room dimensions drawn from Palladio's approved set of ratios (1:1, 1:1.33, 1:1.5, 1:1.67, 1:2, and the square's diagonal)
The Venetian (serliana) window and the Diocletian (thermal) window as the two licensed exotic openings
Five-part composition where the programme allows: main block, low hyphens, terminal pavilions, with a strict hierarchy of ridge heights
Low hipped or pedimented roofs behind a parapet, with chimneys grouped and disciplined into the composition
diagnostic_tells: A pedimented portico standing on a rusticated basement with an exterior stair — if the entrance is at grade, the house is Georgian rather than Palladian
Window aedicules (pediment on consoles or pilasters) on the piano nobile only, with the storeys above and below left completely plain — the vertical hierarchy of ornament is the style's signature
A Venetian window centred in a shallow projecting bay, usually under a relieving arch and often flanked by blind niches
A Diocletian half-round window in a pavilion or attic, semicircular and divided by two mullions
Absolute absence of the giant order, the broken pediment, the banded rustication and the sculpted skyline — the presence of any of these dates the design before 1715 or after 1830

distinguished_from.difference: Correctness against invention. Palladianism restricts itself to what Palladio published; Baroque stretches, bands and breaks the orders for effect. Palladian walls are flat and pale, Baroque walls are modelled and shadowed. A Palladian roof is a low parapeted plane; a Baroque roof is a stage for urns and cupolas.

Palladianism is the aristocratic and theoretical parent; Georgian is its everyday descendant. Georgian drops the piano nobile and puts the door at grade, drops the portico for a doorcase, and applies the proportional system to a brick box built by a speculator. Almost every Palladian rule survives in Georgian, at a quarter of the cost and none of the ceremony.

Adam keeps the Palladian envelope and attacks the interior. Palladian rooms are rectangular boxes with heavy compartmented ceilings and marble chimneypieces; Adam rooms are apsed, niched and screened, with flat low-relief ornament in delicate colour. At fifty feet the difference is that Adam thins everything — the mouldings, the glazing bars, the ornament.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Palladio's published system, module equal to the lower column diameter (subdivided into 60 minutes), with room plans and sections taken from the Quattro Libri's approved ratios and the whole checkable against a printed plate.
typical_ratios: Room plans restricted to 1:1, 1:1.33, 1:1.5, 1:1.67, 1:2, and the square-diagonal ratio 1:1.414
Room height in a rectangular room set as the mean of length and breadth (arithmetic, geometric or harmonic) — commonly the arithmetic mean
Piano nobile storey height 4.5-6.0 m; basement 2.7-3.5 m; attic storey roughly 0.6 of the piano nobile
Sash proportion 1.8:1 to 2:1 height to width on the piano nobile, reducing to near 1:1 in the attic storey
Portico intercolumniation 2.25 to 3 diameters (eustyle or systyle); column height 9-10 diameters for Ionic, 9.5-10 for Corinthian
Main block ridge height to hyphen ridge height not less than 1.5:1
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: An even metronome of bays across the front with a three- or five-bay centrepiece brought slightly forward and pedimented. Bay widths are equal; the centre is distinguished by ornament and projection, never by wider spacing.

massing_affinities.note: The definitive form and the one the massing catalog is named for; Holkham extends it to a main block with four corner pavilions.
The compact Palladian villa — Mereworth, Chiswick and Campbell's smaller designs — is a double-pile block with a central hall and stair.
The portico-plus-flankers composition, which the Americans later take up wholesale for Greek Revival.
The Palladian palace-fronted terrace, where a whole row is composed as one elevation with a pedimented centre — Wood's Queen Square at Bath is the model.

constraints.statement: Every room plan must conform to one of Palladio's approved ratios within 3 percent, and ceiling height must be a stated mean of the room's length and breadth.
The giant order, banded rustication, broken and swan-neck pediments, and skyline statuary are forbidden. These are precisely the features the style was formed to eliminate.
Window aedicules and enriched surrounds occur on the piano nobile only. Ornamenting a basement or attic window inverts the hierarchy and destroys the composition.
Where a portico is used it must be full height of the piano nobile plus its entablature, free-standing or engaged, and land on the rusticated basement — not on a plinth invented for the purpose.
Hyphens and pavilions must be lower and shallower than the main block, with ridge heights stepping down by at least 25 percent at each stage.

exemplars.name: Chiswick House
exemplars.note: Built 1727-29 by Richard Boyle, third Earl of Burlington, for himself, after Palladio's Villa Rotonda and Scamozzi's Rocca Pisana. A manifesto rather than a dwelling: octagonal domed saloon, hexastyle Corinthian portico, and a plan of Palladian ratios throughout.

exemplars.name: Houghton Hall
exemplars.note: Built 1722-35 by Colen Campbell and Thomas Ripley, with interiors by William Kent, for Sir Robert Walpole. The Stone Hall is a 40-foot cube — the clearest surviving demonstration of the system applied at full scale.

exemplars.name: Holkham Hall
exemplars.note: Built 1734-64 by William Kent and Matthew Brettingham for Thomas Coke, first Earl of Leicester, to a scheme developed with Burlington. Yellow brick, a main block with four corner wings, and the alabaster-columned Marble Hall derived from a Roman basilica.

exemplars.name: Mereworth Castle
exemplars.note: Built 1723-25 by Colen Campbell for John Fane. The closest English copy of the Villa Rotonda, with four porticoes and a central dome whose void conceals the chimney flues.

sources: John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)
Rudolf Wittkower, Palladio and English Palladianism (1974)
Colen Campbell, Vitruvius Britannicus, 3 vols (1715-25)
Dan Cruickshank and Peter Wyld, Georgian Buildings of Britain and Ireland (1975)
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)

proportion_packs.note: The loggia and portico order of the type, and the one place in this whole trunk where the source is not mediated at all: this node's own lineage puts the transmission as textual and graphic, direct from I Quattro Libri (1570) via Leoni's 1716 and Ware's 1738 English editions and the Burlington-Kent-Campbell circle, one step closer to Palladio than even English Georgian's own Gibbs- or Chambers-mediated versions, and two steps closer than American Georgian's. The entablature at a fifth of the column rather than Vignola's quarter, and modillions rather than dentils in the cornice, are the two measurable consequences and are exactly this pack's own stated divergence from vignola-ionic.

The order of the grandest porticoes -- this node's own exemplar names Chiswick House's 'hexastyle Corinthian portico' directly. Graded below the Ionic loggia order because it is the exception rather than the working default: most Palladian porticoes in this corpus's exemplars (Mereworth, the smaller villas) are Ionic.

Governs the even metronome of equal bays with a three- or five-bay pedimented centrepiece this node's own bay_rhythm states, and the licensed-ornament-only rule its hard constraint c02 tests: the giant order, banded rustication and broken pediment Baroque permitted are here forbidden outright.

Governs the window aedicule this node's hard constraint c03 restricts to the piano nobile alone -- ornamenting a basement or attic window 'inverts the hierarchy and destroys the composition' -- and the Venetian and Diocletian window types this node names as its two licensed exotic openings.

RE-ANCHORED around the piano nobile rather than the ground floor, the one structural fact that separates this node from every other in the trunk: a rusticated basement (2.7-3.5 m) carries a piano nobile of state rooms (4.5-6.0 m) reached by an external stair, with the attic roughly 0.6 of the piano nobile above it. This is a three-tier hierarchy of RANK -- service, state, subordinate -- not the Georgian four-tier hierarchy of gradually diminishing ordinary storeys, and the datum the pack's default assumes (ground floor tallest) does not hold here at all.

Governs the enfilade of rooms this node describes -- doors aligned so 'you can see through four rooms at once, the alignment is the ornament' -- at the heavy, deeply coffered, rectangular-box register this node's own distinguished_from entry contrasts explicitly against Adam's later thinning.

The room-ratio doctrine's own point of origin in this trunk: this node's hard constraint c01 requires every room plan to conform to one of Palladio's approved ratios (1:1, 1:1.33, 1:1.5, 1:1.67, 1:2, the square's diagonal) within 3 percent, with ceiling height set as a stated mean of length and breadth -- a harder and more literal reading of this pack than any of its Gibbs-mediated descendants apply.

ranch-style.name: Ranch

geography.hearth: San Diego and Los Angeles, California

lineage.note: The direct ancestor: the same builders, the same FHA underwriting, the same trim, the same eight-foot plate. The ranch is the Minimal Traditional house laid on its side across a wider lot once postwar land and lumber allowed it.

The horizontal parti, the low hipped roof with a wide eave, the banded windows, and the open plan reach the ranch through the plan-book Prairie box and, more directly, through Wright's Usonian houses of 1936 onward, which Cliff May and the Sunset editors knew well.

The single-storey habit, the low horizontal spread, the indoor-outdoor terrace relationship, and the informality of the plan are bungalow inheritances carried through Californian practice without interruption.

The claimed ancestry. Cliff May, who grew up among the Estudillo family's adobes, marketed the type as a descendant of the Californian rancho, and the name stuck. The reference is honest in feeling and false in fact: the rancho was a courtyard building of thick adobe walls organized inward, while the ranch is a thin-walled suburban bar organized toward a private rear yard.

description.short: The long, low, single-storey suburban house of postwar America, and the first house type in the world organized around the automobile — a reorganization it accomplished by attaching the garage to the street elevation, a problem it never solved and bequeathed to every traditional style built since.
description.long:
The ranch is the American house at the moment the American house stopped being upright. Everything about it is horizontal: a single storey, a plan one room deep along most of its length, a body twenty-four to thirty-two feet deep and fifty to eighty feet long lying parallel to the street, a roof of three to five in twelve with an eave of eighteen to thirty-six inches, an eight-foot ceiling, and a facade whose width is two and a half to four times its height. Cliff May built the first of them in San Diego in 1932 and spent the next fifty years arguing that it descended from the Californian adobe rancho; Sunset published Western Ranch Houses with him in 1946 and turned a regional idea into a national one. But the ranch that got built ten million times was not May's courtyard house. It was the Minimal Traditional house of the 1930s laid on its side, and the agent of that transformation was land: postwar subdivisions on wider, cheaper, flatter lots made spreading out less expensive than stacking up.

The technology is worth enumerating because each item changed the building. The engineered light wood truss, commercialized in the late 1940s, spanned the full width of the house at twenty-four inches on centre, eliminated interior bearing walls, and made the low pitch structurally trivial and the open plan cheap. Plywood and gypsum board in four-by-eight sheets set the module for everything. The concrete slab on grade removed the basement in the West and put the floor at the level of the yard, which is what actually produces the indoor-outdoor life the marketing promised. Large float glass gave the picture window and the sliding glass door. Forced-air heating in the slab or in the attic removed the chimney's necessity, and residential air conditioning, spreading fast after 1955, removed the porch's — a covered outdoor room facing the street has no function in a house you keep sealed and cooled, and its disappearance is a mechanical fact before it is a social one. The FHA and VA supplied the mortgages, and the 1949 Housing Act supplied the political mandate.

And then there is the car, which is why this node matters more than its architectural quality warrants. The ranch is the first house type in history designed from the outset to receive an automobile at the dwelling. The driveway replaces the front walk as the real approach. The garage stops being an outbuilding at the rear of the lot and becomes a room of the house, attached, and — because the driveway must reach it, and because the cheapest driveway is the shortest one — it lands on the street elevation. A sixteen-foot garage door on a fifty-foot frontage occupies a third of the facade; a two-car door on a forty-foot frontage occupies more. The front door, meanwhile, has become the smallest and least visible opening on the front of the house, and is frequently invisible from the place where visitors actually arrive. This is the unsolved problem of American residential design, and it should be stated plainly: no traditional style has a rule for it, because no traditional style ever had to accommodate a twenty-by-twenty-foot windowless room that must open directly onto the public frontage. Every style in the contemporary-traditional group inherits this problem, and the only strategies that work are the ones the ranch itself occasionally used and then forgot — set the garage face back behind the main facade plane, turn it ninety degrees and side-load it, or push it to an alley.

To be inside a good ranch is more pleasant than its reputation suggests. The ceiling is low and the rooms run into one another, the light comes from two sides in most rooms, and the sliding door to the terrace means the yard is part of the living space in a way that no two-storey house achieves. To stand in front of one is a different experience: the building presents a long low band with a wide garage door, a picture window, and a recessed entry, and it does not address you. It has turned around. The public face of the American house was moved to the back garden in about 1950, and the street elevation has been an unsolved leftover ever since.

defining_characteristics: Single storey, long axis parallel to the street, facade width not less than twice the wall height
Low-pitched hipped or gabled roof, 3:12 to 5:12, with an eave of 18 to 36 in and a long unbroken ridge
Attached garage or carport composed as part of the house rather than as an outbuilding
Plan opened by trussed roof framing: living, dining, and kitchen spaces continuous or only partly divided
Direct indoor-outdoor relationship to a private rear yard through a sliding or french door, with the finish floor near grade
Picture window or window band on the principal elevation, in place of individually punched openings
No habitable front porch; entry as a recessed or hooded stoop
Asymmetrical facade organized by the competing claims of the entry and the garage
diagnostic_tells: The garage door is the largest single element on the street elevation
A picture window composed as a wide fixed centre light flanked by narrow operable sash
Roof ridge running unbroken for 40 ft or more at a pitch under 5:12
Finish floor within about 12 in of exterior grade, with one or two steps at the entry rather than a raised stoop
Decorative shutters, scalloped bargeboard, diamond-pane entry sidelights, or a cupola applied to an otherwise unornamented long low box — the 1955-1970 traditionalizing overlay

distinguished_from.difference: Its parent. Minimal Traditional is a compact upright block with a cellular plan and a detached rear garage; the ranch is a long low bar with an open plan and an attached garage. The 1948-1953 transitional houses have both characters and should be assigned by garage: attached means ranch.

Prairie horizontality is composed and hierarchical, gathered about a dominant chimney with deliberate compression and release; ranch horizontality is extensive and economic, a consequence of plan length. Prairie has a centre; the ranch has an extent.

The bungalow addresses the street with a deep front porch and puts its living room behind it; the ranch turns its living space to the rear yard and gives the street a garage. Both are low Californian single-storey houses; the difference is which side the life is on.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Economic and dimensional. The operative modules are the 4-by-8 sheet of plywood and gypsum board, the 24-inch truss spacing, the 8-foot precut stud, and the 16- or 18-foot garage door. Facade proportion is a residual of plan length rather than a governed quantity, and no vertical hierarchy survives at all — there is no base, no piano nobile, no attic, and frequently no cornice. Where a ranch elevation looks well proportioned it is because someone controlled three things by eye: the ridge line, the head datum, and the position of the garage.
typical_ratios: Facade width to wall height 2.5:1 to 4:1
Body depth 24 to 32 ft; overall length 50 to 80 ft
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12; eave overhang 18 to 36 in
Ceiling 8 ft 0 in; window and door head 6 ft 8 in
Garage door 16 ft (two-car) or 9 ft (one-car); door height 7 ft
Picture window 6 to 9 ft wide, head aligned with the general door head datum
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: None governing. Openings are grouped by room — a picture window at the living room, a pair at each bedroom, a small high sash at the bath — with long blank runs of wall between. The garage terminates the composition at one end.

massing_affinities.note: The L is the type's answer to a corner lot and to the desire for a sheltered rear terrace; it is also the massing in which side-loading the garage becomes natural.
The sloped-lot and cold-climate variant of the same programme, 1955-1975; retains every ranch characteristic except the single floor plane.
Cliff May's own preferred parti and the one closest to the rancho the style claims descent from; almost never built by tract developers because it consumes lot width.
A two-storey cubic mass negates every defining characteristic of the node.

constraints.statement: An attached garage facing the street must have its door plane set back not less than 4 ft behind the primary facade plane; otherwise the garage must be side-loaded, rear-loaded, or alley-served. A garage face forward of the front door is forbidden.

test.note: Tests the attached-street-facing case's 4 ft setback. The side-loaded/rear-loaded/alley-served alternative stays prose (a genuine disjunction; testing setback alone would wrongly fail a legitimately side-loaded garage).

constraints.statement: Total garage door width shall not exceed 33 percent of the street-facing facade width.
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 with eave and rake overhang between 18 and 36 in. Overhang under 12 in disqualifies the node; a pitch over 6:12 makes the horizontal reading impossible.

test.note: Tests the roof-pitch clause. Eave and rake overhang (18-36in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose; the under-12in and over-6:12 figures are illustrative disqualifiers beyond the stated range, not additional bounds.

constraints.statement: Facade width not less than twice the wall plate height, single storey throughout the street-facing mass.

test.note: Tests the width-to-wall-plate-height proportion. 'Single storey throughout the street-facing mass' is separately expressible via the existing storey_count variable as one-of ["1"] but only one test object is permitted per constraint, so it stays prose here.

constraints.statement: The low-pitch, wide-eave, slab-on-grade assembly is native to IECC zones 2 through 5. In zones 6 and 7 the pitch must rise toward 5:12, ice-dam detailing is required at the wide eave, and the slab must be replaced by a frost-protected foundation.

exemplars.name: O'Leary House
exemplars.note: Cliff May's first ranch house, sold for $9,500. The origin point of the type as an idea, if not of the tract house that carried it.

exemplars.name: Levittown ranch model
exemplars.note: The model that replaced the 1947 Cape mid-build-out, with a carport and a rear-facing living room. The moment the East Coast tract industry converted.

exemplars.name: Lakewood
exemplars.note: Boyar, Taper and Weingart, 1949-1953: 17,500 houses at up to 110 completions in a day. The ranch as an industrial product, and the largest single American subdivision of its moment.

sources: Cliff May and the editorial staff of Sunset Magazine, Western Ranch Houses (1946)
Barbara Miller Lane, Houses for a New World: Builders and Buyers in American Suburbs, 1945-1965 (2015)
Dolores Hayden, Building Suburbia: Green Fields and Urban Growth, 1820-2000 (2003)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Kenneth T. Jackson, Crabgrass Frontier (1985)

proportion_packs.note: JUDGMENT BINDING: ranch-style is not in this pack's own applies_to list, but the node's own governing_logic states the elevation's only real discipline in language that restates this pack's central rules almost exactly -- 'no vertical hierarchy survives at all... where a ranch elevation looks well proportioned it is because someone controlled three things by eye: the ridge line, the head datum, and the position of the garage' is this pack's dominance-and-datum logic, with the attached garage standing in as the subordinate mass the composition must rank against the main linear block and the picture window standing in as the pack's one-feature-per-elevation rule. The node's stated eave (18-36 in) also sits close to this pack's own default eave projection (about 21 in, twice the head-datum band's projection) rather than to any classical cornice figure. Bound at moderate confidence given the applies_to gap -- offered as the best-fitting available description of a discipline the node names but the pack library does not otherwise capture, not as a documented source for this specific style.

The node's craftsman lineage (weight 0.25 -- 'the single-storey habit, the low horizontal spread, the indoor-outdoor terrace relationship, and the informality of the plan are bungalow inheritances carried through Californian practice without interruption') is real but modest, and the node's own text never specifies interior trim dimensions. Bound optional and low as the directionally correct family -- flat stock, no order-derived logic, survives a low plate -- rather than as a documented feature of this node; many built ranches in fact ran no applied interior trim at all, which no pack in this library represents since even this one's floor assumes some casing.

french-renaissance-chateau.name: French Renaissance Chateau

revival_periods.note: The French domestic revival under Louis-Philippe and the Second Empire, and the restoration campaigns of Viollet-le-Duc and Felix Duban at Blois from the 1840s.
Richard Morris Hunt and his successors in America; the Loire chateau at Newport and Asheville, with steel and elevators inside.

geography.hearth: The Loire between Amboise and Blois

lineage.note: The substrate is the late-Gothic French manor and fortified house: steep roofs, corner towers, dormers on the roof plane, high chimneys, the corps de logis and cour d'honneur diagram. None of this is Italian and none of it goes away.

Imported bodily by Italian craftsmen brought back from the Italian Wars from 1495 - Fra Giocondo, Domenico da Cortona, later Serlio (in France from 1541) and Primaticcio. The ornament, the pilaster order and the classical mouldings arrive as a vocabulary before the proportional system arrives as a method.

description.short: Italian classical ornament grafted onto the steep-roofed, tower-punctuated, vertically bayed French manor, producing a half-century of unresolved and extraordinarily productive collision.
description.long:
The French Renaissance chateau is what happens when a building culture with a fully formed structural habit imports a foreign decorative system it admires but has no intention of obeying. Charles VIII returned from the Italian campaign of 1494-95 with craftsmen and a taste; his successors kept importing. But the French roof is steep because it snows and rains, the French house has habitable attics because land and heating are expensive, the French wall is organised in vertical strips because the timber floor structure and the window stacking make it so, and none of these facts is negotiable by taste. So the Italian pilaster order arrives and is laid across a wall that is fundamentally vertical, and the two systems argue on every facade for eighty years.

The economic and political conditions are specific and short-lived. The Hundred Years' War ends in 1453 and the internal wars of the fifteenth century subside; the French crown consolidates, the great nobility's private fortifications become militarily pointless against artillery, and an enormous amount of aristocratic capital is suddenly available for building houses rather than defences. What gets built is transitional in the most literal sense: Azay-le-Rideau has a moat and machicolations that could not stop a chicken, and corner turrets that contain nothing but a small room with a good view. The defensive vocabulary is retained as heraldry. Meanwhile the printing of Serlio's books in France from 1537 and du Cerceau's surveys from 1576 begin the process by which the French will eventually digest the Italian system properly - which they do, but not until the next century.

What it was reacting against was its own immediate past: the Flamboyant Gothic of the late fifteenth century, with its melting tracery, ogee curves and structural exhibitionism. The classical vocabulary arrived as a claim to modernity and to a specifically royal, Italianate sophistication. But the reaction was partial by design. Francois I did not want a Roman palazzo; he wanted a hunting lodge in the forest that announced he had been to Italy. Chambord is the extreme case: a strictly symmetrical Greek-cross donjon derived from Italian centralised planning, wrapped in medieval corner towers, and topped with a roofscape of eleven kinds of tower and three kinds of chimney arranged with no symmetry whatsoever - a Renaissance plan under a Gothic sky.

The experience is dominated by the roof. Standing in the court at Blois or on the terrace at Chambord, you are looking at a building whose upper half is as tall as its lower half and far busier - a forest of dormers, finials, chimney stacks and lucarnes carved with the same delicate candelabra ornament as the walls below, all in soft white tufa that weathers to grey and picks up rain in every moulding. The wall below is bright, thin, and pierced by more window than you expect from the period, because the cross-mullioned croisee gets very large very fast once you stop worrying about arrows. Inside, the plan is still medieval - a sequence of rooms without a corridor, each opening into the next, all of it heated by fireplaces the size of a small room and all of it very cold.

defining_characteristics: Steep roofs of 55 to 70 degrees, occupying a height comparable to the wall below, in slate or in flat clay tile
The vertical travee - window over window over dormer, stacked in an unbroken strip from plinth to roofline - as the real organising unit of the wall
Dormers (lucarnes) rising from the wall plane, carried up as stone frontispieces with their own pilasters and pediments, aligned exactly on the travee axes
Corner towers, turrets and machicolation retained as heraldic rather than defensive elements
Italian classical ornament - pilasters, candelabra pilaster panels, shell niches, medallions - applied as surface to a wall it does not proportion
Tall, prominent, individually articulated chimney stacks treated as a designed element of the silhouette
The croisee window: a large opening quartered by a stone mullion and transom, in light-coloured limestone or tufa against a plainer wall
diagnostic_tells: The roof is as tall as the wall - if the roof is subordinate, it is a later French classical building, not a Renaissance chateau
Dormers with full stone surrounds, pilasters and pediments sitting on the wall plane rather than set back on the roof slope
Classical pilasters running past a string course or dying into a moulding rather than carrying an entablature - the ornament does not know what it is holding up
Cylindrical corner turrets with conical roofs on a building that is otherwise symmetrical and undefended
Chimney stacks tall enough to compete with the towers, panelled and moulded on all four faces

distinguished_from.difference: The seventeenth century subordinates the roof, suppresses the towers, and finally makes the classical order govern the wall rather than decorate it. If the orders are proportional and the roof is a mansard rather than a steep pavilion roof with turrets, it is Baroque.

The Italian palazzo is a flat block with a horizontal cornice and an invisible roof; the French chateau is a vertical composition with an enormous visible roof and towers. They share ornament and share almost nothing else.

The American revival compresses the type onto a single dense block, uses machine-cut Indiana limestone with uniform joints, and hangs the whole silhouette on a steel frame with plate glass in the croisees. The revival is always tighter and busier per square metre than the original.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Two systems in unresolved superposition. The French structural system is the travee: a vertical strip of wall containing the stacked openings of every storey plus its dormer, set out at the spacing of the floor framing. Over this the Italian system of superimposed orders and horizontal entablatures is laid. The travee usually wins, and the orders become a grid pinned to a wall that remains fundamentally vertical.
typical_ratios: Travee spacing 4.0 to 6.0 m on centre, uniform along a range
Roof height 0.8 to 1.2 times the wall height below the eave; pitch 55 to 70 degrees (roughly 17:12 to 33:12)
Croisee window opening approximately 1:2 (w:h), quartered by mullion and transom into four lights of roughly 2:3 each
Storey heights near-equal rather than diminishing - typically within 10 percent of each other
Corner pavilion or tower projecting 1/4 to 1/3 of its own width from the range face
Dormer width 0.6 to 0.9 of the travee width, with the dormer's own height (to its finial) 0.5 to 0.8 of the storey below
Chimney stack height above the ridge 1/4 to 1/2 of the roof's own height
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Uniform vertical travees along each range, counted rather than composed, and terminated by corner pavilions or towers that are wider, taller and more ornamented. There is no central accent on the earlier examples; the centre emerges only late, with the staircase frontispiece at Blois and the entrance pavilion at Ecouen.

massing_affinities.note: The cour d'honneur - three ranges around a court opening toward the approach - is the standing French diagram from the fifteenth century onward.
The fully enclosed court survives from the fortified predecessor, as at Chambord's outer enceinte and Ecouen.
A central range with projecting end wings, generally with the wings expressed as pavilions with their own roofs - the same diagram the English are using simultaneously.
Ancy-le-Franc approaches a regular block-and-pavilion hierarchy under Serlio's hand, but it is Italian discipline imposed rather than French habit.
The brisee roof is Francois Mansart's device of the 1630s and later; it postdates this style and its presence indicates a seventeenth-century building or a revival.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch must be between 55 and 70 degrees, and roof height must be at least 0.7 of the wall height. A roof below 45 degrees is a later French classical building.

test.note: Tests the pitch range. The roof-height-to-wall-height ratio (at least 0.7) is a second independent clause with no single named 'roof height' variable to pair against wall height cleanly, and the 45-degree threshold is subsumed by the tested lower bound -- both stay prose.

constraints.statement: Dormers must align on the travee axes below and match their count; a dormer floating between two windows is a hard error.

test.note: Tests that dormer count matches the travee (bay) count. Positional alignment of each dormer on its own travee axis has no offset variable in the vocabulary and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Where corner towers or turrets are used they must be cylindrical or polygonal with their own conical or pyramidal roof carried down independently of the main roof; a turret sharing the main eave line reads as a bay window, not a tower.

Applied pilaster orders must not be given a full projecting entablature that interrupts a travee. In this style the horizontal system yields to the vertical one; where it does not, the building has crossed into seventeenth-century classicism.

Steep slate or flat-tile roofs with the attic occupied require adequate eaves drainage and a habitable dormer at each travee. The type is native to cool, wet, snow-bearing climates (IECC 4A-6A) and reads as costume anywhere warmer.

exemplars.name: Chateau de Chambord
exemplars.note: Begun 6 September 1519 for Francois I, substantially complete 1547. Symmetrical Greek-cross donjon with a double-helix stair, wrapped in corner towers and topped by an asymmetrical roofscape of eleven tower types and three chimney types.

exemplars.name: Chateau d'Azay-le-Rideau
exemplars.note: Built 1518-1527 for Gilles Berthelot. The clearest demonstration of decorative fortification - moat, machicolated cornice and corner turrets with no defensive function - and of the stone-framed dormer running the travee up through the roof.

exemplars.name: Chateau de Blois, Francois I wing
exemplars.note: 1515-1524. The open octagonal spiral staircase on the courtyard front, with the loggia facade behind it, is the single most concentrated statement of the Franco-Italian collision.

exemplars.name: Chateau d'Ancy-le-Franc
exemplars.note: Begun 1544, attributed to Sebastiano Serlio, continued after his death in 1554. Four ranges of equal height around a square court with corner pavilions - the moment Italian regularity briefly overrides French verticality.

sources: Anthony Blunt, Art and Architecture in France 1500-1700, Pelican History of Art
Jean-Marie Perouse de Montclos, Histoire de l'architecture francaise: de la Renaissance a la Revolution (1989)
Jacques Androuet du Cerceau, Les plus excellents bastiments de France (1576-1579)
Sebastiano Serlio, Tutte l'opere d'architettura et prospettiva (1537-1575)
James S. Ackerman, The Villa: Form and Ideology of Country Houses (1990)

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding, bound low and with a real caveat. french-renaissance-chateau is not in vignola-composite's own applies_to, but the American revival it generates, chateauesque, is -- suggesting the corpus already expects a rich order register on this lineage, even though the direct source is not named. Bound optional rather than higher because this style's own c04 is explicit that the applied pilaster order must NOT be given a full projecting entablature that interrupts a travee -- 'the ornament does not know what it is holding up' -- so this covers the imported Italian pilaster VOCABULARY (arriving with Fra Giocondo, Domenico da Cortona and Serlio from 1495) and nothing more; it must not be read as a governing proportional system the way it is for italian-renaissance or beaux-arts-french.

Judgment binding, the weakest room fit in this whole batch and offered as such. Not in room-harmonic's own applies_to. This style's own text states plainly that 'the plan is still medieval -- a sequence of rooms without a corridor,' which argues against a harmonic-mean room system as much as for one. It is bound anyway, narrowly, for the exceptional Italianate-planned examples the style's own text names -- Chambord's centralised Greek-cross donjon and Ancy-le-Franc under Serlio's own hand, 'the moment Italian regularity briefly overrides French verticality' -- and should not be taken as describing the type's norm.

contemporary-traditional.name: Contemporary Traditional

description.short: New Classical, New Urbanist, and the current market idioms — the living attempt to recover traditional design logic under contemporary economics.
description.long:
Since about 1980 a serious body of practice has worked to recover traditional architecture as a living discipline rather than a costume: Krier's urban theory, Duany and Plater-Zyberk's codes at Seaside and Kentlands, the Institute of Classical Architecture and Art, and the Notre Dame school.

The striking thing is the mechanism. These practitioners returned to pattern books and form-based codes — the eighteenth-century solution — because they faced the eighteenth-century problem: how to get correct traditional building out of a trade that no longer carries the knowledge. That is the immediate precedent for encoding design logic in software, and the reason this family sits at the end of the taxonomy rather than as an appendix to it.

defining_characteristics: Deliberate recovery of traditional design logic rather than of style alone
Pattern books and form-based codes revived as the transmission mechanism
Urbanism treated as inseparable from architecture
Contemporary programme, construction, and code accommodated openly
An explicit argument with the market idioms it competes against

charleston-georgian.name: Charleston Georgian

revival_periods.note: Charleston's own preservation movement, the first in the United States (1920 Society for the Preservation of Old Dwellings), produced a revival unusually faithful to local rather than New England precedent.

geography.hearth: Charleston, South Carolina

lineage.note: Shares the Georgian proportional and ornamental system; departs from it in orientation, section, and the treatment of the threshold.

Direct, and unusually direct for a colonial city: Charleston merchants imported British craftsmen, joinery, and pattern books (Gibbs, Langley, Swan) through a port that traded with London more consistently than with Boston.
The Palladian entry, the temple-form portico on the piazza, and the Venetian window are quoted from books rather than inherited from practice.

description.short: The Georgian system as rebuilt for a subtropical port city, where the house turns its narrow end to the street and gives its long southern flank to a stacked open piazza.
description.long:
Charleston in the middle of the eighteenth century was the wealthiest city in British North America and the hottest, and its architecture is what happens when a great deal of money and a great deal of humidity are applied to the same problem at once. The Georgian vocabulary arrived intact — correct entablatures, Flemish-bond brick, Venetian windows, joinery executed by London-trained craftsmen from Gibbs and Swan — and then the plan and the section were quietly rebuilt underneath it.

The rebuilding was climatic. A Georgian house in Boston is a compact double-pile block designed to conserve heat; the same house in Charleston would be uninhabitable for five months a year. So the Charleston version thins its section, raises its ceilings, sets its principal floor above a high service basement to escape ground damp and the mosquito line, and hangs one or two storeys of open piazza along the flank that faces the prevailing southwest breeze. The street elevation, deprived of its usual job, sometimes gives up entirely: a door in the garden wall opens onto the piazza rather than into the house, so that the visitor crosses from public to private through an outdoor room before ever reaching a threshold.

What this produces phenomenologically is unlike anything else in colonial America. You do not confront a facade; you are admitted sideways into a shaded, moving, half-outdoor space, and the house reveals itself in stages. The formality is entirely intact — the drawing room at the top of the stair is as correct as anything in London — but the sequence leading to it has been reorganized around air and shade rather than around symmetry and axis. Georgian architecture is usually described as a system of frontal composition. Charleston demonstrates that the system is more portable than that, and survives being turned ninety degrees.

For a design system this variant is the strongest available argument that style and climate response are separable layers rather than a single package. Everything in the kit of parts above the plan — cornice, sash, panel, order — transfers from Boston to Charleston unchanged. Everything at the level of section, orientation, and threshold has to be re-derived from latitude. A taxonomy that stops at 'Georgian' cannot express that, and a builder working from it will produce a house that looks correct and performs badly.

defining_characteristics: Principal floor raised above a high, often arcaded service basement
Ceiling heights of 12 to 14 feet on the principal floor, markedly taller than Northern Georgian practice
One or two storeys of open piazza on the south or west flank, structurally integral rather than applied
Flemish-bond brick or stucco over brick, with a full classical entablature and modillion cornice
Interior joinery of London quality — full-height raised panelling, carved overmantels, correct orders — executed by immigrant craftsmen
Detached kitchen and service buildings in the rear yard, connected by a covered way
Fenestration and plan organized around cross-ventilation, with aligned openings front to back
diagnostic_tells: A false door in the street wall or garden wall that opens onto a piazza, not into a room
Ceiling heights visibly greater than any Northern colonial house of equivalent status
Superimposed classical orders on the piazza — Tuscan or Doric below, Ionic above
Stuccoed and scored brick imitating ashlar on the principal elevation of the grandest houses
A raised basement of arcaded brick, with the entry stair rising a full storey

distinguished_from.difference: The single house is a plan type — one room wide, end to the street — that persists in Charleston through the Federal and Greek Revival periods and beyond. Charleston Georgian is a style expression that may or may not be housed in a single-house plan; the grandest Georgian examples are double houses, four rooms to a floor, facing the street conventionally.

Tidewater Georgian is a plantation architecture of freestanding five-part compositions on open land, with paired end chimneys and a formal land-and-river front. Charleston Georgian is urban, built on narrow deep town lots with party-wall constraints, and organizes itself around the piazza rather than around a symmetrical land approach.

New England Georgian is clapboarded, compact, low-ceilinged, and centred on heat retention with a tight double-pile plan. Charleston Georgian is brick or stucco, tall, thin in section, and centred on heat rejection.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Standard Georgian classical derivation from the order, with storey heights stretched vertically beyond English or Northern precedent for stack ventilation.
typical_ratios: Principal-floor ceiling 12'-14'; second floor 10'-12'; basement 8'-9'
Sash proportion approximately 2:1 height to width, taller than Northern Georgian at the same width
Piazza depth 10'-14', at least equal to the depth of an interior room
Room proportions commonly 3:4 and 2:3 in plan
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three to five bays on the show elevation; piazza bays set by the order, typically 9'-12' on centre.

massing_affinities.note: The dominant urban expression.
The 'double house' of the wealthiest merchants — Miles Brewton, Colonel William Rhett.
Charleston resisted continuous row building; even attached houses keep a side yard for air.

constraints.statement: The piazza must face within 45 degrees of southwest to catch the prevailing summer breeze and shade the long wall. A piazza on the north flank is decoration and defeats the type.

test.note: 225 degrees is due southwest; the expression is the angular distance from it.

constraints.statement: Principal-floor ceiling height not less than 11'-6'. Below that the vertical proportion of the sash and the stack effect both fail, and the interior reads as a Northern house with Southern trim.

test.note: 11ft6in converted to inches exactly (138in).

constraints.statement: Piazza columns must carry a correct entablature and use superimposed orders where two storeys occur — heavier order below, lighter above. Identical columns on both levels read as a modern deck.
Piazza depth minimum 10 feet, roof structurally continuous with or clearly subordinate to the main roof, never a shed applied to a finished wall.
Openings must align front to back through the plan to permit cross draft; a blocked enfilade of openings removes the reason the section is shaped this way.

exemplars.name: Miles Brewton House
exemplars.note: Ezra Waite, joiner. Double house with a two-storey pedimented portico, superimposed Doric and Ionic; generally considered the finest surviving Georgian town house in America.

exemplars.name: Drayton Hall
exemplars.location: Ashley River, Charleston County, South Carolina
exemplars.note: Palladian double portico, never modernized with plumbing or electricity; the most archaeologically intact Georgian house in the Lowcountry.

exemplars.name: Colonel John Stuart House
exemplars.note: Notable surviving interior joinery.

exemplars.name: Heyward-Washington House
exemplars.note: Double house on a single-house lot; Washington lodged here in 1791.

sources: McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses
Poston, The Buildings of Charleston: A Guide to the City's Architecture
Herman, Town House: Architecture and Material Life in the Early American City
Waterman, The Dwellings of Colonial America
Severens, Charleston: Antebellum Architecture and Civic Destiny

proportion_packs.note: PROMOTED to primary, and this is the one variant where the vertical module is the style. A 12–14 ft principal storey is not a Northern house stretched; it is a stack-ventilation device, and the pack's graduation must be re-anchored on it before any trim rule is run. Note the consequence the trim pack makes explicit: at a 13 ft ceiling the nineteen-part division finally lands where it was designed to, and the derived chair rail (32 3/4 in) is correct without judgment override — Charleston is the American room the classical derivation actually fits.

PROMOTED alongside the Ionic, because the piazza demands superimposed orders — Tuscan or Doric below carrying Ionic above — and the pair must be dimensioned from one authority or the two tiers will not agree. Two identical tiers read as a modern deck.
PROMOTED. Flemish bond over an arcaded raised basement; the basement arcade is a whole-course composition and the entry stair rises a full storey on it.

Retained but marginal. The piazza is framed in timber against a masonry body, so the bay governs the piazza and nothing else; the pack's own bay of 16 ft is too long for a piazza, whose bays run 9–12 ft on centre, set by the order rather than by the frame.

new-classical.name: New Classical

geography.hearth: New York (Classical America and the Institute of Classical Architecture) and South Bend, Indiana (the University of Notre Dame School of Architecture)

lineage.note: The one genuinely unbroken line, and unbroken precisely because it is textual. The Quattro Libri and its successors were never lost; a practitioner in 1985 could open the same book a practitioner in 1735 opened and derive the same building. Descent by treatise is the only kind that survives a century of institutional hostility.

The pedagogy rather than the buildings: the atelier method, the analytique, the esquisse, and the discipline of drawing the orders from measurement. Classical America, founded 1968 by survivors and students of that training, is the institutional bridge across the modernist interval.

The American domestic dialect: the practical means by which classical detail survived in ordinary residential work through the twentieth century, in millwork catalogs and in the offices of a handful of persistent firms.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap, and the reference standard for domestic proportion in the movement's British wing.
The American reference standard, measured and re-measured; the movement's teaching examples are disproportionately Tidewater and Charleston houses.
Quoted for its severity and for its usefulness in civic work, but not descended from — the American Greek Revival's carpenter-classical means are not the means this movement uses.

description.short: The reconstitution of classical architecture as a live, taught, and practised discipline from the late 1960s onward, in which the orders are used as a working proportional system rather than quoted as motifs, and in which the pattern book and the code have returned as the medium of transmission.
description.long:
New Classical is a living tradition, not a revival style, and the distinction is load-bearing. A revival copies the appearance of a past architecture; this movement reconstituted the method — measured drawing, the derivation of every dimension from a chosen module, the correct construction of profiles, the hierarchy of orders — and then designed new buildings with it, including building types (concert halls, university science buildings, apartment towers) that no historical classicism ever addressed. Its practitioners will tell you, correctly, that the orders were the first parametric system with inheritance in the history of design: select Tuscan or Corinthian and several hundred subordinate dimensions follow automatically from the column diameter, cascading through entablature, pedestal, intercolumniation, and door surround. Anyone attempting to encode traditional design as software is re-implementing, with better tools, what Vitruvius, Serlio, and Gibbs each attempted with the tools of their centuries, and this node is where that observation stops being a metaphor.

The institutional history is short and specific. Classical America was founded in 1968, at the low-water mark, to keep the knowledge alive; the Institute of Classical Architecture followed in 1991, and the two merged in 2002 into what is now the ICAA, which teaches the orders in evening courses to practising architects who were never taught them in school. Thomas Gordon Smith became chairman at the University of Notre Dame in 1989 and rebuilt its curriculum around classical and traditional design, producing the only accredited American programme committed to it and, over three decades, a professional cohort. The Richard H. Driehaus Prize, first awarded in 2003, supplied the counterweight to the Pritzker. In Britain, Leon Krier's work for the Duchy of Cornwall at Poundbury from 1993 made the argument at town scale. Underneath the institutions runs a practical condition that is easy to miss: profiled work became affordable again. CNC stone milling, cast stone, computer-controlled millwork, and precision fibre-reinforced concrete made a correct cornice with a six-inch projection a purchasable item rather than a bespoke one, which is the material precondition for everything above.

What the movement reacts against is not modernism as a style — several of its practitioners admire it — but the twentieth-century assumption that architectural knowledge is generated by individual invention rather than accumulated and transmitted. Its answer is the same answer the eighteenth century gave: write it down and make it portable. The handbooks are the evidence. Robert Chitham's Classical Orders of Architecture, Robert Adam's Classical Architecture, and, at the domestic and builder end, Cusato and Hull's Get Your House Right — which is a pattern book in every meaningful sense, organized as a catalog of correct and incorrect versions of the same element. That last book's method, the paired right-and-wrong plate, is the most directly encodable thing in the entire contemporary traditional world, and it is the immediate ancestor of a rule-based constraint system.

What it is like in front of a good one is a matter of shadow and depth, which is precisely what the twentieth century's cost engineering removed. The window is set back four to eight inches from the wall face, so the opening has a dark edge and the wall reads as having thickness. The cornice projects far enough to throw a hard shadow line across the top of the facade at midday, which is what gives a building a top. The door surround stands five or six inches proud, and the mouldings within it are cut to profiles whose curvature has been argued about for two thousand years and which, at forty feet, resolve into a legible sequence of light and dark. Solid dominates void. The centre bay is wider or taller or more articulated than its neighbours, so the eye knows where to enter. None of this depends on ornament or expense in any simple sense: it depends on the willingness to spend the building's money on depth rather than on area, which is the one decision that separates this node from every other node in the contemporary group.

defining_characteristics: Every facade dimension derived from a single declared module — the column diameter of a chosen order, or an equivalent governing unit
Real profile depth: cornices, architraves, sills, and surrounds with projections measured in inches, not fractions of an inch
Wall thickness expressed through window and door reveals rather than assumed; openings recessed from the wall face
Bilateral symmetry about a hierarchically emphasized centre, with the entry as the largest and most articulated element
One order per elevation, correctly proportioned in all its parts, with superimposed orders in canonical sequence
Solid dominant over void on the principal elevation, and storey heights diminishing upward
Materials used structurally or in a manner that convincingly expresses structure: load-bearing or thick-veneer masonry, real stone or cast stone, solid timber joinery
diagnostic_tells: Window reveal depth of four inches or more in masonry — a shadow at the edge of every opening
A cornice that casts a hard continuous shadow line across the whole facade
Correct entablature subdivision, with architrave, frieze, and cornice in canonical proportion rather than as three arbitrary bands
A brick wall with a genuine water table, belt course, and moulded cap, all returning around every corner
No vinyl, no hollow extruded trim, no half-width shutters, no applied veneer with a short return — the absence of the neo-eclectic tells is itself diagnostic

distinguished_from.difference: Colonial Revival interprets freely for picturesque effect and tolerates approximate profiles and eclectic mixing; New Classical is proportionally disciplined and archaeologically informed, and treats a wrong entasis or a compressed entablature as an error rather than a liberty.

Quotation versus system. Both may show a pediment, a keystone, and a Palladian window; in one they are catalog items sized for visibility, in the other they are consequences of a module. Measure the projection of the cornice: under two inches, it is quotation.

A discipline of the building versus a discipline of the street. New Classical will produce a correct building on a bad street; New Urbanist Traditional will produce a good street out of plain buildings. In practice they collaborate, with the classical work taking the civic and terminating positions.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The classical module. A chosen order fixes the column diameter, and column height, entablature depth, intercolumniation, pedestal, storey height, and opening proportions are all derived from it. The system is parametric with inheritance and with declared defaults per order — which is to say it is already a kit-of-parts specification, and the best available model for one.
typical_ratios: Column height 7 diameters (Tuscan) to 10 diameters (Corinthian)
Entablature depth 1/4 to 1/5 of column height
Window opening 1:1.9 to 1:2.1, diminishing in height with each storey above the principal floor
Principal storey 1.2 to 1.4 times the storey above it
Solid to void on the principal elevation 60:40 to 70:30
Cornice projection not less than 1/24 of the wall height it terminates, minimum 8 in
Masonry reveal 4 to 8 in; wood reveal not less than 2 in
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Odd-numbered bays — three, five, seven, nine — with the centre bay emphasized by width, by an order, or by a frontispiece; end bays may be paired or terminated by quoins or pilasters.

massing_affinities.note: Centre block with hyphens and dependencies; the movement's signature parti for large houses and the one that solves the garage by turning it into a dependency.
The workhorse skeleton for houses of moderate size, and the one on which the proportional discipline is most easily verified.
The urban condition, where the movement has produced its most convincing large work.

constraints.statement: All facade dimensions shall be derived from one declared module. The module and the chosen order must be recorded with the design; elements not derivable from it are forbidden.
Window and door openings shall be recessed not less than 4 in from the wall face in masonry, and not less than 2 in in wood construction. Flush-mounted windows are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the looser of the two material-conditional floors (2in, wood construction); masonry's stricter 4in floor is not caught by this test, mirroring the flagged-imprecision pattern used for spanish-colonial-american's wall-slenderness constraint -- there is no schema-honest way to make this one test exact without a material variable.

constraints.statement: Principal cornice projection not less than 1/24 of the wall height it terminates, and in no case less than 8 in.

test.note: Combines both of the statement's clauses exactly: cornice_projection_in must be at least 1/24 of facade_height_ft (converted to inches) AND at least 8in absolute, expressed via max() so neither clause is silently dropped.

constraints.statement: One order per elevation. Where orders are superimposed they must ascend in canonical sequence (Tuscan or Doric below, Ionic, then Corinthian or Composite above) and diminish in diameter upward.
Hollow extruded trim, veneer with returns under 24 in, shutters narrower than the sash they flank, and snap-in muntins without exterior profile are forbidden throughout.

test.note: Tests the veneer-return clause only. 'Hollow extruded trim', 'shutters narrower than the sash they flank' (ambiguous against shutter_leaf_to_sash_ratio, which is calibrated to a paired-leaf-covers-half-opening convention rather than a single full-width shutter panel), and 'snap-in muntins without exterior profile' are categorical/qualitative and stay prose.

exemplars.name: Schermerhorn Symphony Center
exemplars.note: David M. Schwarz Architects. A new building type designed entirely within the classical system, with a full Doric peristyle and correct entablature at civic scale.

exemplars.name: 15 Central Park West
exemplars.note: Robert A. M. Stern Architects. Limestone-clad, base-shaft-cap, with real reveals and cornices at high-rise scale — proof that the system survives the change of building type and the change of structural material.

exemplars.name: Poundbury
exemplars.note: Leon Krier's masterplan for the Duchy of Cornwall, under construction from 1993. The movement's argument made at town scale, and its most-tested and most-criticized case.

sources: Leon Krier, The Architecture of Community (2009)
Robert Chitham, The Classical Orders of Architecture, 2nd ed. (2005)
Robert Adam, Classical Architecture: A Complete Handbook (1990)
Marianne Cusato and Brent Hull, Get Your House Right: Architectural Elements to Use and Avoid (2007)
Andrea Palladio, I Quattro Libri dell'Architettura (1570), still the movement's working reference

proportion_packs.note: Palladio is named directly in the node's own sources as 'still the movement's working reference,' and its lineage weights palladian descent highest of the whole edge list (0.55). Doric bound primary/civic register: constraint c04 requires superimposed orders to ascend 'Tuscan or Doric below, Ionic, then Corinthian or Composite above,' and the movement's own flagship civic exemplar (Schermerhorn Symphony Center, 'a full Doric peristyle and correct entablature at civic scale') is Doric. Palladio's overlay rather than Vignola's because the node's sources list is explicit and singular on this point -- unlike georgian-colonial-american, whose Gibbs choice had to be justified from inventory evidence, this node states its own primary text outright.

The paired upper order in the same c04 superimposition sequence ('Corinthian or Composite above'), and the register the node's own typical_ratios reach for at the top of their column-height range (up to 10 diameters, the Corinthian figure this pack's own module gives). Bound secondary to carry the grander domestic and high-rise register the exemplar 15 Central Park West occupies ('limestone-clad, base-shaft-cap... proof that the system survives the change of building type and the change of structural material') where the civic Doric register alone would not reach.

Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to. Constraint c01 ('All facade dimensions shall be derived from one declared module... elements not derivable from it are forbidden') is this pack's bay-module arithmetic stated as the node's own governing law rather than as a convention, and the canonical massing affinity five-part-palladian is this pack's odd-bay, double-square composition at its most literal. Bound below the two order packs because, per the node's own governing_logic, the order supplies the module the facade divides from -- 'choose the order, take its column height from the storey, and let the bay follow the intercolumniation' is this pack's own instruction and it is New Classical's actual stated working method.

Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to. Constraint c02 (window/door reveal not less than 4 in in masonry, 2 in in wood; flush-mounted windows forbidden) restates this pack's reveal logic as a hard rule, and the node's own diagnostic_tells ('Window reveal depth of four inches or more in masonry -- a shadow at the edge of every opening') is this pack's whole argument about expressed wall thickness stated as the style's signature tell.

Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to. The node's diagnostic_tells ('Correct entablature subdivision, with architrave, frieze, and cornice in canonical proportion rather than as three arbitrary bands') and its distinguished_from entry against neo-eclectic ('Measure the projection of the cornice: under two inches, it is quotation') are this pack's room-as-an-order derivation and cornice-projection rules read outward onto the whole building rather than confined to the interior wall. Bound as the interior system and the source of the cornice-depth diagnostic that separates this node from both neo-eclectic and colonial-revival.

Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to, and about as direct a match as exists anywhere in this assignment: the node's long description frames the orders as 'the first parametric system with inheritance,' which is this pack's own argument in different words, and the node's sources list Palladio's Quattro Libri as the movement's working reference -- the exact treatise this pack transcribes. The node's own typical_ratios ('Principal storey 1.2 to 1.4 times the storey above it') restates this pack's storey-diminution logic directly.

Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to. The node's own typical_ratios ('storey heights diminishing upward' per defining_characteristics; 'Principal storey 1.2 to 1.4 times the storey above it') sit just outside the upper edge of this pack's measured second-storey-over-first band (0.78-0.92, i.e. the inverse of 1.09-1.28), which is itself consistent rather than contradictory: a living practice reasserting the historical convention slightly more strictly than the surviving Georgian and Federal fabric this pack measures against.

queen-anne-american.name: Queen Anne (American)

revival_periods.note: The Neo-Victorian speculative house of the late twentieth century borrows the turret and the wraparound porch while abandoning the dominant-mass and multi-texture rules that make the style cohere.

geography.hearth: Newport and Boston, then nationally by rail

lineage.note: The real parent. Richard Norman Shaw's Old English and free-classic manner, published in The Building News and seen by Americans at the British pavilions of the 1876 Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia.
American practice inheritance: the same architects, carpenters, balloon frame, and millwork supply, and the half-timbered gable panel arrives via the Stick Style's applied board grid.

From the mid-1880s classical columns, Palladian windows, and dentilled cornices enter the style and produce the free classic variant. The mature Colonial Revival node descends from this one, so the substantive inheritance is recorded as the descends_from edge to georgian-colonial-american below.
Against the mansarded symmetrical pile and its French pretension, in favour of an English, domestic, textured, deliberately informal house.

Real transmission of the classical trim: measured drawings and photographs of surviving Georgian colonial work, published from the late 1870s, put correct column, cornice, and sash profiles back into builders' hands.

description.short: The dominant American house style of the 1880s and 1890s: an irregular, multi-textured, tower-bearing composition around one dominant mass, wrapped in porches and covered in machine-made ornament shipped by rail.
description.long:
The name is almost entirely wrong, and correcting it is the first thing a taxonomy owes this node. The American Queen Anne has no relationship to the reign of Queen Anne (1702-1714), nothing to do with English Baroque, and nothing to do with Wren, Vanbrugh, or Hawksmoor. The label was attached in 1860s and 1870s England by Richard Norman Shaw, W. Eden Nesfield, and their circle to a manner assembled from late-medieval and Jacobean English domestic building, tile-hung Sussex and Kent farmhouses, and freely handled classical trim, and the label stuck because it sounded respectable. Americans imported the label with the manner, largely through Shaw's published perspectives and the half-timbered British buildings at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition, and then developed it into something Shaw would barely have recognised. Treating this node as descended from English Baroque, which the name invites, is a category error that a machine-readable graph is well placed to prevent.

What America did with it was industrialise it completely. Shaw's houses were brick and tile, built by craftsmen, individually composed. The American version was balloon-framed pine and its entire ornamental vocabulary came out of a catalogue: turned porch posts, spindle friezes, cut shingles in fish-scale, diamond, and sawtooth patterns, sunburst gable panels, and coloured glass, all of it produced by steam-powered lathes and shingle mills in Michigan, Wisconsin, and the Pacific Northwest and distributed by rail to every town with a siding. The nationwide railroad network, essentially complete after 1869, is the reason a Queen Anne house in Eureka, California and one in Cape May, New Jersey share parts. This is the moment the American house becomes a national product, and it is also the moment placelessness becomes possible, which is a cost the style's enthusiasts rarely price.

Under all the ornament there is a genuine compositional discipline, and it is what separates a good Queen Anne from a bad one. The rule is that one mass must dominate: a great gable, a corner tower, or a broad hip, with everything else clearly subordinate to it. The second rule is that the wall must change texture, usually clapboard below and cut shingle above, with the change occurring at a horizontal band. The third is that the porch is a wrapping, connective element, not a portico. Where those three hold, the style produces houses of real spatial richness. Where they fail, and they fail constantly in the cheap examples and in nearly every modern imitation, the result is a lumpy accumulation of unrelated projections, which is the standing indictment of the whole Victorian century.

Standing in front of a good one is a matter of being kept in motion. The wraparound porch pulls you around the corner, the tower rotates the composition, and the wall changes material as your eye rises, so that the house appears to be built of successive layers, heavy at the ground and increasingly light and decorative toward the sky. Inside, the great innovation is the living hall: a large room containing the fireplace and the stair, opening through wide cased openings into parlour and dining room, so that the ground floor reads as a continuous flowing space rather than as a corridor with rooms off it. That plan, more than any amount of spindlework, is the American Queen Anne's real gift to everything that came after it, including the open plan of the twentieth century.

defining_characteristics: One dominant mass, whether gable, tower, or hip, with all other volumes clearly subordinate to it
At least two distinct wall textures on a principal elevation, changing at a horizontal band or storey line
Steeply pitched irregular roof, 9:12 or greater, with a complex non-rectangular ridge and at least one front-facing gable
A porch that wraps at least one corner, one storey high and of substantial depth
Projecting bays, oriels, or a tower breaking the wall plane on every principal elevation
Asymmetrical plan generating an asymmetrical elevation, with the living hall as the organising interior space
Machine-produced ornament: turned, sawn, or moulded, and concentrated at porch, gable, and cornice
diagnostic_tells: Round or polygonal corner tower with a conical or bell roof: the single fastest identification, though many Queen Annes have none
Cut shingles in fish-scale or diamond patterning filling a gable above clapboarded walls
Wraparound porch turning a corner, often widening into a round porch pavilion at the corner itself
Compared with Stick Style: curves are present. Turned posts, spindles, round towers, and arched porch openings all say Queen Anne
Compared with Shingle Style: the wall is articulated and layered rather than continuous, and the trim is visible and busy rather than suppressed
Windows frequently have a single large pane surrounded by a border of small coloured panes, a Shaw device transmitted intact

distinguished_from.difference: No relationship whatsoever, despite the name. Queen Anne Anne Stuart reigned 1702-1714 and her period produced English Baroque and early Palladianism; this style was named in the 1860s by architects who wanted a friendly English label for a picturesque manner drawn from Tudor, Jacobean, and vernacular sources. The graph must not carry an edge from this node to English Baroque.

The genuine parent, and materially different: Shaw's English work is brick, tile-hung, and craft-built, with real Jacobean and vernacular precedent close at hand. The American descendant is balloon-framed wood with catalogue ornament, and it is far more exuberant and far less disciplined.
Stick Style is rectilinear, panelised, and balanced among comparable masses; Queen Anne is curvilinear, textured, and requires a dominant mass. The presence of a single turned spindle settles it.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Not proportional. Governed by mass hierarchy and by textural layering: one dominant volume, subordinate volumes attached to it, and a wall that grows lighter and more decorative as it rises. The composition is checked in silhouette and in texture, never in module.
typical_ratios: Dominant mass at least 1.5 times the height or plan area of any subordinate mass
Roof pitch 9:12 to 14:12; tower roof steeper than the main roof
Porch depth 7 to 10 ft, wrapping not less than one full corner
Texture change at 60 to 75 percent of wall height, at a belt course or at the second-floor line
Bay or oriel projection 18 to 42 in from the wall plane
Tower diameter 8 to 14 ft where round
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: None regular. Openings are placed by room, and adjacent windows commonly differ in width, height, and head level. Whatever coherence exists comes from texture bands and from porch rhythm.

massing_affinities.note: Round or polygonal in the Queen Anne case, not the square Italianate campanile.
The San Francisco and Philadelphia rows, where the whole style is compressed into a 25 ft frontage.
The modest builder's Queen Anne; the boundary with Folk Victorian sits here.

constraints.statement: One mass shall dominate the composition, exceeding every other mass by at least 50 percent in either height above eave or plan area. A composition of equal masses is not Queen Anne; it is Stick Style or an incoherent accumulation.

Not fewer than two distinct wall textures shall appear on each principal elevation, and each texture change shall occur at a horizontal belt course, water table, or storey line. A texture change at a vertical joint or mid-panel is prohibited.
A porch not less than 7 ft deep shall wrap at least one external corner of the building, continuing not less than 8 ft along the returning elevation.

test.note: Tests the stated porch depth. The wrap-around requirement (turns the corner, continues >=8 ft along the returning elevation) is a linear-extent-along-a-second-elevation fact distinct from gallery_depth_ft's wall-to-outer-support depth measurement, and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Every principal elevation shall carry at least one projection of not less than 18 in: a bay, oriel, tower, or projecting gable. A flat unbroken principal elevation fails the style.
Principal roof pitch shall be 9:12 or greater and the ridge shall be non-rectangular in plan. A simple rectangular hip or gable with applied ornament is Folk Victorian, not Queen Anne.

test.note: Tests the roof-pitch clause. 'The ridge shall be non-rectangular in plan' is a plan-shape fact with no matching vocabulary variable and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Carson Mansion
exemplars.note: Samuel and Joseph Cather Newsom, 1884-86, for the lumber baron William Carson. Redwood, and the most elaborate surviving American Queen Anne; correctly read as Queen Anne with Eastlake, Italianate, and Stick elements.

exemplars.name: Haas-Lilienthal House
exemplars.note: Peter R. Schmidt. Redwood, on the local narrow deep-lot row-house plan; the best-preserved San Francisco Queen Anne open to the public.

exemplars.name: William Watts Sherman House
exemplars.note: H. H. Richardson, 1874-76, with later interiors by Stanford White. The American beginning of the Shaw manner; simultaneously the first American Queen Anne and the prototype of the Shingle Style, which is exactly why the graph needs multiple parents here.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Vincent Scully, The Shingle Style and the Stick Style (1955; rev. ed. 1971)
Mark Girouard, Sweetness and Light: The Queen Anne Movement 1860-1900 (1977)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)

proportion_packs.note: Explicit in this pack's applies_to, and it is close to a direct transcription of the node's own proportional_system: dominant mass at least 1.5x any subordinate (matches the pack's dominance rule range of 1.35-2.5), texture change at a horizontal belt or storey line, a porch that wraps a corner and does the compositional counterweighting. The node's own text states 'governed by mass hierarchy... checked in silhouette and texture, never in module' — this pack is the one system in the library built to formalize exactly that.

Explicit in this pack's applies_to. American Queen Anne windows of 1874-1915 fall in the pack's 1870-1900 glass band (large cylinder and polished plate), typically 1/1 or 2/2 with a single large pane bordered by small coloured panes at the upper sash — the node's own diagnostic tell of a Shaw-derived border-light window, which is a documented late-19th-century departure this pack's light-count arithmetic does not itself derive but does not contradict either.

JUDGMENT BINDING. Not in this pack's applies_to. Bound because American Queen Anne is balloon-framed, and balloon framing still faces the same joist-span and daylight physics room-vernacular reconstructs — no treatise governs these rooms, and the node explicitly says the composition is 'checked in silhouette and texture, never in module,' which rules out room-harmonic's Palladian ratios as squarely as it rules out a bay system on the elevation. The fit is imperfect at the top end: the living hall, described as the style's organising innovation, is often larger than the pack's 14-18 ft measured band and closer to its noted 'halls in houses of pretension' outlier case, which the pack allows for but does not centrally describe. Ordinary parlours and chambers fit the band comfortably.

spanish-classical.name: Spanish Classical

description.short: Plateresque and Churrigueresque — Spanish Renaissance and Baroque, in which classical structure carries an ornament of unmatched density.
description.long:
