Spanish classicism concentrates rather than distributes. A plain wall of great expanse is punctuated by a single entry or retable of overwhelming elaboration — the strategy is one of contrast, not of even articulation, and it is the opposite of the French or English classical habit.

Carried to the Americas, this strategy suited a labour economy in which skilled carving was available for a single focal point and nothing else. The result — vast plain adobe or stone walls with one intensely worked doorway — became the defining move of Spanish Colonial Revival four centuries later.

defining_characteristics: Ornament concentrated at a single focal point against large plain surfaces
Classical structure carrying non-classical densities of decoration
The retable façade as the organizing device
Adaptation to labour economies where skilled carving is scarce

british-vernacular.name: British Vernacular

description.short: The unselfconscious regional building of the English countryside — Cotswold limestone, thatch, cob, and brick — later mined by revivalists for a whole century of cottage imagery.
description.long:
Regional vernacular in Britain is defined by geology. The Cotswolds build in oolitic limestone with stone-slate roofs because that is what the ground yields; East Anglia builds in flint and timber; the West Country in cob. Each produces a distinct language of wall thickness, roof pitch, opening size, and colour without any of it being designed.

The revival of this material from the 1890s onward — and its export to America as the Cotswold cottage and the Storybook style — is a case worth studying closely: a building culture generated entirely by local constraint, reproduced in places where none of those constraints apply.

defining_characteristics: Material determined by local geology, and everything else following from it
Steep roofs sized to the covering material — thatch, stone slate, or clay tile
Small irregular openings and very thick walls
Growth by accretion, producing irregular plans and rooflines
No designer, no date, no name

victorian.name: Victorian

description.short: The high era of American picturesque: Second Empire, Stick, Queen Anne, Richardsonian, Shingle, and the Folk Victorian that carried it to every small town.
description.long:
The Victorian styles share a method rather than a vocabulary: a dominant mass, a complex silhouette, multiple wall textures, and ornament used to animate surface rather than to articulate structure. What changes between them is which historical wardrobe is drawn on and how much of it.

Two nodes in this family carry outsized importance. Shingle Style is the taxonomy's best reticulation case — at least three genuine parents, none dominant. Folk Victorian is the mass-market case: vernacular massing plus catalog-ordered spindlework shipped by rail, ornament fully decoupled from structure and geography. Folk Victorian is the nineteenth century rehearsing exactly the problem a kit-of-parts platform now faces.

defining_characteristics: A dominant mass with a deliberately complex silhouette
Multiple wall textures within a single elevation
Ornament as surface animation rather than structural articulation
Catalog and railroad distribution decoupling ornament from place
Rapid stylistic turnover driven by fashion and by publication

pueblo-revival.name: Pueblo Revival

revival_periods.note: Continuous production as a regional and regulatory default in northern New Mexico; Santa Fe's historic-district ordinance has effectively mandated the style since 1957.

geography.hearth: Santa Fe, New Mexico

lineage.note: The principal claimed ancestor - New Mexican Spanish and Hispano adobe building, itself already a fusion of Iberian technique with Puebloan wall construction. The revival also references Ancestral and historic Puebloan building directly; the taxonomy has no separate node for it.
The mission-church register - buttressed facades, twin towers, deep entry - transmitted through the Franciscan churches of New Mexico, San Esteban del Rey at Acoma above all.

Real transmission. Same decade, same exposition circuit, same professional argument that a Southwestern state needed a Hispanic-derived identity. Retyped: Pueblo Revival originates c.1905-08 at the University of New Mexico, before Spanish Colonial Revival, and the two co-emerge on the same exposition circuit rather than one descending from the other.
The Anglo artist colonies at Santa Fe and Taos, and the Craftsman ethic of visible structure and handled surface, supplied both the clientele and the aesthetic justification.
The Rapp brothers were a conventional commercial practice; the exposition pavilion, the reinforced-concrete frame and the drafting method all come from mainstream professional culture.

The direct Southwestern predecessor in the market and in the professional imagination, though Pueblo Revival takes its forms from Puebloan and New Mexican adobe rather than from the California missions.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The Santa Fe style: flat-roofed, parapeted, earth-coloured buildings with battered walls, projecting vigas, and stepped massing, invented between 1908 and 1917 by Anglo architects and boosters assembling a marketable regional identity from Puebloan and Hispano New Mexican building.
description.long:
Pueblo Revival is unusually well documented as an act of invention, because the people who invented it wrote down what they were doing. New Mexico achieved statehood in 1912; Santa Fe's economy was failing; and a committee of the city's Anglo civic leadership, working with the Museum of New Mexico and the archaeologist Edgar Lee Hewett, resolved to give the town a coherent architectural character that could be sold to tourists. The instrument was the New Mexico Building at the 1915 Panama-California Exposition in San Diego, designed by Rapp & Rapp of Trinidad, Colorado, and modelled on the Franciscan mission church of San Esteban del Rey at Acoma. The same firm then built the permanent version in Santa Fe as the Museum of Fine Arts in 1917, drawing additionally on the mission churches at Laguna, Cochiti, San Felipe, Santa Ana and Pecos. That building fixed the style. From 1957 Santa Fe's historic ordinance made it, in effect, mandatory downtown.

The vocabulary is consistent. Walls are flat-planed, thick, rounded at the corners and arrises, battered outward at the base, and finished in earth-toned stucco over adobe, concrete block, or wood frame. Roofs are flat and drained through canales - projecting spouts - behind parapets whose tops are irregular and gently undulating rather than level. Peeled log roof beams, vigas, project through the wall face; latillas or corbels appear at porch structures. Massing is stepped and terraced, blocks of differing heights set back from one another to recall the multi-storey Puebloan roomblock. Openings are small relative to wall, deeply recessed, and often carry a heavy timber lintel. Portales - post-and-corbel covered porches - run along principal facades.

The appropriation question is not incidental to the style; it is its history. Pueblo Revival takes its imagery from living Native communities - Taos, Acoma, Zuni and the Rio Grande pueblos - who were not consulted, did not profit, and were simultaneously subject to federal assimilation policy that suppressed the culture the style was marketing. It also flattens the Hispano contribution, since New Mexican adobe by 1900 had a substantial Territorial-period vocabulary of milled wood, pediments and porches which the revival stripped out as insufficiently picturesque. Chris Wilson's The Myth of Santa Fe (1997) is the standard critical account and traces in detail how the style was designed, legislated, and sold. It is also true that Pueblo Revival is climatically intelligent, has produced buildings of real quality, and is now a genuine regional tradition with New Mexican practitioners of every background. Both facts are load-bearing and neither cancels the other.

To stand before a good one is to lose the sense of a building as an assembly of parts. There are no eaves, no fascias, no gutters, no corner boards, no visible joints - the whole thing is one continuous rounded surface the colour of the ground it stands on, and the only interruptions are the vigas, which read as a row of dark punctuation, and the shadowed slot of a window. In the high New Mexican light the wall goes almost white at noon and burnt orange at five o'clock. The interiors are low, thick, and quiet, with beamed ceilings and small deep windows, and they hold their temperature the way the earth does, which is the reason the form existed before anyone thought to revive it.

defining_characteristics: Flat roof drained through projecting canales behind an irregular, gently undulating parapet
Thick earth-toned stucco walls with rounded corners and arrises and a visible batter at the base
Projecting peeled log vigas penetrating the wall face below the parapet
Stepped, terraced massing of blocks at differing heights, set back from one another
Small, deeply recessed openings with heavy timber lintels; low solid-to-void ratio favouring wall
Portal - a post-and-corbel covered porch with peeled log posts and carved corbels - on at least one principal elevation
No eave, fascia, gutter, corner board, or applied trim anywhere on the exterior
diagnostic_tells: Flat roof plus vigas plus rounded corners. Any one of the three alone is inconclusive; all three together are decisive.
The parapet top is not level. A dead-straight parapet indicates a Territorial or commercial building rather than Pueblo Revival.
Vigas are round peeled logs 8-12 in. in diameter projecting 12-24 in. Square sawn timbers projecting from a wall are Territorial or Spanish Colonial Revival, not Pueblo Revival.
No brick coping. A brick dentil course capping the parapet marks the Territorial Revival variant, which is a distinct and equally common New Mexican type.

Against the genuine article: real adobe walls are 18-36 in. thick with proportionate reveals and visible settlement; the revival often achieves the look in 2 in. of stucco over frame, and the reveal depth is the tell.

distinguished_from.difference: The original is load-bearing adobe brick, mud-plastered and replastered annually, with walls 18-36 in. thick, a plan generated by adding rooms in single-file, and after 1850 a large admixture of milled Territorial woodwork. The revival is usually frame or block with stucco, is composed as a picturesque whole in one campaign, and deliberately omits the Territorial layer as inauthentic.

Spanish Colonial Revival has pitched red tile roofs, carved or cast entrance ornament, wrought iron and decorative tile. Pueblo Revival has flat roofs, no tile, no worked ornament, and substitutes timber and earth for iron and glaze.
Mission Revival has a pitched tile roof and a curvilinear shaped parapet on smooth machine-flat stucco. Pueblo Revival has a flat roof, an irregular parapet, rounded wall surfaces, and vigas.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The adobe course and the viga span. Wall thickness and the practical clear span of a peeled log - 14 to 18 ft - set room sizes; the absence of any framing module means proportion is judged as sculptural mass rather than as composition.
typical_ratios: Wall base batter 1 in 24 to 1 in 40 over the lower 3-6 ft
Apparent wall thickness at reveals 12-24 in.; genuine adobe 18-36 in.
Vigas 8-12 in. diameter at 24-36 in. on centre, projecting 12-24 in. past the wall face
Parapet height above roof deck 18-30 in., varying by at least 4 in. along its run
Openings 1:1.2 to 1:1.6, solid-to-void ratio 8:1 or greater on principal elevations
Portal posts 8-10 in. square or round at 7-9 ft on centre, with corbels 30-42 in. long
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Additive and irregular. Openings are placed by internal need, do not align between storeys, and are separated by broad blank wall. The only regular rhythm on the building is the viga row and the portal posts.

massing_affinities.note: The stepped, terraced accumulation of flat-roofed blocks at differing heights is the whole formal idea.
The placita house - ranges around an enclosed court - is the historically correct New Mexican domestic plan and the strongest residential option.
Larger institutional and hacienda examples with a fully enclosed placita.
Where a continuous portal fronts a linear range; the standard Santa Fe street condition.
A symmetrical double-pile block with a centred entrance is fundamentally alien to the type.

constraints.statement: Roof must be flat or near-flat, maximum 1/4 in. per foot to internal or canale drainage, concealed behind a parapet 18-30 in. above the roof deck whose top line varies by at least 4 in. over its length. Any pitched roof visible from a principal elevation voids the style.

test.note: Tests the parapet height range concealing the roof. Roof drainage slope (max 1/4in per foot) and the required >=4in variation in the parapet top line over its length (an irregularity requirement, no matching vocabulary variable) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Vigas, where expressed, must be round peeled logs 8-12 in. in diameter projecting 12-24 in. beyond the wall face at 24-36 in. on centre, and must occur only where a roof or ceiling structure could plausibly bear on that wall. Vigas on a gable end, on a parapet above a roof, or on an elevation with no floor behind it are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the viga projection beyond the wall face (this variable's own docstring names viga ends explicitly). Viga diameter (8-12in) and spacing (24-36in o.c.) have no matching vocabulary variable; the plausible-bearing-location clause is qualitative. Both stay prose.

constraints.statement: Wall thickness must be expressed with a minimum 10 in. reveal at all openings, jambs and heads returned in stucco, corners and parapet arrises radiused not less than 3 in. No eave, fascia, gutter, downspout, corner bead line, or applied trim may appear on the exterior.

test.note: Corner/parapet arris radius (>=3in, no matching vocabulary variable) and the prohibition on eave, fascia, gutter, downspout, corner bead, and applied trim stay prose.

constraints.statement: Solid-to-void ratio not less than 6:1 on principal elevations, with no single opening wider than 6'0". Large glass areas belong on courtyard-facing elevations only.

test.note: Tests the 6:1 solid-to-void floor as void/solid <= 1/6 (~0.1667), the same convention as void_to_solid_ratio's other corpus uses. The single-opening width cap (<=6'0", no matching vocabulary variable) stays prose.

constraints.statement: This style quotes the built forms of living Puebloan communities. Where a project is sited in or adjacent to Native land, or is intended to represent Native culture, the design should be developed with the relevant community rather than from the published Santa Fe vocabulary.

exemplars.name: New Mexico Building, Panama-California Exposition
exemplars.note: Rapp & Rapp, modelled on the mission church of San Esteban del Rey at Acoma Pueblo. The founding building of the style; survives as the Balboa Park Club.

exemplars.name: New Mexico Museum of Art (Museum of Fine Arts)
exemplars.note: Rapp, Rapp & Hendrickson, 1915-17. The permanent version of the exposition building, drawing additionally on Laguna, Cochiti, San Felipe, Santa Ana and Pecos. It fixed Santa Fe Style for the century.

exemplars.name: La Fonda on the Plaza
exemplars.note: Rapp & Rapp; substantially remodelled and enlarged by John Gaw Meem from 1929. The commercial and touristic centre of the style.

exemplars.name: Zimmerman Library, University of New Mexico
exemplars.note: John Gaw Meem, 1936-38. Pueblo Revival at institutional scale and at its highest level of design control.

sources: Chris Wilson, The Myth of Santa Fe: Creating a Modern Regional Tradition (1997)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Bainbridge Bunting, John Gaw Meem: Southwestern Architect (1983)
Marc Treib, Sanctuaries of Spanish New Mexico (1993)
City of Los Angeles, SurveyLA Citywide Historic Context Statement: Mediterranean and Indigenous Revival Architecture, 1893-1948

proportion_packs.note: The strongest fit in this whole binding pass. This style's own proportional_system states that 'the practical clear span of a peeled log - 14 to 18 ft - set room sizes', against room-vernacular's own module of a 14 ft joist-span-limited room breadth in an 11-18 ft measured range -- the same physical constraint (a beam's practical span) recovered independently by two different routes. This style's symmetry is recorded as 'additive-vernacular', and room-vernacular's own notes single out Glassie's finding that the vernacular builder 'worked from a square base unit and generated the house by adding, halving and extending it' -- the identical generative logic behind the placita house's single-file room ranges. The direct ancestor new-mexico-adobe is itself listed in the pack's own applies_to. Bind for the module, the daylight-depth rule, and the additive room-count logic; do not carry over the hearth-width rule, since a corner fireplace heats a Pueblo Revival room differently than the cooking-hearth-reach logic that shaped the Anglo-American vernacular record this pack is built from.

Anticipated in the pack's own applies_to list, which already names pueblo-revival directly. This style's c03 forbids essentially all exterior applied trim outright ('no eave, fascia, gutter, downspout, corner bead line, or applied trim may appear on the exterior'), so this binding governs interior door and window casing only, and even there most Pueblo Revival interiors sit close to the pack's own 'plainest work' floor of two members rather than its full three-member assembly. Flat stock and a butted joint are the only trim vocabulary consistent with a style that has no order and, per its own governing_logic, no framing module to derive one from either.

norman-vernacular.name: Norman Vernacular

revival_periods.note: Style balneaire normand — the resort villas of Deauville, Trouville and Cabourg, which invent the picturesque Norman cottage as a leisure product and are the immediate source of what America copied.
American French Normandy Revival: the round stair tower, colombage panels and steep hipped or conical roof, transmitted by soldiers, photographs and architects returning from the First World War.
The looser American French Eclectic mode draws its half-timbered subtype from here.

geography.hearth: Pays d'Auge and the Bocage, Calvados

lineage.note: Not descent in either direction but a genuine exchange zone: Norman and southern English carpentry traded techniques, timber and craftsmen across the Channel continuously from the 12th to the 16th century, and close studding appears on both shores. Kit inheritance is deliberately left off this edge because the two dialects diverge in infill, roof and section.

description.short: The close-studded oak frame, clay-and-straw infill and steep thatched or tiled roof of the Norman bocage, produced by an apple-and-dairy economy on wet clay ground with no good building stone and a great deal of oak.
description.long:
Norman vernacular is what a landscape of hedged fields, cider apples and dairy cattle builds when it has oak and clay and nothing else. The Pays d'Auge sits on heavy impermeable clay: it will not drain, it grows grass superbly, it makes bad foundations and excellent daub. The consequence is a building culture with three fixed rules. Timber does the structure. Clay and straw fill the gaps. And nothing made of either touches the ground — every frame stands on a stone soubassement of forty centimetres or more, because a sill beam set into Auge clay rots inside a decade. Where stone appears at all in this architecture it appears there, at the bottom, doing the one job the frame cannot do.

The framing is close-studded: vertical oak posts set at half a metre to eighty centimetres, far tighter than they need to be structurally, producing the dense vertical striping that reads as Normandy from a kilometre away. The tightness is partly a wealth display — close studding wastes oak, and wasting oak was the point — and partly a practical response to the panel infill, which is torchis, clay mixed with chopped straw and pressed onto riven hazel or chestnut laths. A torchis panel is stable at about half a metre wide and cracks if it is much wider. From the seventeenth century brick nogging arrives and the panels are filled with small bricks in herringbone or in a chequer of red and vitrified black, which is later, harder, and a completely different thing to look at. Roofs are thatch of wheat straw or reed at fifty to sixty degrees, later flat clay tile, and the weather elevation — the west and south-west face that takes the Atlantic rain — is very often hung entirely in slate or split chestnut shingle over the frame, a technique called essentage that shows how seriously the tradition took driving rain.

The farmstead is dispersed rather than merged, and this is the sharpest contrast with the German and Flemish types across the same latitude. A Norman farm is a loose scatter of separate single-purpose buildings inside a walled or hedged enclosure planted with apple trees: the logis, the pressoir with its circular horse-driven apple mill, the charreterie, the etable, the boulangerie, and often a freestanding colombier whose right to exist was a legal privilege of the seigneurie. Nothing is attached to anything. The reason is partly fire, partly the mildness of a maritime winter that does not require the German solution of bringing everything indoors, and partly the specific rhythms of cider-making and dairying, which want separate cool buildings rather than one warm one.

The interior is low, dark and heavily beamed. Ceilings are the underside of the floor above, joists exposed at close centres; the fireplace is a wide open hearth in a gable wall with a bread oven bulging out behind it; the floor is beaten earth or later terracotta tomettes. Windows are small and few, because a torchis panel wall does not want holes in it, so the light comes in hard shafts and the corners of the room stay dark all day. What you notice standing in one is the smell of oak and old smoke and, in autumn, apples, and the fact that everything you can see — every beam, every peg, every panel — was made within a few miles of where you are standing.

defining_characteristics: Close-studded oak frame with posts at roughly 0.5-0.8 m centres, exposed inside and out
Panels of torchis (clay and chopped straw over riven laths), or from the 17th century brick nogging laid in herringbone or chequer
Frame standing on a stone soubassement of at least 400 mm; no structural timber in contact with the ground
Steep roof — 50-60 degrees for thatch, 45 and up for flat clay tile — with a substantial overhang
The rain-bearing elevation frequently hung in slate or split shingle (essentage) over the frame
Dispersed farmstead of separate single-purpose buildings within a hedged or walled enclosure, not merged under one roof
Single-pile ranges, one room deep, lit and ventilated from both faces
diagnostic_tells: Vertical studs far closer together than structure requires, with almost no visible bracing on the front face
A stone base course carrying the whole frame clear of the ground, always visible, never hidden by planting in an authentic example
Panels that are white or ochre earth on early work, red-and-black brick chequer on later work — the two rarely mixed on one elevation
A separate pressoir or colombier standing free in the same enclosure
Slate or shingle hanging on one elevation only, and always the westerly one

distinguished_from.difference: German framing is panel-based with heavy expressive bracing, carved and lettered sill beams, and a jettied multi-storey urban street front. Norman framing is close-studded, almost unbraced on the face, undecorated, rural, and rarely above two storeys.

The manoir is the same craft with money: the same carpenters and masons, but a great hall, croisee windows, a projecting stair turret, a moat or walled cour and an ensemble of ancillary buildings of architectural pretension. A vernacular farm has none of those and does not aspire to them.

The American revival keeps the round stair tower and the half-timber panel and discards the frame, the dispersion, the essentage and the roof pitch. Its half-timbering is nailed to sheathing; the diagnostic is panels not framed on four sides.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Structural and material. Stud spacing of 0.5-0.8 m is fixed by the width at which a torchis panel is stable; range depth of 5-6 m is fixed by the span of an oak floor joist and the pitch of the roof over it. There is no compositional module at all — the elevation is the frame, and the openings are omitted studs.
typical_ratios: Stud spacing 0.5-0.8 m; panel proportion roughly 1:2 to 1:4 (tall and narrow)
Range depth 5-6 m clear; storey height 2.1-2.5 m
Roof pitch 50-60 degrees (thatch), 45-55 (flat tile)
Soubassement 0.4-0.8 m above grade
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Dense, uniform vertical striping with no accentuated bay. Windows and doors are made by leaving out one, two or three studs and framing the gap, so openings always sit on the stud grid.

massing_affinities.note: The one-room-deep, one-or-two-room-long logis is the unit from which everything else in the enclosure is a variation.
Where buildings do connect they connect end to end at the gable, producing a stepped chain rather than a merged volume.
Successive additions at the gable end, each lower and narrower — the same growth grammar as the Chesapeake type, arrived at independently.
Reached only at the top of the vernacular range, where a rich farm begins to behave like a small manoir.

constraints.statement: The bottom sill must rest on a stone or brick soubassement of at least 400 mm above finished grade, with a drip or oversail. Clay ground plus an oak sill at grade is a ten-year building.

test.note: Tests the soubassement height floor. The drip/oversail detailing clause is qualitative and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Stud spacing 0.5-0.8 m; torchis panels must not exceed about 0.6 m clear width. Openings are formed by omitting whole studs and framing the resulting gap — an opening cannot be cut through a stud.

Roof pitch not less than 50 degrees for thatch or 45 for flat tile; overhang at least 350 mm at eave and 250 mm at verge. The rain-bearing westerly elevation should be slate- or shingle-hung, or given a wider overhang.

test.note: Tests the looser of the two material-conditional floors (45deg for flat tile); thatch's stricter 50deg floor is not caught by this test, mirroring the flagged-imprecision pattern used for spanish-colonial-american's wall-slenderness constraint -- there is no schema-honest way to make this one test exact without a material variable. Eave/verge overhang (350mm/250mm) and the westerly-elevation weathering clause are the statement's other claims and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Single-pile only: clear range depth not to exceed 6 m. Depth is added by a second detached building in the enclosure, not by thickening the range.

test.note: Source states clear range depth in metres; kept as stated. 'Depth is added by a second detached building' is qualitative and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Torchis panels and brick nogging belong to different centuries and must not be mixed on one elevation. Where a building has both, the brick marks a later rebuilt wall and should read as such.

exemplars.name: Manoir de Coupesarte
exemplars.note: 15th-16th century; moated timber-framed manor with overhanging turrets, and the best-known demonstration of Auge close studding at any scale. Classe monument historique.

exemplars.name: Aitre Saint-Maclou
exemplars.note: Built 1526-1533 as a plague ossuary; a timber-framed courtyard with carved galleries, showing the urban end of the same carpentry.

exemplars.name: Manoir de Bellou
exemplars.note: 16th century; a colombage manor and its farm ensemble, largely unaltered.

exemplars.name: Beuvron-en-Auge
exemplars.note: A village of 16th-18th century colombage houses retained substantially intact; useful as an ensemble rather than a single object.

sources: Lescroart, Manoirs du Pays d'Auge
Doyon & Hubrecht, L'Architecture rurale et bourgeoise en France
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World
Trochet, Maisons paysannes en France et leur environnement

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to. This node's own single-pile depth constraint (norman-vernacular.c04, clear range depth not exceeding 6 m) sits almost exactly inside the pack's depth_and_pile range (192-264 in / 16-22 ft), because both are the same underlying rule: a single-pile room cannot be deeper than one joist/rafter span. Caveat: the pack's own bay module (16-20 ft, bent-to-bent) is not the close-studded frame's actual visible module — Norman studs stand at 0.5-0.8 m centres, a finer grid the pack does not model (see gaps) — so this is bound for the range-depth and growth-by-addition logic, not for the stud grid itself.

Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to. The logis is the single-pile, two-face-lit, hearth-limited room this pack describes almost verbatim, and its dispersed-farmstead growth (colombier, pressoir and etables as separate single-purpose buildings around a hedged enclosure) is the same generative logic — 'a household that needs more room builds another building' — the pack states as the mechanism behind the whole Anglo-American folk-house catalogue, extended here to the Norman farm.

greek-revival-northern.name: Northern Greek Revival

revival_periods.note: The gable-front-with-returns and the pilastered doorway are absorbed into the generic 'Colonial' kit and detached from their proportional rules.

geography.hearth: the Erie Canal corridor, upstate New York

lineage.note: The same white-painted clapboard carpentry culture, retooled. Asher Benjamin's audience did not change between 1806 and 1830; only his plates did.

description.short: The Greek Revival as a settlement architecture: white clapboard temple fronts and gable-front cottages built by New England carpenters along the Erie Canal and across the Western Reserve, at a density that makes it the default historic house of the northern countryside.
description.long:
Northern Greek Revival is the largest single deposit of any one style in American domestic building, and it is almost entirely wooden. Its ingredients are simple: a rectangular block turned so its gable faces the road, corner pilasters carrying a deep entablature, a frieze board a foot or more tall with small windows cut into it, cornice returns clipped across the gable base to imply a pediment, and a doorway of rectangular transom and sidelights inside a heavy pilastered surround. On the better houses the pediment becomes real and a portico of two, four or six columns stands in front of it, with a lower wing or two set back at the sides. On the ordinary ones the whole classical apparatus reduces to trim boards and a doorway, and it still reads as Greek Revival at three hundred yards because the proportions are right: the roof is low, the eave is heavy, the trim is broad and flat.

The conditions were migration, water transport and cheap sawn pine, arriving together in one decade. The Erie Canal opened in 1825; between then and 1850 the Yankee population moved west along it in enormous numbers into upstate New York, the Western Reserve of Ohio, and then Michigan, northern Indiana and Illinois. They arrived in a landscape with no building traditions they were obliged to respect, carrying a New England carpentry culture and, very often, a copy of Asher Benjamin or Minard Lafever in the tool chest. The water-powered sash and blind mills of the Mohawk and Genesee valleys supplied millwork by canal boat; machine-cut nails and, after the 1830s, balloon framing made a broad flat-trimmed wooden building fast to raise with a small crew. The result is astonishing uniformity across a thousand miles: a farmhouse in Ann Arbor and one near Rochester will share a frieze detail because they share a handbook and a millwork supplier. This is the first time in American history that a style spreads by infrastructure rather than by apprenticeship, and it is the direct ancestor of the mail-order house sixty years later.

What it reacted against was the Federal that its own carpenters had been building. Federal had thinned everything; the Greek generation wanted mass, and in a wooden building mass has to be faked by width of board. The corner pilaster is a twelve-inch plank. The entablature is three boards. The column, where there is one, is built up of staves like a barrel and hollow inside. The whole enterprise is a carpenter's illusion of stone, painted white lead to complete the deception - and the North took the deception further than the South, because in a climate that demands tight walls, small windows and a heated compact plan, the classical body could only ever be a costume over a very practical box.

Standing in front of one on a January afternoon the pleasure is in how the snow explains it. The low roof holds a foot of it and the deep entablature throws a hard blue shadow along the whole flank; the white walls disappear into the field behind and only the shadow line survives, which is why the style photographs so well in winter. Up close the illusion falls apart pleasantly - the flutes on the columns are gouged into pine, the capital is a stack of boards, the marble is paint. Inside, the rooms are taller and plainer than their Federal predecessors, with heavy symmetrical door architraves and corner blocks, deep plain baseboards, and a black-painted or actual marble mantel of two square piers and a slab. The house is colder than the colonial ones it replaced and everybody knew it, which is why so many of them acquired a stove, a wing, and eventually a furnace.

defining_characteristics: Gable turned to the road, with the gable end treated as a pediment by cornice returns or by a full portico
Corner pilasters carrying a continuous deep entablature (frieze board plus cornice) around the building
Frieze-band attic windows where the upper half-storey is habitable
Rectangular-transom entrance with sidelights inside a broad pilastered surround, normally in the end bay (side-hall plan)
Painted white clapboard over braced or balloon frame as the dominant construction, brick in the towns
Low roof pitch (4:12 to 6:12) with no dormers on the principal slope
Subordinate wing or wings set back from the temple block's front plane, holding kitchen and chambers
diagnostic_tells: Clipped cornice returns on a gable-front white clapboard house - the cheapest possible pediment and the most common Greek Revival gesture in North America
Frieze-band windows under the eave in place of dormers
Side-hall doorway pushed to the end bay of a gable front, its asymmetry accepted because the pediment supplies the symmetry
Corner pilaster boards 10-14 inches wide where a Federal house of the same size had a 4-inch corner board
Wing ridge set below the main ridge and its front plane recessed behind the temple block, producing the classic 'upright and wing' silhouette

distinguished_from.difference: The North builds a temple front, a compact heated plan and small windows; the South builds a peripteral or full-width colonnade shading a single-pile plan with 12-foot ceilings and floor-length openings. The Northern portico is a facade; the Southern colonnade is a climate device.

Same carpenters, same clapboard, same paint. Federal thins - 7/8-inch muntins, 4-inch cornice, elliptical fanlight. Northern Greek Revival thickens - 12-inch pilasters, 15-inch frieze, rectangular transom. The transom shape alone settles most cases.

The revival's two-storey entry portico is one storey short of the block or is applied to a facade whose eave is thin; its columns are round mill-turned shafts with Roman bases, and its sash is 6/1 or 8/1. Greek Revival columns are built-up staves without bases under a Doric order.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Greek orders from Benjamin's and Lafever's plates, executed in dimensional pine so that the order's proportions survive but its material logic does not; where no order is used, the same proportions are carried by trim board widths.
typical_ratios: Gable pitch 4:12 to 6:12; pediment height 1/4.5 to 1/5.5 of span
Entablature depth 1/4 to 1/5 of column height where columns exist; 18-30 inches total on a two-storey house without them
Frieze board 10-20 inches; corner pilaster 10-14 inches wide with a projection of 1-1.5 inches
Doric columns 6-7 diameters, Ionic 8.5-9.5
Wing ridge 3-6 feet below main ridge; wing front plane set back 2-6 feet
Clapboard exposure 4-5 inches
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Two or three bays to the gable front with the door in an end bay; three to five bays along the flank at even spacing. The portico, where present, is tetrastyle or hexastyle at 2.25-2.75 diameters intercolumniation and sets the bay module for the wall behind it.

massing_affinities.note: The style's demographic bulk: rotate the house, get a pediment for nothing.
The upright-and-wing, arguably the most-built American house form of the nineteenth century, is Greek Revival in origin before it becomes style-neutral.
The full-dress version for the prosperous farm or the village lawyer.
New York, Brooklyn Heights and Philadelphia rows of the 1830s-40s with heavy Grecian door enframements.

constraints.statement: Portico column height must equal the full facade height of the block, and the entablature it carries must be 1/4 to 1/5 of column height. On a house without columns, the corner pilaster and entablature must still run continuously: total eave assembly depth of at least 18 inches on a two-storey house.

test.note: 1/4 to 1/5 of column height. The column-height-equals-facade-height clause and the columnless corner-pilaster alternative stay prose.

constraints.statement: Frieze-band attic windows and roof dormers must never occur on the same elevation. Where a half-storey is habitable it is lit through the frieze, at a height no greater than one third of the frieze depth.

Wing ridge must sit 3-6 feet below the main ridge and the wing's front plane must be recessed at least 2 feet behind the temple block. A wing flush with the temple front destroys the hierarchy and produces a two-fronted house with no entry logic.

Roof pitch 4:12 to 6:12. In IECC zones 5A-6A this is the practical floor for snow shedding on a wood-shingled or standing-seam roof; below 4:12 the pediment reads correctly and the roof does not work.

Where columns are built up of staves, shaft entasis must be carried through the joint and the column must be ventilated at cap and base; flutes are gouged not applied. Solid round mill-turned shafts with Roman bases are out of period.

exemplars.name: Rose Hill Mansion
exemplars.location: Geneva (town of Fayette), Seneca County, New York
exemplars.note: Hexastyle Ionic portico with a fully pedimented gable and Ionic colonnades on single-storey flanking wings; builders working from Lafever's plates. National Historic Landmark.

exemplars.name: Merchant's House Museum (Seabury Tredwell House)
exemplars.location: 29 East Fourth Street, Manhattan, New York
exemplars.note: Built 1831-32 by Joseph Brewster. Late-Federal brick street front over a thoroughly Greek Revival interior - double parlours with 14-foot ceilings, Ionic columns and Lafever-derived joinery. The only nineteenth-century Manhattan house with both exterior and interior intact.

exemplars.name: Andalusia
exemplars.note: Thomas Ustick Walter's Doric temple front on the river elevation; the professional high-style pole of the Northern variant, against which the carpenter version should be measured.

exemplars.name: Seeley Farmhouse
exemplars.location: 2 Freeman's Bridge Road, Glenville, Schenectady County, New York
exemplars.note: A two-storey pedimented centre pavilion with one-and-a-half-storey flanking wings - the farm-scale, carpenter-built end of the variant, listed on the National Register in 1978.

sources: Talbot Hamlin, Greek Revival Architecture in America (1944)
Asher Benjamin, The Architect, or Practical House Carpenter (1830)
Minard Lafever, The Modern Builder's Guide (1833)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
Roger G. Kennedy, Greek Revival America (1989)

proportion_packs.note: Same choice and same reasoning as the parent style: Benjamin's Practical House Carpenter (1830) Grecian Doric, encoded standalone because Benjamin's own preface names the Doric as the one order where Greek and Roman practice cannot be reconciled by delta. Andalusia -- Thomas Ustick Walter's Doric temple front, this variant's own exemplar -- is the professional high-style pole against which the carpenter-built version is explicitly measured in the style's own exemplar note.

Bound for the same reason as on the parent style -- no dedicated Greek Ionic pack exists in this corpus, so plain Vignola (9 diameters, inside the style's stated 8.5-9.5 Greek Ionic range) stands in honestly rather than inventing a Grecian citation. Directly supported by this variant's own named exemplar: Rose Hill Mansion's hexastyle Ionic portico, 'builders working directly from Lafever's plates.'

The wall_section_greek_revival / casing_greek_revival family, run in dimensional pine rather than the plaster or masonry the numbers were worked out against -- consistent with this variant's own governing_logic, which states the order's proportions 'survive but its material logic does not' when executed in built-up staved columns.

Governs the rectangular-transom entrance in its pilastered surround (constraint c02, the frieze/dormer exclusion) -- ranked ahead of sash-light for the same reason as the parent style: the diagnostic weight sits on transom shape and frieze windows, not muntin count.

The window-glazing module, demoted below opening-proportion for the same reason it is on the parent style -- this variant's diagnostic_tells list clipped cornice returns, frieze-band windows and pilaster board widths, never sash pattern.

Governs the temple-front and gable-front composition and the portico's bay-setting intercolumniation (2.25-2.75 diameters). Where columns are absent, the pack's composed-elevation logic still applies to the continuous corner-pilaster-and-entablature assembly the style requires to run unbroken around the building (constraint c01's columnless alternative: total eave assembly at least 18 in on a two-storey house).

Bound chiefly for the ceiling-height figure and the frieze-window habitable-attic case, as on the parent style; ordinary window-height diminution between floors is not this variant's mechanism. The pack does not model the wing-versus-main-block ridge offset this variant's own constraint (c03: wing ridge 3-6 ft below the main ridge, front plane recessed at least 2 ft) requires for the upright-and-wing silhouette -- that hierarchy is a massing/plan relationship, not a storey relationship, and no pack among the 36 covers it. A genuine, acknowledged gap.

Not listed in this pack's own applies_to cross-reference (which names greek-revival-american and greek-revival-southern-plantation but not this variant), and bound here anyway on architectural grounds stated plainly: this variant's interiors are pattern-book carpenter work off Lafever's and Benjamin's plates -- 'heavy symmetrical door architraves and corner blocks' -- not the accumulated, undesigned rooms room-vernacular covers, which is reserved here for greek-revival-upland-vernacular where the plan genuinely predates the style.

andalusian-spanish-revival.name: Andalusian Spanish Revival

revival_periods.note: Sustained revival in Santa Barbara, Montecito, and coastal Southern California, supported by design review boards that still require it.

geography.hearth: Santa Barbara and Montecito, California

lineage.note: The claimed ancestor, and unusually well studied for a revival: Californian architects travelled to southern Spain and published measured photographs of ordinary farm buildings rather than monuments.
Tilework, courtyard water features, and geometric surface ornament quoted at second hand.
Californian architects had the hacienda in front of them and Andalusia only in books and on summer trips; the built result blends both.
The actual professional lineage. George Washington Smith, Reginald Johnson, and Wallace Neff composed in a Beaux-Arts manner and dressed the result in whitewashed lime.

description.short: The rural, whitewashed, deliberately plain branch of Spanish Colonial Revival, taken from Andalusian farmhouses rather than from Spanish churches, and centred on Santa Barbara in the 1920s.
description.long:
Spanish Colonial Revival at large had a taste for magnificence — carved Churrigueresque portals, twisted columns, ornamental ironwork, the whole retable façade brought down to domestic scale. The Andalusian branch is the reaction against that within the same style, and it is one of the more disciplined acts of restraint in American revival architecture. Its practitioners had noticed that the buildings they actually admired in southern Spain were not the cathedrals but the farms: white lime-washed masses, almost no ornament, tile roofs of a single low pitch, a few small deep-set windows, and a wooden gate opening into a courtyard where all the pleasure of the place was kept.

George Washington Smith is the central figure, and his conversion is instructive. He trained as an architect, went to Paris to become a painter, and came back to build in Montecito a house of such plainness that clients began asking for one like it. What he had understood is that the Andalusian effect depends on subtraction: the power of a whitewashed wall comes from its being uninterrupted, and every additional window, vent, or decorative bracket spends some of it. The 1925 Santa Barbara earthquake, which levelled much of the downtown and prompted the city to rebuild under an architectural review board committed to this idiom, gave the manner a whole city to work on.

Standing before one of these houses, the first thing you register is mass and the second is shadow. There is very little to look at — a plane of lime plaster, a low red-brown roof line, a dark rectangle of opening set back six or eight inches into the wall, a black iron grille. The building withholds. Then a door in a wall opens and the withheld thing is behind it: a court, a fountain or a runnel, tile, shade, a wall of jasmine, and rooms arranged around the court in a single-room-deep range so that every one of them is lit and ventilated from two sides. The sequence is the architecture. The elevation is merely the wall that makes the sequence possible.

Of everything in this taxonomy, this variant has the strongest technical claim on the American Sun Belt today. Its climate logic is exact and it is a logic almost nothing in current production housing uses: thermal mass, minimized and shaded glazing, deep reveals, courtyard microclimate, single-pile ranges for cross ventilation. The idiom is usually sold on romance. It should be sold on physics.

defining_characteristics: Uninterrupted planes of white or cream lime-washed stucco with softened, hand-troweled arrises
Ornament almost wholly absent from the wall, concentrated at a single door, gate, or window grille
Low-pitched clay barrel-tile roof, 3:12 to 5:12, with minimal or no eave overhang and no gutter expressed
Openings small relative to wall area, deeply recessed, and irregularly placed according to interior need rather than facade rhythm
A courtyard or walled garden carrying the principal outdoor life of the house, entered through a controlled gate
Single-pile ranges of rooms wrapping the court, lit and ventilated from two sides
Wrought iron used sparingly and structurally — grilles, gate hardware, a balcony rail — never as applied decoration
diagnostic_tells: Window reveals deep enough to throw a hard shadow at midday — 8 to 14 inches, expressing wall mass
Asymmetrical, apparently accidental fenestration on a formally composed plan
No visible gutters, no fascia board, tile running directly to a plastered edge
A single ornamental event on an otherwise silent elevation
Wall planes meeting at slightly rounded, imperfect corners rather than crisp arrises

distinguished_from.difference: The parent style permits and often features elaborate carved Churrigueresque entries, twisted columns, applied ornament, and a symmetrical show facade. The Andalusian branch systematically refuses all of it and takes its precedent from farm buildings rather than from churches and civic monuments.

Mission Revival is earlier (c. 1890–1920), thinner in wall, and defined by the curvilinear parapet, the arcaded corridor, and a quatrefoil or espadaña quotation from the California mission churches. Andalusian Revival has no curvilinear parapet, expresses far greater wall mass, and refers to Spain directly rather than to California's own Spanish past.

Mediterranean Revival is larger, more symmetrical, more Italianate in its classical detail, and typically has a formal frontal composition with a centred entry. Andalusian Revival is smaller-scaled, asymmetrical, and organizes itself around a court rather than around a facade.

proportional_system.governing_logic: No classical module. Governed by wall mass, opening-to-wall ratio, and the proportion of the courtyard to the height of the ranges enclosing it.
typical_ratios: Glazing 8%-18% of wall area on sun-exposed elevations
Reveal depth 8"-14", not less than one-third the apparent wall thickness
Courtyard width at least 1.5x the height of the tallest enclosing range, so winter sun reaches the floor at 34 degrees latitude
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12, constant across the composition
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and interior-driven; openings are placed by the room behind them, and the elevation is composed by the balance of solid to void rather than by a repeating bay.

massing_affinities.note: The accretive farm cluster reads correctly if the ridge heights step.
A symmetrical double-pile block with a centred entry contradicts the type at the level of plan.

constraints.statement: Window reveal depth not less than 8 inches. A flush window in a stucco wall destroys the expression of mass on which the entire idiom depends, and is the single most common failure in contemporary versions.
Not more than one elaborated ornamental event per elevation — a carved surround, a tiled stair, an iron balcony. Two or more and the composition becomes the parent style, not this variant.
Glazing on south and west elevations not to exceed 18% of wall area unless shaded by an arcade or deep overhang of not less than 4 feet.

test.note: Tests the 18% glazing cap. The shading exception (unshaded, or shaded by an arcade or an overhang of not less than 4 feet) is a conditional escape clause with no vocabulary support for combining a percentage test with an alternate-compliance-path and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 with barrel or two-piece mission tile; eave overhang 0 to 12 inches, terminating in a plastered edge or a shaped rafter tail. Composition shingle and a fascia-and-gutter edge void the type.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch range. Eave overhang (0-12in) and the required barrel/two-piece mission tile roofing material are the statement's other clauses and stay prose.

constraints.statement: The courtyard must be reachable only through a controlled gate or zaguan, and must be enclosed on at least three sides. A patio open to the street is a different building.

exemplars.name: Casa del Herrero
exemplars.note: George Washington Smith, with gardens by Ralph Stevens and Lockwood de Forest; among the most intact Andalusian-mode houses in the United States, and a National Historic Landmark.

exemplars.name: Santa Barbara County Courthouse
exemplars.note: William Mooser III. Civic rather than domestic, and more elaborate than the domestic mode, but the building that fixed the city's post-earthquake idiom.

exemplars.name: Jackling House
exemplars.note: George Washington Smith. Demolished in 2011; documented photographically and worth citing as evidence rather than as a visitable building.

sources: McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses
Gebhard, George Washington Smith, 1876-1930: The Spanish Colonial Revival in California
Byne and Stapley, Spanish Architecture of the Sixteenth Century and Provincial Houses in Spain
Baer, The Architecture of Wallace Neff
Gellner, Storybook Style and Casa California (Winter)

proportion_packs.note: This style's own governing_logic is explicitly non-classical ('No classical module. Governed by wall mass, opening-to-wall ratio, and the proportion of the courtyard') and its symmetry is recorded as 'balanced-asymmetrical' -- the same species of composition facade-picturesque was built to check. Bind only the pack's general compositional invariants: the dominance rule (one mass must clearly outrank the others), the lever-arm/moment rule for balancing a subordinate wing or gate against the main range, the two-continuous-datum rule, and the window-proportion-count and window-grouping rules (2-3 opening proportions at most, adjacent groups differing in count) -- all of which read as a formal restatement, in a different vocabulary, of this style's own c02 constraint (not more than one elaborated ornamental event per elevation) and its 'irregular and interior-driven' bay rhythm. Do NOT apply the pack's datum_stack assembly -- water table as an exposed 'rubble, boulder, brick or shingled skirt', a clapboard-to-shingle material change at the second-floor sill -- because that stack is calibrated to wood-frame, shingled and clapboarded Anglo-American construction and describes nothing about a continuous lime-washed stucco mass with hand-troweled, deliberately imperfect arrises. The style's own real governing numbers -- reveal depth 8-14in, glazing capped at 18% of sun-exposed wall -- are not modeled by this or any pack in the corpus.

Bound for the daylight-depth rule alone, which the pack itself calls 'physics rather than custom... true in 1650, true now.' This style's defining single-pile ranges 'wrapping the court, lit and ventilated from two sides' are exactly the condition the rule describes (max depth ~2 to 2.25x window head height from one window wall), doubled by having a window wall on each side; the style's own courtyard-width rule (>=1.5x the height of the tallest enclosing range, so winter sun reaches the floor at 34 degrees latitude) is the same kind of physically-derived constraint the pack specializes in, applied to the court instead of the room. Do not carry over the pack's hearth-reach or joist-span derivations, or its room-count-from-frontage arithmetic -- this is a masonry/stucco courtyard house with no chimney-count logic and no timber bay to tile against.

italian-renaissance-revival.name: Italian Renaissance Revival

geography.hearth: New York City

lineage.note: The claimed ancestor: the fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Florentine and Roman palazzo, reached through measured plates and photographs rather than through any continuous practice.
Villa parti, arcaded loggia and window aedicule; the villa subtype quotes Palladio directly.
The true descent. Same offices - McKim, Mead & White above all - same draughting room, same clients, differing chiefly in restraint.
Ecole composition and the analytique exercise, which trained the eye that reads a palazzo elevation as a stacked order problem.
The American Victorian palazzo habit - bracketed cornice, round-arched openings, low hipped roof - persisting in builder practice and re-academicised after 1890.
The Villard Houses of 1882-84 are an explicit rebuke of Romanesque weight and rustication in favour of a flat, correct, planar palazzo wall.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The academic American palazzo: a symmetrical masonry block with a low tile-hipped roof, a heavy bracketed or modillioned cornice, differentiated storeys with arcaded openings below and diminishing windows above, built as the sober alternative to Beaux-Arts display.
description.long:
Italian Renaissance Revival begins in 1882 on Madison Avenue, when Joseph Morrill Wells of McKim, Mead & White persuaded his partners to abandon a picturesque scheme for the Villard Houses and instead build a flat-walled palazzo modelled on the Cancelleria in Rome. The building was a professional event. It demonstrated that an American commercial-scale residence could be composed as a single planar block of correctly-proportioned storeys, and it made the palazzo the default for anyone who wanted to appear cultivated rather than merely rich. For fifty years afterwards the same formula was applied to town houses, country villas, clubs, banks, libraries and apartment buildings.

The grammar is compact and unusually rule-bound. The block is symmetrical and rectangular; the roof is low-pitched and hipped, tiled in red or green, with a wide overhang on brackets; the wall is treated as a plane and its storeys are differentiated in the Renaissance manner, so that the ground floor is heavier - rusticated, arcaded, or both - and each storey above it is lighter and shorter, with windows diminishing in height and elaboration as they rise. Openings are round-arched at the ground and rectangular above, often within aedicules of pilasters and pediment. A string course marks each floor. The entrance is recessed under an arch. This system is genuinely proportional in a way Colonial Revival's is not: change the ground storey height and everything above it must change.

What produced it, beyond the Ecole training that produced the whole family, was a specific economic fact - the arrival in America of the professional stone contractor and of terra cotta as a mass-produced substitute for carved stone. Terra cotta could deliver a modillioned cornice, an aedicule, and a full arcade at a fraction of the cost of carving, and it is the reason the style spread from Vanderbilt-scale town houses to speculative apartment blocks in Chicago and Kansas City within twenty years. The buyers were the American haute bourgeoisie - bankers, publishers, professionals - who wanted Renaissance associations for exactly the reasons a Medici would have recognised: mercantile wealth seeking the legitimacy of learning.

A good Italian Renaissance Revival building is calm to the point of severity, and its calm is what people remember. The wall is flat and cool, jointed finely, with no projection except the cornice, and the cornice is enormous - four to six feet of overhang throwing a hard black shadow across the top of the building on any sunny day. The windows sit in the wall rather than on it. There is no picturesque incident anywhere; nothing overhangs, nothing turns a corner, nothing surprises. Standing beneath the cornice on a bright afternoon and looking up into that band of shadow is the whole aesthetic experience the style has to offer, and it is a genuinely good one.

defining_characteristics: Symmetrical rectangular masonry block treated as a planar wall, with no picturesque projection
Low-pitched hipped roof, 3:12 to 5:12, covered in clay tile, often not visible from the street on urban examples
A heavy projecting cornice on modillions or brackets, with an overhang of substantial depth relative to the wall
Storey differentiation in the Renaissance manner: heavier and taller at the ground, progressively lighter and shorter above, with string courses marking each floor
Round-arched openings and/or an arcaded loggia at the ground storey, rectangular openings above, frequently within pilastered aedicules
Recessed entrance under an arch, on the centre line, without a projecting portico
diagnostic_tells: Storey heights diminish upward and windows shrink with them. Colonial and Neoclassical Revival keep storey heights nearly equal and windows identical between floors.
The cornice overhang is 1/12 to 1/16 of the total wall height and is carried on visible modillions - much deeper than any Colonial Revival cornice and much plainer than any Beaux-Arts one.
No portico and no columns in front of the wall. The order, where present, is engaged as pilasters within the wall plane.
Tile roof plus a symmetrical flat-walled block plus arched ground-floor openings. Take away the symmetry and the arcade wraps a courtyard, and it becomes Mediterranean Revival.

Compared with the Italian original: the revival has plate glass, an even and generous fenestration, no ground-floor shops, no rustication above the first storey, and a service plan behind the piano nobile that no palazzo had.

distinguished_from.difference: Italianate, 1840-1885, is a wood or brick Victorian type with a square tower, tall thin round-arched windows with elaborate hoods, and a bracketed cornice that is scaled to a house rather than to a palace. Italian Renaissance Revival is academically proportioned, masonry, and treats the wall as a plane.

Mediterranean Revival is looser, warmer, and organised around outdoor rooms - loggias, courtyards, terraces, arcaded galleries - with rougher stucco and asymmetrical extension. Italian Renaissance Revival is a formal symmetrical block whose exterior spaces, if any, are subordinate.

The original palazzo is a fortified urban courtyard building with a blind or barred ground storey, a cortile as the only source of light to the interior rooms, and 3-4 ft masonry walls. The revival opens the ground floor with an arcaded loggia, glazes generously, and plans on American corridor logic.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The stacked classical order in the Renaissance manner. A nominal order governs each storey, the orders diminish upward in the canonical sequence, and the cornice is proportioned to the full height of the building rather than to the top storey.
typical_ratios: Storey heights descending roughly 1.0 : 0.85 : 0.7 from ground to third
Cornice projection 1/12 to 1/16 of total wall height; on a 40 ft wall, 30-40 in.
Window openings 1:1.8 to 1:2.2 at the ground storey, tightening to 1:1.5 at the top
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 in barrel or pan-and-cover clay tile
Arcade piers 1/3 to 1/2 of the clear arch span; arch springing at 2/3 of opening height
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Strictly even, three to nine bays, with all bays equal except where a centre bay is widened for the entrance arch. Vertical alignment between storeys is absolute - unlike every picturesque style in this family, a single misaligned window is visible from across the street.

massing_affinities.note: The suburban and country version: a symmetrical double-pile block under a low tile hip.
Villa examples with a loggia on the garden side and service wings returning.
The literal palazzo case, a full cortile, as at Vizcaya.
Where the villa subtype is taken directly from Palladio.
The reduced builder version, 1905-1925: a hipped tile-roofed cube with a bracketed cornice and an arched entry.

constraints.statement: Storey heights must diminish upward. Second-storey clear height not more than 90 percent of the first, third not more than 85 percent of the second. Equal storey heights place the building in Colonial or Neoclassical Revival.

test.note: Tests the second-to-first storey diminishment (clear height <=90% of the first, i.e. >=10% reduction). The third-to-second pair (<=85%, >=15% reduction) is the same variable applied one storey pair further up and stays prose, per the corpus's established multi-storey-diminishment pattern.

constraints.statement: Cornice projection not less than 1/16 of total wall height and not less than 24 in. on any two-storey example, carried on modillions or brackets spaced 12-24 in. on centre. A cornice under 12 in. voids the style.

test.note: Tests the absolute 24in floor for a two-storey example. The proportional alternative (not less than 1/16 of total wall height) and bracket/modillion spacing (12-24in o.c.) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12, clay tile only, with no gable facing any principal elevation. Asphalt shingle, or any pitch above 6:12, is forbidden.

test.note: Material (clay tile only) and 'no gable facing any principal elevation' stay prose.

constraints.statement: Masonry walls must express thickness at openings with a minimum 6 in. reveal, and arches must be true arches with visible voussoirs or a moulded archivolt - not flat headers behind a stucco curve.

test.note: Arch construction (true voussoirs/archivolt vs. a flat header behind a stucco curve) is qualitative and stays prose.

constraints.statement: No projecting portico or free-standing column in front of the wall plane. Where an order is used it must be engaged as a pilaster with a projection not exceeding 1/6 of its width.

exemplars.location: 451 Madison Avenue, New York, New York
exemplars.note: Joseph Morrill Wells for McKim, Mead & White, after the Palazzo della Cancelleria in Rome. The founding building of the style in America.

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, which names italian-renaissance-revival directly alongside beaux-arts-american. Bound plain rather than as a Chambers, Gibbs or Palladio overlay, per the batch guidance's steer toward whichever base reading is genuinely period-correct: the style's own diagnostic tells insist the order, 'where present, is engaged as pilasters within the wall plane' rather than free-standing or porticoed, and pilaster orders on the piano nobile of an American palazzo (Villard Houses, the Boston Public Library) are the register Corinthian or Composite pilasters occupy in the real Roman and Florentine palazzi this style claims as ancestor. Corinthian rather than Composite because the style is explicitly the 'sober alternative' to Beaux-Arts display (see distinguished_from) and Corinthian is the lighter, less imperial of the two rich orders.

JUDGMENT BINDING: not confirmed in vignola-doric's own applies_to for this specific node, but general and typological rather than fabricated - the stacked-order palazzo convention (sturdy order at the rusticated ground storey, lighter and richer orders rising) is the ordinary Renaissance grammar Serlio and Alberti both describe and every American Beaux-Arts-trained office inherited. The style's own defining_characteristics call for a ground storey 'heavier - rusticated, arcaded, or both' under a lighter principal storey above; Doric is the order the rest of this corpus consistently assigns to the heaviest, plainest register (see the Georgian template's own doric-for-the-everyday-order note), which is the honest general reasoning this pairing rests on.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs bay count and solid-to-void, though the style's own hard constraint that storey heights must diminish (c01, second not more than 90 percent of the first) is stricter than facade-classical's own default graduation and is better read through storey-graduation below.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Covers the rectangular openings of the upper storeys directly; the round-arched ground-storey openings and arcaded loggia the style's defining_characteristics call for are a further elaboration this pack does not itself model and are covered qualitatively by the style's own constraint c04 (true arches, minimum 6 in reveal).

JUDGMENT BINDING: this specific id is absent from trim-classical's own applies_to list, though the sibling id renaissance-revival-american is present there - almost certainly a curation gap rather than a deliberate exclusion, since nothing about this style's interiors (stacked orders, string courses, a wall read as a classical order) argues against the family and everything argues for it over trim-craftsman, which is not in contention here at all.

JUDGMENT BINDING: this specific id is likewise absent from storey-graduation's own applies_to list (again, renaissance-revival-american is present but not this id), yet the style's own proportional_system states the diminution almost as a paraphrase of the pack's own derived rules - 'Storey heights descending roughly 1.0 : 0.85 : 0.7 from ground to third' against the pack's 0.85-then-0.80 compounding, which resolves to 0.85 : 0.68. The two are close enough that this is a documented near-match, not a fabricated one, and the small numeric gap (0.7 stated vs 0.68 derived) is worth carrying forward rather than silently reconciling.
Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to.

italianate-villa.name: Italianate Villa

geography.hearth: Hudson Valley and the Delaware Valley

lineage.note: The freestanding, picturesque, tower-bearing expression of the parent style.

The asymmetrical farm group with its detached campanile is the observed source, transmitted through English painting and through Barry and Loudon. Typed as reference, not descent: American builders never saw the source, so no construction practice was transmitted and the kit must not cascade.
Not a blend in fabric but a shared compositional method: both were designed by the same men, published in the same books, and composed by the same picturesque rules.

description.short: The freestanding Italianate country house: an L-shaped, low-hipped, deeply bracketed villa with a square campanile in the inner angle and a veranda facing the view, sold as the house of a cultivated gentleman.
description.long:
The Italianate villa is the picturesque programme applied to a client who wanted comfort rather than piety. John Notman built Riverside at Burlington, New Jersey in 1839, Richard Upjohn built the Edward King House at Newport between 1845 and 1847, and Downing reprinted the King House in The Architecture of Country Houses with the verdict that it was one of the most successful specimens of the Italian style in the United States, which effectively made it the national pattern. By the 1850s the type was everywhere a merchant, a mill owner, or a country doctor had money and a slope to build on.

Its compositional logic is genuinely good and is worth extracting cleanly, because it is one of the most reusable arrangements in American traditional architecture. Take an L. Put the principal rooms in the long arm facing the view, the entry and service in the short arm, and the tower in the reentrant angle where the two meet. The tower now contains or adjoins the stair, resolves the awkward internal corner, provides the vertical accent, and, being the tallest element, ties the two arms into one composition. Run a veranda along the outer face of the long arm. Everything the massing needs is produced by a plan decision rather than by an applied motif, which is exactly the property a generative kit should prize.

The technology underneath is the same rupture that produced everything else in this branch. Balloon framing made the L, the tower, and the bay cheap; the steam band saw made the brackets, the hood moulds, the turned posts, and the pierced veranda valance cheap; the railroad made all of it available anywhere. There is an important secondary consequence. Because the brackets marched at a constant spacing regardless of what the plan did underneath, a builder could compose an entirely ad hoc, additive house and still unify it with a single purchased rhythm. The bracket is a coordination device as much as an ornament, and it is a real answer to the problem of holding an irregular building together, which is a problem every kit-of-parts system inherits.

In front of one, the tower does most of the emotional work. It is not tall, usually only a storey and a half above the main cornice, but it is the only vertical in a composition of horizontals and it converts a comfortable house into a small landmark. The eave shadow is deep and continuous and gives the whole building a dark upper edge that reads clearly at half a mile. Inside, the plan is generous and slightly loose, with tall round-headed windows dropping light almost to the floor in the parlour, double doors between the front and back parlours to make one long room for occasions, and a stair in the tower base that arrives, in the best examples, at a small square room with windows on four sides, which is the only genuinely surprising space in the ordinary American nineteenth-century house.

defining_characteristics: Freestanding, asymmetrical L or T plan with principal rooms facing the prospect
Square tower or campanile placed at the reentrant angle, rising above the main cornice
Low-pitched hipped roofs, 3:12 to 5:12, with wide bracketed eaves running continuously across all masses
Tall round-arched or segmental-headed windows, frequently paired, with moulded hoods
Veranda of substantial depth on at least the principal elevation, with chamfered or turned posts and a pierced valance
A single bracket rhythm carried across every mass of the building, unifying the composition
Quoins, string courses, or rusticated corners emphasising the horizontal on each mass
diagnostic_tells: Square tower in the inner angle of an L, capped by a low hipped or pyramidal roof with its own brackets: the type's signature and the fastest identification in American architecture
The tower roof is low and wide, never a spire and never a mansard; a mansarded tower makes it Second Empire
Bracket spacing continues unchanged across the tower, the main block, and the wing, at the same module
Windows are paired within a single hood or surround, giving a two-light rhythm no other style of the period uses so consistently
Roof invisible from the ground, in contrast to the Gothic villa where the roof is the dominant mass

distinguished_from.difference: A Second Empire house is often an Italianate villa with a mansard added, sometimes literally by later remodelling. The test is whether the roof is habitable and visible; if the tower carries a concave mansard rather than a low hip, it is Second Empire.

The same style at a different urban condition. The villa is freestanding, picturesque, and towered; the townhouse is party-walled, symmetrical, stooped, and towerless, and its ornament is masonry rather than sawn wood.
Shared authors and compositional method, inverted geometry: low versus steep, round-headed versus pointed, bracketed eave versus bargeboarded rake, square campanile versus octagonal turret.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Governed by the tower and the eave. The tower height establishes the vertical hierarchy over the two arms of the L; the bracket module establishes the only repeating rhythm and is carried across every mass without adjustment.
typical_ratios: Tower height above main cornice 1.0 to 1.5 storeys; tower plan 12 to 16 ft square
Eave projection 24 to 36 in with brackets at 24 to 48 in on centre
Long arm of the L 1.5 to 2.5 times the length of the short arm
Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12 on all masses including the tower cap
Veranda depth 8 to 12 ft; first-floor ceiling 11 to 14 ft
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: A constant bracket rhythm laid over an irregular plan. Window bays are placed by room and may be unequal; the eave rhythm is what makes the elevation read as ordered.

massing_affinities.note: The bracketed farm villa, common in the Midwest and upstate New York.
The towerless bracketed cube; legitimate but forfeits the type's defining element.
A party-walled row cannot carry a freestanding tower composition; use the townhouse variant.

constraints.statement: Where a tower is used it shall stand at the reentrant angle of the plan and shall rise not less than one full storey above the main cornice, with its own bracketed eave at the same bracket module as the main building.
The tower shall be occupied at every level by a stair, hall, or room. Hollow decorative towers are prohibited.

Bracket spacing shall be constant, between 24 and 48 in on centre, and shall be carried across every mass of the building including tower and wing without change of module. Eave projection 24 to 36 in.

test.note: Tests the eave-projection clause (the statement's second sentence). Bracket spacing (24-48 in on centre, constant across every mass) has no matching bracket-spacing variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: All roof pitches shall be between 3:12 and 5:12. No mansard, no gable steeper than 5:12, and no visible ridge from a viewpoint 40 ft from the facade at eye height.

test.note: Tests the roof-pitch range. 'No mansard' (a roof-form prohibition) and 'no visible ridge from a 40 ft eye-height viewpoint' have no matching variables and stay prose.

constraints.statement: A veranda not less than 8 ft deep shall serve the principal elevation, and its cornice shall carry brackets at the main module or at exactly half the main module.

test.note: Tests the veranda-depth minimum. The bracket-module-matching clause has no matching bracket-spacing variable and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Edward King House
exemplars.note: Richard Upjohn, 1845-47. Praised by Downing in The Architecture of Country Houses and thereby made the American model for the type.

exemplars.name: Morse-Libby House (Victoria Mansion)
exemplars.note: Henry Austin, 1858-60. Brownstone villa with an asymmetrical tower and a complete surviving Gustave Herter interior.

exemplars.name: Litchfield Villa
exemplars.note: Alexander Jackson Davis, 1854-57, for Edwin Clark Litchfield. Davis's most ambitious Italianate villa, with an octagonal and a square tower.

Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: Technology and the Picturesque (1978)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The node's own governing_logic states it directly: 'governed by the tower and the eave... a constant bracket rhythm laid over an irregular plan' - the dominant-mass-with-subordinate-accents method this pack encodes, with the campanile in the reentrant angle as the accent every other mass subordinates to.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the glass-light module of the tall round-arched, frequently paired sash the node's own diagnostic tells single out as giving the style 'a two-light rhythm no other style of the period uses so consistently.'

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the storey-based sizing of the void beneath the arched hood; the paired-window treatment and the round or segmental head itself are carried by the node's own constraints (c03, diagnostic tells) rather than by this pack's default single rectangle.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. Governs the vertical hierarchy the tower sets up - '1.0 to 1.5 storeys above the main cornice' per the node's own typical_ratios - and the first-floor-to-upper-floor diminution across the two arms of the L.

Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to, and the node's own aka list carries 'Tuscan Villa' directly. Bound low and optional for the same reason as its parent italianate-american: the veranda posts are described as 'chamfered or turned posts... a pierced valance,' not literal Tuscan columns, so this pack should be read as supplying the plainest register of the classical apparatus for incidental masonry trim (quoins, a door surround) rather than as governing the porch or the tower.

Judgment binding: not in the pack's own applies_to.
