The node's own interior description - 'the plan is generous and slightly loose... double doors between the front and back parlours to make one long room for occasions' - is additive and practical rather than harmonically proportioned, and the parent style's lineage record states outright that the Renaissance proportional system was not carried over into any Italianate register.

dutch-urban-gable-house.name: Dutch Urban Gable House

revival_periods.note: Dutch Neo-Renaissance (Cuypers, Berlage's teachers) at home, and 'Pont Street Dutch' in London — a deliberate national revival of the gable as an emblem of the Golden Age.
An indirect and much-degraded descent: American Dutch Colonial Revival revives the Hudson Valley gambrel farmhouse, not this urban type, and imports the word 'Dutch' without the gable grammar.

geography.hearth: Amsterdam and the Holland canal towns

lineage.note: After the fall of Antwerp in 1585 a large part of the Flemish merchant and building trades moved north; the Amsterdam Renaissance gable of De Keyser's generation is Antwerp Mannerist practice transplanted onto a Holland lot. This is transmission of people, not of prints.

Pilasters, entablature bands, scrolls and obelisks are quoted from Serlio and from Vredeman de Vries's engraved pattern sheets and applied as a flat surface order to a wall whose structure, plan and section owe Italy nothing.

description.short: The narrow, tall, gable-fronted brick house of the Dutch canal towns, in which an entire architecture is generated by a taxed street frontage, a swampy building ground, and the need to hoist goods into an attic warehouse.
description.long:
The Dutch urban gable house is the most economically legible building type in Europe. Almost every feature that reads as style is the residue of a constraint. Land on the Amsterdam canal belt was sold in deep, narrow lots — commonly twenty to thirty Amsterdam feet wide and up to a hundred and ninety deep — because frontage was the scarce and taxed commodity and depth was not. The house therefore turns its short end to the water, and the short end is the only elevation anyone will ever see. Everything the owner has to say about himself has to be said on a strip of brick five to eight metres wide, which is why the gable becomes an instrument of such concentrated invention: stepped (trapgevel) through the sixteenth century, then the neck gable (halsgevel) that Philips Vingboons introduced at Herengracht 168 in 1638, then the bell gable (klokgevel) and, in the eighteenth century, the horizontal cornice that ends the tradition.

The construction follows from the ground. Holland is peat and clay; every substantial house sits on driven timber piles, which makes masonry expensive and makes it rational to build a light building of thin brick party walls with timber floor beams spanning the narrow dimension wall to wall. Because the beams run across the house, the width is fixed by what a beam will carry, and the house grows upward and backward rather than sideways. Because the party walls are also fire walls, they are carried up past the roof, which is what allows the gable to be a free-standing decorated screen with a roof tucked behind it. Because the merchant's stock lived in the attic and the stair was too tight to carry it, a hoisting beam projects at the apex and the whole facade is deliberately built leaning forward, a centimetre or two per metre of height, so that a bale swinging on the hoist clears the windows below. That forward lean — the vlucht — is the single most Dutch thing about a Dutch house, and it is a logistics decision.

What the type was negotiating with was the arrival of classicism into a culture that had no aristocratic patron for it. There was no court to build palaces and no landed order to be flattered; there were merchants, a Calvinist civic culture suspicious of display, and a building trade already very good at brick. Classicism therefore arrived not as a system of orders governing a whole building but as a set of surface incidents — a pilaster strip, a scrolled console, a triangular pediment on top of a gable that is still doing medieval work behind it. When Jacob van Campen and Vingboons finally imposed a real pilaster order on the whole facade in the 1640s, the gable did not survive it; Dutch classicism kills the gable within two generations.

To stand in a canal house is to be in a tall, narrow, top-lit shaft. The front room is bright and shallow, the middle of the house is dark and reached past a stair squeezed against a party wall, and the back opens again onto a small garden or courtyard that is the only quiet ground in the city. The rooms are not large but they are high, and the windows — small-paned casements below a fixed upper light, with heavy exterior shutters — fill a large fraction of the front wall because the wall carries almost no load. Looking out and up along a canal, the effect is of a ragged, individually-argued skyline over an absolutely disciplined common cornice-to-water rhythm: every owner competing at the top of the wall, every owner obeying the block.

defining_characteristics: Gable end turned to the street or canal; the short elevation is the only designed face
Load-bearing brick party walls carried above the roof as fire walls, with timber floor beams spanning the narrow dimension
A decorated masonry gable screen — stepped, neck, bell, or spout — resolving on a single vertical axis at the apex
Hoisting beam at the gable apex and a facade built deliberately leaning forward (vlucht) so hoisted goods clear the wall
Very high window-to-wall ratio on the front, with cross-mullioned (kruiskozijn) or later sash openings and external shutters
Deep, narrow plan with an internal light court or back garden and a stair pinned against one party wall
Attic used as working warehouse space, expressed by shutter doors under the gable
diagnostic_tells: Facade visibly out of plumb, leaning toward the street — never a settlement failure, always intentional
A steel or timber hoisting beam still in place under the gable peak
White or sandstone horizontal bands (speklagen) crossing dark brick, and a gable that steps or scrolls rather than raking straight
Windows that occupy well over half the front wall, in a masonry building — impossible if the front wall were bearing
Anchor plates (muurankers) expressed on the face at every floor line

distinguished_from.difference: Flemish work is the older, heavier parent: more stone in the wall, stepped gables with fewer and deeper steps, and a small-town or rural distribution. The neck and bell gable, and the extreme narrowness driven by canal-lot taxation, are specifically Holland.

The American descendant loses the gable almost immediately. Hudson Valley and New Jersey Dutch houses are broad, low, one-and-a-half storey, gambrel-roofed and gable-sided; they keep Dutch framing habits, door hardware and stoop, and abandon the entire street-gable grammar because nobody was taxing frontage.
Fachwerk expresses its frame and infills it. The canal house hides its timber entirely inside brick and expresses instead the masonry gable and the anchor plates.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The lot and the beam. Facade width is the taxed frontage (commonly 20-30 Amsterdam feet, 5.7-8.5 m); storey height and room depth follow from the span of a timber floor beam laid across that width onto the two party walls. There is no module derived from a column; the classical elements applied to the face are dimensioned to fit the gable, not the other way round.
typical_ratios: Frontage to depth roughly 1:4 to 1:8 on the canal belt
Facade height (water to gable apex) to width roughly 3:1 to 4:1
Forward lean (vlucht) of 1:25 to 1:60 of facade height
Window area 50-65 percent of the front wall
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Two to four window bays per floor, diminishing in number as the gable narrows toward the apex, terminating in a single opening or oculus under the hoist.

massing_affinities.note: The unit is the house; the subject is the canal wall. Party walls are structural and are shared.
Stair and passage pinned to one party wall, front and back rooms in file — the plan that a two-window frontage forces.
The type is the European ancestor of the gable-to-the-street logic, though the American version is timber-framed and freestanding.
The smallest artisan houses of the side canals are effectively one heated room per floor.

constraints.statement: Floor beams span the full frontage onto the two party walls; unsupported width must not exceed about 7.5 m. Wider houses require an internal bearing wall or a double house of two structural bays.

test.note: Converted from the source's 7.5 m to ft. For a party-wall canal house the floor beams' unsupported span equals the facade width, so facade_width_ft is the same dimension. 'Requires an internal bearing wall or a double house of two structural bays' beyond the threshold stays prose.

constraints.statement: Party walls are fire walls and must be carried a minimum of 300 mm above the roof plane. The gable is a screen in front of the roof, not the end of it.

test.note: Converted from the source's 300 mm to in. Reads the fire wall's rise above the roof plane as this style's parapet condition, the closest vocabulary match. 'Party walls are fire walls' (a fire-rating requirement, not a dimension) stays prose.

constraints.statement: Where a hoisting beam is present the facade must be built leaning forward between 1:25 and 1:60 of its height, and the hoist must be centred on the gable axis.
The gable must resolve on one vertical axis, and every element in it — steps, scrolls, claw-pieces, pediment, finial — must be symmetrical about that axis, whatever the door does below.

External shutters are required on ground and first floor openings; the small-paned casement is a wind and driving-rain assembly, and replacing it with large plate glass removes the reason the wall could be so open.

exemplars.name: Het Houten Huys, Begijnhof 34
exemplars.note: One of two surviving timber-fronted houses in Amsterdam; shows the wooden gable front that brick replaced after the fire ordinances.

exemplars.name: Huis Bartolotti, Herengracht 170-172
exemplars.note: Hendrick de Keyser; the fullest surviving Amsterdam Renaissance stepped gable, brick with sandstone speklagen.

exemplars.name: Huis met de Hoofden, Keizersgracht 123
exemplars.note: Attributed to Hendrick and Pieter de Keyser.

exemplars.name: Herengracht 168
exemplars.note: Philips Vingboons; conventionally identified as the first neck gable (halsgevel).

sources: Meischke & Zantkuijl, Het Nederlandse woonhuis van 1300 tot 1800
Rosenberg, Slive & ter Kuile, Dutch Art and Architecture 1600-1800 (Pelican History of Art)
Kuyper, Dutch Classicist Architecture
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to. The canal house is exactly the coursed, exposed-brick, party-wall building the pack governs: anchor plates (muurankers) at every floor line, a party wall carried above the roof plane matching this node's own parapet minimum (dutch-urban-gable-house.c02), and a facade width capped by an unsupported floor-beam span (dutch-urban-gable-house.c01) that mirrors the pack's own wall-thickness/bond logic for what a wythe count can carry.

Judgment bind: this node is not itself listed in room-vernacular's applies_to, but its family container low-countries-vernacular is, and this node's own text describes a genuinely daylight- and span-limited room type — a shallow bright front room, a dark middle lit by nothing, a stair pinned against one party wall — that the pack's depth-and-pile and second-rank borrowed-light room rules describe directly.

creole-cottage-vernacular.name: Creole Cottage

revival_periods.note: Revived in New Orleans through the Vieux Carré Commission (established 1936) and the restoration work of Richard Koch and Samuel Wilson Jr., more as preservation practice than as new suburban production.

regions: New Orleans (Vieux Carré, Faubourg Marigny, Tremé)
Bayou Teche and the Acadian parishes
geography.hearth: New Orleans and the river parishes above it, on French plan habits reworked through a century of Caribbean practice

lineage.note: The steep double-pitched roof on Norman trusses and the colombage wall are the direct structural inheritance; everything about the plan's climatic behaviour is a New World development.

description.short: A one-storey four-room house with no hallway, two or four equal front doors, and a roof that either extends over a shallow gallery or projects as a bracketed abat-vent, built at the front lot line from the Gulf Coast to the bayous.
description.long:
The Creole cottage is the densest piece of climatic reasoning in American vernacular building, and its most radical decision is a negative one: there is no hall, and there is no front door. There are two front doors, or four, and they are the same size and the same importance, one per front room. Circulation happens by walking from room to room through paired French casement doors, or by stepping outside onto the gallery and re-entering somewhere else. In a climate where a corridor is a dead space with a single opening and no breeze path, this is not primitivism. It is the correct answer, arrived at by people who had been living in the Caribbean for a century before they got to Louisiana.

The plan is a square of four rooms, two wide and two deep, roughly thirty-six by thirty-six feet, with the two front rooms formal and the two rear rooms private. Behind them, at the back wall, two small enclosed rooms — the cabinets — project at the corners with an open recessed loggia between them; one cabinet usually contains the stair to the garret. Chimneys are internal, on the party wall between the paired rooms, so the masonry heats two rooms and stays inside the envelope. Ceilings run eleven to thirteen feet, which puts the hot air well above anyone's head and lets the full-height doors work as a chimney for the room.

The front is where the type divides. The rural and early urban cottage carries a posted gallery six to ten feet deep, roof continuous over it at a flattened pitch. The dense urban cottage, built to the front lot line on Bourbon or Dauphine or Royal, cannot have posts on the banquette, so it uses the abat-vent: the roof plane, or a separate shed, projecting thirty to forty-eight inches over the sidewalk on wrought-iron rods or timber brackets, with nothing touching the ground. That detail is unique to the Gulf Creole tradition and is the single fastest way to identify the type from a passing car.

Walls are colombage — heavy cypress posts with soft brick nogging (briquette-entre-poteaux) or mud-and-moss bousillage — stuccoed on masonry-fronted work and weatherboarded elsewhere, because the local brick was too soft to be left in the weather. The roof is steep, forty to fifty degrees, hipped or side-gabled, and where a gallery exists the pitch breaks at the wall plane.

Inside, on a July afternoon with the blinds closed and the doors open, it is a genuinely comfortable building without a machine in it: high ceilings, deep shade, cross-draught through every room, twelve-inch cypress floorboards two feet off the ground, and light coming in low and green off the shutters. The type persisted into the 1860s almost unchanged for the good reason that nothing better was available.

defining_characteristics: Four-room square plan, two rooms wide and two deep, with no interior corridor and no principal front door
Two (or four) equal full-height French casement doors on the front elevation, one serving each front room
Rear loggia recessed between two projecting corner cabinets, one usually containing the stair
Either a posted galerie 6–10 ft deep with a pitch break at the wall plane, or an abat-vent projecting 30–48 in on iron rods or brackets with no posts
Steep side-gable or hipped roof at 40–50 degrees over the body of the house
Colombage frame with briquette-entre-poteaux or bousillage infill, stuccoed or weatherboarded
Internal chimneys on the partition between paired rooms; ceilings 11–13 ft; floor raised 12–36 in on low brick piers
diagnostic_tells: Two front doors of identical size with no window between them, and no way to tell which is 'the' entrance
An abat-vent — a roof overhang with brackets or rods and no posts — over the sidewalk
Rear elevation showing a recessed open bay with a small square room at each end
Exterior louvred blinds on doors rather than on windows, because the openings are doors
Floor plate visible above grade on low brick piers, with no basement and no water table

distinguished_from.difference: Both are one-storey New Orleans types with no corridor, but the shotgun is one room wide with the gable to the street and rooms in single file; the Creole cottage is two rooms wide and two deep with the eave to the street. The shotgun is also later — post-1810 — and Afro-Caribbean in its transmission.

Same plan logic, radically different section. The raised house sits its principal floor eight to twelve feet up on a full masonry service storey and is reached by an exterior stair to the galerie; the cottage sits at or near grade on low piers.

After about 1830 many Creole cottages acquire Greek Revival door surrounds, wider frieze boards and square box columns. The plan test is decisive: a Greek Revival cottage has a central hall and one front door; a Creole cottage has neither.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Four equal cells sized by cross-ventilation and by the cypress beam, with the gallery or abat-vent depth set by the summer sun angle at the latitude of New Orleans.
typical_ratios: Overall body 32–40 ft wide × 30–38 ft deep; each room 15–19 ft square
Ceiling 11–13 ft on the principal floor
Roof 40–50 degrees on the body; gallery slope 20–30 degrees
Galerie depth 6–10 ft; abat-vent projection 30–48 in
French door opening 5 ft 6 in – 6 ft 6 in wide overall × 8–10 ft high
Floor 12–36 in above grade on brick piers
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Four bays: door–window–window–door, or door–door–door–door. Even-numbered and centreless by design; there is no privileged bay.

massing_affinities.note: The rural version with a posted galerie across the front.
Where flooding forces the whole cottage up onto a low masonry storey.
Superficially similar in room count only; the entry logic is entirely different.

constraints.statement: No interior corridor. Each of the two front rooms has its own exterior door on the front elevation, and every habitable room has openings on two walls.

Ceiling height not less than 11 ft on the principal floor; openings are full-height French casement doors reaching to within 12–18 in of the ceiling. An 8 ft ceiling defeats the stack ventilation the whole type depends on.

test.note: 11ft converted to inches exactly (132in) to match the vocabulary variable's unit.

constraints.statement: Front shelter is either a posted galerie not less than 6 ft deep with a roof pitch break at the wall plane, or an abat-vent projecting 30–48 in on brackets or rods with no posts to grade. A 4 ft posted stoop is neither and belongs to no phase of the type.
Finished floor 12–36 in above grade on brick piers; chimneys internal on the partition between paired rooms, never on the exterior gable wall.

test.note: The chimney-position clause in the same statement is categorical and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Exterior louvred blinds on every opening, leaf width equal to half the clear opening so that a closed pair exactly covers it, hung on strap hinges with holdbacks.

exemplars.name: Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop
exemplars.note: Briquette-entre-poteaux with a steep hipped roof; among the oldest surviving structures in New Orleans and the clearest surviving statement of the urban cottage before the Spanish-period fires.

exemplars.name: Fontenette-Bienvenu House
exemplars.location: 201 North Main Street, St. Martinville, Louisiana
exemplars.note: A one-and-a-half-storey Creole cottage of colombage construction with Federal detailing — the type absorbing Anglo trim while keeping its plan. Listed on the National Register 1997, delisted 2024.

exemplars.name: Kent Plantation House
exemplars.note: Bousillage Creole house, the oldest standing structure in Rapides Parish; a raised cottage version of the same four-room, no-corridor plan with its outbuildings intact.

sources: Jay D. Edwards, 'The Origins of Creole Architecture', Winterthur Portfolio 29 (1994)
Jay D. Edwards and Nicolas Kariouk Pecquet du Bellay de Verton, A Creole Lexicon: Architecture, Landscape, People (2004)
Jessie Poesch and Barbara SoRelle Bacot, eds., Louisiana Buildings, 1720–1940 (1997)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: creole-cottage-vernacular is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. The four-room square plan — no corridor, every room cross-ventilated, size set by breeze reach rather than ratio — is exactly this pack's own subject; its 'THE SQUARE CELL' rule (module by module, a base unit added and extended rather than proportioned, after Glassie's structural analysis of Virginia folk housing) describes this cottage's own room-by-room additive logic closely, even though Glassie's own fieldwork was Virginia rather than Louisiana.

As with the parent style: French casement doors 5'6"-6'6" wide sit within opening-proportion's wide-leaf band where its 2:1 ratio is native rather than forced, and the pack's door-from-storey rule (storey/3.5) is a reasonable proportional starting point for an 11-13 ft ceiling. Preferred over sash-light for the same reason as the parent style: these are doors, not sash windows, and sash-light's glass-supply arithmetic has nothing to derive from here.

french-manoir.name: French Manoir

revival_periods.note: The American Chateauesque draws more from the Loire chateau than from the manoir, but its stair towers, steep hipped roofs and dormer treatment come out of the same French repertoire.
American French Eclectic — the steep hipped roof, through-the-cornice dormers and round entrance tower are manoir features abstracted from photographs.
The half-timbered Norman subtype of the revival is specifically manoir-derived.

geography.hearth: Normandy, the Perche and Brittany

lineage.note: The manoir is the local vernacular executed by the same carpenters and masons with a seigneur's money behind it. The frame, the roof, the single-pile section and the dispersed ensemble are all vernacular; what money buys is dressed stone, a great hall, a stair turret and scale.

From about 1520 the manoir quotes chateau detail — moulded croisee mullions, pedimented lucarnes rising through the cornice, classicising turret caps, candelabra finials — often executed by the same masons moving down the scale between commissions. It is quotation and not descent: the manoir is the older tradition and the chateau's own substrate, so the inheritance runs the other way. See french-renaissance-chateau, which correctly holds the hybridizes_with edge back to this node.

description.short: The fortified-then-domesticated country seat of the minor French nobility: a single-pile hall range with a projecting stair turret, standing with its chapel, dovecote, gatehouse and press inside a walled or moated cour.
description.long:
A manoir is not a small chateau. It is a working agricultural seat that has stopped being defensible and has not become a palace, and its architecture records exactly that middle position. The defensive memory survives in the walled or moated enclosure, the gatehouse, the corner turrets that no longer command anything, and the machicolation-shaped corbelling that is now purely a string course. The agricultural reality survives in the fact that the pressoir, the granges, the etables and the colombier stand in the same cour and are built of the same stone by the same hands. And the social ambition survives in three things: the great hall, the stone-mullioned croisee window, and the stair.

The stair is the diagnostic. A medieval hall range is single-pile — one room deep, because that is what a roof over a stone or framed wall will do and because every room must be lit and cross-ventilated from both faces — which means there is nowhere inside the plan to put a stair without eating a room. The French answer is to push it out: a polygonal or round tower projecting into the courtyard face, containing a stone or oak newel stair, rising above the eave and capped with its own conical or polygonal roof. Because the stair is external, every room on both floors opens off it directly, and the tower becomes the plan's only circulation node and the elevation's only vertical accent. It is also, not coincidentally, the most photogenic feature of the type, which is why it is the one thing the American revival never omits.

The construction divides by region and by what the ground gives. In the Perche and lower Normandy it is limestone or roussard rubble with dressed stone at every opening; in the Pays d'Auge it is colombage over a stone base, the same close-studded frame as the farms but with carved brackets, moulded sills and often a jettied upper storey; in Brittany it is granite throughout, which produces smaller openings and heavier lintels because granite is worked with difficulty. Everywhere the roof is very steep — fifty to sixty degrees, slate or flat tile — and everywhere the dormers are the elevation's rhetoric: stone lucarnes rising through the cornice line, pedimented, finialled, one per bay, each announcing a room in a roof that is doing a full storey of work.

Inside, a manoir is high, cold and thin. The hall is a tall single volume with an open or moulded-beam ceiling and a stone chimneypiece taking most of one gable wall; the rooms beyond it are strung in file, one room deep, each with a window on both faces. There are no corridors, because the stair tower is the corridor, and there is no comfort in the modern sense — the plan is undivided, the windows are large and single-glazed, and the fireplace is the only heat in a stone room with a four-metre ceiling. What is remarkable is the light. A single-pile room with a croisee window on each side is lit from two directions all day, and on a grey Norman afternoon the interior of a manoir is far brighter than the massive walls suggest it should be.

defining_characteristics: Single-pile hall range, one room deep, every principal room lit and ventilated from two faces
A projecting stair turret — round or polygonal — on the courtyard face, rising above the eave with its own roof, serving as the building's only circulation
Stone-mullioned croisee windows: a cross of one vertical mullion and one transom, moulded, with the transom set high
Very steep roof, 50-60 degrees, in slate or flat tile, with stone or timber lucarnes rising through the cornice
An ensemble, not a single object: logis, porterie or gatehouse, chapel, colombier, pressoir and granges within a walled, hedged or moated cour
Defensive vocabulary retained as ornament — corner turrets, corbelled string courses, a gate arch — with no defensive function
Enfilade planning: rooms open directly into one another and off the stair, with no corridors
diagnostic_tells: A stair tower on the inner (courtyard) face rather than the outer face, and taller than the ridge it abuts
Cross-mullioned windows with the transom well above centre, roughly two-thirds up the opening
Dormers whose bases cut through the eave line and stand on the wall below, not perched on the roof slope
A freestanding colombier — round or square, with a conical roof and a ring of flight holes — in the same enclosure
Roof volume equal to or greater than the wall height beneath it

distinguished_from.difference: The vernacular farm has no hall, no dressed stone openings, no stair tower and no ensemble pretension. Everything about a manoir that reads as architecture is what money added to that vernacular.

A chateau is symmetrical, double-pile in its later phases, planned around a formal approach and a garden axis, and has no agricultural function within its walls. A manoir is asymmetrical, single-pile, planned around a working cour, and has a cider press in it.

The English Tudor H-plan reaches its rooms through a screens passage and a great hall on the ground; the French manoir reaches them through an external stair turret. That single difference reorganises both plans.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The hall and the roof. Range depth is fixed at 6-7 m by the single-pile section and the roof span above it; the salle sets the length of the principal range; the croisee window, a stone cross in a rectangular opening, governs the proportion of every principal opening at roughly 2:3 width to height. Nothing here is derived from an order; the vertical accent is the stair turret and it is placed by circulation, not by composition.
typical_ratios: Range depth 6-7 m clear; storey height 3.5-4.5 m in the salle
Croisee opening roughly 2:3, transom at about two-thirds of opening height
Roof pitch 50-60 degrees; roof height equal to or greater than wall height
Stair turret diameter 3-4.5 m, rising 1.5-3 m above the eave
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three to seven bays on the principal range, one dormer per bay, but the rhythm is broken deliberately by the stair turret, which lands where the plan needs it rather than where symmetry wants it.

massing_affinities.note: The developed manoir is a hall range with wings at one or both ends, the skeleton the catalog records as the H- or half-H plan.
Three ranges around a cour, the fourth side closed by a wall and gatehouse.
The ensemble reading — logis, chapel, press and granges as a chain of separately roofed volumes.
The stair turret gives the manoir the same compositional device the Italianate villa uses, arrived at three centuries earlier and for a structural reason rather than a picturesque one.

constraints.statement: Principal ranges are single-pile, clear depth not exceeding 7 m. A double-pile manoir requires an internal bearing wall and an internal stair, at which point it has become a chateau or a later house.

test.note: Source states clear depth in metres; kept as stated (matching the precedent in english-georgian-townhouse.c04). The double-pile/bearing-wall/stair reclassification clause is categorical and stays prose.

constraints.statement: The stair turret must project into the courtyard or a reentrant angle, never from the outer face, and must rise above the eave of the range it serves. A stair turret on the entrance front is a revival invention.

Croisee windows are divided by a stone mullion and transom, the transom at roughly two-thirds of the opening height. Removing the mullion to gain glass area destroys the proportion the whole elevation depends on.

Roof pitch 50-60 degrees in slate or flat tile. Dormers must be wall dormers rising through the eave line and carried on the wall below; dormers sitting on the roof slope belong to a later and different tradition.

test.note: Dormer type (wall dormer rising through the eave line, carried on the wall below) is categorical and stays prose.

constraints.statement: A manoir is defined by its ensemble. A freestanding logis without a gate, a chapel, a dovecote or a working range is a large house; the type requires the enclosure and at least two ancillary buildings.

exemplars.name: Manoir du Catel
exemplars.note: c. 1270; one of the oldest surviving non-fortified manor houses in France, and a rare survival of the pre-Renaissance hall-and-solar plan. Classe monument historique.

exemplars.name: Manoir de Courboyer
exemplars.note: 15th-16th century; the canonical Perche manoir, with corner turrets, stair tower and an intact agricultural domaine. Facades, roofs and four chimneypieces classes monument historique.

exemplars.name: Manoir d'Ango
exemplars.note: Built 1532-1544 for the shipowner Jean Ango; the Renaissance hybrid in its clearest form, with a polychrome flint-and-brick colombier at the centre of the cour.

exemplars.name: Manoir de Coupesarte
exemplars.note: 15th-16th century; the timber-framed variant of the type, moated, with overhanging corner turrets carried on brackets.

sources: Lescroart, Manoirs du Pays d'Auge
Mesqui, Chateaux et enceintes de la France medievale
Blunt, Art and Architecture in France 1500-1700 (Pelican History of Art)
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World

proportion_packs.note: Judgment bind: french-manoir is not itself listed in room-vernacular's applies_to, but its family container french-vernacular is. The salle and the single-pile rooms strung off the stair turret are span-limited exactly as the pack describes — 'every principal room lit and ventilated from two faces' because a single-pile section cannot be built any deeper — and this node's own constraint (french-manoir.c01, depth not exceeding 7 m) is the same joist/roof-span ceiling the pack's depth_and_pile rule encodes.

Judgment bind: french-manoir itself is not listed, but its two direct architectural descendants — chateauesque and french-normandy-revival, both named in this node's own revival_periods — are, and this node states outright that its symmetry is 'balanced-asymmetrical' with the stair turret 'placed by circulation, not by composition,' the identical dominant-mass-plus-subordinate-accent logic the pack's dominance and lever-arm rules formalise. Used narrowly for that compositional logic; the pack's own numeric dominance ratio and datum-band figures are calibrated to 19th-century American eclectic fronts and should be treated as a diagnostic to check a drawing against, not a historical rule for this medieval type.

saltbox-colonial.name: Saltbox Colonial

revival_periods.note: A staple of the Colonial Revival cottage, and of Royal Barry Wills's practice, from the 1920s.

geography.hearth: eastern Massachusetts and the Connecticut River valley

lineage.note: The outshut or lean-to behind a two-storey range is an English medieval move; New England only had to make it universal.

description.short: A two-storey New England house with a single-storey lean-to across the rear, producing an asymmetric roof whose long rear slope runs almost to the ground.
description.long:
The saltbox is not a designed form. It is the visible record of a decision that thousands of families made independently: that the cheapest square footage in New England is under an extension of the roof you already have. A two-storey hall-and-parlor house needed more room — for a kitchen that could be got out of the hall, for a buttery to keep milk cool, for a borning room off the warm chimney wall. Building out the back at one storey and running the rafters down over it required no new plate, no new chimney and no second-floor framing. The result is a roof with a short front slope and a long rear catslide, a ridge that sits well forward of the plan centre, and a rear eave you can touch.

What the section does thermally is the reason the form persisted after it stopped being merely cheap. The long rear slope faces north in the standard siting, so the winter wind hits a surface it cannot get under and is deflected up and over; the low rear wall presents almost no elevation to it; and the unheated service rooms are stacked on the cold side, buffering the heated rooms from it. The house is, in effect, a windbreak with rooms inside. Once builders understood this, they began framing the lean-to from the start rather than adding it, which is why the distinction between integral and added lean-tos matters so much in the field. An added lean-to shows a pitch change at the original plate line, a break in the rafter run, and often a different sheathing; an integral one is a single unbroken slope from ridge to rear eave.

The front is the same face as any First Period house — five bays, central door, central chimney stack, small windows tight under the eave, riven clapboard — so the type is invisible from the road and obvious from the side. That asymmetry between the public and the working faces of the building is worth naming: the saltbox has one elevation for the world and three for the household, and it does not pretend otherwise.

Inside, the lean-to rooms feel entirely different from the front rooms. The ceiling follows the rafters down, so the far wall of the kitchen may be five feet high; the light is low and level, coming through small windows just above the counter; and the fireplace at the back of the central stack is the biggest one in the house, with the oven in its cheek. It is the room the family actually lived in, and it is the room the roof was extended to make.

defining_characteristics: Two full storeys at the front, one storey plus loft at the rear, under one continuous roof plane
Asymmetric roof: short front slope, long rear catslide, ridge set forward at 35–45% of the plan depth
Rear eave 6 ft 6 in – 8 ft 6 in above grade — low enough to reach
Central chimney stack serving front rooms and the rear kitchen fireplace, with the oven in the rear cheek
Lean-to depth 10–14 ft, holding kitchen, buttery and borning room
Five-bay symmetrical front with centre door; no corresponding order on the rear elevation
No dormers, and few or no second-floor openings on the rear slope
diagnostic_tells: From the gable end the roof is visibly lopsided — this is the only First Period type you can identify from a single oblique view
The rear eave is at head height while the front eave is at eighteen feet
A pitch change part-way down the rear slope means the lean-to was added; an unbroken slope means it was framed integrally
Rear windows are small, few, and set at odd heights because the ceiling is following the rafters
One chimney, dead centre, breaking the ridge forward of its midpoint

distinguished_from.difference: A Cape is one-and-a-half storeys with a symmetrical roof; a saltbox is two storeys in front with an asymmetric roof. A Cape with a rear lean-to is still a Cape — the front eave stays at nine feet.

A garrison is two full storeys front and rear with a framed overhang at the second-floor line and a symmetrical roof. Many garrisons later acquired lean-tos and became jettied saltboxes; the overhang is the deciding feature.

Revival saltboxes carry the asymmetric roof but give the rear slope dormers, full-height rear walls behind a false catslide, symmetrical windows on all elevations, an 8:12 pitch and an attached garage. If the rear eave is above ten feet, the section is fake.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The original two-storey frame governs; the lean-to is whatever the rafter can reach at the working pitch.
typical_ratios: Main body 38–42 ft × 18–20 ft; lean-to adds 10–14 ft of depth, total depth 28–34 ft
Ridge at 35–45% of total depth from the front wall
Front slope 45–52 degrees; rear slope 38–45 degrees if broken, equal to the front if integral
Front eave 16–18 ft above grade; rear eave 6 ft 6 in – 8 ft 6 in
Lean-to ceiling 7 ft 0 in at the wall of the main house, falling to 5 ft 0 in – 6 ft 0 in at the rear wall
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five bays on the front, unequal, set by post positions with the narrow entry bay centred on the stack; the rear has no rhythm at all.

massing_affinities.note: The two-room core that the lean-to is added behind.
Half-house saltboxes exist, as at the Hoxie House.
A jettied two-storey front with a lean-to behind is a common hybrid.

constraints.statement: Rear eave height 6 ft 6 in to 8 ft 6 in above finished grade. Above 10 ft the catslide is cosmetic and the type is not present.

Front roof slope 45–52 degrees. Where the rear slope is broken it runs 38–45 degrees; where integral it matches the front exactly. A rear slope shallower than 35 degrees will not clear a usable lean-to ceiling.

test.note: Tests the front slope. The rear/catslide slope (38-45deg when broken, or matching the front when integral) is the statement's other, conditional claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: No dormers on the rear catslide. The slope exists to shed weather and hold heat; puncturing it is the revival's habit, not the colonial one.
Lean-to depth 10–14 ft — the practical reach of a single rafter run past the plate. Beyond 14 ft the rear eave drops below head height at the door.

test.note: Reuses the general shed/lean-to depth concept.

constraints.statement: Sash 12/12 or 12/8 before c. 1750, 9/6 thereafter, with heads within 8 in of the front eave and no frieze band.

test.note: Tests the head-to-eave clause. The date-conditional sash pattern (12/12 or 12/8 before c.1750, 9/6 after) is OQ 22 territory and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Hoxie House
exemplars.note: A two-and-a-half-storey half house with an integral rear lean-to; frequently called the oldest house on Cape Cod, and a saltbox rather than a Cape despite its location.

exemplars.name: John Quincy Adams Birthplace
exemplars.note: Central-chimney saltbox with two rooms per floor flanking the stack; the lean-to was added c. 1764, so the rear slope shows the classic break. Often mis-dated to 1663 in popular sources.

exemplars.name: Stanley-Whitman House
exemplars.note: A jettied saltbox — the type in its hybrid form, with a framed overhang on the front and a catslide behind.

exemplars.name: Boardman House
exemplars.note: Unusually unaltered First Period frame with an integral lean-to; the framing is legible throughout.

sources: Abbott Lowell Cummings, The Framed Houses of Massachusetts Bay, 1625–1725 (1979)
J. Frederick Kelly, Early Domestic Architecture of Connecticut (1924)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)

proportion_packs.note: Inherits new-england-colonial's bay-generated frame in full -- same 16-20 ft bay, same central-stack logic -- and adds the one framing move that defines this variant: the lean-to is a NEW, shorter frame leaned on the main block's rear plate, not an extension of the main bay. This pack's wing_strategy rule (module x 0.8, giving 12-16 ft against the 16-20 ft main bay) sits close to this node's own recorded lean-to depth of 10-14 ft, and the pack states the mechanism in almost these words: 'this is why the saltbox reads the way it does: the rear lean-to is a shorter span leaned on the main frame's rear plate, and the catslide roof is the honest consequence.' The diagnostic distinction this node leads with -- a break in the rafter run means an added lean-to, an unbroken slope means an integral one -- is a fact about framing sequence, not about style, and this is the pack that explains it. As on new-england-colonial, no facade-system pack is bound: the front is generated by post position exactly as there, and the rear has no composed rhythm at all, being 'one elevation for the world and three for the household' in this node's own words.

The front roof follows the main block exactly as new-england-colonial (45-52 degrees, rafter length set by the 16-20 ft bay). The rear catslide is a second, independent structural decision: where it is integral the same rafter run simply continues past the plate at the same pitch; where it is added, a second and shallower run (38-45 degrees) is framed against the existing wall -- two different framing histories producing the same silhouette, which is exactly this node's own point about reading the break rather than the roof shape. The very low rear eave (6 ft 6 in - 8 ft 6 in) follows directly from this pack's near-zero eave allowance for First Period work: there is no boxed overhang to lift it, so the rafter foot is close to being the wall's top.

Governs the front openings on the same date sequence as new-england-colonial -- 12/12 or 12/8 to c. 1750, 9/6 thereafter -- which is this node's own co-occurrence constraint (c05) stated as a dating rule.

Bound for the single head-datum rule only, matching this node's own c05 (heads within 8 in of the front eave, no frieze). Not bound for its 13:6 window ratio, which this tradition's casement- and frame-set openings do not follow -- see new-england-colonial's binding for the same caveat.

The lean-to rooms are this pack's own 'service room' case by name: its service_zone_strategy rule (module x 0.8 = 11 ft 4 in) sits inside this node's recorded 8-11 ft lean-to breadth, and the pack calls that dimension 'one of the most characteristic dimensions in the whole vernacular catalogue' and names the saltbox directly as what it produces. Lean-to ceiling height is a section problem rather than a ratio -- the roof simply comes down to the rafters -- which the pack itself concedes when it says the governing dimension in a sloped space is the knee-wall head height, not a fraction of the storey below.

spanish-colonial-american.name: Spanish Colonial American

revival_periods.note: The California mission quadrangle rediscovered by railroad publicity and the Landmarks Club.
Triggered by Bertram Goodhue's Panama-California Exposition at San Diego, which imported a Mexican Churrigueresque vocabulary the borderlands themselves never possessed.
The New Mexico branch, largely invented in Santa Fe between 1912 and 1930.

geography.hearth: two independent hearths — St. Augustine, Florida (1565) and the upper Rio Grande, New Mexico (1598–1610) — with a later and separate Californian foundation from 1769

lineage.note: The borderlands were governed, supplied and staffed from New Spain, not from Spain. Master masons, tile, ironwork and pattern all came up the Camino Real from Mexico City, Zacatecas and Puebla.
The plan diagram — closed street wall, inward courtyard, ornament reserved for the doorway — is Andalusian and arrives via Mexico.

Attenuated but real: Mudéjar carpentry (the artesonado ceiling), the tile tradition, the reja and the blind wall are Islamic inheritances carried inside Spanish practice for eight centuries before they crossed the Atlantic.

description.short: Massive earth and rubble construction, small openings, deep shade and an inward turn to a courtyard, built at the far edge of a supply line so long that the architecture arrived stripped to its diagram.
description.long:
Spanish colonial architecture in what is now the United States is the product of extreme remoteness. Santa Fe in 1610 was six months from Mexico City by ox-cart, and the cart brought a bell, a chalice, some ironwork and a friar with a sketch. It did not bring stone-cutters, lime kilns, glass, or the Baroque. So what got built was the plan diagram of a Spanish building executed in whatever the ground provided, by labour that was overwhelmingly indigenous and already possessed sophisticated earth-building practice of its own. That combination — a Mediterranean spatial idea, a local material, and an indigenous workforce with its own tradition — produced something genuinely new rather than a degraded copy, and mistaking it for a degraded copy is the standard error.

The constant across all five provinces is the wall. It is load-bearing, it is between eighteen inches and five feet thick, and it is made of what is there: sun-dried adobe in New Mexico and Texas, coquina shellstone in St. Augustine, rubble and adobe in California and Arizona. That thickness does three jobs at once — it carries the roof, it stores the day's heat and releases it at night in climates with a thirty-degree diurnal swing, and it makes the building defensible. It also has consequences the builder cannot escape. Openings must be small, because every opening is a hole in a gravity structure with no tensile capacity, and glass had to be carried a thousand miles. Windows therefore occupy well under fifteen percent of the wall, sit deep in splayed reveals, and are often simply barred rather than glazed. The room can be no wider than the available beam, so plans are strings of rooms one span deep, joined end to end and folded around a court rather than stacked into a block.

The court is the second constant, and it is a social instrument as much as a climatic one. The street elevation is a wall with a door in it; the good rooms, the loggia, the fountain, the trees and the family face inward. An Anglo house presents itself to the road and hides its yard; the Spanish house does the opposite. Where the plan does not fully close, it produces the portal or corredor — a covered walk on posts, six to twelve feet deep, functioning as the corridor of a building that has no corridors, so that one crosses the open air to move from room to room.

Ornament is concentrated to the point of drama. The domestic building is unornamented — mud plaster, whitewash, a carved corbel over a post, an iron grille. Everything the province could afford in the way of carving, colour and figural sculpture went onto one surface: the portada of the church door. That extreme rationing is why the borderlands read as austere and why the twentieth-century revivals, which distributed Mexican ornament evenly across a stucco house, look nothing like the thing they claim to revive. To stand in a New Mexican sala, or under the arcade of a California mission at four in the afternoon, is to feel the buildings doing their work: three feet of earth between you and a hundred degrees, the light knocked down to a warm reflected glow, and every surface radiating the temperature of yesterday.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing mass walls of adobe, rammed earth, rubble stone or coquina, 18 in to 5 ft thick, plastered in mud or lime
Small openings, well under 15% of wall area, set in deep splayed reveals and often barred rather than glazed
Inward orientation: the principal rooms and the loggia face a placita or patio, and the exterior street wall is substantially closed
Rooms one structural span deep (12–18 ft), strung in linear files and folded around the court rather than composed into a block
A portal or corredor — a posted or arcaded covered walk 8–14 ft deep — serving as the building's circulation
Roof either flat on round beams behind a parapet (New Mexico, Texas, Arizona) or low-pitched under half-round clay tile (California, later Texas); never steeply pitched
Ornament rationed to a single point — the church portada, the doorway, the campanario — with all other surfaces plain
diagnostic_tells: Wall depth visible at every reveal: the window is a tunnel, not a hole
No gable roof anywhere in the compound
The building presents a nearly blind wall to the public side and opens entirely on the court side
Ornament appears once, at the entrance, and nowhere else
Wall surfaces undulate — hand-applied plaster over irregular adobe gives no straight arris and no true plane

distinguished_from.difference: The single most instructive misidentification in the Southwest. The revival is stucco over wood frame or block: walls four to eight inches thick, sharp arrises, machine-true planes, large windows, ornament distributed over the facade in a Churrigueresque or Andalusian vocabulary the borderlands never had, and often a two-storey plan the material could never have carried. The colonial original is a gravity structure; the revival is a costume over a frame.

The parent had cities, guilds, quarries, lime, and money. Mexican colonial buildings are cut-stone, vaulted, domed and richly carved. The borderlands version is the same plan diagram in earth, with the vaulting replaced by beams and the carving reduced to one door.

Both are Latin colonial and both shade their walls, but the French tradition frames in timber, opens the wall almost completely, raises the floor and faces outward to a gallery; the Spanish builds mass walls, minimizes openings, sits on the ground and faces inward to a court.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The clear span of the available roof beam sets room width absolutely; wall thickness is set by the height it must carry; the court is what is left over.
typical_ratios: Room clear width 12–18 ft (beam span), length 1.5–2.5 times the width
Wall thickness 1:6 to 1:10 of wall height; adobe not less than 1:10
Glazed or open area 6–15% of wall area
Portal depth 8–14 ft, posts at 6–9 ft on centre
Placita 30–60 ft across for a house, 150–300 ft for a mission quadrangle
Tile roof pitch 3:12–5:12; flat roof drainage 1/4 in per ft to canales
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Set by the post or pier spacing of the portal, not by the wall openings, which are placed by interior need and frequently do not align with the posts.

massing_affinities.note: The three-sided placita house, the commonest domestic form.
The closed quadrangle of the mission, presidio and larger hacienda.
The additive room-file before it closes into a court.
The one-room jacal or adobe cell of first settlement.
Where the portal fronts a linear block rather than enclosing a court.

constraints.statement: Mass wall height shall not exceed ten times its thickness for adobe, or eight times for unreinforced rubble, without buttressing. This is the rule that keeps the plan single-storey and the openings small.

test.note: Tests the looser (adobe, 10x) bound. Unreinforced rubble's stricter 8x limit is the statement's other case -- a rubble wall between 8x and 10x passes this test while still being able to violate its own material's real limit. Flagged as a known imprecision rather than silently resolved.

constraints.statement: Room clear span limited to the beam length: 12–18 ft for vigas or hand-hewn timbers. Any room wider than 18 ft requires an intermediate support and reads as a later intervention.
Total window and door area not more than 15% of exterior wall area, with reveals showing the full wall depth. Punched openings in a thin plane are the revival's tell, not the original's.
Roof pitch either flat (1/4 in per ft to canales, behind a parapet 12–24 in high) or 3:12–5:12 under half-round clay tile. Pitches above 6:12 are foreign to the tradition.

test.note: The statement is a disjunction (flat, or 3:12-5:12 tile) but also gives a single unconditional ceiling ('pitches above 6:12 are foreign') that covers both branches safely -- flat is 0, the pitched range tops out at 5 -- so this is the one clean test, not a union guess.

constraints.statement: Carved, moulded or coloured ornament is permitted at exactly one location per building — the principal doorway or the campanario. Distributed ornament converts the building into a revival.

exemplars.name: Palacio de los Gobernadores (Palace of the Governors)
exemplars.note: Founded with the villa in 1610 though the surviving fabric largely postdates the 1680 Pueblo Revolt and the 1731 rebuilding. Caution: the famous portal is a 1909–13 reconstruction by Jesse Nussbaum, not colonial fabric.

exemplars.name: Mission San Esteban del Rey
exemplars.note: Adobe walls up to nine feet thick on a mesa top, timbers carried on foot from Mount Taylor thirty miles away — the clearest statement of what remoteness did to the architecture.

exemplars.name: González-Alvarez House ('The Oldest House')
exemplars.note: Coquina shellstone ground storey with a later frame upper floor; the surviving example of the Florida branch, which used shellstone where the Southwest used adobe.

exemplars.name: Mission San Xavier del Bac
exemplars.note: Fired brick, lime-plastered, vaulted and domed — the one borderlands building where a full Mexican Baroque portada was actually achieved, and therefore the exception that proves the rationing rule.

sources: Bainbridge Bunting, Early Architecture in New Mexico (1976)
George Kubler, The Religious Architecture of New Mexico (1940)
Rexford Newcomb, Spanish-Colonial Architecture in the United States (1937)
Chris Wilson, The Myth of Santa Fe: Creating a Modern Regional Tradition (1997)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: The one pack in this corpus whose physical logic actually matches this tradition: its span constraint -- room breadth capped by the available beam, 14-18 ft in the pack's own measured band -- is very nearly a restatement of this node's own governing_logic ('the clear span of the available roof beam sets room width absolutely'), and its 12-18 ft room clear span constraint (c02) sits inside the pack's band almost exactly. The pack's hearth and daylight constraints fit less precisely -- there is no single central hearth heating the house the way there is in New England, and the small deep-set opening here limits light by depth of reveal rather than by the pack's single-window-wall model -- but the outcome the pack predicts (narrow, elongated, span-limited rooms strung rather than stacked) is exactly this node's own recorded room shape. Nothing else in this corpus binds. No pack in this corpus governs the load-bearing mass wall itself -- its height-to-thickness ratio (this node's own hard constraint c01, 1:8 to 1:10), the portal or corredor's post-and-beam proportion, or the small, deep-set, barred-rather-than-glazed opening. That is a genuine absence, not an oversight in this binding: none of the 36 available packs -- the two facade systems, the material modules (brick-course, log-module, sash-light, storey-graduation, timber-bay) or the two opening systems -- was built against fired-brick coursing, log-cabin notching, sawn-timber framing or a Palladian treatise proportion, and none of those is the physics of a load-bearing earth or rubble wall. A dedicated mass-wall/adobe module and a portal/arcade system are both missing from the corpus.

north-american.name: North American

description.short: Four centuries of transplanted European traditions hybridizing with new climates, new materials, new technologies, and a new social order to produce the world's most stylistically promiscuous residential architecture.
description.long:
North American residential architecture is not a style but a laboratory. Every European tradition arrives, meets a climate it was not designed for and a labor market that cannot supply its craft, and mutates. The mutations are the interesting part: the Georgian box grows a porch it never had in England, the Dutch gambrel outlives the Dutch, the Spanish courtyard opens up when it reaches a wetter latitude, and the log pen from Scandinavia becomes the substrate of an entire Appalachian building culture.

Three technological ruptures organize the whole story. Balloon framing and machine-cut nails around 1840 make complex irregular massing cheap for the first time, and the Victorian era is the immediate consequence. The railroad and the mail-order catalog around 1890 make a house in Iowa identical to a house in Oregon, which produces both national styles and the first crisis of placelessness. The automobile after 1930 reorganizes the plan around the garage and the lot around the driveway, a problem no traditional style solved because none had to.

The fourth rupture is happening now, and it is worth naming plainly: design knowledge is moving from the drafting room into software. The question this taxonomy exists to answer is whether that movement carries the traditional grammar with it or leaves it behind. Every previous rupture that democratized building — the pattern book, the catalog, the tract plan — degraded proportion while extending access. There is no law requiring the next one to do the same.

defining_characteristics: Continuous hybridization of transplanted traditions under new climatic and economic conditions
The porch, the ell, and the accretive plan as characteristically American adaptations
Technological ruptures (balloon frame, catalog, automobile) as primary drivers of stylistic change
Revivalism as a permanent condition rather than an episode
Regional variation of national styles as the level at which real buildability lives

british-isles.name: British Isles

description.short: The insular stream that fused Norman masonry, medieval timber framing, and imported classicism into the pattern-book culture that furnished colonial America with most of its architecture.
description.long:
Britain's building tradition is a hybrid from the start: Romanesque masonry from Normandy laid over Anglo-Saxon timber practice, then Gothic, then a late and reluctant Renaissance arriving through Netherlandish intermediaries rather than directly from Italy. The reluctance matters. English classicism is never purely classical; it is classicism negotiated with a stubborn vernacular of steep roofs, tall chimneys, and small-paned windows suited to a cold, wet, cloudy island.

The decisive British contribution to world architecture is not a style but a medium: the pattern book. Beginning in the early eighteenth century, builders' guides by Gibbs, Langley, Swan, and later Asher Benjamin in America converted architectural knowledge from guild apprenticeship into printed, purchasable instruction. A carpenter in rural Connecticut who had never seen a classical building could execute a correct Ionic door surround from a plate. This is the historical precedent for what a design platform now attempts, and it is worth studying closely — including its failures, which were mostly failures of proportion at unusual scales.

The second British contribution is the picturesque: the deliberate composition of irregular, asymmetrical, historically allusive buildings for their visual and emotional effect. This is the ancestor of Gothic Revival, Queen Anne, Shingle Style, and eventually of the entire Anglo-American suburban imagination.

defining_characteristics: Steep roof pitches and prominent chimney stacks as climatic and compositional constants
Classicism absorbed and domesticated rather than adopted wholesale
Pattern-book transmission of design knowledge from the early 18th century onward
A strong parallel vernacular of local stone, brick, and timber that never fully surrenders to fashion
The picturesque as a legitimate compositional method alongside the classical

norman-romanesque-english.name: Norman Romanesque (English)

revival_periods.note: The Norman Revival, a short-lived and unpopular branch of the British Gothic Revival. It failed because the Ecclesiologists judged the round arch doctrinally inferior to the pointed one, which tells you how much the nineteenth century thought was at stake in an arch.

geography.hearth: Normandy, transplanted wholesale by the post-Conquest royal and monastic building programme

lineage.note: The round arch, the barrel and groin vault, the ashlar course and the very idea of a masonry order reach Normandy through Carolingian and Lombard intermediaries, not by direct study of Roman buildings. Transmission is real but attenuated: no Norman mason had read Vitruvius.

description.short: The masonry architecture the Conquest imposed on England: round-arched, immensely thick-walled, cut rather than assembled, and in its domestic form a defensible stone hall raised over a vaulted undercroft.
description.long:
Norman Romanesque is what happens when a conquering minority builds in stone to make a political fact permanent. Within two generations of 1066 the Normans rebuilt nearly every English cathedral and major abbey and planted several hundred castles, and the surviving domestic examples — a scatter of twelfth-century stone houses in Lincoln, Bury St Edmunds, Southampton and Boothby Pagnell — belong to the same programme in miniature. The style is defined by mass rather than by line. Walls three to six feet thick carry everything; openings are small holes punched through that thickness and splayed inward to gather what light they can; ornament is chevron, billet and beakhead chiselled into the arris of a voussoir rather than applied to a surface. Nothing about it is skeletal, and nothing about it is delicate.

The conditions that produced it were military, monastic and administrative. A Norman lord in a hostile countryside needed a hall he could hold, and the standard answer was the first-floor hall: a vaulted stone undercroft at grade for storage, the living hall above it reached by an external stair that could be defended or removed. That plan is a security diagram before it is an architectural one, and it recurs across Europe wherever a landholding class lived among a population it did not trust. The technology was equally specific: quarried limestone, lime mortar of indifferent quality that took years to cure and therefore demanded very thick walls, and a mason-contractor tradition organised around the church-building lodge, which is where nearly all skilled stonecutting in England lived for two centuries.

There was nothing to react against, which is part of what makes the style so blunt. Anglo-Saxon England built substantially in timber; the Normans simply did not continue that practice at the top of the social scale, and the discontinuity is visible in the archaeology as a hard edge rather than a gradient. The one concession to what was already here is the survival of native carpentry in roofs, floors and everything below the rank of a lord, which continued unbroken and eventually produced the timber-frame tradition that is Norman Romanesque's true domestic sibling.

Standing in a Norman undercroft is a distinct bodily experience, and it is not a pleasant one in the ordinary sense. The room is cold in a way that has nothing to do with air temperature; the vault is low and the piers are fat out of all proportion to the load they carry; sound dies immediately in the stone. Upstairs in the hall the geometry loosens — a twin-light window with a central colonnette, a great round-backed fireplace with an ashlar hood — but the wall is still the dominant fact in the room, and every opening announces its own depth. The experience is of being inside a solid rather than under a shelter, and no later British style ever reproduces it, because no later British style could afford to.

defining_characteristics: The semicircular arch used universally and without exception — doors, windows, arcades, vaults — with the rise exactly half the span
Load carried by wall mass, not by frame: principal walls 900 mm to 1.8 m thick, with openings expressed as deep splayed reveals through that thickness
Coursed rubble field walling with ashlar reserved for quoins, jambs, voussoirs, string courses and shafts
Cushion, scalloped or volute capitals of cubic derivation; ornament (chevron, billet, beakhead, cable) cut into the stone's arris rather than applied to its face
In domestic work, the first-floor hall raised over a vaulted or beamed undercroft and entered by an external stair
Openings small in relation to wall area, grouped as twin lights under a shared containing arch where more light is needed
diagnostic_tells: A round arch and a cushion capital in the same building, with no pointed arch anywhere — the moment a pointed arch appears you are in the Transitional or in Early English Gothic
Window reveals splayed so steeply that the internal opening is two or three times the external one; the wall's thickness is legible from inside
Chevron (zigzag) cut around an arch order — an ornament essentially confined to Anglo-Norman work and its revivals
Domestic entrance at first-floor level with a blind or barred undercroft below, no ground-floor front door at all
Buttresses that are flat pilaster strips of shallow projection rather than the deep stepped buttresses of Gothic

distinguished_from.difference: Round arch versus pointed; wall-as-mass versus wall-as-frame. Norman puts stone everywhere and light nowhere; Gothic concentrates stone into piers and buttresses so that the intervening wall can dissolve into glass. A Norman window is a hole; a Gothic window is what is left over.

Contemporaneous and complementary rather than competing. Norman Romanesque is the masonry practice of the lordly and ecclesiastical class; the timber tradition is the carpentry practice of everyone else, including the same lords' outbuildings. They share a century and almost no details.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Wall thickness and the semicircle. The arch's rise is fixed at half its span, so span sets height throughout; the vault bay and the ashlar course height are the working modules. There is no order, no entablature and no applied system of proportion.
typical_ratios: Arch rise to span exactly 1:2 — the defining and non-negotiable ratio
Wall thickness 1/8 to 1/5 of the clear span it encloses
Pier or respond width 1/3 to 1/2 of the opening it flanks
External window opening height to width roughly 2.5:1 to 3:1; internal splayed opening roughly 1.5:1
Undercroft clear height 2.4-3.0 m; hall above 4.5-6.0 m
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Heavy and slow: piers or vault responds at 3.0-5.0 m centres, with the bay set by what a groin vault of the available mortar could be trusted to span. Windows do not establish a rhythm of their own; they sit where the wall can spare the material.

massing_affinities.note: The first-floor hall over an undercroft is a single-cell type stacked vertically — one room per level, entered directly.
The Jew's House at Lincoln and the Norman stone houses of Southampton stand in a street line with party or near-party walls; twelfth-century urban stone housing is genuinely a row type.
Where a chamber is partitioned off the upper hall, but the division is a screen, not a structural bay.
The H-plan belongs to the developed ground-floor hall of the later Middle Ages. Norman work reaching that plan has generally been rebuilt into it.

constraints.statement: Every arched opening is semicircular with rise equal to half the span. Segmental, stilted, four-centred and pointed heads are forbidden; a single pointed arch reclassifies the building as Transitional.
Principal masonry walls not less than 900 mm thick, and openings must express that thickness with reveals splayed at 30-45 degrees. A thin wall with a round-headed opening is a stage set.

test.note: Tests the minimum wall thickness. The reveal-splay-angle clause (30-45deg) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose -- no vocabulary variable expresses a reveal splay angle.

constraints.statement: Ashlar is permitted only at quoins, jambs, voussoirs, string courses, shafts and fireplace hoods; field walling must be coursed rubble. Continuous fine ashlar over a whole elevation reads as Georgian regardless of the arch profile.
Glazed area not to exceed roughly 8 percent of the elevation. Beyond that the wall stops reading as mass and the style collapses.
Domestic entry at first-floor level by an external stair, with the undercroft either blind or given only slit openings.

exemplars.name: Boothby Manor House (Boothby Pagnell Manor House)
exemplars.note: Historic England dates it late twelfth century. The most complete surviving Norman domestic first-floor hall in England: two-chamber vaulted undercroft, hall above with a round-backed fireplace under a massive ashlar hood.

exemplars.name: The Jew's House
exemplars.note: A twelfth-century stone town house standing in the street line, its ground-floor doorway carrying the chimney of the hall above — one of the oldest inhabited houses in Europe.

exemplars.name: Oakham Castle Great Hall
exemplars.note: A late-Norman aisled hall with carved capitals of exceptional quality, and the rare case of a domestic hall of this date surviving substantially intact.

exemplars.name: Durham Cathedral nave
exemplars.note: Not domestic, but the fullest statement of the structural and ornamental logic — chevron-cut piers, the first large-scale ribbed high vault in Europe — that the domestic work abbreviates.

sources: Eric Fernie, The Architecture of Norman England (2000)
Margaret Wood, The English Mediaeval House (1965)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England (county volumes)
R. W. Brunskill, Traditional Buildings of Britain (1981)
John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (for the later reception of the Romanesque)

proportion_packs.note: Judgment binding, and a narrow one: norman-romanesque-english is not in room-vernacular's applies_to, and almost none of the pack's module transfers — this is single-cell, vertically stacked, vaulted masonry construction (undercroft 2.4-3.0 m, hall above 4.5-6.0 m) with no joist-span or hearth-reach logic resembling the pack's 14 ft timber room at all. What does transfer is the one rule the pack itself calls 'physics rather than custom': the daylight-depth relationship. This style's own text confirms the same constraint by observation ('openings small in relation to wall area... splayed inward to gather what light they can'), so the daylight rule is bound as the sole governing content of this pack for this node; the module, hearth and span figures should be disregarded here. No dedicated masonry-mass room or facade system exists in the library for this style — see gaps.

chateauesque.name: Chateauesque

geography.hearth: New York City and Newport, Rhode Island

lineage.note: Blois, Chambord, Chenonceau and Azay-le-Rideau, measured and drawn by American students in Paris and reassembled at American scale.
Late Gothic tracery, crockets and pinnacles supply the vertical ornament that the French Renaissance model itself inherited.
The true parent. Richard Morris Hunt was the first American admitted to the Ecole; this style is the direct output of that training applied to American fortunes.
Shares the American taste for heavy load-bearing ashlar and the craft base of cut-stone masons trained in the 1880s building boom.
The immediate American precursor for a tall, steep, dormered French roof as a status marker.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The briefest and most expensive American revival: a full-scale reconstruction of the sixteenth-century Loire chateau in load-bearing cut stone, built for perhaps two hundred families between 1880 and 1910 and effectively impossible thereafter.
description.long:
Chateauesque is the one style in this branch that does not cheat. Where Tudor Revival veneers brick over a wood frame and Colonial Revival buys its cornice from a catalog, the Chateauesque house is genuinely a masonry building: bearing walls of dressed limestone or granite, carved on site by immigrant French, Italian and Scottish masons, with steep slate roofs framed heavily enough to carry them. This is why the style lasted only thirty years. It required a labour supply and a tolerance of cost that the American economy offered exactly once, in the window between the 1880s building boom and the First World War, and it required clients of the Vanderbilt order, of whom there were never many.

The style is one man's argument before it is anything else. Richard Morris Hunt, the first American to train at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts, built the William K. Vanderbilt house on Fifth Avenue in 1882 and made the case that a new American fortune could purchase not merely a large house but a specific historical dignity - that of the French crown at the moment when the Gothic was giving way to the Renaissance. The reference was chosen with care. The Francois I chateau is itself a hybrid, medieval in silhouette and Italian in detail, built by a new monarchy consolidating power. American railroad money recognised itself in that, and the recognition was flattering enough to justify the expense.

The necessary features are constant across every real example. A steeply pitched hipped roof, usually 14:12 or more, in slate. Multiple vertical elements piercing the eave line: tall wall dormers with elaborated stone surrounds carried up through the cornice, corbelled turrets, and finialed pinnacles. Round or polygonal towers, often at the corners, frequently containing stairs. Massive corbelled chimneys treated as compositional elements. Round-arched or basket-arched openings with pilastered and pedimented stone surrounds. And, decisively, a wall of load-bearing ashlar with real carved detail, since every element of the style presupposes stone that can be cut.

Standing in front of Biltmore or Ochre Court, what strikes first is not the size but the density of incident above the eave. The building keeps going after it should have stopped - dormer, turret, cresting, chimney, finial - so that the skyline is busier than the wall, and the eye is pulled upward and never settles. The stone is pale and finely jointed and the shadows are sharp. Up close the carving is genuinely good, and its goodness is disconcerting, because it makes no allowance for the fact that nobody standing at ground level can read it. That surplus of craft delivered where it cannot be seen is what a Chateauesque house is for.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing masonry of dressed ashlar with carved detail executed in stone, not cast or veneered
Steeply pitched hipped roof, typically 14:12 or steeper, in slate, with a busy skyline of vertical incident
Tall wall dormers whose stone surrounds rise through the cornice line and terminate in pediments, finials, or crockets
Round or polygonal towers and corbelled turrets, usually engaged with the mass rather than free-standing
Massive multi-flue chimneys treated as compositional elements and often corbelled or panelled
Openings with elaborated stone surrounds - pilasters, entablatures, basket or round arches - and multi-light casement or transomed sash
diagnostic_tells: If the dormers stop at the eave rather than cutting through it, it is not Chateauesque; the through-cornice wall dormer is the style's signature move.
Stone is load-bearing and coursed with joints under 3/8 in.; any veneered or cast-stone wall places the building in a later, cheaper style borrowing the imagery.
The roof is taller than the top storey it covers. A Second Empire mansard is flat-topped and boxy; the Chateauesque roof is a steep hip or a set of steep hips that come to ridges and points.
Ornament is late Gothic in vocabulary - crockets, finials, tracery - but the openings underneath are Renaissance and round-arched. That specific collision dates the reference to about 1520.
Almost never suburban and almost never wood. A frame house with a corner turret is Queen Anne, not Chateauesque.

distinguished_from.difference: Second Empire, 1855-1885, uses a mansard: a double-pitched roof with a flat deck, dormers set in the lower slope, and generally symmetrical massing. Chateauesque uses a steep single-pitch hip with dormers rising through the cornice, and is asymmetrical.

The original is a defensive-descended structure with a moat-derived plan, walls 3-5 ft thick, tiny interior circulation and no central heating; it was built over decades in campaigns. The revival is a single-campaign house with a Beaux-Arts axial plan, plumbing, and an American service wing behind a French face.

Beaux-Arts is horizontal, classical, and Roman or Italian in reference - balustraded parapet, low roof, paired columns. Chateauesque is vertical, late Gothic in ornament, and defined by an enormous roof.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Vertical accumulation. There is no governing module; proportion is set by the roof, which is designed as an inhabited mass roughly equal in height to the top two storeys, and by the stone course heights, which regulate the wall.
typical_ratios: Roof height from eave to ridge 0.8 to 1.2 times the height of the storey below it
Roof pitch 14:12 to 20:12 on principal masses; conical tower roofs steeper still
Wall dormer width 6-10 ft, projecting above the cornice by 1/2 to 1 full storey height
Tower diameter 12-18 ft, height to eave 1.2 to 1.5 times the adjacent wall height
Ashlar course heights 12-18 in. with joints 1/4 to 3/8 in.
