proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Grouped and interrupted. Openings gather into vertical stacks aligned with the dormers above and are separated by wide plain ashlar; the rhythm is set by the roof furniture rather than by the wall.

massing_affinities.note: An assembly of towered and gabled masses of differing height, resolved by the roof rather than by the plan.
Estate examples with projecting wings enclosing an entrance forecourt.
Biltmore and the largest examples; a genuine cour d'honneur.
A symmetrical double-pile block cannot support the skyline the style requires.

constraints.statement: Wall construction must be, or must convincingly express, load-bearing masonry: minimum 16 in. apparent wall thickness at window reveals, jambs returned in the same stone as the face, and heads carried on real arches or lintels. Thin-set veneer with 1 in. reveals voids the style.

test.note: Tests the apparent wall thickness minimum. Jamb-material matching and real-arch/lintel head construction are qualitative and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Principal roof pitch not less than 14:12. Roof height from eave to ridge not less than 0.8 times the height of the storey immediately below. A Chateauesque composition with a shallow roof does not exist.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch floor. 'Roof height from eave to ridge not less than 0.8 times the storey height below' has no matching vocabulary variable (no absolute storey-height variable exists to form the ratio) and stays prose.

constraints.statement: At least two wall dormers must break the cornice line and rise a minimum of half a storey above it, with their stone surrounds continuous from the window sill below the cornice to the dormer pediment above. Roof-set dormers that begin above the eave are forbidden as the primary dormer type.

test.note: Tests the minimum wall-dormer count. 'Rise a minimum of half a storey above the cornice' and stone-surround continuity are qualitative and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Chimney stacks a minimum of 4'0" x 2'6" in plan, rising at least 4'0" above the adjacent ridge, with corbelled or panelled shafts. Flush metal flues are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the ridge-rise minimum. The 4'0"x2'6" plan footprint (no matching vocabulary variable) and corbelled/panelled shaft treatment stay prose.

constraints.statement: Do not apply this style below roughly 8,000 sq ft or outside masonry construction. Every economy available to the other revivals in this family - veneer, cast ornament, catalog trim, shallow roof - destroys it, and the reduced version is Queen Anne with a turret.

exemplars.name: Biltmore House
exemplars.note: Richard Morris Hunt for George Washington Vanderbilt; begun 1889. Explicitly composed after Blois, Chambord and Chenonceau. 178,926 sq ft, the largest private house in the United States.

exemplars.name: Ochre Court
exemplars.note: Richard Morris Hunt for Ogden Goelet. Louis XIII register - steep roofs, turrets, tall chimneys, elaborate dormers - on a compact Newport site.

exemplars.name: William K. Vanderbilt House ('Petit Chateau')
exemplars.location: 660 Fifth Avenue, New York, New York
exemplars.note: Richard Morris Hunt. The founding building of the style in America. Demolished 1926, which is itself the clearest statement of the style's economics.

exemplars.name: Casa Loma
exemplars.note: E. J. Lennox for Henry Pellatt; begun 1911. Late, Canadian, and eclectic enough to show the style dissolving into general castellated romance.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Paul R. Baker, Richard Morris Hunt (1980)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)
Richard Guy Wilson, The American Renaissance 1876-1917 (1979)

proportion_packs.note: The style's own proportional_system says so directly: 'There is no governing module; proportion is set by the roof' and symmetry is 'balanced-asymmetrical'. Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The dominant mass is the roof-and-tower assembly rather than any single wall plane, and the dominance rule (one mass must exceed the next by at least 1.35x in elevation area) is exactly the discipline that separates a genuine Biltmore-scale composition from 'Queen Anne with a turret', which is the style's own stated failure mode at reduced scale.

Confirmed directly in the pack's own applies_to, which names chateauesque explicitly alongside beaux-arts-american and second-empire. This is the honest way to bind the collision the style's diagnostic tells describe outright: 'Ornament is late Gothic in vocabulary - crockets, finials, tracery - but the openings underneath are Renaissance and round-arched. That specific collision dates the reference to about 1520.' Composite is the order whose capital genuinely fuses two registers (Ionic volute over Corinthian acanthus), which is a defensible formal echo of a style built at the exact historical seam between Gothic structure and Renaissance ornament. Bind it only at the round-arched, pilastered and pedimented stone door and window surrounds the defining_characteristics call out - never at the roof, the dormers, the turrets or any crocketed or finialed member, which are Gothic vocabulary this order does not touch and which no pack in this corpus models.

The style's own distinguished_from entry against french-renaissance-chateau states the plan directly: 'The revival is a single-campaign house with a Beaux-Arts axial plan, plumbing, and an American service wing behind a French face.' Hunt's training was Ecole des Beaux-Arts (lineage edge to beaux-arts-french, weight 1.0), and room-harmonic is that same Ecole-adjacent classical room discipline. It governs the principal reception rooms behind the French face, not the towers, stair turrets or service ranges, which the plan explicitly treats as a separate, un-composed American wing.

Bound narrowly and at low precedence. It reaches only the formally planned principal rooms implied by the Beaux-Arts axial plan noted above - the great hall, the stair, the salon - and it says nothing about the Gothic register that dominates the exterior (crockets, finials, tracery) or the room-harmonic pack does not already cover. This is the honest ceiling of what a classical trim family can claim on a building whose ornamental vocabulary is genuinely bifurcated; no pack in this corpus encodes the late-Gothic half.

early-republic.name: Early Republic

description.short: Federal, Jeffersonian, and Greek Revival — the one period when American architecture was explicitly and self-consciously ideological.
description.long:
For roughly seventy years after independence, Americans chose architectural styles as political arguments. Federal continued English Adamesque practice while the country was still culturally British. Jefferson deliberately bypassed England to quote Rome and Palladio directly, because a republic should look to a republic. Greek Revival, arriving with Greek independence and Jacksonian democracy, made the temple front a national form and put it on farmhouses, banks, and courthouses alike.

The mechanism was the American pattern book, and the mechanism has a name: Asher Benjamin published *The American Builder's Companion* in 1806 as a Federal manual and *The Architect, or Practical House Carpenter* in 1830 as a Grecian one. Same author, same audience, same carpenters — new plates. Style change here is a change in the reference material distributed to the trade, which is worth sitting with if you are building the next reference material.

defining_characteristics: Style chosen as explicit political and civic argument
Pattern books as the operative mechanism of stylistic change
A decisive shift from Federal attenuation to Greek Revival mass and weight
The temple front applied across every building type without embarrassment
Classical correctness pursued from published plates rather than from travel

american-folk-vernacular.name: American Folk Vernacular

description.short: Log, shotgun, farmhouse, and the other unstyled house types that most Americans actually lived in.
description.long:
Most American houses were never designed and never carried a style name. They were built from types — a log pen, a double pen, a shotgun, a gable-front-and-wing farmhouse — that encode generations of accumulated judgment about span, heating, ventilation, and how a family grows.

Treating this family as residual would be a mistake. These types are the substrate the styled architecture sits on, they are the direct ancestors of the current market's most popular idiom, and their expansion logic — how a house grows without breaking — is the property that formal styles most conspicuously lack and that a generative design system most needs.

defining_characteristics: Type rather than style as the unit of design
Structural and climatic logic governing form directly
Ornament minimal, applied late, and bought rather than made
Expansion and accretion as designed-in properties
Transmission entirely by craft memory and imitation

new-england-federal.name: New England Federal

revival_periods.note: New England Federal is the single largest donor to the Colonial Revival image bank: the fanlighted door, the Palladian window over it, and the balustraded hip roof.

geography.hearth: Boston and Salem, Massachusetts

lineage.note: Direct craft continuity. The same housewrights, the same white pine clapboard over braced frame, the same central-chimney-derived plan discipline; only the mouldings changed.
Bulfinch saw Adam's work in England in 1785-87 and carried it back as first-hand observation rather than as printed plates - the one American case where the Adam transmission is direct.

description.short: The Federal style executed in white-painted clapboard and Charlestown brick by the housewrights of Boston, Salem and the Maine coast, at its best a wooden architecture pretending, very thinly, to be a masonry one.
description.long:
New England Federal is what happens when a masonry style is handed to a carpentry culture with the best softwood in the Atlantic world and a shortage of both stone and plasterers. The urban version - Bulfinch's Boston, the brick fronts of Beacon Hill and Salem's Chestnut Street - is genuinely Adamesque: three-storey brick with graduated storey heights, a marble stringcourse, a fanlighted door, and a hipped roof behind a balustrade. The rural and coastal version is the more interesting one, because there everything Adam did in stucco and stone is being executed in clear white pine with moulding planes. Fluted pilasters at the corners are boards. The 'quoins' are cut into a board. The elliptical fanlight is joinery. The whole facade is painted white so that at a distance it does not read as wood at all, which is exactly the intention: this is a carpenter's imitation of a mason's architecture, performed so competently that the imitation became the regional idiom.

The conditions were maritime and brief. Between the Peace of Paris and the Embargo of 1807, the New England carrying trade made a class of merchants in Boston, Salem, Newburyport, Portsmouth, Providence and the Maine ports rich very quickly, and they built. Salem's Chestnut Street and Portsmouth's Middle Street are the physical residue of the East Indies and the neutral-carrying trade. Samuel McIntire in Salem, Charles Bulfinch in Boston, Asher Benjamin as the publishing intermediary, and dozens of housewrights working from Benjamin's plates supplied the design. Timber supply mattered as much as taste: eastern white pine in wide clear widths, easily worked and dimensionally stable, made possible the very thin muntins and crisp shallow mouldings that define the style, and made it cheap to imitate stone forms in wood. When the trade collapsed after 1807 and again after 1812, so did the building, and the coast is full of superb Federal houses that were essentially the last thing their towns could afford - Wiscasset and Columbia Falls, Maine, are museums of this fact.

What it reacts against, within New England, is the massive central chimney and the steep dark roof of the colonial house. The Federal generation moved the chimneys to the gable ends or into paired interior stacks, dropped the pitch, opened the plan around a stair hall, and doubled the glass area. The result is a demonstrably brighter, colder, more expensive house - a deliberate trade of thermal sense for light and formality, made by people who could now afford to heat four fireplaces instead of hoarding one. The three-storey brick townhouse version goes further still and abandons the free-standing house entirely for the party wall, which in Boston produced the finest American urbanism before 1850.

Inside a good one the effect is of thinness and light. Rooms are eleven or twelve feet high on the principal floor with windows nearly to the ceiling, and the woodwork is all edge: reeded pilasters an inch and a half wide, a mantel of applied composition swags, a chair rail that is a band rather than a moulding. McIntire's carving in Salem is so shallow you have to stand at an angle to see it. The stair, where the money went, curves out of the hall and rises without any visible means of support - the Ruggles House in Columbia Falls has one built by a housewright in a town of a few hundred people, and standing under it is the closest American domestic architecture gets to a magic trick.

defining_characteristics: Federal proportions and Adamesque detail executed predominantly in painted white pine over a braced timber frame, or in brick in the seaport cities
Gable-end or paired interior chimneys replacing the colonial central stack, with a low hip or side-gable roof
Roof frequently hipped and screened by a balustrade or captain's walk; pitch dropped well below colonial practice
Elliptical fanlight and sidelight entrance, often with a small semicircular or elliptical portico on slender colonnettes
Palladian or triple window centred over the entrance on the principal facade
Corner treatment by flat fluted pilasters or applied wood 'quoins' - masonry gestures executed in board
Wide, thin, crisply run mouldings possible only in clear eastern white pine
diagnostic_tells: Wood imitating masonry: flat pilasters at the corners, rusticated or quoined boards, all painted white
A semicircular or elliptical entrance portico so small and slender it shelters nothing - it is a frame, not a roof
Palladian window stacked directly over the fanlight door, a New England signature the South used far less
Balustrade or captain's walk on a low hip roof, in a region whose colonial houses had steep gables and a huge central chimney
Four-chimney silhouette (paired interior stacks) rather than one massive central stack

distinguished_from.difference: Same frame, same clapboard, same town. The Georgian house has a central chimney or heavy paired stacks, a steeper roof, a projecting pedimented door frontispiece, and muntins over an inch. The Federal house has a lower hip, thin muntins, a fanlight set flush in the wall, and graduated storey heights.

New England builds tight, tall and closed - three storeys, low hip, no porch, windows shut against the winter. Southern Federal builds wide and one room deep with piazzas, taller ground-floor ceilings, and often a raised basement. The plan responds to opposite climates within an identical ornamental vocabulary.

Revival work enlarges the fanlight assembly, thickens muntins, and combines Federal doorways with gambrel roofs, sunrooms and attached garages. Genuine New England Federal doorways are smaller than photographs suggest and sit on a house whose upper windows are visibly shorter than its lower ones.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Adamesque classical proportion transmitted through Bulfinch's first-hand observation and Asher Benjamin's plates, executed to the tolerances of hand-run wood mouldings rather than plaster.
typical_ratios: Three-storey brick townhouse: storey heights approximately 12 : 10 : 7.5 feet
Two-and-a-half-storey frame house: 9.5-11 feet ground floor, second floor 0.85-0.9 of it
Colonnette height 10-11 diameters on entrance porticoes
Clapboard exposure 4-5 inches on principal facades, 5-6 inches on secondary elevations
Roof pitch 6:12 to 8:12 hipped, against 9:12-12:12 in the colonial work it replaced
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five-bay frame houses and three-bay townhouses with even spacing; the Palladian window over the door is the only permitted disturbance of the rhythm and it must be centred.

massing_affinities.note: Beacon Hill, Salem's Chestnut Street, Providence's Benefit Street.
Gore Place is the outstanding New England case and is rare precisely because the region's wealth was mercantile and urban rather than agricultural.

constraints.statement: Where masonry forms are executed in wood (pilasters, quoins, rustication), the board thickness must not exceed 1-1/4 inch and the whole assembly must be painted a single light colour. Exposed wood grain or contrasting trim colour destroys the masonry illusion the variant depends on.
Sash 6/6 or 6/9 with muntins 5/8 to 7/8 inch; glass 10 x 14 to 12 x 18 inches. Upper-storey window height must be 0.80-0.90 of the principal storey, and third-storey 0.60-0.75.

test.note: Tests the upper-storey-to-principal-storey window/storey height diminishing pair (10-20 percent, ratio 0.80-0.90). Sash light pattern, muntin width (5/8-7/8in), glass size (10x14-12x18in) and the third-storey diminishing ratio (0.60-0.75) are left as prose.

constraints.statement: Central chimney is forbidden. Chimneys must be at the gable ends or paired as interior stacks flanking the stair hall - the plan liberation that distinguishes the variant from its colonial parent.

test.note: Tests that chimney_position excludes interior-central, capturing 'central chimney is forbidden'. paired-exterior is the closest available vocabulary match for 'paired as interior stacks flanking the stair hall' -- the enum has no paired-interior value -- so this is a flagged approximation, not an exact test of the interior-stack claim.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 6:12 to 8:12 (hip or low side gable) - low enough to read Federal, steep enough to shed New England snow. Below 5:12 the assembly fails in zone 5A-6A snow loads and above 9:12 it reads colonial.
Entrance portico, where present, is limited to a single storey and a projection of 4-6 feet on colonnettes no more than 7 inches in diameter. It is a frame for the door, not a shelter.

test.note: Tests the portico projection depth (4-6ft) via balcony_depth_ft, reused for a comparable cantilevered/posted projection -- flagged as an approximation since the vocabulary entry's canonical case is a balcony, not a portico. The single-storey limit and the 7in colonnette-diameter cap are left as prose -- no column-diameter vocabulary variable exists.

exemplars.name: First Harrison Gray Otis House
exemplars.note: Charles Bulfinch; brick, three storeys, five bays, Palladian window above the entrance with a lunette above that.

exemplars.name: Gore Place
exemplars.note: Five-part brick country house about 190 feet long with bowed oval projections; plans developed with the French architect Jacques-Guillaume Legrand.

exemplars.name: Nickels-Sortwell House
exemplars.location: Main and Federal Streets, Wiscasset, Maine
exemplars.note: Built 1807-08 for shipmaster William Nickels; the fullest expression of the coastal Maine merchant Federal, with a monumental two-storey entrance frontispiece in wood.

exemplars.name: Ruggles House
exemplars.note: Built 1818-20 by housewright Aaron Sherman with carving by Alvah Peterson; the free-flying stair rises to a landing and reverses without visible support in a village of a few hundred people.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
Asher Benjamin, The American Builder's Companion (1806)
Abbott Lowell Cummings, The Framed Houses of Massachusetts Bay, 1625-1725 (1979), for the framing tradition this variant inherits
William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: The Colonial and Neoclassical Styles (1970)
Historic New England property files (Otis House, Nickels-Sortwell House)

proportion_packs.note: The one order run throughout this variant rather than a graded primary/secondary pair -- unlike georgian-colonial-american's Ionic-for-best-rooms/Doric-for-everyday-work hierarchy, Federal ornament is uniformly thin, and this style's own defining_characteristics name the SAME order for both the corner pilasters and the entrance: 'fluted pilasters at the corners' and, in its own typical_ratios, 'colonnette height 10-11 diameters on entrance porticoes.' This pack's column is 20 semidiameter-modules, i.e. exactly 10 diameters -- the bottom of that stated range on the nose. Benjamin over Gibbs because Bulfinch (who designed this variant's own leading exemplar, the Otis House) saw Adam's work in England first-hand in 1785-87 and Benjamin's 1816 plates are the documented transmission for everyone who came after him.

The wall_section_federal / casing_federal family. McIntire's Salem carving is 'so shallow you have to stand at an angle to see it' per the style's own description -- the flattest possible expression of the family this pack encodes, executed here in clear eastern white pine rather than plaster, which is what let the mouldings run this thin and crisp in the first place.

Ranked ahead of opening-proportion, matching the parent style: constraint c02 states the muntin ceiling directly (5/8-7/8 in) and glass size (10x14 to 12x18 in), and the pack's own rule that it wins any disagreement with opening-proportion on window ratio is the reason for the ordering.

Governs door and window sizing beneath the fanlight-and-sidelight co-occurrence rule the parent style states (single-storey entrance treatment only; a two-storey portico is forbidden). This variant's own description notes the entrance portico 'shelters nothing -- it is a frame, not a roof,' which constraint c05 makes explicit: single storey, 4-6 ft projection, colonnettes no more than 7 in diameter.

Governs the elevation composition -- five-bay frame houses, three-bay townhouses, the centred Palladian window as the only tolerated disturbance of the bay rhythm -- through the same reduced-projection ceiling federal-style's own binding of this pack states (3 in general, 6 in at the door surround).

This variant states its own three-storey townhouse ratio directly -- storey heights approximately 12 : 10 : 7.5 ft -- which is close to but slightly steeper than this pack's default compounding (0.85 then 0.80, i.e. 12 / 10.2 / 8.16 on a 12 ft base); the variant's own figure is bound as the governing case and the pack supplies the general mechanism and the window-follows-the-storey rule that makes the diminution legible from the street.

Listed directly in this pack's applies_to cross-reference. Bound for the oval and circular rooms this variant's own description names as its interior signature -- Gore Place's bowed oval projections, the free-flying stair at the Ruggles House -- composed geometry rather than accumulated framing.

PROMOTED ABOVE brick-course here, the reverse of southern-federal's ordering. This variant's own description states plainly that 'the rural and coastal version is the more interesting one' and that the whole enterprise is 'a carpenter's imitation of a mason's architecture' -- clear white pine over a braced frame is the characteristic fabric, with the Boston/Salem brick townhouse as the secondary, urban case.
The seaport brick minority -- Beacon Hill, Salem's Chestnut Street -- bound optional and demoted below timber-bay for this variant specifically, the inverse of the ranking on southern-federal.

antique-classical.name: Antique Classical

description.short: The Greek and Roman architecture of antiquity, in which the orders were first codified and the proportional method invented.
description.long:
Everything downstream in the classical stream is a reading of this material. Greek building gave the West a system of proportion derived from a module rather than from absolute measure, and a set of orders that graduate character from robust to delicate. Roman building gave it the arch, the vault, the dome, and a bureaucratic capacity to standardize and export the whole apparatus across three continents.

What matters for a design system is that these are the only two bodies of ancient architecture the West has ever possessed complete enough to reverse-engineer. Every revival since the fifteenth century has worked from surviving Roman fabric and, after the 1750s, from measured Greek fabric — which is why the revivals differ so sharply in the accuracy of what they reproduce.

defining_characteristics: Proportional derivation from a module rather than absolute dimension
The orders as a graduated system of architectural character
Trabeated Greek construction and arcuated Roman construction as two distinct structural logics
Temple and domus as the two type-diagrams the West kept returning to

federal-style.name: Federal

revival_periods.note: The fanlight-and-sidelight door surround becomes the single most-copied American ornamental motif, usually enlarged by a third and hung on a house with no Federal proportions behind it.
Academic revival that reads Federal and Georgian as one continuous 'Colonial' and habitually thickens Federal trim back toward Georgian weight.

geography.hearth: Boston and Salem, Massachusetts

lineage.note: Unbroken transmission: the same housewrights, the same framing, the same four-over-four plan. What changed was the book on the bench, not the hand holding the plane.

Federal and Adam are the same impulse on two sides of an ocean and a revolution. Robert and James Adam's Works in Architecture (1773-78) reached American builders through abridgments, imported mantelpieces, and Asher Benjamin's translations of Adam detail into carpenter-buildable mouldings.

The Adam vocabulary of paterae, swags, husks and grotesques is quoted from Roman domestic decoration (Spalato, Herculaneum) at third hand. No American builder had a line of transmission to it; it arrived as printed plates and composition castings.

description.short: The classicism of the new republic: Georgian bones stripped of their Baroque weight and re-dressed in the thin, linear, attenuated ornament of Robert Adam, built in brick and clapboard from Portsmouth to Savannah between the Peace of Paris and the Missouri Compromise.
description.long:
Federal is Georgian with the pressure taken out of it. The plan is the same four-over-four box around a stair hall, the symmetry is the same strict bilateral discipline, the framing is the same braced heavy timber or the same Flemish-bond brick. What changes is the wall's relationship to its own ornament. Georgian ornament projects: bolection mouldings stand proud, door frontispieces advance on engaged columns and carry a broken pediment, quoins turn the corner in relief, muntins are an inch and a quarter of solid wood. Federal ornament recedes into the plane: the door becomes an opening rather than an object, crowned by an elliptical fanlight with lead cames spun into a fan of impossible thinness; mouldings flatten into bands and reeds; the swag and the urn arrive as applied composition castings glued to a flat frieze. The Federal facade is a taut membrane. Nothing on it is more than two inches deep.

The conditions are precise and they are commercial before they are ideological. The Revolution did not change the building trade; the same carpenters were at work in 1790 that had been at work in 1770, and continuity of craft is why the style has Georgian bones at all. What arrived new was print and money. Robert Adam's neoclassicism, already fashionable in Britain since the 1760s, crossed in books, in imported Coade stone and Wellford composition ornament, and above all in Asher Benjamin's Country Builder's Assistant (1797) and American Builder's Companion (1806), which did the essential translation: they reduced Adam's aristocratic surfaces to plates a New England housewright could execute with a set of moulding planes and no plasterer. The money came from the post-1790 neutral-carrying trade, which made Salem, Portsmouth, Providence, Baltimore and Charleston rich enough to build in brick. The technology cooperated: thinner and cheaper crown glass allowed larger lights and slimmer muntins, so a Federal 6/6 sash could carry glass of 12 by 18 inches behind muntins under seven-eighths of an inch, where a Georgian sash carried 8 by 10 glass behind muntins twice that width. The whole visual difference between the two styles at fifty feet is contained in that one dimension.

What it was reacting to is subtler than rebellion. A Federalist merchant in 1795 was building an English fashion at the precise moment his government was defining itself against England, and that contradiction is the most interesting thing about the style. He was not quoting the Republic; he was quoting London's West End. The reaction was against weight, cost, and provincial coarseness rather than against monarchy — Federal is Georgian made lighter, cheaper per square foot of visible richness, and more obviously up to date. Jefferson understood the contradiction perfectly and built the alternative, which is why jeffersonian-classicism exists as a separate node rather than as a Federal sub-variant: he went around England to Rome, while the Federalist merchants went straight to Portland Place. Both were classical; only one was arguing.

Standing in front of one, the eye is given nothing to hold. A Salem or Charleston Federal front presents a plane of brick with punched openings, a thin marble or brownstone stringcourse, and a cornice so shallow it casts a shadow only an inch wide at noon. Storey heights graduate downward — twelve feet, ten, seven — so the building visibly settles rather than floats, and the third-floor windows are squat by design. The whole composition is held together by tension rather than mass, and it fails badly if any single element is thickened. Inside, the compensation arrives: the oval and circular rooms that Bulfinch and the Charleston builders cut into the rectangular box, the cantilevered stair that turns out of sight without visible support, the plaster ceiling of husks and paterae picked out in three colours. A Georgian interior impresses you with the quantity of carved wood. A Federal interior impresses you with the apparent absence of structure.

defining_characteristics: Strict bilateral symmetry inherited intact from Georgian practice, three or five bays, with vertically aligned openings
Ornament reduced to low relief and applied to a flat wall plane; nothing projects more than two or three inches from the facade
Elliptical or semicircular fanlight over the entrance, normally with flanking sidelights, set within the wall plane rather than in a projecting frontispiece
Attenuated proportions: slender columns and pilasters, narrow muntins, shallow cornices, storey heights that graduate downward
Double-hung 6/6 or 6/9 sash with muntins under seven-eighths of an inch and larger panes than Georgian practice permitted
Curved and polygonal geometry introduced into the plan (oval rooms, bowed bays, elliptical stair) without disturbing the rectangular exterior box
Ornamental vocabulary of swags, urns, paterae, husks and reeding, frequently in cast composition rather than carved wood
diagnostic_tells: At fifty feet, Federal versus Georgian is a muntin-width and cornice-depth judgement: if the sash grid looks thin and the cornice casts almost no shadow, it is Federal
Fanlight elliptical rather than semicircular, and set flush in the wall rather than under a projecting pedimented hood
A shallow curved or polygonal bay pushing out of an otherwise flat rear or garden elevation
Third-storey windows noticeably shorter than the second, giving the facade a downward graduation Georgian rarely bothers with
Roof low-pitched or hipped and often hidden behind a balustrade; the Georgian steep gable with heavy dormers has gone quiet

distinguished_from.difference: Same plan and same symmetry; the difference is entirely one of relief and slenderness. Georgian ornament is carved and projecting, Federal ornament is applied and flat. If the door surround is an object standing in front of the wall, it is Georgian; if the door is a hole in the wall with a fan of glass above it, it is Federal.

A proportional inversion before it is an ornamental one. Federal thins everything; Greek Revival thickens everything. Federal has no full-height portico, no heavy entablature, and elliptical rather than rectangular transom lights.

Revival versions enlarge the fanlight and sidelight assembly by a third or more, thicken muntins back to Georgian weight for durability, and combine Federal doorways with massing (gambrel, wide dormered roofs) no Federal builder used. Scale is the tell: a genuine Federal doorway is smaller than you expect.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Classical orders as transmitted through Adam and the American pattern books, but consciously attenuated: the module remains the column diameter while the columns themselves are drawn slenderer than any antique authority permits. Delicacy is a proportional decision, not a decorative one.
typical_ratios: Column and pilaster height 9-11 diameters (Adam-attenuated Ionic and Corinthian), against 7-8 in Georgian practice
Storey heights graduate downward, second floor 0.80-0.90 of the first, third floor 0.60-0.75 of the first
Window openings roughly 1:2 width to height; sash muntins 5/8 to 7/8 inch
Cornice projection 1/25 to 1/30 of facade height; entablature depth under 1/8 of the storey it crowns
Facade width to height (eave) commonly 1.4:1 to 1.7:1 for a five-bay block
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even three or five bay rhythm with equal interbay spacing; the centre bay is emphasised only by the doorway, never by projection or by a wider bay.

massing_affinities.note: The Georgian double-pile plan carried over unchanged; the style operates on its surfaces.
Federal is the first American style whose finest surviving work is urban and party-walled: Beacon Hill, Society Hill, Mount Vernon Place.
Homewood and Gore Place; the hierarchy is Palladian but the trim is Adam.
The Lowcountry variant; see charleston-single-house.

constraints.statement: Sash must be 6/6 or 6/9 double-hung with muntins no wider than 7/8 inch and glass no smaller than 10 x 14 inches. Muntins at Georgian width (1-1/4 inch and up) collapse the style at any distance beyond fifty feet, regardless of the quality of the rest of the trim.

test.note: Tests the muntin-width ceiling (7/8in). Sash light pattern (6/6 or 6/9) and minimum glass pane size (10x14in) are left as prose -- sash_light_pattern is categorical and no vocabulary variable expresses glass pane dimensions.

constraints.statement: No element of the principal facade may project more than 3 inches from the wall plane except the door surround, which is limited to 6 inches. Cornice projection must not exceed 1/25 of facade height, and frieze depth must not exceed 14 inches.

test.note: Tests the cornice-to-facade-height ratio (1/25). The general 3in projection cap with its 6in door-surround exception has no safe shared bound to test generically -- testing at 3in would false-reject a legitimate door surround, testing at 6in would false-accept other ornament between 3 and 6in -- and the 14in frieze-depth cap has no matching vocabulary variable; both stay prose.

constraints.statement: An elliptical fanlight requires flanking sidelights and a single-storey entrance treatment (flat entablature, small portico, or nothing). A two-storey portico is forbidden; it converts the building to Greek Revival or Neoclassical Revival regardless of trim.
Storey heights must graduate downward: second floor 0.80-0.90 of the first, third floor 0.60-0.75. Equal storey heights read as twentieth-century Colonial Revival.

test.note: Tests the second-floor-to-first-floor diminishing pair (10-20 percent, i.e. ratio 0.80-0.90). The third-floor pair (0.60-0.75, i.e. 25-40 percent) is the same variable applied to a further storey pair and stays prose, per the english-georgian precedent.

constraints.statement: Masonry is laid in Flemish bond with joints no wider than 3/8 inch and no quoins. Belt courses are limited to a two-course brick band or a marble stringcourse no more than 4 inches deep. Rusticated or heavily articulated masonry belongs to Georgian or later revivals.

test.note: Tests the stringcourse/belt-course depth cap. Flemish bond, joint width (3/8in), the no-quoins rule, and the two-course-brick-band alternative form are left as prose -- no vocabulary variable expresses brick joint width or bond pattern.

exemplars.name: First Harrison Gray Otis House
exemplars.note: Charles Bulfinch. Three-storey brick, five bays, Palladian window over the entrance with a lunette above it; the canonical urban Federal front.

exemplars.name: Gore Place
exemplars.note: Five-part plan roughly 190 feet long with bowed oval projections; the most fully realised Federal country house in New England.

exemplars.name: Nathaniel Russell House
exemplars.note: Begun 1803. Free-flying cantilevered stair, rectangular, oval and square rooms stacked in one block, full-height polygonal bay on the garden front.

exemplars.name: Homewood
exemplars.note: Begun 1801 for Charles Carroll Jr.; five-part Palladian parti with Adamesque detail throughout - the clearest demonstration that Federal is a surface treatment applied to an inherited plan.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
Asher Benjamin, The American Builder's Companion (1806)
Asher Benjamin, The Country Builder's Assistant (1797)
William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: The Colonial and Neoclassical Styles (1970)
Robert and James Adam, The Works in Architecture of Robert and James Adam (1773-78)

proportion_packs.note: The order that supplies the module for the attenuated Federal apparatus. Benjamin over Gibbs or Chambers directly because Benjamin's American Builder's Companion, 3rd ed. (Boston, 1816) is the documented Federal-era successor to Gibbs's role in the Georgian generation -- the pattern book that actually retooled New England and Chesapeake housewrights after 1797 -- and because the fit is exact rather than approximate: this pack's column stands 20 semidiameter-modules tall, i.e. 10 diameters, which lands squarely inside the style's own stated range of '9-11 diameters (Adam-attenuated Ionic and Corinthian)'. Gibbs's Ionic, correct for Georgian at 7-8 diameters, would rebuild a Georgian house with Federal ornament glued on -- exactly the failure mode the style's own distinguished_from clause warns against.

The style's own typical_ratios name Ionic AND Corinthian in one breath as the two Adam-attenuated orders of Federal practice, so both are bound rather than one. This is also the best-sourced of the four Benjamin overlays: alone among his five orders he sets the Corinthian out member by member in the letterpress of the 1816 American Builder's Companion -- 'the entablature is two diameters high; cornice, forty eight minutes; frieze, forty one; architrave, thirty one; capital, seventy; base, thirty minutes; column, including base and capital, eleven diameters' -- figures that sum exactly and are encoded at high confidence rather than apportioned.

Bind the wall_section_federal / casing_federal family specifically, not the Georgian or Greek Revival sections in the same pack. The pack's own comparison states it plainly: Federal's baseboard is 6 1/8 in in three members against Georgian's 6 7/8 in, and its casing is 4 1/2 in in seven members 'with the interest reeded into the face rather than proud of it' -- Federal is not Georgian made smaller, it is Georgian made flatter, with composition ornament standing in for carved wood, which is the entire proportional argument of this style.

The module that dates a Federal building and the fastest fifty-foot tell the style names for itself: 6/6 or 6/9 sash, muntins under 7/8 in (constraint c01, hard), glass up to 12 x 18 in behind them -- twice the glass area a Georgian sash of the same date carried behind muntins twice as wide. Ranked ahead of opening-proportion for the same reason it is in the Georgian kit: where the two disagree on the window ratio, the measured light module wins.

Governs the void itself -- door and window sizing from the storey, head datum discipline per storey -- beneath the elliptical fanlight and sidelight assembly that constraint c03 lays on top as a co-occurrence rule (fanlight requires flanking sidelights and a single-storey entrance treatment; a two-storey portico is forbidden and converts the building to Greek Revival). The fanlight's own elliptical geometry is not expressed by any of the 36 packs and is carried entirely as prose in the style file -- a genuine, acknowledged gap rather than an omission.

Governs bay count, pier width and the elevation's overall proportion exactly as it does for Georgian, but every dimension it yields must be read through Federal's own hard ceiling: no element may project more than 3 in from the wall plane (6 in at the door surround), and cornice projection is capped at 1/25 of facade height (constraint c02). The pack composes the elevation; the style file overrides its depth.

A near-verbatim match. The style's own hard constraint (c04) states second floor 0.80-0.90 of the first and third floor 0.60-0.75, which is this pack's compounding rule (0.85 then 0.80, yielding a third storey at 0.68 of the first) almost to the decimal. Federal reads correctly only when this diminution is visible in the windows, per the pack's own 'the window follows the storey' rule -- and the style's third-storey windows being 'noticeably shorter than the second' is listed as a diagnostic tell in its own right.

Bound for the oval, circular and polygonal rooms Bulfinch and the Charleston builders cut into the rectangular Georgian box -- Gore Place's bowed oval projections, the Nathaniel Russell House's oval drawing room. These are still classically proportioned interiors, composed rather than accumulated, which is exactly this pack's domain; it is not bound for anything the plan does not compose (garrets, service rooms).

Bound optional at the parent level because the style spans both the seaport brick fronts (Beacon Hill, Salem's Chestnut Street, Baltimore) and the far more common rural clapboard house. It is promoted to primary construction on southern-federal, where Flemish-bond brick is the prestige wall, and demoted below timber-bay on new-england-federal, where clear white pine is the more characteristic and more interesting fabric per the style's own description.

Bound optional and low for the same reason as on georgian-colonial-american: a Federal house is designed from a drawing, not from a frame, so the bay no longer sets the plan. It is promoted above brick-course on new-england-federal, where the frame clapboard house is the majority fabric.

california-bungalow.name: California Bungalow

geography.hearth: Pasadena and Los Angeles, California, spreading through the Central Valley and the Southwest

lineage.note: The Southern Californian expression, and the one in which the style was invented before it was exported. The regional differences are all climatic: no snow load permits a lower pitch, no freeze permits single-wall construction, and a dry warm year permits rooms that are outdoors.

Shares the Californian stucco trade, the low-pitched tile or composition roof, and the pergola. Produces the common Los Angeles hybrid of a Craftsman body with stucco walls and a shaped parapet or tiled porch roof.

From 1915 onward the same builders and the same plaster crews shift toward the Spanish idiom; late California bungalows carry arched openings, red tile accents, and wrought iron while keeping the bungalow plan intact. This hybrid is what supplants the node rather than a separate style displacing it.

The gable-end truss displayed as a face, the projecting purlin, and the deep bracketed rake are more pronounced here than in the national type, because Californian builders learned them from the chalet pattern books that circulated on the West Coast in the 1880s and 1890s.

description.short: The Southern Californian bungalow in which the Craftsman grammar was first assembled, distinguished from the national type by lower pitches, deeper shading eaves, stucco and boulder masonry, and a set of genuinely outdoor rooms — sleeping porch, pergola, court — that only its climate permits.
description.long:
The California bungalow is the parent form pretending to be a child. The Craftsman style was assembled here, in Pasadena and Los Angeles between roughly 1903 and 1909, out of the chalet books, the British reform journals, the Japanese timber work at the expositions, and the local availability of redwood, arroyo boulders, and over-fired clinker brick from the Los Angeles yards. It then travelled east through Stickley's magazine and the plan-book trade and returned to the rest of the country in a form adapted for frost, snow load, and a heating bill. This node holds what was left behind in the adaptation, and almost all of it is climatic.

The climate does four things. It removes the snow load, which allows the roof to drop to three or four in twelve and to spread wide and flat, so that the Californian bungalow reads as a shelter placed on the ground rather than as a house with a lid. It makes shade rather than warmth the design problem, so eaves grow to three and four feet, porches deepen past eight, and pergolas, trellises, and vine-covered lattice extend the roof plane beyond the building. It removes the need for a continuous thermal envelope, which permits single-wall board-and-batten construction in the Central Valley and unheated rooms everywhere: the sleeping porch, screened and open on two or three sides, is a genuine room of the plan and not an afterthought. And it makes the year-round outdoor room possible, which produces the bungalow court — a row of small detached bungalows facing a shared landscaped walk rather than the street, of which Arthur and Alfred Heineman's Bowen Court in Pasadena, twenty-three units built 1910-1912, is the largest surviving example, and which remains one of the best pieces of low-rise dense housing ever built in America.

What produced it economically was the Southern California land boom that ran from about 1904 to 1913: the Pacific Electric interurban network opening subdivisions at a rate no other American city matched, a fifty-by-one-hundred-and-fifty-foot lot as the standard unit, and a house that could be built for fifteen hundred to three thousand dollars. Health migration supplied a large share of the buyers, and the sleeping porch is partly a tuberculosis prescription made architectural. The bungalow was marketed as a way of life more explicitly than any American house before it — informal, servantless, sunlit, out of doors — and the marketing was accurate, which is why the type survived the style.

The experience is of a building whose most important space is not enclosed. You arrive under a pergola or through a low masonry gate, cross a porch deep enough to be dim at midday, and the transition from outside to inside takes twenty feet and three changes of light. The masonry is deliberately rough — river boulders with mortar raked back, clinker brick warped and glazed by overfiring — set against woodwork that is machined flat and finished smooth, and the collision of the two textures is the whole aesthetic argument in one wall. The wood is redwood or Douglas fir, stained rather than painted, and in the surviving unmodernized examples it is very dark. Outside at the eave, the rafter tails are cut to a profile and the ends are sanded, which is the Japanese lesson: the end of a piece of wood is a face.

defining_characteristics: Very low roof pitch, 3:12 to 5:12, with eaves and rakes of 30 to 48 in shading the wall for most of the day
Porch of 8 ft or more depth, framed under the primary roof, with the roof plane frequently extended further by pergola, trellis, or beam extension
At least one genuinely outdoor or unheated room integral to the plan — sleeping porch, screened porch, or open court
Rustic local masonry — arroyo boulder, clinker brick, or cobble — at foundation, porch base, chimney, and site walls
Stucco, redwood shingle, or wide board-and-batten wall surfaces rather than the eastern type's clapboard
Exposed and shaped structural members: rafter tails cut to a profile, purlins projecting through the gable, beam ends sanded and finished
Single storey or single storey with one raised sleeping room; no full second floor
diagnostic_tells: Roof pitch visibly below 5:12 with an overhang deep enough to stand under
Arroyo boulder or clinker brick used raw against smooth machined woodwork on the same porch
A pergola, trellis, or extended open beam structure continuing the roof plane past the enclosed wall
Sleeping porch on the upper level, screened rather than glazed, often with its own small hipped roof
In the airplane subtype, a single room raised above the main roof with windows on all four sides and no dormer relationship to the roof below

distinguished_from.difference: The national plan-book type has steeper pitch (4:12-6:12), shallower eaves, clapboard or shingle rather than stucco, and no unheated rooms. It is a Californian design rebuilt for winter.

Mission Revival organizes the elevation around a shaped parapet, arcade, and red tile roof, and has no exposed timber. Where both appear, look at the gable: an exposed truss with projecting purlins is bungalow, a curvilinear parapet is Mission.

Spanish Colonial Revival turns the wall into a smooth plastic mass with deeply recessed openings and no eave; the bungalow keeps the wall thin and the eave deep. If the roof stops at the wall, it is Spanish; if the roof flies past it, it is bungalow.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The Craftsman datums with a shade override. Roof plane and eave depth are set first, by the sun angle and by the depth of shadow wanted on the wall, and the enclosed volume is then fitted beneath. This inverts the usual sequence — the roof is designed before the plan — and is why the type tolerates such wide dimensional variation without losing coherence.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 3:12 to 5:12
Eave and rake overhang 30 to 48 in
Porch depth 8 to 12 ft clear
Ceiling 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft 6 in — taller than the eastern type, for stack ventilation
Body width 24 to 30 ft; depth 36 to 50 ft
Masonry porch base 24 to 36 in wide, carrying a tapered post no more than half its width
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Grouped openings of two to four sash between exposed posts, with the porch reading as one very wide bay occupying the whole street elevation.

massing_affinities.note: Invented in and largely confined to California and the Central Valley; the raised room is a sleeping porch catching the evening breeze.
The bungalow court reads as a courtyard-U at site scale, with the units detached rather than continuous.

constraints.statement: This assembly — 3:12 to 5:12 pitch, unlined deep eaves, single-wall or minimally insulated walls, unheated rooms — is native to IECC zones 2B, 3B and 3C only. In zones 5 and above the pitch must rise to 4:12-6:12, the eave shorten to 24-36 in, and the outdoor rooms be glazed, at which point the node becomes craftsman-bungalow.

test.note: Tests the pitch range this node is native to. The IECC-zone gating and the zone-5-and-above conversion to craftsman-bungalow are conditional/descriptive rather than a bound on this node's own values, and there is no climate-zone vocabulary variable -- both stay prose.

constraints.statement: Eave and rake overhang not less than 30 in; porch depth not less than 8 ft clear.

test.note: Tests the eave/rake overhang. Porch depth (not less than 8 ft, expressible via gallery_depth_ft) is a second independent numeric clause and is left as prose rather than combined into this test.

constraints.statement: Masonry at porch base, chimney, and foundation must be a locally rough material laid with raked joints; smooth-faced manufactured veneer with returns of less than 24 in is forbidden.
Rafter tails, purlin ends, and beam ends must be cut to a declared profile and finished on the end grain; square sawn-off ends are permitted only on secondary structures.
At least one unheated or open room — sleeping porch, screened porch, pergola-covered terrace of not less than 80 sq ft — must be present in the plan.

exemplars.name: Bowen Court
exemplars.note: Arthur and Alfred Heineman, 1910-1912. Twenty-three bungalows in an L about a shared garden walk; one of the largest bungalow courts in Southern California.

exemplars.name: Bungalow Heaven Landmark District
exemplars.note: More than 800 bungalows, c. 1900-1930, designated 1989 — the Californian type at street scale rather than at exhibition scale.

exemplars.name: Gamble House
exemplars.note: Greene and Greene. Included as the type's apotheosis and its explicit outlier: a bungalow grammar executed at ten times the normal budget, with the sleeping porches, terraces, and boulder masonry of the modest type at full scale.

sources: Robert Winter, The California Bungalow (1980)
Clay Lancaster, The American Bungalow, 1880-1930 (1985)
Edward R. Bosley, Greene and Greene (2000)
Stefanos Polyzoides, Roger Sherwood and James Tice, Courtyard Housing in Los Angeles (1982)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)

proportion_packs.note: Inherited from the parent craftsman style (regional_of, weight 1) with the same datum-band and roof-dominance logic, and especially apt here: this node's own porch_depth figure (8-12 ft clear) sits almost exactly on this pack's own porch_depth rule ('eight feet... close to a hard number rather than a soft one... the band in which a porch is both usable and survivable for the rooms behind'), and the pack's roof_form ratio (dominant roof covers at least half to 0.85 of the elevation) matches this variant's even lower 3:12-5:12 pitch and 30-48 in eaves better than it matches the national type's.

Carried from the parent style: the same catalog carpentry logic, built here in redwood and Douglas fir rather than eastern species, which the pack itself does not distinguish by wood type and does not need to.

Bound narrowly for one mechanism: this pack's daylight-strategy conflict entry states plainly that 'an eight-foot porch across a south front costs the rooms behind it about four feet of usable depth' and that the historic answer was to raise the storey to buy the loss back -- which is exactly this variant's own defining move (ceilings 8 ft 6 in to 9 ft 6 in, 'taller than the eastern type, for stack ventilation,' per its own typical_ratios) and exactly why its sleeping porches and courts are genuinely unheated rooms rather than mere ornament. Not bound for room proportion generally: this is an architect- and pattern-book-derived type, not a span/hearth-constrained folk one, and its rooms are sized by the plan-book programme, which the node's own text describes directly.

georgian-colonial-american.name: Georgian Colonial American

revival_periods.note: The most durable American revival; by the 1920s the standard vocabulary of banks, schools, fraternity houses and upper-middle-class suburbs.
The looser, more numerous suburban descendant.

regions: South Carolina and Georgia low country
geography.hearth: the colonial port cities — Boston, Newport, New York, Philadelphia, Annapolis, Charleston — where merchants had the money and the books arrived first

lineage.note: Direct and documented: the same books, the same mouldings, often the same immigrant joiners. William Buckland arrived in Virginia in 1755 as an indentured joiner with a working library.
The five-part composition, the piano nobile, the temple portico and the Venetian window all arrive through the Burlington–Kent–Campbell circle rather than from Italy.

Palladio himself is quoted rather than descended from. Drayton Hall's portico derives from a plate in the Quattro Libri that its builder knew through Leoni's English edition; almost no colonial builder had seen an Italian building.

description.short: The first American architecture designed rather than accumulated — a symmetrical, proportioned, classically detailed box whose grammar arrived not with craftsmen but in books.
description.long:
Georgian is the moment when American building stops being a craft tradition and becomes a design system, and the mechanism of that change is the pattern book. Before about 1720 a colonial carpenter built what his master had built. After 1720 he could buy a quarto volume of plates and execute an Ionic entablature he had never seen, at any scale he liked, by following a rule of proportion. The books were specific and their influence is traceable in surviving fabric: James Gibbs's A Book of Architecture (1728) and Rules for Drawing the Several Parts of Architecture (1732), which supplied door surrounds and the rusticated 'Gibbs surround' from Annapolis to Charleston; Batty Langley's The City and Country Builder's and Workman's Treasury of Designs (1740), the workhorse of the middling builder; William Salmon's Palladio Londinensis (1734), whose doorway plates appear repeatedly in Virginia; Abraham Swan's The British Architect (1745), the first architectural book reprinted in America, at Philadelphia in 1775; and William Halfpenny's Practical Architecture (1724). What crossed the Atlantic was not a style but an algorithm — a module, a set of ratios, and instructions for deriving everything else.

The result is a plan and an elevation that are the same argument. The centre passage runs front to back, ten to fourteen feet wide, dividing the house into two equal halves and putting the stair on display for the first time in American building. Two rooms on each side, one deep or two, arranged so that no room is entered through another — the emergence of privacy as an architectural value. The elevation follows: five bays with the door at the middle, an odd number so there is a centre to occupy, windows of a fixed proportion diminishing in height from ground to attic, a water table below and a cornice above, and a doorway that receives all the classical attention in the building. Roof pitches drop from the First Period's 12:12 or steeper to 8:12–10:12. Ceilings rise. Sash lights shrink and multiply — twelve-over-twelve, then nine-over-six, then six-over-six by the 1770s as glass got cheaper and bigger.

What it was negotiating against is worth stating plainly, because it was social rather than aesthetic. Colonial society between 1720 and 1770 was stratifying fast, and the Georgian house is a machine for making that stratification legible and liveable. It separates family from servants and enslaved workers, front from back, public from private, and it announces the owner's participation in metropolitan culture to anyone approaching down the drive. The regularity is a claim about the owner's mind. Even at its most modest — a five-bay farmhouse with a plain pedimented door — it is saying that its builder knows the rules.

Inside, it feels ordered in a way nothing before it in America does. The passage is cool and cross-lit, doors align on axis so that you can see through the house at the moment of entry, the panelled chimney breast in the best room is the most expensive object the family owns, and every moulding in the room belongs to a single order and therefore agrees with every other. That coherence is the actual achievement, and it is the reason the Georgian grammar has been revived continuously for a hundred and forty years without ever quite dying.

defining_characteristics: Strict bilateral symmetry about a central entrance, with an odd number of bays — five is normative, three on smaller houses, seven on the largest
A central passage running front to back, 10–14 ft wide, containing the principal stair, with rooms opening off it rather than through one another
Classical detail derived from a printed order: entablature, modillion or dentil cornice, pilasters, and a fully worked door surround
Double-hung sash of fixed proportion, diminishing in height by storey, with muntin patterns keyed to date (12/12, then 9/6, then 6/6)
Side-gable or hipped roof at 8:12–10:12, markedly lower than seventeenth-century work, with a boxed cornice returning at the gable
Chimneys paired and symmetrically placed — interior on either side of the ridge, or at both gable ends — never a single central stack
A composed elevation in which the rear and ends are treated as elevations too, not as leftovers
diagnostic_tells: Five bays, door dead centre, and the same window rhythm carried around to the rear
A doorway that is plainly copied from a plate — pilasters or engaged columns carrying a pediment, or a Gibbs surround with alternating blocks
Windows shorter on the second floor than the first by roughly 15%, and shorter again in the attic
A modillion or dentil cornice with a full return across the gable end (not a clipped 'pork chop')
A water table with a moulded or beveled brick or wood course 24–36 in above grade

distinguished_from.difference: The defining confusion in American architecture. A colonial Georgian house has hand-made brick or riven clapboard, mouldings cut with a specific order's proportions, muntins 7/8 to 1-1/8 in wide, true divided lights, shutters whose leaves actually cover the opening, and a plan without closets, bathrooms or a garage. A revival house has muntins under 3/4 in or applied grilles, machine-perfect trim of generic profile, shutters half the required width, an attached garage, and often a two-storey portico on a house whose eave cannot support one. Trim consistency on all four elevations is a revival tell; so is a fanlight on a house dated before 1780.

Federal (from c. 1785) keeps the symmetry but thins everything: flatter, more attenuated mouldings, elliptical fanlights and sidelights, oval and polygonal rooms, lower-relief ornament in the Adam manner, and often a low hipped roof with a balustrade. Georgian is heavier, bolder in relief, and has no fanlight.

The First Period house has one enormous central chimney, a 12:12+ roof, window heads jammed under the eave and no classical order. Many surviving houses are First Period frames wearing Georgian doors and cornices; read the chimney and the roof pitch, not the trim.

proportional_system.governing_logic: A classical order chosen from a pattern book supplies the module; the entablature, door surround and cornice are derived from it, and the facade is divided so that the window openings and piers fall into a regular arithmetic rhythm.
typical_ratios: Window opening height:width 1.9:1 to 2.1:1 on the principal floor
Second-floor window height 82–88% of first-floor; attic 60–70%
Pier (wall between windows) 0.6 to 1.0 times the window width
Cornice height roughly 1/12 to 1/14 of the wall height from water table to cornice
Passage width 10–14 ft, roughly one-third of the facade on a five-bay front
Ceiling 9–11 ft ground floor, 8–10 ft second, in a plan 32–40 ft deep if double-pile
Roof rise:run 8:12 to 10:12
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Odd, even and unaccented: a-a-A-a-a on five bays, with the centre bay differentiated only by the doorway, never by a projecting mass, except on the most ambitious Palladian compositions where a pedimented pavilion breaks forward 18–36 in.

massing_affinities.note: The Southern and modest Northern norm — one room deep, passage through.
The double-pile Georgian box, four rooms per floor around a central passage.
Main block, hyphens, dependencies — the ambition of the plantation and the great town seat.
The urban lot version, three bays wide with the passage at one side.
Chesapeake growth pattern where dependencies step down from the main block.
Rare, and mostly a survival of Jacobean planning as at Stratford Hall.

constraints.statement: The front elevation must have an odd number of bays (3, 5 or 7) with the entrance in the centre bay. An even-bay Georgian front is a contradiction: there is no centre to enter.

test.note: The centred-entrance clause is the vocabulary's own documented corollary of an odd bay count (entrance_bay_index == (bay_count+1)/2) rather than a second independent test.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 8:12 to 10:12. Below 7:12 the cornice loses its relationship to the roof and the house reads Federal or later; above 11:12 it reads First Period.
Sash lights by date: 12/12 or 12/8 to c. 1750; 9/6 c. 1740–1770; 6/6 from c. 1765. Fanlights and sidelights do not appear before c. 1780 and are a Federal marker, not a Georgian one.
Shutter leaf width equals half the clear opening width so that a closed pair exactly covers the window, and shutter height equals the sash height. Anything narrower is applied decoration.

Brick laid in Flemish bond on the entrance elevation (with glazed headers in the Chesapeake), common or English bond elsewhere; water table 24–36 in above grade; flat or segmental gauged arches over openings with a 4–6 in rise.

test.note: Tests the water table height. Brick bond pattern and gauged-arch rise (4-6in) are the same statement's other clauses and stay prose.

exemplars.name: Westover
exemplars.note: Built by William Byrd III shortly after a 1749 fire destroyed the earlier house — a correction to the long-standing attribution to William Byrd II. Steep hipped roof, tall paired interior-end chimneys, Portland stone doorways added c. 1767.

exemplars.name: Drayton Hall
exemplars.location: Ashley River, Charleston County, South Carolina
exemplars.note: Built 1738–42; the earliest fully realized two-tier Palladian portico in British North America, derived from a plate in Palladio known through its English editions. Never modernized — no plumbing or wiring — so the fabric is exceptionally legible.

exemplars.name: Mount Pleasant
exemplars.note: Built 1762–65 for John Macpherson; stuccoed and scored rubble with brick quoins, pedimented central pavilion, flanking dependencies — the Mid-Atlantic Palladian composition at full strength.

exemplars.name: Hammond-Harwood House
exemplars.note: William Buckland's last work. The entrance is a Gibbs surround executed in southern pine and rusticated to imitate stone, taken directly from Gibbs's A Book of Architecture (1728), as are the oeil-de-boeuf windows in the pediment — pattern-book transmission caught in the act.

sources: Thomas Tileston Waterman, The Mansions of Virginia, 1706–1776 (1946)
Fiske Kimball, Domestic Architecture of the American Colonies and of the Early Republic (1922)
Helen Park, A List of Architectural Books Available in America before the Revolution (1973)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)

proportion_packs.note: The order that supplies the module for the whole classical apparatus — doorway, cornice, pilaster, modillion. Gibbs rather than Vignola or Palladio because Gibbs is the book colonial builders actually owned: A Book of Architecture (1728) and Rules for Drawing the Several Parts of Architecture (1732) are the two most frequently recorded architectural titles in colonial American inventories, and the Hammond-Harwood House entrance is a Gibbs plate executed in southern pine. The choice is load-bearing and not decorative: Gibbs's entablature is one FIFTH of the column where Vignola's is one quarter, so at a 10 in diameter Gibbs gives 1'-6" of entablature against Vignola's 1'-10 1/2". A Georgian doorhead drawn to Vignola is four and a half inches too tall.

The everyday order. Ionic is the order of the entrance frontispiece and the best room; Doric is the order of the eave cornice, the porch, the secondary doorway and the plainer house. A five-bay farmhouse with a pedimented door is Doric throughout and is no less correct for it. Bind both and grade them by rank — the graduation of orders within one building is a period habit and is almost entirely absent from modern work.

Governs the elevation as a composition: odd bay count, pier width, the position and projection of water table and belt course, cornice projection, the width the whole entrance composition is permitted, and the ratio of the front's height to its width. This is the pack that enforces the style's single hard proportional constraint — an odd number of bays with the entrance in the centre. Palladio Book I chs. XXI–XXVI read against measured Anglo-American fronts of 1700–1860.

Governs the void before anything is put round it: door size taken from the storey (storey / 3.5), the 13:6 window ratio, the 5/6 diminution of window height by storey, and the one rule that most disciplines a Georgian elevation — one head datum per storey on every elevation without exception. Palladio Book I chs. XXV–XXVI with Vitruvius IV.vi.

The measured counterpart to opening-proportion, and the pack that dates the building. The light of glass is the real module of a Georgian window: 12/12 and 12/8 to c. 1750, 9/6 c. 1740–70, 6/6 from c. 1765, because the glasshouse could supply a larger pane each decade at a price a builder would pay. It also carries the muntin section (7/8 in) and the shutter rule (leaf = half the clear opening less the meeting clearance), which are the two fastest tells of a fake. Where it and opening-proportion disagree on the window ratio — 2.1 measured against 13/6 = 2.167 treatise — prefer this one; the pack says so itself.

The interior. Its wall_section_georgian assembly is the profile family for every internal moulding, and its nineteen-part division of the wall (pedestal 4 : field 12 : entablature 3) is Vignola's general rule applied to a room, which is exactly what the eighteenth-century builders' companions did. Bind this one family and no other: the Federal and Greek Revival sections in the same pack are the successor styles and mixing them is the interior equivalent of mixing typefaces. Read its calibration warning — the derivation was worked out for rooms of 11–13 ft and misbehaves below about 9 ft 6 in.

Governs the vertical: second storey at 0.85 of the first, attic at 0.62, the sill datum that does not move (30 in), the head at 0.78 of the storey, and the position of the belt course at the second-floor STRUCTURE rather than its finish. The graduation is the thing that makes a Georgian front sit down on the ground instead of floating, and it is the first casualty of a modern equal-storey frame.

Governs room shape and the relation of ceiling height to plan. Bound because the Georgian plan is the first American plan designed rather than accumulated, and its rooms are set out to ratios (3:4, 2:3, and the square passage bay) rather than to what the frame gave. Applies to the principal floor only; garrets and service rooms are not composed.

Primary on the masonry variants, absent on the frame ones — which is why it is bound optional here and promoted on the children. Where the wall is brick it is the real module of everything horizontal: four courses to eleven inches on a 2 1/4 in brick with a 1/2 in bed joint, water table at ten courses (27 1/2 in), belt course two courses, quoins on a whole number of courses, window head snapped to a course line. The tidewater-georgian node previously stated a 3/8 in joint, which is arithmetically impossible over four courses; corrected 2026-08-18 to the pack's 1/2 in figure.

Bound optional and low: the Georgian house is designed from a drawing rather than from a frame, and the bay no longer sets the plan the way it does in First Period work. It still governs where the house is framed — the 16 ft bay is why a New England Georgian is 32–38 ft deep and not 40 — so it is bound rather than dropped, and it is promoted on new-england-georgian.

tudor-jacobean.name: Tudor & Jacobean

description.short: The transitional century in which English building acquired Renaissance ornament without surrendering its medieval plan and silhouette.
description.long:
Between the end of the Wars of the Roses and the arrival of Inigo Jones, English architecture took on classical motifs — pilasters, strapwork, shaped gables — while keeping medieval massing, medieval framing, and the medieval hall. The result is a hybrid that later purists disliked and that later revivalists loved precisely because of its irregularity.

The transmission channel is worth noting: the ornament arrived largely through Netherlandish engravings and immigrant craftsmen, not from Italy directly. It is a second-hand Renaissance, which explains its cheerful indifference to proportional correctness.

defining_characteristics: Renaissance ornament applied to medieval massing and plan
Tall multi-flued chimney stacks and large mullioned, transomed windows
Strapwork and shaped gables transmitted via the Low Countries
The H- and E-plan great house with hall at the centre

elizabethan.name: Elizabethan

revival_periods.note: The Victorian 'Jacobethan', which fused Elizabethan and Jacobean sources indiscriminately and supplied the model for a generation of country houses and grammar schools.

geography.hearth: The Midlands and the North, above all Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire, where Robert Smythson and the Smythson office worked for Bess of Hardwick and her circle

lineage.note: Continuous practice: the same masons, the same mullion-and-transom window, the same absence of a real classical system. What changes is composition, not craft.

The orders reach England as printed plates — Serlio's Book IV in its Flemish and Dutch editions, John Shute's First and Chief Groundes of Architecture of 1563 — and are used as applied frontispieces. No Elizabethan mason had seen an Italian building, and it shows in every entablature they cut.

Real transmission by hand and by press: Protestant refugee craftsmen from the Low Countries settling in East Anglia and the ports from the 1560s, and Vredeman de Vries's Antwerp engravings, which are the direct source of English strapwork.

description.short: The first English style to compose an entire house as a symmetrical object rather than a set of accreted ranges, spending its new wealth on glass, height and silhouette rather than on defence or ornament.
description.long:
Elizabethan architecture is what a newly secure, newly rich and intensely competitive gentry built when the monarch travelled. The prodigy houses — Longleat, Wollaton, Hardwick, Burghley — were designed in significant part to receive a royal progress, an event which could ruin the host and make his family. Their extravagance is therefore not decadence but investment, and their strangeness is the strangeness of a building type with no precedent: a very large private house, undefended, in open country, meant to be seen from a distance and approached frontally.

The technical enabler is glass. English glassmaking capacity expanded sharply in the second half of the century, and the Elizabethans spent the windfall immediately and conspicuously. Hardwick Hall, built 1590-97 to Robert Smythson's design for Bess of Hardwick, has so much of it that the contemporary jingle 'Hardwick Hall, more glass than wall' is a plain description rather than a joke. The consequence is a wall that reads as a grid of mullions and transoms with stone piers between — structurally a masonry building, visually something much closer to a frame. This is the moment when English domestic architecture acquires its taste for the great window, which never afterwards leaves it.

Compositionally the change is decisive. The courtyard collapses into a compact block, often only one room deep so that every room is lit from both sides; the hall is turned through ninety degrees to lie on the entrance axis, which finally kills the screens passage as an organising device; the long gallery migrates to the top floor and runs the length of the house; and the silhouette becomes the primary subject, crowded with turrets, banqueting houses, chimneys disguised as classical piers and strapwork cresting. The orders appear on a central frontispiece, superimposed Doric-Ionic-Corinthian in the standard sequence, entirely as a piece of applied heraldry — Wollaton and Burghley cut them beautifully and use them structurally not at all. What the Elizabethans were reacting against was the medieval plan itself: its inwardness, its irregularity, its refusal to present a face. They wanted a house that could be drawn.

Inside, the experience is of light and cold in equal measure, and of a relentless upward pull. At Hardwick the stone stair rises through the whole house in a series of turns, gaining light at every landing, and delivers you at the top into the High Great Chamber, which is the largest and grandest room in the building and is on the second floor — an arrangement that makes no sense until you understand that ascent was the ceremony. The great windows flood these rooms and, in a Derbyshire winter, empty them of heat as fast as the fires fill them. Elizabethan houses were uncomfortable in a way their builders knew about and accepted, which is a useful reminder that comfort has never been the only thing architecture optimises for.

defining_characteristics: The house composed as a single symmetrical block, frontally and from a distance, with the courtyard abandoned or reduced to a forecourt
Glazed area approaching or exceeding solid wall on principal elevations, in grids of stone mullions and transoms
A central frontispiece of superimposed classical orders — usually Doric over Ionic over Corinthian — applied as ornament around the entrance and carrying no load
The hall turned onto the entrance axis, ending the medieval screens-passage sequence
A long gallery on the top floor running the full length of a range
Strapwork ornament (interlaced flat bands derived from Antwerp engraving) on parapets, gables, chimneypieces and plaster ceilings
An animated skyline of turrets, banqueting rooms, obelisks, balustraded parapets and chimneys treated as classical piers
diagnostic_tells: More window than wall on a principal elevation, with the glazing in a regular mullion-and-transom grid — the single quickest Elizabethan identification
Strapwork cresting standing free above the parapet line, often incorporating the owner's initials or device in cut stone
Superimposed orders stacked on the entrance bay of a facade that is otherwise entirely unclassical, with the entablatures stopping abruptly at the edges of the frontispiece
Rooftop banqueting turrets and a leaded roof walk — the house is meant to be occupied on top as well as inside
Windows without hood moulds: by the 1580s the label mould is dropped and the mullion grid runs flush, which distinguishes Elizabethan from Tudor at fifty feet

distinguished_from.difference: Tudor composes a gatehouse and hides a medieval plan; Elizabethan composes the whole building. Tudor keeps the hood mould and the four-centred arch and uses far less glass; Elizabethan drops the hood mould, flattens or squares the openings, and glazes to the limit of what the wall can carry.

A matter of degree and detail rather than of kind. Jacobean adds the Netherlandish shaped and scrolled gable, uses a columned porch rather than a flat frontispiece, is far more often brick with stone dressings, and lays on plasterwork and joinery with a heaviness the Elizabethans avoided. Elizabethan silhouettes are spiky; Jacobean silhouettes are curved.
