A century apart and philosophically opposed. Baroque uses the orders structurally and at colossal scale to model mass and shadow; Elizabethan uses them as flat applied heraldry on a wall of glass. If the wall is being sculpted, it is Baroque; if it is being dissolved, it is Elizabethan.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Symmetry about a central axis, with the mullion-and-transom grid as the working module and a rough, self-taught use of the orders on the frontispiece only. Devised by mason-architects such as Robert Smythson working from plans and from engraved plates, not from any theory of proportion.
typical_ratios: Mullion light 400-550 mm wide; transom divisions producing panels of roughly 1:1.2 to 1:1.5
Glazed to solid ratio on a principal elevation 45-60 percent, and higher at Hardwick
Storey heights increasing upward at Hardwick (roughly 1 : 1.1 : 1.3) to mark the ascent to the state rooms — the exact inverse of the Georgian rule
Long gallery 5-8 m wide by 30-50 m long, proportion 1:6 to 1:8
Frontispiece order height 1/4 to 1/3 of the elevation height, in three superimposed storeys
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Regular and grid-like, established by the window mullions rather than by structural bays; projecting towers or bay windows at the ends and centre punctuate the rhythm without breaking its module. Elevations read as a woven field with accents, not as a colonnade.

massing_affinities.note: The E-plan and H-plan are the standard Elizabethan gentry forms, with the porch as the middle stroke.
Retained at the very largest houses such as Burghley, though increasingly as a forecourt rather than an enclosed life.
The compact symmetrical block of Hardwick and Wollaton anticipates the double-pile plan by fifty years, but with a central hall or great chamber rather than a stair passage.
Wollaton's raised central prospect room over the hall is a tower-and-block composition, and Smythson's smaller lodges make the type explicit.

constraints.statement: Principal elevations must be at least 40 percent glazed, in a mullion-and-transom grid of 400-550 mm lights. A solid-walled elevation with punched openings is not Elizabethan whatever its ornament.

test.note: Tests the glazing-percentage floor. The mullion-and-transom light size (400-550 mm) has no matching vocabulary variable -- glazing_bar_width_in is muntin sight-width, not individual light size -- and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Classical orders occur only on the entrance frontispiece and only as superimposed applied storeys; they may not run across a whole elevation, carry a roof, or form a portico.
Facade symmetry about the entrance axis is absolute on the principal front, including chimney and turret placement. Side elevations may relax.
Roof pitch is low or concealed behind a balustraded or strapwork parapet; a dominant visible roof slope belongs to Tudor or to the vernacular, not here.
Skyline incident — turrets, banqueting rooms, cresting, chimney piers — must be symmetrically disposed and structurally reachable. Decorative turrets with no interior are a Victorian habit.

exemplars.name: Hardwick Hall
exemplars.note: Built 1590-97 by Robert Smythson for Elizabeth Talbot, Countess of Shrewsbury. Storey heights increase upward, the parapet carries her initials in cut stone, and the glazing ratio has never been exceeded in a house of its date.

exemplars.name: Longleat House
exemplars.note: Rebuilt 1568-80 for Sir John Thynne with Robert Smythson among the masons. The first fully symmetrical, outward-facing English country house elevation, with superimposed orders as flat pilaster strips.

exemplars.name: Wollaton Hall
exemplars.note: Built 1580-88 by Robert Smythson for Sir Francis Willoughby on coal money. A compact block with corner towers and a raised clerestoried prospect room over the hall — the most theatrical English house of its century.

exemplars.name: Montacute House
exemplars.note: Built 1598-1601 for Sir Edward Phelips in Ham Hill stone. E-plan, top-floor long gallery of 52 m, and a facade whose glazing and statuary niches show the style at its most disciplined.

sources: Mark Girouard, Robert Smythson and the Elizabethan Country House (1983)
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)
John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)
Malcolm Airs, The Tudor and Jacobean Country House: A Building History (1995)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England (county volumes)

proportion_packs.note: elizabethan is named directly in timber-bay's applies_to. The prodigy houses themselves (Hardwick, Wollaton, Longleat) are stone, but the bay module still governs the great mass of lesser Elizabethan gentry building, which remained timber-framed at this date, and it governs the roof and floor carpentry even at the great houses. No order pack is bound here despite the style's own text describing superimposed classical orders on the entrance frontispiece: proportional_system is explicit that the orders were used 'by rule of thumb' from engraved plates 'not from any theory of proportion,' so a Vignola-derived pack would attribute a precision (a real module, real entasis, a sourced entablature ratio) that the style's own masons did not have and did not intend. This is a deliberate exclusion, matching the corpus-wide guidance that no order pack belongs on this node.

Judgment binding (not in applies_to). Scoped narrowly to the subsidiary chambers off the state apartments, not to the great chamber, long gallery or hall — those are governed by this style's own figured ratios (storey heights increasing upward, gallery 1:6 to 1:8) and are far outside the pack's ordinary-room scale. The chamber-and-service-room band the pack records (9-14 ft) is a reasonable approximation for the smaller private rooms this style's own text notes were multiplying by the 1590s.

cape-dutch.name: Cape Dutch

revival_periods.note: Cape Dutch Revival, begun when Cecil Rhodes bought Groote Schuur and commissioned Herbert Baker to rebuild it in 1893; subsequently adopted as a settler-national style across South Africa.
Continuous Western Cape wine-estate practice — genuinely living building, not only restoration.

geography.hearth: Cape Town, Stellenbosch and the Boland winelands

lineage.note: The gable itself, the joinery, the small-paned casement, the brickwork and the whole idea that the centre of the front wall is where a house makes its statement. Transmitted by VOC servants and free burghers, most of them from Holland, in a single generation.

About two hundred Huguenots settled at Franschhoek and Drakenstein from 1688, roughly one in six of the free-burgher population. They brought vine and cellar practice, French joinery and panelling, and a rural farmstead habit of a long single-pile logis in a walled werf — which is why the Cape house is a farm building and not a town house.

A very large share of VOC employees were German, and the enormous reed-thatch roof of a Cape homestead — undressed rafters, no ceiling over the loft, a roof volume larger than the walls beneath it — is Low German and rural Dutch thatching practice, not Amsterdam practice.

The late gables of the 1790s-1810s, and the work of Louis Michel Thibault and the sculptor Anton Anreith, quote Louis XVI neoclassical profiles — concave-convex holbol curves, urns, pediments, fluted pilasters — onto a wall and plan that do not change at all.

description.short: The whitewashed, thatched, centrally gabled homestead of the Cape winelands, produced by Dutch gable practice, Huguenot farm craft and enslaved Cape Malay and African labour meeting a Mediterranean climate at the far end of a shipping route.
description.long:
Cape Dutch is the clearest demonstration in this taxonomy that a tree is the wrong data structure for architectural descent. Three transmissions arrive at the same place within forty years and none of them is subordinate to the others. From Holland comes the gable — the conviction that the centre of a front wall should rise into a shaped, moulded, whitewashed screen with a date on it — along with brickmaking, casement joinery and the anchor-plate. From France, after 1688, comes a Huguenot population large enough to reshape the free-burgher economy, bringing viticulture, cellar planning, panelling and a rural habit of long single-pile ranges arranged in a walled yard. And from the Cape itself, and from Batavia, comes the labour and much of the technical intelligence: enslaved craftsmen from the Indonesian archipelago, India and Madagascar, and Khoi and slave labour drawn from across the colony, who did the thatching, the lime-burning, the sun-dried brickmaking, the plaster modelling and, in many documented cases, the carpentry and joinery. The moulded gable is habitually credited to Dutch taste and Anreith's chisel. The people who mixed the lime, modelled the plaster and set the reed were overwhelmingly not Dutch, and any account of the style that leaves them out is not describing the building.

The climate did the rest. The Boland has hot dry summers, wet north-westerly winters and a wind — the south-easter — that arrives with a force nothing in Holland prepares a builder for. There is no useful building timber in the Western Cape: what forest existed was small, and structural timber was imported at ruinous cost from Batavia and later from Europe. Every consequence follows from that scarcity. Walls are thick sun-dried brick or rubble, lime-plastered and whitewashed annually, because the material is free and the finish is a performance layer against driving rain. Rooms are one room deep, because the roof span is set by what an undressed rafter will do. Roofs are steeply pitched reed thatch cut from the vleis, because it is local and free, and because thatch on a 45 to 50 degree pitch sheds Cape winter rain and insulates against Cape summer heat better than anything else available. And beneath the thatch, by law and by hard experience, sits the brandsolder — a brick-on-timber fire floor over the whole house, because a thatch fire in a dry summer wind is total.

The plan grows by letters. A single range is a langhuis. Add a rear wing and it is a T; add two and it is a U; close the two wings with a back range and it is an H, and the H-plan Cape homestead is the fully evolved type — a pinwheel of one-room-deep ranges around a small back court, with the front gable centred on the front door and the voorkamer behind it. Around the house, and part of the composition, is the werf: a low whitewashed wall enclosing the wine cellar, the slave quarters, the dovecote, the jonkershuis and the oak avenue. The werf is not a garden. It is the boundary of the working farm and the boundary of the household in the widest colonial sense of that word, and it is the part of the ensemble that most plainly records who lived there and on what terms.

Inside, the house is dark, cool, and much simpler than the front suggests. The voorkamer is high and its ceiling is exposed beams carrying a brick brandsolder, so you are looking at a floor rather than a ceiling. Walls are lime-plastered and thick enough that a window is a small bright cave. Floors are peach-pip, brick or later yellowwood. The gable that reads from three hundred metres away as a piece of European rhetoric turns out, from inside, to be a plastered blank — it is a wall the house never sees. That gap between what the front says and what the interior does is the essential Cape Dutch experience, and it is a colonial condition made architectural.

defining_characteristics: A moulded, plastered, whitewashed gable centred on the front door, standing free above the eave line of a thatched roof
Thick sun-dried brick or rubble walls, lime-plastered and limewashed white, on a raised stoep
Steeply pitched reed thatch over a brandsolder — a brick-on-timber fire floor spanning the whole plan
Single-pile ranges only, room depth fixed by the span of undressed imported or local rafters
Additive letter-plan growth: langhuis to T to U to H, ranges pinwheeling around a small rear court
Small-paned casements or sash in deep reveals, with external shutters, symmetrically disposed about the central door
An enclosed werf of outbuildings — cellar, jonkershuis, dovecote, slave quarters — bounded by a low whitewashed wall and read as part of the house
diagnostic_tells: Front gable rising clear of a thatched roof, moulded in plaster and usually dated in relief
Whitewash over a wall whose corners are visibly rounded and soft — plastered earth brick, not stone
The eave of a thatch roof cut square and level over a stoep supported on plain plastered piers
Green or dark-painted shutters and joinery against uniform white — the only colour on the building
A second, plainer gable over the rear or wing door, always subordinate to the front one

distinguished_from.difference: The Cape gable is centred on a broad, low, freestanding farm range and is a decorated wall panel above an eave. The Amsterdam gable is the end wall of a tall narrow urban house and contains the attic. One is a farm's face; the other is a merchant's whole building.

Both are whitewashed, thick-walled and hot-climate. The Cape house faces outward across a werf and puts everything into a front elevation; the Andalusian house faces inward to a patio and gives the street nothing.

Superficially similar — white walls, working precinct, single-pile ranges. But the hacienda's organising element is a continuous arcaded corredor around a patio, and it has no gable; the Cape house has no arcade and lives entirely off its gable and stoep.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The roof span and the wall. Room depth is fixed by what an undressed rafter will carry over a thatch roof — about 5.5 to 6.5 m clear — so every range is one room deep and the house grows in length and in wings. The front elevation is then set out from the door: the gable is centred on it, the windows are paired either side, and the gable width is roughly one third of the range's length.
typical_ratios: Range depth 5.5-6.5 m clear; wall thickness 450-600 mm
Thatch pitch 45-50 degrees
Gable width to front elevation length roughly 1:3
Gable height above eave 2.5-4 m; stoep height 400-600 mm above the werf
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five to nine openings on the front range, evenly spaced, with the door centred under the gable. The rhythm is even and unaccented — there is no order and no pilaster rhythm, only repetition against a long white wall.

massing_affinities.note: The developed Cape homestead is an H: a front range, two wings, and a rear range around a small court. The skeleton is Tudor in the catalog and Cape in this style; that is exactly why massing is separated from style.
The U-plan stage, wings running back from a front range with the fourth side open or closed by a wall.
The T-plan and the werf ensemble: a chain of single-pile ranges and outbuildings under separate thatched roofs.
The original langhuis and the surviving labourers' cottages of the winelands.

constraints.statement: All ranges are single-pile. Clear internal depth must not exceed 6.5 m; a double-pile Cape house is not a Cape house, because the roof cannot be made without an interior bearing wall the type does not have.

test.note: Converted from the source's 6.5 m to ft. Tests the internal-depth ceiling that makes a single-pile section possible; 'all ranges are single-pile' itself (depth_and_pile, categorical) is the same rule's consequence and is left as prose rather than tested a second way.

constraints.statement: Thatch pitch between 45 and 50 degrees. A continuous brandsolder — brick laid on timber beams over the full plan — is required beneath any thatch roof; it is both a fire barrier and the visible ceiling.

test.note: Tests the thatch-pitch range. The brandsolder requirement (a fire-barrier/ceiling assembly beneath the thatch) is a construction-method fact with no matching vocabulary variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: External walls minimum 450 mm, lime-plastered and limewashed. Cement render is prohibited: it traps moisture in an earth wall and destroys it. Openings on the north-west (summer sun and south-easter) elevation limited to about 15 percent of wall area.

test.note: Converted from the source's 450 mm to in. Tests the wall-thickness minimum only. 'Cement render is prohibited' (a material prohibition) and 'openings on the north-west elevation limited to about 15 percent of wall area' (glazed_area_pct_wall has no per-orientation variant) both stay prose.

constraints.statement: A moulded front gable requires a centred front door directly beneath it and at least one subordinate, plainer gable elsewhere on the house. A single decorative gable with no counterpart reads as scenery.

test.note: Reads 'a moulded front gable plus at least one subordinate gable' as a minimum total of two. The centred-front-door-under-the-front-gable alignment clause stays prose.

constraints.statement: The homestead is incomplete without its werf: a low limewashed enclosing wall and at least the cellar and one outbuilding. Isolating the manor house from its working precinct misrepresents the type.

exemplars.name: Groot Constantia
exemplars.note: Granted to Simon van der Stel 1685; manor house substantially remodelled for Hendrik Cloete in the 1790s, with the wine cellar pediment by Anton Anreith, 1791.

exemplars.name: Meerlust
exemplars.note: Homestead gable dated 1776; one of the least-altered surviving H-plan werf ensembles.

exemplars.name: Boschendal Manor House
exemplars.note: Built on a Huguenot grant of 1685; the surviving H-plan manor with holbol gables is dated 1812.

exemplars.name: Groote Schuur
exemplars.note: Herbert Baker's rebuilding for Cecil Rhodes — the origin point of the Cape Dutch Revival, and therefore the hinge between the living tradition and its later national use.

sources: Fransen & Cook, The Old Buildings of the Cape
Lewcock, Early Nineteenth Century Architecture in South Africa
Walton, Homesteads and Villages of South Africa
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to. The voorkamer — one room deep, lit through thick lime-plastered reveals, roofed by a brandsolder fire-floor over exposed beams — is the daylight- and span-limited vernacular room this pack describes, and its single-pile constraint (cape-dutch.c01, depth not exceeding 6.5 m) is the same physical limit — what an undressed rafter will carry — that generates the pack's own depth_and_pile rule.

Judgment bind, though this node id is itself listed in the pack's applies_to. Cape Dutch walls are masonry, not a timber frame, so the pack does not govern wall construction here — but its depth_and_pile rule (single-pile depth 192-264 in / 16-22 ft) matches this node's own stated range depth of 5.5-6.5 m (18-21 ft) closely, because both are the same underlying constraint restated: a room cannot be deeper than the span an available roof member will carry without an interior bearing wall. Bound narrowly for that depth-governing logic, not for framing. brick-course was checked and rejected: Cape Dutch walls are lime-plastered and limewashed sun-dried brick or rubble, and the coursing brick-course models (exposed bond, moulded water-table courses, gauged arches) is invisible under a plastered finish and does not apply.

garrison-colonial.name: Garrison Colonial

revival_periods.note: A post-war builder type: two-storey box, a token 12–18 in overhang across the front only, and the folk-etymological name that came with it.

geography.hearth: Essex County, Massachusetts and the Connecticut River towns — the wealthier First Period settlements

lineage.note: The jetty is straightforwardly English. It is a standard device of late-medieval urban timber framing in East Anglia, Kent and the West Country, and the New England carpenters who used it had learned it there.

description.short: A two-storey New England house whose second floor projects on a framed overhang, with carved drop pendants at the posts — an English timber-framing survival that American folklore has misread as a defensive device for three hundred years.
description.long:
The overhang needs its story corrected before anything else can be said about the type, because the folk etymology is nearly universal and it is wrong. The jetty — a projection of the second-floor framing eight to twenty inches beyond the wall below — is a late-medieval English carpentry practice with three ordinary explanations, none of them military. Structurally it is the simplest way to land a second-floor girt: you cantilever the joists past the plate and set the upper posts on their ends, which gains floor area upstairs without lengthening the sill and puts the joint in compression where the carpenter wants it. Urbanistically it gained the upper room a foot or two of space over a narrow street or way without encroaching at ground level. Socially, by the time it reached New England it was already an old-fashioned, expensive, visibly skilled detail that a prosperous man could pay for and a poor one could not — which is why it clusters in the wealthiest First Period towns and appears on the houses of ministers, magistrates and merchants.

It is not a fighting platform. There are no loopholes in a New England jetty; the projection is far too shallow to shoot down through; the drop pendants beneath it are decorative turnings, not gun ports; and the boiling-oil story is a nineteenth-century invention that circulated with the general Romantic reimagining of the colonial frontier. There were genuine garrison houses in seventeenth-century New England — fortified dwellings with heavy horizontal plank or squared-log walls, small high openings, and sometimes a palisade, designated by the town as places of refuge — but those buildings are a different type and they generally did not have jetties. The twentieth-century real-estate label 'Garrison Colonial' fused the two, attaching a military name to a domestic detail. This node uses the received name because the industry does, and corrects the reading.

What the type actually is, then, is the display end of the First Period house: two full storeys front and rear (unlike the saltbox, which gives the rear away), a central chimney, a steep 45–55 degree roof, and a jetty across the front, sometimes carried around the gable ends as a second overhang and occasionally a third at the gable peak. Where the overhang is 'hewn' — cut from the solid of the post — it projects only two to six inches and reads as a shadow line. Where it is truly framed, with the second-floor girt bearing on cantilevered joist ends, it projects fourteen to twenty inches and casts a real shadow across the facade at midday, which is the whole point of it.

Standing under one, the effect is oddly protective and entirely visual: a horizontal band of deep shade at the twelve-foot line, four turned pendants hanging from it like punctuation, and above that a second storey whose windows are noticeably smaller than the ones below. It is the closest thing seventeenth-century New England had to a facade.

defining_characteristics: Two full storeys front and rear under a symmetrical side-gable roof — no lean-to reduction of the rear elevation
A framed overhang (jetty) at the second-floor line projecting 8–20 in on the front, occasionally repeated at the gable ends and at the gable peak
Carved drop pendants at the exposed post ends beneath the overhang, normally four across the front
Central chimney stack, as in all First Period New England work
Second-floor windows measurably smaller than the first-floor windows — 10–20% shorter and often narrower
Steep roof, 45–55 degrees, with the ridge on the long axis
Riven or sawn clapboard over the frame, with the overhang fascia and pendants the only worked exterior joinery
diagnostic_tells: A continuous shadow line across the facade at the second-floor level, with turned drops at four points
Where the overhang is hewn rather than framed, the projection is only 2–6 in — look for the shadow, then measure
Central chimney plus two full storeys plus jetty: the combination occurs nowhere else
No openings in the overhang soffit — the absence of loopholes is itself the diagnostic against the defensive story
The gable-end overhang, where present, sits at the attic floor line rather than the second-floor line

distinguished_from.difference: The post-1930 builder type has a shallow 12–18 in overhang across the front only, with no pendants or with applied ones, gable-end or no chimneys, an 8:12 roof, six-over-six or picture windows the same size on both floors, and an attached garage. It also, almost universally, carries the defensive folk etymology in its marketing. The colonial original has a central chimney, a 12:12+ roof, and smaller upper windows.
Both are two storeys at the front and both often carry a jetty. The saltbox gives up its rear elevation to a single-storey lean-to under a catslide; the garrison keeps two full storeys all round.

The English parent leaves the frame exposed with infill panels, and jetties often on two or three storeys; New England covers the frame in clapboard, uses one jetty, and stops building them by about 1730.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The frame bay and the cantilever capacity of the second-floor joists; the overhang dimension is set by how far a 7–9 in joist can project without a visible sag.
typical_ratios: Framed overhang 14–20 in; hewn overhang 2–6 in; never more than 24 in
Main body 38–44 ft × 18–22 ft, two storeys
First-floor ceiling 7 ft 0 in – 7 ft 8 in; second floor 6 ft 8 in – 7 ft 2 in
Second-floor window height 80–90% of first-floor
Drop pendant length 8–14 in, diameter 4–6 in, at post positions only
Roof rise:run 12:12 to 17:12
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five bays on the front where the frame allows, the door bay narrow and centred on the stack; the pendants mark the post lines and therefore do not coincide with the window rhythm.

massing_affinities.note: The plan under the jetty is the ordinary First Period two-room plan.
Very many jettied houses acquired a lean-to and became saltboxes.
Jettied half-houses exist, awaiting the second cell that was sometimes never built.

constraints.statement: Framed overhang 14–20 in maximum, hewn overhang 2–6 in; never exceed 24 in. The projection is the cantilever of a 7–9 in second-floor joist and cannot be increased without changing the structure to something the tradition never built.

test.note: Tests the statement's absolute ceiling ('never exceed 24 in'), which covers both the framed (14-20in) and hewn (2-6in) sub-cases without needing to know which construction method is used.

constraints.statement: Drop pendants occur only at post positions and only where the overhang is framed — four across a five-bay front. Pendants on a hewn overhang, or spaced to suit the windows, are decoration without structure.
One central chimney within the plan. Gable-end chimneys with a jetty produce a combination that does not occur in surviving First Period fabric.
Second-floor window height 80–90% of first-floor height. Equal windows on both floors is a revival signature.

Do not model or describe the overhang as defensive. No loopholes, no firing platform, no boiling oil. Where a genuinely fortified frontier garrison house is wanted, the correct assembly is heavy horizontal plank or squared-log walls with small high openings and no jetty.

exemplars.name: Parson Capen House
exemplars.note: The canonical example: framed overhangs on the front and both gables, four carved drop pendants, central chimney, casement openings.

exemplars.name: Stanley-Whitman House
exemplars.note: Framed overhang projecting 18 in with four drop pendants, two of them original. Long dated to c. 1660 in older literature; documentary evidence now places construction between 1709 and 1720.

exemplars.name: Paul Revere House
exemplars.note: The urban case, where the jetty does the thing it did in England — gains upper-floor area over a narrow street.

exemplars.name: John Whipple House
exemplars.note: Second-phase block carries the overhang; Ipswich retains the densest surviving group of jettied First Period houses in America.

sources: Abbott Lowell Cummings, The Framed Houses of Massachusetts Bay, 1625–1725 (1979)
J. Frederick Kelly, Early Domestic Architecture of Connecticut (1924)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Historic Ipswich / Historic Massachusetts, 'Jetties of the New England Post-Medieval Renaissance' (survey of Essex County First Period fabric)

proportion_packs.note: Same generative bay as new-england-colonial: the 16-20 ft frame bay sets the room, the central stack takes over half a bay (hearth_position rule), and the plan is the ordinary First Period hall-and-parlor under the overhang. What this pack does NOT derive is the jetty itself -- the 8-20 in cantilever of the second-floor girt past the wall below is a real gap in this binding: no pack in this corpus dimensions a framed overhang, and the 14-20 in framed / 2-6 in hewn figures in this node's own record are not recoverable from any of the 36 packs available. As on new-england-colonial, no facade-system pack is bound: the front is generated by post position, and the pendants mark the post lines rather than the window rhythm, which this node states directly.

The best-fitting single number in this whole cluster. This pack's height_proportion rule for a box frame -- second-floor post shorter than the ground-floor post, ratio 0.88, explicitly marked judgment -- lands almost exactly inside this node's own hard-adjacent constraint (c04): second-floor window height 80-90% of first-floor. Roof pitch (12:12-17:12) and the near-flush eave follow the same framing logic as new-england-colonial.
Same date sequence as new-england-colonial -- casement to c. 1700, then progressively larger-paned sash -- governing the window openings on both floors.
Bound for the single head-datum rule only, as on new-england-colonial; not for its 13:6 window ratio, which the recorded openings here do not follow.
The plan under the jetty is the ordinary First Period hall-and-parlor two-room plan; room breadth, hearth reach and Glassie's generative square-cell logic apply exactly as on new-england-colonial.

english-georgian-townhouse.name: English Georgian Town House

revival_periods.note: Neo-Georgian infill and mansion flats, which borrow the elevation and abandon the section.
The Georgian terrace is the single most-cited precedent in contemporary urbanist practice, generally reproduced without the basement, the mews or the leasehold system that made it work.

geography.hearth: London's West End estates — Grosvenor, Bedford, Portman — and after them Bath, Dublin, Edinburgh New Town and Bristol

lineage.note: The urban expression of the parent style. Everything in the kit is inherited; what changes is that the plan is turned through ninety degrees onto a narrow lot, the composition becomes the street wall rather than the house, and statutory regulation replaces taste as the enforcing mechanism.

The type is fixed by the post-Fire rebuilding: the Act of 1667 defined four rates of house and banned timber facades, and the surviving Queen Anne houses of Spitalfields and the City are the immediate ancestors of the whole Georgian terrace.

description.short: The rated, party-walled, leasehold-built terrace house whose individual facade is deliberately unremarkable so that the street wall can be magnificent.
description.long:
The Georgian town house is a product, in the industrial sense, and understanding it as one explains everything about its form. A ground landlord let land on a building lease of sixty to ninety-nine years; a speculating builder — often a carpenter or bricklayer with very little capital — took a plot or three, put up carcasses to a standard section, and sold the leases on to fit out. Because the builder could fail at any point and frequently did, the section had to be conventional enough that another tradesman could finish it. Because the ground landlord wanted a coherent estate, the elevation was controlled by covenant. And because Parliament kept legislating after each fire and each collapse, the construction was controlled by statute: the 1667 Act's four rates, the 1707 Act banning the projecting timber eaves cornice and requiring a parapet, the 1709 Act setting window frames back four inches from the wall face, and the consolidating Act of 1774, which fixed the rates by floor area and value and gave London the terraces of Bloomsbury and Marylebone.

The plan is the side-hall double pile turned onto a narrow frontage: entrance and stair against one party wall, front and back rooms lit only from the two short ends, a closet wing projecting into the yard, and the whole service life pushed down into a basement lit by an area cut in front of the pavement and up a back stair. The vaults under the pavement take the coal, delivered through a round iron plate; the mews behind takes the horses; the servants sleep in the garret behind the parapet. Vertically the house is a social section, and it is worth stating the one place where it departs from the country-house rule: in a town house the principal storey is usually the first floor, not the ground floor. The drawing room is up one flight, away from the street noise and the smell of the area, and its windows are the tallest in the elevation, frequently reaching the floor and opening onto a shallow iron balcony. The ground floor, holding the dining room and the front parlour, is broad but slightly lower; above the drawing room the bedroom floor drops sharply and the garret drops again.

What the type was reacting against was the timber-fronted, jettied, gabled London street that burned in 1666. What it produced instead is the most successful piece of urban design in the English-speaking world: a wall of nearly identical houses, brick or stucco, with a continuous cornice or parapet line, uniform floor levels, uniform railings, and a rhythm of doorcases at the pavement. No individual house asks for attention. The doorcase is the one licensed indulgence, and in Dublin the fanlight above it becomes an art form in its own right.

To walk a Georgian street is to be held by a wall of consistent height with a floor of consistent width, and the effect on the body is unmistakable — the street is a room. To enter one of the houses is a compression: up three or four steps, past the railings and the void of the area, through a narrow doorcase into a passage the width of a coffin, and then a release upward into the stair, which is nearly always the best-lit part of the plan. The rooms themselves are simple boxes, deep-silled, chair-railed, and if you sit in the drawing-room window on a spring afternoon with the sash raised you will understand exactly why the first floor became the principal one.

defining_characteristics: Party-wall construction in a continuous terrace, with the street wall rather than the individual house as the compositional subject
Side-hall double-pile plan on a narrow lot: entrance passage and stair against one party wall, front and back rooms lit only from the ends
A vertical social section — basement service, ground-floor dining, first-floor principal drawing room, bedroom floor, garret — expressed in graduated window heights
The first floor as the principal storey, with the tallest windows, often taken to the floor with an iron balcony
A front area with railings, steps up to a raised entrance, and coal vaults extending under the pavement
Regulated construction: brick or stucco facades, parapet with concealed gutter and no projecting eaves, window frames set back from the wall face
Ornament restricted to the doorcase, fanlight, railings and, at grander scale, a shared pediment or giant order across a whole terrace
diagnostic_tells: First-floor windows taller than ground-floor windows — the reverse of the country-house rule and the quickest way to identify an urban Georgian elevation
A parapet with no visible eaves, and dormers set back behind it so the garret is invisible from the opposite pavement
The area: a sunken open trench across the front with railings above and a bridge to the front steps, admitting light to the basement kitchen
Round cast-iron coal plates set into the pavement in front of each house, marking the vaults beneath
A doorcase and fanlight that differ from house to house on a street where nothing else does

distinguished_from.difference: The same style solving the opposite problem. The country house is free-standing, lit on four sides, entered on the ground floor at the centre of a symmetrical front, with the principal rooms at grade. The town house is party-walled, lit on two sides, entered off-centre, and puts its principal room on the first floor.

Chronological successor on the same plan. Regency stuccoes the brick, bows the front, thins the glazing bars, and hangs iron balconies with tented canopies. If the terrace is brick with a plain flat front, it is Georgian; if it is cream stucco with bows and ironwork, it is Regency.

The American and mid-Victorian successor: taller storeys, a high stoop, heavy bracketed cornice, segmental-arched windows with pronounced hood mouldings, and one-over-one or two-over-two glazing. Georgian terraces are flat-fronted, small-paned and cornice-light.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The statutory rates of house, which fix floor area, storey heights and wall thicknesses, combined with the inherited Georgian sash and bay proportions. The unit of composition is the terrace, not the house; the unit of construction is the party-wall bay.
typical_ratios: Frontage 5.0-7.5 m for a second- or third-rate house, giving three bays; 4.0-5.0 m and two bays for a fourth rate
Depth front wall to rear wall 9.0-12.5 m, beyond which the middle of the plan goes dark
Storey heights: basement 2.4-2.7 m, ground 3.0-3.4 m, first floor 3.3-3.9 m (the tallest), second 2.7-3.0 m, garret 2.3-2.6 m
Sash proportion 1.6:1 to 1.9:1 at ground and second floors, 2:1 to 2.4:1 at the first floor
Solid to void ratio on the facade 1:1 to 1.4:1; pier between windows not less than 450 mm
Front steps 3-6 risers above pavement level; area 1.2-2.0 m wide and one full storey deep
Party wall one and a half bricks (330 mm) minimum, carried up above the roof as a fire break
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Two or three equal bays per house, the door taking one of them, repeated without variation along the terrace. Where a whole row is composed as a palace front, the rhythm is broken only by a pedimented centre and slightly advanced end pavilions.

massing_affinities.note: The type is the massing; the individual house has no independent silhouette.
The plan behind the facade, with a closet wing or rear ell extending into the yard.
Only at the widest first-rate houses and at the ends of terraces, where a centred door and a genuine centre hall become possible.

constraints.statement: Facades in brick, stone or stucco only; no timber-fronted elevation, and no projecting timber eaves cornice. Rainwater is taken behind a parapet into a concealed gutter, following the London Act of 1707.
Window frames set back not less than 100 mm from the external wall face, per the Act of 1709; sash boxes concealed within the reveal.

test.note: London Building Act of 1709.

constraints.statement: First-floor storey height must exceed the ground floor by 5-20 percent, and first-floor windows must be the tallest on the elevation. Applying the country-house graduation to a terrace produces a facade that looks top-heavy and wrong.

test.note: Here the differential runs the other direction from the usual ground>first hierarchy -- first floor is the tallest, piano-nobile-like storey of a London terrace. Same variable, applied to the first-over-ground pair.

constraints.statement: Party walls carried up through the roof as a fire break, and no window on a party wall elevation. Plan depth not to exceed 12.5 m without a light well or closet-wing set-back.

test.note: Source states the figure in metres directly. The fire-break party wall and no-window-on-party-wall clauses in the same statement are categorical, not numeric, and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Cornice or parapet line, floor levels, material and railing pattern must be continuous across the terrace. Individual expression is confined to the doorcase, fanlight and door colour.

exemplars.name: Bedford Square
exemplars.note: Built 1775-83 for the Bedford estate, probably by Thomas Leverton with the builders William Scott and Robert Grews. Each side treated as a palace front with a stuccoed pedimented centre; Coade stone doorcases throughout.

exemplars.name: Charlotte Square
exemplars.note: Designed by Robert Adam in 1791 and built 1792-1820. The north side is a single palace-fronted composition in polished ashlar — the Georgian terrace at its most disciplined, and No. 7 survives as a furnished Georgian House museum.

exemplars.name: Fournier Street
exemplars.note: Built 1725-c.1730 for Huguenot silk masters. Early Georgian brick with wooden doorcases on carved brackets and long attic weavers' lofts glazed for north light — the type before its facades were fully regulated.

exemplars.name: Merrion Square
exemplars.note: Laid out from 1762 and built over four decades. Dublin brick with granite steps, wrought-iron railings and the finest radiating fanlights in the British Isles.

sources: John Summerson, Georgian London (1945)
Dan Cruickshank and Peter Wyld, Georgian Buildings of Britain and Ireland (1975)
Dan Cruickshank and Neil Burton, Life in the Georgian City (1990)
Peter Guillery, The Small House in Eighteenth-Century London (2004)
John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)

proportion_packs.note: Bound here, not at the trunk style, for a reason specific to this variant rather than to Gibbs's colonial export: the 'Gibbs surround' -- alternating rusticated blocks around an opening -- is an ENGLISH device, first given currency on Gibbs's own window architraves at St Martin-in-the-Fields (1722-26), and it is exactly the licensed doorcase indulgence this node names as the terrace's one point of individual expression. Where the American template binds Gibbs for the book colonial builders owned, this node binds him for the surround he invented and that London, Dublin and Edinburgh speculators used on their own streets before it ever crossed the Atlantic.
The plainer doorcase of the fourth-rate and lower third-rate house, where the budget does not run to a fanlight-and-pilasters frontispiece; Doric is graded below Ionic exactly as in the trunk style.

Governs the street WALL rather than the individual house -- this node's own governing_logic states the unit of composition is the terrace, not the house -- so the pack's cornice-line, floor-level and material continuity rules apply across the whole run per the node's hard constraint c05, and a single facade's departure from its neighbours is the failure this pack exists to catch here.

Governs the sash ratio, but INVERTED from the country-house default: this node's own hard constraint c03 sets the first floor, not the ground floor, as the tallest storey and its windows as the tallest on the elevation -- the piano-nobile-like drawing-room floor this node's long description explains at length. Apply the pack's ratio logic to the first-over-ground pair, not ground-over-first.

Carries the same inversion at measured scale: 2:1 to 2.4:1 at the first floor against 1.6:1 to 1.9:1 at ground and second, per this node's own typical_ratios -- the tallest panes are one flight up, not at the door.

RE-ANCHORED, following the tidewater-georgian precedent for a different divergence: the storey this node graduates UP to before graduating down is the first floor (3.3-3.9 m, the tallest in the section), not the ground floor (3.0-3.4 m) the pack assumes by default. Basement (2.4-2.7 m), ground, first, second (2.7-3.0 m) and garret (2.3-2.6 m) form a five-tier social section rather than the country house's four-tier decorative one, and the peak sits one storey up.

Governs the drawing-room chair rail and cornice on the principal (first) floor at full Georgian richness, diminishing toward the plainer ground-floor dining room and the bare bedroom and garret floors above -- the vertical social section expressed in trim as much as in window height.

Constrained by the narrow lot this node's own plan_depth_ft constraint (c04) tests: front and back rooms lit only from the two short ends, a closet wing into the yard, and a plan depth capped at 12.5 m without a light well -- the Georgian ratio set is still the governing logic, but it is solved for a shape the free-standing country house never has to face.

The party wall this node's own hard constraint c04 requires -- one and a half bricks (330 mm) minimum, carried up through the roof as a fire break -- and the coursing behind the regulated brick or stucco facade the 1667 and 1774 Acts controlled.

regency.name: Regency

revival_periods.note: Regency Revival — the stuccoed, iron-balconied seaside and suburban manner of the interwar years, and the source of the American 'Regency Moderne' of the 1930s.

geography.hearth: Nash's London — Regent Street and the Regent's Park terraces — and the new resort towns of Brighton, Cheltenham, Leamington and Hove

lineage.note: Unbroken. The plan, the sash, the terrace, the leasehold building system and the trades are Georgian; Regency changes the surface, the roof line and the relation to the garden.
The thinning of every profile, the attenuated order and the taste for shaped rooms carry straight through from the Adam office into the Regency generation.
By the 1790s Adam's manner was being attacked as frippery and confectionery. The Greek turn is explicitly a demand for severity, mass and correctness against Adam's decorative delicacy.

Quoted from measured drawings, not descended from. Stuart and Revett's Antiquities of Athens, from 1762 onward, made the baseless Greek Doric column and the anthemion available to men who had never been to Greece, and Regency uses them as motifs on wholly English plans.

Directoire and Empire taste crosses the Channel through emigres, through Percier and Fontaine's plates, and through Thomas Hope's Household Furniture and Interior Decoration (1807). Regency interiors are as French as they are Greek.

description.short: Georgian construction rendered in stucco and opened to the garden: bow fronts, floor-length windows, cast-iron balconies under tented canopies, wide bracketed eaves, and Greek detail applied with a light hand.
description.long:
Regency is the moment the English house stops facing the street and starts facing the view. Almost everything structural is inherited — the brick carcass, the double-pile plan, the sash window, the terrace — but the priorities have shifted. Windows on the principal floor are taken down to the floor and turned into casements or long sashes opening onto a balcony, so that the drawing room and the garden become continuous; the front bows outward to catch a sea view or an oblique light; the roof, once hidden behind a parapet, comes out over the wall on brackets in a wide shallow overhang of Welsh slate. Underneath it all the brick is covered in stucco, ruled and lined to imitate ashlar and painted a pale stone colour. That last decision is the one everything else follows from: stucco is cheap, fast, moulds into any profile, and hides the fact that a magnificent terrace is a row of thin speculative shells.

The conditions are war, boom and leisure. The French wars cut off the Grand Tour and turned English travel inward, which built Brighton, Cheltenham, Leamington and Weymouth; peace and agricultural wealth after 1815 built the Regent's Park terraces; and the Prince Regent's own extravagance gave the period its name and its most conspicuous building. John Nash is the central figure not because he was the best architect of the period — Soane was, and knew it — but because he understood development. Regent Street, cut through London between 1811 and 1825, is simultaneously a piece of speculative real estate, a social boundary and a picturesque composition, and the Regent's Park terraces behind it dress rows of ordinary houses as single vast stuccoed palaces with giant orders and pediments. The trick is entirely scenographic and completely successful.

What Regency reacted against was Adam's prettiness, and what it reached for was severity — the baseless Greek Doric column, the plain incised anthemion, the unmoulded architrave. But it reached for a great deal else at the same time. The same decades produce the Royal Pavilion at Brighton, which is Indian outside and Chinese inside; the cottage orne with its thatch, tree-trunk verandas and diamond casements; Egyptian, Etruscan and Gothic rooms in the same house. Regency is where British classicism stops being a system and becomes a menu, and the eclecticism of the whole Victorian century starts here.

Standing in a Regency room is the first recognisably modern domestic experience in Britain. The window comes to the floor and the light is horizontal and abundant; you can walk out onto a balcony with a curved iron rail and a striped copper awning above it; the ceiling is plain or very lightly enriched; the walls are painted a strong flat colour; the furniture is light enough to be moved around the room rather than lined up against the walls. Outside, the stucco terrace works as a single wall of pale, softly modelled surface — bows, balconies and canopies casting shallow shadows — and it looks, correctly, like scenery. Nash was criticised in his own lifetime for building in lath and plaster; the buildings are still there, and still lovely, and still require repainting every few years.

defining_characteristics: Stuccoed walls, ruled and lined to imitate ashlar, painted in pale stone or cream, over a brick carcass
Bow, bay or canted fronts giving oblique views and modelling the terrace wall in shallow curves
Floor-length windows on the principal storey opening onto a cast-iron balcony, frequently under a tented copper canopy
Cast and wrought iron used as the principal ornament: balconies, verandas, railings, porches, in anthemion, lyre, heart and trellis patterns
Low-pitched hipped roofs of Welsh slate with wide overhanging eaves on plain or scrolled brackets, or alternatively a very shallow parapet
Greek rather than Roman detail, sparingly used: baseless Doric columns, incised anthemion and Greek key, unmoulded flat architraves
Very thin glazing bars, often with margin lights and occasionally coloured glass, and glazing patterns of 6-over-6, 3-over-6 or margin-light arrangements
diagnostic_tells: A cast-iron balcony with an ogee-tented copper hood over a floor-length window — the single most reliable Regency signature and one that appears in no earlier style
Stucco scored with ruled joints at the ground floor and left smooth above, so that a rendered wall imitates a rusticated base under ashlar
Wide eaves projecting 450-750 mm on brackets over a shallow slate roof, where Georgian would have a parapet or a modillion cornice tight to the wall
Glazing bars of 12-18 mm, thinner than anything before, sometimes with a narrow margin light framing the main panes
A Greek Doric porch with baseless, unfluted or partly fluted columns and a plain entablature, against the Roman Doric or Ionic doorcase of Georgian work

distinguished_from.difference: Material honesty is the dividing line. Georgian shows brick or ashlar and keeps its windows in the wall plane's discipline; Regency renders everything in stucco, bows the front, brings the windows to the floor, hangs ironwork on the facade and lets the eaves overhang. Georgian faces the street; Regency faces the garden.

Adam is Roman, floral, polychrome and interior-driven; Regency is Greek, linear, pale and exterior-driven. Adam thins the Georgian moulding; Regency deletes it — a Regency architrave is often a plain flat band with a single incised line.

The American cousin takes the Greek quotation far more literally, with full temple fronts, heavy pedimented gables and columns of structural scale, usually in painted wood. Regency uses Greek detail as light incident on a stuccoed box and rarely builds a full portico.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Georgian proportional habits, loosened and lightened, with Greek orders used as motifs rather than as a generative module. Composition is increasingly scenographic — the terrace or the villa is designed for how it reads from a moving viewpoint in a landscape.
typical_ratios: Ground-floor window 2:1 to 2.4:1 height to width, taken down to floor level; upper windows 1.6:1 to 1.8:1
Storey graduation retained: ground floor exceeds first by 10-15 percent, second floor 0.65-0.75 of the first
Eaves overhang 450-750 mm; roof pitch 22-30 degrees in slate
Bow front radius 3.5-6.0 m, projecting 0.6-1.2 m from the wall plane
Balcony depth 900-1200 mm, rail height 900-1050 mm
Greek Doric column height 6-7 diameters, baseless, with a plain unmoulded abacus
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Even Georgian spacing, interrupted by the bow, which usually occupies the centre of a villa front or one end of a terrace unit. At the largest scale — Nash's Regent's Park terraces — a whole row is composed as a palace with a giant-order centre and end pavilions, and the individual house disappears entirely.

massing_affinities.note: The stuccoed terrace, palace-fronted or bow-fronted, is the style's defining urban form.
The Regency villa: a compact double-pile block with a hipped slate roof, wide eaves and a veranda, standing free in a small landscaped plot.
The standard terrace plan, unchanged from Georgian practice.
The full-width iron veranda, exported to and reimported from India and the colonies, makes the Regency villa a genuine gallery type in warm climates.
The castellated and Italianate villas of Nash and his contemporaries — Luscombe, Cronkhill — begin the picturesque asymmetrical house within an otherwise classical practice.

constraints.statement: Stucco must be continuous over all visible elevations of a rendered mass, with ruled ashlar lining confined to the ground storey where a rusticated base is intended. Stucco on the front with bare brick returns is forbidden.

Principal-floor windows extend to within 150 mm of the finished floor and open onto a balcony or veranda not less than 900 mm deep. A floor-length window with no balcony is a hazard and a period error.

test.note: Tests the balcony/veranda depth clause. The window-to-floor gap (within 150mm) is the same statement's other numeric claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Glazing bars 12-18 mm. Heavier bars date the work to before 1780; the thin bar is what makes a Regency window read as a sheet of light.

Where wide eaves are used they project 450-750 mm on visible brackets or a plain soffit, and the roof pitch stays between 22 and 30 degrees in slate. A steep roof under wide eaves belongs to the Italianate, forty years later.

test.note: The eave-projection figure (450-750mm) stated in the same clause applies only 'where wide eaves are used' and is conditional, so it stays prose rather than being folded into this test.

constraints.statement: Greek and Roman detail may not be mixed on one elevation. Exotic modes — Indian, Egyptian, Chinese, Gothic — are permitted but must be complete within a room or a whole building, never blended.

exemplars.name: Cumberland Terrace
exemplars.note: Designed by John Nash and executed by James Thomson. A row of ordinary houses fronted as a single stuccoed palace with a giant Ionic order and a sculptured pediment — the scenographic method at full strength.

exemplars.name: Royal Pavilion
exemplars.note: Remodelled by Nash 1815-23 for the Prince Regent from Henry Holland's earlier villa. Indian outside, Chinese inside, and structurally a cast-iron frame — the period's eclecticism and its technology in one building.

exemplars.name: Park Crescent
exemplars.note: Built 1806-21 by Nash. A semicircular stuccoed crescent with a continuous paired Ionic colonnade at ground level, and the hinge between Portland Place and Regent's Park.

exemplars.name: Sir John Soane's Museum, 12-14 Lincoln's Inn Fields
exemplars.note: Built and rebuilt by Soane for himself 1792-1824. The period's other pole: incised linear ornament, top-lit spaces, mirrors and shallow domes, and a classicism reduced almost to abstraction.

sources: John Summerson, Architecture in Britain 1530-1830 (9th ed., 1993)
John Summerson, The Life and Work of John Nash, Architect (1980)
Dan Cruickshank and Peter Wyld, Georgian Buildings of Britain and Ireland (1975)
Thomas Hope, Household Furniture and Interior Decoration (1807)
Nikolaus Pevsner et al., The Buildings of England (county volumes)

proportion_packs.note: Bound as the top-governing pack in place of an order, because this node's own governing_logic says so directly: 'Georgian proportional habits, loosened and lightened, with Greek orders used as motifs rather than as a generative module.' No order pack is bound primary or secondary on this node -- see the chambers-doric entry below for why. What actually generates a Regency elevation is the composition itself: the retained Georgian bay and pier discipline, now loosened to admit a bow or a canted front at the centre of a villa or the end of a terrace, and at the largest scale (Nash's Regent's Park terraces) a whole row composed as one palace-fronted scenographic object.

Governs the diagnostic proportion this node's own hard constraint c02 tests: principal-floor windows extending to within 150 mm of the finished floor, opening onto a balcony or veranda not less than 900 mm deep. A floor-length window with no balcony is, in this node's own words, 'a hazard and a period error' -- the constraint the pack exists to catch here.

Carries the thinnest glazing bars anywhere in this trunk -- 12-18 mm, against Adam's 16-20 and core Georgian's 25-32 -- per this node's own hard constraint c03, sometimes with margin lights and occasionally coloured glass at the edges of the main panes.

Retained but loosened from the trunk style's own figures: ground floor exceeds first by 10-15 percent here against Georgian's 10-20, second floor at 0.65-0.75 of the first against Georgian's 0.7-0.8 -- a shallower diminution consistent with a style that is softening every Georgian rule rather than replacing it.

Governs the family the node's own distinguished_from entry describes as reduced nearly to a diagram: 'a Regency architrave is often a plain flat band with a single incised line' -- Adam thins the Georgian moulding, Regency deletes most of what is left of it, but it is still this family and not a different one; there is no separate Greek-linear trim pack in this corpus.

NOT the style's real order, and bound only as the nearest available analogue -- flagged as a genuine gap. This node's own typical_ratios give exactly one order-specific figure, 'Greek Doric column height 6-7 diameters, baseless,' and its diagnostic_tells name 'a Greek Doric porch with baseless, unfluted or partly fluted columns and a plain entablature' as the single most reliable signature next to the iron balcony. That is Stuart and Revett's Grecian Doric after the Antiquities of Athens (1762), which this node's own lineage cites directly -- a different order-family entirely from the five Roman orders Vignola, Chambers, Gibbs and Palladio all overlay in this corpus. None of the 36 available packs encodes a Greek order. Chambers's Roman Doric is bound at low precedence and optional role only as the nearest available Roman-tradition cornice/proportion reference where a Regency design needs one; it should not be read as the porch order itself.

The ratio system is retained, but this node's own long description states plainly what changes: 'the drawing room and the garden become continuous' through the floor-length window, so the room's proportion is increasingly negotiated against the opening onto the balcony rather than resolved as a closed box the way the Georgian trunk states it.

The structural module survives entirely hidden: 'almost everything structural is inherited -- the brick carcass... but... the brick is covered in stucco, ruled and lined to imitate ashlar.' The coursing this pack governs is real and still sets the wall's dimensions; it is simply never seen.

pennsylvania-bank-house.name: Pennsylvania Bank House

revival_periods.note: Revived weakly and mostly as an aesthetic — fieldstone with an exposed lower level on a sloping lot — rather than as the working refrigeration strategy it was.

regions: Lancaster, Berks, Lebanon and Montgomery counties, Pennsylvania
geography.hearth: the rolling limestone country of the Pennsylvania German counties, where cross-slopes of one in six to one in ten are the normal condition of a farm site

lineage.note: The Alpine and Rhenish habit of setting a house across a slope so that the byre or cellar opens at the lower grade arrives with the Palatine and Swiss migration and is applied here to a dwelling rather than a farm building.

description.short: A Pennsylvania German stone house set across a hillside so that its lower storey opens at grade on the downhill side and is buried on the uphill side, giving a cool service level and two front doors at two different levels.
description.long:
The bank house is the most literal piece of environmental engineering in colonial American domestic building, and it is almost entirely invisible from the uphill approach. Set a house across a slope of one in six or steeper. Cut into the hill on the upper side and build the lower storey against the cut, so that three of its walls are surrounded by earth and only the downhill wall sees daylight. That lower storey is now a room that will not freeze in January and will not exceed the mid fifties in August. Put the kitchen, the dairy, the root store and the meat there. If the site has a spring — and the limestone country is full of them — build directly over it so that the water runs across the floor and out through an arched opening in the downhill wall, and you have running cold water and a dairy at fifty degrees, permanently, for the cost of moving earth.

The consequences run right through the building. There are two front doors on two different levels: one entering the lower service storey from the downhill grade, one entering the Stube level from the upper grade, sometimes across a short bridge or a stone stoop. The uphill elevation is one storey shorter than the downhill one, so the same house presents two entirely different faces. The uphill wall carries earth pressure and therefore has few openings or none. And because the lower level is doing the work of a cellar without being underground, the principal floor above it is dry — a serious matter in a period when the alternative was a damp cellar under a damp floor.

The rest is standard Pennsylvania German: eighteen to thirty inches of squared limestone or sandstone with oversized quoins, a steep forty-five to fifty degree roof framed with a liegender Stuhl leaning truss, small irregular windows placed for the rooms behind them, a pent roof across the facade at the second-floor line, and a central chimney serving an open kitchen hearth on one side and a closed jamb stove on the other. Later examples regularize the front to five bays under Anglo pressure while keeping the section entirely unchanged, which is the standard fate of every immigrant tradition here.

To arrive at one from above is to see a modest one-and-a-half-storey stone cottage. To walk around it and look back from the field below is to see a three-storey stone wall with a spring running out of it. That gap between the two readings is the pleasure of the type, and it is also the reason it is under-recognized: half the building is a fact about the ground.

defining_characteristics: Sited across a slope so that the lowest storey is fully exposed on the downhill elevation and earth-bermed on the uphill elevation
Two principal entrances at two different grades — one to the service level, one to the living level — of unequal architectural status
Lower storey of 18–30 in squared stone housing kitchen, dairy and cold storage, frequently built over a spring discharging through an arched opening
Barrel-vaulted or heavy-beamed masonry ceiling over the lower storey
Uphill elevation with few or no openings; downhill elevation a full storey taller than the uphill one
Steep gable roof, 45–50 degrees, on a liegender Stuhl leaning-post truss over a usable loft
Central chimney serving an open hearth in the service level or kitchen and a closed jamb stove in the Stube above or alongside
diagnostic_tells: Two front doors at two different levels on two different elevations — decisive, and visible from a passing road
An arched opening at the base of the downhill wall with water running out of it
The uphill gable shows a one-and-a-half-storey house; the downhill gable shows two-and-a-half
No basement windows on the uphill side, and often no openings at all in that wall below the first floor
A pent roof band across the facade with no posts beneath it

distinguished_from.difference: The parent style covers both banked and level-sited houses. This variant is specifically the banked case, and it is worth separating because the section, the door count, the circulation and the room programme all change when the house is set into a hill.

A Georgian house on a slope gets an exposed English basement and keeps one front door on the piano nobile, entered up a flight of steps, with symmetrical windows above. The bank house gets two doors of equal practical importance, an asymmetric plan, unaligned windows and no ceremonial approach at all.

The revival 'Pennsylvania farmhouse' on a sloping lot exposes a walkout basement with a garage in it, keeps a symmetrical five-bay front with a centred classical door, and uses four inches of veneer stone. The bank house has two feet of load-bearing masonry, a vaulted service ceiling and no ceremonial entrance.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The slope sets the section: the fall across the building footprint must equal roughly one storey height (7–9 ft) for the type to work at all.
typical_ratios: Cross-slope 1:6 to 1:10 across the building depth; total fall 6–10 ft across 22–30 ft
Footprint 26–38 ft × 22–30 ft
Lower-storey wall 22–30 in; upper storey 18–24 in
Lower-storey ceiling 6 ft 6 in – 7 ft 6 in; principal floor 7 ft 6 in – 8 ft 6 in
Roof rise:run 12:12 to 14:12
Pent roof projection 30–42 in at the second-floor line, pitch 25–35 degrees
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and driven by the plan; a nominal three- or five-bay front emerges after about 1790 but rarely aligns floor to floor.

massing_affinities.note: The nearest catalogued skeleton to the banked Flurküchenhaus.
The regularized nineteenth-century banked farmhouse.
Small tenant bank houses of a single room per level.
Growth along the contour with a summer-kitchen wing.

constraints.statement: Requires a cross-slope of at least 1:8 (12.5%) across the building depth, giving a fall of not less than 6 ft. On a level site the type cannot exist; a house with a walkout basement on flat ground is not a bank house.

test.note: 1:8. The fall figure (not less than 6ft) restates the same requirement over the building's actual depth and stays prose.

constraints.statement: The lower-storey finished floor sits within 12 in of the downhill grade at the exposed wall, and the uphill wall is bermed to within 12 in of the principal floor level. Lower-storey walls not less than 22 in of load-bearing stone to carry earth pressure.

test.note: Tests the lower-storey wall thickness, the cleanest single claim in a compound statement. The two grade-relationship clauses (finished floor within 12in of downhill grade; uphill wall bermed within 12in of principal floor) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Two exterior doors at two levels, on different elevations. A single ceremonial entrance destroys the type: the service level must be enterable without passing through the house.
No openings in the bermed (uphill) wall below the principal floor. Where a spring is captured, the discharge is through an arched opening 18–30 in wide at the base of the downhill wall.
Roof pitch 12:12 to 14:12; pent roof, where used, projects 30–42 in at the second-floor line, unposted, returning 12–24 in at the corners.

test.note: The pent roof clause restates the same feature already tested on german-pennsylvania-colonial and stays prose here.

exemplars.name: Heinrich Zeller House (Fort Zeller)
exemplars.note: Limestone house built into a bank over an everflowing spring that discharges from an arched opening in the basement; narrow irregularly placed windows, steep gable, central twelve-foot fireplace.

exemplars.name: Schifferstadt
exemplars.note: Built by Elias Bruner of the Palatinate; central wishbone chimney, liegender Stuhl truss, vaulted cellar and five-plate jamb stove all survive, making the section unusually legible.

exemplars.name: Furnace Hills Tenant House
exemplars.location: West Cocalico Township, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: A 19th-century banked sandstone dwelling of about 19 by 26 ft, explicitly documented as a vernacular Pennsylvania German perpendicular bank house — the modest end of the type.

sources: Sally McMurry and Nancy Van Dolsen, eds., Architecture and Landscape of the Pennsylvania Germans, 1720–1920 (2011)
Robert F. Ensminger, The Pennsylvania Barn: Its Origin, Evolution, and Distribution in North America (2nd ed., 2003)
Bernard L. Herman and Gabrielle Lanier, Everyday Architecture of the Mid-Atlantic (1997)
Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission, Pennsylvania Architectural Field Guide: Pennsylvania German Traditional, 1700–1870

proportion_packs.note: Inherits the parent style's stone construction directly and is explicitly named in brick-course's own applies_to. The lower (banked) storey wall is specified at not less than 22 in of load-bearing stone to carry earth pressure — the pack's reveal_masonry rule (wall thickness in whole wythes) applies exactly, and its window_head_masonry segmental/flat-arch rules govern the few, deliberately placed openings in the exposed downhill wall.

pennsylvania-bank-house is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. The banked plan is, if anything, more function-constrained than the parent's: room size follows the slope, the spring and the stove wall, never a ratio.

Bound cautiously, as an analogy rather than a direct fit. storey-graduation's own 'GROUND STOREY UNDER A PIANO NOBILE' rule (a markedly lower storey below the principal floor, ratio about 0.72) describes the same geometric shape this variant's own typical_ratios record — a lower-storey ceiling of 6'6"-7'6" against a principal floor of 7'6"-8'6" — even though the reason for the height difference is entirely different: the pack's rule is about architectural hierarchy under a piano nobile, while the bank house's lower storey is a working refrigeration cellar set by the cross-slope, not by design ambition. The ratio is offered as a usable starting point for the section, not as evidence the two traditions share a rationale. No pack among the 36 models hillside/bank siting directly, which is the more honest statement of this variant's real governing geometry.

new-england-colonial.name: New England Colonial

revival_periods.note: The Centennial and the 1877 Longfellow-circle sketching tours of Portsmouth and Marblehead began a revival that never ended; by 1935 it was the default American suburban house.

geography.hearth: Massachusetts Bay — the Boston–Ipswich–Salem arc and the Connecticut River towns

lineage.note: Direct craft transmission. The carpenters who framed the Fairbanks House had served apprenticeships in East Anglia and the West Country; the joinery, the scarf joints, the summer-beam-and-girt system and the chamfer stops are English medieval practice executed in American oak.
Plan logic — the single-cell hall and the hall-and-parlor pair — comes from the English yeoman cottage rather than from anything grand.

description.short: The post-medieval English timber house rebuilt in a colder country around a single enormous masonry chimney, stripped of ornament by Puritan taste and by the total absence of a leisured client.
description.long:
New England Colonial is what happens when late-medieval English carpentry lands in a climate roughly eight degrees colder than the one it evolved for and has to solve heating before it solves anything else. The answer was the central chimney stack: a masonry mass eight to twelve feet square at the base, occupying the middle of the plan, serving two or three fireplaces plus an oven, and functioning as a thermal flywheel that holds heat through a February night. Everything else in the plan is arranged around that block. The stair is a cramped winder squeezed between the stack and the front door. The rooms are pushed to the corners. The entry is not a hall but a porch — a vestibule barely large enough to close the door behind you before you turn left or right into the heated rooms. The plan is an argument with winter, and the argument is won by mass.

The materials tell the second half of the story. England was short of oak and long on skilled labour; New England was the reverse. So the frame becomes generous — sills a foot square, summer beams spanning the room, posts flared at the head into gunstock shoulders to receive both the plate and the girt — while the finish becomes plain. Riven oak clapboard, four to five inches to the weather, nailed to studs; roofs of split shingle at forty-five to fifty-five degrees, steep enough for the thatch that was never actually used here and kept because that was the pitch the framing tradition knew. Glass was imported and taxed; windows stayed small, casement, leaded in diamond quarries, and only after about 1700 did the counterweighted double-hung sash arrive with twelve-over-twelve lights. There is no classical ornament to speak of before 1700 because there was no one to pay for it and, in a colony that had abolished bishops, a certain suspicion of anyone who would.

What it was negotiating against was not another style but scarcity — of lime, of glass, of nails, of a second generation of trained joiners — and against a settlement pattern that put a house in a clearing rather than on a street. The house therefore has no urban face. It is symmetrical only by accident of the chimney's centrality, and its elevations are wildly unequal: five bays and a doorway on the front, a blank wall of clapboard behind, a gable end that may carry nothing at all.

To stand in one is to be surprised by how low and how dark it is. Ceilings run six-foot-eight to seven-foot-six under the exposed summer beam, so a modern adult reads the room with the beam at eye level; the space is measured in wood rather than in air. The fire end of the hall is enormous and the far corner is cold. Light comes in small hard patches from windows set high and tight under the plate, and the plastered ceiling between joists, when there is one, throws that light back down with a chalky softness. There is no moulding anywhere except a chamfer and its stop, and the chamfer stop — lamb's-tongue, ogee, taper — is the only decorative decision the carpenter made and therefore the one he made carefully.

defining_characteristics: A single massive central masonry chimney serving back-to-back fireplaces, occupying the middle of the plan and dictating the circulation
Braced oak post-and-beam frame with summer beam, gunstock posts, and mortise-and-tenon joinery, the frame exposed on the interior
Steep side-gable roof, 45–55 degrees, of split shingle, with the ridge running the long dimension
Small openings: leaded casements before c. 1700, twelve-over-twelve double-hung after, set tight under the eave with no frieze between head and cornice
Riven or sawn clapboard (or shingle in coastal Massachusetts) at 4–5 inch exposure over the frame; no masonry veneer
Plan grown by accretion from the single-cell hall — hall, then hall-and-parlor, then a rear lean-to — rather than composed
Ornament confined to the chamfer stop, the drop pendant, and after 1700 a modest entry frame; no classical order anywhere before c. 1710
diagnostic_tells: One chimney, in the middle, and it is enormous — if the chimneys are at the gable ends you are looking at a Southern colonial or a post-1740 Georgian house
Front door opens onto a chimney stack four feet away, not into a passage
Window heads within a few inches of the eave, with no frieze band; a wide frieze means Georgian influence has arrived
Casement openings (or the ghost of them in the framing) rather than sash on anything pre-1700
Second-floor windows visibly shorter than the first-floor windows, and both shorter than a Georgian house would use

distinguished_from.difference: The single most common misidentification in American architecture. A real First Period house is asymmetrical in the rear, has one central chimney, window heads jammed under the eave, a 12:12-or-steeper roof, and no cornice returns before about 1700. A Colonial Revival house has paired end chimneys or none, a symmetrical five-bay front carried through to the back, a 8:12 roof, wide window trim with a backband, shutters that could not close over the opening, an attached garage, and machine-milled dentils. If the mouldings are consistent on all four elevations, it is a revival.

Georgian arrives in New England after about 1720 and replaces the central chimney with a center passage and paired interior chimneys, raises the ceilings, regularizes the fenestration front and back, adds a classical frontispiece and a modillion cornice, and lowers the roof to 9:12–11:12. A First Period house that has had a Georgian door and cornice added is a common and legible hybrid — read the chimney, not the trim.

The English parent shows its frame on the outside with infill panels between studs; New England covers the frame entirely in clapboard because the climate destroys exposed wattle-and-daub and lime infill in a decade of freeze-thaw.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The structural bay of the timber frame, set by the practical span of a hand-hewn summer beam — 16 to 20 feet — and by the plan dimension of the chimney stack.
typical_ratios: Room 16–20 ft square, the frame bay; hall-and-parlor overall 38–42 ft × 18–20 ft
Ceiling height 6 ft 8 in – 7 ft 6 in under the summer beam, 7 ft 0 in – 8 ft 0 in to the joists
Chimney stack 8–12 ft square at the base, i.e. roughly one-third of the plan depth
Window opening 2 ft 6 in – 3 ft 4 in wide × 4 ft 0 in – 5 ft 6 in high, ratio near 1:1.7
Roof rise:run 1:1 to 1.2:1 (45–50 degrees)
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five bays on the front where the frame permits, but unequal: the door bay is narrow and centred on the chimney, and the flanking pairs are set by post positions, not by division of the facade. Four-bay and three-bay fronts are equally correct.

massing_affinities.note: The irreducible starting point; many surviving houses are a hall that was later doubled.
The mature First Period plan: two rooms flanking the stack, entry porch and winder stair between.
The lean-to addition, integral or added, is the normal growth move after about 1660.
The one-and-a-half-storey coastal expression.
Two full storeys with a framed overhang.
Only after Georgian influence, at which point the node has changed.
