constraints.statement: Exactly one chimney, positioned within the plan (not at a gable end), with a base not less than 7 ft × 7 ft and typically 8–12 ft square. A First Period massing with end chimneys is incoherent: the plan diagram depends on the stack occupying the centre.

test.note: Tests the count. Base size (7x7ft minimum, typically 8-12ft square) is a two-dimensional claim the vocabulary has no single variable for and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 10:12 to 14:12 (40–50 degrees). Below 9:12 the massing reads Georgian or later; above 14:12 it reads as a thatch survival not built here.
The head of a second-floor window sits 0–8 in below the underside of the cornice or plate. There is no frieze band. Introducing a frieze of more than 4 in converts the elevation to Georgian.

test.note: The no-frieze-band clause (a frieze over 4in converts the elevation to Georgian) is the same statement's other claim and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Sash by period: leaded casement to c. 1700; twelve-over-twelve or twelve-over-eight c. 1700–1750; nine-over-six c. 1740–1770. Six-over-six on a First Period massing is an anachronism of at least fifty years.
Clapboard exposure 4–5 in on the weather elevation, up to 6 in elsewhere; shingle at 5–6 in exposure on the coast. Wider exposures read Victorian.

test.note: Tests the weather-elevation clapboard exposure. The up-to-6in-elsewhere and coastal shingle-exposure clauses stay prose.

exemplars.name: Fairbanks House
exemplars.note: The oldest surviving timber-frame dwelling in North America; dendrochronology supports a construction date in the late 1630s. Later lean-tos and wings make it a textbook of accretive growth.

exemplars.name: Paul Revere House
exemplars.note: Urban two-storey house with a framed overhang; the only surviving 17th-century dwelling in downtown Boston.

exemplars.name: Parson Capen House
exemplars.note: The canonical post-medieval elevation: front and gable overhangs, carved drop pendants, central stack, casement openings.

exemplars.name: John Whipple House
exemplars.note: Two-phase First Period house; the later block carries the jetty. Ipswich preserves the densest surviving concentration of the type.

sources: Abbott Lowell Cummings, The Framed Houses of Massachusetts Bay, 1625–1725 (1979)
J. Frederick Kelly, Early Domestic Architecture of Connecticut (1924)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)

proportion_packs.note: The generative module of the whole type: this is a house framed to a bay, not designed to a proportion, and the plan, the chimney position, the window rhythm and the roof all follow from one 16-20 ft structural dimension (Cummings' survey of Massachusetts Bay frames is the primary evidence for the figure). The central stack alone occupies over half a bay in plan -- this pack's hearth_position rule (module x 0.55) lands at 8'-10', matching this node's own recorded chimney base of '8-12 ft square, roughly one-third of the plan depth' almost exactly -- which is why the frame needs a narrow third bay to hold the stack and why the front door sits hard against it rather than opening onto a passage: there is nowhere else for the door to go. No facade-system pack is bound on this node, deliberately: facade-classical's module is a uniform bay chosen by design, and this node's own bay_rhythm record states plainly that its bays 'are set by post positions, not by division of the facade' and that three- and four-bay fronts are 'equally correct' -- the direct opposite of facade-classical's odd-bay rule. The bay arithmetic bound here, not a facade system, is what actually generates this elevation.

Roof pitch and eave follow the frame rather than a style choice. A common-rafter roof over an 18-20 ft bay at 45-50 degrees gives about a 13 ft rafter -- close to the longest stick that pairs conveniently with a joist cut from the same tree -- which is this node's own 10:12-14:12 constraint (c02) read from the framing side. The eave is flush or nearly so (this pack's default is 6 in or less, 'often nothing'), because a 17th-century rafter foot lands ON the plate rather than past it; the boxed cornice arrives in the 18th century as applied joinery, not as part of the frame, and its appearance is one of the better date markers available on a First Period house. Storey graduation is correspondingly weak: this pack's own height_proportion rule for a box frame is 0.88 and is explicitly marked judgment, against the 0.78-0.92 band storey-graduation records for classically composed work, because a First Period post is a single hewn stick and the carpenter took the length the tree gave rather than proportioning one storey against another.

The dating system for the openings, and the one genuinely diagnostic pack in this binding. This node's own co-occurrence constraint (c04) is this pack's content stated in prose -- leaded casement to c. 1700, then twelve-over-twelve or twelve-over-eight to c. 1750, nine-over-six to c. 1770 -- and sash-light derives that same sequence from the glasshouse's own maximum pane size by decade, with the muntin (heavy, 1 1/8-1 3/8 in before 1760) and the glazing ratio (6-10% of floor area, the luxury-import band) that go with it. A leaded diamond-quarry casement is what this pack predicts before 1700, ahead of the point where its light-count arithmetic even applies.

Bound for one rule and one rule only, and it is the pack's strongest: 'the windows... ought to be all equal in the same order or story' -- a single head datum per storey, without exception. That is exactly this node's own hard constraint (c03), that the second-floor head sits 0-8 in below the plate with no frieze -- a head-datum rule before it is anything else. The pack's canonical 13:6 (2.167:1) window ratio does NOT govern here: this node's own measured openings run nearer 1:1.7 (height over width), outside even sash-light's 1.85-2.6 measured band, because the First Period window is set by the casement and the frame bay rather than by a treatise proportion. Where the two disagree, this node's own recorded ratio and sash-light's period dimensions govern, not this pack's default figure.

The physics that generates the plan. Room breadth is capped by the summer beam's span (14-18 ft here, against this pack's 14 ft default), room area is capped by what one fireplace will warm (250-320 sq ft -- which is why the hall, holding the cooking hearth, is the widest room in the house and the parlor is smaller), and Glassie's square-base-unit reading of the vernacular plan -- additive, generated, not proportioned to a chosen ratio -- is exactly this node's own account of a house 'grown by accretion from the single-cell hall... rather than composed.' room-harmonic, the treatise counterpart, is not bound: there is no evidence any First Period builder proportioned a room to a ratio, and this node's own record confirms it.

cotswold-cottage-revival.name: Cotswold Cottage Revival

geography.hearth: Philadelphia's Chestnut Hill; Kansas City; Detroit's Palmer Woods

lineage.note: The small, all-masonry, cottage-scaled wing of the parent style. Shares the kit but drops the half-timbering that the parent depends on.
The claimed ancestor: the limestone villages of Gloucestershire and Oxfordshire, with graduated stone slate roofs, steep pitches and thick walls.
The broader thatched and half-timbered cottage register - the catslide roof, the eyebrow dormer, and the sagging ridge that American builders imitated with sawn rafters.

The real transmission. Voysey, Baillie Scott and Ernest Gimson had already reduced the Cotswold cottage to a designable set of moves, and American architects learned it from them, not from Gloucestershire.
The craft ethic, the taste for handled surface, and the client base that would pay for irregular stonework.
Deliberate resurrection after a gap. Recorded separately from the reference edge so revival relationships are queryable across the graph.

description.short: The small, all-stone or stone-and-stucco wing of the English revival, imitating the Gloucestershire cottage: very steep roofs with rolled or swept eaves, a massive chimney on the entrance facade, tiny casements, and an arched door under a catslide.
description.long:
Cotswold Cottage Revival is Tudor Revival reduced to a house rather than a manor, and reduced with more care than that description suggests. Its necessary elements are a steeply pitched roof, 12:12 or steeper, in slate or in wood shingle laid to imitate stone slate, with the courses graduated - larger at the eave, smaller at the ridge - and the eaves rolled, swept, or clipped around the corners in imitation of thatch; a massive chimney placed on the front elevation, often flanking or even framing the entrance; walls of irregular coursed stone or of stucco over stone; casement windows in small groups with leaded or diamond glazing; and a low, arched, plank door recessed under a projecting bay or a catslide roof that runs down to head height.

The conditions were specific and mostly Philadelphian. A group of practices in Chestnut Hill and the Main Line - Mellor, Meigs & Howe, Robert Rodes McGoodwin, Edmund Gilchrist, H. Louis Duhring - spent the 1910s and 1920s working out an American version of English and Norman cottage building on real sites with real stone, and the Wissahickon schist of the Philadelphia region turned out to be a nearly perfect substitute for Cotswold limestone. McGoodwin's French Village at Chestnut Hill, built 1925-28, is the fullest demonstration. Their work was published continuously, and by the late 1920s the vocabulary had reached builders in Kansas City, Detroit, Chicago and Los Angeles, usually in a thinner form.

What the buyer was claiming was not lineage and not scholarship but retreat. This is the one variant in the branch whose imagery is explicitly anti-monumental: a small, old, hand-made building in a garden, deliberately modest, deliberately English, and deliberately not the house of a magnate. It arrives at exactly the moment when the American professional class was moving out of cities that had become large and loud, and its charm is not incidental to it - the style was sold as charm, and the best examples earn it.

What you notice standing in front of one is that nothing is straight. The eave rolls; the ridge sags slightly; the stone courses vary; the chimney leans out at its base and steps back twice as it rises; the door is not on centre and the window beside it is smaller than the one above. All of this is designed irregularity, executed by masons paid to do it, and its success is entirely a matter of restraint - two or three deviations read as age, six read as whimsy, and past that point the building becomes Storybook, which was a real and different Californian style. Inside, the rooms are small, the ceilings are low and often beamed, the windows are deep-set, and the fireplace is enormous relative to the room, which is precisely the effect the whole exercise is aiming at.

defining_characteristics: Steeply pitched roof, 12:12 or steeper, in slate, stone slate, or shingle laid to imitate it, with graduated courses
Rolled, swept, or clipped eaves and rakes, softening every roof edge in imitation of thatch or stone slate
Massive chimney on the entrance facade, frequently adjacent to or framing the front door
Walls of irregular coursed stone, or stucco over masonry, without applied half-timbering
Small casement windows in groups of two or three with leaded, diamond, or small rectangular glazing
Low arched or plank entrance door, recessed, under a catslide roof, a projecting gable, or a hood
Small overall footprint and a deliberately irregular, cottage-scaled massing
diagnostic_tells: Rolled eaves. If the roof edge curves around the corner or over a dormer rather than terminating in a straight fascia, this is the variant.
The chimney is on the front and it is disproportionately large - often 1/4 to 1/3 of the elevation's width.
No half-timbering. Its presence returns the building to the parent Tudor Revival.
A catslide - one roof plane running much further down than the other, often to below head height - over the entrance or a side wing.

Against the genuine Cotswold original: real Cotswold cottages have level dripstones, square-cut mullions, stone slate roofs of enormous weight requiring 55-degree pitches, no dormer eyebrows, and are almost never picturesque on purpose. The revival adds the picturesque and subtracts the weight.

distinguished_from.difference: The parent style is larger, taller, and depends on applied half-timbering over masonry and on grouped bands of double-hung or steel casement windows. This variant is small, all-masonry, has rolled eaves and a front chimney, and never uses timbering.

The original is a load-bearing limestone building 18-24 in. thick with a stone slate roof weighing 15-25 lb per square foot, tiny openings, and irregularity that results from centuries of repair. The revival is usually veneer or thin masonry with a light roof, larger glazing, and irregularity that was drawn.

The Norman variant adds a round entrance tower with a conical roof, uses steeper and taller wall dormers, and mixes brick, stone and stucco with half-timbering. The Cotswold variant is lower, all-stone, tower-less, and defined by rolled eaves.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Roof geometry and apparent wall mass at a domestic scale. The roof is the dominant proportional figure and typically occupies half or more of the elevation height; wall thickness is expressed at reveals to make a small building feel heavy.
typical_ratios: Roof pitch 12:12 to 18:12; roof height eave to ridge 0.9 to 1.4 times the wall height below it
Eave roll radius 6-12 in.; rake and eave carried around corners without a break
Chimney width 1/4 to 1/3 of the elevation it stands on, projecting 12-18 in. from the wall
Casement leaf 14-20 in. wide by 36-48 in. high; groups of two or three under one head
Wall reveal 6-10 in. at openings; door head 6'4"-6'10", deliberately low
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: None. Openings are placed by internal need and by picturesque judgement, in twos and threes, with wide blank stone between. Any repeating rhythm defeats the variant's whole premise.

massing_affinities.note: An irregular accumulation of small gabled volumes with a dominant front chimney.
The suburban builder version - a simple block with one steep front gable and a rolled eave.
Where the cottage is reduced to a rectangular one-and-a-half-storey box; rare and usually weak.
The plan-form belongs to jacobethan-revival; at this scale it is inappropriate.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch not less than 12:12 on all principal planes, with the roof occupying not less than 45 percent of the elevation height. Eaves and rakes must be rolled, swept, or clipped with a radius of 6-12 in. and carried continuously around external corners; a straight fascia and a square rake void the variant.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch floor. 'Roof occupying not less than 45 percent of the elevation height' and the eave/rake sweep radius (6-12in) have no matching vocabulary variable and stay prose.

constraints.statement: A masonry chimney must be expressed on the entrance elevation, occupying between 1/4 and 1/3 of that elevation's width, projecting not less than 12 in. from the wall, and rising not less than 3'0" above the ridge.

test.note: Tests the ridge-rise minimum. Chimney width as a fraction of the entrance elevation (1/4-1/3, no matching vocabulary variable) and wall projection (>=12in, matching wall_plane_advance_recess_in but not tested here) stay prose -- one test per constraint.

constraints.statement: Applied half-timbering is forbidden. Wall material is irregular coursed stone, or stucco over masonry, or the two combined; the material change must occur at a chimney, a corner, or a wing junction, never mid-plane.

Wall thickness expressed with a minimum 6 in. reveal at all openings, with stone or wood lintels visible over doors and principal windows. Windows are casements with true divided lights, leaves 14-20 in. wide.

test.note: Lintel material (stone or wood) is qualitative. Casement leaf width (14-20in) has no matching vocabulary variable -- a casement-leaf-width variable is missing -- and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Limit deliberate irregularities to three per elevation - for example a swept eave, a stepped chimney, and a catslide. Beyond that the building reads as Storybook rather than as a cottage, which is a different style.

exemplars.name: French Village
exemplars.location: Chestnut Hill / Mount Airy, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: Robert Rodes McGoodwin, 1925-28, for Dr. George Woodward. A complete development in Wissahickon schist; the fullest American realisation of the English and Norman cottage idea.

exemplars.name: Woodward development houses, Chestnut Hill
exemplars.note: H. Louis Duhring Jr., with Edmund B. Gilchrist and McGoodwin, built roughly 180 houses for George Woodward between 1910 and 1930, dozens of them explicitly Cotswold in register. The Quadruple Houses on Benezet and Nippon Streets (from 1910) are the best documented.

exemplars.name: Sulgrave Manor house, 200 West Willow Grove Avenue
exemplars.note: H. Louis Duhring Jr. for George Woodward, incorporating interiors from the Sulgrave Manor replica shown at the 1926 Sesquicentennial Exposition.

exemplars.name: Cotswold Cottage, Greenfield Village
exemplars.note: Not a revival building: a genuine c. 1620 Cotswold cottage from Chedworth, Gloucestershire, dismantled and re-erected by Henry Ford in 1929-30. The reference object against which any revival example should be judged.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Robert A. M. Stern, ed., The Anglo-American Suburb (1981)
William Morrison, The Main Line: Country Houses of Philadelphia's Storied Suburb, 1870-1930 (2002)
David R. Contosta, Suburb in the City: Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, 1850-1990 (1992)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969, rev. 1992)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in the pack's own applies_to. The variant's own bay_rhythm entry states the picturesque premise more strongly than any other node in this batch: 'None. Openings are placed by internal need and by picturesque judgement... Any repeating rhythm defeats the variant's whole premise.' The roof as dominant proportional figure (occupying 45 percent or more of elevation height per the style's own hard constraint c01) and the disproportionate front chimney (c02, 1/4 to 1/3 of the elevation) both map directly onto facade-picturesque's dominance and chimney derived_rules.

The lineage record is unusually direct for this node: 'arts-and-crafts-british, descends_from, weight 0.9 - Voysey, Baillie Scott and Ernest Gimson had already reduced the Cotswold cottage to a designable set of moves, and American architects learned it from them, not from Gloucestershire.' That is the highest lineage weight to any single ancestor in this whole batch and it names named Arts and Crafts designers directly. No classical order or entablature-derived trim is claimed anywhere in the style's defining_characteristics or constraints - trim-classical is not in contention here.

new-urbanist-traditional.name: New Urbanist Traditional

geography.hearth: Seaside, Walton County, Florida

lineage.note: The Gulf Coast and Southern wood vernacular — raised floor, deep porch, tall shuttered openings, metal roof, simple trim — is the grammar the Seaside code actually encodes, chosen because Duany and Plater-Zyberk measured surviving examples in small Southern towns before drawing it.

The side-piazza type is one of the code's canonical frontage solutions: it delivers a private outdoor room and a narrow street frontage simultaneously, which is exactly what a dense traditional block requires.

The American small-town default of 1830-1860 — pedimented gable, simple pilaster and entablature, tall narrow openings — survives here as the plainest available classical vocabulary and the one most easily specified in a code.
Supplies the Northeastern and Mid-Atlantic dialects of the movement, notably at Kentlands.

Shared personnel, shared institutions, and a shared theory of transmission. New Classical supplies the civic buildings and the terminated vistas; New Urbanist Traditional supplies the fabric around them.

The defining opposition, and a precise one: the movement's codes read as an itemized prohibition of neo-eclectic practice — no street-facing garage, no front-only masonry, no misaligned heads, no arbitrary gables.
Against the whole postwar settlement pattern the ranch belongs to: the cul-de-sac, the deep setback, the single-use pod, and the house that turns its back on the street.

description.short: The traditional architecture produced under form-based codes in walkable new towns from Seaside onward, in which the street section, the build-to line, the frontage type, and the relegation of the garage are specified before style, and the style itself is drawn from a single regional vernacular.
description.long:
New Urbanist Traditional is the only node in this branch whose unit of design is not the house. It is the block and the street, and the building is what happens at the edge of them. This inverts the entire logic of the preceding fifty years: rather than designing a house and placing it on a lot, the movement specifies the public space first — a street of eighteen to twenty-four feet of pavement, a sidewalk, a planted verge, a build-to line ten to twenty feet back, an alley behind — and then writes rules for the building envelope, the frontage type, the height in storeys, and the transparency of the ground floor that will produce a coherent wall along it. Style enters last, and it enters as a regional constraint: use the vernacular of this place, correctly, rather than a menu of six vernaculars from elsewhere.

The origin is precise. Robert Davis inherited eighty acres on the Florida panhandle in 1978, engaged Andres Duany and Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk, and the three of them drove the American South looking at small towns before drawing anything. Construction began in 1981 with two houses and a street. The Seaside urban code — famously compressed onto a single sheet, organized by street type, and legible to a builder in ten minutes — is the pivotal artifact, and it is worth being explicit about what kind of artifact it is. It is a pattern book. It works exactly as Gibbs and Langley and Asher Benjamin worked in the eighteenth century: it externalizes design knowledge into a portable, purchasable, enforceable document so that builders who have never seen the exemplar can produce coherent work. The eighteenth century transmitted proportion by engraved plate; Seaside transmits it by regulating plan and section; and the direct next step — encoding the same logic in software so that it can be checked, cascaded, and generated — is the reason this taxonomy exists. Kentlands followed a week-long charrette in June 1988 and began construction in 1989. Windsor, in Vero Beach, was founded in 1989 with a DPZ code and later a town hall by Leon Krier. The Congress for the New Urbanism organized in 1993, and the SmartCode of 2003 generalized the method into a transect-based model ordinance that hundreds of municipalities have since adapted.

What produced it, beyond conviction, was the exhaustion of Euclidean zoning. Use-segregated, setback-driven, parking-minimum zoning cannot produce a walkable street no matter who designs the buildings, because it prohibits the geometry. The movement's central technical insight is that the enforceable instrument is the code, not the style — a builder will not follow taste but must follow an ordinance — and that once the code has fixed the section, a surprisingly wide range of architectural quality still produces a decent street. The corollary is uncomfortable and worth stating: much New Urbanist architecture is mediocre, and the places work anyway. That is a finding about which rules matter, and it should discipline any system that proposes to encode design.

Standing in one, the differences from ordinary suburb are all dimensional and all felt immediately. The street is narrow enough that the buildings on both sides are in your visual field at once. The porch is eight to twelve feet deep and twelve to eighteen feet from the sidewalk, which is close enough to speak across and far enough not to be intruded upon — a distance the movement rediscovered empirically. There are no garage doors; they are on the alley, and the alley absorbs the bins, the meters, and the parked cars. Vistas terminate in something — a civic building, a tower, a tree. The buildings are various in colour and detail but identical in the two things that matter, setback and height, so the street reads as one room. What is under construction here is not a style but a demonstration that design logic, written down and enforced, produces a public good that individual good intentions do not.

defining_characteristics: A form-based code governing build-to line, frontage type, height in storeys, and street section, adopted before any building is designed
The garage relegated to an alley, or set well behind the front facade; no street-facing garage door on an alley-served lot
A front porch or equivalent frontage element of habitable depth at a shallow setback, in direct conversational relation to the sidewalk
A continuous street wall formed by a limited set of permitted frontage types rather than by a uniform setback
Stylistic vocabulary drawn from a single regional tradition per building, specified by the code and applied consistently on all elevations
Narrow street sections with on-street parking and terminated vistas, designed as public rooms rather than as traffic conduits
Mixed lot widths, building types, and uses within a single block
diagnostic_tells: No garage doors visible from the street anywhere on the block
Front porches at eight feet or more of depth, at setbacks of twelve to eighteen feet, occupied by actual furniture
A hard build-to line: adjacent facades line up within a foot or two, and the fence or hedge continues the line across the gaps
Streets narrow enough that two moving cars must negotiate, with parking on both sides
The same material and detail carried around all four elevations of every building, including the alley face

distinguished_from.difference: A code versus a menu. Both build traditional-looking houses for the same market; one enforces alignment, material return, garage relegation, and a single grammar per building, and the other selects an elevation package. The diagnostic is the side elevation and the alley.

A difference of scale and commitment. New Classical is a discipline of the individual building organized around the correct use of the orders; New Urbanist Traditional is a discipline of the street that accepts plain vernacular buildings and often prefers them. The civic buildings in a New Urbanist town are usually New Classical.

Colonial Revival is a style that can be built on any lot in any pattern; this node is not usable outside a coded street. A single New Urbanist house in a conventional subdivision is simply a Colonial Revival or vernacular revival house.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The code first, the order second. Build-to line, lot width, height in storeys, frontage type, and required transparency are fixed by ordinance; within that envelope, building proportion follows regional vernacular precedent — a vertical window proportion, a single head datum per storey, a porch depth, and a plate height. The significant point for this project is that the code is a rule set of exactly the kind a generator consumes: it is enumerable, checkable, and independent of taste.
typical_ratios: Front setback 10 to 20 ft, with facade occupying not less than 70 percent of the lot width at that line
Porch depth 8 to 12 ft clear; porch height one full storey
Window opening proportion 1:1.8 to 1:2.2, heads aligned to one datum per storey
Ground storey plate 9 to 11 ft; upper storey 8 to 9 ft
Street pavement 18 to 24 ft with parking on one or both sides; building height to street width roughly 1:2 to 1:3
Alley 12 to 20 ft, garages set 5 to 20 ft off it
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Regular vertical openings at 8 to 12 ft centres on the principal frontage, with solid-to-void of roughly 60:40 on the ground storey and more solid above.

massing_affinities.note: The canonical narrow-lot frontage solution in the Southern codes: side piazza, gable to the street, entry through a false door onto the porch.
The type that makes the transect work at its denser calibrations, and the one most often missing from conventional zoning.

constraints.statement: Where an alley serves the lot, garages must be alley-loaded and street-facing garage doors are forbidden. Where no alley exists, the garage face must be set back not less than 20 ft behind the front facade plane, or be side-loaded.
Front porch not less than 8 ft clear depth and not less than 60 percent of the facade width, at a front setback of 10 to 20 ft.

test.note: Tests the clear-depth floor. The 60-percent-of-facade-width clause has no matching porch-width variable (gallery_depth_ft is depth only) and stays prose; the 10-20ft front setback is separately expressible via the existing setback_front_ft variable but only one test object is permitted per constraint, so it also stays prose here.

constraints.statement: The principal facade must occupy not less than 70 percent of the lot width at the build-to line; gaps must be closed by a fence, wall, or hedge of not less than 3 ft continuing the line.

test.note: Tests the build-to-line coverage ratio. The fence/wall/hedge gap-closure requirement (minimum 3ft) is the statement's other clause and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Window openings vertically proportioned between 1:1.8 and 1:2.2, with all heads on a storey aligned to a single datum. Ground storey transparency on the principal frontage not less than 30 percent.

test.note: Tests the window-proportion range. 'All heads on a storey aligned to a single datum' has no vocabulary variable for same-storey cross-elevation head alignment (opening_vertical_alignment_in is storey-to-storey, a different comparison) and stays prose, as does ground-storey transparency (30 percent) -- glazed_area_pct_wall exists but is not scoped to a single storey.

constraints.statement: One regional stylistic vocabulary per building, applied to all elevations including alley and side. Mixing grammars on a single building, or changing material at an outside corner, is forbidden.

exemplars.name: Seaside
exemplars.note: Robert Davis with Duany Plater-Zyberk; land assembled 1978, construction begun 1981, urban code drawn in the early 1980s. The founding case and the origin of the single-sheet form-based code.

exemplars.name: Kentlands
exemplars.note: DPZ charrette June 1988, construction from 1989, first residents 1991. The first full-scale test of the method in a cold-climate Mid-Atlantic context and on a conventional developer's pro forma.

exemplars.name: Windsor
exemplars.note: Founded 1989 by Hilary and Galen Weston with a DPZ plan and code; town hall by Leon Krier, 1999. The movement's most tightly coded and most expensively executed village.

sources: Andres Duany, Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk and Jeff Speck, Suburban Nation: The Rise of Sprawl and the Decline of the American Dream (2000)
Andres Duany and Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk, The Lexicon of the New Urbanism, and the SmartCode (2003- )
Leon Krier, The Architecture of Community (2009)
Robert A. M. Stern, David Fishman and Jacob Tilove, Paradise Planned: The Garden Suburb and the Modern City (2013)
Witold Rybczynski, Last Harvest: How a Cornfield Became New Daleville (2007)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to. Constraint c03 (principal facade not less than 70 percent of lot width at the build-to line, gaps closed by a fence, wall or hedge continuing the line) is a code-enforced version of this pack's odd-bay, wall-dominant composition discipline, and the node's own symmetry attribute (near-symmetrical) sits inside this pack's solid-to-void and window-proportion bands rather than in the picturesque pack's massed-and-subordinated logic -- itself diagnostic, since the node explicitly opposes itself to the ranch and the cul-de-sac suburb it reacts against (weight 0.5 in the lineage) rather than to the composed classical front.

Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to. Constraint c04 ('all heads on a storey aligned to a single datum... Ground storey transparency not less than 30 percent') restates this pack's single-head-datum rule (target_slot window_head_wood: 'DISTINCT HEAD DATUMS PERMITTED ON ONE STOREY: ONE') as code language rather than as convention -- one of the most direct quotations of a proportion-pack rule into a node constraint found anywhere in this assignment.

Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to. The node's own typical_ratios ('Ground storey plate 9 to 11 ft; upper storey 8 to 9 ft') sits inside this pack's second-storey-diminution band (0.78-0.92), stated here as a code-permitted range for the town's building envelope rather than as a style convention. The node shares this pack with new-classical, its explicit institutional sibling ('shared personnel, shared institutions, and a shared theory of transmission' per the hybridizes_with lineage entry).

Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to, alongside greek-revival-upland-vernacular and colonial-revival -- precisely the company this node's own lineage keeps: greek-revival-american descends into this node at weight 0.3, named explicitly as 'the American small-town default of 1830-1860... the plainest available classical vocabulary and the one most easily specified in a code.' Bound optional and low because the node's own text is explicit that style is a per-place regional choice made by the individual code, not a single order this style-level node should assert as governing across every child; Tuscan is bound rather than a richer order because it is the one the node's own lineage names as the code-legible default, reserved for the occasional civic or terminating building a New Urbanist code permits within an otherwise plain-vernacular fabric -- per the distinguished_from entry, 'the civic buildings in a New Urbanist town are usually New Classical,' so this node's ordinary fabric buildings do not carry an order and its rare civic ones may.

modern-farmhouse-traditional.name: Modern Farmhouse

geography.hearth: No design hearth. Its transmission hearth is Waco, Texas, by way of television and a retail brand, and its production hearth is the Sun Belt builder market.

lineage.note: Silhouette only, and this edge is deliberately typed as a reference rather than a descent. What is quoted is the outline: a simple steep gable, vertical boarding, a metal roof, a porch. What is not transmitted is everything that made the original work — the 10:12 to 12:12 pitch, the 12-to-18-inch overhang with a moulded rake return, the full-depth working porch, the small openings in a thick wall, and the accretive plan that grew by ells over generations.
The economy, and the specific habit of deleting the overhang first. The lineage of cost engineering runs unbroken from the 1936 FHA bulletin to a 2020 elevation with a 6-inch rake.

The apparatus: production builders, elevation packages, engineered trusses, sheet-goods modules, the 9-to-10-foot plate, and the street-facing garage. Structurally this is a neo-eclectic house with a different skin.

And at the same time a genuine reaction against it: monochrome instead of contrasting materials, one grammar instead of six, simple gables instead of stacked ones, restraint instead of accumulation. Both edges are true, which is the most interesting fact about this node.
The plan and the section: open great room, island kitchen, indoor-outdoor rear relationship, attached garage on the frontage.

description.short: The market-dominant American idiom of the 2010s and 2020s: white board-and-batten or lap siding with black windows and black metal accents under a simple gable, descending in silhouette from the farmhouse vernacular, in economy from minimal traditional, in apparatus from the production builder, and in section from contemporary open planning.
description.long:
Modern Farmhouse is the first traditional idiom selected by photograph. Its predecessors were transmitted by pattern book, magazine, catalog, or code — media that carry plans, sections, and dimensions. This one was transmitted by television and by image feeds: HGTV's Fixer Upper ran from 2013 to 2018 out of Waco, Texas, and the Magnolia brand that grew from it converted a renovation aesthetic into a national exterior style; Pinterest and Instagram did the rest. That transmission medium has a specific consequence which explains nearly every characteristic of the style: an image at thumbnail size carries value contrast and silhouette and carries nothing at all of profile depth, reveal, or shadow. So the style optimizes hard for the first two and abandons the third. White wall, black window, black roof, simple outline: it is extremely legible on a screen, and it is thin in front of you.

The material and technical conditions are as specific as the media ones. Fibre-cement board-and-batten and lap siding — Hardie, LP SmartSide — made a durable, paintable, dead-flat vertical wall available in four-by-eight and four-by-ten panels at production-builder prices; this is the actual enabler, and it is why the wall is flat, because the panel is. Black-clad aluminium and vinyl windows fell in price in the 2010s and became a stock item rather than an upcharge. Standing-seam metal, formerly agricultural and industrial, became a residential accent product. Meanwhile the open great room with an island kitchen pushed the ground-floor plate to nine and often ten feet, which raised the window head to eight feet, which left one to two feet of blank wall between head and soffit — a gap the historical farmhouse never had, because its heads died into the frieze within six to ten inches. The garage remained where the ranch left it, on the street.

Where it characteristically fails is worth stating precisely, because these are five measurable deviations from the thing it quotes, and correcting them would cost very little. Roof pitch: the vernacular farmhouse gable runs 10:12 to 12:12; the market version flattens to 6:12 or 8:12 to reduce truss cost and attic volume, and the result reads as a shed with a tall wall rather than a house under a roof. Overhang: the historical eave projected twelve to eighteen inches with a moulded rake and a cornice return at the gable corner; the market version boxes it at zero to eight inches, so the wall meets the sky at a knife edge, the gable never terminates, and no part of the wall is ever in shadow. Window head height: heads set by the plate rather than by the wall composition, leaving twelve to twenty-four inches of blank siding above them and misaligning heads between storeys. Porch: reduced from a full-width working porch of eight to ten feet to an entry shed of five or six, which is a gesture rather than a room and is never furnished. And contrast substituting for depth: black on white is being asked to do the work that three to six inches of projection used to do. It photographs beautifully and, at twenty feet, produces a house made entirely of outline.

The fair assessment is that this is the closest thing to a shared national traditional idiom since the ranch, and that it is a real improvement on what it replaced. It is restrained, it is coherent, it uses one grammar per building, and it has largely stopped applying half-width shutters and three-material fronts. Its interiors are genuinely good — light from two or three sides, generous circulation, an intelligible plan. The deficiency is precisely five dimensions deep: pitch, eave overhang, rake overhang, head-to-soffit distance, and porch depth. Fix those five and the idiom becomes a good style rather than a photographed one — which is a nearly perfect demonstration of what a small, enforceable, numeric rule set can be worth, and the reason this node is included in a design system rather than merely described in a field guide.

defining_characteristics: Simple dominant gable forms with minimal cross-gabling and a legible single roof hierarchy
Vertical board-and-batten or narrow lap siding, or the two combined by storey, in a single light value
High-contrast dark window frames, trim, and roof accents against a light wall — a strict two-value palette
Standing-seam metal roofing at porches, dormers, or the whole roof
A covered entry or partial porch under a shed or extended gable roof
Open great-room plan with a 9 to 10 ft ground-floor plate and correspondingly high window heads
Ornament essentially absent: no shutters, no keystones, no applied classical elements, no material changes at an outside corner
diagnostic_tells: Black windows in a white wall, with no trim colour in between
Board-and-batten to the gable or upper storey over lap siding below, with the change occurring at a floor line
A standing-seam shed roof over the entry, in a different plane and material from the main roof
Overhangs under 12 in, boxed, with no rake return at the gable corner
Gooseneck barn lights over the garage doors and a sliding barn door somewhere visible through the glazing

distinguished_from.difference: The original has a steeper roof (10:12-12:12), a real eave and rake overhang with a cornice return, small openings in proportion to solid wall, a full-width porch of habitable depth, and an accreted plan of ells built over decades. The modern version has one mass, a flat eave, a high plate, and a shed porch. Almost every difference is measurable.

Simplification versus accumulation. Neo-eclectic multiplies gables, materials, window shapes, and quoted motifs; modern farmhouse reduces to one gable family, one material, one window type, and no motifs. Both are production-builder products with the same plans behind them.

A look versus a code. New Urbanist towns frequently build in this idiom, and when they do the code forces the porch depth, the pitch, and the garage relegation — which produces a visibly better version of the same style and demonstrates that the failures listed here are enforcement failures, not stylistic ones.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Photographic and economic. The operative modules are the fibre-cement panel (4 x 8 and 4 x 10 ft), the 24-inch truss, the 9-to-10-foot plate, and the 16- or 18-foot garage door. Composition proceeds by silhouette and colour value rather than by profile and shadow, and that single substitution is what separates the idiom from every style it quotes. Recording the as-built and the source dimensions side by side, as below, is the most useful thing this node can carry.
typical_ratios: Principal gable pitch as built 6:12 to 8:12; vernacular source 10:12 to 12:12
Eave and rake overhang as built 0 to 8 in; vernacular source 12 to 18 in with a cornice return
Window head to soffit or frieze as built 12 to 24 in; vernacular source 6 to 10 in
Window opening proportion 1:1.7 to 1:2.0, commonly ganged in twos and threes
Ground plate 9 to 10 ft; window head 8 ft 0 in
Entry porch depth as built 5 to 6 ft; vernacular source 8 to 10 ft full width
Wall-to-trim luminance contrast greater than 8:1, doing the work of profile depth
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Regular ganged openings at 8 to 14 ft centres on the principal elevation, with the garage terminating one end; heads generally aligned within a storey, which is a genuine advance over the preceding node.

massing_affinities.note: The quoted skeleton, and the one the idiom handles best because the ell gives a secondary mass without requiring a stacked gable.
The single-storey market version, particularly in the Sun Belt.
Works surprisingly well, because a hipped or steep-gabled square mass tolerates the flat wall and the high plate better than a long elevation does.

constraints.statement: Principal gable pitch not less than 6:12, and 10:12 preferred. Below 8:12 the mass reads as a shed and the quoted vernacular silhouette is lost.

test.note: Tests the hard 6:12 floor. '10:12 preferred' and 'below 8:12 reads as a shed' are softer descriptive guidance beyond the hard floor and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Rake overhang not less than 8 in and eave overhang not less than 12 in, with a returned or moulded termination at every gable corner. Zero-overhang boxed rakes are forbidden.

test.note: Tests the eave-overhang floor. Rake overhang (8in) is the statement's other numeric claim and stays prose -- no vocabulary variable distinctly expresses rake-overhang projection depth (rake_trim_width_in is the rake trim board's face width, a different measurement). The returned/moulded gable-corner termination is categorical and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Window heads shall sit not more than 10 in below the soffit or frieze line, and shall align to one datum per storey. Where the plate exceeds 9 ft, either raise the head or introduce a transom to close the gap.

test.note: Tests the head-to-soffit/frieze offset ceiling. 'Align to one datum per storey' has no vocabulary variable for same-storey cross-elevation head alignment (opening_vertical_alignment_in is storey-to-storey, a different comparison) and stays prose, as does the plate-exceeds-9ft transom clause.

constraints.statement: Board-and-batten battens at 16 or 24 in on centre aligned to the framing, minimum 1x2 nominal with not less than 3/4 in projection. Battens at 12 in centres or with projection under 1/2 in read as stripes rather than as boarding.
A covered space may be described as a porch only at 8 ft or more of clear depth across not less than 40 percent of the facade. Shallower entry roofs are hoods and must be detailed as such.

test.note: Tests the clear-depth floor. The 40-percent-of-facade-width clause has no matching porch-width variable (gallery_depth_ft is depth only) and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Fixer Upper renovations
exemplars.note: The 2013-2018 television series and the Magnolia brand that followed. Listed as the style's transmission event rather than as architectural authorship, because that is honestly what it is: the idiom has no canonical designed building, and saying so is more useful than inventing one.

exemplars.name: Serenbe, Selborne hamlet
exemplars.note: Steve Nygren's New Urbanist community, first houses sold 2005 and built out since. The same farmhouse idiom under a form-based code that enforces porch depth, setback, and garage relegation — the control case showing what the style looks like when the five failing dimensions are regulated.

sources: Thomas C. Hubka, Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn: The Connected Farm Buildings of New England (1984)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses, rev. ed. (2013)
Marianne Cusato and Brent Hull, Get Your House Right: Architectural Elements to Use and Avoid (2007)
Dolores Hayden, Building Suburbia: Green Fields and Urban Growth, 1820-2000 (2003)

proportion_packs.note: Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to. The node's defining_characteristics ('Simple dominant gable forms with minimal cross-gabling and a legible single roof hierarchy') is this pack's dominance rule intact, and its canonical massing (linear-ell-farmhouse -- 'the ell gives a secondary mass without requiring a stacked gable') is a dominant-block-plus-subordinate-ell composition of exactly the kind this pack's wing_strategy and dominance rules describe. Bound primary/facade with the deviation stated plainly, because the node itself states it with unusual precision -- pitch as built 6:12-8:12 against the pack's picturesque-vernacular expectation and the node's own named 10:12-12:12 source; eave as built 0-8 in against this pack's own default eave projection of about 21 in; window head as built 12-24 in below soffit against a 6-10 in vernacular source. This is the same relationship this pack has to american-farmhouse-vernacular one link up the lineage, except here the node's own long description supplies the deviation table itself ('Recording the as-built and the source dimensions side by side... is the most useful thing this node can carry'), so the binding is confirmed by the node's own text rather than merely inferred.

Confirmed in this pack's own applies_to, and a materially closer fit here than on its ancestor american-farmhouse-vernacular (where it is bound optional and only for the 1900-1920 tail). Constraint c04 -- board-and-batten battens at 16 or 24 in on centre aligned to the framing, minimum 1x2 nominal, not less than 3/4 in projection -- is this pack's flat-stock, board-series logic almost exactly: a batten sized against the framing module is precisely how this pack's whole family is generated ('the base is a one-by-eight because a one-by-eight is a board'). Unlike american-farmhouse-vernacular, this node has no surviving classical-order-derived trim tradition competing with it -- defining_characteristics state 'ornament essentially absent: no shutters, no keystones, no applied classical elements, no material changes at an outside corner' -- so this is the primary and effectively only trim system genuinely present, bound at role interior (this schema's slot for a governing trim family) rather than optional.

swiss-chalet.name: Swiss Chalet

revival_periods.note: The Swiss Chalet fashion in Britain and America. Downing's The Architecture of Country Houses (1850) and Vaux's Villas and Cottages (1857) both publish 'Swiss cottage' designs; the mode spreads through pattern books, and through the Swiss pavilions at the international exhibitions.
The Chalet as a resort and railroad type in the American mountain West and Pacific Northwest, and as the 'Swiss Chalet style' in American style guides.

The decisive downstream transmission. Exposed rafter tails, wide unsupported eaves, expressed purlin ends and brackets, flat sawn balusters and a broad low gable to the street pass from the American Chalet fashion into Craftsman and the California bungalow, where they become normative and the Swiss origin is forgotten.

geography.hearth: Bernese Oberland and central Switzerland

lineage.note: Genuine and technical, not general: the Swiss Mittelland and the northern cantons build Bohlenstanderbau and Standerbau — a post-and-beam skeleton with horizontal plank or log infill — which is Fachwerk carpentry hybridised with Blockbau. Basel and Schaffhausen build straightforward Fachwerk. The chalet proper is the alpine end of one continuous carpentry region.

description.short: The horizontally-logged, shallow-roofed, deeply overhanging alpine farmhouse whose entire form is dictated by the length of a log, the settlement of a log wall, and the need to keep snow and water off both.
description.long:
Almost everything a non-Alpine observer believes about the chalet is wrong, starting with the roof. A real high-alpine chalet has a low roof — eighteen to twenty-five degrees, sometimes less — not a steep one. The steep-roofed chalet is a nineteenth-century invention of the lowlands and the resorts, and it inverts the original logic. Snow on an alpine roof is not a problem to be shed; it is the best insulation available, free, delivered annually, and a metre of settled snow on a shallow shingle roof holds the building's heat far better than the roof itself. The roofs were built shallow deliberately, covered in heavy split larch shingles, and weighted down with rows of stones so that the whole assembly would not lift in a foehn wind. Where pitches are steeper — in the Bernese Mittelland, in the Emmental, in the lower valleys — it is because those places get rain rather than dry cold, and the roof form follows the precipitation type, not the altitude.

The wall is the second thing that governs everything. Blockbau — horizontally stacked squared logs, corner-notched — is a superb structure in an alpine forest, where straight softwood of eight metres is abundant and a mason is a week's walk away, and it imposes two absolute constraints. First, no wall can be longer than a log, which fixes the building's plan dimensions at roughly six to nine metres and means growth happens by stacking storeys or by adding a whole new building, never by lengthening a room. Second, a green log wall shrinks across the grain and settles by two to four per cent of its height over the first several years, which means every door and window frame must be built with a settlement gap above it and every vertical element that passes through the wall — a post, a chimney, a stair — must be detailed to slide. Openings must be small and grouped, because each one interrupts the continuity of the courses, and this is why chalet windows come in bands of three, four or six small lights rather than as isolated large openings. The Fensterband is not a design preference. It is what a log wall permits.

From those two constraints the whole image follows. Because the log wall must be kept dry — a wetted, sun-baked log wall checks and rots — the eave overhang is enormous, one and a half to two metres on the gable face, and the gable face is where all the ornament goes: the carved bargeboard, the sawn balustrade of the Lauben (the galleries running the full width under the overhang), the painted or carved inscription band across the facade, and the exposed and shaped purlin ends stepping out to carry that overhang. Because the log wall must never touch the ground, the ground storey is masonry or is built into the hillside, holding the byre and the cellar, and the timber house sits on top of it. And because the sun-blackened larch of a two-hundred-year-old south face is the finest weathering material in Europe, the building gets better looking for a century and a half.

Inside, a chalet is small, low, and extremely warm. The Stube — the one heated room — has a plank floor, log walls left bare and scrubbed to a pale silver, a ceiling under two and a half metres, a corner bench, and a masonry stove (Kachelofen) fired from the passage so that no smoke or draught enters the room. The windows are small and grouped in one wall, so the light is directional and low. It smells strongly of pine. And what is genuinely striking, if you have come to it from Craftsman houses in California, is how completely familiar the exterior detail is: the exposed rafter tails, the bracketed overhang, the horizontal board banding, the flat sawn baluster. Those details crossed the Atlantic in the 1850s as an exotic Swiss fashion, were absorbed into American resort and railroad building, and by 1905 had become the ordinary structural expression of the American bungalow, at which point nobody remembered where they came from.

defining_characteristics: Horizontally stacked, corner-notched squared log walls (Blockbau), left exposed and unpainted
Plan dimensions bounded by log length — no wall longer than about 9 m without an intersecting cross-wall
Openings small, grouped into horizontal bands, and framed with a settlement gap above each head
Masonry or earth-set ground storey holding byre and cellar; the log storey never meets grade
Very deep roof overhang — 1.2 to 2.0 m on the gable face — carried on stepped, shaped purlin ends
Shallow roof pitch (18-25 degrees) in the high alps, rising to 35-45 in the wetter lower valleys; heavy split shingle, historically stone-weighted
Galleries (Lauben) running the full width of the gable face under the overhang, with sawn or turned balustrades
All ornament — bargeboard, balustrade, carved and inscribed facade band — concentrated on the gable face
diagnostic_tells: Log courses visibly continuous across the whole wall, with the corner notching exposed and projecting at the corners
Window heads with a visible gap or slip joint above the frame — the settlement allowance
Purlin ends stepping outward in a stack of three to five, each shorter than the one below, to carry the overhang
A masonry or stone ground storey under a timber upper storey, with the change of material sharp and unconcealed
A dated and inscribed board running the full width of the facade below the gallery

distinguished_from.difference: Both are Blockbau, and they share the log-length constraint and the settlement problem. The Nordic farm disperses into many small single-purpose log buildings around a yard and paints them Falu red; the Alpine chalet concentrates house, byre and hay store in one tall building set into a slope, leaves the timber bare, and puts a gallery and an enormous overhang on the gable.

Fachwerk is a skeleton frame with infill panels; Blockbau is a solid stacked wall with no frame at all. The two meet in the Swiss Mittelland but are structurally opposite systems, and they settle and behave differently.

The American descendant keeps the eave brackets, exposed rafter tails, wide overhang and horizontal banding and abandons the log wall, the settlement detailing, the gallery and the byre. Craftsman is stud-framed and clad; the resemblance is real inheritance, not convergence.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The log. Wall length is bounded by the available straight trunk, 6-9 m, which fixes the plan; the log course of roughly 18-25 mm x 200-250 mm sets a coursing module that all openings must land on; storey height is a whole number of courses. The overhang is dimensioned by what is needed to keep rain off a log wall, and the roof pitch by the local precipitation type. There is no compositional module anywhere in the system.
typical_ratios: Wall length 6-9 m maximum without a cross-wall; plan roughly 1:1 to 1:1.4
Log course height 180-250 mm; settlement allowance 2-4 percent of wall height
Gable overhang 1.2-2.0 m; eave overhang 0.8-1.5 m
Roof pitch 18-25 degrees (high alps), 35-45 (lower valleys and Mittelland)
Gallery depth 1.0-1.5 m
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Horizontal bands of ganged small windows — typically three to six lights in a continuous row — repeated at each storey. The rhythm is a band, not a bay: individual openings do not read separately.

massing_affinities.note: The chalet is emphatically gable-fronted; the gable face carries the gallery, the ornament and the whole architectural argument.
The Lauben are integral, not applied: they are circulation, drying space for hay and washing, and the social edge of the house.
The Stube plus a cold passage is the irreducible plan, and small chalets are little more than that stacked twice.
The Emmental Einfirsthaus puts house, byre and barn under one enormous roof; a merged rather than a linked variant of the connected farm.
A log wall cannot be a party wall and the type cannot be built in a row.

constraints.statement: No log wall may exceed about 9 m without an intersecting cross-wall to lock the corners. Plan dimensions are bounded by log length; the type grows by stacking storeys or adding a separate building, never by lengthening a wall.

test.note: 9 m converted to 29.5 ft ('about 9 m' in the source -- an approximate stated ceiling, not an invented one).

constraints.statement: A settlement gap of 2-4 percent of wall height must be provided above every door and window head and at every point where a rigid element passes through the log wall. Log walls shrink across the grain; ignoring this splits frames and cracks chimneys within five years.
Gable overhang not less than 1.2 m, eave overhang not less than 0.8 m. The overhang exists to keep water and direct sun off the log wall; reducing it to a conventional 300 mm eave destroys the wall.

test.note: Tests the eave-overhang clause, the vocabulary term that names it exactly. The gable-overhang minimum (1.2m) stated in the same sentence is a distinct measurement the vocabulary does not separate from eave overhang and stays prose.

constraints.statement: The log storey must sit on a masonry base or on the uphill grade, never on the ground. Roof pitch 18-25 degrees where the precipitation is snow, 35-45 where it is rain — pitch follows precipitation type, not altitude.

Ornament belongs on the bargeboard, the gallery balustrade, the purlin ends and the inscription band. The log wall itself stays plain; carving or applied trim on the log courses is outside the tradition.

exemplars.name: Haus Bethlehem
exemplars.note: Dendro-dated to 1287; among the oldest surviving timber dwellings in Europe and an intact demonstration of medieval Blockbau.

exemplars.name: Haus Nideroest
exemplars.note: Timbers dendro-dated to 1176; discovered during demolition in 2002 and dismantled for conservation. Cited with that caveat — it is evidence rather than a visitable building.

exemplars.name: Ballenberg Swiss Open-Air Museum
exemplars.note: Over a hundred relocated rural buildings of the 14th-19th centuries from every canton; the only place where the regional range of the type can be compared directly.

exemplars.name: Chalet-Museum / farmhouses of the Simmental
exemplars.note: 17th-18th century; the Simmental facade, with its stepped purlin overhang, carved and painted inscription band and full-width gallery, is the type specimen for what the 19th century exported as 'the chalet'.

sources: Die Bauernhauser der Schweiz (Schweizerische Gesellschaft fur Volkskunde, multi-volume survey)
Hunziker, Das Schweizerhaus nach seinen landschaftlichen Formen
Oliver (ed.), Encyclopedia of Vernacular Architecture of the World
Downing, The Architecture of Country Houses (1850) — for the American transmission

proportion_packs.note: Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to and directly documented among the pack's own sources. Blockbau is the identical construction system the pack derives from — wall length bounded by log length (6-9 m), a settlement gap required above every opening, gable-end-only chimneys — and this node's own constraints (c01-c04) restate the same limits in the same units.

Explicitly listed in the pack's applies_to. The chalet's gable face is a genuinely composed asymmetrical-about-a-datum elevation in the pack's own sense: a dominant gable mass carrying the gallery (Lauben), stepped purlin overhang and inscription band, with a continuous water-table and head datum running through it — the two-datum discipline the pack states as its one firmly evidenced (non-judgment) rule. massing:gallery-house, cross-referenced by the pack's own module note, is one of this node's own canonical massing affinities.

Judgment bind: this node is not individually listed in room-vernacular's applies_to, but its family container nordic-alpine-vernacular is, and the Stube — small, low-ceilinged (under 2.5 m), lit from one banded wall of small ganged windows, warmed by one masonry stove — is squarely the span/hearth/daylight-limited room this pack models. Note that the elaborate bracket, gallery-balustrade and stepped-purlin-end ornament vocabulary this node describes as the building's whole decorative content is not captured by this or any of the 36 packs (see gaps).
